Several times she seemed about to speak, but finally only sighed and shook her head, setting her earrings swaying.

“Say whatever you wish,” Wang urged, taking her hand. “If I can do it, I will. If I can't, I'll explain why. Don't worry; we can discuss it.” “With whom? Only His Majesty the Emperor!” Her form of address for the emperor struck Wang as novel, especially in her soft southern accent. He smiled. “Is it so momentous that only the emperor can solve it?” “Naturally!” She seemed entirely convinced. “Unless His Majesty issues an edict promoting you to an appointment in Shanghai...” After all these turns, she merely wished to say she could not bear to be parted from him. Wang himself offered no answer for the moment; his helper spoke. “Wanxiang, do you mean that sincerely?” “Oh, Mr Hu!” She looked very solemn. “Must I cut out my heart and show it to you?” “I believe you, I believe you!” Wang hastened to reassure her.

“So do I,” Hu put in with a smile. “Wanxiang, why not return to Hangzhou on the same boat as His Honour on the seventh?” “Why wouldn't I? I'm only afraid he wouldn't agree.” “He agrees a thousand times over. He could wish for nothing better! There are only three days left. Begin your preparations.” Even Wang was surprised. Why was Hu so rashly deciding on another man's behalf that he should take a concubine? But knowing him well, he said nothing and watched. If Wang was surprised, Wanxiang was more bewildered still—and alarmed that pretence might become reality, leaving her unable to retreat. “Well?” Hu asked. “Shall we discuss it directly, face to face? Shall I speak to Third Aunt? Or should Brother You intervene?” Now he was talking about the price of releasing her. It sounded more real than ever. Wanxiang blinked repeatedly and looked awkward, but she was no novice. Composing herself, she sat down and answered with a suggestion of gratification. “Very well. It's my own person; I can negotiate for myself. First, may I ask what His Honour has in mind?”

How could Wang possibly answer? Naturally, Hu replied for him. “Don't you already know what he has in mind?” It was an evasion. His original proposal had been a bluff to test the depth of Wanxiang's feeling for Wang. Their exchanges had now given him a fair idea. It was time to discover Wang's wishes instead. “Of course I know,” she answered. “But I don't dare say it aloud. I can't imagine being so fortunate.” Now even Wang understood that, if he wished to take her as a concubine, she might not agree. Fearing that further discussion would embarrass them both, he put the matter aside. “We can talk about it later. Let us drink first.” That suited Hu exactly. He too thought her intentions sufficiently clear and saw no need to pursue the subject. “Yes, let's drink. You can discuss the rest in bed later.” Wanxiang knew she had lost the advantage. Apparently Wang had no serious intention either. Had she known, she could have made a more generous declaration. Now his position remained concealed while hers was exposed. Her hope of extracting a large sum during the remaining three days would probably come to nothing. Hu had tricked her into this. The grievance in her heart became a mournful expression and silence, which greatly stirred Wang's pity.

“What is it?” he asked, gently touching her shoulder. “Why are you suddenly unhappy?” At the question, she gave herself up to tears. With a sob, she covered her face with her handkerchief and hurried into the back room. Soft weeping followed. Wang felt distressed and, still more, moved. He wanted to do something, but Hu stopped him. “Leave her,” he said quietly. “Their tears are easily shed. Whenever they remember something painful, they can have a cry. It doesn't necessarily mean she's been hurt just now.” Wang felt suddenly bereft. He thought Hu's judgement too harsh, but nodded and remained seated to show his confidence in him.

“Mr Xuexuan, tell me what you want, and I'll arrange it.” “What I want...” Wang paused for a long while. “If I brought her home, I'm afraid people would talk.” His attachment was plain. Hu thought it right that he should consider his official reputation, but felt the point should be made more clearly. “Wanxiang may not want to go to Hangzhou either, so there's no need to consider bringing her into your household. I expect you'll often be coming to Shanghai. Why not keep her in a separate establishment? In the second or third month of spring, or in autumn when West Lake is at its best, you could bring her to Hangzhou for a while. I'd arrange a small house for you. What do you think?” “Excellent!” This exactly suited Wang. “Please discuss it with her and find out what it would cost.” “It would only mean contributing to her monthly expenses. Any extra money you give her when you visit, or jewellery and clothes you have made for her, would be a matter between you two. Nobody else could intervene.” Then Hu called, “Wanxiang!”

She came out slowly. Her powder and rouge had been renewed, but her eyes were still red. Looking fragile and pitiful, she sat close to Wang, frowning slightly and saying nothing. “What were you crying about?” he asked. “Who offended you?” “Ah, Mr Xuexuan, there's no need to ask,” Hu interposed. “Don't you understand her difficulty? If she goes to Hangzhou with you, she can't bear to leave Third Aunt. If she stays, she doesn't want to be parted from you. Torn between the two, she naturally feels unhappy. Am I right, Wanxiang?” Instead of answering him, she turned to Wang. “Just look at you. After all we've meant to each other, you understand less than Mr Hu.” “The bystander sees more clearly,” Wang said, while signalling to Hu to propose their arrangement. Hu gave a slight nod, then returned a glance asking him to leave them alone. “I'm a little dizzy,” Wang said. “I'll lie down on your bed for a while.” Once he had stretched out in the back room, Hu began negotiating with Wanxiang. How much did she need each month?

“I live quite frugally. Twenty or thirty taels at most.” “If His Honour gave you thirty taels a month, could you close your door to visitors and live quietly?” “Nothing could be better. But...” She shook her head and stopped. “Go on,” Hu urged. “Do you have debts? You may tell me.” “Truly, nobody is more understanding than you, Mr Hu. Who wouldn't wish to leave this life? But there are so many difficulties. If one tells other people, they think one is asking for an outrageous sum. Speaking only harms the friendship. Better to say nothing.”

From that tone, the sum would not be small. If she claimed debts of eighteen thousand taels, should they pay them? Hu had heard of a practice called “taking a bath.” A popular courtesan burdened with debts would seize upon a wealthy fool, swear eternal love beside his pillow, and declare that she would marry nobody else. He would spend a fortune paying her debts and buying her release, as though purchasing a bride with pearls. Yet within six months, or a year at most, she would grow restless in married life and devise every means of leaving him. It had been a scheme from the beginning. Wanxiang did not appear quite that sort. Still, even if her demands were met and she agreed to stop receiving clients, her conduct might not match her promise. If she continued attracting admirers while known as Wang's mistress, his reputation would suffer. Wouldn't that be foolish? Hu therefore smiled. “If you have so many difficulties, naturally we can't press you. But you should know that His Honour's feeling for you is quite sincere.” “I know. We all have hearts. Besides, with Fifth Master You's standing to consider, I could hardly fail to do my best. As long as His Honour is here, I shall certainly attend to him wholeheartedly.”

“You've clearly seen something of the world,” Hu praised her. “You speak differently from girls just entering the profession. I suppose I count as a matchmaker, and must consider both sides. Wanxiang, I think you and His Honour should be husband and wife for short periods, two or three times a year.” She broadly understood, but deliberately asked, “How would that work?” “For example, when he comes to Shanghai, he stays here. Naturally, you make yourself available to keep him company. Or, if he wishes, he brings you to Hangzhou to offer incense and see West Lake. Again, you'd be husband and wife for a little while. For ordinary expenses, he'd contribute twenty-five taels a month. There would certainly be extras as well; how much would depend on your own skill.” This was certainly acceptable. “Only one thing worries me. What if His Honour arrives while I'm occupied?” she asked hesitantly. “That would be awkward. Once one sets up in this business, every visitor provides one's livelihood. I can't afford to offend any of them. Mr Hu, I'm speaking frankly. Please don't be angry.” “Frankness is precisely what I like. If an earlier guest won't make way for a later one, there's still a solution. You can stay at an inn with His Honour as Mrs Wang and tell people here that you've gone to the country. Would that manoeuvre work?” Of course it would. Her difficulty solved, Wanxiang was delighted. “Really, Mr Hu, one would think you'd worked in our profession yourself. You know all the tricks!”

“Then shall I become your male attendant?” In a courtesan household, an unmarried female servant was called an elder sister, a married one an aunt, and a male servant an attendant. Only at his reply did Wanxiang realise her serious mistake. One could speak of working in any other trade, but to say that a man had worked in hers amounted to insulting the women of his family. An ill-tempered client, especially a northerner, might take immediate offence. She blushed deeply and hurried to apologise. “Mr Hu, a great man overlooks a small person's fault. I spoke wrongly. I truly deserve a beating.” Taking his hand, she pressed and rubbed it, repeatedly saying, “You mustn't be angry. Punish me however you wish, but please don't be angry.” Her voice grew loud enough to disturb Wang, who could not resist coming out to see what was happening. Hu was smiling silently while Wanxiang apologised in alarm. Wang was more puzzled still. Once the incident was explained, they all laughed and let it pass. Wanxiang's manner changed again. She felt that she now occupied a distinct position, and the division between Wang as host and Hu as guest became more pronounced. Wang naturally sensed it. He felt as unrestrained as though in his own home. They rinsed their cups, poured more wine, and drank with renewed pleasure.

“Xueyan, I have something to ask you too,” Wang said with lively interest. “I hear A'zhu's heart is entirely yours. What is going on?” Before Hu could answer, Wanxiang asked, “Who is A'zhu?” “Ask him.” Wang pointed to Hu. “The boatman's daughter,” Hu replied. “I have no mind for that sort of thing at present.” This vague explanation did not satisfy her curiosity. She pressed Wang for the full story, and he repeated what he had heard, adding considerable embellishment. Where he strayed too far from the facts, Hu corrected him with a word or two. Minor discrepancies he let pass.

“Why, that's splendid!” Wanxiang was eager to intervene. “Mr Hu, shall I be your matchmaker?” Not only Hu but Wang found the proposal extraordinary. “You don't even know her,” Wang said. “How could you arrange it?” “What does that matter? From the sound of it, the match depends upon her mother's agreement. And A'zhu seems to have something on her mind that she won't tell you men. Only if I go can we discover what it is.” Wang thought this reasonable. Nodding, he asked, “What do you say, Xueyan? Let Wanxiang try.” “Thank you, thank you,” Hu answered. “We'll see later.”

“I understand.” Wanxiang deliberately provoked him. “A devoted woman and a faithless man! You must not care for her.” “Now you're wronging him,” Wang laughed. “Whenever he has a free moment, he hides away on the boat. He and A'zhu never run out of things to say.” “Then why doesn't he take her home? Is the first wife formidable?” “He could rent another house and let her live separately.” “Exactly!” Wanxiang looked directly at Hu. “Priceless treasure is easier to find than a loving heart.” “That's what I think too.” Wang raised his voice and recited, “What was ordained in a former life—do not let the destined marriage pass!” They urged him on in turn, each supporting the other. Hu had made up his mind, but there was much he could not say in Wanxiang's presence. He only smiled and shook his head. Seeing that he would not be persuaded, she finally abandoned the attempt.

CHAPTER FIVE

When the boats reached Hangzhou, Wang rested briefly at home, changed into official robes, and went to see the governor. He personally reported the journey and presented a letter from Huang's family acknowledging safe receipt of the twenty thousand taels. Both the public and private aspects of the assignment had been handled handsomely. Huang was exceedingly pleased. “You've worked hard. I know what you've done,” he said. “I have plans of my own. You'll hear something within a few days.” “Yes, Your Excellency.” Wang dared not inquire further. Leaving the governor's yamen, he went to call on Treasurer Lingui. Knowing how difficult Huang could be, Lingui had previously treated Wang rather like a spirit best respected from a distance. Whether things went well or badly, someone taller would hold up the falling sky. He sought no merit, only freedom from blame and trouble. Now Wang's tactful, thorough handling of the journey, together with his understanding of the “rules,” had exceeded Lingui's hopes. Zhou's praise made him regard Wang more highly still. As soon as the visiting card went in, a message came out: “Ask His Honour Wang to change into ordinary clothes and meet me in my private office.” This was how one received an intimate friend of roughly equal standing. Wang knew that Zhou's favourable account had produced the result, and that Hu deserved the credit for winning Zhou over. Thinking of Hu and of Lingui's exceptional courtesy, he suddenly had an idea: he would ask Lingui to recommend Hu for advancement.

They met in ordinary clothes in the private office. The Manchus were ceremonious, and Lingui took Wang's hand, asked whether the journey had gone smoothly and whether everyone at home was well, then, after these affectionate greetings, led him into the western room. The office occupied a small courtyard, with a single-storey building of three rooms: an open central reception room and an enclosed room on either side. Documents were signed and business conducted in the eastern room; the western was Lingui's everyday sitting room. As the curtain lifted, Wang saw an opium tray on a rosewood couch. A maid with a long plait and slender waist had just lit a bright Taigu lamp. “Please,” Lingui said, indicating the upper end of the couch. “You take it, Your Excellency.” Wang smiled. “I don't know how to enjoy that pleasure.” “It's just as well that you don't.” Lingui dispensed with polite pretence. “In truth, the stuff does more harm than good. But you can lie down and keep me company.” That was harmless enough. Provided one did not become addicted, conversation beside an opium tray could be entertaining, and lying head to head across the little flame could deepen a friendship. Wang readily agreed and reclined at the lower end. The pretty maid immediately held his feet, removed his boots, arranged a square stool beneath them, and covered his lower body with a Russian blanket.

Another maid brought four small dishes of fruit and two exquisite little teapots. Setting them beside the tray, she sat on a low stool to prepare the opium. Once a pipe was filled, she offered its jade-inlaid ivory stem to Wang's lips. “Give it to your master. I don't smoke.” Lingui accepted without ceremony, finished the pipe in one sustained breath, drank from the hot teapot, and put a pine-nut sweet into his mouth. Then, slowly letting smoke escape through his nostrils, he closed his eyes as though transported. “Brother Xuexuan,” he began, turning to business, “you've done Zhejiang great credit on this journey. If all official business went as smoothly as yours, I could live comfortably.” “It was entirely due to Your Excellency's support. Subordinates can act freely only when their superiors trust them.” “One must first feel secure before allowing a free hand. Frankly, I couldn't feel more secure about you. With the governor standing behind everything, whatever you propose is acceptable.” Lingui added, “The governor is a shrewd man too. If he puts himself in my position, he's certain to look after me.” He smoked a second pipe. Wang considered his words and concluded that the latter remark meant he must not forget Lingui's proper share while attending to the governor. In fact, there was no need to say it: Hu had already thought of that.

But Wang had learned one principle of official life: anything not meant for outsiders' knowledge must be kept completely secret. Though they faced each other on the same couch, the presence of the maid preparing the pipe prevented him from making any sign. “Quite so,” he answered. “There are two sorts of superior one hopes to serve. The best is naturally someone like Your Excellency, generous, tolerant, and considerate of his subordinates. Failing that, I would prefer Governor Huang. Shrewd though he is, he certainly knows merit from fault and right from wrong.” “Merit from fault, perhaps. Right from wrong—not necessarily.” Lingui regretted the remark as soon as he made it. “Brother Xuexuan,” he added with deliberate irony, “you might mention these words to the governor when you have a chance.” Wang was quick to respond. “That is an honour I must decline!” he said with a smile. “I never care to carry tales behind people's backs. It causes needless trouble, harms others, and benefits oneself not at all. Why do it?” The answer impressed Lingui deeply. This man truly knew how to handle every situation. He could be trusted.

With his last psychological guard removed, Lingui spoke without reserve and with increasing pleasure. He discussed conditions in the capital and the rules and precedents of the six ministries, greatly enlarging Wang's knowledge. Finally he returned to official business. “We must press ahead with this year's new grain. Jiangsu and Zhejiang bear exceptionally heavy tax quotas, yet Zhejiang is really no match for Jiangsu. How can Hangzhou, Jiaxing, and Huzhou compare with Suzhou, Songjiang, and Taicang? Of our three prefectures, Huzhou is the richest, but its affairs are the hardest to manage.” He sighed. “The prefect of Huzhou has been dismissed for delaying the grain, and for the moment I can't find anyone to take over. A real headache!” Chunshou had lost his life over Huzhou, so Lingui could not help being wary. Wang understood the difficulty, but feared that pursuing it would lead to Chunshou's case and all its awkward implications. He merely listened. “I do have an idea!” Lingui suddenly exclaimed, then fell silent. After a long pause, he answered himself. “No. It won't work. There's no precedent.” Wang could not imagine what he meant, but it was not his place to ask. During the ensuing silence, Lingui finished his twenty-fourth pipe and ordered dinner. The maids went out to pass on the instruction. With nobody else present, Wang could produce what he had brought.

“I've brought Your Excellency a little curiosity.” From an inner pocket he took a paper parcel and passed it across the opium lamp. Inside was an exquisite wallet of exceptionally soft leather. Its pattern immediately showed that it came from the West. Lingui examined the outside and was about to open it when Wang spoke again. “Perhaps later.” Plainly there was something special within. Lingui smiled, thanked him, and put it away. When dinner was served, he excused himself, slipped outside, and opened it privately. The wallet held a bank draft for five thousand taels. Wang had acted in great secrecy, but Lingui showed no concern about his servants. Returning to invite his guest to the table, his first words were, “I am much indebted to you. What about the grain intendant?” “A little something for him too.” “How much?” “Three.” He meant three thousand taels. Lingui nodded. “Delivered already?” “Not yet. Naturally, I had to call on Your Excellency before visiting him.” “It's too late today. Go early tomorrow. He takes these matters very seriously.”

The tone was that of affectionate advice to one of his own people. Wang felt that their relationship had advanced another step. “Thank you for the guidance, Your Excellency,” he answered gratefully. “Could you put away that ‘Your Excellency’?” Lingui set down his wine cup and frowned. “It's unbearably commonplace and spoils the pleasure of drinking.” Wang smiled. “Obedience is better than ceremony. I shall call you Mr Lin, with every respect. Let us drink a cup!” “Excellent!” Lingui drank gladly, then continued, “I hadn't finished what I was saying. Do you know the grain intendant's particular passion?” “No. I must ask you to enlighten me.” “In fact, everyone shares it, but his case is exceptional.” Lingui smiled. “He loves what lies beneath a man's knees.” Wang was baffled by the riddle. “Your learning is as broad as the sea. Can this unfinished proverb defeat you?” So that was it! The saying ran, “There is gold beneath a man's knees.” The unspoken words were “there is gold.” The Manchus' attempts at literary wit could sometimes be oddly contrived. Wang was genuinely amused.

“So I advise you not to send a bank draft. Exchange it for gold leaf.” Lingui could scarcely suppress his amusement. “They say he delights in counting his gold sheets every night before bed. Otherwise he feels something is missing and cannot sleep peacefully.” “That is a curious habit. What happens when he travels?” Wang asked. “Does he take the gold with him? Wouldn't that invite thieves?” “That I don't know.” Their joking over, they returned to business. Lingui asked about official circles in Shanghai. Wang told him of Ni's grievances and complaints and his own promise to look after Ni's family. “I can say nothing about that,” Lingui replied. “I can't even concern myself with Ni's family. I know how suspicious the governor is.”

“Yes.” “So I advise you to look after them discreetly and keep it from the governor.” Lingui lowered his voice. “I truly don't understand why our Mr Huang is so harsh. What has the treasurer of Jiangsu to do with the governor of Zhejiang? Why torment him like that? And there's something else, even less defensible...” At the crucial point he stopped. Plainly the matter was important enough that Wang's status as Huang's favourite still troubled him. Understanding this, Wang thought it better not to press. He raised his cup and considered how to change the subject. Lingui, however, felt embarrassed. “I may as well tell you. He's done something to benefit himself at another man's expense. Looking after oneself is natural enough, but one ought to consider whom one harms. To injure a man from one's own examination cohort is hardly generous.” Which fellow graduate had Huang injured? Their cohort's remarkable advancement depended upon mutual support. Had Huang himself not relied upon Grand Councillor Peng Yunzhang and He Guiqing to intercede and shield him in the case of Chunshou's forced suicide? Wang therefore half doubted Lingui's story.

“There was an edict recently about the defence of Jiangsu and Zhejiang,” Lingui asked. “Did you see it?” “No. I was in Shanghai and haven't read the court bulletins for some time.” “It said: ‘Governor Huang Zonghan of Zhejiang reports the dispatch of troops to Jiangsu and arrangements for preventing an incursion into Zhejiang.’ The imperial response was: ‘Excellent. In the present military affairs, submit any useful observations you may have without distinguishing between the concerns of one province and another.’” Wang listened with surprise and delight. Sending troops beyond the provincial boundary to meet the enemy had been his suggestion. Huang had adopted it—and, more unexpectedly, received imperial praise! He therefore felt bound to defend it. “There seems nothing wrong with sending troops beyond the province.” “Indeed! Nobody says there is. But an official of Zhejiang should attend to Zhejiang's affairs. Even if the edict says not to distinguish between provinces, we must observe proper limits and not take over another man's duties. Yet Governor Huang sends memorial after memorial, indiscriminately telling the throne how Jiangsu's military affairs should be arranged. Tell me,” Lingui leaned forward, “if you were governor of Jiangsu, how would you feel?” Now Wang understood. For the sake of imperial favour, Huang was leaving no room for his fellow graduate Xu Naizhao, governor of Jiangsu. That was indefensible. His conduct also suggested an ambition to be transferred there. If so, it was still less wise. Jiangsu was certainly one of the empire's richest regions, but war made it an undesirable posting. If an opportunity arose, Wang ought to advise him against it.

Unaware of these further thoughts, Lingui mistook Wang's silence for disagreement. He asked frankly, “Brother Xuexuan, what do you think of what I've said?” Wang came to himself and hurried to prevent a misunderstanding. “Your Excellency's intentions are generous, and your view is naturally just. Unfortunately, my position is too insignificant for my words to carry weight. Otherwise I would find an opportunity to advise him.” “No need!” Lingui waved his hands. “I'm speaking in confidence because I regard you as a good friend. Nobody else need hear of it.” “Of course.” Wang was solemn. “I wouldn't dare repeat a word of what you've said. But since the matter appears in a publicly issued edict, even if I spoke to the governor, he would have no reason to suspect anyone else.” “That is up to you. The Xu family is prominent in Hangzhou, but has no connection with me. I'm merely judging the matter and speaking fairly.” The subject was dropped. They had drunk enough, so Wang asked his host for rice, ate, and took his leave. Knowing that he had only just returned and must have much to do at home, Lingui did not detain him. He personally escorted him to the middle gate, and they parted in good spirits.

Wang spent the following day making more calls, bringing gifts to everyone with whom he had even a slight acquaintance. Coming from Shanghai, these “local products” were in fact foreign goods. Maritime trade had only recently opened. Objects worth little in their Western countries became rare treasures in China. Even a linen handkerchief won unusual appreciation. The round of visits therefore gained Wang many more friends. When he returned home that evening, Hu was in the reception room, joking with his young son. They had been apart for only a day, yet Wang felt as though meeting an old friend after years of separation, with a great deal he urgently wished to say. “Have you eaten?” “No. I meant to invite you up City God Hill for yousuobing cakes, but it's too late now.” The suggestion appealed to Wang. “Not too late! The summer solstice is approaching, the days are long, and the weather is warm. Even if it gets late, it doesn't matter. How shall we go?” “Surely not with gongs and cries to clear the road!” Hu laughed. Wang was amused too. “Naturally, I'll change into ordinary clothes. I meant that we needn't even take a chair or servants. We can walk.” “Good. Put on dark crystal spectacles, and you needn't greet acquaintances if we meet any.” Wang changed into a sapphire-blue satin robe with a dark tribute-satin waistcoat, light cotton socks, and double-ridged shoes. Wearing his large dark spectacles and carrying a folding fan, he walked with Hu through Dajing Lane and straight up City God Hill, both looking at ease.

“Let's have tea where we first met,” Wang said. “A gentleman doesn't forget his beginnings. We ought to give him some good custom today.” By “him,” he meant the proprietor of the tea place. This was Wang's second visit with Hu, but his circumstances and state of mind were worlds apart from the first. Once seated, he looked about calmly and contentedly. Less than a year had passed; the lake and hills were unchanged, yet to his eyes they seemed transformed. West Lake, the beautiful Xizi, looked more graceful, and the green hills more charming. “Wine or tea, gentlemen?” Their bearing and clothes made the proprietor unwilling to neglect them, and he came himself. “Both.” Wang imitated the Hangzhou accent. “The new tea is on sale. Tell us what good leaves you have.” “I don't dare keep anything too costly in stock. I'd have to buy it specially.” “No need for that.” After thinking for a long time, Wang said, “Bring a pot of chrysanthemum tea.” The proprietor found him odd. He had begun by asking for fine tea and ended with chrysanthemums. Apparently he was a man of grand words and small expenditure.

Hu too was surprised. “Why chrysanthemum?” “It took me a while to remember. That's what I drank last year.” Only Hu understood. The recollection stirred him as well, but his nature was to look ahead, with little time for the past. He quickly set it aside and ordered the meal. “One chicken prepared three ways; vinegar fish prepared daibin. Do you have a live crucian carp, about a jin in weight?” “I can get one from below the hill. For soup?” “Yes, crucian carp in milky broth. Warm two bowls of Zhuyeqing, bring four small dishes and a few yousuobing cakes, and we'll begin.” “Certainly. They'll be here at once.” When the tea arrived, Wang held his cup and gazed at the dark blue-green and pale purple of the evening haze. Remembering his circumstances here the previous year, he was suddenly overcome by feeling. “Xueyan,” he said with great force, “with the two of us together, what couldn't we accomplish? We must really make something of it.” “That's my thought too. It's what I came to discuss with you today.”

“Tell me!” “I still want to return to my old trade.” “Not to Xinhe, I hope?” Wang was half joking. In truth, he did fear that Xinhe's proprietor might persuade Hu to return. “I've already said it: I won't be bean curd warmed over in the same broth, and I mean to set up for myself. With the war, silver prices are constantly moving. With sound judgement, one can profit on both buying and selling. We mustn't miss the opportunity.” Wang said nothing. His chopsticks moved incessantly over a dish of sprouted beans. Hu knew it was not fondness for the dish: he was calculating. Naturally, he was thinking about capital. There was no need, for Hu had already planned where it would come from. But he could not conveniently say so first. Wang eventually spoke. “Xueyan, frankly, I don't want you opening a bank just now. I need your help, and helping me means helping yourself. Couldn't you purchase an official qualification and stay with me wherever I go? The governor has already spoken of another arrangement shortly. Presumably he'll give me an additional assignment, and then I'll need help all the more. You can't stand aside and watch me neglect one thing while attending to another.” “I've thought of that already. Opening a bank is one matter, helping you another. I can manage both. Rest assured.” “Of course. Nobody knows your ability better than I. Naturally I trust you...”

Seeing that his words did not match his continuing reluctance, Hu lowered his voice. “You've only just begun to succeed, Mr Xuexuan. Frankly, people outside don't yet know much about you. That's precisely why this is the moment for me to open a bank. Once every official and merchant in Zhejiang knows His Honour Wang, and everyone knows our relationship, what will they say if I open one then?” “Only that I supplied the capital. There's no need to conceal our friendship. My financing a bank for you would be perfectly ordinary.” “True. But as the saying goes, only a mediocre man never arouses envy. If we could avoid it and deliberately invite it instead, we'd be foolish. People would say you were using public money for private profit. Someone might amuse himself by filing an accusation against you. How could I feel at ease then?” This struck home. Wang felt the danger could not be ignored and hesitated. “Things must be done without leaving obvious traces.” Hu spoke still more quietly. “A bank has one particular advantage: it can act for circuit and county treasuries. Public funds bear no interest, so they're effectively capital borrowed for nothing. Sooner or later you'll receive a local appointment. If I open a bank then and immediately take over your treasury's business, the connection will be too obvious. That's why I must act now. Do you understand?” “Ah!” Wang saw the matter differently. “I understand.”

“Perhaps not all the subtleties yet. Different trades are separated as though by mountains. Let me explain.” Hu's plan was to establish a firm first, however modest its resources. Outwardly it must look busy and prosperous; inwardly it would have little substance. Once Wang was appointed to a department or county, the bank would handle its treasury business. Public funds being remitted to the provincial capital would flow in continuously, turning appearance into reality. “Brilliant!” Wang laughed and imitated the Hangzhou accent. “Xueyan, you really know how to perform conjuring tricks!” “A trick is still an illusion. One or two may be useful; too many lose their value. What matters is eventually producing something real.” “That's sound sense.” Wang stopped laughing and spoke seriously. “Let us plan it. First, how much capital is needed?”

Over wine, they discussed opening the bank. The main question was the source of capital, which first required a reckoning of the official-procurement affair. Hu had an extraordinary memory and calculated rapidly in his head. Item by item, the account came to a deficit of more than fourteen thousand taels, all entered in Xinhe's books. To obtain so desirable an assignment at the Sea Transport Bureau, gain nothing from it, and instead incur a deficit seemed hard to justify. Wang, however, did not mind. It was an investment. Judged by the achievements of the past two months and the connections established on every side, the return was already considerable. Yet finding capital for a bank on top of this debt seemed difficult. “If we announce capital of two hundred thousand taels, even a quarter actually paid in means fifty thousand. That may be a strain just now.” “We don't need fifty thousand,” Hu said. “Twenty thousand at most. For the moment, we need a few thousand to establish a proper appearance.” “A few thousand is available at any time. I'll transfer it to you at once.” “Then we're set. There's also a price-difference allowance of several tens of thousands to draw from the provincial treasury. It was meant for Tongyu, but we can hold it back for a while.” “Yes!” Wang saw the point. “Tongyu has borrowed a hundred thousand, and we've secretly guaranteed it. A little delay in paying this allowance isn't unreasonable.” “Exactly. But drawing it from the treasury will take several months unless we work through the right connections.”

Wang understood that well. Even the most urgently needed military pay faced obstruction at every stage before release. The treasury clerks were particularly difficult. “‘The King of Hell is easy to see; his little demons are hard to manage!’” he said. “I can deal with Treasurer Lin, but I don't yet see a way through the clerks below him.” “Leave them to me.” Hu was about to say, “You go and see the King of Hell; I'll deal with the demons.” Then he remembered that telling someone to see the King of Hell was an ill-omened joke. He answered plainly instead. “Send an official document pressing for payment. I'll find a way among the subordinates. At worst, it will mean a little more in gratuities.” With that settled, Wang drew five thousand taels from the bureau's public funds the following day and handed it to Hu. The money was available, but smooth progress required people too. If Hu were merely opening a bank and could attend to it himself all day, the lack of a good assistant would not matter for the moment. But he had to coordinate matters in many directions and could not be tied down by daily business. He therefore needed a capable, trustworthy manager.

Two former colleagues at Xinhe had promise, but he did not want to approach them. First, he would be taking good men from Zhang. Neither the obligations of the trade nor their personal friendship permitted it. Second, they knew his background too well. They had joked together as equals. Suddenly becoming employer and employees would embarrass him and make it difficult for them to regard him with proper respect. After much thought, he remembered another man in the trade with whom he had little personal connection. He worked at the counter of a bank in Qinghefang. Hu had dealt with him once and found him clear-headed, with an appearance and manner of speaking well above the ordinary. He was worth recruiting. Zhang would be the best person to approach him. That brought up another problem. Ever since deciding to open a bank on the return voyage from Shanghai, Hu had wondered whether to tell Zhang first or wait until everything was ready and an auspicious opening date selected. A moment's serious thought made the answer plain. Early disclosure might bring no benefit, but late disclosure would certainly do harm. It would first suggest a lack of friendship, as though he were concealing something, and invite suspicion. Zhang was currently bearing substantial risks for him and Wang. Any loss of trust would cause trouble. Besides, gathering staff and opening a bank could not be kept secret. If Zhang discovered it and came to ask, the position would be more awkward still.

Having decided, Hu made a special visit to Xinhe at Salt Bridge. Their meeting was cordial. After chatting in the shop, he said, “Mr Zhang, I have something important to discuss,” and glanced around. “Come inside.” Zhang led him to his bedroom. It was small, and a safe recently purchased from a foreign firm in Shanghai made it more cramped still. They sat on the bed. “Mr Zhang, I've decided to establish a firm of my own.” “Excellent!” Zhang's pleasure sounded somewhat forced. Hu understood: he feared that Hu's bank would affect Xinhe's business. Its dealings with the Sea Transport Bureau were naturally likely to change. He therefore began with reassurance. “Don't worry. A rabbit doesn't eat the grass beside its own burrow. If I meant to take your business, I wouldn't be telling you first. The bureau's dealings will remain with Xinhe. I'll find a different path.” “Oh? What path?” “That will emerge in time. In short, whatever business Xinhe is pursuing, I'll keep clear of it.” “Good.” Their relationship had changed, and Zhang no longer offered insincere courtesies. He answered frankly. “I trust your character. If you're willing to make that concession, I appreciate it. Whatever help I can give, I'll give wholeheartedly. Tell me what you need.”

“Naturally, I must ask your help. First, support me on opening day.” “That goes without saying. I'll bring fellow bankers to make a show of deposits. I can't promise a great deal, but there'll be ten thousand taels or so in silver.” “Excellent. Thank you in advance. Second, I've made it a rule not to take any of Xinhe's good men. I've found someone else and would like you to help bring us together.” “Who?” “At Dayuan in Qinghefang there's a young fellow, surnamed Liu, I think. A presentable man who knows how to deal with people. I'd like to meet him.” “Liu? Presentable?” Zhang frowned in thought, then remembered. “You have a good eye. But I know both Dayuan's proprietor and its manager well, so I can't intervene openly. I'll have someone arrange a meeting. If it works out, you mustn't reveal that I brought you together.”

“I understand.” Zhang had not spoken idly. He did all he could to help and immediately asked someone to contact Liu. That night, close to the second watch, a visitor knocked at Hu's house. Hu took an oil lamp to the door and raised it towards the man's face. It was Liu. “Mr Hu, Mr Zhang of Xinhe asked me to call.” “Yes, indeed. Come inside.” Once they were in the reception room, Hu asked his full name. It was Liu Qingsheng, and Hu addressed him as “Brother Qingsheng.” “Where is your family home?” “Yuyao.” “Ah, a fine place! I've been there,” Hu said with interest. They discussed Yuyao's sights and customs, moved on to Ningbo, then back to Shaoxing. Hu spoke endlessly on every imaginable subject, bewildering Liu. Several times Liu tried to return to the purpose of the visit and asked how he could be of service. Hu always gave a brief, evasive answer and wandered off again, as though bored by the long night and wanting someone to listen to fantastic tales from the Classic of Mountains and Seas.

Liu grew increasingly puzzled and somewhat annoyed. But he too had great perseverance. Neither Hu nor Wang ever told others the story of their remarkable connection. Zhang, however, knew half or more of it and embellished it freely in conversation. Everyone in the trade therefore knew Hu as an unfathomable man of consequence. Liu thought, “He must have a reason for bringing me here. I mean to see what he has to say.” That decision enabled him to endure. Hu was testing precisely that patience. After an hour of empty talk, Liu showed no irritation. Satisfied, Hu considered the first test—and in truth the hardest—passed. Only then did he turn to banking. An expert himself, he disguised his examination as casual conversation and set difficult questions. Liu answered to the best of his knowledge, mostly correctly. The second test was passed as well.

“Brother Qingsheng, I've been away from banking for some time. How many firms are there in the city now?” “Eight large banks. There are more of the smaller establishments: thirty-three altogether.” “Which thirty-three?” Now Liu's ability truly appeared. From the Upper City to the Lower, he named every one of the thirty-three smaller firms whose main business was exchanging silver and copper cash. He gave the names without a pause and missed none. Even Hu felt his own memory inferior.

By now Hu had all but decided to employ him, though he would not yet say so. “Is your family in Hangzhou?” “They're all in Yuyao.” “Why don't you bring them here?” “I can't afford it yet.” “I take it you're married?” “Yes. I have two children.” “Who else is in your household?” “Both my parents are alive, and I have a younger brother at an elementary school.” “Then, including yourself, there are seven mouths to feed. That's quite a burden.” “Yes. That's why I don't dare bring them to Hangzhou. It's easier to manage in our home district.”

“If you did move them here, what would the monthly expenses be?” Hu asked. “I don't mean a life of hardship. At least a meat dish and a vegetable dish at meals, silk as well as cotton clothes—even a wife and a concubine wouldn't be excessive.” Liu laughed. “You're joking, Mr Hu.” “Then treat it as a joke. Give me a figure.” “On that basis, even ten taels a month might not be enough.” “That isn't much.” Hu continued, “Hangzhou's eight large banks are about to become nine.” “Oh?” Liu asked attentively. “Another is opening?” “Yes, very soon.” “What's its name? Where will it be?” “The name hasn't been decided, nor the location.” “Then... what do you mean?”

Hu ignored the question. “Brother Qingsheng, if this bank asked you to be its manager, would Dayuan let you go?” “What?” Liu thought he had misheard. “Please say that again.” This time he heard clearly, but could scarcely believe it. Studying Hu's face and finding no sign of a joke, he realised that his opportunity had arrived. “Dayuan would have no reason to refuse. I've got on well with everyone there. If such an opportunity came, my colleagues would be pleased for me.” “Good. Then I invite you to manage this new bank.” “You're opening it yourself, Mr Hu?” Liu was slightly surprised. “The proprietor isn't me, though you could say that I am. In any case, I have full authority. You say your expenses would be at least ten taels a month, or a hundred and twenty a year. Here's my offer: two hundred taels a year, with a bonus at year's end. What do you think?”

What more could he ask? Yet the generosity was so great that it was difficult to believe. Reading his expression, Hu understood. He excused himself, went inside, and returned with four ingots of fifty taels each, which he set before Liu. “This is for the year from this fourth month to the third month next year. Take it in advance.” “No, no!” Deeply moved, Liu pushed the silver away almost as though quarrelling. “Mr Hu, frankly, I've never even heard of anyone treating a man like this. Money can be spent, but our hearts are what matter. Just give me your instructions. Whatever you say, I'll do.” While Liu was agitated, Hu remained calm. He spoke earnestly. “Brother Qingsheng, you must take these two hundred taels today. Money gives a man confidence. With it in your hands, your mind will be settled and your thoughts more active. Any ideas you devise will naturally be better.” “That isn't what I mean...” “No more ceremony. It's money you're properly entitled to. Why refuse it? If you won't accept, I'll find it difficult to speak freely.” “Very well. Let us leave that for now and discuss the business.”

“Exactly. When you go back today, put the affairs you've handled at Dayuan in order. Our first task is to find premises. The building must be handsome and well appointed, with convenient access, and it must be in the Upper City. Ask the property brokers to show you several places. We can buy it outright or take it in pledge. Once you've chosen, tell me.” “Yes. The second task?” “Find employees. Choose whomever you think suitable.” “And the third?” “After that, it's decorating the premises, buying furniture, and so on. You handle it all. I won't interfere.” Liu considered. “I understand. Tomorrow, please open an account with a thousand taels available and give me the seal, so I can draw funds as required.” “Quite right. Write a note to Mr Zhang at Xinhe, asking him to advance a thousand taels and open the account.” This was another test, of his writing. Liu handled it easily. Hu read the note, approved it, added his written signature mark, and sent Liu away with both the note and the two hundred taels in silver.

In that single evening, Hu had completely won Liu over. Liu normally lived alone at the bank, but with so much to plan that night, he deliberately took a quiet room at an inn. He borrowed brush and inkstone from the desk, asked for two sheets of plain writing paper, and sat beneath an oil lamp listing everything he must do. The cocks were crowing by the time he finished. He lay down in his clothes for a little while and rose at daybreak. Though he had slept very little, good fortune gave him energy. Taking his silver, he went straight back to Dayuan. His colleagues, assuming that his night away had been spent with a courtesan, teased him. Liu was firm inwardly and accommodating in manner. He only smiled and began putting his accounts in order. His abacus clicked rapidly, and by noon everything was settled. After lunch, he said he was going to collect debts and went out to attend to Hu's business. First came the premises, for which he needed a property broker. At the brokers' customary teahouse meeting place, he found an acquaintance and described the layout required. He added one condition: a small residence must be rented near the bank. He intended to bring his family to Hangzhou and live close enough to attend to the business whenever needed. After arranging when to hear the broker's reply, he turned to recruiting staff. With people coming and going, he needed somewhere to meet them, and once he left Dayuan he would need lodging too. Fortunately, he had two hundred taels. He rented a small courtyard of three rooms at an inn by the month, then went to an employment agency and selected an honest, industrious general servant, who began work at the inn that day.

By dusk, Dayuan's manager, Sun Deqing, had gone home. Liu prepared four carefully chosen gifts of fresh provisions and called on him. “Oh!” Sun was bewildered. “Gifts out of the blue? What's the occasion?” “There's something on which I must ask your help...” “I know!” Sun interrupted. “I've already spoken to the proprietor. You'll get a raise after the festival. Why spend money on presents? Qingsheng, money isn't easily earned. These must have cost at least four taels—two months of your wages. Why do it?” He had completely misunderstood. Yet his kindness made Liu's news harder to deliver. Smiling, Liu said, “It seems I owe both you and the proprietor an apology.” “What?” Sun was alarmed. “What trouble have you caused? Taken on a bad debt?” “No.” Liu placed the account book he had brought before him. “Everything is settled. There isn't a single uncollectable account. Mr Sun, I'm leaving.”

“Going where?” “You'll be pleased for me when I tell you. A friend is opening a bank and wants me as manager.” “Congratulations!” Then Sun looked doubtful. “But tell me: what sort of friend? Why was there no hint of this beforehand?” “I only came upon this exceptional opportunity yesterday. You must know the man: Hu Xueyan.” “The Hu Xueyan formerly at Xinhe? He's your new employer?” Those words showed that Sun had accepted his departure. Greatly relieved, Liu smiled. “I suppose so.” “That's not right. An employer is an employer. What do you mean, ‘suppose’? I've met Hu too. Every movement of his eyebrows means another scheme. I think...” At last Sun said frankly, “He's not entirely dependable.”

“He is dependable. And if he really isn't, I'll come back. You're like an elder to me, Mr Sun. You wouldn't laugh at me.” These words pleased Sun, who nodded. “Water flows downwards, but a man seeks to rise. Going straight into a manager's position does Dayuan credit too. I only hope it doesn't become a laughing matter. If he proves unreliable, be very careful. Leave promptly and come back to us.” There had been fraudulent banks before: empty establishments that took deposits and then collapsed. That was the danger behind Sun's warning. If the proprietor fled, the manager would face legal proceedings. Nothing of the kind could happen here, Liu felt, but the warning was well meant. He had intended to suggest that the new bank establish an affiliation with Dayuan. Now there was no point in offering that overture. He answered, “I shall certainly heed your advice,” and took his leave.

From Sun's house he went to Hu's and briefly reported the day's activities. Hearing that he had rented a courtyard at an inn, Hu knew that he could act freely and decisively. He had previously feared that Liu might be too constrained to develop his abilities fully. That last doubt now disappeared. “Excellent. Go ahead. Decide anything within your authority without asking me.” “There is one thing you must decide yourself,” Liu said. “Have you settled on the firm's name? Once you have, we need someone to write it so the signboard can be made.” “Yes, that is important. But I too must consult someone wiser. I'll tell you tomorrow.”

CHAPTER SIX

The person he consulted was none other than Wang. “This is my first attempt at naming a business,” Wang laughed. “I don't even know how to begin. What are the requirements?” “First, it must sound impressive and be easy to say. Second, the characters must be distinctive, so nobody confuses it with another firm. Naturally, it must suit a bank and be auspicious.” “Very well. Let me think.” He was rather at a loss. Taking a book at random, he intended to select a few characters, write them down, and then try different combinations. The volume he pulled from the shelf was the Chronicles of Huayang. He opened it and read a few lines. By a fortunate coincidence, two characters lay ready to hand. “What about these?” He wrote out a passage: “The age is peaceful, the way well governed; the people and their possessions flourish in abundance and well-being.” He circled the characters fu and kang. “Fukang, Fukang!” Hu repeated the name twice, then answered gladly, “Excellent! Both abundance and well-being. That's the one.”

As Hu rose to leave, Wang called him back. “Xueyan, I have news. I'm to receive a regular appointment.” “Oh! Which department or county?” “I don't know yet. Liu Er from the governor's office came to say that Governor Huang wishes to see me this evening. He let the news slip. I suppose it is time I received a post.” Just then a figure hurried past the window. Hu's sharp eyes recognised him. “It's Commissioner Wu.” The curtain lifted to reveal a smiling face. As Wu stepped inside, he saluted and announced loudly, “Congratulations, Your Honour! Wonderful news!” Wang paused, then understood. Wu had connections at the provincial treasury and must have heard of the appointment. He stood and repeatedly clasped his hands. “Thank you!” “I've just come from the treasurer's office,” Wu said, stepping closer. “The news is certain: you are to act as prefect of Huzhou.” Even Hu, who knew comparatively little of official practice, was astonished. An expectant department or county magistrate, who had not served a single day in a regular post of his own grade, was suddenly to leap to an acting prefecture? Surely that was extraordinary. Wang found it still harder to believe. “That... that doesn't sound quite right.” “There can be no mistake! The appointment will be posted tomorrow.”

Wang considered, still feeling that something was strange. He begged Wu to inquire further and sent Gao to ask Liu Er, who might have definite information. The news was both abrupt and intensely exciting. Torn between hope and fear, Wang could neither sit nor stand comfortably in his office. Hu urged him to remain calm. “Even if it isn't a prefecture, it must be a large county. You'll know when you see the governor tonight.” “I was thinking...” Wang's answer followed his own thoughts. “I paid little attention to what the treasurer said the other day. Now it seems significant.” “What did he say?” “First, that Huzhou's prefect had been dismissed for delaying the grain and that no replacement could be found. Then he said he had an idea, but immediately rejected it, muttering that it wouldn't work, that there was no precedent. Could it be connected with this news?” “Then that explains it!” Hu slapped his thigh. “Either the treasurer recommended you and the governor agreed, or the governor proposed it and the treasurer was happy to oblige. Let's hear what Liu Er tells Gao. If the treasurer has just been to see the governor, the news is eight-tenths certain.” “That makes sense.” Wang was greatly reassured.

“But remember, Mr Xuexuan: Huzhou has a great many powerful households. Its affairs are very difficult.” “Exactly! That's why you must still help me and come with me.” Hu could not agree to that. He put it aside for the moment. “We can discuss it later. There's another matter we must guard against. What happens to your assignment here?” “Here” meant the Sea Transport Bureau. The question reminded Wang of all that handing over its executive directorship would involve: the deficit must be made good and every affair under his management explained. A successor would have his own methods. If the bureau's funds ceased to be deposited with Xinhe and the relationship ended, their guarantee for the Songjiang association's loan could create serious trouble. It was indeed a danger to consider. “Yes!” Wang drew a breath. “A great deal depends on that. We must act early. I think I should tell the governor frankly and ask to retain the bureau as an additional duty. But if he says I couldn't manage provincial-capital business from Huzhou, we'll be in considerable difficulty.” “Then let me ask you this. If you reach the point where you can't have both, what will you choose?” “I'd rather decline the regular appointment and preserve our position here. I owe my present standing to my friends' help. I can't leave a burden that harms you, Zhang, and You.” Hu nodded deeply and spoke word by word. “With that principle, you'll never lack friends.” Having clarified his ultimate position, Wang felt calmer.

They discussed how he should address Huang under various circumstances. After about an hour, Gao returned. As Hu had expected, Huang had specially summoned Lingui that morning for a private consultation. Wu's news plainly had a basis. Soon Wu himself brought fuller confirmation: Wang was to act as magistrate of Wucheng County and concurrently as prefect of Huzhou. There could be no further doubt. Everyone at the bureau had heard and came together to congratulate their director. They also discussed subscribing for a feast and theatrical performance in his honour. Wang thought this far too ostentatious and firmly refused. He asked Wu to thank them and make absolutely clear that no such celebration should be held. Half a day of commotion produced no agreement. At last he put the matter aside and went punctually to the governor's summons.

“We must find a way to collect this year's full revenue. Military expenses are enormous. Ministry dispatches demanding remittances to the capital arrive one after another. Look—another edict.” Wang rose and took the document from Huang. Its lengthy text concerned raising military funds and encouraging contributions. The final passage read: “As provincial appropriations have failed to arrive on schedule, the Board of Revenue proposes suspending salary payments for one year, according to rank. We consider that princes and senior ministers have long enjoyed generous emoluments, so a temporary suspension is practicable. For civil officials below the fourth rank and military officials below the third, however, let the Board pay in full the salaries withheld this spring. Let five hundred thousand taels also be released from the privy treasury into the Board's treasury to meet essential salary and military expenditure.” Would princes and senior ministers tolerate a prolonged interruption of their salaries? Naturally, the provinces would face relentless demands for funds. Wang took warning: this year, local officials must give revenue collection precedence over everything. “Our province depends on Hangzhou, Jiaxing, and Huzhou, with Huzhou its particular lifeblood,” Huang continued. “Treasurer Lin and I have agreed that you must go. In this crisis, unparalleled in two hundred years, the court has repeatedly urged practical results and exceptional appointments where necessary. I therefore doubt it will reject my recommendation that you act as prefect.” Wang was prepared. As soon as Huang paused, he rose and saluted. “Such favour overwhelms me with gratitude and apprehension. I don't know how to repay it.” “Handle the public business properly, and that will be repayment enough. Huzhou is unlike other places, Brother Xuexuan. You must bring all your ability to bear.” “Yes. But there is a personal difficulty for which I must ask your special consideration.” “Speak. Anything that benefits the public business can be accommodated.”

“It concerns the Sea Transport Bureau. I've only recently taken charge. Your Excellency understands every complication of the official-procurement arrangement. Matters are still unfinished. If a successor, unaware of the circumstances, objects at every turn, then even apart from possible financial liabilities, the correspondence needed to explain and justify everything would consume enormous time. With me in Huzhou, how could I devote my full attention to revenue collection? I venture to ask you to remove this concern.” “What would you have me do?” “Allow me to hand over only after this affair has been concluded.” Huang fell silent, gazing into space as though calculating. Wang tried to read his thoughts. Had the post already been promised to someone else? “There is no objection in principle to your holding both duties,” Huang said slowly, bringing his eyes back to Wang. “But can you manage them?” The question was expected. “Rest assured, I can. I have an exceptionally capable man under me. Without his work in making contacts and negotiating on every side, the procurement affair could never have proceeded so smoothly.”

“Oh? What is his name? What qualifications does he hold? Bring him to see me sometime.” “His name is Hu Guangyong. He is young, and though a man of commerce, he has extraordinary abilities. At present he holds no official or scholarly qualification, so it may not be proper for him to seek an audience.” “That doesn't matter. There is much to be done. A talented man need not fear being overlooked. What business is he in?” “He...” Wang exaggerated on Hu's behalf. “He comes from a prosperous banking family and has now established a bank of his own.” “A bank? Good. Very good indeed!” The repeated approval had a strange tone. Wang feared some concealed implication and grew watchful. “Speaking of banks reminds me of something,” Huang continued. “Senior officials in the capital and governors throughout the provinces are contributing to military funds. I too must make an effort. I intend to assemble ten thousand taels as a modest contribution. In a few days, ask this Mr Hu's bank to remit it for me.” “Certainly. We should be honoured to serve. Please send the money whenever convenient.”

At that, Huang lifted his tea bowl, signalling the end of the audience. Nothing further was said about retaining the bureau. Wang was anxious. Left suspended between possibilities, he could not see how to obtain a definite answer. As soon as he left, he sent Gao to find Hu. Hu arrived just after him. Without even changing his clothes, Wang took him into the study, closed the door, and recounted everything. “The bureau is now hanging in mid-air. I don't know where to begin. Isn't that maddening? If he'd simply refused, I could have stated my decision. As it is, I can neither advance nor retreat.” “Never mind. It's very easy,” Hu said casually. “A little more silver will settle it.” “Why, I don't believe you! How can you be so sure? And how much is ‘a little’? How would it be spent?” “Mr Xuexuan, you're clever all your life and muddled for a moment. He's already named his price: ten thousand taels.” “Ah!” Wang understood. “No wonder!” He reconsidered the scene. Because he had failed to grasp the implication, he had asked Huang to send the money at his convenience. Hearing that he had missed the point, Huang had immediately dismissed him. The abrupt coldness was disheartening.

“No more talk. Act quickly. The right medicine cures the illness; there's no reason to delay.” “Certainly.” Wang considered. “Tomorrow I'll have Xinhe remit ten thousand to the ministry.” “Wait. Give me that money. I have another use for it.” The words were puzzling, but Wang did not ask. Showing complete trust was one of his methods of securing Hu's loyalty. He nodded. “Come to the bureau tomorrow morning to collect it.” “No. You'll be very busy. I won't disturb you. Send the draft to me, and I'll finish the business during the morning. We'll meet at noon.” “Wait, let me think.” Wang anticipated the next day's schedule. “Assuming the appointment is posted early, I'll immediately go to thank the treasurer, then to the governor...” “No.” Hu interrupted and waved his hand. “See the governor in the afternoon. When you return from the treasury, there's something important to do at the bureau. Gather the staff and let them know you're retaining the directorship. Why? To settle their minds. In banking, when a manager changes, the employees begin talking outside, or answer questions they cannot avoid. Many internal secrets escape that way. I imagine official life is the same. Once people feel secure, there'll be no rumours and needless trouble. Don't you agree?” “Of course!” Wang smiled. “My mind is quick enough, but always one step behind yours. We'll do that and discuss the rest at noon.”

After ten the following morning, the bureau's general affairs officer brought a draft drawn on Xinhe. Hu immediately went to Liu Qingsheng. His reasoning was this: Liu had promise, but his sudden promotion from counter clerk to manager might provoke disdain among fellow bankers. His standing and reputation must be developed. Handling the governor's remittance would demonstrate powerful connections. Within the province, the governor was the foremost possible client. With such a customer, everyone would view Liu differently. Once Hu explained, Liu was delighted—but not merely for himself. “What an unexpectedly splendid opportunity!” Then he grew serious. “Mr Hu, there's something I can tell you now. Mr Sun at Dayuan still doubts your backing and resources. It annoyed me, but I couldn't refute him. Empty words were useless, so I said nothing. If I arrange this remittance through Dayuan, they'll see your influence for themselves.” “So that's how it is?” Hu smiled. “Wait until our signboard is up. I'll show them a little more.” “Then I mustn't delay. I'll do it now and bring the documents to your house afterwards.”

Liu's standing had changed. He put on a silk robe and jacket bought at a second-hand clothing shop on Yanda Street, added new shoes and socks, and hired a small chair to Dayuan. The employees all looked up, expecting an important customer. When the curtain lifted and revealed Liu, they were astonished, envious, and admiring. He felt a little awkward, but his naturally smiling face made them reluctant to mock him. After a few civilities with Sun, he came to business. “I have a remittance to send to the capital through Dayuan. Send it to Rishengchang. That remittance house deals with the Board of Revenue, which will make things convenient.” “How much? Money to purchase office?” “No. Governor Huang's contribution to military funds: ten thousand taels of standard silver.” Sun's expression changed at once. “Why, Qingsheng!” He was surprised and impressed. “You've done well indeed, reaching the governor's circle.” “I have no such ability. Someone else entrusted it to me.” “Who?” Liu merely smiled, deliberately leaving him to guess. He knew the answer would be immediate but wanted the satisfaction of hearing Sun say it. “Hu Xueyan?” “Yes.” Liu looked at him and slowly nodded, as though asking whether he understood Hu now.

Puzzled and envious, Sun took the draft to the counter for processing, then returned. “Have you settled on a name for your firm?” “Yes. Fukang.” “Fukang!” Sun leaned closer and asked mysteriously, “Does Governor Huang have a share in it?” The notion surprised Liu. It was a serious suggestion. Repeated outside, it could become a boast of official backing and cause trouble. He answered immediately, “I don't know, but I shouldn't think so. How could a provincial governor open a bank in his own province?” “Of course you wouldn't know the inside story...” Sun smiled knowingly and said no more, wearing the reserved expression of a man possessing a private secret. Liu really did not know whether the governor held shares and could not deny it on anyone's behalf. He nevertheless felt uneasy. Once the remittance draft was ready, he took a chair to Hu's house, delivered it, and honestly reported Sun's speculation. Hu smiled with satisfaction. “Let them guess. The more excitement in the market, the easier Fukang's business will be.”

Reassured, Liu departed happily. Hu went to the bureau, where several chairs stood outside. Hangzhou's prefectural seat contained two counties, Qiantang and Renhe, with Qiantang the principal one. Its runners were clearing onlookers and managing traffic. Knowing that congratulatory visitors had arrived in numbers, Hu avoided the main entrance, slipped through a side door in the lane, and quietly entered his usual small room beside the private office. “Mr Hu!” Li Cheng, the office attendant, smiled as he delivered the news. “Our master has been promoted.” “Oh? To what?” “Wucheng County, with acting charge of Huzhou Prefecture, while retaining his bureau duties. Our master's official fortune is flourishing, and we servants benefit too. Mr Hu, I have a favour to ask.” “Go on.” “I have an uncle who's very good with his pen. A lawsuit ruined him, and he's in miserable circumstances. Could you put in a word and have him taken to Huzhou?” “Good with his pen in what way?” “People praise his social letters. He can also use an abacus and keep accounts.” Hu considered. “I'd like to try him first. Ask him to come and see me.” “Yes!” Li was excited. “When will you be free?”

Before Hu could answer, footsteps sounded and Wang's figure appeared outside the window. Li hurried to lift the curtain. Instead of entering his office, Wang came directly into Hu's small room. His face was radiant, his pace composed, and his bearing seemed altogether altered. “Congratulations!” Hu rose with a smile and bowed. “To both of us!” Wang took his hand. “Come and talk in my room.” He led Hu into the inner room of his office, and they sat side by side on the small bed where he took his afternoon rest. His excitement was irrepressible. “Xueyan, I couldn't believe it until I saw the treasurer this morning. Less than a year! Who could have imagined my position today? Misfortune lurks beside good fortune. I'm almost uneasy.” “You must remain steady. Today's result comes from yesterday's causes. Don't dwell on the past; look ahead. Never mind your present standing. Think only of what you've done today and what you ought to do.”

Taking his advice, Wang restrained himself and grew calmer. “First, there's something to discuss. The treasurer wants me to take office quickly. Someone else suggests accepting the seal on the first day of the fifth month, so I can collect the festival gifts already due. What do you think?” This baffled Hu. After careful thought, he answered, “I don't know official customs, but human feelings are the same. Before taking a ready-made benefit, consider whether it harms anyone. If it doesn't, well and good. Otherwise you're taking someone else's advantage. Put yourself in his place.” “That's exactly why I hesitate. There's only one set of festival gifts. If I take them, the present acting magistrate loses them...” “Then you absolutely mustn't!” Hu interrupted. “He's held the post for some time and deserves this payment. You shouldn't take it away. Money can be spent, but offending someone isn't easily repaired...” “Enough,” Wang interrupted in turn. “I've decided to receive the seal after the Dragon Boat Festival.” “Exactly. Your fortune is rising. You must handle things handsomely.” As he spoke, Hu handed over the remittance draft.

“This is important. I'll go to the governor after lunch. But even if I send in my card, he may have no time to see me.” Wang was earnest. “This must be settled promptly.” “He needn't necessarily see you. Enough heat will cook the pig's head: he only needs to see the draft. Write a letter beforehand and send that in if you can't get an audience. While you're there, distribute the customary festival gifts in his office early. Then you can rest easy; someone will bring news.” “Yes, that's what I'll do.” Wang paused. “Xueyan, taking up a regular post will mean advancing another ten thousand taels or so. The hole grows bigger and bigger. I'm worried.” “Don't be. You have me. Don't delay—go before the governor takes his nap.”

Wang followed the advice. He wrote a short letter, enclosed the draft, and prepared the festival gratuities, each in a red envelope. With a thick stack tucked inside his boot flap, he called for his chair and went to the governor's yamen. Liu Er hurried over with congratulations. Wang's standing had changed, and he could not resist assuming some importance. But while dignity showed on his face, a reward was ready in his hand. Once he passed over an envelope containing a twenty-tael note, the grander his manner, the more respectful Liu became. “Your Honour,” Liu said with great determination, “do you want to see the governor today? If you do, I'll make certain of it.” “Why? Is he very busy?” “Indeed. Otherwise I wouldn't say so.” Liu lowered his voice. “Someone has come from the capital. They've been behind closed doors in the private office all morning. The garrison general has also sent an orderly asking him over to discuss military affairs. Once he goes, he may not return until evening. If you must see him, I'll announce you now and contrive something. But even if you get in, there won't be much time.” “Before he visits the general, would he have time to read a letter?” “Certainly. Give it to me. I'll stay beside him and make sure he opens it.” Wang handed it over. “Then I rely on you. If the governor has any message, please come and let me know.” “Naturally. I understand.”

“One more favour.” Wang drew the handful of red envelopes from his boot and gave them to Liu. “A few small festival tokens. Please distribute them for me.” This was a duty Liu welcomed. With repeated assurances, he escorted Wang to his chair. Back at the bureau, the entrance was busier than ever, crowded with strangers. They rose respectfully at the sight of his chair. Sitting upright behind his dark spectacles, Wang examined them. Most were plainly seeking employment. He feared there were too many monks for too little porridge: he could not satisfy them all and would inevitably offend some. Sure enough, as soon as he sat down, a great bundle of cards and letters came in. Here was one of the hardships of office. Everyone had to be answered. Depending upon the importance of the connection, he received them personally or asked Zhou and others to do so. He had to devise countless polite phrases explaining what he could not do. Only when the sun touched the hills did the business briefly subside. Then he remembered Liu Er. Why had no message arrived? By lamplight there was still none, and Wang grew restless. Following Hu's advice, he had announced that morning, after returning from the treasury, that he would retain the bureau's directorship. He had hoped to steady the staff. If things changed and the pretence were exposed, the story would become a joke at his expense. He could not bear that loss of face. As he worried, Hu arrived. Hearing the situation, he too found it puzzling, but retained his confidence. There was no good news, but no bad news either. There was no need for alarm.

“Even so, Liu should have told me something.” “He doesn't know why you're waiting. If he understood your anxiety, he'd certainly have come.” Hu thought a moment. “Go home first, and send Gao to invite him over. We can ask how the governor responded.” “That makes sense.” Gao too was gone a long time without word. Wang and Hu drank together at home while they waited. Not until the clock struck nine did Gao appear with a lantern, lighting Liu's way inside. Now that the man had arrived, Wang became composed and first asked whether he had eaten. Liu had eaten long before. “When Second Master Gao came, I was still reporting upstairs. There were many instructions, which delayed me. The governor read your letter early, but only now gave me a message.” “Oh?” Liu's unhurried manner made Wang impatient, though he would not show it. “His Excellency says: after His Honour Wang has received the seal at Huzhou and put things in order, he is to return promptly to the provincial capital. The business here is important too.” “Here” naturally meant the Sea Transport Bureau. Wang was overwhelmed with joy. He and Hu exchanged a smile that needed no words.

Only then did Liu understand. Wang's retention of the bureau had not been certain until this moment. He regretted his ignorance. Had he known, this news could have been made a valuable commodity, with a more elaborate account of his own services. But it was not too late. He immediately bent his knees in salute. “Congratulations, Your Honour! Knowing how anxiously you awaited news, I stayed beside our master without daring to move. At last I obtained the good word.” “I am most grateful.” Wang understood and sent him away with another envelope containing ten taels.

“At last you've got what you wished, and everyone can be satisfied.” Hu joked, “Your Honour Wang, I have an assignment to request. Let me hire the boat for your journey to take office.” Naturally, this meant giving A'zhu's family the business. Wang laughed too. “Any other assignment is yours. Only that one is out of the question.” Their laughter drew Mrs Wang out to inquire. That was her excuse; she really wanted to hear the news and share the joy of her husband's rising fortune. They had become intimate family friends, so she no longer avoided Hu. Sitting with them, she thanked him repeatedly, then asked, “Young Master Hu, why don't you purchase an official title?” “Exactly!” Wang seized on it. “This is important. A qualification would make your work much easier. At the bureau, for instance, if you held a department or county magistrate's qualification, I could recommend you as a commissioner to oversee everything for me. Wouldn't that simplify matters?” “True. But my first concern is getting Fukang established.” Hu glanced at Mrs Wang. Understanding that some things could not be said before her, Wang found an excuse to send her away. “Fukang must open soon,” Hu continued. “We need those tens of thousands from the treasury as capital. Press them again tomorrow. I've already found someone to work on the matter below.” “That can be done. My mind is in such confusion that I don't know what to do first.” “I don't fully understand official practice. Let's discuss it patiently. We have the whole night to put things in order.” They talked through the night, writing down each task and its priority. Hu busied himself preparing Fukang. Wang's first major duty was to find private secretaries.

Private secretaries came in many varieties. Besides the legal and revenue advisers, there were accountants handling receipts and payments, correspondence secretaries, tutors for the official's children, examination assistants who read papers, collection specialists, and others. The legal and revenue posts were naturally the most important. Secretary Yu at the judicial commissioner's yamen had long promised to find suitable men, so Wang made a special call. His purpose needed no explanation. Yu had already chosen his own pupil for the legal post. This pupil, Qin Shoumen, was in fact nearly Yu's age and no novice. The profession was sometimes dismissed as a last resort for men who failed in their studies, but a secretary's life could be that of “an immortal, a tiger, or a dog.” Celebrated secretaries enjoyed great prestige. They needed not only command of statutes and precedents and a fluent pen, but sound professional lineage, broad knowledge, and experience. Their training was therefore crucial. Qin had followed Yu for years, beginning at county and department level, progressing through prefectural and circuit offices, and finally reaching the provincial judicial commission. He understood the entire local judicial process and the powers and characteristics of every level. This comprehensive experience made him superior to men trained only in a county office or only at the provincial commission. He had begun independent practice ten years earlier and had never lacked employment. Two years before, both parents died. He returned to Shaoxing for their funerals, then fell ill himself. Recently recovered, he had come to his teacher for assistance. Yu could now recommend him to Wang. They met and conversed agreeably.
