Mulberry trees alone were useless, but too many worms and too few trees also caused difficulties. Sometimes people had to discard worms already halfway through their painstaking upbringing. Nothing was more painful to a silkworm-raising household.

Her account brought back what Hu already knew of silk. “Isn't the very best called Jili silk?” he asked. “That's what everyone says,” A’zhu's mother answered. “The place is seven li from Nanxun.” “So it's Qili—‘seven li’—silk, rather than Jili!” Hu exclaimed, pleased with his discovery. “You really must consult those who know the trade.” The characters for “seven” and the first syllable of Jili were different, but sounded alike in their speech. A’zhu was therefore puzzled and laughed at him. “What do you mean, ‘Qili silk, not Qili silk’? A man named Hu isn't named Hu? What sort of nonsense is that?”

Hu smiled without answering. He had no inclination to exchange jokes just then. Seven or eight ideas were turning in his mind. He quietened himself, began to put them in order, and returned to the interrupted subject. “I understand how the worms are raised now. What I still don't quite understand is how the silk is reeled and then sold.” A’zhu's mother explained the traditional method. Water was boiled in a large pot, a sheng measure of cocoons tipped in, and the contents stirred with a wooden stick. Two small reels stood above the pot, with a bamboo tube beneath. Once stirring had drawn out the filament ends, these were passed through the tube, taken once round a small reel, and led to the large reel on the ground. As the silk was drawn off, the pupae appeared. If a thread broke, one stirred again to find its end, continuing until all the silk had been reeled. “Reeling is hard work too,” she said. “Unless the cocoons are reeled quickly, the creatures inside break through them and make them useless. So the whole family, young and old, has to work day and night until it's finished. Imagine standing beside a pot of boiling water, stirring and drawing silk without stopping, with that smell from the scalded pupae. It's real suffering. If the cocoons are damp and soft and won't reel easily, it's worse still. Some won't yield an end however long you stir. They're called water cocoons. You can only fish them out and throw them away—all that work wasted.”

“Hard as it is, there must be happy times too.” “Of course. Nobody in the world would do something that was nothing but misery. Once the silk is reeled and the travelling silk buyers reach town, the happy time begins. Silk prices rise every year. The money from the new silk really does come in useful.” Here was what Hu most needed to understand. He knew the term “travelling silk buyer”: a merchant who brought large quantities of ready silver to purchase silk where it was produced. Those who operated local firms, gathering new silk for the buyers and making a profit in the process, were known as “silk hosts.” Every third and fourth month, lending to the travelling buyers was one of the banks' chief lines of business. Why, Hu thought, should he lend them money to buy silk and collect interest, instead of becoming a buyer himself? “I'd like to try being a silk buyer too. Are there any special tricks to it?” “That I couldn't tell you,” A’zhu's mother replied. “I suppose the first thing is to recognise good silk. The second is to know the market. Prices go up and down each year, but buying the new season's silk is always cheaper.”

“What makes the price rise and fall? If less silk is produced, the price goes up; or if more people want to buy it, that raises the price too. Is that how it works?” “I suppose all business works that way. But,” she added, “I've heard that silk prices are mostly made by people. They're in the hands of a few big firms.” Hu's spirits rose. So prices depended on manipulation by the large operators. That was a game he understood exceptionally well. A’zhu's mother was becoming increasingly animated, and she was discussing exactly what he wanted to know: the buying and selling of cocoons and silk. “Some families sell their cocoons because they don't have enough hands, or for some other reason,” she said. “Cocoon firms buy them. To open one, you have to obtain a broker's licence from the authorities. The trade has its Cocoon Guild. When the new cocoons reach the market, the members agree on the day buying begins and the day it ends. They agree on the prices too; nobody may raise them independently. But country people often lose out by selling cocoons. Unless they have no other choice, they sell silk.”

“Why do they lose out?” “Don't you understand even that?” A’zhu interrupted. “If the cocoon firm beats down your price, you have to sell. Leave them unsold, and the creatures inside break through. Then they're not worth a single copper!” “Yes, yes! I wasn't thinking.” Hu asked another question. “Once the cocoon firm has bought them, how does it sell them on?” “There are two ways. It can sell them to a reeling establishment, or reel the silk itself and sell that.” “Ah, I see. Now tell me about the silk firms. Do they also need a broker's licence from the ministry? And do they have a guild?”

“Of course. There are far more varieties of silk firm than cocoon firm, each with its own business. Only the larger ones are properly called silk firms. The smaller ones are ‘users,’ buying locally for local use. Those that buy and resell wholesale are called ‘transfer houses.’ Then there are Cantonese houses and export houses, which deal exclusively with the foreign devils. Those require even more capital. They may hold tens of thousands of liang in silk, waiting for a good price before selling it to the foreigners. Think how much capital that ties up! And the foreign devils are very cunning. If you ask a higher price, they don't tell you you're expensive. They smile pleasantly while secretly looking elsewhere. There's always someone with too much money tied up, desperate to sell for cash and willing to take a lower price. You go on waiting while they've already bought cheap stock, put it on a steamship, and sent it to the West...” “Wait, wait!” Hu interrupted loudly. “Let me think.”

Neither mother nor daughter knew what he wanted to think about. They saw him frown, tilt his head, and stare into space in deep concentration. He was thinking how to make money out of the foreigners. The great danger in business was lack of unity. Dealing with foreigners should be like the cocoon firms' buying arrangements: this was the price; take it or leave it. Then the foreigners would have to submit. But people's minds differed as much as their faces. Nor could one really blame them. With insufficient capital and no money circulating, they had no choice but to sell for cash, unless... Suddenly he saw it! Unless he could bring all the export houses under his influence. Naturally, no one person could swallow every opportunity in the world. He must bring his fellow merchants together and persuade them to follow his lead.

That would not be difficult either. Who would object to higher prices for export silk? For those who needed to sell for cash, there were two solutions. First: instead of selling to the foreigners, sell to him. Second: if they would not sell to him, they should still refrain from selling to the foreigners. Whatever funds they needed, they could borrow against their goods; he would guarantee them a better profit later than they could make now. If a man still insisted on selling to the foreigners, he must be receiving secret benefits from them, deliberately lowering his own price and betraying his fellows for outsiders. Hu could rally the trade to cut off all dealings with him. Then how far could his defiance go? “That's it! That's it!” Carried away by his cleverness, he clapped and laughed to himself as though possessed, making A’zhu double up with laughter. Her mother was different: she partly guessed his thoughts. “Are you planning to enter the silk trade, Mr Hu?” she asked with a smile. “I mean to become a travelling silk buyer.” “Just as I thought!” she said triumphantly. “Mr Hu means to trade in silk.” A’zhu, of course, was even more delighted. It was not only that she would have frequent opportunities to see him. Her own wish seemed to have come true so quickly that she felt the joyful surprise of an unexpected gift.

“But, Auntie...” Hu addressed A’zhu's mother as ganniang, a form familiar in Hangzhou and inherited from the Southern Song. It could mean an adoptive mother or a paternal aunt, and could be used for any older woman towards whom the speaker voluntarily assumed the respectful position of a younger relation. A’zhu's mother was overwhelmed by the honour. “Oh, I couldn't accept that!” she protested repeatedly, almost alarmed. “You mustn't call me that, Mr Hu!” While her mother demurred, A’zhu grew anxious. To her, “Auntie” meant almost the same thing as his earlier joke about calling Mother his mother-in-law. She appeared calm, but her heart kept racing. He was trying to draw closer, and Mother insisted on refusing. What sense did that make? Before Hu could answer, she spoke. “He's honouring you. Don't be so ungracious!” No one understands a daughter better than her mother. Hu's new “Auntie” immediately grasped what A’zhu meant and realised that there was no need to refuse so firmly. Yet she could hardly take back her words. Best to let the matter pass vaguely, then make no objection when he used the name again. That would settle her new position. She laughed and scolded A’zhu. “Look at you! Now you're the one lecturing me!”

Hu noticed every tone and glance exchanged by mother and daughter, but he was too eager to discuss serious business to attend to their meaning. “Auntie,” he said, “if I become a travelling silk buyer, how would you like to become a silk host?” “You're joking, Mr Hu.” Being a silk host meant operating a local silk firm. “I haven't got a silk firm. Where would I find silk to sell you?” “Never mind. I'll help you open one.” “Open what?” A’zhu broke in again. “A silk firm?” “Yes!” His answer was crisp and confident. Her mother looked from him to her daughter. He did not seem to be joking. But if he was serious, that was even more puzzling. “Mr Hu,” she asked cautiously, “why don't you open one yourself?” “That's exactly the right question!” Hu nodded repeatedly. “Why don't I? First, I'm not from Huzhou, and in business, to be frank, people do take advantage of newcomers. Second, Mr Wang will be prefect there. If I come as a visiting buyer, that's harmless; if I become a local proprietor, people will gossip. Though Mr Wang has nothing to do with it, they'll say such-and-such a firm has the prefect behind it. That breeds resentment and makes business difficult.”

Now A’zhu's mother understood. At the thought of stepping straight into the role of a business proprietor, she smiled until her eyes narrowed to two slits. “So you want me to represent the firm, Mr Hu. But...” Her spirits suddenly sank. “How can a woman take that public role?” “That's no difficulty. Have Old Zhang apply for the licence in his name. Behind the scenes, you'll run everything as the proprietress. Won't that amount to the same thing?” “Oh my! The proprietress!” A’zhu tossed her braid and laughed. “An auntie and a proprietress! I shall have to make myself very agreeable to you from now on!” Her laughter was rather exuberant and brought her father to see what was happening. As he peered in, Hu noticed him and beckoned. “Come in, Old Zhang! There's something I want to discuss with you.” An honest, simple man, Old Zhang was quite constrained in Hu's presence. He perched sideways on the edge of a chair, listening for instructions like a subordinate before his superior. Seeing this, Hu thought a solemn business discussion would be unsuitable and asked A’zhu to explain.

“Mr Hu wants to make you a proprietor!” A’zhu began, in the tone of someone who had no personal interest in the matter. Then she carefully explained his proposal. Old Zhang had never dreamed that obeying his wife's instruction to visit Xinhe and inquire for Hu's address would lead to such good fortune. Yet he had doubts. It was all too sudden and might not be as favourable as A’zhu made it sound. He therefore answered cautiously. “Thank you, Mr Hu,” he said slowly. “It sounds a good opportunity. I do have one or two friends in silk firms. But I'm afraid I might not manage it properly.” “Who is born knowing everything? Listen, Old Zhang. In business, the first thing is to work together; the second is to get on with people. I imagine you're well liked. As long as you follow my advice, I won't promise anything else, but I'll certainly make your life more comfortable than it is on the boat.” He added, “A man must think about the latter half of his life. Drifting about in a boat for ever is no lasting arrangement.” That sentence immediately touched Old Zhang. His wife and daughter naturally found it even more welcome. “That's sound sense, Mr Hu!” his wife said. “He's nearly fifty. He can't go on bearing hard work for ever. Better make plans while there's time. If we can help you establish this firm, we'll at least have a fixed place to return to, like leaves falling back to their roots.”

“You aren't helping me open a silk firm. I'm helping you open one,” Hu said firmly. “And if you already have friends in the trade, so much the better. First, Old Zhang, how much capital would it take?” “That depends on the size. A shopfront, some fittings, and two or three hundred taels in ready money would let you act as an intermediary for customers. That's a silk firm. Buying silk yourself, holding it in stock, and waiting for customers to come—that's a silk firm too.” “Then a thousand taels would be enough to begin?” “With a thousand taels, you wouldn't count as one of the smaller firms.” “Good!” Hu looked round at the couple and their daughter, finally fixing his gaze on Old Zhang. “I won't call it a gift. I'll lend you a thousand taels. You open the firm, and I'll commission you to buy silk. There'll be no interest on the thousand. Repay me when you've made a profit. How does that sound?”

“How could it be anything but good?” Old Zhang answered. “But, Mr Hu, business can make losses as well as profits. What if I lose the whole capital?” “Really!” His wife was indignant. “You haven't even begun, and already you're saying unlucky things.” “No, Auntie.” Hu approved of Old Zhang's attitude. “That's exactly how one ought to approach business. You won't succeed if you look only ahead, neglect what lies behind, and think of nothing but profit. Here is my advice, Old Zhang: don't sell this boat. Hire it out. If the silk firm fails, you can still live on the rent.” Old Zhang stared without speaking. His attention had wandered. Why had Mr Hu suddenly begun calling his wife “Auntie”?

“Father!” A’zhu nudged him. “He's talking to you! What are you thinking about?” “Oh, yes!” Old Zhang collected himself and recalled what Hu had said. “Mr Hu, surely it's too late for this year.” “Why?” “A silk firm needs a broker's licence. I hear it has to come from the capital. Sending the application and getting it back takes at least three months. By then the silk-buying season will be long past.” “Does buying silk have a season too?” “Naturally!” A’zhu's mother laughed. “You don't even know that, Mr Hu?” “Different trades are worlds apart. I've never handled this business. Though,” he added, “now I remember: bank loans to silk merchants are always made in the fourth and fifth months.” “Exactly. The new silk comes on the market then, and everyone wants to sell quickly. First, the lean fifth and sixth months fall between harvests, and people in the countryside are waiting for money. Second, if snow-white silk lies at home until it yellows, its price falls. Some people hold on for a better price, but even they wait only another month or so. Most silk firms do their year's business in a single season.”

This made Hu hesitate, for he had a plan of his own. Once Wang arrived in Huzhou, Fukang would naturally handle the prefectural treasury's receipts and payments, including public funds to be remitted to the provincial capital. Hu intended to use the silver received in Huzhou to buy silk there, ship it to Hangzhou, sell it for cash, and pay the money into the provincial treasury. It was business requiring no capital of his own. Outsiders must not see how this conjuring trick worked; that was why he was willing to help Old Zhang open a silk firm. Now, if the firm could not be established immediately, his plan to buy silk and ship it to Hangzhou would fail.

“What about this?” he asked Old Zhang. “We take over someone else's licence, or rent one. Would that work?” “I've heard of it being done. But I don't know what it would cost. Perhaps three or five hundred taels just for a year!” “Then let it be three or five hundred,” Hu said. “You can't make big money without spending a little. Go to Huzhou tomorrow and arrange it!” Why such haste to act the instant an idea occurred? Nothing was clear yet. How were they to begin once they reached Huzhou? Old Zhang, his wife, and his daughter all found themselves at a loss. Again it was A’zhu's mother who produced an idea. “Mr Hu, why don't you accompany Mr Wang when he takes up his post? We could row straight to Huzhou and deal with things there. With you on the spot to decide everything, it would all go smoothly.” “It would, but there are two difficulties. First, everyone knows how close Mr Wang and I are. I must avoid appearances that might excite suspicion, so I shouldn't accompany him to his appointment. Second, I have a bank about to open. I really can't get away.” “Oh, you have a bank as well?” “Yes,” Hu said. “I represent it publicly. There are major shareholders behind me.”

A’zhu's mother regarded him with still greater respect. She glanced at her husband, then turned back to Hu. “Then the journey to Linping...” “That stands as arranged,” he quickly assured her. “Tomorrow I'll have a banknote made out for a thousand taels, and Old Zhang can take it to Huzhou. He can find a licence and look for premises at the same time, getting the shop set up first. I should come to buy silk around the middle of the month. I suppose the boat can manage without Old Zhang?” “Of course it can,” she replied. “If we're short of hands, we can hire someone temporarily.” By now there was little room for objections. Old Zhang had spent decades rowing a boat. Suddenly to leave it, go ashore, and set out alone for Huzhou with a thousand taels to open a silk firm naturally frightened him. But under the encouragement and urging of Hu, his wife, and his daughter, he at last gained confidence. On arriving, he would first consult a few friends in the trade. After all, he had spent decades travelling the waterways. Even if he could not recognise every danger at a glance, he could judge whether a person's character was good or bad. As long as he held firm to that judgement, he should not be taken advantage of.

They talked in high spirits until late at night. A’zhu's mother prepared a late supper for Hu, and after he had eaten, A’zhu made up his bed herself. They wished one another a good night's rest and went to their separate berths. She had much she wanted to say to him, but being alone with a man in the middle of the night seemed to her a shocking impropriety. Reluctantly, she returned to her own bed. Of the five people aboard that night, only A’si had nothing on his mind. The other four were all thinking about the silk firm, and all connected it in their thoughts with A’zhu. Yet each saw it differently.

Her mother was the happiest. Two knots of worry had been undone at once. First, Old Zhang was nearly fifty. In such ballad books as Flowers Raining from Heaven and Destined to Meet Again, an official “approaching half a century” would “retire to his native place,” buy fields and land, and enjoy a comfortable old age as a country gentleman. Yet her husband was still rowing a boat! Now at last they could return to their roots and have a home in which to grow old and die. Her second worry concerned A’zhu. She was entirely willing for her daughter to marry Hu, but feared that as a concubine she would suffer. Mrs Hu seemed kind, yet there was only one husband. When he lavished affection on one woman, the other would be left lonely. Over time, resentment was inevitable. If A’zhu stayed in Huzhou, however, she would be free of the senior wife's temper, and her mother would be there to look after her. Could any arrangement be better? The thought left her perfectly content.

A’zhu imagined an even happier prospect. If she entered the Hu household, domestic quarrels would be the lesser concern. The very word “concubine” meant accepting an inferior position. How devoted and thoughtful he was to have found a way of giving each of his two households a wife of equal standing! He had not said so yet, but someone so considerate must have that in mind. First he would raise her father's status, making him a proprietor fit to become his father-in-law. Then she would be married openly and properly, with a matchmaker, a phoenix crown, and a ceremonial cape. She would ride in a bridal chair and perform the wedding bows like any other bride. People would call her “Mrs Hu.” No one would know she was only “the Mrs Hu in Huzhou”!

While she indulged these hopes, Hu too congratulated himself on his cleverness. Helping Old Zhang establish the firm was certainly intended, in part, to provide an arrangement for A’zhu. He believed in physiognomy and fortune-telling, though only halfway: half was destiny, half human action, and determined human effort could overcome fate. It was true that one should avoid romantic entanglements when passing from one phase of fortune to another. Yet surely that depended on the form the entanglement took. If he brought A’zhu home and wife and concubine quarrelled every few days, turning the house upside down, how could he concentrate on business? Under the present arrangement, it would be as though he had opened his own silk firm in Huzhou, with A’zhu and her parents doing their utmost to manage it. Naturally he would stay there when he visited. A’zhu would be neither senior wife nor household concubine, but a woman maintained in a separate establishment. They could decide the future as circumstances developed. If the firm prospered, she would have rendered the Hu family a real service. When he brought her home then, his wife would have little ground for objection. His plan seemed to cover every angle and make everything practicable. It was indeed a beautifully calculated piece of wishful thinking.

What he could never have imagined was that Old Zhang's mind had changed. A boatman with little education he might be, but he had self-respect. A’zhu wished to marry Hu and was willing to accept the lesser position; her mother strongly approved. Since mother and daughter were united, he would not oppose them. He had assumed that whether the two women lived together or in separate households, A’zhu would in any case be in Hangzhou. He could carry on his own business, keeping out of what did not concern him, and no one would gossip. Now it was different. Opening a silk firm and becoming a proprietor was certainly a miraculous rise, more than he could have wished for. But people would inevitably ask, “How did Old Zhang the boatman suddenly become a proprietor?” And what followed would be ugly. He could hardly go about explaining to everyone: “A’zhu is becoming Hu's concubine purely because she loves him. The silk firm is for his own business convenience. Even without the marriage, he'd still open it and still ask me to put my name to it and become the proprietor!” Even if he could say all this, others might not believe him. He therefore resolved that opening the silk firm and A’zhu's marriage to Hu must never be mixed together.

“Listen,” Old Zhang said softly, nudging his wife as they lay in their berth. “Have you spoken about A’zhu's future?” “No.” “Then why does he call you ‘Auntie’?” “He's being polite and honouring us.” “It is an honour. But cold rice and cold porridge are easy to swallow; cold, cutting words are not.” “What cutting words?” his wife asked in surprise. “Who's been gossiping?” “No one. It's just something I've been thinking...” “There, that's enough!” she interrupted impatiently. “Don't fail to recognise good fortune when it comes! Think about what matters. Which friends will you look up in Huzhou? Where will you find premises?” Old Zhang's feelings towards his wife were seven parts affection and respect, three parts fear. From her tone, he knew that explaining his thoughts would provoke a serious quarrel that very night. He therefore kept them to himself.

The night passed without incident. Early next morning Hu rose, and A’zhu helped him wash and rinse his mouth. In his haste to go ashore on business, he could not even stay for breakfast. Before leaving, he arranged to meet them at midday at a tavern called Chunhao, near Yan Bridge, and said that A’zhu and her mother might come along for an outing if they liked. Naturally, both were delighted. Yan Bridge Street had plenty of cloth shops and shops selling second-hand clothes. A’zhu consulted her mother. “Father's going to be a proprietor. He can't go on wearing a boatman's short jacket. Let's buy him a long gown at a second-hand shop first, then get some cloth and make him more clothes ourselves.” “Good!” her mother agreed happily. “Let's go early!” While they cheerfully dressed their hair and prepared to go out, Old Zhang sat alone in the bow, sunk in gloom. When they met at noon, Hu would surely hand him the money. Once he accepted it, anything he might say afterwards would come too late and look bad. He must speak first—or decline to take the money today and wait until everything had been settled. He wanted to discuss it with his wife, but with A’zhu there he could not open his mouth. While he hesitated helplessly, mother and daughter finished making themselves immaculate, put on their visiting clothes, and stood ready to leave.

“Time to go!” his wife urged. A’zhu, too, found fault with her father's rustic appearance. “Father, will you change that little blue cotton jacket? You look such a bumpkin! You'll disgrace us completely.” Old Zhang spoiled his daughter and generally let her impudent remarks pass as if he had not heard them. Still, even if he ignored her words, he ought to have done something. Instead he stared at the two of them as though his soul had left his body, remaining silent for a long time. “Why!” his wife exclaimed in astonishment. “What's the matter?” He shook his head, then said, “You two go. I'm staying here.” “Why ever not?” After a moment's thought, he answered, “I have to help A’si take the boat back to Wan'an Bridge.” It was no excuse at all. The expressions on mother and daughter changed as quickly as the uncertain weather outside. “What strange notions have you got into your head now?” His wife's face lost every trace of a smile, and her eyes reddened. “You were born to toil! You haven't enjoyed a single comfortable day yet, and already you're making trouble for yourself!” The Hangzhou expression she used normally described a tiresome child who was dissatisfied whichever way things went. Applied to Old Zhang, it carried the sharper implication that he was bringing his own ruin upon himself. Her words were harsh and her resentment deep. He had to make his position somewhat clearer.

“Don't think of nobody but yourself,” he said. “A thousand taels of good silver is no trifling sum. What happens if we lose it all?” “You! You'd fear a falling leaf might split your head! You haven't begun trading, and all you can talk about is losses. If that's the way you look at it, you might as well spend your whole life rowing. Row till you're seventy or eighty, and when you draw your last breath we needn't even buy a coffin. Just push you into the river and let the fish have you!” Whenever her parents quarrelled, A’zhu sided with her father at the critical moment. Now she protested, “Mother! Why say such things? If Father doesn't want to go, let him stay.” “Very well!” Her mother was truly angry. “Some head of the family he is! We give him his due and he won't accept it. Let him please himself. We're going!” This angry declaration troubled A’zhu in turn. After thinking for a moment, she could only ask, “How are we to get there? It's such a long walk.” Besides the distance, the country paths were deep in mud. Even if they managed to walk into town, their shoes and stockings would be a sorry sight. This did not defeat her mother, however. “A’si! A’si!” she shouted. “A’si's gone to Wan'an Bridge,” Old Zhang answered. Fortunately, this reply prevented a complete deadlock. His wife's anger subsided a little, though her voice remained loud. “We'll have this out today. Just what do you mean?”

“We'll talk about it later,” Old Zhang replied, with a glance at A’zhu. Both women now understood. A’zhu felt embarrassed, annoyed, and, above all, anxious. Judging by her father's expression, their plans might fall through. “A’zhu! Go and look at the tendons stewing on the stove. They may need more water.” Having sent her daughter away on this pretext, his wife drew close to him for a private conversation. His very first question was, “Tell me this: what exactly does that fellow Hu intend to do about A’zhu?” “Why ask me? Can't you see for yourself?” “Of course I can. Or I could yesterday. Today I'm not so sure.” “What do you mean by that?” He considered, then asked, “Does he want to trade in silk, does he want our A’zhu, or does he want both?” “Both, naturally.” “He may want both, but I'll agree to only one. If he wants our A’zhu, let him find someone else to run his silk firm. If he wants me to work for him and act as its proprietor, there can be no question of his marrying her.” “Why?” she demanded, her eyes widening. “Give me one good reason.” His reason was that he would not let people laugh at him for becoming a proprietor through his daughter's skirts. “In a word,” he said earnestly, “poor I may be, but I won't have a name for selling my daughter!” Every person had a reputation to protect, just as every tree had its bark. His wife could not say he had no grounds for his objection. But since they could not have everything, she could only urge him to swallow his pride a little.

“Don't be so stubborn. Everyone has enough to do sweeping the snow from his own doorstep. Nobody will meddle in our affairs.” “Nobody?” Old Zhang shook his head vigorously. “You're a woman. You seldom visit teahouses or taverns, so you don't hear what people say. I have to go about outside. How am I to live with people pointing at me behind my back? Enough, enough!” The more he thought about it, the more intolerable it seemed. He raised his voice. “I've made up my mind. If you absolutely refuse to listen, I have a way of dealing with it.” “What way?” she asked uneasily. “You run the silk firm. Call yourself the proprietor or the proprietor's wife, as you please. I shan't interfere. I'll go back to my old trade, working each day for my daily bread. Whenever business takes me to Huzhou, I'll come and see you and our daughter.”

He spoke of this fantastic scheme so seriously that she could not help laughing. “So you'll be coming as a visitor?” she asked deliberately. “Yes. As a visitor.” “In that case, you've no conscience: you're casting me off?” She was half joking, but the accusation struck him like a slap across the face. His cheeks burned as he protested, “How can you say I've no conscience? You mustn't accuse me unjustly!” “I'm not accusing you unjustly. If you have a conscience, can't you put up with a little humiliation for my sake?” He fell silent. She could see that, if she insisted, she could have her way. But he would submit without agreeing in his heart, and they were husband and wife, after all. Why make him suffer? Better to persuade him to accept willingly. Only then would the matter sit comfortably with them both.

As she thought it over, she reached the same conclusion as her daughter. “Would this do?” she asked. “All you're afraid of is gossip behind your back. Suppose he gives a proper wedding feast in Huzhou, observes the ceremonies, and establishes her as his wife there. Surely there could be no objection then?” Since his wife had yielded a little, he must do the same. He nodded. “That would be more like it.” “Good. I'll find a way. Peel a radish a piece at a time as you eat it; let's deal with what's urgent first. Change your clothes so that we can go.” Old Zhang changed into a short outfit he kept for visits: black shoes, white stockings, trousers tied at the ankles, and a lined jacket of fine woollen cloth. Just then A’si returned in a small boat with the provisions he had bought. Leaving him to watch the larger vessel, Old Zhang rowed his wife and daughter to Yan Bridge himself. They landed and climbed from the waterside to the crowded street.

Families who lived on the water seldom visited this busy thoroughfare, where shoulders brushed and carriage wheels almost touched. A’zhu was dazzled by everything around her. Looking up without watching her feet, she stumbled on an uneven stretch and stepped on a loose stone slab. Mud splashed up and stained the new mauve pleated skirt she was wearing. Her involuntary cry made the passers-by turn to look. “Careful, careful! Watch where you're going!” A sleek-haired loafer in his twenties pretended to help her, taking the opportunity to pinch her arm. Her face flamed. She flung her arm away so violently that the back of her hand caught his face with a resounding slap. “Oh! What a fierce one!” Some bystanders exclaimed in surprise; others laughed. This made it still harder for the man to save face. Clutching his cheek, he stamped and cursed. A’zhu and her mother turned pale. Seeing trouble, Old Zhang hurried forward, smiling apologetically. “I'm sorry, I'm sorry! It was an accident!”

In Hangzhou a slap on the face was considered a terrible disgrace, and to be struck by a woman was thought particularly unlucky. The sleek-haired fellow was also one of the petty street ruffians known locally as liaoguier, which made matters worse. Five or six companions immediately surrounded them. One seized Old Zhang's clothing at the chest, showering him with abuse, and raised his fist. “Don't hit him! Don't hit him! We can talk this over!” A’zhu's mother cried. “Talk to your bloody mother—” A fist shot out. Old Zhang caught it. A kick followed, and he dodged. He had trained in boxing for several months, practised with a weighted carrying pole, and tossed stone exercise weights. His arms had the strength to lift a hundred or two hundred jin, and he could have dealt with these five or six men. But he felt that his side was in the wrong, and his honest, peaceable nature made him unwilling to fight. He merely ducked and pleaded. In the scuffle he took two blows, while others used the confusion to crowd against A’zhu and molest her. She was on the verge of tears when a rescuer appeared.

“Third Monk! What's going on?” The fact that the newcomer knew a name made all the difference: the man immediately relaxed his grip. A’zhu's mother felt as though she had been reprieved. She hurried forward. “Mr Zhang! Mr Zhang! Please say a word for us! There was nothing to begin with—” “Nothing?” The man who had been slapped also rushed to present his complaint, pointing at A’zhu. “Mr Zhang, you judge for yourself! I thought she was about to fall and kindly tried to help her. Who'd have expected her to slap me across the mouth? With the Dragon Boat Festival so close, isn't that a fine piece of bad luck?” Fat Zhang understood perfectly: the fellow had been pestering the girl and had brought it on himself. He was rather amused, however, and deliberately asked, “A’zhu, why did you hit him?” Hearing him address her by name, the man holding Old Zhang realised that they knew one another and instinctively let go. A’zhu, blushing scarlet with embarrassment, felt safe at last. Sure of her ground, she straightened up. “I didn't mean to hit him. It was his own fault.” “All right, all right!” her mother hastily intervened. “You needn't say any more.” “Let it pass for my sake. She's my niece,” Zhang told the injured party. “I'll buy you all a drink later.” A quarrel that had seemed impossible to resolve was settled in a few words. Old Zhang and his wife thanked him again and again. A’zhu stood silent beside them, unable to define her own feelings: she seemed both disappointed and reassured. “This is no place to talk,” Fat Zhang said. “Aren't you meeting at Chunhao? Look, there it is.”

Chunhao was famous for its Shaoxing spirits. Its shopfront was two bays wide, half the space taken up by a high, L-shaped counter. On this stood large porcelain dishes more than a foot across, holding a dozen or so foods to accompany a drink, from humble sprouted beans to fresh seafood in season. A number of customers were already drinking at the counter. The market stallholders and the porters from the Yan Bridge waterfront had finished their morning's work and come to enjoy themselves: a bowl of spirits, a small dish, a brief rest leaning against the counter, and away again. Several knew Old Zhang. Seeing him neatly dressed with his wife and daughter, they naturally had questions to ask. By the time he had dealt with them, Fat Zhang and the two ladies were seated inside. This inner room had more comfortable seating. Only two sides of their square table were occupied, A’zhu and her mother sharing a bench. Old Zhang took a third side, leaving the place of honour for Hu. “What a lucky encounter!” Fat Zhang said. “Xueyan asked me to meet him here too. He came to the bank first thing this morning. He's gone back to the bureau on business and will be here shortly. Let's eat while we wait.” They ordered food and wine and talked over their drinks. Respectable women seldom entered taverns, and A’zhu was striking enough to attract still more attention. People kept craning their necks from both inside and outside. She felt awkward and a little pleased, but all she really wanted was for Hu to arrive.

At last he did. As soon as he sat down, Fat Zhang related the entertaining story of her accidental blow to the street ruffian, plainly proud of having settled the dispute. “A’zhu!” Hu laughed when he had heard it. “We never knew you were such a terror.” Feeling that he was calling her a tigress, she flushed and protested, “He did it on purpose. What business had he putting his hands on me in the street? I panicked and flung my arm away, and it caught his face. What has that to do with being a terror? If I were such a terror, nobody would bully me!” Hu merely smiled. From the way she spoke to him, Fat Zhang saw that they had reached a stage where ceremony was unnecessary and nothing need go unsaid. A joke would do no harm.

“Old Zhang,” he began, looking at A’zhu and her mother, “when are you inviting me to the wedding feast?” Old Zhang had no answer. A’zhu lowered her head in embarrassment, but her mother had been hoping to ask Fat Zhang for help and answered with a broad smile, “That depends on you, Mr Zhang!” “Why! What have I to do with it?” She checked the words on her lips and said instead, “Where do you live, Mr Zhang? I'd like to prepare a couple of dishes for you and Mrs Zhang.” Hu alone understood that she meant to ask Fat Zhang to act as matchmaker. It would be a good thing to discuss the matter through someone they knew, he thought, and prompted him: “Perhaps she has something to ask of you.” “Oh! Oh!” Understanding at last, Fat Zhang replied, “I live right at the end of Stone Pagoda Street. When you can't go any farther, turn into Sairan Lane. It's the second house from the end, facing south.” Rattled off in a single breath, the address sounded so like a tongue-twister that A’zhu burst out laughing.

He teased her a little more, stopped before the jokes went too far, and then changed the subject. Looking at Hu, he said, “Let's get down to our business.” That word “our” showed that he, too, had a share in the Huzhou silk venture. Hu had already settled matters with him. For the present, Hengli Bank, Xinhe's affiliated establishment in Huzhou, would lend the money to buy silk. Besides paying interest at the prevailing market rate, Hu had promised Fat Zhang personally twenty per cent of the eventual profits. He offered such generous terms partly to make financing easy, partly because he feared he could not supervise everything himself and hoped Zhang would share the burden, and partly out of friendship. Xinhe Bank had gained the Sea Transport Bureau's business, but Fat Zhang had made nothing personally from it. Hu was using this opportunity to give him a chance to earn something.

“Old Zhang! There are two things I want to settle with you today. First, here are the thousand taels. Keep them safe.” Hu produced a bundle wrapped in a towel and opened it. Inside were two banknotes for five hundred taels each. “Mr Zhang's bank issued these. Hengli in Huzhou will honour them.” “Hengli is in front of the City God Temple,” Fat Zhang added. “Open a passbook account there, Old Zhang. You can withdraw whatever you need as you need it. Very convenient.” “Yes,” Old Zhang answered with difficulty. “Second, Mr Zhang has recommended someone to help you—” “Oh!” Old Zhang interrupted gladly. “That's excellent! I was afraid I'd be like a crab without legs, unable to manage on my own.”

“But there's one thing you must understand clearly.” Hu glanced at Fat Zhang and spoke with great seriousness. “It's your silk firm, and you must make the decisions. The person recommended to you will be your employee. He takes his orders from you, not the other way round. I want to make that clear today in Mr Zhang's presence.” “Quite right, quite right,” Fat Zhang agreed. “The young fellow's surname is Li. He's a younger relative of mine, quite capable, and he understands the silk trade. But he's young and fond of amusement. I'll rely on you to keep him in order.” Old Zhang considered what both men had said, then nodded. “Business is business, friendship is friendship. I understand.” “Exactly!” Hu said, greatly pleased. “If you can say that, Old Zhang, you're bound to do well. Go ahead with confidence! And one more thing: as soon as you reach Huzhou, find an experienced man with a good eye whom you can trust. Don't begrudge him a generous salary. You get what you pay for, and that's as true of hiring people as of anything else.” Encouraged, Old Zhang nodded repeatedly, understanding much that had been unclear. “When shall we meet this Mr Li?” he asked. “Come to the bank after we've eaten,” Fat Zhang answered. “I'll send for him to meet you.”

With so much serious business to attend to, they brought the meal to a hurried end. Outside Chunhao the party divided. Fat Zhang took Old Zhang to Xinhe, while A’zhu and her mother went to a second-hand clothes shop to equip him for his new role. That left Hu. A’zhu had assumed that he would go to the bank too, but to her surprise he preferred to accompany the women. Nothing could have pleased her more. Yet she would not walk beside him in the street. Taking her mother's arm, she deliberately lagged well behind. Hu, intent on pleasing her, stopped outside a large cloth shop to wait for them. “I know this place well. I guarantee you won't be cheated. Choose whatever cloth you want. You don't often come shopping, so don't stint yourselves.” The more he urged them, the less willing they were to put him to expense. They selected only a few modest additions and would have stopped there. Hu wanted them to buy more. “Auntie, this is a lovely piece,” he kept saying. “That colour would suit A’zhu.” But neither would agree. Rather than say plainly that she could not bear to let him spend so much, A’zhu found fault with every fabric: the colour was wrong, the pattern old-fashioned, the width too narrow, or it would shrink in water. Her baseless accusations, made against her own better judgement, left the shop assistant speechless with anger.

The second-hand clothes shop was next door. When it came to buying Old Zhang's clothes, Hu firmly took charge. “You must leave this to me,” he said. “Business isn't what it used to be. A man's appearance has to look thoroughly respectable. You've seen Shanghai's miles of foreign settlement. Wherever men come out from, don't they all look trim and smart? A Buddha needs gilding, and a man needs clothes. Watch me dress Old Zhang: I guarantee he'll look like a great merchant.” A’zhu smiled at his persuasive speech, then nudged her mother and whispered, “You'll have to dress up too. Otherwise you won't look like a proprietor's wife!” A proprietor's wife—she really was going to become one! Only yesterday it had been so much talk, with no certainty of what would happen. Now it was solid fact beyond doubt. Whatever else might be uncertain, those thousand taels were certainly real. Her thoughts wandered far ahead. Absorbed in imagining how she would conduct herself and what it would feel like, she forgot where she was.

By the time she came to herself, Hu had chosen a great pile of clothes for Old Zhang: long gowns, short outer jackets, padded garments, and lined ones. He even wanted to buy a dark lambskin robe, but she stopped him. “When we've made some money, we'll have a new one made.” The bill came to more than twenty taels. Hu pulled out a large handful of banknotes, selected one for thirty taels, and paid. When the change came, he took A’zhu's handkerchief bundle and wrapped the money inside it. “What's this for?” she asked, though she knew perfectly well. “There's a branch of Dai Chunlin across the street. I know nothing about rouge and powder. You'll have to choose those yourself.” She did choose a great many things, spending freely and buying only the best. Besides local products such as egg-shaped powder cakes, she bought liquid face powder, scented toilet water, and foreign soap brought from Shanghai. She would use them to dress herself up and earn a word of praise from Hu.

The day after Old Zhang left for Huzhou, A’zhu's mother prepared several exquisite dishes, rose early, and hired a small sedan chair to take her to Fat Zhang's house on Stone Pagoda Street. After the customary greetings to Mrs Zhang, conversation soon turned from the four dishes she had brought to the purpose of her visit. Mrs Zhang protested at the trouble she had taken, but her husband laughed. “Thirteen and a half chickens! I've a good deal of eating ahead of me yet.” It was said that a matchmaker had to go between the two families at least thirteen times, from the first exchange of names to the completion of the six marriage rites. At every visit, the host would kill a chicken for the guest. There was another chicken on the wedding day, but with the bride due to enter her sedan chair, there was no time to linger over it: at most, half could be eaten. The total was thirteen and a half. Originally a facetious remark, the phrase had gradually become a synonym for matchmaking. Mrs Zhang immediately took an interest. “Does our visitor represent the bride or the groom?” she asked.

“The bride.” “Oh, congratulations, congratulations!” She smiled at her guest, then asked her husband, “And who is the groom?” “Guess! You know him very well.” She began with the capable, unmarried employees at Xinhe and went on to the young sons of their close friends and relations. She offered seven or eight names, and seven or eight times Fat Zhang shook his head. “Enough, enough! You could guess till dawn tomorrow and never get it.” He steered her towards the inner rooms. “Never mind the talk. Off to the kitchen with you. With such good food today, I'll have an early lunch at home before going to the bank. I'll tell you later.” As he ushered her away, he gave her a meaningful glance, telling her not to come out again.

This was where Fat Zhang's experience and tact showed. First, the outcome of the proposed match between Hu and A’zhu remained uncertain, and he did not know whether Hu intended to keep it from his family. For the moment, secrecy was necessary. His wife had lately been visiting the Hu household often. An inadvertent word might damage his friendship with Hu, now his closest and most important friend, whom he could not afford to lose. Second, he was thinking of A’zhu's mother. Giving one's daughter to a man as a concubine was hardly a glorious subject, and he feared she might find it difficult to discuss before someone she had only just met. She naturally understood this consideration and felt all the more certain that she had chosen the right man: he was thoughtful and experienced.

“Mr Zhang,” she said, “you know why I've come. Whether this marriage can be arranged depends entirely on your kindness.” “There's no need to say that,” he answered earnestly. “Xueyan is a good friend of mine. Even if neither family asked me, I'd still want to help arrange the wedding.” “Oh!” she asked eagerly. “Has Mr Hu asked you too? What did he say?” “He hasn't asked me. By ‘neither family’ I meant either side, the bride's or the groom's. Isn't it all the same?” “No, no.” She shook her head. “Mr Hu is your good friend, certainly. But I'm the one who has come to ask you today. If you agree, you're the matchmaker for our side and ought to speak up for A’zhu. Don't you think so?” Fat Zhang laughed. “My good sister, I take my hat off to you. Your scholarly upbringing shows: the moment you speak, you go straight to the heart of the matter. Very well, tell me what you want. I'll do all I can.”

“Thank you, my honoured matchmaker!” She paused to think. “I won't be afraid of your laughing at me. To tell the truth, our A’zhu has set her whole heart on Mr Hu. It's entirely a matter of affection, with no thought of wealth or position.” “I know that.” “Let affection bring the families together. There's no need to discuss betrothal gifts or a dowry. Mr Hu seems fond of our A’zhu too. Surely he wouldn't wish to slight her.” Fat Zhang began to feel uneasy. If she sought neither future wealth nor immediate marriage gifts, what exactly did she mean by not slighting A’zhu? “I'll speak plainly. As to her standing in the family... I want you to press her claim, Mr Zhang.” How was he to do that? Surely Hu could not be expected to marry again as though he had no wife! Suddenly he understood. “Do you mean... two wives of equal standing?” “Mr Zhang, do you think that arrangement could be made?” she asked in return. Unwilling to give a definite answer, he smiled. “If it were up to me, of course it could.”

This implied that, with Hu, it might be difficult. Naturally she asked why. He could offer no reason: he was merely afraid the match might fail and was leaving himself room to retreat. In truth, he knew too little about Hu's household to foresee the obstacles. Nevertheless, he promised to do his utmost and, whatever happened, to obtain a definite answer as soon as possible. He also urged patience. Matters settled better when allowed time; haste could create unexpected difficulties. A girl like A’zhu, he said, was like a rare article whose owner could afford to wait. Best to make Hu feel he could not bear to lose her, until he proposed of his own accord. Then everything would be easier. Her initial disappointment faded as she heard these final words. They made excellent sense. A’zhu must not be too accommodating to Hu. In such matters it was just like business: indulge a customer too much and he began to suspect that the goods were inferior. She took the lesson deeply to heart, though she still pressed Zhang to help. The sooner things were settled, the sooner she would have one less worry.

As soon as Fat Zhang reached the bank, he sent a young apprentice to the Hu house with an invitation to dine at Xinhe that evening. There was something important to discuss, and Hu must please come, however late. Towards dusk Zhang had food and wine prepared and waited especially for him. Hu did not arrive until about eight, apologising repeatedly and explaining that there had been a great deal of official business at Wang's office. “This isn't my affair; it's yours. And it's a matter that will be all the pleasanter discussed over a drink.” Zhang courteously showed him to his seat and instructed the bank's employees not to come in unless called. Then, cup in hand, he took up his duties as matchmaker and related A’zhu's mother's request in full.

“Of course the matter must be dealt with,” Hu said. “I hadn't expected her to be in such a hurry.” “I advised her against hurrying too.” Suddenly Zhang gave a knowing smile, leaned closer, and lowered his voice. “Xueyan, let me ask you something. Have you and A’zhu been intimate?” “Nothing of the kind. Nothing has happened.” “Then why is her mother so anxious?” Zhang looked relieved on his behalf. “I thought the rice was already cooked and they meant to make you eat it!” “I could eat it if I had to. But just now I don't want to, and I really haven't the time. My business is only getting started. Even devoting all my energy to it scarcely seems enough. Where am I to find the leisure for romance?” Fat Zhang understood. Hu was willing to amuse himself as occasion offered, but the time had not come to establish another household and take on another burden. Their fortunes were linked, so Zhang naturally preferred him to concentrate on business. Forgetting the bride's mother's solemn commission, he now took Hu's side instead.

“Then tell me what you want to do. I'll help you manage it.” Hu hesitated. A’zhu's every smile and frown came into his mind, and he could not bear to disappoint her. “In my view, there's only one thing to do: delay,” Zhang advised. “Dragging it out solves nothing,” Hu objected. “We must make things clear.” “How?” Hu hesitated again. “I'm afraid someone will be hurt if I say what I think.” He meant A’zhu, of course. “Tell me first,” Zhang said. “Standing outside the situation, I can see it more clearly.” “I think business is business and affection is affection. The two shouldn't be mixed.” “Exactly!” Fat Zhang applauded. “What a clear head you have! But let me ask you this: if you aren't opening the Huzhou silk firm to provide for A’zhu, why choose Old Zhang? He knows nothing of the trade.” “He may not know the trade, but he's honest and hardworking. That's enough. Were you and I born knowing how to turn somersaults through the hole in a copper coin?”

“True enough. But now affection has got mixed up in it, and that makes things difficult.” “Difficult, perhaps, but affection is still a good thing. It's because of that bond that Old Zhang and his wife will give their whole hearts to the business.” “And now we've come round in a circle,” Zhang laughed. “What we're discussing is how to preserve that affection without letting it distract you.” “Precisely. That's why we mustn't let it drag on. With nothing settled, how can Old Zhang and his wife concentrate on business? And if it drags on long enough, affection will turn to resentment, and we'll surely fall out. What would be the point?” Fat Zhang reflected that, whichever way the argument turned, Hu had an answer. He considered himself clear-headed and no poor speaker, yet he could not get the better of him. He might as well let Hu decide what he wanted and then do as he was told.

Seeing Zhang silently occupied with his cup and chopsticks, Hu asked, “Mr Zhang, do you feel that if the match doesn't come off, you won't know how to face A’zhu's mother?” “Not exactly,” Zhang replied. “But it would be a happy thing if it could be arranged.” “It certainly can be arranged. But the matchmaker eats thirteen and a half chickens; nobody settles everything on the first visit.” Hu smiled. “A’zhu's mother is a wonderful cook. Get it all settled at once, and you won't have any more of her good dishes.” Zhang laughed too, feeling that Hu's remark contained something worth considering. “Then what if I put it this way?” he asked. “I'll tell her mother that, since the two wives are to have equal standing, nothing can be done carelessly. First we'll compare the birth horoscopes for any clash. Then we'll explain matters to your mother, and your first wife must be consulted too. Once those two obstacles are past, we can choose a date. All that will take a year or so. It still comes back to what I said: delay.” “This delay is different from yours. Yours offers no definite word and leaves everyone uncertain. Mine follows the formalities, which necessarily take time. Even if it fails later—because the birth horoscopes clash, for instance—that will be fate, and nobody will have grounds for complaint.” Zhang thought about it and saw the distinction. “Xueyan!” He raised his cup in a toast. “Whatever you undertake, you always think first of a way to retreat. That's what I admire most about you. It's why people feel secure and are willing to join you in business.”

Hu smiled without answering, asking only, “When will you take your answer back to the bride's family?” “I'll see whether she comes tomorrow. If she doesn't, it won't matter. I'm bound to see her the day after.” That was the day Wang would leave to take up his new post. Hu and Fat Zhang were to accompany him as far as Linping aboard the Zhang family's boat. A’zhu's mother had to prepare an excellent banquet and could not spare a moment. Anxious though she was for news, she could only do as Fat Zhang had planned and wait until they came aboard.

On the appointed day, Wang boarded his vessel at the wharf by the salt administration, while Hu and Zhang embarked at Wan'an Bridge. They were to meet outside the Beixin customs barrier by Gongchen Bridge. As the two men stepped aboard, A’zhu, beautifully dressed and radiant, welcomed them into the cabin with a smile. Both noticed her expression. There was no embarrassment or awkwardness, so they knew she had heard nothing of her mother's marriage negotiations. Hu immediately signalled to Zhang not to mention them. “Mr Hu, Mr Zhang!” A’zhu's mother came out to greet them. “Please make yourselves comfortable. You'll excuse me if I can't sit with you.” The greeting was merely a pretext for studying their faces, but both men were too practised to reveal anything. Fat Zhang simply said, “Attend to whatever you must. We'll talk when you have a moment to spare.” Reassured by this, she went back to the stern to prepare the feast, and the boat cast off and headed north. When Hu and A’zhu were absorbed in laughing and talking, Fat Zhang slipped aft on the pretext of seeing what dishes were being prepared.

“My good sister, congratulations!” he said softly, clasping his hands. That single sentence made her beam. She could only repeat her thanks, unable to think of anything else to say. “Everything will be as you wish,” he continued. “But this isn't simply taking a concubine. It must be done properly, step by step. Even if you were willing to dispense with formalities, I, as matchmaker, would not. Isn't that right?” “Yes, absolutely. Tell me what to do, Mr Zhang.” “First, then, I'll need her birth particulars. How old is A’zhu this year?” “She was born in the eighteenth year of Daoguang, the wuxu year. She's sixteen this year.” “So she was born in the Year of the Dog. Xueyan was born in the Year of the Sheep. Sheep and Dog can get along; there's no clash there. What month is her birthday?”

This reference to a clash alerted her. Naturally, the matchmaker would take A’zhu's birth particulars to a fortune-teller to compare with Hu's. If anything proved incompatible, Hu himself might not care, but with an elderly mother still living he could not disregard it. Better to find out Hu's birth particulars first and have someone examine them privately. If anything failed to agree, she could alter A’zhu's birth month, day, or hour to make the two horoscopes compatible. Having decided this, she would reveal nothing further yet. “We'll certainly do that, Mr Zhang,” she said. “When I return to Hangzhou, I'll have the particulars written out and sent to your house.” “Good, good. That's settled.” In those few exchanges, Fat Zhang had satisfactorily discharged the bride's family's commission. He returned to the middle cabin and, out of A’zhu's sight, smiled at Hu to show that everything had gone smoothly.

At the Beixin barrier they waited for Wang's official boat. When it arrived, they obtained clearance and passed through the lock, then invited Wang, Qin Shoumen, and Yang Yongzhi aboard the Zhang family's vessel. As it moved slowly over the still waters of the canal, A’zhu served them and they drank with pleasure. With the two secretaries, Qin and Yang, present, however, they could neither speak their hearts without reserve nor abandon propriety to discuss romantic adventures. The entire meal therefore passed in gentle, agreeable conversation. It lasted from Gongchen Bridge to Linping—from noon until evening. Afterwards they moved to Wang's boat for tea and more talk. At the first night watch, Qin and Yang took leave and returned to their own vessel. Fat Zhang followed them away. Wang detained only Hu for a private farewell.

They had been together for merely a few months, and only two days' journey along a navigable waterway would separate them, yet Wang felt an immense sorrow at parting. Besides affection, he felt something close to the fear of being left alone and helpless. In recent months he had relied on Hu as on his own hands and had grown so accustomed to him that he could scarcely do without him for a day. Yet he knew that he could not ask Hu to abandon his business and become a resident adviser at the yamen, available for consultation whenever anything arose. Even if it were possible, where would that leave Qin and Yang? He had therefore given up that hope. His next best wish was that they should meet often. “Xueyan, when are you coming to Huzhou?” he asked. “Before long.” Hu calculated the days. As soon as Fukang opened, he would go to Huzhou to see how Old Zhang was getting on. “In a fortnight at the earliest; by the end of the month at the latest.”

“That reminds me,” Wang said. “I've been so busy these last two days that I haven't had time to ask you. What's this about your opening a silk firm in Huzhou?” “I meant to discuss it with you when I got there. But I may as well tell you now.” Hu explained the whole story in detail, including the proposed marriage to A’zhu. It was rather complicated, and Wang could not immediately grasp all its threads. Deeply interested, he merely remarked, “You certainly keep things lively.” “Mr Xuexuan, all this activity comes from you.” Hu lowered his voice. “Naturally, there's a share in the silk firm for you.” “No need for that. If word got out, it wouldn't do my reputation any good. There's nothing you and I can't discuss in any case; we needn't talk about these things now. But you must find some way to work on Yang Yongzhi. Otherwise, with his own views, he may make it difficult to arrange the movement of public funds.” “I've already thought of that. But again, I intend to act in your name.” “How?” Wang asked. “I've found out where both Qin's and Yang's families live. I'll send people to look after them, providing gifts when gifts are called for and money when money is called for. Their families will naturally write to Huzhou. When Qin and Yang hear of it, they'll feel grateful to you. Then everything will be easy.”

“Yes, yes!” Wang approved delightedly. “That's the best way. I needn't explain beforehand. When they come to thank me, I'll make sure you get the credit.” Hu smiled and quoted a Hangzhou saying: “We take turns carrying one another's flowered sedan chairs!” “Speaking of which,” Wang said, suddenly smiling mischievously, “when will you put A’zhu in a bridal sedan chair?” “It's too soon to talk of that. We'll take things as they come.” “Does your wife know?” Hu shook his head. “I'd rather she didn't.” “There I disagree,” Wang said. “A man as clever as you should surely know those two sayings: ‘Do not turn out the wife who shared your coarse meals and hardship; do not forget the friends you made in poverty.’ You're not dismissing your wife to marry another, but you ought to discuss the matter with her all the same.” Hu said nothing. He felt that Wang's words had something of an official sermon about them.

CHAPTER EIGHT

Fukang Bank opened for business. Its premises had been handsomely fitted out, and the four clerks behind the counter, all in brand-new gowns of imported blue cotton, greeted everyone with smiles. Liu Qingsheng wore a silk gown and a gauze jacket. His face glowing, he personally attended to customers with tremendous energy. Hu Xueyan received the fellow bankers and guests from official and commercial circles who came to offer their congratulations. Fat Zhang of Xinhe and Sun Deqing of Dayuan were both there. Everyone knew that Hu could get a hearing even with the governor, and might someday be needed to put in a word. Moreover, he was exceptionally well liked. His fellow bankers therefore gave him enthusiastic support, placing several tens of thousands of taels in goodwill deposits. Freshly cast horseshoe ingots and round silver ingots, dazzlingly bright, lay in casual heaps behind the counter, making passers-by stare. A banquet was served at noon, and it was after three before the guests dispersed. Left quietly alone, Hu considered the situation. The first day had gone well, but he must secure a few substantial accounts before the business could really develop. His first step must be to build a name. Once Fukang was well known, business would be brisk.

Suddenly an idea came to him. He sent for Liu. “Make me a list.” He carried a small notebook filled with symbols intelligible only to himself. It contained accounts of his dealings, the names of his acquaintances, and the birthdays of important officials and their mothers, wives, concubines, sons, and daughters. Consulting it, he dictated a series of account names: Fuji, Xiangji, Heji, Shende Hall, and others. When Liu had written them down, he asked, “Are we to open passbooks?” “Exactly. How many are there?” Liu counted them with the shaft of his brush. “Twelve altogether.” “Put twenty taels in each. Two hundred and forty in all. Charge it to my account.”

Only after Liu had completed the arrangements and brought the twelve passbooks did Hu explain the device. The names belonged to members of the governor's and provincial treasurer's households. Once accounts had been opened, deposits provided, and the passbooks presented, business would naturally follow. “The ladies' private savings may not amount to much,” Hu said. “They may scarcely count as business. But once word gets about, people will see Fukang's connections in quite a different light.” “So that's it!” Liu nodded in understanding. “How are we to get these passbooks inside?” “A good question! Tomorrow, take my card to Mr Liu Er at the governor's gate. The Fuji passbook is for him. Ask him to deliver the others. Cultivate him properly. Noon is the best time to go, when he has less to do. You might invite him out to a restaurant and ask him to explain the ways of official life. Our business depends entirely on knowing official circles and keeping well informed.” Liu agreed repeatedly. Hu's decision to let him approach Liu Er was a sign of trust, and he was very pleased.

At noon the following day, Liu went expressly to call on Liu Er, as Hu had directed. Since they shared a surname, he addressed him as “Second Uncle.” The affectionate form of address won Liu Er's goodwill; respect for Hu helped too, and the reception was most courteous. The eloquent young manager delivered a series of compliments and expressions of admiration before turning to business. He produced the Fuji passbook and presented it with both hands. Liu Er opened it, saw the twenty-tael deposit already entered, and asked in surprise, “What does this mean?” “We hope Second Uncle will favour Fukang with his business, so we have paid a little interest in advance.” Liu Er laughed. “Your proprietor's ideas really are like nobody else's!” Then, with a little hesitation, he added, “Now I can hardly avoid doing business with Fukang. Here, someone has just repaid me a sum. I'll deposit it with you.”

He opened the visiting-card box beside him, took out two notes, and handed them to Liu. At first glance they looked unlike the usual notes issued by remittance houses or private banks. Closer inspection confirmed it. They were printed on bark-fibre paper, with the words “Board of Revenue Official Note” in both Manchu and Chinese. The central inscription read, “One Hundred Taels of Full-Fineness Silver, Treasury Standard Weight.” Below came several lines: “These official notes are issued by the Board of Revenue with imperial sanction. For any person wishing to exchange official notes for silver or cash, they shall be treated on the same basis as silver. They may also be tendered as a proportion of payments due to the government, in accordance with regulations laid down by the Board. Counterfeiters shall be punished according to law.” Liu had not even known such official notes existed. “I haven't seen these in circulation,” he said with a smile. “This is an education for me.” “They have only just come into use in the capital,” Liu Er replied. “I hear the provincial treasury has already sent someone there to collect a supply. They'll soon be circulating here.”

One of the notes was for a hundred taels and the other for eighty. Liu entered their receipt in the passbook, although they were not yet in local circulation. He then produced the remaining passbooks and asked Liu Er to deliver them. “That's easily done. Leave them all to me. Now, what else can I do for you?” “You are too kind, Second Uncle. That is all.” “Then I won't keep you. Between ourselves, I have official business to report upstairs. We'll talk another day.” Leaving the governor's office, Liu did not return directly to Fukang. He stopped at Dayuan to see Sun Deqing, producing the two official notes for everyone to inspect and hoping to learn how the affair had come about. “I'd heard a vague report that official notes were to be issued. There seemed to be no further news, and now here they are! The authorities have been quick.” “The need for military funds is urgent. They have to be quick,” said another Dayuan shareholder. “I expect they'll soon be circulating in Zhejiang.” “I wonder how many of these notes they intend to issue. They say anyone wishing to exchange them for silver or cash will be treated as though holding silver, but if there are too many notes and too little actual silver, then...” Sun shook his head and left the rest unsaid.

Liu understood his meaning and became wary. Back at the bank, finding Hu still there, he described his visit to Liu Er and finally mentioned the official notes. Hu examined them carefully. “Business grows harder every day, but the greater the difficulty, the greater the opportunity. Qingsheng, there will be all sorts of possibilities in these notes. Think them through carefully.” “I believe they'll certainly lose their value.” Hu thought this too sweeping. Confidence had to be sustained by everyone. If the notes were not issued excessively, if sound regulations were established and the notes could be used conveniently, then, with support from private banks and remittance houses, they ought to retain a stable value. Otherwise, the abuses that might arise were beyond imagining. What he wanted Liu to think through was the various problems that might develop if confidence in the notes weakened: how to avoid those problems, and even how to profit from them.

“Remember this,” he said. “Everything in the world has two sides. When one side gains, the other loses. That is particularly true of business. Buyer and seller, one taking in and the other paying out, are natural opponents. Sometimes the advantage lies in buying, sometimes in selling. A capable businessman must gain both ways: sell when prices have risen far enough, buy when they have fallen far enough. That is how you gain on both sides.” Liu was intelligent; he merely lacked experience. He understood Hu's guidance and felt he had learned a great deal. But how was one to anticipate the rises and falls? By one's own judgement, of course—but where did that judgement come from? He put the question to Hu, who looked gratified. “An excellent question. However shrewd you are, however perfectly you work your thirteen-column abacus, counting every penny in and out without the slightest error, that isn't the great thing. What matters most is vision. The larger your business, the farther you must look. In a small business, for instance, if hot weather comes early and you think the summer will be long, you stock up on palm-leaf fans ahead of time. That too is vision. But a great business requires a view of the whole situation. If your vision takes in a province, you can do business throughout that province. If it takes in the empire, you can do business throughout the empire. If it takes in foreign countries, you can do business abroad.”

Liu had never heard anything like this. Along with heartfelt admiration, he felt some bewilderment. “Then may I ask, Mr Hu, what is your own view of things at present?” “I look at the whole empire.” Hu usually spoke with easy assurance. Now his expression grew grave, as though he bore a heavy burden on his shoulders. “The Longhairs will achieve nothing lasting. They are bound to be defeated. But it won't happen in two or three years. There is a great deal of fighting still to come. The guiding purpose of my business is to help the imperial armies win.” “Mr Hu,” Liu murmured, frowning slightly, “I still don't quite understand.” “Then I'll put it plainly. I'll undertake any business that helps the imperial armies win, even at a loss. You must understand that it isn't really a loss: it is capital invested. Once the imperial armies win and peace returns, what business won't prosper? By then you will have made a contribution. The government will naturally repay you, and every path will be open to your business. Think of it! How could you fail to rise?” Liu immediately thought of Wang Youling. It was Hu's foresight in investing capital in Wang that had brought him to his present position. With delighted understanding, he said, “I see! I see!”

This understanding changed his view of the official notes. Previously he had assumed that they would depreciate and ought to be avoided as far as possible. Now he believed their first need, on being issued, was help in establishing themselves. As Hu had said, confidence had to be sustained by everyone. Since he had authority to act for Fukang, he resolved then and there to support the notes with all his strength. Two days later, the bankers' guild circulated a notice summoning its members to discuss how the official notes were to be distributed—in practice, how the obligation to take them was to be apportioned. Besides the Board of Revenue silver notes, there were notes denominated in copper cash. The guild's presiding officer for the year brought samples, which passed from hand to hand. Their form resembled that of the silver notes. Across the top stood “Great Qing Treasure Note”; down the centre, “Equivalent to ... Standard Copper Cash.” At the sides were the words, “Currency throughout the realm; equal value in payment and receipt.” The inscription below read, “This note shall circulate in place of standard copper cash. It may also be used, in the prescribed proportions, to pay land and poll taxes, grain levies, and all other taxes and contributions. All treasuries, in the capital and the provinces, shall accept and remit it.” The presiding officer explained, “The authorities have assigned us two hundred thousand taels in silver notes and a hundred thousand strings in cash notes. At the prescribed rate of two thousand cash to one tael, those hundred thousand strings equal fifty thousand taels. The total is therefore two hundred and fifty thousand taels.” He paused. “How should we apportion the distribution among the large and small banks? Let us discuss it together.”

“Since the ministry has issued these notes, the market cannot refuse to use them. But that depends on people trusting them,” said Fat Zhang. “If a customer wants actual silver, a bank cannot insist that he accept paper. I suggest this: let the guild collect the silver and cash notes from the provincial treasury and distribute them fairly among the banks, according to their size. We shall use as many as we can, and settle every ten or fifteen days, paying in actual money for whatever we have put into circulation. The banks will take no profit; we shall perform the service for nothing.” Though the proposal offered no profit, it imposed no risk either, and the bankers promptly voiced their approval. The presiding officer shook his head. “That won't do. The authorities wanted full payment. After lengthy negotiations, they agreed to accept sixty per cent immediately, with the remaining forty per cent paid over two months.” They looked at one another in dismay. Everyone knew that the presiding officer had always defended the trade's interests zealously. If a favourable condition could be obtained, he would fight to the utmost for it. What he could not secure, no one else could. The only question left was how to divide the obligation.

Here, too, opinion split. The larger banks wanted an equitable allocation according to size; the smaller ones wanted the larger houses to subscribe first, so that if the total was covered, nothing need be imposed on them. Argument followed argument, with no resolution. As a newcomer and a junior, Liu had not ventured to speak first. But when all the influential men had spoken without reaching agreement, he felt he should no longer hold back. “I have a view which I should like to submit to my seniors for correction,” he said. “We pay sixty per cent and receive the full value in notes. That amounts to an interest-free government loan of forty per cent. The calculation is not unreasonable. Besides, these notes have only just been issued. We cannot yet know how they will turn out, but we ought to look for a good outcome rather than assume a bad one. Everyone will use them, certainly, but the banks have the closest interest of all. If confidence in the notes fails, we shall be the first to suffer. We must therefore help establish that confidence.” “Well!” Fat Zhang interrupted with his usual frankness. “Who would have expected young Liu to produce such an argument?” “A sound argument!” The presiding officer nodded at Liu with warm approval. “Please continue, my young friend.”

Encouraged, Liu became still more animated. “Fukang has only just opened, and our standing is still modest. But where loyalty to our fellow bankers is concerned, we shall never hold back. Whether the notes are allotted or taken by voluntary subscription, Fukang is willing.” “If we proceed by subscription, how much would Fukang take?” The presiding officer had recognised Liu's attitude and deliberately asked the question, hoping to make him an example. Liu calculated at once. There had been eight large banks; with Fukang there were now nine. The smaller banks still numbered thirty-three. If the two hundred and fifty thousand taels were divided on the basis of one share for a large bank and half a share for a small one, each full share would be approximately ten thousand taels.
