Trusting in the closeness of their friendship, he thought he must explain plainly, or the conversation would go no further. “Mrs Wang, a little over a year ago, before Mr Xuexuan went to the capital, I knew something of your circumstances. It was your management that carried the household through those hard times and allowed his fortune to turn. Naturally, then, you couldn't do without a capable helper like Ruiyun...” “Ah!” She interrupted before he could finish, her face full of uneasy remorse. “You're right, Brother! Thank you for reminding me.” He had made her see the difference between then and now. The masters were enjoying official success and rising rapidly; what of the servants? Ruiyun had helped them endure hardship and deserved some reward. How could Mrs Wang bear to neglect her future and let her youth slip away? She was now not merely uneasy but anxious to find, immediately if possible, a promising husband of suitable age and appearance for Ruiyun.

“Tell me, Brother, whose family is it? What is the man's background? How old is he? If the proposal seems suitable, I want to see him for myself.” Her eager concern showed that her expectations were high. Ji could not take Ruiyun as a formally married successor to his late wife, and he had six children still under age. Mention either fact, and Mrs Wang would shake her head at once. If Hu met a refusal at the outset, recovering the position would be difficult even if possible. His first words must move her and leave no room for rejection. That required a little manoeuvring. However much she cared for Ruiyun, she cared more for her husband. He could begin there. “Mrs Wang, this marriage concerns Mr Xuexuan closely too. If I arrange it, everything will go smoothly. If I fail, trouble may follow.”

As he had expected, her expression changed again. Concern was joined by vigilance. “Brother, if you're arranging it, there's no reason it shouldn't succeed. Whatever you do is sound.” It was an excellent answer. It made Hu feel the weight of responsibility and obliged him to consider Ruiyun's interests. Instead of replying immediately, he reviewed Ji's qualities once more. In that brief silence, Mrs Wang understood. “Is the man you mean Mr Ji?” she asked directly. “It is.” Hu had finished his deliberation. “Let me speak frankly. If Ruiyun hopes to marry an official, she'll have to accept some disadvantages for the first few years. As for Ji himself, you can imagine his qualities. His character and ability are first-rate. He's certain to succeed. If she marries him, she will have good days ahead.” Mrs Wang considered silently, then asked, “How old is he?” “Just over forty. He looks young—only in his thirties—and is full of energy.” “What about his temper?” “Talented men generally have a temper, but they don't vent it at home. A man who's a tiger in his house and a timid cat beside the stove outside it is the most hopeless kind.” “Indeed!” Mrs Wang smiled. “What sort of man can do nothing but beat his wife at home?” Then she added, “That reminds me: why did you say Ruiyun must accept disadvantages for a couple of years? I don't quite understand.”

“I mean she wouldn't have the status of principal wife when she first entered his household. After two or three years, he would naturally elevate her to that position.” Mrs Wang had to consider this, less for the present than for the future. “Brother, you're being frank. But if Mr Ji later marries someone else to replace his wife, wouldn't Ruiyun's hopes come to nothing?” “We can make the condition clear beforehand.” Hu tapped his chest. “If he fails to honour it, come to me, the matchmaker.” “A full bowl is easy to eat; a sweeping promise is hard to keep. I trust you in everything, but on this matter, frankly, I've seen more than you. Many matchmakers labour hard and earn only blame. Otherwise, why would people talk about pounding the matchmaker into paste? Naturally our two families would never behave like that towards each other. If it happened, Ruiyun would simply have to suffer.” “It depends on the man. Ji's word is his bond. He may refuse to promise, but once he agrees, he'll keep faith. In short, if Ruiyun is truly capable and virtuous, they will grow old together.”

“Very well, leave that aside,” Mrs Wang said. “Does Mr Ji have elderly parents?” “No parents above him, but six little devils below!” This was the greatest obstacle to the match, and Hu deliberately raised it himself. “Still, don't worry. The family is well brought up. All six children are very good.” She shook her head as he spoke. “That makes it difficult! What do you men know of the labour of running a household? With six children, making shoes alone would keep her busy all year. If she later has children of her own, wouldn't that add hardship to hardship?” From this point Hu spent a great many words. His eloquence was extraordinary and had usually carried everything before it. Now, however, nothing could persuade Mrs Wang. He praised Ruiyun's ability: she could make light work of the most complicated household. He said Ji would soon advance and could employ more servants to share the burden. Every argument failed before her single answer: “Ruiyun has suffered for years. I won't send her out to suffer again!” Further talk was useless. Hu gradually drew back. Though the affair had failed, goodwill remained intact. Mrs Wang, deeply apologetic, left an opening: “We can discuss it again later.”

Hu could not wait. A favour of this sort had to be carried through briskly if its recipient was to feel its full value. He therefore tried another route, through Wang. But if Wang simply overruled his wife, she would be unhappy and their marriage might suffer. Hu devised a gentler plan. “My dear,” Wang said in a consultative tone, “Ji Heling is doing our whole family a great service. We've just settled it over dinner: he'll leave for Xincheng the day after tomorrow. Since he's helping us, we must consider his difficulties too.” “Naturally. What difficulties does he have just now, and how can we help?” “He's acting as both father and mother. Once he leaves, the old family servant won't be able to manage everything. I'd like Ruiyun to keep house for him for a few days.” Mrs Wang smiled. “This must be one of Xueyan's devices.” “He's exceptionally clever. A device of his won't go wrong.”

“I'm not saying it's wrong,” she replied. “But you must explain the device before I can understand it.” “This is what he means. First, Ruiyun can manage Ji's household for a few days so he can leave without domestic worries. Second, she can see the situation for herself. If she finds him agreeable, the children obedient, and the household within her abilities, nothing could be better. Otherwise we abandon the idea and never mention it again, leaving no trace of the proposal. Wouldn't that be excellent?” “Yes, yes!” Mrs Wang nodded vigorously. “I have no objection to that.” “But let me offer some advice too,” Wang continued. “To be fair, a man like Ji has real talent. If he becomes a little more accommodating, his bearing and ability will certainly bring success. Ruiyun may have some hardship at first, but later she will enjoy prosperity. Besides, once we're close friends and this marriage links us too, you could visit each other often. Wouldn't that be pleasant?” This persuaded her. Affection required some consideration for herself as well as for Ruiyun. Whether Ruiyun became wife or concubine, relations between the women would depend first on relations between the men. Differences of rank or generation, or husbands who rarely met, made it difficult for their households' women to associate comfortably. Wang and Ji would certainly see much of each other. As friends whose families visited freely, they would give her ample opportunity to see Ruiyun. She therefore happily summoned the maid and explained the entire proposal, emphasising first that they could visit often, then promising a dowry, and finally asking what she thought.

Ruiyun had already been listening through the wall while Hu and Wang discussed the matter with their mistress. It concerned the rest of her life, and she had been considering it throughout. She felt it best not to declare herself yet. “Mr Ji is undertaking official business for the master. With no one to manage his household, naturally I should do it for a few days. Who can say what comes afterwards?” “That's reasonable too.” Mrs Wang wanted her to make a special effort and win Ji's heart, but could not say so openly. Instead she challenged her pride. “Only I'm a little worried. He has so many children, and the household will be hard to manage. It would sound very bad if people later said, ‘Her being there made no difference.’” Ruiyun said nothing, but inwardly scoffed. No difference? She would show them what proper management looked like tomorrow. Then they would know.

Early the next morning, Ruiyun took a clothes chest and travelled in a small sedan chair to Ji's house, accompanied by Gao Sheng. Hu had already explained the arrangement to Ji, who was deeply grateful. He treated Ruiyun with special respect, calling her “Miss Rui” and telling his children to address her as “Aunt Rui.” “Miss Rui, I'm putting you to a great deal of trouble,” he said earnestly. “With your help I can set my mind at rest. From today, I entrust this household to you. If the children misbehave, scold or punish them as necessary. Don't hesitate.” “How could I do such a thing?” she answered with a faint smile, drawing his youngest, large-eyed daughter into her arms while surveying the five older children. There were exactly three boys and three girls. The eldest, a boy, looked thoroughly honest and good-natured. The second was a thin girl of about twelve, with unusually lively eyes and more to say than anyone else. She was plainly not easy to manage. To run this household well, Ruiyun thought, she must first win over this Second Miss. “Miss Rui!” Ji interrupted her thoughts. “Let me give you the keys.” A housekeeper's keys were like an official's seal. Ruiyun accepted the heavy bunch without hesitation. Ji then summoned Zhang Gui and a young maid named Xiaoqing and introduced them. Having explained these arrangements, he rose to go out.

“Mr Ji, will you be home for a meal?” Ruiyun asked. “I leave tomorrow, and there's much to arrange today. I can't get back for lunch, and I have a dinner engagement.” “Then your luggage needs packing?” “I must trouble you with that. I won't take much. I usually bring Zhang Gui when I travel, but this time he needn't come. He knows what I require.” Ji did not return until the second watch that evening, bringing a guest: Hu Xueyan. The moment he entered, he felt the difference. The passage was no longer so dark that he could scarcely see. Pale moonlight made it quite bright. Looking closely, he saw that the windows had been repapered. Inside, everything stood in order. All the miscellaneous objects that had cluttered the reception room had been removed. The fresh clarity of the house immediately recalled the days when his wife was alive.

“Mr Ji is home!” Ruiyun came from the inner rooms to greet him, then welcomed Hu. “You've taken such trouble!” Ji smiled broadly and clasped his hands in thanks. “Well?” Hu asked with satisfaction. “Didn't I say Miss Rui was capable?” “More than capable. She has both ability and virtue.” This was plainly the language of assessing a bride. Otherwise, why speak of “ability and virtue” in a guest temporarily managing the house? Ruiyun understood, but felt she must pretend not to. Calmly she directed Xiaoqing to pour tea and prepare the water pipe. Only when host and guest were seated did she say that she had cooked some fragrant rice congee, ready to serve whenever they felt hungry. Before Ji could answer, Hu welcomed the suggestion. “Just what I was wanting!” Ruiyun went out and returned with a tray: four small dishes, a pot of Ji's usual rose spirit, and an earthenware pot of hot congee. Whatever the food might taste like, the utensils were exceptionally clean and fine. Since his wife's death, Ji had made do with the barest arrangements. To see even a simple supper presented properly naturally pleased him.

“Come, come!” he urged his guest. “This truly is offering the Buddha someone else's flowers. Without Miss Rui, I'd have nothing fit to serve you.” “Mr Ji!” Ruiyun was pleased too, though she thought his repeated courtesies unnecessary. “You'll embarrass me. Since I've come here, these things are simply my duty. I only hope you'll forgive anything I fail to do properly.” She gave him a deep look before lowering her head to ladle the congee. From their manner, Hu knew the match would succeed and could not resist a joke. “Brother Heling, you really do treat each other with the respect due to honoured guests!” “She is a guest,” Ji replied. “Of course I should respect her.” The phrase also described the mutual courtesy of an exemplary married couple. Ruiyun understood Hu's meaning but could think of no suitable answer. Still pretending not to understand, she quietly withdrew.

Watching her disappear, Hu moved from the seat opposite Ji to one beside him, across the corner of the table. He lowered his voice. “Brother Heling, now for serious business. What do you think?” Pressed so directly, Ji felt embarrassed. He smiled and tried to postpone the matter. “There'll be time to discuss it when I return from Xincheng.” “Certainly. Ordinarily that would be right. But the moment you leave, I must hurry to Shanghai. We're close friends now, so I'll be frank: everything I own is tied up in those boatloads of silk. I'm afraid of trouble on the journey. That's too complicated to explain now, so let it pass. Once in Shanghai, I must wait for an opportunity to sell. It may be two or three months before I return. You'll be back in Hangzhou long before then. Suppose you two are fond of each other and have to wait for the matchmaker. You'd be anxious, and so would I. Better to arrange the match now, before I leave. Whether I make it back for the wedding feast doesn't matter.” “You are kindness itself!” Ji offered him a toast, using the pause to consider. He still felt they should not hurry. “Could you give me a little longer to observe?” he asked apologetically.

“What more is there to observe?” Hu objected. “First, with your judgement and mine, can't we see what sort of person she is? Second, unless she possessed the ability and virtue you praised, would Mrs Wang have treasured her so much that she kept her unmarried until this age?” “That's true.” “And frankly, taking a concubine isn't the same as marrying a principal wife. There's no need for so much deliberation.” “Very well. I'll obey.” Ji offered another toast, thanking him as matchmaker. “Not so fast! You promise to obey, but I haven't given my instructions yet. I've pledged my word to Mrs Wang: if after two or three years Ruiyun has given no cause for complaint, you must be ready to obtain an imperial patent of rank for her.” “Naturally. I shan't marry another principal wife. In due course I'll raise her to that position.” “Those are your own words.” Hu deliberately pressed the point. “Will you turn into a Cai Bojie or a Chen Shimei and abandon her later? We must settle this beforehand, so I can answer for it.” Ji laughed. “What an idea! I'm not going to become the top examination graduate. Where would a prime minister's offer of his daughter's hand come from?”

“I don't believe you're that sort of man either. Then my work as matchmaker is done. You can choose the auspicious day yourselves. Mrs Wang will provide a dowry as though marrying off a daughter. As for your betrothal gift, there are two ways. Choose one.” “That's a new idea. Tell me the amount, and I'll find it. What is there to choose?” “I always do things differently. First, given the friendship among all three parties, I think the gift could be waived. Second, if you insist on doing your future companion proper honour, I'll lend you the money. Choose for yourself.” “Naturally I must do her honour. Besides, I already owe Mrs Wang a great deal. The betrothal gift cannot be omitted.” Ji reflected. “Borrowing is easy; repayment is difficult.” “Not difficult at all. Once you complete the Xincheng assignment, Governor Huang is certain to give you a post—perhaps a county under Mr Xuexuan's Huzhou prefecture. Would you still fear being unable to repay?” Ji considered the matter as a whole and decided the loan was reasonable. He nodded. “I'll borrow a thousand taels from your bank. But charge the usual interest, or I won't take it.”

Without a word, Hu took a sheaf of banknotes from an inner pocket of his jacket, selected one, and laid it before Ji. It was for exactly a thousand taels. “You certainly act promptly!” Ji laughed. “And you certainly cultivate your customers!” “I run a bank. How could I do otherwise? Put the note away safely. If you'd like to open an account at Fukang, ask for my chief clerk, Liu Qingsheng.” “Thank you. First let me write a promissory note.” Hu was prepared for this too. He carried a leather writing wallet containing blank plum-red paper ruled in eight columns, an inkbox, and a brush. In his calligraphy after Su Shi, dignified yet graceful, Ji wrote out the note on the spot and handed it back together with the banknote. “Why this?” Hu asked in surprise, pointing to the money. “The betrothal gift! I leave early tomorrow, so I must trouble you, my distinguished matchmaker, to prepare the formal card and deliver it for me.” “There's no need for so much...” “No, no!” Ji interrupted. “Even ten measures of pearls would seem a meagre gift to me.”

Hu considered. “Very well. Now tell me, when do you intend to hold the wedding?” “Since it's settled, naturally the sooner the better. Otherwise I fear Ruiyun will be left in an awkward position.” Ji continued, “If, as you say, I return successfully from Xincheng and receive a magistrate's seal, won't she be an official's lady?” “If that's your thinking, I must advise you...” Hu, too, produced a literary phrase. “Have patience; do not be hasty.” “Quite right. I'll follow your advice.” Ji agreed gladly. “Besides, we must wait for you to return. I'll have her thank the matchmaker at the feast!”

At first the two men had discussed Ruiyun in lowered voices, with some restraint. As they went on, they spoke louder and louder. Ruiyun could not have avoided hearing even if she had wished. Sitting quietly behind the door, she felt her heart tighten again and again until she almost struggled for breath. The words “an official's lady” were particularly sweet, like a piece of sugar in her mouth. Yet something continued to trouble her. Surely they ought at least to sound out her wishes first! They seemed so certain of her, so confident of their hold, that they were already deciding the wedding date between themselves. And “thank the matchmaker”! How did they know she would not object? Did they suppose she would accept whatever they said and let herself be arranged as they pleased? While she was thinking this, Ji called, “Miss Rui!” “Coming!” Her hand reached the curtain, then withdrew. She touched her face. It was indeed warm. She could hardly appear like this. Yet failing to come would reveal that she had been listening. After a moment she lifted the curtain and went out, but stood some distance away with her hands at her sides.

“Ruiyun,” Hu said, “I'm leaving.” “I'll light the lantern.” She welcomed the excuse to withdraw again. “No hurry. I have something to ask you.” “Yes, Mr Hu?” “Mr Ji is deeply grateful for your management of his household. He's asked me to buy you something in Shanghai. Don't be shy. Tell me what you'd like.” “I couldn't accept such kindness,” she replied. “How could I let Mr Ji spend money on me?” “Don't stand on ceremony. Tell me yourself. If you don't,” Hu added, “I'll buy a whole heap of things and charge them to your Mr Ji. That would cost him far more!”

What a formidable man this Mr Hu was, Ruiyun thought. She could not tell whether he was serious. If he really brought back a pile of useless things, she would regret the waste even though it was not her own money. Apparently it would be better to state her wishes. Yet Ruiyun also knew how to speak. “You're Mr Ji's good friend. You wouldn't let him spend too much.” She glanced at Ji and added, “I'll leave it to your judgement.” “That's an answer too. With your permission, I can act. In short, I'll satisfy you both: one won't feel it in the heart, and the other won't feel it in the purse.” There was a hidden judgement beneath the teasing. Ji frowned and Ruiyun blushed. Unwilling to remain there, she curtsied. “Thank you, Mr Hu and Mr Ji.” Then she turned away. “Well?” Hu said triumphantly. “She's protecting your interests at every turn. She's hardly entered the house and is already a devoted helpmate!” Ji pressed two fingers to his lips for silence, pointed towards the inner rooms, and asked softly, “Why embarrass her?” Hu laughed again. “Good! She protects you, and you protect her. It seems this match really will earn me merit for doing good.” Still talking, he moved towards the door. Ruiyun had roused the drowsing Zhang Gui and lit the lantern. Master and servant accompanied Hu outside, returning only after he had entered his chair.

Ji checked his luggage, then instructed Zhang Gui to obey Miss Rui in everything and guard the house carefully. When the servant had withdrawn, he asked, “Which room are you using, Miss Rui?” “I'm sharing with the Second Miss...” “Miss Rui,” Ji interrupted, “she's only a child. She doesn't deserve such a formal title from you. Call her by her name. It's Danhe...” He told her the names of all six children. “I wouldn't presume to call them simply by name either,” Ruiyun answered calmly. “I'll use guan.” In Jiangnan gentry households, children were commonly addressed with guan, attached either to their place in the family or to part of their name. Danhe would thus become Heguan. It was a customary form that implied neither superiority nor inferiority, so Ji offered no further polite objection.

“Let me say again, Miss Rui: I entrust the entire household to you, and all the children to your care.” “Set your mind at rest, Mr Ji. I'll attend to everything here.” Ruiyun now felt differently about him. A vague sense that he might become her lifelong support made her concerned for his safety on this journey. Yet she could not say so plainly and merely asked, “When do you expect to return?” “It shouldn't take long. A fortnight if things go quickly, a month at most. I'm confident I can settle the business.” “I hear it's a very troublesome affair?” “Much depends on the man.” Afraid she might not understand the saying, Ji explained, “It depends on who handles it. If I go, I should be able to manage.” “And if you can't?” If he failed, his life would be at stake. But he understood her feelings and would not frighten her with the truth. “Don't worry,” he said with complete confidence. “I shall certainly manage it.”

Ruiyun's face did indeed relax. She had many more questions, but it was their first day together, and the limits of her position made them hard to ask. Yet she could not bear to leave. She stood with her head lowered, as though waiting for further instructions. Ji found the atmosphere stiff and unsuitable for deeper conversation. “Please sit down. We shall have many more days together. If we're so constrained, we won't feel like one family.” The words were quite explicit. Sitting as he asked would amount to acknowledging that they were one family. Though she cared greatly about him, she did not want to show openly that she had given him her heart and her future. She was shy; besides, a trace of inexplicable resentment towards him and Hu remained, prompting deliberate reserve. Seeing her still standing, Ji quickly repeated, “Do sit down.” “I'm quite all right.” She still would not comply. Without realising it, Ji rose too. Holding his water pipe and twisting paper spills, he talked with her, chiefly asking about her family background. She answered every question. They continued until the third watch before finally going to their separate rooms.

This should have been Ji's most comfortable night since his bereavement. Ruiyun had thoroughly put his bed in order: spotless white ramie curtains, a scrupulously wiped sleeping mat, and a fresh pillow cover. The shelf behind the large bed was neatly arranged, with tea and books ready. Outside the curtains, the oil lamp had been trimmed to burn brightly, so he could read if unable to sleep. He could not sleep, but he did not read. His eyes were already dry and tired, while his mind remained excited and crowded with thoughts. Above all, he was assessing the journey to Xincheng. At first, moved by Hu's friendship and Wang's courtesy, he had volunteered without counting the consequences. Now he saw that he could not simply act on courage and consider the rest afterwards. What to do on arrival would necessarily depend on circumstances, but success and failure both required forethought. No one entering a city in danger could devise an entirely safe plan. If he were killed, what would become of his six children? Naturally there would be an allowance from the court and help from his superiors. But these depended on others' generosity. He needed someone truly dependable to whom he could entrust the children if they were orphaned.

This naturally brought Hu to mind. Ji regretted not having considered it sooner. Had he done so, he could have made a serious, explicit request that evening. Now he could only leave something like a will. He rose again, moved the lamp to the table, and laid out paper and brush, but hesitated. A will seemed too grave. It would place a heavy burden on Hu. He considered for a long while, then suddenly found an ingenious solution that pleased him greatly.

CHAPTER TWELVE

To reach Xincheng, one first travelled to Fuyang by water along the Qiantang River. Once Wang, who had come to see him off, had left, Ji asked Hu to stay a little longer. There were still a few things he wished to say. Seated in the cabin, he took a plum-red card from his visiting-card box and placed it before Hu. It read: “Ji Heling, known by his courtesy name. Native of Luotian, Hubei. Born at the noon hour on the fourth day of the tenth month, in the twenty-first year of Jiaqing.” “Oh!” Hu laughed. “You certainly don't waste time. I ought to have obtained Ruiyun's birth particulars for you first. Though really, we could dispense with this.” “No, no!” Ji waved his hand. “The card is for you. Brother Xueyan, I hope you will grant me the honour of becoming my sworn brother.” “This...” Hu paused in surprise, then beamed. “The honour would be mine! I haven't time to prepare a card now, but we must at least bow.” “That can all be arranged. We can perform the ceremony when I return from Xincheng. What matters in friendship is understanding each other's hearts. If you accept me, let's change our forms of address now. How old are you?”

“Much younger than you.” Hu adopted the new form at once. “Elder Brother!” Then he knelt to bow to him. Ji hastily knelt in return, naturally calling him “Second Brother.” They exchanged a bow and became brothers of different surnames without even taking a pinch of earth to serve as incense. When they rose, each felt a change in the weight on his shoulders. Ji's had lightened; Hu's had grown heavier. “Elder Brother,” Hu said, “go to Xincheng with your mind at ease and devote yourself entirely to the work. Don't spend a moment worrying about things at home. I'll attend to everything.” “Naturally I must rely on you. But with Ruiyun there now, I have little cause for anxiety. Once I've gone, hurry to Shanghai yourself. Go early and return early, and we'll exchange cards and give a feast.” “Very well. I understand. A safe journey!”

Hu left the boat, went ashore, and took a chair into the city. He reached Wang's house just after Wang himself, unable to suppress his smile. Both husband and wife wondered what had made him so happy. “You'd never guess! In the few moments after Mr Xuexuan went ashore, Heling and I became sworn brothers.” “Splendid! Congratulations!” Wang turned to his wife. “My dear, this changes our relationship with Heling too.” “Now we really are one family. The more close relations and good friends, the better.” “That reminds me.” Hu took a red envelope from his jacket pocket and offered it to Mrs Wang. She would not accept it. “What is this?” “Ruiyun's betrothal money...” Before he could finish, Wang protested loudly. “No, no! How could we take his money? Give it back.”

“Wait. Don't make such a noise!” Mrs Wang waved a hand. “First I want to be clear about Ruiyun. Has she agreed herself?” “She seems willing a thousand times over.” “How could it happen so quickly?” Mrs Wang was unconvinced. “What exactly did she say?” “It hardly needs to be said outright.” Hu recounted the previous evening. Affection conveyed in looks and unspoken understanding always made an engaging story, and he deliberately described every nuance. The couple listened with relish, mouths slightly open and the corners lifted, ready to burst out laughing at any moment. “It seems nearly settled,” Wang said with a nod when Hu finished. “Nearly isn't ‘willing a thousand times over,’” Mrs Wang replied. “I shall still have to say a few words before she gives her consent.”

“Then I entrust it to you!” Hu clasped his hands and used the opportunity to offer the red envelope again. Mrs Wang had just taken it when her husband snatched it back and thrust it at Hu. “We can't accept this.” “Of course we can,” she answered. “Ruiyun is being honourably betrothed, not given away as though she were worth nothing. Brother, give me the money. I have another use for it.” “What use?” Wang was thoroughly displeased and on the verge of quarrelling with her. “I'll tell you!” Her voice rose too. “We shall provide Ruiyun's dowry ourselves. These thousand taels will go to her separately, as money of her own. May I ask whether Your Honour Wang permits that?” His expression changed at once. He smiled apologetically, though his reply sounded reproachful. “My dear, why didn't you say so earlier?” “It isn't too late to say it now.” Mrs Wang carried off the envelope in triumph.

“Xueyan.” Wang looked a little worried. “We ought to discuss what comes next if Ji fails.” Their principle had long been settled: conciliation first, force afterwards. If conciliation failed, naturally troops would be sent. Why ask? But Hu understood what was troubling him and would not answer so literally. “Don't worry too much. Heling told me that whatever happened, he had ways to protect himself. He must be very confident. Besides, happy events lift a man's spirits. He has no domestic worries now and can concentrate entirely on the public business. Of course he'll succeed.” Hu spoke fluently and with such assurance that Wang was unconsciously encouraged. His worries eased, and he nodded repeatedly. “And another thing, Mr Xuexuan. Your fortune is at its height. Ruiyun will share your good luck, and she has a fortunate face herself. She looks certain to bring prosperity to her husband. Heling is bound to succeed at once. Sooner or later Ruiyun will be an official's lady!” Wang was still more pleased. “Quite right! I too feel this cannot possibly be an unlucky time. When Heling returns successfully to the provincial capital, I'll strongly recommend him for Gui'an County. That post brings in at least fifty thousand taels a year.”

Hu reflected that Wang was currently acting magistrate of Gui'an himself. Recommending Ji would be like taking fifty thousand taels out of his own pocket. A moment's generosity would eventually bring regret, and regret he could not express. A friendship brought to that point could hardly end as well as it had begun. Hu ought to dissuade him. “Gui'an is a large county of the first class. The authorities might not agree. A refusal would be awkward for both of you. I have another idea.” “Tell me! It's sure to be a good one.” “See what you think. You can't give proper attention to the Sea Transport Bureau as well. Why not recommend Heling to succeed you there?” “Ah!” Wang understood. “Exactly! That would achieve several things at once.” Hu knew what he meant. The benefits would include Hu's own convenience: with Ji in charge of the bureau, the advances and loans Hu had arranged would be easier to settle.

“That's what we'll do,” Wang said. “When are you leaving?” “The day after tomorrow at the latest. I really must go.” “Good. Come back as soon as your business is finished.” Wang lowered his voice. “I'd like you to take some money for me.” For whom? Neither needed to say. Hu asked only, “How much?” “Give her two or three hundred taels.” “Understood. I'll advance two hundred and settle with you when I return.” Hu went home to repack. The next day he found time to buy a variety of tea snacks himself and visit Ji's children. Seeing all six clean and well cared for by Ruiyun greatly reassured him. He did not tell the children about his sworn brotherhood with their father, but he told Ruiyun. As they talked, an unexpected lady visitor arrived: Mrs Wang. Hu understood why she had come. He had no reason to obstruct their serious conversation, so he smiled and left.

On reaching Songjiang, Hu again went ashore at Xiuye Bridge, famed for its four-gilled perch. He had brought no attendant, but carried many small pieces of luggage, mostly local products from Hangzhou. He had no fear of being unable to manage them. He asked the boatman to fetch a chair and porters and told them to go to Tongyu Rice Firm. There was no need even to bargain over the price. Carters, boatmen, innkeepers, porters, and brokers might be difficult people, but they understood how the world worked. Everyone at the wharf knew who stood behind Tongyu, and everyone respected his influence. Chen Shilong happened to be at the door when Hu arrived. “Mr Hu, I've been waiting for you every day! Why have you only just come?” “It's a long story. Is Brother You in Songjiang?” “He came back from Shanghai only last night.” “Good. Let's go inside and talk.”

Hearing them, Tongyu's staff came out to welcome Hu. They settled with the chair-bearers and porters, treated him as an honoured guest, and hurried to send word to You. “No need!” Hu stopped them. “I'll call on Brother You and go with him to pay my respects to the old master.” He checked the gifts and told Chen to carry them and follow. You's house was near enough to require neither chair nor horse. As they walked, Chen briefly reported what had happened since their arrival in Songjiang. The party was staying separately: Chen at Tongyu, Old Zhang aboard the boat, and A’zhu at You's house. Hu understood that You still regarded her as his beloved and was therefore treating her with special courtesy. He put her aside for the moment; his concern was the goods. “The silk is in a warehouse in Shanghai,” Chen said. “Uncle You arranged it. It's at Yuji Silk Warehouse, on North Street by Eryangjing Bridge. He has the warehouse receipt. He offered it to me, but I wouldn't take it. I do have a tally of the quantities.” Chen showed some caution: while another man held the receipt, he kept a written tally as a form of evidence. Yet it was really useless. The proper course was to accept the warehouse receipt. Otherwise, he might as well show complete trust. What was the point of clinging to a tally? This showed Chen's inexperience, precisely the sort of thing Hu must teach him. But the time and place were unsuitable for a lecture, so he merely nodded.

They found You's house full of important visitors. Hu was hesitating when You came out with exceptional warmth. They exchanged clasped-hand greetings, and You took his hand. “I thought you wouldn't arrive for several more days. Has Mr Wang's official business begun to take shape?” How did he know about Wang's business? Hu glanced at Chen, whose expression was quite natural. Evidently Chen had not told him. How, then, was You so well informed? The question flashed through Hu's mind while he answered, “Yes. Otherwise I couldn't have got away.” “Good. We'll discuss it later.” You drew him aside and lowered his voice. “I won't introduce you to those ‘divinities’ in the hall. Do you understand?” Hu understood after a moment's thought and answered crisply, “Yes.” “Then go back to Tongyu first. I'll come as soon as I've seen these ‘ghosts’ out.” “No hurry. Let's meet at the old master's instead.” “He often speaks of you. I'll send someone to take you.” You patted Chen's shoulder. “This young fellow has met him too. He's quite fond of him.” Chen's face shone as though gilded. “Only out of regard for Mr Hu.” It was partly modesty and partly the truth.

A man sent by You accompanied them to Old Master Wei's house. The old man had retired and concerned himself only with matters affecting the brotherhood as a whole. Most of his leisure passed in conversation with disciples of various generations. He had been out of spirits lately, but Hu's arrival delighted him. There were several reasons, the chief one being that Hu suited him perfectly. After receiving Hu's greetings and gifts, he ordered everything opened. Most were tea snacks and similar delicacies. He tried a little of each and repeatedly praised them. Once the bustle had subsided and they were seated, he instructed the others, “Go outside for a while. I have something to discuss with Mr Hu.” Usually only You was admitted to such private conversations. To dismiss everyone for a visiting outsider surprised them, but no one dared ask why. The dozen or so people in the room withdrew silently. “Xueyan,” the old man said, resting a hand on him, “I've been very low lately. With war and disorder everywhere, there's much to worry about. Old Five is capable enough, but his luck is poor. Since it became his turn to bear this burden, he hasn't had a single easy day. As his old master, I feel I've failed him.” “The younger generation has its own good fortune! You can afford to take an easier view. A boat straightens as it reaches the bridge. With Brother Five's standing outside, he can manage anything. Why worry so much about the younger men?”

“Among men of the waterways, perhaps. But when it comes to officials—and an imperial edict at that—what can he do? Xueyan, consider our position!” Hu understood. The transfer of grain transport to the sea route threatened the brotherhood's very existence. He had thought about this before and meant to help, but one development after another had kept him too busy even to consider it. The old man's words immediately filled him with remorse. “Officials nowadays—I don't mean to disparage them—are like the Jiangxi bowl-mender in the saying: each looks after himself. Wife, wealth, children, and salary come first! Otherwise things would never have reached this state...” The old man poured out his grievances, but there was truth in what he said. Hu understood that his anger concerned the sea transport of grain, or rather the failure to make provision for the brotherhood afterwards. Yet Hu felt the authorities could not bear all the blame. This was neither the moment to say so nor likely to do any good. He remained silent until he could discover what the old man wanted, then decide how to respond.

“I'm not flattering you, but the people who can actually serve the court and the common people now are men like you,” the old master continued. “I know something of Mr Wang's official reputation too. He's a reasonable man, willing to work. That's why there's something I want to say to you.” “Please give me your instructions. The brotherhood's men are all my good friends. Wherever I can help, I'll treat their business as my own.” “That's why I want to speak to you. Besides being a good friend who values loyalty, you see things clearly and won't misunderstand me.” He leaned closer and lowered his voice. “A man must always be left a way out. A desperate dog leaps a wall; a desperate man may hang himself. And you know our brotherhood: when we're amenable, we're very amenable; when we're not, we're hard to manage. Arrangements must be made beforehand. Once relations have broken down, restoring peace is painfully difficult. Xueyan, Mr Wang still holds the Sea Transport Bureau appointment. Ask him not to look only at what lies ahead and forget what follows behind. He must spare a thought for our brethren too.”

Hu was inwardly alarmed. Resentment within the brotherhood must be running high. Once the paper could no longer contain the fire, it might spread across the plains. The situation was chaotic enough already. He had heard that the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom had links with the Hongmen society. If the Anqing brotherhood rose as well, matters would be still more terrible. Trade required peaceful conditions, and peace could not depend on the authorities alone: everyone must work together. Hu had always thought so. Considering the interests involved, he now felt duty-bound to make a serious effort for the brotherhood. “Your words aren't merely for your own benefit,” he said solemnly. “You're thinking of the whole region. The canal runs from south to north; provincial boundaries cannot divide its concerns. Wherever I can be useful, I shall help.” “Exactly!” The old man patted his back. “That's why I say you see clearly. Once we understand that our fortunes are linked and cease dividing ourselves from others, matters become easier.”

“Then tell me what I should say when I return.” The old master thought briefly. “First, times have changed. Sea transport certainly has advantages, but canal transport isn't entirely useless. Ask Mr Wang to preserve it wherever possible.” He meant that not all grain shipments need be transferred to the sea route. The request was not excessive. Hu nodded. “That ought to be possible.” “Second, some provision must be made for the brotherhood's transport workers. Mr Wang should speak for us on that point too.” This was still more clearly a duty. “Certainly!” Hu agreed readily. “He certainly will.” “I know you can shoulder responsibility.” The old master clasped his hands. “Officials understand little of the hardships below. How fortunate that someone like you can connect those above and those below and open a path for us. I entrust this to you! I bow in thanks on behalf of our whole association.”

“You do me too much honour! But there's something I'd like to say, though you may not welcome it.” “Go ahead.” “I think the brotherhood should seek a livelihood for itself too. For instance, could the garrison lands be put in order?” “You're right in principle. But those lands are a long story. Over the years, who knows how many have been privately sold or pledged? Songjiang has an exceptional amount of land held under other men's registered names. That's why ours has become an impoverished association.” Hu had never heard this term, so the old master explained. Garrison farmland had originally been public property assigned to registered cultivators, who were in effect the emperor's tenants. They therefore bore a double burden: first, the regular land tax payable to the authorities; second, a silver payment per mu to subsidise the transport workers. This was called transport-support silver and ranged from one fen to three or four fen of silver per mu. Thus, despite being called garrison land, it carried heavier obligations than ordinary private farmland. Many abuses followed. Some cultivators fled, leaving fields untended. Other land was seized by local bullies, unscrupulous gentry, or clerks in the garrison offices. Still more was privately sold or pledged. Under the law governing the unauthorised pledging of military land, both parties to such a transaction were punishable. Hence the practice of holding land under another's registered name: the purchaser or pledge-holder kept it entered under the original cultivator or transport worker and paid the taxes through that name, leaving the registered tenure a mere fiction.

“Between the thirteenth year of Yongzheng and the eighteenth year of Daoguang, these lands were investigated seven times. The authorities know every abuse, yet they've never managed to put things in order.” The old man spread his hands. “Consider it: if the court can't deal with the problem, how are we to reform it ourselves?” “I understand!” Hu said. “Since the land has become a burden to the brotherhood, that actually makes things easier.” This sounded puzzling and required explanation. Hu regarded land as something that could tie a man's hands and feet. Countless people remained rooted in their native places, unwilling to leave a plot behind and venture boldly into business. If the Songjiang brotherhood's lands offered real benefits, cultivators and transport workers might fight over them at home, making matters troublesome. Since they were a burden, why not let them go? Provided the authorities could devise an arrangement, the men could change occupations without hesitation or disputes over what they were leaving. Wouldn't that make things simpler? “I truly admire you!” the old master exclaimed. “Heroes arise among the young. Your insight is far above the ordinary.”

At this point You came in. The old master briefly recounted his conversation with Hu. You listened very attentively, but this was chiefly a display of filial respect. He thought the matter important yet impossible to influence; they could only let events take their course. At least for the present, it was not urgent. “I'll discuss it with Young Uncle in due course,” he answered, then changed the subject. He spoke casually of A’zhu's stay and how well she got on with the women of his household. Hu naturally expressed his thanks. From the turn of the conversation, he sensed that You had something to discuss with his old master and that the small talk concealed an awkwardness about Hu's presence. Taking the hint, Hu rose and said he would rest at Tongyu until You joined him for a meal and a discussion of business. Before he had finished, You caught his arm. “Wait a moment, Young Uncle. I only need a few words with the old master. Then we'll go together.” “Very well. I'll sit outside.” “No need,” the old master told You. “Your Young Uncle is no stranger. You needn't keep anything from him.” “It isn't that I wish to keep it from him. We have no choice: when people bring things to us, we can't stop our ears. But he has no part in this. Why make him know about it? What he doesn't see needn't trouble him.” “That's true. Then sit outside for a while, Xueyan.” The old man raised his voice. “Someone come and show our guest my orchids!”

The old master kept several hundred pots of jianlan orchids, tended by a specialist. This man escorted Hu round them, finding much to say about every flower and leaf. Hu had no such refined interest. He responded politely to pass the time, thinking only of the confidential and troublesome business You regarded so gravely. Then he remembered You's phrase about seeing the “ghosts” out and understood. Those “divinities” were probably members of the Small Swords Society, or at least connected with Liu Lichuan. The thought both alarmed and pleased him. Alarmed him because this meant rebellion: he hoped neither You nor the old master would be drawn in. Pleased him because You knew what the Small Swords were doing. Information that helped him avoid danger and seize favourable chances could greatly benefit his trade. Benefits without harm! He must discuss that carefully with You. Only after a long while did You emerge. They called Chen and left together. “Young Uncle, shall we go to my house or Tongyu? Tongyu is quieter and better for talking.” Going to You's house would mean seeing A’zhu first. Hu felt no need for that just now. “Tongyu,” he answered without hesitation. “I have much to discuss with you alone.” Taking the hint, You arranged matters so that only the two of them sat drinking and talking privately there.

“I took the decision to put your goods in a silk warehouse. Here is the receipt.” You began by settling that matter. In Hu's hands, the receipt could serve many purposes. At the least it was evidence of his resources and credit. There was no need for empty politeness: he accepted it and laid it aside. “I know the warehouse well,” You continued. “They're charging a specially low rate. But if you can sell early, do so. Silk yellows when it lies in store, and the price suffers.” “You're right, Brother Five. But...” Hu paused. “I have a new idea to discuss with you.” “I don't understand this business particularly well, but never mind. Tell me first.” “You know the foreign trading houses well?” “Yes. Do you want introductions to foreign merchants?” “More than that. There's another question I'm not sure I ought to ask. If it's improper, tell me plainly. We're brothers: there must be no awkwardness between us.”

“I understand. ‘A man of the world has many thoughts, as coarse cloth has many fibres.’ Sometimes I can't avoid being cautious. But you're different.” You now thought more highly of Hu than even a little earlier. “The old master said your insight was exceptional. You see things that men of our world can't.” “I thank him for the compliment. Frankly, I claim no other virtues, but first, I've never knowingly failed a friend; second, I understand very clearly the weight and implications of a matter. So you needn't worry about this question I perhaps ought not to ask.” Hu was repeatedly assuring him that he would keep a confidence. You's worldly intelligence understood. Why wait to be asked? Wouldn't volunteering the information be more generous? “You want to ask about those ‘divinities’ you saw at my house today?” “Exactly.” Hu nodded gravely. “For my sake you wanted to spare me the trouble of knowing. But I have a business plan in mind.” You did not reply immediately. He slowly drank some wine, chewed a piece of dried fish for a long while, spat out the residue, and then spoke. “I don't know what your business plan is. But I'll tell you plainly about this. The Small Swords will rise within the next few days. They came to invite me to join them. I've decided to let them do it on their own.”

Just as Hu had thought! He first offered You a toast. “You've made the right decision, Brother Five. It isn't worth entering those muddy waters with them.” “Deciding is easy. Acting on it isn't. When muddy water is splashed at you, it's hard to keep clear.” This meant that although You had not joined them, he could scarcely oppose them either. Hu understood his difficulty. What he did not understand was the Small Swords' potential. “Then let me ask one more thing. Do you think they can become a real force?” “Hard to say. With foreigners mixed up in it, things become complicated.” “What?” Hu was startled. “Foreigners are involved too?” “That's through Liu Lichuan.” “Then the foreign settlements are certain to remain peaceful?” “The foreigners deal with Liu precisely to preserve order in the settlements,” You replied. “Why else would I have sent your silk to a warehouse there?” Hu said nothing. He carefully considered these words and felt that another excellent opportunity had arrived.

Naturally he must share the opportunity with You. In fact, he could not proceed without You's influence. “Brother Five, as I see it, once the Small Swords rise, the affair won't be over in three or five months. Silk supplies will be cut off, and export prices will strengthen. We can make a good profit.” “I'd certainly like to,” You answered. “The association grows poorer, and the burden on my shoulders grows heavier. I only wish I knew how. Buying silk, holding it, and selling when the export price rises—I understand that too. But tell me, where's the capital?” Capital was the chief difficulty. Hu already had a plan, but first he needed to know You's position. “How much can you raise? Give me a figure you're sure of, and we'll discuss it.” “I've already renewed the hundred-thousand-tael loan from the Big Three once. I can't renew it again. My immediate task is to raise the repayment. How could I think of anything else?” “How much have you raised towards it?” “Only half.” “Half means fifty thousand. How much more could you find within three days?” “Twenty thousand at most.” “Then that's seventy thousand. Good. Go ahead and raise it. Leave the renewal with the Big Three to me.”

Hu went on to ask, “There's something I don't quite understand. Do foreign trading houses lend money against goods?” “I've never heard of it.” “Then please make inquiries, Brother Five. Even with little capital, we can do a very lively business. There are two ways.” His first proposal was to pledge the goods in the Yuji Silk Warehouse for a loan from a foreign firm, turn the warehouse receipt into ready silver, and buy silk locally in Shanghai. If no foreign firm would lend, he would approach the banks. “Wait!” You interrupted. “That's a clever idea, but why not go directly to a bank for the loan?” Hu smiled, a little sheepishly. “Brother Five, I want to perform a conjuring trick with that receipt.” Lowering his voice, he explained, “We need a reason for asking the Big Three to renew your loan. We can say I have a sum to transfer to you, but can't settle it until my silk is sold. Show them the receipt, with the goods still untouched in the warehouse, and they'll naturally feel reassured. How are they to know I've already pledged the receipt elsewhere?” You laughed too. “You're formidable! No one can beat you at business. I understand. The receipt must stay out of banking circles if the trick is to remain hidden. If the foreign firms won't do it, I can try private lenders, so long as there's something to pledge.”

“Nothing could be better. Now for the second way.” Hu had long cherished the idea of uniting silk merchants to deal with foreign trading houses, so that they could dictate terms instead of having terms dictated to them. Such an ambition could not be achieved at a stroke, but they might begin on a small scale. With You's connections and his own powers of persuasion, he meant to win the cooperation of fellow silk dealers in Shanghai whose goods were intended for export. “Here again, there are two possible arrangements. First, we pay a deposit of a quarter or a third, and the goods are reserved for us. Six months later we pay the balance and collect them. Taking the price as a whole, the seller must of course get a better bargain than by selling now, or he won't agree.” The other arrangement was to bring all the dealers together and secure their agreement to withhold their silk from sale. Hu and You would then negotiate prices with the foreigners and take a commission on concluded deals. Hu explained carefully, and You listened closely, calculating as he listened. By Hu's method, a hundred thousand taels could finance trade worth five hundred thousand. If they divided the profits equally, each would receive fifty thousand. Added to the fifty thousand already in You's hands, that would exactly repay his loan from the Big Three. He could hardly remain indifferent. “Young Uncle, you calculate brilliantly. I'll certainly join you. When shall we leave for Shanghai?” “What do you think? For me, the sooner the better.” “Tomorrow at the earliest.” “Tomorrow it is. Agreed.”

Business settled, they turned to lighter talk. You mentioned A’zhu and asked with a smile when Hu would take her as a concubine, so that he could prepare a present. “You've misunderstood!” Hu answered, then felt that this was not quite right. “No, it isn't that you've misunderstood. The truth is that no one knows what's in my mind. First let me ask you something, Brother Five. What do you think of A’zhu's character? We're among ourselves; there's no need for polite phrases.” “She's a good girl, though she seems rather strong-tempered. Frankly, a girl like that would be a fine helpmate for a young fellow willing to make his way in the world. Married to you...” You suddenly asked, “What is your wife's temper like?” “I couldn't call it good, but I couldn't call it bad either. Never mind her. In any case, she won't concern A’zhu.” “Young Uncle, that's a strange thing to say!” You exclaimed. “You sound as if you don't intend to marry the girl. Yet she tells my wife everything and says you've promised to establish a separate household for her in Huzhou. Those two accounts don't fit together.” “True. I don't know whether I'm doing the right thing. Let me tell you, Brother Five, and you can help me think it through.” He then explained in detail his plan to redirect A’zhu's affections and persuade her to marry Chen Shilong.

“So that's it!” You said with a laugh. “Young Uncle, you're as shrewd at managing people as you are at managing money. Yes, young Chen Shilong has a future. I approve of your idea.” “Good! I've wanted someone to talk it over with, to discover whether it was only wishful thinking on my part. Since you approve, I've decided to go ahead.” In his enthusiasm, You immediately volunteered his services. “It's a good idea, but it won't be easy. Her whole heart is set on you. Getting her to give you up all of a sudden will be very difficult. Would you like my help?” The offer was well meant; Hu had no reason to refuse. “Of course. But how would you go about it?” “Haven't I told you she confides everything to my wife? Shall I ask my wife to act as matchmaker?” “That would be excellent. Only...” Hu added, “this is something we mustn't rush.” You understood at once: this was a tactful refusal. He nodded. “Very well. We'll wait and see. Whenever you need me, I'm at your service.”

“You're too kind!” Hu suddenly changed his mind again. “I'd like your wife to sound her out first. What did she think of Chen Shilong on the journey? If she thinks well of him, your wife could go a little further and try persuading her. Then we'll see what she says.” “That isn't the way to put it!” You shook his head. Hu felt somewhat unconvinced. Surely, knowing A’zhu as he did, he knew how to approach her? “Then how should it be put?” he asked. “First, she must understand that becoming anyone's concubine would be unfair to her. Next, she must understand that becoming yours might not give her a comfortable life.” On reflection, Hu saw that he was right. “I'm too involved to see clearly.” He clasped his hands respectfully. “I leave it entirely to you. I shall put the matter out of my mind.” Only when that concern was off his mind could he devote himself wholly to the silk trade. You thought that they simply must bring the affair to a successful conclusion. Otherwise it would distract Hu, and both their interests were at stake.

Returning home that day, You held a private consultation with his wife. They had just finished when A’zhu passed the window. He called her in. “Miss Zhang, I have something to tell you.” Considering herself Hu's woman, A’zhu used his form of address. “Brother Five!” she said, and entered to sit beside her Fifth Sister-in-Law. In her presence, however, You did not refer to Hu as “Young Uncle.” “Xueyan asked me to tell you that he won't be visiting today. He has something to attend to this evening.” A’zhu was naturally disappointed, but she told herself that he had many things to do and ought to be forgiven. She nodded. “I understand.” “He's leaving tomorrow, and I'm going with him. I'm afraid he won't have time to see you before we leave, either.” This was strange. “Aren't we all going to Shanghai together?” “No,” You replied. “He means you to stay here with us.” “Stay here,” Mrs You added, taking her hand. “In a few days I'm going to Shanghai too. You can come with me, and we'll enjoy ourselves.” A’zhu held back the tears welling in her eyes. The kinder her hosts were, the more hateful Hu seemed. It looked as though his feelings for her were changing!

“Miss Zhang, I'm meeting him early tomorrow. Is there anything you'd like me to tell him? I'll pass it on.” “No!” A’zhu's anger made her answer sharply. As soon as she spoke, she felt it was wrong to treat You that way. She hastily softened her voice. “Thank you, Brother Five. There's nothing I want to say to him.” “Very well. I'll tell him exactly that.” Now she felt uneasy again. She was angry and even wanted to scold Hu to his face, but she did not want other people carrying her angry words back and forth. Nor could she make out what You meant, so she could hardly say more. She merely asked, “What about my father and Chen Shilong? Are they leaving too?” “Of course. There's a great deal to do in Shanghai, and we're short of people. How could they stay behind?” “All right. Then I'll go to the boat tomorrow to see my father.” Her mind was made up. Once aboard, she would surely meet Hu, and she would teach him a lesson. What sort of lesson she had not yet decided. She would have to think it over.

“What hot weather!” Mrs You rose, still holding her hand. “Let's cool off in the pavilion.” The You family's back garden had its share of pleasant flowers and trees, as well as an artificial hill with a pavilion on top. Its name was odd: the Bumai, or “No Purchase,” Pavilion, presumably because a clear breeze and a bright moon cost nothing to enjoy. Oddly named though it was, the pavilion had a pleasingly simple, old-fashioned design and an excellent position. From its height, the green fields and distant mountains made a delightful prospect. The garden wall was low. Those on the hill could see passers-by, while those passing below could glimpse only the women's hair and graceful silhouettes inside the pavilion. In a strictly proper household, the women would not have been allowed up there. You's family was different. Its women never hid themselves from view, and no outsider dared entertain designs on them. Since her arrival, A’zhu had therefore gone almost every evening with Mrs You to enjoy the cool air in the Bumai Pavilion.

They were often joined by You's younger sister, seventh among the children, whom the household called the Seventh Lady. Widowed young, she had quarrelled with her parents-in-law and returned to her own family. She was about thirty and strikingly beautiful. Sitting in silence, she was a woman of exceptional loveliness; once she opened her mouth, she could frighten timid men away. She had a man's bold, forthright manner and a strong flavour of the rougher world beyond respectable society. Her speech was sharp and her face expressive: she could lower her brows, glare, and look positively murderous. What men found hardest to bear was her utterly unguarded tongue, especially when she was abusing someone. There was no coarse expression she would not use. Her sister-in-law therefore called her “the female Zhang Fei,” after the famously fierce and outspoken warrior.

The female Zhang Fei had a warm heart and was particularly fond of A’zhu. Seeing the unhappiness that flickered across the girl's face, she could not help asking, “What's the matter? Tell me what's troubling you.” How could A’zhu confide in anyone about this, especially her? “Nothing, nothing!” She did her best to sound carefree. “I couldn't be more comfortable here. What could trouble me?” “There's something I don't understand.” The Seventh Lady spoke her mind without much thought for the consequences. “Since your Mr Hu has arrived, why hasn't he come to see you?” A’zhu was deeply embarrassed. Alarmed, Mrs You hurried to stop her. “There you go again! A true headstrong Zhang Fei.” “Why? What's wrong with asking?” Mrs You was no fool either. Seeing how matters stood, she suddenly decided to use the female Zhang Fei to her advantage. She sighed deliberately. “Every household has its own difficult scripture to recite. We must try to persuade our Sister Zhang to understand Mr Hu's difficulties.” To speak of understanding and persuasion implied that Hu was at fault. While A’zhu was still considering those words, the Seventh Lady could contain herself no longer. Taking her hand and looking straight at her, she said, “Of course something's troubling you! You've been badly treated. However busy he is, he can't spare a moment to see you? Tell that to the ghosts! Men are contemptible creatures. When they want you, you're an empress. Once they change their minds, you can kowtow to them and get a fist in return. I've seen plenty of that sort.”

“My dear lady, my dear lady!” Mrs You sounded almost as though she were pleading for mercy. “Will you spare me? What is all this shouting about?” “Very well!” The Seventh Lady lowered her voice but spoke still faster and more urgently. Holding A’zhu with one hand, she pointed at her sister-in-law with the other. “Sister Zhang couldn't have made it clearer. He agreed to establish a household in each place. Why hasn't it been done long ago? Now he comes to Songjiang and won't even see her. What is that supposed to mean?” Turning to A’zhu, she continued, “I thought there was something wrong from the beginning and felt it unfair to you. At first I wondered whether I'd misjudged him. Now it's plain enough: a devoted woman and a faithless man!” “Headstrong Zhang Fei, headstrong Zhang Fei! You really are...” Mrs You left the sentence unfinished. Listening beside them, A’zhu felt acutely uncomfortable, though she could not immediately tell whether the cause was the Seventh Lady or Hu. Ashamed and angry, she shifted quietly until her face was in shadow, hidden from the two women.

They would not allow even that. Both turned towards her. Taking her other hand, Mrs You comforted her. “Sister Zhang, don't listen to her. That's her nature: the moment she opens her mouth, she offends someone.” A’zhu now had to be gracious. “Seventh Sister means well by me. I don't blame her.” “That's a fair-minded thing to say!” The Seventh Lady looked still more indignant on her behalf. “This concerns your whole life. Now that we've brought it into the open, let's think it through properly.” She asked Mrs You, “What exactly is Mr Hu thinking, behaving like this?” “Nine out of ten of your questions are impossible to answer,” Mrs You replied with a smile. “Still...” She deliberately stopped and watched A’zhu carefully, trying to read her feelings. That was not easy. A’zhu considered their concern unnecessary and maintained her composure as a way of refusing their kindness.

The Seventh Lady hardly understood this signal; even if she had, it would not have restrained her tongue. Assuming a gentler manner, she said, “Sister Zhang, you're such a fine young woman. Why accept an inferior place?” Hearing her express the same view as her brother, Mrs You saw a chance to speak through her. When A’zhu remained silent, she supplied the next line like a performer in a duet. “What do you mean, an inferior place?” “Bowing and scraping as a lesser wife—isn't that accepting an inferior place?” The speaker meant no particular wound, but her listener felt one. The words touched A’zhu's hidden sore, and composure became impossible. “Besides, it might be tolerable if the wife were good-tempered. Otherwise, lowering yourself like that is simply pressing your warm face against someone's cold backside.” Another of her coarse expressions! Mrs You had repeatedly warned her that their guest was a young lady and such language must be restrained. Yet nature would have its way. Just now, however, she needed the Seventh Lady as her supporting player and could not stop to scold. She merely sighed. “Yes, that's precisely Mr Hu's difficulty.” There was a meaning behind this that A’zhu must discover, but someone else asked for her. “What? Is the woman at home a tigress?” “From what Mr Hu says, she's very fierce.” “Then he's at fault! With a jar of vinegar at home, why deceive our Sister Zhang?” “I must say something fair on his behalf,” Mrs You answered earnestly. “He intended to settle matters with his wife before holding the wedding. When she wouldn't agree, he had to retreat. That's hardly deception.”

“What?” A’zhu exclaimed. “Fifth Sister-in-Law, how do you know?” “Her brother—Brother Five—told me everything.” Mrs You indicated the Seventh Lady. “Mr Hu really does have difficulties. He couldn't bring himself to tell you, but keeping them to himself was no solution either, so he spoke to a close friend. Don't worry, Sister Zhang. We'll think of a way.” What way? The meaning was unclear, and A’zhu's mind was too tangled to examine it. Her sole wish was to speak to Hu face to face. “There's always a way. We needn't stand on ceremony with a heartless man. But...” The Seventh Lady lowered her voice. “Tell me honestly. You've travelled back and forth together on the boat and stayed in the same place in Huzhou. Have you and he ever...” Before she could finish, A’zhu cried out in embarrassment and alarm. “No!” Afraid they might not believe her, she spoke with absolute firmness. “Absolutely not! I'm not that sort of girl.” “I know, I know.” The Seventh Lady sounded greatly relieved. “If he hasn't taken advantage of you, things are easier still.” “Exactly,” Mrs You agreed. “This isn't such a difficult affair yet. It all depends on you.” Again there was a deeper meaning for A’zhu to consider, but the Seventh Lady talked too much to give her time.

“It's fortunate you found out early,” she said. “Out of ten men, eleven want something new. If he's treating you like this before he's even won you over, imagine what he'll do once he's had his way. He'll cast you aside, and then even your tears will do no good.” She considered this restrained language, but A’zhu, who understood relations between men and women only imperfectly, flushed and lowered her head, not knowing where to look. Coarse though the female Zhang Fei's words were, they revealed a side of the matter she had never grasped. She had heard that men tired of the familiar and sought the new, but never had it been explained so plainly. She remembered how Hu had sometimes overstepped the bounds, pressing further and further, and how she had stood firm when it mattered. She had been right to do so.

This sense of relief eased her embarrassment. Nor did her whole heart now seem bound so immovably to Hu. She raised her face, smoothed her hair, and sipped the honeysuckle tea intended to clear heat and toxins. Calmly she asked, “Fifth Sister-in-Law, Seventh Sister, you say you'll think of a way for me. What way?” Mrs You had been waiting for the question. They had reached a crucial point, and she must choose her words carefully. Pressing the Seventh Lady's hand to keep her from interrupting, she asked in return, “That depends on your own wishes. The main decision must be yours. If you want to go east, we'll find a road east. If you want to go west, we'll see whether that road is open.” A’zhu understood. There were two paths: continue with Hu, or wipe away all the sweet words and solemn promises of the past. Understanding them was one thing; making the choice on the spot was beyond her.

“In my view, such things require willingness on both sides. Since he has said this, it wouldn't be right to force him. Leaving everything else aside, you must at least preserve your own dignity.” “Exactly!” The Seventh Lady could hold back no longer. “Fifth Sister-in-Law is absolutely right. You're a delicate flower, not stale fish left on the market stall that we must force on him before it spoils!” The words struck A’zhu like mustard, sending resentment up into her nose until she nearly wept. She was a delicate flower, yet Hu treated her like unwanted fish, behaving strangely and scarcely deigning to notice her. It hurt to think of it. Through clenched teeth she said, “Who would be so cheap as to force herself on him?” “Good. You've seen it clearly,” the Seventh Lady answered. “To be honest, even having equal standing in two households was a terrible concession for you. And still he talks of difficulties! A man like that can keep his whole family to himself, thank you!”

Half the task was accomplished. Why continue abusing Hu and merely create an enemy? Mrs You defended him. “Seventh Sister, you're going too far. Mr Hu is as good a man as one could find. There are things beyond his power, and he doesn't wish to waste Sister Zhang's youth. Don't misjudge him.” One virtue of the Seventh Lady was her readiness to admit an error. Hu had had many opportunities to win A’zhu, yet nothing had happened between them. He had also done a great deal for the Zhang family. A man like that was indeed uncommon. She smiled. “On reflection, you're right. After all his trouble and effort, he gets nothing—and is scolded into the bargain. It really is unfair.” A’zhu's unsettled heart had been rising and falling with the two women's words. Now she remembered all Hu's kindness and could hardly bear to give him up. Yet her defiant words had already been spoken. A sail once lowered was difficult to raise again. Regret stirred within her, but she could not express the pain. Two tears rolled down her cheeks.

“Why!” the Seventh Lady asked in astonishment. “What are you crying for?” “Don't be sad,” Mrs You urged. “You nearly took the wrong road and have turned back in time. You ought to be happy.” How could she be happy? The Seventh Lady had said Hu's efforts had come to nothing. Hadn't hers too? His disappointment was of his own choosing; she had no choice in hers. In the stillness of the night, all the past happiness and future plans would become reflections in a mirror, moonlight on water. How was she to live with that? As A’zhu sat lost in thought, Mrs You took the opportunity to signal to her sister-in-law that enough had been said. But the Seventh Lady did not understand. When Mrs You rose to pour tea, she followed and asked quietly, “Have you something to tell me?” There had been nothing, but since she asked, they might as well talk. “A word or two. Only I'm afraid your tongue will run away with you. Half the affair is settled, but unless the other half succeeds, none of it does.” “What do you mean?” “Mr Hu intends...” Mrs You glanced at A’zhu and drew the Seventh Lady outside the pavilion before lowering her voice. “He also wants to arrange a marriage for our Sister Zhang.”

“To whom?” “That young fellow surnamed Chen.” “Him!” The Seventh Lady cried out in delighted surprise. “Softly, softly!” Mrs You reproached her. “A true headstrong Zhang Fei! You never consider anything.” “He's a good young man.” The Seventh Lady dropped her voice almost to a whisper. Her warm heart was overflowing with joy for A’zhu. “That's the right match! Exactly right!” “Don't rejoice yet. We don't know how things will turn out.” “I'll persuade her. I'll make her agree. She's told me she thinks very well of him.” “Oh?” Mrs You listened closely. “What did she say?” “It's really funny. She told me he was capable and kind, and that she meant to find him a good wife one day. Little did she know: as the old joke goes, a girl raised as a future bride starts matchmaking, but cannot secure her own fate!” At this she burst into laughter, bending and stamping until she looked quite foolish. Even A’zhu was amused. “What are you laughing at?” “You!” Her laughter, only just subsiding, broke out again. “Silly creature!” Mrs You gave her a look, but could not help laughing too. Their mysterious behaviour only increased A’zhu's suspicions. She kept asking what she had done to amuse them so much. Quick-witted Mrs You invented a story and put her off.

They turned to other subjects, ate a late-night snack, and found that it was already midnight. Mrs You was tired from managing the household all day. She did not do the actual drudgery herself, but You Laowu entertained many guests and supported plenty of people who lived at his expense. Every day they fed four or five tables of people. Directing the servants in their reception was work enough. By now she could hardly stay awake. “What about you two?” she asked. “It's cool now. You should go to bed too.” “I'm not sleepy yet. I'd like to sit a little longer,” A’zhu replied. In truth, her troubles would keep her awake even in bed. “I'm not sleepy either,” the Seventh Lady said. “Now that it's cool, we can enjoy sitting out.” Mrs You reflected that, left together, they would certainly return to Hu and Chen. She feared the Seventh Lady lacked the composure to proceed slowly and might ruin a promising affair through haste. She hesitated uneasily. “Go to your room,” the Seventh Lady reassured her, guessing her concern. “We'll sit a little longer, then go to bed.” “Anything more can wait until tomorrow.” Mrs You gave her another pointed hint. “Things settle better when allowed time. I'm always telling you, but you never seem willing to listen.” “I know, I know. Don't worry.” This exchange plainly concealed much that had not been said. As soon as Mrs You left, A’zhu asked, “What did she mean about things settling better when allowed time?”

“Your affair, of course.” The Seventh Lady considered. “After all our talk, what do you intend to do? It isn't that he doesn't want you. A girl like you needn't fear that nobody will. But Mr Hu is afraid to eat the steamed bun already at his lips, and you can't force it into his mouth.” A’zhu found the first half pleasant enough, but the ending made her frown. “Seventh Sister, your comparisons are always so strange that I don't know how to answer.” “Why? I speak the truth. Whatever I think, I say. There's not a scrap of pretence in me.” “I know you're sincere with people. But...” How was she to explain? Many things could be thought but not spoken. A’zhu understood this, yet could not make the principle clear. She could only smile helplessly. “But what?” The Seventh Lady began to understand. “You blame me for being too blunt and saying things you don't like to hear?” That was partly right, but A’zhu could not admit it. “No, no, I don't blame you at all. Everyone here—Brother Five, Fifth Sister-in-Law, and you—has been as kind as possible. Since we're like family, of course we should speak frankly.”

“Good!” Once again the Seventh Lady could not restrain herself. “You know my nature. I take other people's affairs as seriously as my own, especially yours. Now let's make a long story short. What exactly do you mean to do about Mr Hu?” A’zhu wanted to evade the question but could not. After thinking, she could only offer an excuse. “My mother arranged this, Seventh Sister. I'll have to ask her.” “That's a strange thing to say! Have you no opinion of your own?” “I can't disregard my parents.” “Oh, oh! What a dutiful daughter!” The sarcasm embarrassed A’zhu. “Seventh Sister,” she appealed, “let me think. I'll talk to you tomorrow morning.” From years of observing her own household, the Seventh Lady knew very well how to read an expression. Seeing A’zhu's face, she realised that pressing further would be tactless. “Take your time, take your time. Once you've decided what you want, I'll certainly help.” “Thank you.” A’zhu took her hand. “It's fortunate I'm staying with you. Anywhere else, I wouldn't even have someone to tell my troubles to.”

Much of this was intended to strengthen their friendship. In fact, she already felt the misery of having nobody she could confide in. The Seventh Lady's warmth was almost hot enough to burn one's hands. Mrs You was smooth and worldly, apparently taking Hu's side for reasons of interest. That left only Chen. They had almost reached the point where they could talk of anything, but whether she should discuss this particular matter with him was doubtful. Even if she did, he worked for Hu and depended on him for advancement. Would he help her stand against him? That was doubtful too.
