Reading his expression, Hu saw the change in the air and tactfully turned the conversation elsewhere. Nor did he wish to linger. At a suitable moment, he suggested ending the gathering. It was nearly midnight, but the lane outside Yiqing House was still lively. Food hawkers passed continually, calling their wares. At the entrance stood numerous little sedan chairs, finely made, with tasselled curtains and small glass windows. They catered especially to weary late-night seekers of pleasure. On this occasion alone, one carried a lady—the Seventh Lady. Back at the Yuji Silk Warehouse, she was first out of her chair and hurried towards the rear. Scarcely on the stairs, she called at the top of her voice, “Sister Zhang, are you asleep?” A’zhu was still awake. At first she had stayed up to let the Seventh Lady in, worried about her. Later, chatting and eating snacks with Chen, she had become so absorbed that she forgot whom she was waiting for. The call from below startled her, and she hurried out. They met at the head of the stairs. Seeing the Seventh Lady's rosy cheeks, sparkling eyes, and exuberant glow, A’zhu exclaimed, “Where have you been drinking to come back so tipsy?”

“Look what I've brought you!” The Seventh Lady handed her a finely woven bamboo basket. Hu and You had now come upstairs too. With Chen and Old Zhang, who had risen at the noise, the room was crowded, yet only the Seventh Lady's voice could be heard, recounting how she had spent the evening at Yiqing House. To Old Zhang and his daughter, it was an unheard-of adventure. Even Chen marvelled at her audacity. “Have some!” At last she lifted the basket lid, revealing six large Yangcheng Lake crabs. Beneath her rough manner, she was remarkably thoughtful: even the ginger vinegar was ready to hand. Her kindness could not be refused, and the crabs themselves were tempting. Old Zhang, A’zhu, and Chen began shelling them as they listened to her description of life at Yiqing House. You, meanwhile, signalled to Hu, and the two withdrew into the inner room for a private conversation.

“Young Uncle,” You said with a frown, “my sister's behaviour grows more improper every day. What are we to do?” “Don't say that!” Hu replied cheerfully. “Brother Five, I shall be asking for wedding wine soon. Do you know what Gu said to me? He wants me to arrange a marriage.” You was astonished. After a long silence, he asked, “He wants to marry our A’qi?” “Exactly. Love at first sight! Marriage really is a matter of destiny.” “What destiny?” You frowned still more deeply. “Think how it would sound: they met in a courtesan house!” This response surprised Hu. He could not immediately think how to defend Gu and the Seventh Lady, and stood speechless for some time. “There's something I don't understand,” You continued. “How did Gu know that A’qi is living with her own family now? Does he think she's still an unmarried young lady?” “No. He knows she's a widow. The Second Miss told him—no, he asked her.” Hu then described Gu's family circumstances.

“Well, Young Uncle, what did you tell him?” “I told him to see for himself. I think they are destined for each other. We should be able to drink that wedding wine.” You shook his head emphatically. “Let it be. We shouldn't ruin a man's life.” “There's no need to put our lady down so harshly!” Hu spoke with indignation. “With her looks and abilities, I think even marrying Gu would scarcely do her justice. As for her temper, that cuts both ways. A woman's mind is a strange thing: if she herself wishes to, she will naturally change. Look at her today—refined and perfectly at ease. Clearly, she's changing already.” Persuasive though the words were, they led to no conclusion. A marriage could hardly be settled immediately in any case. They must leave it for later and first arrange the following day's departure.

They went aboard at noon: Hu and his pupil, Old Zhang and his daughter, and the Seventh Lady—five in all. Apart from Old Zhang, each had private concerns that could be discussed only in close confidence, never openly. Moreover, the route was unsettled, and every disturbance required vigilance. Even the talkative Seventh Lady remained silent much of the time. As they approached Songjiang the following day, Hu had to decide whether she should escort them as far as Jiaxing. If unnecessary, they could leave her in Songjiang and sail on after stopping no more than half a day to collect the luggage he and A’zhu had left with the You family. Otherwise, they must stay at least a day while she gathered news and perhaps brought along someone to run errands. “Young Uncle!” As soon as he raised the matter, she interrupted. “Whether I escort you or not, you must stay a day at our house before leaving.” “They're waiting urgently in Hangzhou...” “One day won't make all the difference. Fifth Sister-in-Law has something to say to you.” That was strange. What could Mrs You want to say? And if she did have something to say, how could the Seventh Lady know? Whenever faced with a difficulty, Hu tried to reason it through from beginning to end before asking questions.

His mind worked exceptionally quickly. Watching her expression, he could see only one possibility. “Seventh Sister, is there something you find awkward to say yourself and want Fifth Sister-in-Law to ask me?” She smiled, partly mischievous and partly shy. “Young Uncle, you are very clever.” “Then why not tell me directly?” “It would still be better to let her ask you herself.” That sounded as though it concerned You and his wife. Puzzled, Hu considered it further. Could it be about the Second Miss? Perhaps the Seventh Lady meant to meddle and report her brother's activities, giving Mrs You questions to ask. Or perhaps she intended kindness. Having taken to the Second Miss, she might persuade her sister-in-law to let her husband take the courtesan as a concubine. In that case, Mrs You would have even more to ask. Questions might be alike in form, yet some could be answered freely and others could not. What sort of inquiry awaited him? He must establish its direction beforehand, or risk being caught at a disadvantage. “Seventh Sister, do you know whether what she wants to ask concerns something good?” “Naturally.”

Hu was reassured. At Songjiang they went ashore and directly to the You house for a rest. Taking the opportunity, Hu paid a visit to the old master and dined with him. Back at the house, he had scarcely exchanged a few words when Mrs You rose. “Young Uncle, I have a favour to ask.” She wanted him to act as matchmaker. It was not, however, to bring the Second Miss into You's household, but to secure a happy marriage for the Seventh Lady. Mrs You explained that, while Hu and You had been discussing Gu privately at the Yuji Silk Warehouse, the Seventh Lady had taken advantage of the others' absorption in their crabs to listen at the wall. She knew Gu's intentions and had declared that she would marry nobody else. Having heard that her brother seemed opposed, she had come especially to discuss it with his wife. Hu laughed at himself. He had misread the Seventh Lady's tone and fallen victim to his own cleverness. If he approached a major business transaction with such wild guesses and self-assurance, he would surely lose heavily.

“Young Uncle,” Mrs You asked, “how did A’qi come to know this Mr Gu? It seems they had only just met. Where was it?” That was not easy to answer, especially to her. As You had said, meeting in a courtesan house sounded disgraceful. Her next question would be why the Seventh Lady had gone there, which would bring in the Second Miss. Mrs You would naturally not interfere with a man like her husband occasionally visiting the pleasure quarters. But knowing that he was the Second Miss's favoured patron and maintained a separate little house might well make her jealous. Hu therefore said, “At the Yuji Silk Warehouse. Gu, Brother Five, and I are now partners. The marriage would be quite natural. He is willing and so is she. What more is there to say? As for arranging it, I am not only bound to help; you might say nobody else is so well placed. But, Fifth Sister-in-Law, we have an idea. Let me put it to you and see what you think.” “Your judgement is sound, Young Uncle. Tell me.”

“In Hangzhou, we say a matchmaker eats thirteen and a half chickens. It means the messages must be carried back and forth over and over, so everything takes time. Other marriages seem too slow to arrange; this one is moving too fast. I think it would be better to proceed more slowly.” “I understand. You're afraid that, if things move too quickly, neither will see the other clearly, and they may regret it later?” “Exactly.” “Your intention is good. But you know how impatient our lady is.” “Then you must persuade her.” Hu lowered his voice. “There's something else. From what Seventh Sister says, she seems a little determined to spite Brother Five: if he doesn't quite approve, she'll marry Gu all the more. Spite is no basis for such an important decision.” Mrs You considered, then nodded deeply. “You're right, Young Uncle. That hadn't occurred to me.”

Hu craned his neck to make sure the Seventh Lady was not listening at the wall before continuing. “She's impatient, but you mustn't give in. Let matters wait until Brother Five returns and you can all discuss them properly. Say that arranging a marriage must follow the rules, and that you first want to meet the prospective groom yourself. That should take up half a month.” “I understand. I'll find a way to delay things. But let me ask one more question. What sort of man is this Mr Gu, really?” “You had better see for yourself.” That was hardly a matchmaker's answer. In fact, Hu was beginning to regret his involvement. The Seventh Lady was too impatient and was acting partly out of defiance, while You had objections. Hu vaguely foresaw complications. His enthusiasm suddenly cooled. For that reason, he wanted to avoid the Seventh Lady and firmly declined her kind offer to escort him to Jiaxing. The next day he boarded the boat and continued down the canal. Fortunately, the journey went smoothly. They entered Zhejiang without incident, and from there to Hangzhou there would be no further danger.

CHAPTER FIFTEEN

With his anxiety relieved, Hu Xueyan once more devoted all his attention to business. There was little to do aboard the boat, so it was a good opportunity to go over his accounts. When he worked out the total, he could scarcely believe it himself. In barely half a year, as much as five hundred thousand taels had passed through his hands. With business in Hangzhou, Huzhou, and Shanghai, he had certainly built up a lively operation, and everything was going smoothly. Yet if anything unexpected happened, a tug at one thread could disturb the whole fabric. He would not fall alone: many others would be dragged down with him—first Wang Youling, then Fat Zhang, then Yu Si, and then You Laowu. At this thought, the autumn wind on the river felt especially cold. Pushing aside his abacus, he sat alone before the lamp and considered everything, growing deeply cautious. He must not rely on his quick mind and flexible methods to expand without restraint. One man's energy was limited. Anything he overlooked could open a gap that would rapidly widen; by the time he discovered it, matters might already be beyond repair.

Two conclusions followed naturally. First, he must conserve his energy and stop meddling in unnecessary disputes. Second, he must find more help. Liu Qingsheng had been a good choice and could now take charge independently. Chen Shilong had promise, but Hu had not yet made proper use of him. During the remaining journey to Hangzhou, he would teach Chen the tricks and practices of business, then put him in charge of the Shanghai affairs. Before teaching him the trade, however, he must arrange his marriage. That would also settle Hu's own relationship with A’zhu and remove another worry: a further way of conserving his energy. After considering the matter for some time, he decided how to begin.

The boat set off early the next morning. Apart from Old Zhang, who was helping at the helm in the stern, everyone was at leisure. Hu deliberately called Chen into the cabin for a talk. Since boarding, A’zhu had spent most of her time in the after cabin, saying little even when they ate together. Chen, of course, often went back to see her. Hu felt certain that she would listen carefully from there to whatever the two men said in the middle cabin. He therefore meant to appear to speak casually while addressing his words to her. “Shilong, my business has taken shape now. But one man can't eat all the rice himself: we must all lend a hand. Tell me, would you rather be in Huzhou or Shanghai?” Unaware that Hu had a settled plan and was asking deliberately, Chen thought he really was being offered a choice. Shanghai might be prosperous, but he was unsure of himself there. Huzhou was home, and he could stay close to A’zhu. Naturally he preferred Huzhou. “I'd like to get the silk firm properly established in Huzhou first.” “I knew you'd choose Huzhou.” With his back to the after cabin, Hu could make a face without A’zhu seeing. He winked emphatically at Chen, warning him that the next words had a purpose. “You can't bear to leave A’zhu!” Chen was quick to understand and gave an embarrassed smile of acknowledgment. With one man making the assertion and the other accepting it, the relationship among all three was settled in that single exchange—unless A’zhu herself came out and plainly declared that she would not marry Chen Shilong.

Listening from the after cabin, A’zhu was furious. They were treating a person like a bale of silk: a few words between them, and the transaction was complete! How could they take everything upon themselves like that? Yet, for all her angry thoughts, she remained where she was, scarcely breathing as she listened. Hu was speaking again. “My idea is that the silk firm has your father-in-law and mother-in-law there...” At this, A’zhu was astonished. Whom did he mean by “father-in-law and mother-in-law”? Listening on, she could not mistake it. Who could Chen's parents-in-law be but her own parents? Bewilderment, shame, and resentment mingled with an excitement she could not describe. Her thoughts raced like ten thousand horses, and only by repeatedly mastering herself could she make out what was being said. “To tell the truth, A’zhu's mother hasn't quite the right idea. Because I helped the family, she thinks she ought to give me her daughter in marriage as repayment. But those are separate matters. I didn't help them because I wanted their daughter.” Hypocrite! A’zhu cursed inwardly. Remembering the many ways Hu had once tried to win her affection, she felt her face grow warm and silently added, Shameless!

What followed made her feel rather better. “In all conscience,” Hu said, “do I like A’zhu? Of course I do. But I won't put her at a disadvantage. Her character is spotless, and even a young lady of a great family might not equal her in looks and qualities. Shilong, even marrying you would be beneath her.” “I know.” Chen nodded with a sense of his own unworthiness. “It's good that you know. You must be especially considerate towards her.” Chen repeated the same answer. “I know.” He kept agreeing as though he had already married her! A’zhu deeply resented it. She was puzzled too. From their tone, it sounded as though they had long since made a private bargain behind her back. She must first discover exactly what had happened, then consider how to get her own back. This time Chen spoke. “Mr Hu, what do you think I ought to do about the marriage? I have nothing—no means at all.” “You have me!” Hu answered readily. “I have three matches to arrange at present. One has already succeeded; another needs more consideration; and then there's yours. A word from me will settle Old Zhang. Your mother-in-law is easier still: she always listens to me. A’zhu is devoted to her parents. Once they agree, we needn't fear she won't.” So that was it! They meant to use her parents to pressure her. No wonder they were so confident. They thought nothing of her at all. Her first step must be to speak to her father and prevent him from agreeing too readily. Then they could stand there looking helpless!

She had scarcely settled this plan when she was startled again: Hu seemed to read her thoughts aloud. “But A’zhu is extremely proud. Kindness moves her; force doesn't. We must allow for that too. Even if she obeyed her parents unwillingly, with a thousand resentments in her heart, she wouldn't treat you particularly well afterwards. In the end, what matters most is that both people should be willing. Always remember what I've told you: A’zhu responds to kindness, not force. Give way to her in everything, and you'll have happiness all your life.” These words left a mixture of sweetness and pain in her heart. They also took the wind out of her sails: she could no longer summon any resistance. Yet she still resented being managed in this way and felt that Chen ought not to have things so easily. “My plan,” Hu continued, “is to see whether we can hold the wedding before the year's end. If there isn't time, we can complete the formal betrothal this year and have you marry into her household next year...” “Marry into her household!” Chen interrupted loudly. His voice alone showed his reluctance, and A’zhu's heart tightened as she listened. “You aren't being asked to change your surname to Zhang. The two households will simply become one. There's nothing disgraceful about it.” “As long as I don't have to change my surname.”

“Don't fail to appreciate your good fortune!” Hu deliberately pitched this at A’zhu. “Even if you wanted to change your surname, she might not think you good enough.” Chen showed his white teeth in an embarrassed smile. Through a crack in the partition, A’zhu saw it and felt a pleasant sense of triumph. “A good wife is all very well,” Hu continued, “but a man who never moves a step from her apron strings won't amount to much. With your parents-in-law at the Huzhou silk firm, they can manage it perfectly well. I want you to help me in Shanghai. Learn the foreign language properly from Old Gu, and it will serve you all your life.” “Gladly!” Chen was excited. “Mr Gu speaks it wonderfully well. I'll make sure I learn it from him.” “That's the spirit!” Hu sounded pleased. “Fortunately, the silk business will bring you back to Huzhou often. You'll have plenty of time to show A’zhu your affection.” The wretch! Her face flushed crimson. She did not know whether to sit or stand, yet dared make no sound for fear that the men would discover her eavesdropping. She tiptoed back to her berth and, with a hand over her racing heart, carefully considered all they had said.

She became so absorbed that she lost track of time. Only when Old Zhang called did she come to herself. Looking out, she saw the sun overhead: it was noon already. “Come and eat! A’zhu, what have you been doing? I haven't seen you all morning.” “I fell asleep!” She was pleased with that answer. Being asleep meant that she could not have heard Hu and Chen talking, which would make it easier to pretend ignorance when she faced them. They were pretending too. At the table, both men behaved as usual. It was Old Zhang who had much to say. The boat would stop at Deqing that afternoon, where they would part: Hu and Chen would continue south to Hangzhou, while Old Zhang took his daughter north towards home in the same boat. Naturally, various things had to be settled. They reached Deqing early that afternoon. As soon as the boat was moored, Hu invited Old Zhang ashore for a stroll. A’zhu immediately guessed that they had something concerning her to discuss. While lying in her berth that morning, she had decided that, whatever happened, she must first return to Huzhou and talk to her mother about this lifelong matter. If her father agreed now, there would be no room left for discussion. Unwilling to let others arrange everything for her, she resolved to remain beside him all day and give Hu no opportunity to speak. What could she do now? There was only one way: follow them. Surely Hu would not openly discuss matchmaking with her standing there!

“Father, I'm coming too!” she called. Naturally Hu did not want her along. Preventing it was easy; he did not even need to think. “A’zhu, would you do me a favour and pack my odds and ends?” “Yes!” Honest Old Zhang agreed. “We're changing boats. Everyone's things need sorting out. You stay here.” This gave Hu another opening. “Exactly! Shilong, go through the presents that are to be taken to Huzhou, and explain everything to A’zhu. We mustn't have any mistakes.” With that, he strode ashore with Old Zhang, deliberately leaving Chen behind to confide his feelings to her. A’zhu could scarcely contain her indignation. She felt like Monkey in Journey to the West: however she tried, she could never escape Hu Xueyan's palm. For the moment, Chen would naturally have to bear the brunt of her frustration.

“What have they gone ashore for?” she demanded angrily. Chen was naturally clever. During his time with Hu, he had also picked up many ways of handling people and situations simply by watching and listening. In something affecting his entire future, he could hardly afford carelessness. Rather than answer at once, he looked up and considered her carefully, determined to understand her attitude first. That question proved she had heard their whole conversation that morning. Now she suspected that Hu had gone ashore to discuss her marriage with her father. If so, why had she not come forward to speak that morning? Why fly into a temper now? Clearly, this was a fit of temper. He understood that too: the more he opposed her, the fiercer she would become. The best course was to leave her nothing on which to vent her anger. Smiling apologetically, he said, “I really don't know. Shall I run after them and ask?” “How obliging of you!” One wave subsided, and another rose. “And what were you and your master talking about all morning? What was all that nonsense?” With the secret out, how could he deny it? But how should he acknowledge it? A smile without an answer would annoy her; a full account would undo the effect of Hu's carefully planned words, which had reached her heart so precisely. Neither course would do. He was at a loss, and his silence seemed about to anger her again.

Urgency brought him an idea. It was like building an embankment: after days of labour by many hands, the moment came to close the final breach. Then one had to see clearly, act quickly, and seize the opportunity. At a critical closing, an official in charge might leap into the gap himself and use his body to resist the flood. Moved by such selfless courage, the others would put forth all their strength, and the work would succeed. Chen too must dare that leap if this great undertaking was to succeed. Without hesitation, he dropped onto both knees and knelt upright before her. “Since you've heard everything, I needn't say much more. A’zhu, my whole life is in your hands.” She had not expected this. Her heart raced with alarm: what if someone saw them? “What are you doing?” she demanded in a low voice. “Get up, quickly!” “Getting up is easy. Say one word, and I will.” She knew what that word was. But even if she agreed in her heart, she could not say it. She must first try frightening him. “The more you behave like this, the less I'll say! Get up, or I'll never speak to you again.” Chen had resolved to settle the matter once and for all. His voice allowed no argument. “Until you say it, I'll kneel here for ever.”

“I've never known anyone like you!” A’zhu said resentfully. “What do you want me to say?” “You know.” “Exactly! You know, and I know. Isn't that enough?” At those words, Chen's heart settled. Smiling, he asked, “Then is it really settled?” “Stop pestering!” Her face grew stern. “If you don't get up, even what's settled will be unsettled!” He could no longer refuse to obey, but he wanted one more test. “I'll get up. Give me a hand.” “I won't! Why should I pull you up?” She drew a finger down her cheek to shame him. “‘A man's knees are worth gold.’ Apparently yours are worth nothing.” “For the sake of that gold beneath my knees, help me up!” As he spoke, he held out his hand.

A’zhu truly meant to ignore him, yet her right hand seemed independent of her intentions. Somehow it reached out, and once Chen had taken it, he would not let go. Rising, he kept hold of her hand and sat beside her. His other hand reached swiftly for the window. With a clatter, the wooden shutter closed, plunging the cabin into darkness. “What are you doing?” she asked sharply but quietly. “Nothing! I only want to kiss you.” “Don't you dare!” Before she had finished, he ignored her objection and became more intimate than she was prepared to accept. She felt embarrassed, anxious, and conflicted. Beyond the dark cabin it was still broad daylight, and the thought of being discovered made her deeply uneasy. “Let go,” she finally managed to say, turning her head aside. “Just one more kiss!” “Again?” she said angrily. “Don't make me afraid of you!” It was a serious warning. Chen stopped, released her, and helped her sit up. “Shall I open the window?” he asked gently. “Of course.” She reached out and opened it herself. As the light came in, she quickly withdrew into a corner hidden from anyone outside, smoothed her hair, straightened her clothes, and sat with closed lips and lowered eyes, looking as though she had been hurt.

“A’zhu...” “Don't pester me again!” she interrupted. “Behave yourself and talk sensibly, or kindly leave.” Chen said nothing. He merely smiled and kept looking at her, making her both embarrassed and annoyed. “Would you stop staring at me like that?” She gave him a reproachful glance. “It's not as though you don't know me.” “I'm sorry,” he said with a smile. “I can't bear to stop looking.” The words stirred something different in her heart, and her tone softened. “You can keep your affection in your heart. Must you display it all on your face? You're thick-skinned and don't mind being laughed at, but you ought to think of someone else.” Chen looked away. Almost at once, however, his gaze returned. Without sight of her face, he felt as though he had mislaid something important and could not be at ease until he found it again.

During this brief silence, A’zhu felt her heart grow calmer. Touching her face, she found it no longer so hot. “I want to ask you some serious questions,” she said. “Whether you answer honestly is a matter for your conscience.” “Very well!” Chen answered firmly. “I'll answer in good conscience. Ask me.” “You and your master discussed me long ago?” “Yes, long ago.” “What did you say?” “That's hard to explain. We said so much that I don't know where to begin.” “Then heaven knows how many times you've plotted about me!” Recalling the hateful way they had disposed of her privately, she complained, “You could probably sell me to a foreign country without my knowing it.” “Who would dare plot against you?” Chen assumed a solemn air. “I'd be the first to object!”

“Hmph!” A’zhu curled her lip. “You're such a good man! If you're so good, why haven't you let a word slip all these days?” “It wasn't that I wouldn't. I didn't dare.” “Why not?” “I was afraid you'd reject me outright. After that, it would be hard to say anything more.” On reflection, that was probably true. But she also realised that, although her girl friends considered her formidable, she was no match for Hu or Chen. If they really intended anything heartless, they could manoeuvre her into a position with no escape. What, then, could she rely on? Chen's heart. Only by winning that could she feel secure. She must combine kindness with firmness. Consideration mattered, but she must also establish rules and refuse to give way. That was for the future, however. For now, she must learn more about what concerned her. “What exactly did Mr Hu say about me?” To Chen, “Mr Hu” was an entirely new form of address from her. He had never heard her call him that before. The change suggested both that her relationship with Hu had reached its end and that she would follow her husband's lead, using the same address Chen used. This understanding delighted him, and once again he stared at her with a foolish smile. She had never seen such an expression on Hu's face. Like the smile of a mischievous big boy, it had a charm of its own. This time she felt like reaching out to touch his face.

“What did you just ask?” Chen suddenly said. Her thoughts elsewhere, A’zhu was startled. But in such situations she had a way of turning the accusation back on the other person. “Look at you!” she complained. “You forget everything the moment it's said. How can you claim to care about me?” “I'm sorry!” He smiled apologetically. “I'm so happy that I've rather lost my head.” During this delay, she remembered her question and repeated it. “I asked what Mr Hu said about me.” “You heard for yourself! A thousand words, all meaning one thing: you're wonderful.” He was referring to her eavesdropping. She could hardly deny it. “I mean at other times. Surely he's said more than that.”

“Don't inquire into that any more.” Chen waved a hand. “Let's talk about ourselves.” “Yes!” The word escaped her, followed by another question. “What have they gone ashore to discuss? Me?” “Certainly.” “Then why did you play innocent just now and say you didn't know?” “Then was then, and now is now. Now I needn't call you A’zhu. I can call you my wife!” “Shame on you!” she said, blushing. “Don't be so embarrassing.” “It's really extraordinary!” Chen sounded full of wonder. “First I called you Miss Zhang, then A’zhu, and now my wife. So much has changed in only a few months!” Thinking it over, she felt the same. Life was astonishing. From the time she had met Hu to this moment, how many new and strange experiences had she had? These six months had certainly been eventful.

“I was thinking,” Chen continued, “a person depends entirely on luck. Meeting Mr Hu was the day my luck began.” “Don't put it like that! Nobody can depend on luck alone. Luck lasts only a while; you must always try to improve yourself.” There was something admonishing in her words, and Chen found them a little disagreeable. Then he reflected that she spoke this way precisely because she already thought of them as husband and wife, sharing the same fortunes. His slight resentment quickly disappeared. He said no more, and neither did she. Their silence did not mean that they had nothing to say. As they looked at one another, his lingering gaze and her swiftly averted glances conveyed more than words could tell.

“It's dark!” A’zhu exclaimed. “Why hasn't Father come back?” “They must be drinking in town. It'll be a while yet.” “Are you hungry?” “I'm not. Are you?” “Neither am I. But...” She stopped, thinking. If she was not hungry, she was not hungry. What could that “but” mean? Chen could not resist asking. “But what?” “Let's go outside.” A’zhu stood up. “What sort of scene is this, the two of us sitting here in the dark?” Chen would have preferred to remain close beside her in the darkness, talking softly. To oblige her, however, he answered against his wishes, “Yes, let's go out, light the lamp, and wait for them.”

In the middle cabin, they lit the kerosene lamp and found four dishes, four sets of cups and chopsticks, and a pot of wine already on the square table. When had the boatman come in? Only one partition away, they had known nothing about it. It was astonishing. Thinking a little further, A’zhu blushed again. “Look!” she reproached Chen quietly. “They must have heard everything we said in there.” He understood too. While laying out the meal, the boatman must have heard their private conversation in the after cabin and chosen not to disturb them. He had left the dishes without lighting the lamp or calling them to eat, allowing events to take their course. Evidently he was a very tactful man. “We said nothing we need be ashamed of. It doesn't matter if they heard,” Chen said reassuringly. “They'll find out sooner or later anyway, and there's no need to hide it. If you simply take no notice, like the Seventh Lady, people won't tease you.”

Mention of the Seventh Lady aroused both concern and curiosity in A’zhu, along with an unpleasant feeling she could not describe. “Let me ask you something. How do you feel when she keeps calling you A’long?” Before considering his own feelings, Chen detected a trace of jealousy in the question and immediately became cautious. “If she chooses to call me that, I can only answer. To tell the truth...” The words were on his lips, but he felt they would be unkind. He waved a hand. “Oh, let's not discuss it.” “Why?” A’zhu pressed him. “Why not?” “It's nothing to do with us. Why talk about it?” “There's no harm in talking.” Seeing how intent she was, Chen had to answer, though against his conscience. “Honestly, it makes me rather uncomfortable.” She smiled faintly, showing that the reply pleased her, and asked no more.

Chen felt as though a weight had been lifted. He helped A’zhu with the lamp, and they sat opposite each other to eat. Ordinarily each had attended to their own needs. Even if he cared for her, he could hardly show his attentions openly. Now things were different. He served her rice and selected dishes for her, laughingly calling himself a “big-footed maid”—a Hangzhou expression he had heard used to mock a man who liked waiting on women. The meal lasted an hour. Chen talked a great deal about one thing and another, though seldom about himself, and A’zhu listened with absorbing interest. “They're back!” he suddenly called. She turned and saw two lanterns approaching slowly. At once she became anxious. What expression should she wear when facing her father and Hu? Naturally, she could not hide in the after cabin. All she could do was try to look calm, clear the table, and respond as circumstances required once they came aboard. Chen hurried out, helped the boatman lay the gangplank, and supported Old Zhang across. When he turned to help Hu, Hu squeezed his hand firmly, signalling that the great matter had been settled.

“Well!” Hu began teasing as soon as he entered. “How long have you two been eating this meal?” “We've been waiting for you all this time.” Seeing both men's red faces and smelling the wine on them, A’zhu issued a warning in advance. “Don't come talking nonsense because you're drunk!” “We shan't!” Hu replied with an unmistakably drunken air. “No nonsense. Serious matters.” “What serious matters can you discuss when you've been drinking? I'll make a strong pot of tea. Have some and go to sleep—that would be best.” She called the boatman to clear away the food, then took the porcelain teapot to make tea. Though outside the cabin, her thoughts remained within it. She listened for what Hu would say, but heard Old Zhang's voice instead. “Shilong!” “Yes!” Chen answered emphatically. That call and response alone made her anxious. One hand held a handful of tea leaves; the other was damp with nervous sweat. What would her father say? Yet he fell silent again, leaving his daughter more bewildered and uneasy than ever.

“Old Zhang,” Hu said, breaking the unbearable silence, “you talk to A’zhu. I'll talk to Shilong.” “Yes, yes! I don't know what to say to him. You do it!” Then Old Zhang called, “A’zhu! A’zhu!” From his tone, her father must already have agreed. This was something to discuss quietly, she thought. Why shout it out? A little annoyed, she answered loudly, “I'm making tea!” “Come out when you've finished. I have something to tell you.” “Can't you come in and tell me?” “I'm coming.” He left the cabin. He had drunk rather too much and stumbled unsteadily as he walked.

A’zhu hurried to support him. “You ought to drink less of that yellow stuff! Why have you had so much?” “Because I'm happy!” Old Zhang answered. “Life only seems worthwhile on an evening like this.” His fatherly love showed in every word. She was moved and felt truly fortunate, though her reply naturally retained the affectionate complaining tone of a daughter accustomed to indulgence. “Drunken talk from the first word! I've never heard you speak of ‘life’ before. All that elegant language is embarrassing.” Despite her words, she remained devoted to him. She helped him sit down, brewed the tea, and brought him the first cup. Catching her hand and looking up, Old Zhang said, “A’zhu, you must thank Mr Hu.” “Why?” “He's arranged a good match for you.” Lowering his voice to say it, he nodded repeatedly. “This is the best way. The very best.”

She found it rather funny but could hardly show it. Her feelings were contradictory. On the one hand, she wanted her father to stop before he embarrassed her further. On the other, she wanted to hear exactly what Hu had told him. Naturally, Old Zhang went on. “A’zhu,” he said solemnly, “Mr Hu is the matchmaker, and I've given him my consent. I hope you'll live happily together and grow old side by side.” After all this, whom did he mean? Although she knew, and knew too that her father was no speaker, she still felt anxious. She wanted to hear the name “Chen Shilong” before she could be at ease. What she said, however, was full of bashfulness. “Father, I say you're talking drunkenly, and still you won't admit it. Enough! Don't say any more.” “Yes. You understand already, so it doesn't matter if I say nothing. But marriage is an important business. I ought to tell you.” He was rambling and hardly reaching the point. Hu, outside, could no longer bear it. “Will you two come out? I have a few things to say.” “Yes, yes!” Old Zhang called back. “You had better say them after all.” He rose and pulled his daughter along. Too shy to come out willingly, she could not resist his insistence and at last entered the middle cabin. Her lively eyes passed briefly over Chen's face, then withdrew. She stood by the doorway with her head lowered.

“A’zhu, you've always been perfectly natural. There's no need for embarrassment,” Hu said. “I've arranged the match, your father has agreed, and Chen could wish for nothing better. We're waiting only for your consent. Then I'll have him bow to your father and establish the relationship. Tell us plainly: do you like Shilong or not?” “I don't know.” Her answer was loud and quick. She turned her face aside, looking almost resentful. “You must be too embarrassed to say. Then give us a sign. If you don't like him, go outside. If you do, sit here.” What a tormentor Hu was! She cursed him inwardly. Naturally she did not want to leave, yet she could not bring herself to sit. She could only continue pretending not to understand. “I don't know what you mean.” “Saying you don't understand means you do!” Hu laughed. “Very well. We've had our joke. Now I'll ask you seriously. If you feel too shy to tell me, tell your father and let him report it. Shilong is my pupil, so I am both the matchmaker and the elder representing him. Marriage is for life, no childish game. Whatever there is to say should be made clear now. What do you require of the bridegroom's family?” This showed Hu's experience. He knew that the couple were deeply attached and willing, and that his services to the Zhang family gave him considerable influence as matchmaker. Even so, he asked clearly, so that the bride's family would have no grievance afterwards.

Old Zhang thought the question unnecessary. “Nothing, nothing!” he said, waving his hands. “How could we make demands? Whatever our honoured matchmaker says, we shall follow.” “It's precisely because you think that way that I must ask.” Hu turned again. “A’zhu, this concerns your whole life. You mustn't be embarrassed. Tell me what you want, and I'll see whether it can be done. If it can't, I shall have nothing more to do with the matter.” This was a way of putting pressure on her from the opposite direction. If she really refused to speak, he might say he would withdraw. Then a happy prospect could fall through, leaving a deadlock that was difficult to resolve. Alarm overcame her shyness. With her head down, she said softly, “I don't ask anything. I only want him to try to get ahead and never change his feelings.” “Did you hear that, Shilong? If you refuse to improve yourself and become idle and self-indulgent, or if prosperity later leads you to bring home a concubine and upset A’zhu, you'll be deliberately disgracing me as your matchmaker.” “Time reveals a man's heart, Mr Hu. You shall see.” “Good. I believe you. A’zhu, be at ease. With me supervising him, he won't dare neglect his future. As for a change of heart, if anything like that happens, tell me. I'll stand up for you.” She wanted to thank him but felt too shy. Instead, she looked at him and nodded slightly to show her gratitude.

“Very well! Shilong, bow to your father-in-law. You shall use the new form of address from today.” A’zhu hurried away at once. Old Zhang repeatedly protested that it was unnecessary, but Chen knelt, touched his forehead firmly to the floor, and called with a broad smile, “Father!” “Please get up!” Old Zhang was both delighted and uneasy, grinning as he clumsily tried to help him rise. Chen stood, then knelt again to bow to Hu. At Hu's instruction, he fetched a presentation box. Hu had planned ahead and bought four kinds of jewellery in Shanghai: a pair of jadeite earrings, a pair of gold bracelets, two pearl flowers, and four gemstone rings. Together they must have been worth five or six hundred taels. They were the betrothal gifts for the bride's family. Old Zhang naturally felt overwhelmed, but there was no need for formal refusals. After thanking Hu, he called loudly, “Come and look! You're fortunate indeed. Your mother has never worn jewellery as fine as this.”

Hidden in the after cabin and peering through a crack, A’zhu was already deeply moved. At those words from her father, something swept through her heart, and hot tears suddenly covered her face. She could not suppress her sobs. “Why, what's the matter...?” “Don't question her.” Hu waved a hand, interrupting Old Zhang. “She's probably feeling sorry for her mother.” The words touched A’zhu's heart exactly. Whether she felt gratitude towards her parents or towards Hu, she could not have said. She simply lay down on her berth and wept. The more she cried, the more relieved and confident she became. When she had finished, she wiped her eyes and walked openly into the cabin. She was still too embarrassed to smile, however, and sat with a solemn face, waiting for her father or Hu to speak so that she could join in. Hu obliged. “A’zhu, where's the tea you made us?” “Oh dear, I'd forgotten!” She rose. “I'm afraid it's cold.” “Cold tea is just what we want. Bring it here.” She fetched it and poured a cup for Hu, then one for her father. Chen sat shyly to one side, looking very much like a bridegroom. After a little hesitation, she poured him a cup too. She neither carried it over nor spoke, merely pushing it towards the edge of the table to indicate that he should take it himself.

“Look for yourself. Do you like them?” Hu opened the presentation box. Faced with the glitter of pearls and gems, A’zhu was astonished. Were these really hers? She could scarcely believe it. “Never display your wealth!” Old Zhang's long experience of the world made him genuinely uneasy. “Put them away carefully. You can look when you get home.” She had to obey, though reluctantly. Closing the box, she lowered her head and said softly, “Mr Hu, thank you.” “A mere trifle!” Hu smiled. “When Shilong prospers, he'll buy you diamonds.” Old Zhang too was moved, and his words now came more readily. “Shilong, you must never forget how well Mr Hu has treated you both. You must repay him.” Chen nodded earnestly. While he was trying to find words that would express his gratitude, Hu spoke first. “That isn't entirely right, Old Zhang. There's no question of repayment. I've asked you to help me, and naturally I regard you as family. We share good fortune and bad. If we run the business well, everyone benefits. Now...” He gave Old Zhang a meaningful glance. “Let's go to bed. A’zhu and Shilong can sort out our things so that we can part tomorrow morning.”

He deliberately gave them a chance to be alone and exchange a few heartfelt words. Chen took a lamp and saw the men to their berths. Returning, he first shut the cabin window, then placed a mirror on the table. “Do try on the jewellery,” he said gently. Nothing could have pleased her more. She opened the box and first put on the jadeite earrings shaped like autumn leaves. Then she slipped a gold bracelet onto each wrist and put on a ruby ring. Only the pearl flowers could not be worn: they belonged in a woman's hair bun, and she still wore her hair in a braid. Seated opposite, Chen watched with a delighted smile. A’zhu had never looked particularly like a girl from a modest household. Adorned with jewellery, her oval face seemed still more gracious and distinguished. She did not look at all like a boatman's daughter. Turning this way and that before the mirror, she suddenly stopped smiling. Slowly, she removed the ornaments and put each away. Chen was puzzled. What had made her lose interest?

“You...” he began awkwardly. “You don't seem very happy.” “It's not that I'm unhappy. It's a pity, that's all.” “What's a pity?” he asked anxiously. “Surely you don't think a woman like you is unworthy of wearing such things?” “That isn't what I mean. ‘A capable woman doesn't keep wearing the clothes she married in.’ It's a pity you didn't buy these for me.” Her words struck him deeply. His thoughts turned over and over: how could he prove himself worthy of her? After remaining lost in thought for some time, he finally forced out an answer. “You have ambition, and so do I. But unless you're willing to share a few years of hardship with me, I shan't be able to buy you jewellery like this one day.” “Do you think I can't bear hardship? Wait and see!” “I believe you.” Chen smiled. “In truth, how could I bear to make you suffer? As things are, the business is going very smoothly, and we should live comfortably. We owe it all to Mr Hu's help.” “We must never forget how we began.” At last A’zhu voiced a heartfelt thought. “Our first duty is to look after every part of his business. Only then shall we deserve what he's done for us.” The night was late and still. Even though they spoke quietly, Hu could just hear them from his berth. He felt that he had managed this affair extremely well. Pleased with the result and proud of himself, he fell peacefully asleep, his mind free of care.

On reaching Hangzhou, Hu Xueyan stopped briefly at home, then went straight to Fukang. Chen Shilong had already brought the luggage there and was waiting. There was a great deal of it, but everything was a present for someone. With Liu Qingsheng's help, the gifts were sorted, and one of the bank's errand clerks was sent with Chen to deliver them from house to house. Hu used the interval to hear Liu's report. “Mr Hu, please examine the accounts first,” Liu said gravely, bringing a pile of ledgers. “No hurry, no hurry. Give me a general account first.” “Please look at the books before we talk.” His insistence suggested that the books themselves would show how business had gone. Hu nodded and began with the deposits. What he saw astonished him. There were many names such as Zhang Debiao, Li Desheng, Wang Zhankui, and Zhao Huchen, with sums ranging from a few hundred to more than ten thousand taels. Nine out of ten entries bore the brief annotation: “Long-term; no interest.” “Well, well!” Hu exclaimed. “Fukang really is going to prosper! How did we acquire so many accounts?” With restrained pride, Liu said, “Please look at this entry too.” He turned to a payment: “Twenty-fifth day of the eighth month: paid out eleven thousand taels, principal standing in Luo Shangde's name. Interest waived.” “Oh! So Luo has withdrawn his deposit?” “No. Luo Shangde was killed in action. In effect, I returned the money. I don't know whether I did the right thing...”

Liu explained what had happened. On the twenty-fifth of the eighth month, two officers had come to ask whether it was true that Luo had deposited money at Fukang. They said he had been killed in action but still had relatives in Sichuan. If the deposit existed, they wished to withdraw it and send it home. Luo's passbook was in Liu's keeping. Had he denied the account's existence, there would have been no other witness. But he refused to act that way. He acknowledged it at once, produced the passbook, and verified the amount. He made clear, however, that he could not pay out the deposit on the two men's unsupported statement. “What should we do, then?” “I know that Mr Luo was a friend of Mr Liu Er at the governor's office. Mr Liu Er and your commanding officer must jointly give Fukang written authorisation,” Liu replied. “Provided Luo really has been killed in action and you gentlemen accept responsibility, Fukang will pay immediately.” The two officers brought Liu Er that same day, and a joint receipt was signed. Liu immediately produced eleven thousand taels and offered to calculate the interest as well, but they naturally refused anything more. The following day, Zhang Debiao, Li Desheng, and the others began coming to the bank.

Hu was exceedingly pleased by the story. “Qingsheng, Fukang's reputation is made! You handled it brilliantly.” “To be honest,” Liu said, feeling much comforted himself, “I learned the method from you. To deal honestly, one need only hold firm to one's principles. But to make customers know of that honesty and speak of it everywhere requires some thought. I had a sudden idea and managed to seize the opportunity.” “Exactly. Seizing opportunities is the highest art in business. I'm delighted that you can do it. Qingsheng, I haven't enough assistants. You must take more off my hands. From now on, the bank's business is all yours to manage. I shall leave everything to your direction.” Alongside his excitement, Liu felt overwhelming apprehension. “I'm afraid I may not be able to carry such a burden.” “Don't worry. Put more thought into things and work them out before acting. A little risk doesn't matter. Everyone can do business that involves no risk. How could that put you ahead? As long as it's worthwhile, go ahead boldly.”

“That's difficult to judge. What counts as worthwhile and what doesn't? People see things differently.” “In life, people seek either profit or a good name. Business is the same. Whether a risk is worth taking depends on whether you can gain one of the two.” Hu paused and pointed to the ledger. “Take this loan. I know the borrower is a rice merchant, using the money for trade. You must establish where he's sending his rice. If it's going somewhere that hasn't fallen, that's all right. If it's going to the Longhairs, you mustn't lend. Why? If the loan goes bad, people will say, ‘Who asked you to help the Longhairs? You deserved to lose your money.’ You lose both profit and reputation. Naturally, that risk isn't worth taking.” Liu nodded firmly. “I understand. There must always be a way to fall back. Even if something goes wrong, we must be able to justify ourselves openly.” “Exactly, Qingsheng!” Hu patted his shoulder. “You understand completely. Whatever business we do, that is our principle: if we fail, we must have an explanation. If others can forgive us, we still have a chance to begin again. Defeated, but not destroyed!” Liu repeated the phrase inwardly several times and grasped much from it. They then discussed plans for expanding the business. Since Hu could remain in Hangzhou only a few days, delay might leave matters unsettled. He therefore gave an immediate decision, yes or no, on each proposal.

In the midst of their deliberations, someone came in calling, “Second Brother! Second Brother!” The form of address could belong only to Ji Heling. Hu hurried out to greet him. His face glowed, and his queue was black and glossy. He wore a crisp, lined robe of purplish-brown xianchun cloth beneath a black satin baturu waistcoat, with a row of coral fastening buttons level with the shoulders. His rolled sleeves revealed snowy-white silk cuffs. In his left hand he turned a pair of walnuts; in his right he held a short pipe of spotted bamboo mounted with jade. He looked every inch the fashionable young gentleman. Not a trace remained of his former careless scholar's appearance. “Elder Brother!” Hu laughed. “You look more than ten years younger. I hardly recognised you.” “It's all Ruiyun!” Ji could not suppress his delight. “After dressing up the children, she insists on dressing me up too. If we never did anything useless, how would we pass our allotted years? But never mind that. I've been ordered to invite you. Ruiyun says we're to give you a welcome-home dinner tonight. There won't be much to eat, but you must come.” “Certainly. Only I may not be very early.” “You mean to call on Mr Xuexuan first? There's no need. I've invited him too. He'll meet you at my house, and you can leave together after dinner.” “Excellent. That saves me a great deal of trouble.” Hu smiled. “How is Miss Rui?” “That goes without saying. In a word, I'm endlessly grateful.”

“Mr Xuexuan wrote to tell me about the Xincheng affair, but without much detail. I've been concerned about it in Shanghai. Has an arrangement been made for you?” Hu asked. “Yes. I was just going to tell you all about it.” Ji hesitated. “But it's a long story. Once I begin, there'll be no end. Let's do this: I still have an errand to run. Ruiyun wants me to buy a few pots of chrysanthemums. I'll leave my chair here for you to come in later. Try to arrive early, so that we can talk properly before Mr Xuexuan comes.” Seeing his cheerful expression and fine clothes, and now discovering that he maintained his own chair-bearers, Hu could tell that matters were going reasonably well. Reassured, he nodded and promised to come as soon as possible. After dealing with several urgent matters at Fukang, he took the chair straight to Ji's house. Ji had only recently returned and was wearing short working clothes while directing a gardener in arranging the chrysanthemums. “Go inside and sit down,” he said on seeing Hu. “I'll wash my hands and join you.” Zhang Gui came to receive the guest, exceptionally respectful and warmly attentive. Bowing as he led the way and inquiring after Hu's well-being, he took him directly to the rear hall, where they met Ruiyun.

“Second Master!” she said with a smile, using the title because Hu and Ji were sworn brothers. After studying him briefly, she added, “You've grown a little thinner. The journey must have been tiring. But your spirits and complexion are just the same.” “You seem to have filled out.” Hu smiled. “Are you happy with life here?” “Thanks to you, Second Master.” She called inside, “Heguan, bring your younger brothers and sisters to greet Second Uncle!” “Yes!” came a sweet voice. Danhe led the little troop out. They toddled forward in clean clothes and stopped as soon as she did. “Greet him—Second Uncle,” Ruiyun told her. Danhe spoke first, then instructed the others to follow. Seeing this, Hu admired Ruiyun enormously. She had followed the principle of catching the bandits' chief first. Somehow, she had won over the most mischievous child, Danhe, so completely that the rest had settled down too. “Where's the eldest?” he asked. “I've sent him to join another household's school,” Ji answered as he entered. The two youngest immediately rushed to him. Hu truly envied Ji, and felt deeply comforted as well. He took Danhe's hand, asked her all manner of questions, and did not let go for a long time. “Enough, enough!” Ruiyun said loudly. “Follow your second sister inside. Don't bother Second Uncle.”

After sending the children away, Ruiyun excused herself and returned to the kitchen. Ji then described what had happened since they parted. The policy for Xincheng—conciliation first, force afterwards if needed—had been correct. The local gentry admired his courage in going alone into the endangered county town and recognised his sincerity. They willingly cooperated, finding a way to persuade the leader, the “bandit monk” Huixin, to come to the county office and surrender. A snake cannot move without its head: the disorganised followers scattered completely. The whole affair had taken no more than half a month. When Ji returned successful, Wang naturally treated him with special respect and warmth, offering him five hundred taels from his own purse in gratitude. Ji refused, and Wang insisted. “In the end, we almost quarrelled,” Ji said. “Then I thought of your close friendship with him and our own brotherhood. On the strength of that indirect connection, I accepted.” Hu nodded. “You are scrupulous indeed about what to accept and what to decline. There's no harm in using a little of his money. But leave that aside. What about a substantive appointment? Mr Xuexuan said he would take responsibility for securing you a permanent post. Where does that stand now?”

“It's rather exasperating.” Ji hastened to add, “Though I have nothing to complain of in Mr Xuexuan. He recommended me as acting magistrate of Gui'an, but Governor Huang refused. Then he proposed that I take over the Sea Transport Bureau, and Huang refused that too, saying we must wait for the decision on the recommendations for reward.” When a major local undertaking—suppressing disorder, repairing waterways, or changing grain transport from the canal to the sea—had been completed and reported to the throne, it was customary to recommend rewards for those who had contributed. Such recommendations might be public or confidential. Naturally, the confidential kind was more valuable. “Governor Huang has put me forward publicly, whereas Mr Xuexuan has received a confidential recommendation...” “That's most unfair,” Hu interrupted. “Could there be something underhand behind it?” “Ah!” Ji slapped his thigh. “Nobody is sharper than you. One of the governor's clerical commissioners asked me for two thousand taels. I don't know whether he wants it for himself or on Huang's behalf. In any case, even if I had the money—which I don't—I wouldn't pour it down that dog's hole.” “What does Mr Xuexuan say?” “He knows nothing of it. I haven't told him. If I did, he'd certainly pay the two thousand for me. Why should I put myself under yet another obligation to him?”

There were few men of such unbending integrity left in official life. Hu felt a deep respect for him. Yet although Ji might take that view, Hu himself ought to explain matters to Wang. They must secure the Sea Transport Bureau post somehow, even if the money had to be poured down the dog's hole after all. “Elder Brother, leave this alone,” he said. “Mr Xuexuan will have an answer. Let me speak to him.” “There's really no need to force matters.” Ji shook his head. “I'm tired of the changing warmth and coldness of official society. I'm quite comfortable as I am. We can think again when the five hundred taels are spent. Surely nobody need starve in this world.” “A true scholar's spirit!” Hu laughed. “Without boasting, I could afford to keep you in your present style. But you certainly wouldn't agree, and I wouldn't want you idle either. A comfortable life is not enough to satisfy a man.” Ji nodded deeply. “Exactly. I have plans of my own, of course. If I can't make my way in Zhejiang, I mean to return to Hubei and organise local militia.” “There's no need. We have ample scope here in Zhejiang. When Mr Xuexuan comes, we'll discuss it properly.”

As the saying went, speak of Cao Cao and Cao Cao arrives. Wang was now a familiar visitor. Zhang Gui had barely announced him before he came through the door, calling as he walked, “Xueyan! Xueyan!” “Mr Xuexuan!” Hu went to meet him and greeted him with clasped hands. “I've been waiting for you every day. Now you're here, I can finally fix a day to return to Huzhou.” “Master!” Ruiyun called, still using the form of address she had used in Wang's household. “Please come inside. Let's have dinner. Mr Hu must be hungry too.” “Yes, yes! Let's eat and drink,” Wang replied happily. “Today we must have a few good cups.” They went into the rear hall, where the table was already covered with dishes. There was Ruiyun's speciality, chicken in red fermented-rice lees, and an ingenious rich hotpot combining fish offal and bean curd in the style of Ji's home region with Hangzhou's fish-head-and-bean-curd dish. It was just the thing for an evening of west wind and falling leaves.

“This is the foreign liquor Mr Hu sent.” Holding a bottle of brandy, Ruiyun smiled. “I don't even know how to open it.” “Give it to me.” Ji took the bottle, then quite naturally laid both hands on her shoulders. “This saves trouble. It doesn't need warming. Go back to the kitchen. There's no hurry with the dishes. Come and drink a toast later.” He spoke with gentle affection, finding nothing improper in it, but Ruiyun was embarrassed. With a shy smile and a reproachful glance, she murmured, “You do talk too much!” Wang looked at Hu. As soon as she disappeared, he burst out laughing. “Xueyan, now I understand your pleasure. To see all lovers united in marriage is a delightful thing indeed.” The couplet at the Temple of the Old Man under the Moon by West Lake expressed the wish that all lovers should be united. Ji laughed. “An excellent change of one word—from wishing to seeing! With that spirit, Mr Xuexuan, you will always find joy.” “You are too kind. Both of you have helped me greatly. Today I'll borrow another's flowers to offer to the Buddha and express a little of my gratitude.” The three emptied their cups. Brandy was unlike Shaoxing wine. Ji drank too quickly, choked, and coughed until his face and neck were red. Hearing him from the kitchen, Ruiyun hurried out, asking what had happened while patting his back. Wang and Hu exchanged another smile.

“And your Miss Zhu?” Wang asked Hu. “Now it's your turn.” “That too is something to be pleased about...” “What?” Wang interrupted with concern. “Has the match failed?” “It's still a happy outcome for A’zhu. But leave that aside. As for Wanxiang, I sent someone to see her in Shanghai. She's still in Meijia Lane and hasn't suffered any serious fright. She'd like to come for a visit. What do you think?” “We'll see later.” Wang's expression was cool; he plainly did not wish to discuss it. Ji had meant to ask who Wanxiang was, but took the hint and remained silent. Naturally, Hu did not pursue the matter either. He turned the conversation towards his own acquaintances and business in Shanghai.

There were two matters to discuss: the foreign guns he had bought on Wang's behalf, and the plan for the sea-going grain shipments to leave by Liuhe, with You Laowu handling the lighterage. The latter was connected with Ji's future employment. An idea came to Hu: he could present the proposal as Ji's own, demonstrating that he possessed exceptional ability in this field too. He therefore began with the guns. “Mr Xuexuan, how is the Huzhou militia getting on?” The question delighted Wang. “Very well! Of all the militia organisations in the province, Huzhou's is proceeding most smoothly. To be fair, the credit belongs to Zhao Jingxian.” He turned to Ji. “His abilities are no less than yours. I must introduce you sometime.” “I've heard that he is both worthy and capable, and have long wanted to know him. An introduction from you would be a great pleasure.” Contentedly, Ji raised his cup and drained it.

“Mr Xuexuan,” Hu said, bringing the conversation back, “I've bought a consignment of foreign guns for you.” He described the whole transaction. “Then I must drink a full cup too!” Wang was delighted. “Xueyan, you've done splendidly. Only the other day, the governor was telling me that troops must be good, not merely numerous, and that a man who means to do his work well must first sharpen his tools. Gong Zhenlin and his son have experience in making cannon, but unfortunately they cannot make guns. Now that we can buy foreign guns, our defences will benefit enormously. Tomorrow I'll call on the governor and work out a comprehensive arrangement. The more foreign guns, the better.” “That's for later. What about this consignment?” “Huzhou will buy it, naturally. Quite apart from what these guns may achieve in future, their immediate effect on the militia's morale will be important. I can hardly imagine how pleased Zhao Jingxian will be when he hears.”

“Mr Xuexuan,” Ji intervened, “if Huzhou is determined to obtain them, that isn't the way to proceed. You must guard against the governor keeping this consignment for himself. Better say nothing for the moment.” “When should I tell him, then?” “I suggest the following steps,” Ji answered deliberately. “First, obtain a transport permit for the foreign guns from the provincial treasurer. Then collect them and send them to Huzhou. Only afterwards tell Governor Huang. By that time they'll have been distributed. Surely he couldn't order every one called back for his own personal troops?” “Exactly, exactly!” Wang agreed. “With the two of you advising me, nothing can go wrong. Come, let's drink!”

Over their wine, Hu explained another advantage of buying the guns: it would draw the British merchants towards them and make them less inclined to deal with the Taiping leaders Hong and Yang. Ji listened silently, thinking of Hu's interests. When the conversation paused, he offered a reminder. “Xueyan, shouldn't you discuss the price of this consignment with Mr Xuexuan?” Before Hu could answer, Wang suddenly recalled something. “That reminds me. The militia is under official supervision but organised locally. The locality raises its own funds and keeps charge of them. Huzhou is wealthy, its people are enthusiastic, and the militia has ample money. I had meant to ask Zhao Jingxian to deposit the public funds at Fukang, but feared a polite refusal that would embarrass me, so I never raised it. Now these guns will be just the catalyst we need. Zhao will be grateful to you, and I can speak easily. As for the price, whatever you say will be accepted. The rebate is yours, naturally.” Hu's greatest difficulties were a shortage of assistants and insufficient ready funds. A large deposit from the Huzhou militia would be like water to a fish: nothing could be better. With substantial business in prospect, he would not chase a small profit. “No,” he said. “I want this done handsomely. Let the rebate go into the public funds or be divided among Jingxian's staff. I'll perform the service for nothing.” “There's no need to work for nothing,” Wang replied. “Leave this to me. I'll speak to Zhao Jingxian.”

One of the two matters had been settled. The other had to begin with Ji Heling. “Mr Xuexuan,” Hu asked directly, “what has happened about Heling?” Wang lowered the glass he had almost raised to his lips and sighed dispiritedly. “It has been keeping me awake at night. I was waiting to discuss it with you. I don’t know what the governor intends. It looks very much as though he means to destroy the bridge after crossing the river. How can I face Brother Heling?” He described his successive approaches to Huang Zonghan. He had first made a request; when no definite answer came, he had submitted a recommendation. That too had achieved nothing, so he had argued the case forcefully. Still there had been no result. “Xueyan, you judge these things more accurately than anyone. What do you make of it?” “There is no death without a ghost at work,” Hu said bluntly. “There must be something underhand behind this.” “I thought so too. I asked the men handling the correspondence whether some little inducement was needed. They answered quite sincerely that everything depended on the governor. They did not dare accept anything yet, for fear of taking a favor and then failing to accomplish the business. Once Mr Ji’s appointment order was issued, of course, they would expect him to treat them to a celebratory drink. Xueyan, surely that says all there is to say?”

Comparing Wang’s account with Ji’s, Hu understood at once. The two thousand taels were wanted by Huang Zonghan, who was unwilling to have Wang supply them. That explained these answers. If the money were merely for the correspondence staff, why would they care whether it belonged to Wang or Ji, so long as the silver was good? Hu understood, but would not reveal it. If he did, Wang would still feel guilty that he had failed to do enough for Ji, even if he paid. And Ji, having declared that he would not buy an office, might bring the whole affair to an impasse. Hu therefore smiled. “Let them play their ghostly tricks. I am a Maoshan Taoist who specializes in catching such ghosts. Just watch me!” “And how do you intend to catch them?” Wang asked. “Heaven’s secrets must not be disclosed.” Hu pointed to Ji. “Mr Xuexuan, in his letter Heling mentioned that the tribute rice would go out to sea through Liuhe. Because the Small Swords uprising might cause trouble, he suggested a plan. See what you think of it.” Ji was astonished. When had he suggested any plan? He was about to speak when someone gave him a light kick. Recognizing Hu’s signal, he remained silent.

“What plan?” Wang asked attentively. “Our superiors are worrying about it, and it is giving me a headache too. Escorting tribute grain is a public duty, yet the troops make demands at every turn. The whole Green Standard Army ought to be abolished!” “Then this suggestion will be useful,” Hu said calmly. “Heling knows my friendship with You Laowu and the extent of You’s influence. His idea is to contract the transshipment to You. What do you think?” Wang considered, then struck the table in approval. “A splendid idea! You belongs to the Songjiang grain-transport brotherhood, so the benefit would not go to outsiders. It can be justified on every side. Brother Heling, you truly have remarkable talent. Please draw up a memorandum today, and I’ll present it to the governor in person tomorrow. If he still raises objections, there really must be a ghost at work!” “Certainly, certainly,” Ji replied. His face and ears grew hot, though the wine concealed his embarrassment. “Excellent!” Wang raised his glass. “I have drunk brandy several times, but none seemed as fragrant or mellow as this.” “‘Friendship with Zhou Gongjin is like drinking mellow wine,’” Ji quoted from the Records of the Three Kingdoms. He raised his glass toward Wang, but his eyes rested on Hu. After they drank, Wang said, “That is enough wine. Brother Heling still has his memorandum to write tonight. Come to my house tomorrow evening, and we’ll enjoy a proper drink.”

As he finished, Ruiyun lifted the curtain and came out smiling. “But I haven’t yet offered a toast to Master Hu or to you, sir.” “You certainly ought to toast Master Hu—to thank your matchmaker!” That had indeed been her intention, but Wang’s saying it aloud made things difficult. With the wine pot in one hand and a cup in the other, she stood awkwardly at a loss. It lasted only a moment before Ji came cleverly to her rescue. “Mr Xuexuan should be toasted first,” he said, taking the pot. “Xueyan and I are brothers. He is one of the family.” “How unfortunate!” Wang laughed. “You are all family, and I’m the only outsider.” “You mustn’t say that, sir.” Ruiyun recovered her composure and her skill in social conversation. “Neither Master Hu nor Master Ji regards you as an outsider.” “Exactly!” A little wine had sharpened Wang’s wit. “A woman’s heart turns toward her husband. It is you who regard me as an outsider.” “I would never dare.” Though he was joking, she answered seriously. “I spent more than ten years in your household. I could never forget your kindness and your wife’s.” Even with wine as an excuse, Wang could hardly continue teasing after that. He accepted her toast with proper courtesy. She then toasted Hu and put down the cup to leave, but Hu stopped her and insisted she toast Ji as well. Now she could not remain at ease. The more she demurred, the more Hu teased, until several children gathered behind the curtain to peep at the fun. Danhe, the most mischievous, giggled incessantly. By turning to scold his children, Ji gave Ruiyun another opportunity to escape.

After dinner they returned to the study for tea and resumed their business. “Have you discussed the transshipment with You?” Wang asked Hu. “We have discussed it, but nothing is settled. I did not know your wishes.” “You might just as well have decided yourself. What does You say?” “One word is enough with him. The cost can be negotiated; he only needs an official communication from Zhejiang to the Jiangsu grain transport circuit intendant.” “The document is easily arranged. Even a letter to Governor Xu of Jiangsu would be no trouble. But we need an approximate figure for the expense before we can plan.” “I imagine it will be much cheaper than having Green Standard troops provide an escort.” “Then that will do.” Wang considered carefully. “If You can truly guarantee its safety, this is an excellent arrangement.” Hu heard the uncertainty about You. There were many things he could not conveniently explain, such as You’s friendship with Zhou Lichun. Yet Wang’s concern, and the fact that the proposal was now being attributed to Ji, made reconsideration necessary. If something went wrong, it would jeopardize both men’s careers. “I am reasonably confident, but we must guard against the one chance in ten thousand,” Hu said, looking at Ji. “Perhaps the memorial should leave some room for maneuver and let Governor Huang decide.” “No, no!” Wang waved his hand. “He will not take the responsibility.”

The whole matter seemed to require fresh discussion. Hu felt the responsibility was too heavy for any plan to be entirely secure. While he was pondering, Ji spoke. “We must first circle the horse and bend the bow—prepare the ground before acting. Defense is pressing everywhere, and every locality needs more troops. The existing forces are already insufficient. How could men be spared to escort the tribute rice?” “Ah!” Wang exclaimed. “I understand.” “So do I,” Hu said. “But it would be better if those words did not come from you, Mr Xuexuan.” “You mean the Green Standard officers should say it themselves?” Wang shook his head. “They won’t. It is a comfortable and profitable assignment. Why would they refuse?” “Not necessarily comfortable. If they really encounter the Small Swords forces and have to fight, they will be no match for them.” “Unfortunately, they do not think so, and I cannot say it. I’ll see the governor myself and act as circumstances require.” “What about the memorandum?” “Have it drafted tonight all the same. I’ll take it with me. Better to have it ready and not need it than need it and not have it.” “Then I’ll finish it tonight,” Ji said. After a pause, he added, “I should like Xueyan to stay so that we can discuss it and make it as sound as possible. What do you think?” “Very well.” Wang looked at Hu. “We shall meet tomorrow morning, then.”

With that agreed, Wang took his leave. Hu and Ji began immediately. One arranged the arguments clearly; the other wrote fluently. They soon produced a draft, reconsidered it, settled the final wording and made a fair copy for Hu to take away. The next morning Wang stayed home especially to await Hu. As soon as he arrived, they shut themselves in the study. Since the Xincheng disturbances had been put down, Wang had gained still more of Huang’s confidence. That also meant more jealous rivals and more obstruction. He had many troubles to pour out to Hu. “Xueyan, there is an important matter I want to discuss. I hear that Governor Huang may be transferred. If he leaves, who knows what his successor will be like? I am strongly tempted to withdraw while things are going well.” Hu was greatly alarmed. “Mr Xuexuan, why should you think of that? We have only just built things up, and everything is running smoothly. Why retreat now?” “First, if the new man and I do not get on, winding up the affairs I have handled could become troublesome. It would be easier to hand them over while Governor Huang is here. Second, Jiang Zhongyuan has been promoted from judicial commissioner of Hubei to governor of Anhui. We are old acquaintances, and he has written to ask whether I would join him there. He and Zeng Guofan are both enjoying great imperial favor. Going to him might be a good move.” “I disagree!” Hu shook his head vigorously. “You do not know Anhui, and neither do I. To speak plainly, if you go there, I shall not go with you, because I could do nothing to help you there.” “Very well.” Wang nodded. “Since you put it that way, there is no more to say. I will write today to decline Jiang’s kind invitation.”

Hu was naturally reassured, but felt his responsibility grow heavier. After reflecting, he asked, “Is the report of Governor Huang’s transfer reliable?” “There is such a rumor, and we must be prepared. Besides, disturbances by bandits are occurring throughout Zhejiang. A spark can set the prairie ablaze. The governor takes the matter very seriously. Because the Xincheng affair was handled well, I fear all these assignments will fall to me in future. Meanwhile I cannot get free of the Sea Transport Bureau. I really am beginning to lack the strength for everything.” This made Ji’s appointment all the more important. In truth, Wang was more anxious about it than Ji himself, but he could not exert his full influence with Huang. In allocating the rewards for Xincheng, Wang had made a wrong move—or rather, failed to make a move at all. Huang had decided from the outset that Wang and Ji would receive one confidential recommendation and one open recommendation between them. He had no preference as to which man received which. Had Wang said when the report went forward, “Ji Heling did more of the work; please favor him with the confidential recommendation,” Huang would have agreed. Because Wang had failed to say this, the confidential recommendation had gone to him. To press Ji’s claims again now might look opportunistic, and he feared displeasing Huang. That was why he had never dared say too much. He could hardly confess this difficulty even to Hu. As time passed, his sense of guilt, almost as though he had appropriated another man’s merit, deepened. He longed for Hu to devise a way to settle the appointment quickly. “As things stand,” Wang continued, “it will probably take more than a day or two. I must first discuss defense and make the governor see that no troops can be spared. Then I must wait for him to ask whether there is another way. Only then can I produce Heling’s memorandum. Think how many turns we have to take!”

Hu agreed. Reviewing the causes and consequences once more, he realized that he had been mistaken. He had wanted Ji to display his abilities. But the memorandum had little bearing on whether Ji could take over the Sea Transport Bureau. The decisive point still lay with the correspondence office. A pig’s head cooks when the fire is brought to it; official business proceeds when the money arrives. How had he forgotten such familiar sayings? “Mr Xuexuan, please wait a little. See the governor tomorrow at the earliest, or the day after at the latest.” “Why? What are you arranging now?” “The same answer as before.” Hu smiled. “Heaven’s secrets must not be disclosed.” “Very well. I won’t ask. I’ll wait for your word.” They went on to talk about events in Shanghai and Hangzhou.
