On one side, live frugally and save little by little until you have some capital. On the other, behave responsibly and help them establish the shop, so that you can ask for their support. Together, those things might put Liu Jingde Hall's signboard up again. As you think now, spending everything you have for present pleasure, what plans have you made for the future? Tell me, Third Uncle, isn't that boasting?” Her sustained argument left him speechless. Thinking it over, he had to admit how clearly she saw and how carefully she had planned. For a clerk aspiring to become a proprietor, no path could be sounder. Yet he still could not answer. Judging himself honestly, he had no confidence that he could live frugally and behave responsibly as she demanded.

During the silence, a young man hurried in. Liu went to the doorway and recognised Chen. “Little Monk!” He wondered how Chen knew Mrs Yu too: they were facing each other, speaking in low voices, as only acquaintances would. Chen answered and came over. Seeing Furong, he respectfully greeted his teacher's wife. “Madam!” Then he turned to Liu. “Third Master Liu, I've arranged the meeting. We can leave whenever you're ready.” “Yes, let's go.” Liu told his niece, “It's the man who proposed the partnership.” Furong took Little Rabbit, and she and A’qi departed in their chairs. Liu invited Chen to sit, wanting first to understand who the other man was and where they would meet. “At Jucheng Bank, Mrs Yu's...” “Wait!” Liu interrupted. “That Mrs Yu is Yu Si's wife?” “Yes. Didn't you know her?” “No, and it never occurred to me. I'd only heard that Yu's concubine had parted from him after a quarrel some time ago. I never imagined she was the Mrs Yu here.” An idea struck him. “Then the proposed partner must be Hu Xueyan?” There was no need to conceal it now. Chen nodded. “Exactly. Mr Hu. A partnership between close relations—what could be better? A man needn't fear lack of success or luck, Third Master Liu. He should fear missing an opportunity. Failure to recognise one may be excusable. Seeing it clearly and letting it pass brings the bitterest regret.”

Liu remained silent. It had come so suddenly that he needed to think. “Gambling requires coolness, accuracy, and daring,” Chen said. “Here's a splendid opening. If you don't seize it, you'll truly deserve the name Liu Bucai and never recover.” “Is it really such an opening?” “Of course. Take Uncle Four alone!” From Yu, Chen went on to You Laowu, from Wang Youling to Ji Heling, then from Old Zhang to himself. His conclusion was that everyone who associated with Hu found good fortune. Half fact and half skilful embellishment, the account held Liu's complete attention. He missed not a word. “Very well!” Liu declared with the heroic air of a gambler staking everything in a final battle. “I'll take your advice. I'll make this wager!”

Chen slowly drank his tea to ease his thirst while considering the next move. Calling Hu his teacher was no empty form: he had learned much about managing people. Liu was enthusiastic now and would not change his mind. The question was how to win his wholehearted loyalty at once. “Well?” Liu could not understand his silence. “You've made me talk till my throat is dry. Give me time to moisten it.” Chen set down the cup and rose. “I'll go ahead and arrange matters concerning your difficulties. Come to Jucheng yourself at noon. Will that do?” “You mean you'll first find money for me? There's no need to worry about that now.” “No ceremony! Ceremony will only make you suffer. Frankly, your circumstances aren't good. You might find even a dinner party difficult to afford. If you have to attend to business while scraping money together for creditors, your situation will be exposed and your dignity lost. Better to let me arrange it beforehand.” Liu saw the sense of this and left it to him, promising to meet Hu at Jucheng at noon.

At the appointed hour, Chen was waiting at the entrance. He led Liu into the reception room, where Hu greeted him with a deep bow and called him “Third Uncle.” A sumptuous banquet with silver tableware was ready, including four dishes of dried fruit and four of fresh. Liu addressed him as “Brother Xueyan,” speaking only of his admiration and avoiding the family connection. Yu kept them company, while Chen helped the conversation along. Treated as the guest of honour, Liu felt wonderfully flattered. After tea they took their places, Liu at the head, Yu and Chen on either side, and Hu in the host's seat. Following three rounds of wine, Yu introduced the business. “Brother Liu, I didn't originally approve of Old Hu's plan for a medicine shop. Now I think it makes sense. Doing good and helping people is always worthwhile. I mean to invest too. But he and I know nothing of the trade. We must rely on you for everything.” “You flatter me. This is my own trade, and I'll gladly do whatever I can. But I don't yet know the plan or its scale.” “That's where we need your advice, Third Uncle. As for scale...” Hu considered. “To begin with, I mean to raise a hundred thousand taels.” A hundred thousand, merely to begin! Without Chen's advance account and Yu's promise to invest, backed by his reputation for wealth, Liu would hardly have believed it. Excited but cautious, he said, “That would be a very large concern. But in troubled times, trade may not be as good as in peaceful years.”

“In peaceful times, people take nourishing medicinal pastes. In troubled times, we should sell medicines that save lives and fewer tonics,” Hu replied. “Don't worry about trade, Third Uncle. Great wars are followed by great epidemics. Refugees suffer hunger in the morning, cold at night, and difficulty adapting to unfamiliar conditions. When they fall ill, they must buy medicine. Those who can't afford it shall receive it free.” Liu nodded, thinking that the man certainly spoke on a grand scale. Yet there was calculation behind the grand words. “The principles of business are the same everywhere,” Hu continued with a smile. “Establishing a name comes first. That's why I propose giving medicine away.” “I understand that,” Liu answered calmly. “Every medicine shop gives to the poor and sick. It doesn't do much beyond being a good deed.” “Then they're doing it the wrong way. I heard an interesting story in Shanghai. Let me tell you.”

The story concerned a small medicine shop in the capital during Yongzheng's reign. It supplied medicines to the palace dispensary, choosing particularly genuine, high-quality ingredients, and the emperor trusted its products. In one of the Dragon, Dog, Ox, or Goat years when the great examination was held, the metropolitan examination fell in the third month and was known as the Spring Examination. The preceding winter had been mild, with little snow. Abnormal weather in early spring brought an epidemic, and many provincial examination graduates fell ill. Even those who could carry on often had no appetite and felt listless. The shop's owner prepared a remedy for the seasonal illness and asked a minister of the Imperial Household Department to inform the emperor that he wished to give it to every candidate to carry into the examination compound for use if needed. The cells there were so small that a man could neither stand fully upright nor stretch out his legs when reclining. After three sessions, a weak constitution might give way even in good health, let alone when unwell. Yongzheng, an emperor keenly attentive to people's circumstances, had already been worrying about the candidates. He warmly approved. Acting by imperial command, the shop stationed men at the entrance to the examination compound. As the candidates entered, a packet of medicine was placed in each examination basket without anyone needing to ask. The wrappers were elegantly printed and bore the words “By Imperial Command.” Each packet also contained a leaflet listing the shop's celebrated pills, powders, ointments, and elixirs. The outcome owed something to the quality of the medicines and something to the shop's good fortune: no more candidates withdrew through illness than in previous examinations. This was taken as evidence of the remedy's effectiveness. Afterwards, whether they had passed or failed, the candidates all went to buy the shop's medicines, and business flourished extraordinarily.

“Think of it,” Hu said. “People in all eighteen provinces, even distant Yunnan and Guizhou, came to know their medicines. However much you spent hiring men to put up notices throughout the empire, you couldn't achieve that effect. It all depends on whether you use your head.” “Exactly!” Yu laughed. “That's what makes you so formidable in business. You think of things nobody else can.” Liu's attitude had changed too. Eagerly, he asked, “Then how shall we give ours away?” “To the military camps...” “Nothing could be better!” Liu interrupted. “I have a formula for Zhuge Marching Powder. Its ingredients are quite exceptional, and its effects are miraculous.” “Excellent indeed! We'll need to give large quantities to the camps, and naturally there's a method. I'll devise ways to have others provide the money, while we charge only cost. People contributing to the army, including those donating military funds, can specify quantities of our Zhuge Marching Powder and other medicines, with their value calculated in silver. As long as the medicines are good and the soldiers trust them, I have a second step that will bring a profit.” Hu deliberately withheld the next step to test Liu's ability to guess. Liu could not, but Chen spoke. “I understand! Do you mean to deal with the military supply offices?” Naturally Liu had failed to guess: he knew nothing of army arrangements. Hu nodded earnestly at Chen, looking pleased with such a promising pupil, then developed his explanation.

“A military supply office attends to almost everything except fighting at the front. The most troublesome business is naturally dealing with casualties after a battle, so it uses enormous quantities of medicine. That's what we would sell it. Prices must be low and goods good. We can extend credit, making the public accounts easier to manage. Privately, of course, we'll pay the usual kickbacks...” “What a business!” Liu exclaimed. Interrupting was a habit of his. “But what an amount of capital it would require!” “Yes. Though the reverse also holds: if we can allow credit, we can request payment in advance. It depends on whether the supply office has money. The Jiangnan Grand Camp relies on military subsidies from the provinces. Vice Minister Zeng of Xiangxiang in Hunan also relies on contributions from various places to support his volunteer troops beyond his own province. With the right connections, payment for our medicines might be deducted directly from those subsidies. It depends on how one goes about it.” “On how one uses one's head!” Liu raised his cup. “Brother Xueyan, I drink to you.” “You do me too much honour. We shall still rely on you, Third Uncle.” “There's only one thing to say!” Liu pointed at Chen. “He knows my temperament. I've told him already: I'll stake everything on this one wager!”

From a white pouch worn against his skin, Liu produced a small, beautifully made book, bound with silk thread, its cover of red silk and its corners protected with blue. He handed it over. Seeing the title, Secrets of the Apricot Grove, Hu knew what it contained. “Here's my stake. When I say I'll stake it, I do.” Liu looked again at Chen. “Tell me, am I doing the right thing?” Chen thought not only that it was right, but that Liu had acted splendidly. As Hu's advance negotiator, he shared the credit. Smiling broadly, he nodded repeatedly. “Please put it away,” Hu said. “Since you approve of my proposal, matters are easy. We'll discuss them carefully afterwards.” Both men behaved generously: one offered his treasure to prove his sincerity, while the other would not casually accept it. They pressed and declined for some time until Chen proposed a solution. He fetched a sheet of mulberry-bark paper used for wrapping silver dollars, wrapped the book, sealed it, and marked the closure with a personal sign. It was entrusted to Yu, who immediately locked it in the safe.

After dinner, over tea, Liu did all the talking. He explained how to open a medicine shop, hire staff, obtain supplies, and prepare the medicines; what advantages and difficulties to expect; and what required caution. He spoke enthusiastically while the others listened intently. Everyone took the matter seriously. “Third Uncle,” Hu said when he finished, “I can't grasp all these rules and practices at once. We shall depend on you. But I have one thought. Nothing could be worse than quoting genuine formulas and selling false medicines. Customers must see plainly for themselves before they'll trust us.” “That can be arranged. If we're preparing Shiquan Dabu Pills, for example, we could announce it beforehand and invite people to see whether the ingredients are genuine and worth the price.” “That's precisely the difficulty. How do I know whether what you're using is genuine?” Liu paused. “By that reasoning, if we sell deer velvet, must we keep a deer in the shop?” He sounded thoroughly puzzled. Hu answered without hesitation. “Yes! Why not?” This opened Liu's eyes. After consideration, many ideas occurred to him. “Then let's give ourselves a free hand. If we're willing to spend, there'll be no shortage of fresh ideas.” “We aren't devising tricks merely for their own sake. We want business to be both honest and lively.” “Honest and lively!” Liu repeated, committing the words firmly to memory.

At this point, some further gesture was needed. Judging the moment right, Chen gave Liu a meaningful glance. Hu noticed too and rose before Liu could respond. “Stay a little, Third Uncle. Brother Yu and I have something to discuss.” In fact, there was nothing. He merely went inside to lie on the opium couch with Yu, leaving Chen free to speak. “Third Master Liu, look at this.” Chen handed him a booklet. It was a passbook issued by Jucheng, but when Liu opened it, there was no balance entered. It looked like a useless blank book. “Why is there no amount written in it?” Chen asked. “Third Uncle, do you understand the meaning?” “Honestly, no. Xueyan has so many ingenious devices that I'm convinced of his ability. Tell me what this means.” “It's for whatever you need. You can withdraw as much as you require, so there's no need to enter an amount. Only, you may withdraw no more than once a day.” Liu had never heard of anything so fortunate. Naturally, he did not suspect Hu of joking. After considering, he tested the offer. “Such unlimited freedom shows real trust. Suppose I wanted, say, eighteen thousand taels?” “That depends on the purpose. With sufficient credit, even eighteen thousand would not be impossible.”

Now Liu understood the deeper meaning. Naturally, Hu had given instructions and set a limit. Beyond it, Jucheng's clerks would find a reason to refuse. The daily restriction guarded against his taking the money to a gambling house. For a proper purpose, any shortfall could wait until tomorrow. Bets alone could not be placed on credit. This thought revived his haughty temper. He handed the book back. “Thank you.” His voice was cold. “I'm afraid I can't control myself. With an inexhaustible source of money, I'd certainly gamble until I no longer knew my way home.” Chen remained calm. “Third Master Liu, you said you'd stake everything on this one wager. Did you mean it?” “Naturally! Those formulas are my stake, and I've handed over every one. What more is there to say?” “That isn't the stake. Mr Hu says that, if you're truly determined, there's one thing you must do to show that you have really committed yourself. It isn't altogether difficult, nor altogether easy. I'll wait until you've thought it through before telling you.”

Liu considered. “Is it something I can do?” “Of course.” “Very well. Tell me.” Chen became unusually solemn. “A man who goes about in the world must keep his word.” “Need you say that? Little Monk, you look at people through a crack in the door!” Liu was offended. Hu had instructed Chen, and Furong had described her uncle fully. Deliberately seeking to rouse Liu's resolve, Chen answered casually, “I'm not looking through a crack to make you seem small. I'm much like you myself and know this won't be easy. Besides, mentioning it might hurt our friendship. That's why I have to be certain.” He gave a calculated sigh. “Perhaps I'd better not say it.” Liu ground his teeth but could hardly lose his temper. After restraining himself repeatedly, he managed, “Say it or don't, as you please! I refuse to believe that I, Liu, will give you reason to despise me.” “That's hard to say. There's one thing you may not be able to do.” “Tell me!” Liu struck the table with his fist and rose, bracing both hands on it and leaning forward, looming like a mountain about to crush Chen to the floor.

“Then can you do as I've done and never enter a gambling house again?” At the question, Liu's body sank involuntarily back into his chair. For a long time he could not speak. “Mr Hu says that only such a resolution will prove your sincerity. He asks nothing else. Of fine food, clothes, brothels, and gambling, he only wants you to give up one. In my view, if you can't abandon even that...” Chen shook his head. “There's no need to say more. It would sound unpleasant.” Even without the words, Liu could imagine them. Indulging all four would certainly reduce him to beggary. “Mr Hu also says that gambling is a contest of minds, and business is a contest of minds too. Why not put your gambler's ingenuity into business? Once you learn its ways, you'll naturally find it interesting. Then you won't want to gamble.” Liu considered in silence. Gradually his expression changed. The flightiness, impatience, and anger faded, giving way to calm and steadiness. At last he nodded. “That's sound advice.” His words were clear. “I'm giving up gambling!” “Congratulations!” Chen smiled and clasped his hands, pushing the passbook towards him again.

“Then let's discuss business. After all this talk, how should I begin? I want to understand.” That naturally required Hu. With matters settled, there was no further need to borrow Jucheng's premises. Hu easily persuaded Liu to come home with him, and the estrangement between uncle and niece dissolved almost without their noticing. An evening's discussion brought the undertaking into shape. The shop would be called Hu Qingyu Hall, and Liu would take charge of preparations. They agreed that he would accompany Hu to Hangzhou in three days. Details could be discussed there. “Third Uncle,” Furong urged, “you really ought to settle down. If there's a suitable woman, marry her and give me a new aunt.” “It's too early for that.” Liu shook his head. “My whole mind is on Hu Qingyu Hall.” He immediately changed the subject. “Xueyan, I think we should draw up plans and build our own premises.” “I think so too. Start everything from the beginning!” “Exactly,” Liu replied. “That's what I'm doing myself.”

He truly began afresh. During those three days, he produced a detailed plan for Hu Qingyu Hall, covering the purchase of land, construction, staffing, supplies, layout, and management. Hu had never before planned a business so thoroughly. Yet never before had he undertaken one on so uncertain a basis. This time the boastful man was Hu, not Liu. He had spoken of raising an initial hundred thousand taels, but did not know where the money would come from. Yu had offered to invest, yet was already supporting him to the limit of his resources. Hu could hardly ask him to sell his land, and in these unsettled times property could scarcely be turned into cash anyway. Fortunately, no immediate payment was required. Hu intended to consult Wang Youling in Hangzhou. A medicine shop was a sound business, with the admirable purpose of saving lives and helping people. Perhaps Huang Zonghan would contribute part of his well-filled official purse, investing under a member of his family's name. With Governor Huang taking the lead, finding other wealthy officials to provide the rest would be easier. This was only an initial plan, aimed at getting the enterprise established. There could be no talk yet of profits, much less of conducting it entirely according to Hu's ideals. Liu never imagined these calculations. Still enthusiastic, he talked of the shop whenever they met, all the way to Hangzhou. There Hu lodged him at the bank and assigned a young clerk to accompany him on daily outings, treating him with the greatest consideration.

CHAPTER NINETEEN

Spending every day at leisure could not go on. What tormented Liu Bucai most was having nothing to do. His fingers itched, and he kept wanting to gamble. But whenever the thought arose, he remembered what he had told Chen Shilong and fought it down. After ten days of this, he could bear it no longer. What he could no longer bear was waiting for Hu Xueyan to tell him something definite. He waited another two days and finally caught him on the third. “Xueyan!” he said with some agitation. “I’ve been here more than half a month and haven’t done a thing. I know you’re busy, but if this goes on I shall fall ill from boredom.” “I know, I know! I’m terribly sorry. There were matters in several places that I had to attend to myself. Most are now in hand. Above all, the transfer of cargo for sea transport has at last been settled. I can spare some time. Tomorrow we shall begin by looking at sites.” Then Hu asked, “Third Uncle, how much can you drink?” “I can hold my own.” “Then let me introduce you to a friend.”

The friend was Qiu Fengyan. He had carried out the escort of the foreign guns very efficiently. Wang Youling had given him a sum of money and praised him warmly, so he had lately been in excellent spirits. He and Liu took to one another at once. Moreover, Hu had asked Qiu to look after him, and Qiu made a special effort to please. Liu felt that acquiring such a friend was something to be happy about. Qiu therefore undertook to accompany him in looking at land. Every morning they began with tea at a teahouse by Fengle Bridge. Qiu had lived in Yangzhou and was particular about his morning meal. He ordered two stir-fried dishes to go with his early wine, followed by noodles. Then a broker led them out to inspect sites. Some were too small; elsewhere they could not agree on the price. By the time they had weighed one consideration against another, it was three in the afternoon, and Qiu wanted tea and wine again. With his company, Liu was no longer so bored. The days passed peaceably, and his desire to gamble subsided.

One morning Hu unexpectedly came to see Liu and began, “Third Uncle, I need you to entertain a guest. He knows everything about women, gambling, fine food and clothes. You are the only man who can keep him company.” For a moment Liu could not answer. First, the request was unexpected. Second, it contradicted Hu’s original intention: he had wanted Liu to give up gambling, and now was asking him to gamble. Third, Liu had promised to stop and had actually done so. To break that resolution now, throwing away his hard-won determination and self-control, seemed a pity. “Third Uncle,” Hu said seriously, “have no misgivings. This is precisely where I need your help. To put it plainly, I am making use of your strengths.” There was nothing more to say. “If it will help you, of course I shall do it. But first you must explain what it is all about.” Hu hesitated. “It is a long story, with complications I cannot explain in a moment.” He paused. “In a word, if we keep this young gentleman amused, it will be a great help to my business.” “Mm, I understand. You want me to be his companion and entertainer?” “Not a dependent companion—a wealthy guest. Of course, a wealthy guest who also entertains him will be all the more effective!” Only now did Liu truly understand. Nodding gravely, he said, “Provided you don’t mind the expense, I know how to play the rich man, and how to make friends with rich men.”

“Of course! Why should I mind the expense? Third Uncle, what is the most you have ever lost at one sitting?” “I once lost...” Liu said. “I lost a pawnshop. Not a large one. It was worth thirty thousand taels.” “Good. You have seen high play. That will do. Have no worries: I can put thirty or fifty thousand taels in ready silver into your hands. More would be no trouble either. I can raise it whenever it is needed. Losing does not matter. What matters is never to look small-minded or mean.” “You can trust me there. At the gaming table my nerve is second to none.” They agreed that Hu would return that afternoon and accompany him to meet the young gentleman, bringing banknotes then. Liu went off in high spirits to have his head shaved and dressed himself as an elegant man of the world, then sat waiting. Shortly after noon Hu returned. Liu wore a grey-squirrel fur robe faced with iron-grey satin, a maroon Baturu waistcoat, and a little black satin cap with a coral knot on top and a piece of green jade carved with the longevity character at the front. There was a snow-white spun-silk jacket, crisply fitted trousers bound at the ankles, and a pair of double-ridged Zhangzhou velvet shoes. “Splendid! I have brought two things that will go perfectly with your clothes.” One was a gold repeating watch on a very thick gold chain; the other, a thumb ring of mutton-fat white jade. There were also twenty thousand taels in banknotes, none smaller than five hundred taels.

“It is still early. Let me tell you who this rich young gentleman is.” His surname was Pang. Hu had met him during his two days in Nanxun, and everyone called him Second Master Pang. His family had been in the silk trade for generations, accumulating wealth; then, when foreign trade opened late in the Daoguang reign, they had made large profits in the export business. Even if their fortune did not rival a state’s, its depth was far beyond what outsiders imagined. Second Master Pang was an idler of the first rank, but his family upbringing had given him a thorough knowledge of business. That was why Hu wanted to deal with him. He had purchased the rank of circuit intendant, though naturally he would never wait at an official headquarters for an appointment or an assignment. He did not ordinarily wear official dress. But if any prefectural or county official put on airs before him, Pang could outdo them all in official grandeur. That alone showed his character: he could be won by courtesy, but never bullied. So that was the man! Liu listened and considered. As a fellow Huzhou man, he naturally knew of Second Master Pang, but among wealthy young gentlemen he himself had stood at least two grades lower. Now he had fallen on hard times as well. To be introduced as “the third son of the old Liu Jingde Hall family” was hardly glorious. He could not help wondering beforehand what Pang would think.

“Third Uncle,” Hu continued, “to draw Second Master Pang closer, I specially asked Prefect Wang to give this party. He is your district’s governing official. However busy Pang may be, he cannot refuse. Today is only a dinner, so the gaming will not be on a very large scale—just some mahjong. You must show your skill and make him want a second game with you after the first. That is how the friendship will grow.” “I understand. You can rely on me for that. But...” Liu found it difficult to say. “We have never met, and he spends most of his time in Shanghai, but he probably knows who I am.” “That does not matter. A prodigal who reforms is worth more than gold. Nobody will laugh at you. Besides, I have spoken to Prefect Wang. He will treat you with particular courtesy. With the host showing you such respect, nobody will be able to fathom your circumstances.” Hearing this, Liu looked down at his finery and then at the twenty thousand taels in notes. His outlook changed. Everything else might be a pretence, but money was real. Money gave a man courage. What was there to fear? “You are right, Xueyan.” His spirits rose. “When do we leave?” He opened the repeating watch. It was only two in the afternoon. “We are expected at four. Naturally I must arrive early. Rest a little longer and come to Mr Wang’s residence at the appointed time.” Hu left a slip of paper bearing the address. With this agreed, they parted. Liu duly reclined on a couch and closed his eyes, carefully considering Pang’s temperament and how best to approach him. Feeling fairly confident, he opened his eyes cheerfully, made a few further adjustments to his appearance and hired a small chair to take him to the party.

At the Wang residence the host was indeed most courteous, addressing him at every turn as “Brother Sancai.” They sat exchanging civilities while the other guests arrived. Apart from Ji Heling and Qiu Fengyan, there were two wealthy young men. One was Zhou Wu, fifth in his family and a younger brother of the former Tianjin customs intendant. The other was Gao Si, the fourth son of a family whose members combined official service with commerce. Their conversation had no serious purpose. Either they spoke of how much they had lost at pai gow, or of some extraordinary beauty newly appeared aboard the Jiangshan pleasure boats. Second Master Pang arrived last. He was thirty-four or thirty-five, with a broad, pale face like a silver basin, resembling Cao Cao on the stage. His grandfather had recently died, so mourning restrictions obliged him to wear a plain grey-cloth robe lined with sheepskin. Yet on his hand was an “oil diamond” ring full of fire. He wore the stone turned inwards; whenever he raised his hand, flashes from his palm caught the eye all the more. The host made the introductions. Only Ji, Qiu and Liu were new acquaintances for Pang. Hearing Liu’s Huzhou accent, he warmed to him. “Brother Liu,” he asked, “where do you live? How is it that we have never met?” Liu gave his address. “I have long heard of you, Second Master Pang. I am delighted to make your acquaintance.” “The pleasure is mutual.” Pang was courteous, without the airs of a grand young idler. “Come, come!” cried the impatient Zhou. “Time to play!” Their host led them into a side room, where a mahjong table had been prepared. They stood discussing who should join. Pang, Zhou and Gao were obvious choices. For the fourth place, the host deferred to Ji, Ji to Liu, and Liu to Hu. Hu declined, settling the matter: Liu would play.

They drew seats and agreed on “one-two” mahjong, a base stake of ten thousand taels, a forty-point base score and sixteen rounds. Soon the tiles were clattering. Liu was in no hurry to go out; first he studied the others’ play. Pang and Gao were both highly skilful, but Gao had one weakness: he liked building elaborate hands. Zhou played as impatiently as he did everything else, taking any winning hand, large or small. Once he needed only one tile, he turned his tiles face down and stared into the pool of discards as though longing to snatch out the one he wanted. Yet bad player though he was, luck favoured him. In four rounds he made two all-one-suit hands and a Three Dragons hand. He had won nearly a full base stake and was delighted. “All because Gao insists on building big hands and discards so freely,” Pang said coolly as he threw the dice to change seats. “If you sit below me this time, watch out!” As it turned out, Liu sat immediately before Zhou, with Gao before him and Pang opposite. Gao persisted in his old habit: if seven of his thirteen tiles belonged to the same suit, he aimed for an all-one-suit hand. His discards were therefore still generous. Liu decided he must not claim too many of them. Otherwise his own discards would become loose, allowing Zhou to profit; once Zhou’s luck gained momentum, it would be hard to check. He refused even tiles that would complete an edge or a gap in a sequence and concentrated on the player after him, keeping Zhou firmly pinned down. Within two rounds, Zhou had lost half his winnings. But Pang, the heaviest loser, had made no recovery. Liu now decided that besides restraining Zhou, he must help Pang win. He played so well that a little attention to the tiles Pang drew and discarded showed him what Pang needed. Just as Pang reached a waiting hand, Liu would discard the winning tile. Pang went out twice in succession; his luck turned and he recovered his losses. When they stopped for dinner after eight rounds and counted up, three were winning from one. Gao was the heavy loser.

“You play extremely well,” Pang told Liu as they left the table. “And I admire your conduct at play still more.” “You are too kind!” Liu was gratified, and felt some admiration in return: Pang was a man who appreciated a favour. After dinner Pang’s luck grew stronger. Whenever he became dealer he retained the position, and his winning hands grew larger. This too owed something to Liu. He no longer fed Pang winning tiles, but concentrated on holding Zhou and Gao back, particularly preventing either from making a big hand. At any sign of danger, he either went out quickly himself or let someone else win a small hand. By the final reckoning, Pang was the great winner and Zhou the great loser. “Always the same—win first, lose afterwards!” Zhou said bitterly. “Losing is nothing, but the tiles are infuriating. That is why I dislike mahjong. There is no pleasure in it.” Pang and Gao, accustomed to this performance, merely exchanged smiles. Liu spoke. “Brother Zhou is impatient. Pai gow would suit him better.” “Exactly! Let me take the bank.”

Gao was willing either way, and Liu said nothing. Only Pang hesitated. “Isn’t it too late? We ought not impose on our host.” “Not at all!” Hu answered for Wang. “Please enjoy yourselves. Shall we have supper before playing, or...” “Too early for supper,” Zhou broke in. “Let me bank a game first.” Pang knew his temper. If Zhou took the bank, win or lose he would not stop before daylight. Pang therefore spoke at once. “We are all friends. Let us keep it modest. We can rotate the bank, playing big or small pai gow as you please, with ten thousand taels to each bank. Lose it all and give way; even a winning banker may play only four sets.” “Four is too few. At least eight.” “Come now. Four each makes sixteen sets. After that, we can enjoy our host’s supper and go home to bed.” “Quite right,” Gao agreed. “I have business tomorrow morning. Let us finish early.”

Zhou could not carry the argument alone and had to agree. When the dominoes appeared, Zhou naturally banked first. From his clothes he produced an ivory case shaped like a bean pod, slid off its lid and tipped out four dice. He had many little rituals. He threw all four until they showed a four and a five, then removed the red die. He threw the other three until he obtained a four and a six, and only then would he use the red one. Four and five made nine, which sounded like the word for wine; six and four made ten, made to sound like meat. He called it “treating the dice to wine and meat.” “Mahjong should be quiet, but pai gow needs a lively crowd,” he announced loudly. “Everyone must join in. You can bet even a single tael.” Qiu had not yet left. Liu gave him two hundred taels of “luck money” so that he could place bets of five or ten. Wang was persuaded to play too. Hu disliked gambling, but naturally had to contribute to the fun. Taking a hundred-tael note, he placed it on the upper gate, where Pang sat. “Big pai gow or small?” Pang asked. “You’ll know when I open the hands.” With Zhou’s temperament, it was bound to be small pai gow, where the whole issue was settled at a single turn of the tiles. His bank lasted only two sets before Pang and Gao broke it. Pang banked next and went through his four sets without much gain or loss. Zhou, however, lost over ten thousand more. Gao was the chief winner, while Liu won five or six thousand taels.

Liu was the third banker. Rolling up his snow-white cuffs, he shuffled and stacked the dominoes. As he opened the hands, he said, “Since Brother Zhou likes small pai gow, I shall play that too.” Zhou’s temper was rising with his losses. “Exactly! ‘In spring, never ask the way.’ I’m sitting at Heaven’s Gate, so that is the gate I’ll back.” He pulled a sheaf of notes from his clothes and slapped them on the table. “I’ll take the whole stake!” “Come now!” Pang objected sharply. “We are all here to enjoy ourselves. What pleasure is there if you leave nobody else room to bet?” “Why not? Each man can play his own game. If you fancy your lower gate, shift my stake over to it. Isn’t that just as good?” “Shifting stakes” meant that players at the side gates gambled against one another. If the banker won from all or paid all, the person who had shifted a bet was unaffected. But if one gate won and another lost, the difference was considerable. In pai gow and dice-shaking games, some players particularly liked shifting other people’s bets. If the original gate lost and theirs won, they won from both banker and fellow player, doubling their profit. They could also congratulate themselves on their judgment, which was very satisfying. But shifting stakes often became a contest of pride. One man shifted a stake across; the other shifted it back. Back and forth it went, each move doubling the gain or loss at issue, until the gambling grew wild. Zhou and Pang were now showing signs of such a quarrel. When gambling spoiled the harmony, others naturally had to intervene. But both were wealthy young gentlemen who could afford to lose money and could not endure losing a single word of argument. Making peace was difficult, and Hu grew anxious.

Just as Pang, beginning to lose his temper, was about to shift Zhou’s stake by declaring that Heaven’s Gate must follow the lower gate, Liu spoke first. “Brother Pang is quite right. We are all friends. This is only a friendly parlour game...” As expected, the hot-tempered Zhou interrupted. “What sort of thing is that for the banker to say? Tell me—if he is right, am I wrong?” “You are right too,” Liu answered calmly. “And Brother Pang need not shift any stakes. Since Brother Zhou is keen to play, I ought to oblige him. How about a private side bet of ten thousand taels?” It was Qiu who cried, “Good! That satisfies both sides.” A separate wager between the banker and another player was nobody else’s concern. There could be no reasonable objection. With ten thousand taels Liu had given both men a way to save face. It was skilfully done, and the money was not necessarily lost. Hu silently approved. Liu certainly knew how to handle a social occasion.

The dice showed seven. Zhou seized the two dominoes dealt on the outside and turned them up. Now he truly stared: an Ox-head and a Three–Six. His face turned livid with anger. “What do they call that?” Qiu said. “I heard a saying in Songjiang: ‘A black devil shouldering a foreign rifle!’” He spoke without a smile, in complete seriousness, so it did not sound like mockery. Everyone laughed, and Zhou laughed too. The banker swept all the gates. Liu could have put aside the ten thousand taels won on the private side bet, recovering his original stake and making the rest of his bank pure profit with nothing left to lose. Instead, with a fine gesture, he left it in play. He counted the money and announced the total—twenty-seven thousand taels—so that the other players could judge how much to bet.

His bank was steady, taking more than it paid and showing a gain on every deal. By the third deal of the third set, custom called for omitting the final deal and shuffling again. Instead, Liu offered to play on. “Only one set remains,” he said. “I’ll play the last deal. Place your bets quickly!” “My friend,” Pang cautioned him, “the remaining tiles favour the lower gate. You had better leave this deal alone.” “Thank you for the warning. But that is the pleasure of banking at pai gow. If the dice help, the banker alone may have the high hand and sweep everything in. It happens often enough.” “Then let’s try it! I don’t believe the lower gate will come up empty.” Zhou took out another handful of notes. “How much has the banker?” Liu counted: forty thousand taels in all. “Let everything follow the lower gate.” Zhou put his notes there. “I’ll take whatever remains.” Everyone grew tense. There were no draws in small pai gow. On this one deal, the banker would either turn his forty thousand into eighty thousand or lose everything and surrender the bank. It was the largest single wager of the evening. So much money changing hands commanded even Pang’s close attention.

Liu’s face and voice remained unchanged as he cast the dice. The three gates showed their hands: the upper gate had nine points, Heaven’s Gate seven, and the lower gate a Heaven tile with a Red Nine. They had agreed that this combination would count as one point, not as the special Heaven Nine hand. “You see? The lower gate is the live one!” Zhou declared, with something of bravado covering unease. “One hand overcomes the next. What else would you call it?” “Live it may be, but the point count is too small,” Pang replied. “The last deal often produces strange hands. A full bowl of rice is easy to swallow, Old Five; a mouthful of boasting is harder.” “Any points will bring money!” Zhou persisted. “If this hand loses, I’ll eat the dominoes.” The enormous wager was interesting enough. But Zhou’s boast, which might make the outcome impossible to manage, fascinated everyone in the room, from the players seated at the table to the servants and maids standing beside them. All longed to see what the banker would turn up. A Mixed Seven and a Mixed Five would make an ordinary two-point hand, enough to beat the lower gate’s one-point Heaven Nine. What an expression Zhou would wear then, after his sweeping claim! Yet nobody, not even Pang, expected what happened. Liu did not turn over his dominoes at all. “Brother Zhou, you are right. Your single point is worth a great deal.” With a calm, natural smile, he pushed the money forward. He seemed to lose to Zhou entirely willingly—indeed, almost to have defeated him.

By now Pang liked Liu very much and sided with him at every turn. “You haven’t even looked at your tiles!” he reminded him. “Can you really fail to beat one point?” “All the other tiles are out,” Liu said. “There is no need to look. One point loses to one point.” “I don’t believe it.” Pang began sorting through the exposed tiles, starting with the highest “Treasure” combination. He found a Two–Four but no Ding tile. If the banker’s one point lost to the other one point, his hand ought to be a Man-and-Ding One. Pang searched for the Man tiles. Sure enough, only one was there. When the banker’s tiles were turned over, there it was: a Man-and-Ding One. Ten red spots made the single black spot stand out all the more sharply. The silent room erupted in regret and laughter, astonishment and exclamations. Naturally, Zhou was the loudest. “Come, come! I’ll make the payments.” He drew the bank’s money and his own notes in front of him, paid the smaller wagers and kept the remainder as his winnings. “To think there really was such a hand!” Pang shook his head. “He couldn’t even turn up two points.” He regretted the banker’s loss so keenly that he almost resented it. Liu, however, behaved as though nothing had happened and pushed the dominoes towards Gao. This was the last bank. Its four sets also passed without much gain or loss. Their host then invited everyone into the hall for supper. As they ate and talked, the conversation inevitably returned to Liu’s hand.

“You have a remarkable eye,” Pang said. “You saw at once that a Man tile and a Ding were missing. That is a skill one cannot acquire in three or five years.” “Old Liu is a man of real quality,” even Zhou admitted. “Losing to you is a pleasure. We must have a proper game some time.” “Why some time?” Pang put in. “Tomorrow.” “But we have already agreed to dine with Old Hu tomorrow. Make it the day after.” “Tomorrow will do just as well,” Hu said. “Tell me whom you would like to play with, and I can send additional invitations.” “No need,” Pang replied. “The day after tomorrow, I shall invite you all to dinner and bring in a few friends for a proper game.” He turned particularly to Liu. “Are you free that day?” “I am free any day.” “Good. Come early, then. I hope everyone will honour me. Those who like to play can play; the others can simply dine. I have a new cook who does shark’s fin rather well. Come and try it.” “Thank you,” Wang said, “but I return to Huzhou the day after tomorrow.” They settled it there and then: everyone except Wang would accept Pang’s invitation. Ji Heling was naturally included. Pang admired him greatly, said they must be sure to have him and expressly asked Hu to convey the invitation.

The next day, Hu Xueyan borrowed Wang Youling's house to entertain the guests, again for “a little play.” Over the two days, Liu Bucai won more than ten thousand taels and was greatly excited. Hu reminded him, however, not to let this alter his original intentions: gambling could never establish a man's career. Once more, he urged Liu to win Pang over completely, then find an opportunity to put their proposal to him. “We seem to get on very well,” Liu said. “A long line flies the kite far; enough fire will soften the pig's head...” “No!” Hu would not allow such leisurely patience. “What I need from him is urgent. Third Uncle, you must use tomorrow's opportunity to win him over. Yesterday you did wonderfully. Even I admired you. But today you went wrong. You put your whole mind into gambling and neglected the real business.” “The opportunity was good today. I wanted to win something first, to use as gambling capital.” Liu smiled sheepishly. “There may be no chance later. Let me off this once.” “You needn't worry about capital. Naturally, if there's a chance to win something, I've no reason to object and insist on your losing. But remember why you went there to gamble.” Hu emphasised his point. “That's how business works. Wherever you are, never forget what you're there for.” Liu considered, then nodded. “Very well. Tomorrow I'll give all my attention to Pang Er.”

Pang's entertainment was on a grand scale. His family had a villa at the foot of Geling Hill beside West Lake, and he received his guests there. Outside, the north-west wind of the eleventh month penetrated even heavy furs. Inside the villa, it was warm as spring. The luncheon was served in a heated room with the hill behind it and the lake in front. There were three tables of guests, drawn from widely differing ranks, though their informal clothes made those distinctions difficult to see. By the time they finished eating, it was already two in the afternoon. Apart from a few exceptions, they were all well-known gamblers. As soon as they left the tables, they discussed what to play. “Let our host bank a dice-shaking game!” Others immediately agreed. Pang was famous for his fondness for the game, and of everyone present he was naturally the best qualified to act as banker. Willing though he was, he hesitated: he lacked an assistant. Then he caught sight of Liu and readily agreed. “Very well! Since you're in the mood, I'll shake a few dozen rounds first.” Apart from one table of mahjong, nearly twenty people prepared to play. While servants arranged the table, seats, and equipment, Pang drew Liu aside.

“Old Liu, let's be partners. Sixty per cent for me, forty for you. How does that sound?” “Excellent, of course. But let me first feel out the scale of the game. I've only thirty thousand taels on me. If the stakes are too large, I'll have to send home for more.” “No need. I have the money. You needn't put up any capital beforehand; we'll settle when the game breaks up. There's just one thing: I'd like you to handle the collection and payment of bets.” Pang continued, “I've a bad habit at this game. If the man settling the bets isn't up to the mark, I lose all enthusiasm. The other day, at Zhou's, I asked a friend to help at short notice. I'd only thrown five Old Treasures and lost less than twenty thousand taels when his hands began to tremble. It's not that I fail to appreciate someone helping me and still complain about him, but the way that fellow handled the settlements made me lose all face!” “I've never done it for you before. Naturally, if you ask, there's nothing more to say. I'm only afraid I won't be able to manage.” “Don't be modest.” Pang clasped his hands. “Help me put on a good show. I'll be grateful indeed.”

Liu took his place to settle the bets. The table was already prepared. Made specially for the game, it had a zitan-wood frame and a boxwood top and was one size larger than an ordinary square table. Ivory inlay marked the boundaries at its four corners. Each side also had ivory dots the size of teacups: one on the banker's side, three opposite, two to his right, and four to his left. The left was the Green Dragon, the right the White Tiger. The settling clerk customarily stood at the upper-left corner between three and four, the auspicious Green Dragon Corner. Once Liu stood there, a servant brought him a box of counters. They were ivory tallies four cun long, engraved in gold with the identifying words “Pang of Shizai Hall.” There were five kinds. Four bore the Heaven, Earth, Man, and Harmony markings from domino tiles; the fifth bore only the hall's name and was naturally the lowest denomination. Liu assigned them five values: one thousand, five hundred, one hundred, fifty, and ten taels. Only when the players had bought their counters did Pang, the “emperor,” sit down. He picked up a blue-and-white shaking bowl from the Chenghua kilns of the Ming dynasty and gave it three rattling shakes. Opening it, he found twelve points, which counted as four. “Good! An opening Green Dragon!” he said, and shook again.

The first three throws were called “showing the game,” allowing the players to chart its course. There were many kinds of patterns: main patterns, minor patterns, “meat” patterns, and “vegetable” patterns. Each player believed in his own. Only after the fourth shake did betting formally begin. The scene grew lively, and Liu had to display his ability. Of all gambling games, this was the fairest: the players suffered no disadvantage, and they had the widest variety of wagers. As in pai gow, besides betting a “corner” or “across the hall,” they could bet a “big head.” With corner and across-the-hall bets, player and banker each held two of the four numbers, so the wager was one against one. A big-head bet also gave each side two numbers, but the method of winning differed. With a two-led big head carrying one, a White Tiger paid double, while an Entrance was a draw. Then there was “flying a kite”: the player backed three numbers, and on a win the settlement was “take two, pay three.” In money terms, this meant staking three to win one: large capital for a small return, seemingly a disadvantage. With the dice, however, the player held the advantage, winning on three numbers and losing on only one. Of course, the unbacked number could still come up. Then all three stakes were taken, the whole force was wiped out, and the flying kite's string had snapped.

Whether the wager was a kite or a single-number bet, collecting and paying it was straightforward enough. The difficult part was a changed wager. One player might turn a big head into a single-number bet; another might transfer his stake from one number to another without moving the counters, merely announcing the change. The settling clerk had to remember it all. Nobody complained if he paid a bet that did not deserve payment, but if he collected a stake that should not have been taken, someone would protest. Losing money was a small matter. Making a mistake showed incompetence and would embarrass Pang. Liu dared neglect nothing; he watched every wager. Inwardly attentive but outwardly at ease, he waited for the bowl to be opened, then collected the losing bets and calculated each payment and its proper multiple. There were no complaints and no disputes. He worked not only accurately but exceptionally fast, so the banker never grew bored waiting and shook with increasing enthusiasm. Before long, twenty rounds were over. Halfway through his turn as banker, Pang finally looked at the banknotes in front of him. The settling clerk kept only counters and less than ten thousand taels in notes beside him. Once the notes reached ten thousand, he had to put them before the banker. This was auspiciously called “bringing money into the bank,” but its real purpose was to prevent the clerk from slipping money into his own pocket. Newly acquainted with Pang and charged with winning his trust, Liu was especially careful over such details. Pang made a quick count: there were fourteen or fifteen stacks. His own capital had been a hundred thousand taels. The winnings were by no means small.

The second half went less well. Liu kept reaching towards Pang for money, and before long only seven stacks remained. The sequence was worse still: a Green Dragon followed by a White Tiger, swinging back and forth. This was called a “swaying course,” or “rowing.” Zhou judged it ripe and placed twenty thousand taels on White Tiger as a single-number bet. Another ten thousand or so was already on that number. If the banker threw a two, he would have to pay ninety thousand taels. Although he could collect the stakes on the other three numbers, they were negligible. The money before him would not cover the loss. It was the settling clerk's responsibility to warn him, but some bankers disliked being told that even everything they had would not cover the payouts. Liu hesitated. Looking up, he happened to catch Hu's eye and frowned involuntarily. Hu immediately gave him a warning glance. Liu took the hint, indicated the money before Pang with his lips, and resumed his usual expression. “Old Liu, how is it?” Pang naturally had his own reckoning. He meant: was the capital enough? Liu must not discourage him, yet could not confidently undertake to cover everything. He merely answered, “Open it.” The result was three. Liu breathed freely. When collection and payment were complete, a servant of the Pang household quietly laid two banknotes before Pang. He glanced at them, looked slightly surprised, and nodded without speaking. Whether in understanding or approval, it was hard to tell. “Old Five,” he told Zhou, “go on betting. I've added more capital—another hundred thousand.” Strangely enough, the extra capital seemed to change his luck. The sequence became unpredictable, repeatedly favouring whichever number carried the smallest stake. When the forty rounds were over, the accounts showed a profit of seventy thousand taels.

Zhou took the bank next and also asked Liu to settle the bets. After twenty rounds, they saw that it was eight in the evening and stopped for dinner. Pang used the interval to take Liu into his study. Opening a drawer, he brought out two envelopes and offered them to him. Liu would not take them. “Brother Pang, what are these?” “Open them and see.” The first held three banknotes. Two, issued by Fukang Bank, were for fifty thousand taels each; the third, from another bank, was for five thousand. “Old Hu is a true friend. He had my servant bring me a hundred thousand taels to add to my capital. I didn't need it, but I appreciate the kindness. The five thousand is a share of the luck. Please take it to him.” “Xueyan won't accept...” “Never mind that,” Pang interrupted. “I'm only asking you to deliver it.” Liu too had been brought up as a wealthy young master. He knew that refusing on Hu's behalf would offend Pang, so he accepted the envelope.

The second envelope held more than thirty-two thousand taels in notes. “This is your share,” Pang explained. “We agreed on forty and sixty per cent, but I think an even division would be better.” Even in his former days of extravagant gambling, Liu had seldom played on a scale that involved thirty thousand taels in a single session. Now, almost without understanding how, he had won such a sum. He could scarcely believe it and stood speechless. Pang found this puzzling. Could Liu be dissatisfied? The suspicion vanished as soon as it arose. That was impossible. He must be considering what to say. A mere thank-you would hardly suffice: thirty-two thousand taels was no small sum. Pang already felt pleased with himself for being able to confer so great a benefit. Naturally, he wanted a few words that would give him further satisfaction. Such was the temperament of a wealthy young master.

Liu was deeply moved, but the unexpected windfall had not turned his head. Hu wanted him to win Pang's confidence and, if possible, place Pang under some obligation to him. Accepting this enormous sum would put the obligation the other way round. Besides, ready money was what counted at a gambling table. Having agreed to a partnership on a forty-sixty basis, Liu should have supplied his capital first and handed over the thirty thousand taels in notes he carried. Then he could take his profit with a clear conscience. Pang was famously wealthy and might not care, but if the other man behaved generously, Liu must conduct himself handsomely too. Only then could they be friends on equal terms. Otherwise, he would become a hanger-on clinging to a powerful patron, and his words would carry quite a different weight. The principle was clear. To gain Pang's friendship and carry out Hu's business, he must refuse the money. Yet it was thirty-two thousand taels. Added to the ten thousand and more he had won the previous day, it would provide enough capital to restore Liu Jingde Hall. So much was at stake that the decision was agonising. There was no time for leisurely reflection. Gritting his teeth, he told himself that silver and copper could be spent to the last coin; another chance to make friends like Hu and Pang might never come.

With an awkward, apologetic expression, Liu smiled. “Brother Pang, everyone knows how generous you are. This is as good as giving me thirty-two thousand taels. To refuse would be ungrateful, but to accept would leave me very uneasy. Let me suggest this. Friendship isn't a matter of one day. Whether we play together again or undertake some proper business, we'll have other chances to be partners. I'll leave this money on deposit with you.” He put the envelope back before Pang. “You...” Pang scratched his head. “That won't do! Let's settle one account at a time. Whatever we do later, gambling or business, there'll always be a share for you.” Liu hastily clasped his hands. “If you say that and regard me as a friend, Brother Pang, that's more than enough. Come, let's eat.” Speaking as he went, he walked out. Pang could only write “Liu's deposit” on the envelope and put it in the drawer.

When play resumed after dinner, Liu felt that his conduct had fulfilled Hu's commission. With that concern removed, he gave his whole mind to gambling, following the three rules of coolness, precision, and ruthlessness. During Zhou's twenty rounds, he bet only three times. Judging Old Treasure to be the right number, he staked two thousand taels on it alone and won six thousand. He put down capital and winnings together once more, and the sum became eighteen thousand. On the third bet, he set aside ten thousand and wagered eight thousand. If he won, his original two thousand would have become thirty-four thousand; after deducting the capital, the profit would exactly equal the thirty-two thousand he had declined. Instead, the stake was taken, and Zhou's turn as banker ended. Liu had won eight thousand taels. They changed to pai gow and played until dawn without any substantial change in his fortunes. Having won twenty thousand taels in three or four days, Liu felt he had every reason to be satisfied.

Stretching, he left the card table and drew back a window curtain. The sudden brightness dazzled him. He closed his eyes for a moment, then looked through the foreign glass, a luxury few households possessed. “What a snowfall!” he exclaimed. “Indeed!” Gao said. “We've gambled ourselves blind to the world. We didn't even know it was snowing so heavily.” “The view is magnificent.” Liu looked over West Lake, white as far as he could see. “Brother Pang's villa is wonderfully situated—a paradise.” “Then don't leave,” said Zhou, whose appetite for gambling remained unsatisfied. “There are plenty of guest rooms. Sleep a while, and we'll return to battle.” Ordinarily, Liu never refused a game. But now he remembered Hu's business. Hu had long since returned to the city, and he must meet him before considering anything else. He therefore pleaded an important appointment: he would rather return to town and come out again. “There's no need to come again,” Pang said. “Let's rest today. If you're interested, we could tour West Lake. I'll send a boat to wait at the Yongjin Gate wharf.” Zhou drew in his neck at once. “I haven't that refined taste. Better come to my place for hotpot, then another game.” “No!” Pang laughed. “This is the best place to admire the snow. I'll imitate the elegant scholars for once and stay out of town today.” Gao too said he had business, and several other guests said nothing. Zhou's proposal came to nothing. After a plentiful breakfast, they each took a sedan chair into the city. Liu went directly to a bathhouse called Huaqing Pool instead of returning to the bank. He soaked in its scalding communal bath, then lay on a padded couch and fell asleep while an attendant pounded his legs.

He did not wake until two in the afternoon and still felt no wish to leave the bathhouse. He called an attendant to order dishes from a restaurant and, at the same time, wrote a note for delivery to Hu's house, giving his whereabouts and asking Hu to meet him. By the time Hu arrived, Liu had been enjoying a hotpot of ten varieties of sliced raw ingredients, had drunk four liang of strong clear spirits, and was eating his rice. Looking at him closely, Hu said, “You look particularly well today. Things must have gone your way.” “Quite well. Everything went smoothly. Let me finish this bowl of rice, then I'll tell you all about it. It's bitterly cold. Go and have a soak first.” Hu undressed and entered the pool. When he returned to his place, Liu was waiting at ease over his tea. An envelope lay on the low table, bearing two lines of writing: “Kindly deliver by hand to my elder friend Xueyan.”

“Why did you leave yesterday before Pang finished his turn?” Liu asked. “Naturally, I had to leave early. Getting the city gate opened at night would have been troublesome. I had two notes drawn up and carried them with me. I'd handed them to Pang, but I didn't know whether the bank had enough deposits to cover them. I had to hurry back into town and make the arrangements.” “Fortunately, Pang didn't lose the money. Otherwise, there would have been trouble.” Liu shuddered at the thought. “I'd agreed to a forty-sixty partnership. If he had lost everything, including your hundred thousand, that would have been two hundred thousand. My forty per cent would be eighty thousand. After offsetting the accounts, there would be only twenty thousand to give back. A hundred thousand reduced to twenty thousand! What a risk. We must never do that again.” “So you know it shouldn't be done!” Hu laughed. “You were gambling at the table, and I was gambling outside it. But my gamble would have been worthwhile whether you won or lost.” “Winning made it especially worthwhile. Look!” Liu pushed the envelope towards him and explained what had happened.

Only then did Hu open the envelope. He put away his own two banknotes and held up Pang's note for five thousand taels. “Naturally, I can't take this five thousand. But it would be awkward to return it. There's only one course: donate it to a charitable institution in his name. After last night's heavy snow, there must be at least twenty or thirty bodies lying in the roads. My bank has already given four coffins.” “Good works are only right. I'll give a thousand taels too.” “No, no!” Hu could hardly say that, once Liu had money, his wealthy young master's habits would return. Instead he checked him with, “If you want to do good works, you should do them in Huzhou. Hangzhou has me; you needn't trouble yourself.” Liu sensed something of his meaning and smiled a little awkwardly. “In truth, I need other people to do good works for me. What standing have I to do them myself?” “Enough of that. This isn't the place to talk. Let's go to my house.”

They dressed and got up to leave. This would be Liu's first visit to Hu's home, and the thought of his niece made him uneasy. Did Mrs Hu know that her husband had established another household in Huzhou? If she did, Liu's position would be awkward. He felt apprehensive. Then he reflected that this was an opportunity to see what sort of woman she was and whether she and Furong might get on in future. Torn between these thoughts, he lagged as they left Huaqing Pool. Hu looked back, read his expression, and realised that he must say something. “Third Uncle, when you meet my wife, there's no need to mention Huzhou.” This removed one obstacle from Liu's mind, and his thoughts began to move freely again. “Then you mustn't call me Third Uncle either. If it slips out, you'll give yourself away.” “That doesn't matter. If she asks, I'll say I knew your nephew first and followed the younger generation's form of address. That happens often enough.” “Never mind. Call me something else. I don't want to be your elder anyway. I'd rather be your friend.” “Certainly, Third Master Liu.” This was his formal social title, and he readily accepted it. They took sedan chairs to Hu's house and paid their respects to his mother and wife. Liu addressed them as Auntie and Sister-in-Law. He found that Mrs Hu, though shrewd, had a proper regard for social appearances and was no unreasonable shrew. Half his anxiety on Furong's behalf disappeared.

Sitting round the brazier with wine, Hu began to discuss Pang. “As you know, the most important business before me is the silk in Shanghai. Since I've entrusted this matter to you and we shall be working together, there's no need to conceal anything. The year's end is approaching. Accounts must be settled everywhere, and expenses must be met. That silk in Shanghai has to be sold.” “Yes, yes.” Growing up in Huzhou had naturally given Liu considerable knowledge of silk for the foreign market. “Prices are good now. Better sell early. If you keep it until next year, the silk will yellow, and the new crop will come on the market. You'll lose heavily.” “Exactly. Prices are good now, but they could be better. You may not believe this, but I can name my own price.” “As good as that?” Liu was indeed doubtful. “Then what are you doing here? Get to Shanghai at once!” “Quite right. I must leave within the next few days. I'm only waiting for Pang's word.” That word was a promise that, in selling silk to foreign merchants in Shanghai, Pang would follow the same course as Hu. Hu had received highly confidential news: Jiangsu's governor-general and governor had submitted a joint memorial. Because foreigners in the Shanghai settlement were continually supplying Liu Lichuan with arms and provisions, they had decided on a blockade, cutting off trade between the interior and the foreigners to force them to support the imperial side. Supplies of both silk and tea would then cease. Foreigners would buy as much of the stock in Shanghai as possible. Whoever could control the supply could naturally hold it for an exceptional price.

“So that's it!” Liu said confidently. “Pang will certainly agree. You're helping him make money. Why wouldn't he?” “It isn't as simple as that.” Hu shook his head emphatically. “Don't take it too lightly.” Liu was not easily convinced. “I don't believe it. There's no reason for him to refuse.” “With enough friendship, naturally he'll agree. Without it, one can't be sure. First, he's traded with foreigners for years and has friendships among them. Sometimes he must accommodate them. Second, there's his standing in business. People would say Pang has to take instructions from me about his silk. How could a man in his position accept that?” On reflection, this was true. Liu yielded again and smiled. “Your mind works differently from other people's. Put like that, I really must be careful.” “Exactly. There's a way of saying things.” Hu then taught him how to put the proposal.

Liu nodded with full understanding. Since their fortunes were linked, however, he could not help asking, “What if you hold firmly to your price and the foreigners decide it isn't worth their while? If no sale takes place, won't you have made yourself unpleasant for nothing? And how would you explain it to Pang?” “That won't happen. Foreign silk originally came from a country called Italy, and from France too. Six or eight years ago, a disease struck their silkworms and killed more than half their stock. So they depend entirely on silk shipped from China. Without enough raw material, their silk mills and weaving workshops must close. Think how many people's livelihoods depend on them! They have to buy our silk. The wool comes from the sheep, and boats rise with the water: the foreign silk merchants won't lose their own capital. What is there to fear?” “You even know the foreign market!” Much of this was entirely new to Liu. “No wonder other people can't compete with you.” “Enough! Stop flattering me,” Hu laughed. “Save those words for Pang.”

Following Hu's advice, Liu made a special call on Pang the next day. He began by praising Pang's boldness and ability in business, then explained that Hu wished to support him as their leader. “Xueyan thinks the foreigners have grown shrewder and more difficult these last few years. They see that some dealers need to sell quickly for cash and deliberately force down prices. Once one firm's price falls, it's hard for the others to raise theirs. So he'd like you to give the call and bring the trade together to deal with the foreigners.” “Yes, I've thought of that myself. The trouble is that people won't act together. I mean it for everyone's benefit, but they behave as though I were begging a favour.” Pang shook his head and sighed. “Why should I give up a comfortable life for thankless work and invite vexation?” “You were born a young master and have never had to put up with an insult. Naturally, you can't go humbly begging others. Xueyan understands that. He asks only that you stand at the head and lend the movement your prestige. He'll do the work.” “I couldn't accept such an honour,” Pang answered. “Old Hu gives me far too much credit.” The words needed careful interpretation. They might be sincere, or merely an excuse. If an excuse, why? As he continued to flatter Pang, Liu studied his expression closely. Here his experience proved useful. Pang's modesty was indeed a pretence. He admired Hu, but they did not know each other well. He had heard something of the remarkable story of Hu's rise, like a leap through the Dragon Gate, from a poor young fellow to a man who could operate on such a scale. Yet he thought Hu's real resources must still be limited. Afraid there might be some trick behind the proposal, he remained on his guard.

As the conversation continued, Liu grew anxious. “Brother Pang, you've been kind enough to take to me as an old friend from the moment we met. That's why I immediately agreed when Xueyan asked me to undertake this. Now you keep declining so modestly that you seem to regard me as an outsider.” Realising that he had gone a little too far, he smiled. “Never mind! I won't meddle in this any longer. Let me invite you to drink with the courtesans on a Jiangshan pleasure boat.” The final turn was well judged. Pang felt that Liu was a true friend. Though Pang had remained suspicious, Liu still treated him warmly. That was rare. The thought softened him, and he felt he must give some definite answer. “Old Liu, don't be impatient. If not for the monk, then for the Buddha: this is the first time you've brought me a business proposal, and it benefits both sides. How could I refuse you consideration? But let me speak frankly. If such a scheme succeeds, nobody thanks you. If it fails, the trade will have plenty to say. Chinese minds are sharper than foreign ones; the trouble is excessive self-interest. That's why I dare not rush to take the lead. Let me talk to Old Hu first. If it can be done, I'll certainly do it. I won't be a tiresome obstruction. Will that suit you?” “How could it not? Where shall you meet?” “I've another appointment today and no time. Tomorrow, then. Didn't you offer me a courtesans' drinking party? We can talk on the Jiangshan boat.” “Agreed. Tomorrow I'll entertain you there. I'll send an invitation.”

“No need for that. Whose boat will you use?” Pang knew this world well too. “Xiao Jingui's is the best, but it may already be booked. Next best is He Xiangu's.” “Then one of those two. There's no time to lose. I'll arrange it now. Once I've secured the boat, I'll send an invitation all the same.” “Very well. I'll await your word. But don't invite too many people. We want some quiet to discuss business.” Liu agreed and took his leave. Returning to the city, he went directly to Hu and recounted the conversation. He admired Hu's foresight: the business had indeed proved difficult. He also apologised deeply for failing to complete his mission satisfactorily. “What are you saying?” Hu reassured him. “To my mind, this is already an excellent result.” “How will you approach him, then?” “Naturally, I'll adapt as we talk. It seems he doesn't quite trust me yet, since this would be our first undertaking together. Even if this one doesn't succeed, there will be other opportunities for us to work together. So, Third Master, if we can't agree, don't take it to heart as though you'd failed me or he weren't a good friend. Treat everything as usual and think nothing of it. Do you understand?” “Of course.” Liu nodded earnestly. “This is a friendship for the long term.” “Exactly!” Hu was deeply pleased. “That shows you truly understand.”

Liu took his leave and asked Liu Qingsheng to send someone to book Xiao Jingui's boat. He also sent the invitations. The preparations occupied the whole afternoon. That night, unexpectedly, a letter arrived from Pang. He had received news from home and must return to Nanxun the following day, so he could no longer attend the party. He hoped to discuss Hu's business that very evening and was waiting for an immediate reply about where they should meet. The letter came by Pang's servant. After a few inquiries, Liu learned that there was trouble within Pang's family. He would hardly be in good spirits or interested in Hu's affairs; whether they discussed the proposal now seemed to matter little. But remembering their “friendship for the long term,” Liu felt he should offer some sympathy. He told the servant that he would fetch Hu and call on Pang immediately. As soon as the servant left, Liu hurried to Hu's house and explained. Hu frowned deeply and considered for some time, then suddenly rose as though his plan were settled. “Let's go. The boat will straighten itself when it reaches the bridge.” They took chairs out of the city. On seeing Pang, Hu detected worry in his expression. Instead of raising his own business, he asked what urgent matter required Pang to return home. “Someone has brought a case against me,” Pang answered frankly. “I may have to appear in court.” “Most unfortunate. What is it about?” “That's a long story. In short, some members of my clan see that I'm fairly comfortably off and are making unreasonable trouble. I don't mind spending money. It's the insult I can't swallow.”

Hu understood at once that the clansmen were after Pang's property. Without the particulars, he could offer no specific advice. He could only urge, “Brother Pang, lawsuits end badly. Peace is best.” “Peace must be possible first.” Pang shook his head. “Never mind. Let's not discuss it.” But Hu could not let the subject drop, nor should he: he could help. “If you're willing to settle, I guarantee a settlement. You needn't fear a lawsuit, Brother Pang. If right is on your side, I guarantee you'll win. But the saying is sound: the rich shouldn't fight the poor. Even winning your case would bring little satisfaction.” “Ah!” Pang's eyes suddenly brightened. “Of course! You're a close friend of Prefect Wang. You can help me.” “Naturally. I'll go with you first. Your affairs are urgent. My business in Shanghai will have to wait.” This was a retreat intended to gain ground. Reminded of Hu's business, Pang showed the decisiveness of a wealthy young master. “Old Hu, don't worry about Shanghai. Leave it all to me. Tell me what you want me to do.”

“Third Master Liu has told you the general idea. I'd like you to take the lead. I'll persuade the trade to act together, then accompany you to negotiate with the foreigners.” “I won't have time to handle it myself. How much silk have you in Shanghai?” “Twenty thousand bales.” “Then that's enough. Yours and mine together already account for seventy per cent. We have ample strength. You negotiate with the foreigners. I'll hand you my warehouse receipts and authorise you to sell on my behalf. Whatever you decide goes. Surely that will do?” The result surpassed Hu's hopes. With Pang's full authority, he could not only bring the transaction with the foreign merchants to a successful conclusion but immediately raise his own standing. Yet such easily won good fortune made him uneasy. He dared show no triumph. “Brother Pang, you're placing a heavy responsibility on me. I'm afraid that if I make a mess of it, I shan't know how to face you.” “You won't. Old Liu has told me about you. You know the silk trade. Remember just one thing: don't stretch your banner too far in a favourable wind. Then nothing can go wrong.” “Yes,” Hu answered with sincere respect. “I'll follow your advice. As for the price, I shall still consult you. I won't decide everything on my own.”

“No need. Use your own judgement. As for your commission...” “No, no!” Hu hastily waved his hands. “After such support, I couldn't take a commission as well. You could have handled the transaction yourself. Why should you lose that amount? I know you're generous, but you have ‘friends’ working under you. If they criticised you behind your back, I should have done you a disservice.” Pang felt still more strongly that Hu understood how things should be done and was a man with whom he could cooperate wholeheartedly. If the other man behaved handsomely, he would not be careless in return. He insisted on paying. Hu was equally definite: if Pang insisted, he could not refuse, but after deducting necessary expenses, he would give the balance to Pang's “friends.” “That's up to you. I won't interfere. I'll write to Shanghai tonight and have the warehouse receipts sent to you. Where should they go?” “Not that way. Please just give me a letter of authorisation and notify your firm's manager of the arrangement. The receipts needn't be handed to me.”

That arrangement was equally acceptable. With Hu's business settled, they returned to Pang's. Hu thought he could entrust the Shanghai transaction to someone else and accompany Pang to Huzhou to help with the lawsuit. Liu supported him, saying that Hu excelled at resolving disputes and was indispensable to the journey.
