Yet this very argument made Pang hesitate. “Old Hu, with your full help, I can already set my mind at rest. At worst there'll be a few troublesome days and a few strings of cash to spend. Nothing very serious. But I don't want a reputation for using influence to bully people. It would be good to have you with me, except for one thing. Many people in Huzhou know you're a close friend of Prefect Wang. If you appear, they'll say I used connections even if he handles the case with complete impartiality.” After a pause, Pang added, “I wouldn't like that, and it would harm his official reputation too.” Hearing this, Hu thought that anyone who called Pang an ignorant rich idler was a blind fool himself. With heartfelt admiration, he replied, “You see matters very clearly indeed, Brother Pang. In that case, I'll do as you wish.” “You flatter me. All I ask is that you write me a proper, substantial letter, to keep in reserve rather than use.” “Certainly. I'll write two: one to Prefect Wang and one to Secretary Qin, his legal secretary. I'm friendly with him too. If you have any difficulty, consult him freely.”

“That's the formal side. There's the forceful side too.” Liu asked Pang, “Do you know Yu Si?” “I know him, but not well. Frankly, I don't much care to get involved with such men of the streets and waterways.” “Keep him in reserve too,” Hu said. “I'll write him a letter as well, though it scarcely matters. Once Yu hears that it's your business, Brother Pang, he won't dare spare any effort.” Hu was flattering him, implying that the Pang family's prestige would naturally make Yu eager to oblige. The compliment was subtle enough to give Pang great pleasure. He thought of the Hangzhou saying: people take turns carrying one another's decorated chairs. The more Hu spoke like this, the more Pang ought to honour him. “Old Hu, from what you say, you and Yu must be good friends. Your friends are mine. When I return to Huzhou, I should like to get to know him. Please write me an introduction.” “Consider it done.” Hu rose to leave. “You're going tomorrow and must still have things to arrange. I won't take up your time. I'll bring the letters early in the morning.” That night, Hu prepared three letters, all giving firm and practical support, and took them to Pang the next morning. Returning favour for favour, Pang gave him two equally substantial letters: one was an authorisation; the other was addressed to his manager in Shanghai. He had deliberately left the latter unsealed and asked Hu to send it, meaning that Hu should read it first and be reassured. This gave Hu a deeper understanding of Pang. He was not only generous and forthright; in attending to every detail of an arrangement, he was scrupulous and admirable.

CHAPTER TWENTY

Now that he had the letter of authorisation, Hu Xueyan needed to think carefully. He had kept up a steady correspondence with Gu Yingchun, who handled his business contacts in Shanghai and passed on all news of You Laowu. Once the agreement with Pang Er was settled, his first act was to write to Gu. Then he attended to the affairs in his charge in Hangzhou, intending to leave for Shanghai early in the twelfth month and sell the silk before mid-month to meet his public and private obligations. After the New Year, he would launch fresh plans and make a great effort. Gu's reply arrived a few days later with an unpleasant surprise: the foreign merchants had changed their minds and had no intention of buying silk before the year ended. They claimed that letters from home reported ample stocks and advised suspending purchases. In Gu's view, however, they had grown shrewd. They knew the Chinese business custom of settling accounts at the three major festivals and making a final reckoning at year-end, when large sums of ready money were needed. They meant to “slaughter the New Year pig.” Yet if Hu did not hold out for too high a price, their interest in future dealings would keep them from driving him entirely to the wall. “This makes things difficult!” Hu told Liu Bucai. “My own need for funds is secondary. Many small dealers won't get through the year. They'll have to turn round and beg the foreigners. Their small quantities won't affect the whole market, but we Chinese will lose face!” Liu now admired him so completely that he thought no difficulty could defeat him. His answer was therefore quite casual. “There's only one solution. Raise some money to help the small dealers: buy their goods or lend against them. Keep them out of the foreigners' trap, and the problem is solved.” That had been Hu's original plan. The difficulty was the lack of money. He could only smile bitterly. Liu understood. “Old Hu, I think Pang Er responds to persuasion but resists pressure. He won't swallow such behaviour from the foreigners. Why not discuss it with him? He has ample resources. If he agrees to your plan, won't that see you through?” True enough. But Hu also had many public and private accounts of his own to settle. What was he to say about those? The whole matter required careful consideration.

That night Hu and Liu Qingsheng worked over the accounts until morning. They extended whatever payments could be extended and postponed whatever could be postponed, but still needed three hundred thousand taels to get through the year. Receivables and funds that could be mobilised amounted to less than a hundred and fifty thousand. Half the required sum was still missing, even before finding year-end cash for the small silk dealers. He had reached the point of having to submit to the foreign merchants. The thought was intolerable. So much time and effort had gone into securing the advantage of a unified grip on the business. With Pang's support, that advantage was finally taking shape. Yet he could not maintain his grip and would still lose to the foreigners. How could this be? Unwilling to yield, with the year's end fast approaching and time running out, he worried through the night without finding an answer. Anxiety brought grey hairs to his temples. Liu Qingsheng added a warning: failure to pay what was due would look very bad. Hu understood what that meant. If word spread that he was short of working funds, Fukang's depositors would rush to withdraw their money. Such a run would make matters worse and force the bank to close. He thought again of Liu Bucai's suggestion. Pang Er seemed a man with whom one could share adversity. Better to let one of their own profit than the foreigners. Asking him for help would certainly cost face, but the same principle applied: better to lose face before one of their own. “Third Master, come with me to Huzhou,” he said. “This journey will depend on my luck. If Pang's family dispute has been settled smoothly, I can speak more easily. If his own affairs are in a muddle, how can I open my mouth?” “Very well. I think we should go straight to Nanxun. Going to Huzhou first and then doubling back would waste time.” Hu nodded without committing himself. He was considering the arrangements needed in both Hangzhou and Shanghai. On reflection, even three or five days were hard to spare. Business at year-end might not change every instant, but unexpected developments were frequent. If something happened while he was unprepared, it could ruin everything. Seeing his hesitation and understanding that he must remain in charge in Hangzhou, Liu ventured, “Xueyan, why don't I go in your place?”

That offered a solution. Liu had the ability to handle such a mission, but one concern remained. “Third Master, when you arrive, you mustn't look desperate...” “Surely you don't need to tell me that!” Liu interrupted. “I understand that much.” “No, there's more. If it doesn't seem desperately urgent, there will seem to be time to spare. You know that rich young master's temper better than anyone.” Imitating Pang, Hu said, “‘All right, all right. Leave everything to me. Let's have a game first.’ What will you do then?” Liu saw the point. Once they started gambling, he might delay Hu's business. He must not play. “I'll tell him I have a great deal to attend to in Hangzhou and must hurry back. On New Year's Eve I'll come to Nanxun and play as many games as he likes.” “Exactly. Say just that.” Hu added solemnly, “Third Master, you mustn't let me down!” “If you don't trust me, don't send me.” After that, Hu could say no more. He wrote the letter and hired a boat, adding extra hands to speed it on its way through the night to Nanxun. They agreed that, successful or not, Liu must return in three days.

Those three days naturally seemed like years. But Hu would never sit helplessly with his troubles and leave everything to fate. He needed a fallback. Each morning he took his place at Fukang and kept sending people out to make contacts and test possibilities, hoping to find some means of raising the large sum. The first two days produced nothing. On the third he was beginning to lose his composure. While he sat frowning in thought, Ji Heling called at the bank. “Xueyan!” Ji exclaimed. “It's only been a few days since I saw you. How have you grown so thin?” There was no need to conceal anything from a sworn brother. “I'm still three hundred thousand taels short,” Hu said frankly. “How could I help worrying myself thin?” Ji was shocked. “Why didn't you tell me? When I asked the other day, didn't you say you could put everything in order?” There was reproach in his voice. “What good would it do to make you anxious too?” Hu adopted a reassuring tone. “As long as you can keep that outstanding Sea Transport Bureau account from being pressed, the rest isn't too serious.” Not serious? Plainly he was trying to put Ji at ease. After thinking a moment, Ji asked, “But you must be doing something?” “Yes.” Hu explained Liu's mission to Nanxun. “In my letter, I offered to sell Pang a quantity of silk at the current market price, so the benefit would stay among ourselves. Since I'm accepting a loss and swallowing my pride, he ought to help.” “Raising three hundred thousand at once at the year's end is no easy matter.” “Actually, half would see me through.” “A hundred and fifty thousand is no small sum either.” Ji beckoned. “Come here. I have something to tell you.”

In a secluded spot, Ji passed on news from Qiu Fengyan. A foreign merchant had approached Gong Zhenlin of the Cannon Bureau and his son Gong Zhitang. They in turn had approached Governor Huang's third concubine, and a purchase of fifteen thousand foreign guns had been agreed at thirty-two taels apiece, with sixty per cent paid in advance. The contract was to be signed and the money paid within the next day or two. Hu was astonished. Buying foreign guns had been his own initiative. If the trial proved satisfactory and a large purchase followed, surely he, as the original agent, should handle it. Why had the business changed hands, with the Gongs acting as intermediaries? Obviously there must be some trick behind it. “Do you know the merchant's name?” he asked. “No. I hear he's Prussian.” “Then it isn't Hudson. There's at least twelve taels of padding in the price of each gun. On fifteen thousand guns, that's a hundred and eighty thousand, before counting any commission. Their consciences must be very black to handle public business like this.” “Leave that aside. I'm telling you so that you can consider whether the money might pass through your hands. If that could be arranged, wouldn't it solve your immediate difficulty?” It was a fresh suggestion. Hu always took an interest in an idea that had not occurred to him. Counting on his fingers, he said, “Fifteen thousand times thirty-two makes four hundred and eighty thousand taels. Sixty per cent in advance is two hundred and eighty-eight thousand. If I could get roughly half of that, it would be about enough.” “Do you know the Gongs? A friend of mine knows the younger Gong well and could introduce you.” “Excellent! Let me think. This avenue is bound to be useful.”

A little thought revealed a weakness in the transaction. Fifteen thousand foreign guns were a consignment of arms that would attract enormous attention. The Small Swords Society nearby in Shanghai and the Taiping forces farther away in Jinling would certainly covet them. Whether sent from Shanghai by land or water, they would be vulnerable along the route. “If only we could discover what the contract says,” Hu murmured. “I suspect something isn't sound here.” “Not sound? The information is absolutely certain.” “I don't doubt that the transaction exists. I mean it may go wrong and land the Gongs in serious trouble.” He explained his concerns. “I see,” Ji said. “The crucial point is where delivery takes place. If it's Shanghai, Governor Huang will have to send a strong escort. That would be troublesome.” “I have it!” Hu summoned Liu Qingsheng. “Have we sent Second Master Liu at the governor's yamen his festival gift?” “It's still early.” “Send it ahead of time. I recall it's a hundred taels at each festival and two hundred at New Year. Put another four hundred in a separate envelope and send both. Tell him I have a favour to ask and beg him to take special care.” The favour was to obtain a copy of the original draft contract. For two red envelopes containing banknotes worth six hundred taels, Liu Er could hardly refuse. Besides, he resented the Gongs for bypassing him. As people from the same native place, their womenfolk called frequently on the governor's household, and they had used that advantage to approach the third concubine directly. Liu guessed that Hu meant to find a way to stop the purchase, a prospect he welcomed. He was particularly obliging. That same day, fifty taels bought the cooperation of Huang Zonghan's young male favourite, who also served as a junior attendant in the official signing room. The attendant stole out the draft. Liu shut the door, copied it himself, and delivered the copy to Hu in complete secrecy.

The contract specified delivery by boat at the Zhejiang border. Hu was puzzled. What remarkable powers did this Prussian, Rudolf, possess that would let him pass safely along the waterway from Shanghai to Jiashan? If trouble prevented delivery, what would happen? A closer reading revealed a tremendous loophole. The seller had guarantors, two Shanghai banks, but their guarantee covered only shortages in quantity and discrepancies in specifications. There was also a special clause: “After the seller has transported the guns from overseas to Shanghai, the Zhejiang governor's yamen shall be requested to appoint commissioners to inspect them jointly at the customs house. Only after the specifications and quantities have been verified as conforming may the goods be released for onward shipment.” It looked like careful administration, wholly intended to protect the buyer. In reality, it provided precisely the means for the seller to escape responsibility. “What skilful legal drafting!” Ji, studying the contract beside him, could not suppress a scholar's indignation. “This is how public business is done! They think themselves clever and fall into someone else's trap.” “Perhaps they're pretending to be clever,” Hu replied. “Under this contract, once the guns reach Shanghai and the Zhejiang commissioners have verified their quantity and specifications at customs, the seller has discharged his responsibility. If they're robbed on the way, it's like the rule on a pawn ticket: ‘The pawnbroker is not liable for natural or human disasters.’ The guarantors don't cover war risks. If a dispute arises, the foreigner need only say, ‘They were stolen in your country. If you can't maintain order in your own territory, what has that to do with us?’ We couldn't refute him. We'd have to hold our noses and swallow it.” Ji, himself exceptionally able and perceptive, nodded repeatedly. A deep, cryptic smile appeared at the corners of his mouth. His eyes kept blinking, as though he had reached some further understanding.

“Elder Brother, have you another thought?” Hu asked. “I'm taking your argument a step further. Perhaps it's a base suspicion, but the others may not be honourable men. My guess needn't be wrong.” What, after all that, did he mean? Hu grew impatient. “Tell me quickly! There may be some way forward in this. Time is short. We must think and act fast.” Ji needed only one question to make his point. “Could it be a fraud?” Under the contract, fraud was certainly possible. The guns would reach Shanghai customs, and Zhejiang's commissioners would report the quantity and specifications correct. During onward shipment, the seller could claim robbery, an unforeseen calamity for which he bore no responsibility. Whether the guns had actually been stolen would be impossible to establish. That opened the way to a swindle. With collusion arranged beforehand, the commissioners might merely go through the motions. Even if the quantity were short and the specifications wrong, they could report conformity. Once the goods were said to have been stolen, investigation would be equally impossible. That would be an even greater fraud. Hu was, after all, a businessman. Hesitantly he said, “Surely they wouldn't dare go that far?” “Ha!” Ji sneered. “You don't know how filthy official life is! Here are the facts: there's a loophole in the contract. Why should everyone else be less intelligent than we are? We saw it at a glance. So many people have examined it. Who could believe none of them noticed?” “Yes.” Hu nodded, then asked the essential question. “Now that we've seen it, what should we do?” Ji smiled. “With your intelligence, why ask me? Decide on a plan, and I'll see how I can help.” Hu thought Ji remained a gentleman. Even with the closeness of sworn brotherhood between them and time pressing so urgently, he would not suggest an underhanded scheme when the opportunity arose. That was rare indeed.

“There are plenty of ways,” Hu said after a little thought. “A man of the world doesn't cut off another's livelihood. If they aren't committing fraud, let them keep the business. Still, Governor Huang shouldn't treat me this way. I've helped him often enough, and I opened the way to buying foreign guns. To see someone else given the transaction now—it's hard to accept.” Ji understood the way Hu's words advanced and retreated. So long as the matter helped him through his immediate difficulty, he did not want further trouble. On that basis, Ji thought they ought to negotiate with the Gongs. “Who should negotiate?” Hu asked. “Your friend?” “No. Neither of us should appear at this stage. Send Qiu Fengyan.” “Excellent!” Hu clapped his hands. “Let's get him here at once.” They used Ji's house, where Ruiyun set out a brazier and wine, and sent for Qiu. It was late and cold. Having drunk himself pleasantly tipsy at dusk, Qiu had long since gone to bed. But the invitation to a late supper round the brazier brought him up at once. He dressed and hurried eagerly to Ji's through the bitter north-westerly wind. On entering, he altered the poetic line “On a cold night, a guest arrives; tea takes the place of wine,” and declaimed, “On a cold night, a guest arrives; wine takes the place of tea!” Ji and Hu exchanged smiles. Even Ruiyun in the next room laughed. A little maid lifted the door curtain, and Ruiyun appeared with a bottle in one hand and a wine pot in the other. Raising them, she said, “Mr Qiu, there's plenty! Chinese wine and foreign wine—drink all you please!”

“My thanks, Madam!” Qiu bowed deeply, took a bottle of brandy, pulled out the stopper, and drank straight from its mouth. Ruiyun laughed again. “Mr Qiu makes drinking so easy. There's no need to prepare food!” “You might say that elsewhere, but I won't let you say it here.” “Why not?” “Because I'd lose by it. At the risk of being laughed at, I've spent the last few days positively drooling over the thought of your sea conch and chicken in red wine lees.” “Then you are fortunate. We happen to have both today.” She smiled. “Only I'm ashamed to serve them to guests. They've already been eaten from.” “What does that matter? Coming here is like coming home. Nobody objects to leftovers in his own house.” Using what was ready, Ruiyun prepared a hotpot and four small dishes for the three men's supper. As Ji urged Qiu to drink, he explained the faults in the gun contract. Though he said nothing of Hu, Qiu, already a little tipsy and always friendly towards him, felt indignant on his behalf. “If this can be tolerated, what cannot? We must have the rights and wrongs of this properly argued!”

“Calm yourself.” Ji took his hand. “We invited you precisely to discuss how to put this injustice right. We've found the weakness, but you don't undertake to mend porcelain without a diamond drill. The Gongs aren't easy men to deal with. We must discuss it calmly.” “Very well!” Qiu drank, put a piece of chicken in his mouth, and said indistinctly as he chewed, “With you two here, I've no opinion to offer. You discuss it. I'll drink and listen.” Ji and Hu exchanged a glance. Even an honest fellow could be hard to manage. They had planned to play off one another, approaching the matter indirectly until Qiu volunteered. Now that he was placing himself entirely at their disposal, further circumlocution would be unfriendly. It left them in an awkward position. Naturally Ji had to speak. After a moment's thought, he looked at Hu. “There is one rather forceful approach. But it's a matter of drawing the bow and holding the threat. It won't produce an immediate result.” “Never mind. Tell us.” “Qiu has already handled the collection and transport of foreign guns, so he can claim experience. He might submit a memorandum saying that a British merchant has approached him and is willing to sell guns to Zhejiang on exactly the same terms, but at only twenty-five taels apiece. Let's see what they say.” “An excellent plan!” Qiu, despite his promise of silence, could not contain himself. “With that memorandum before him, Governor Huang couldn't shield them. Otherwise a censor might impeach him and the court send a high official to investigate secretly. I'd come forward then and see how he explained himself!” “It won't go that far. Once the memorandum is submitted, the Gongs are certain to approach you. Then there'll be something to discuss.” Ji turned to Hu. “Any benefit will come after the New Year.” Not understanding the purpose, Qiu said, “After the New Year, then! It's only a few days away.” Ji slowly raised his eyes to Hu, questioning and prompting him to make some explanation. Hu understood but did not want to reveal his real purpose. It would do no good with Qiu. An excellent fellow in other ways, he could not manage too many threads in serious business. If told, he might only find it troublesome and say, “Make it short! I can't remember all that.” Why invite a rebuff? Hu therefore said only, “Whenever it produces results, this can only benefit Qiu. Let's submit it first and see.” “Very well.” Ji turned back. “What do you think?”

“Ask me nothing beyond the wine cup!” Qiu answered in something like a line of verse, his drunken eyes misty as he reached again for the bottle. “No more!” Ji caught his hand. “You mustn't get drunk when there's work to do. Once it's finished, I'll give you a bottle to take home.” Reluctantly Qiu let go. Ruiyun, alert to the situation from the next room, promptly cleared away the remaining food and wine. She brought a pot of rice gruel simmered with a roast-duck carcass and four accompaniments. With ivory-coloured winter-pickled vegetables, Qiu ate three bowls. “How comfortable!” he said, rubbing his stomach. “Full of wine and food—now for business. Are we drafting the memorandum?” “Exactly. Can you still wield a brush?” “Why not? ‘A measure of wine, a hundred poems from Li Bai.’ Surely I can manage one plain memorandum!” “Good. Have some tea, smoke a couple of pipes, and rest while Xueyan and I discuss it.” They moved to the window and spoke quietly. Some things could not be said before Qiu. First they must consider the consequences for him personally.

“Once the memorandum goes in, Governor Huang will hate Qiu. He may suffer for it later. As his friends, we must consider that.” “Of course. But, Elder Brother, I see it a little differently. Governor Huang has always responded to pressure better than courtesy. This might even make him regard Qiu with new respect.” Ji reflected. “Leave that aside for now. The memorandum must at least look genuine.” “We must be prepared to make it genuine. If we actually take over the transaction, we can certainly supply guns at twenty-five taels each and still make a profit.” Once that was clear, drafting was easy. They moved the inkstone towards the lamp. Ji and Hu considered each point and dictated it, and Qiu wrote each one down. Then they reviewed the whole and settled on a final text. Qiu would have three fair copies made, one for the governor and one for the provincial treasurer. This must be done the next morning. “Very well. Leave all that to me. Now, the next step: once it's submitted, what should I say if Governor Huang sends for me?” “He won't,” Ji replied with complete confidence. “It will be the Gongs who come.” “I still need something to say.” “There's no hurry. When they come to you, come to me.” “By the time I come to you, your New Year expenses will be provided for,” Hu added. Feeling this was ill-judged, he immediately laughed. “I'm joking. Whatever happens, don't worry about this New Year. Leave everything to me!” “Thank you, thank you!” Qiu beamed. “To tell the truth, with friends like you two, I had no need to worry anyway.” He rose to leave. Hu did not detain him and left Ji's house with him. They agreed to meet there again at supper the following evening, whether there was news or not.

Moved by their appreciation, Qiu exerted himself unusually hard. Back home, he did not return to bed. Fortunately, the effects of the foreign liquor wore off readily. After washing his face and drinking two cups of strong tea, he felt clear-headed. He trimmed the lamp, rubbed the ink, and resolved to copy the memorandum properly so that he could take it to the governor's yamen first thing in the morning. His activity disturbed his stout wife's sleep. “You wretch!” she scolded affectionately from behind the bed curtains. “In the middle of the night, in weather this cold, why don't you drag yourself to bed? What are you up to?” “Go back to sleep. I have official business.” This was news indeed. Qiu spent his days being busy about nothing and had never put brush to paper on official work. To claim it at such an hour was extraordinary. “Tell that to the ghosts! What official business? You're playing some foolish trick for amusement again. New Year's nearly here. Think about that! How are you going to get through New Year's Eve?” “It's precisely to get through it that I'm working myself to death. Stop bothering me. Once I finish, I still have to go to the governor's yamen.” That could hardly be a prank. Half disbelieving, and unwilling to let her old companion work himself to death alone, she rose and came over. Seeing “Memorandum” on the cover of the plain folded paper, she finally believed him. “Go to bed,” he said, rubbing his hands. “Why stand here freezing with me?” “How could I sleep alone while you're doing official work?” Her words made him feel delightfully light. He reached out and gently pinched her cheek, soft as starch paste, then took up his brush and wrote rapidly with his head bent. His small regular script was both swift and elegant. He finished by the fifth watch. His wife urged him to sleep a little, but he refused. After an early cup of liquor to keep out the cold, he walked, fortified by it, to the governor's yamen, found Liu Er, and explained his errand.

Qiu's amiability made him well liked. Liu Er was accustomed to joking with him, punning on “Master Qiu” by calling him “Uncle.” “It's winter already,” he laughed. “The autumn wind has long passed. These two memoranda of yours won't do any good!” “Does submitting a memorandum always mean coming to cadge money? I haven't troubled you once this year. You must help me this time.” “How?” “Put it into the governor's hands at once—and ask him to read it at once too.” “Is it that urgent?” Liu was doubtful. “Tell me what it's about first.” From Ji and Hu, Qiu knew that Liu resented the Gongs. There was no need to conceal this from him. He beckoned him aside and whispered, “I have a client who wants to sell foreign guns. If it succeeds, there'll naturally be a share of the commission for you.” “Foreign guns!” Thinking it over and taking Qiu's connection with Hu into account, Liu understood. He answered without hesitation, “I see. Where shall I send word if there's news?” That stumped Qiu. What sort of news? If it meant a summons from Governor Huang, Ji had said none would come. Perhaps the prediction was uncertain after all, and he ought to prepare. “You mean the governor might send for me?” he asked after a moment. “I'm hard to find. I'll come again this afternoon.” “Very well. If there's news and I'm out, I'll leave a message. If there's none, you can go home.” With that settled, Qiu returned to make up his lost sleep. He did not wake until two in the afternoon, when his wife handed him a letter from Hu asking him to come to Fukang at three. They had agreed to meet at Ji's that evening. There must be a reason for the earlier appointment. Qiu hurriedly washed, rinsed his mouth, and went out.

The first person he met at Fukang was Chen Shilong, an old acquaintance. After a few words of greeting, he went to Hu and found him looking radiant and delighted. “Well!” Qiu exclaimed. “You look like a bridegroom today!” Hu smiled, ignored the remark, and asked only, “Has that thing been submitted?” “When I got home last night...” Qiu described the whole business, with no intention of boasting, simply to show how sincerely he had worked for his friends. “Excellent! Matters settle better when we take our time. Trouble yourself to go once more and see whether there's news. After that, we'll drink at Ji's this evening.” “Certainly. I'll go now. But there's something I don't understand. Did you specially ask me here now just to ask that?” “Yes. If you hadn't sent it in, I meant to hold it back until I'd been to Shanghai and learned more about that Prussian. Since it's already gone, that's fine too.” Qiu was more puzzled. “Why this sudden thought of Shanghai? When are you leaving?” “No date is fixed, but within the next day or two. Oh!” Remembering something, Hu took a red envelope from his pocket and pushed it into Qiu's hand. “Hurry home and report to your stout wife, so she can start buying for the New Year.” Qiu opened it and found a banknote for four hundred taels. Gratitude mingled with a sense of unworthiness, and his eyes reddened. Hu would not let him say anything. Gently urging him away, he said, “Off you go! I won't keep you. See you at Ji's later.”

Chen's unexpected arrival had surprised Hu, but the explanation was simple: Liu Bucai had pressed him into service. Negotiations at the Pang household had gone fairly smoothly, largely because of Hu's own earlier efforts. His two letters had naturally led Wang Youling to treat Pang with special consideration and instruct his legal secretary to mediate the inheritance dispute. The plaintiff, a distant uncle of Pang's, saw that with the prefect intervening, continuing the lawsuit would bring him no advantage. It would be foolish to reject a cup offered courteously only to drink one imposed as punishment, so he accepted mediation. Pang had already said that he did not mind spending a little, provided he could avoid litigation and appearing in court. That would put his mind at rest. After reading Hu's letter and hearing Liu's explanation, he agreed at once to help. But with the year's end so close, and himself in Nanxun, assembling a large sum in cash immediately was difficult. “I'll find a way. I certainly will! Don't trouble yourself. Let's enjoy a game first.” Exactly as Hu had predicted. Liu thought that refusal would offend Pang and might undo the good result. Yet sitting down to gamble would delay Hu's business. Then he hit upon a way to satisfy both. “Brother Pang, I've been entrusted with something and must see it through. I ought to hurry back. But since you want me to stay and play, I'm reluctant to leave too. Let me enjoy it properly, without something weighing on my mind. How about this...” He paused as though considering, then spoke as though nothing could be taken on trust and this was the only arrangement that would do. “Settle what Xueyan asked you to do, and I'll get someone from Huzhou to take the news back!” “Good!” Pang agreed readily. “Sit here. I'll ask in the counting house.” Liu would not waste time while he was away. He wrote at once and asked the Pang household to send someone to Huzhou for Chen Shilong, who was to come and await instructions.

“There is some silver in the house,” Pang said, “but I must keep it for New Year gambling and for poor friends and relations who come to borrow. I can't give that to Old Hu. I have several hundred thousand owing to me in Shanghai. I'll assign him two hundred and fifty thousand, but he'll have to collect it himself. Two debts may prove uncollectable. That will depend on his ability.” “Excellent!” Liu was thoroughly satisfied. “On his behalf, thank you for such a great favour. But how is this money to be treated? Do you want goods for it, or something else? Tell me so that I can notify Xueyan.” “What goods? It's a loan. He can repay me when he's sold that consignment of silk.” “Yes. And the interest?” “None!” “Surely that's too much to ask...” Liu hesitated. Pang lowered his voice. “Old Liu, we get on well, so I'll speak frankly. Two of those debts, amounting to perhaps seventy or eighty thousand, will be hard to collect. I hear Old Hu is very close to You Laowu of the Songjiang Grain Transport Brotherhood. If he asks You to collect them, we should recover seventy per cent, even if we can't get it all. I'd be deeply grateful for that. I'll thank You separately, of course. I'll discuss it all with Hu when we meet.”

Chen Shilong was eager to oblige. The moment he received the letter, he went to Nanxun. Liu Bucai was already at the pai gow table and could spare no time to write. Drawing Chen aside, he explained everything, gave him Pang Er's documents authorizing collection of the debts, and made sure he understood every detail. Chen then took the fast boat Liu had hired and travelled through the night to Hangzhou. A weight lifted from Hu Xueyan's heart. Yet matters were still complicated enough to require a journey to Shanghai, while miscellaneous business in Hangzhou also needed his attention. The unexpected discovery of the foreign gun transaction was a particular concern. Properly handled, it could become a substantial piece of business, and closer dealings with the foreigners would help his silk trade. Handled badly, it could offend Governor Huang and the Gongs. If their resentment spread to Wang Youling and Ji Heling, the consequences would be grave. He could hardly leave it unattended. Seeing his dilemma, Chen volunteered. “Mr Hu, if it's something I can manage, let me make the journey.” Hu considered this. It was a possible solution. “You couldn't do it alone. You'll have to ask You Laowu.” His decision made, he continued firmly, “Go to Songjiang first. Whatever happens, get him to stay with you and help. I'll entrust the other business to Old Gu.” They talked throughout the evening, until Hu had made every instruction clear. Chen left early the next morning. That same day, Qiu Fengyan's memorandum produced a response. Early in the morning, a large sedan chair covered in blue woollen cloth arrived outside Qiu's house. An attendant took a visiting card from his card case and handed it to the doorkeeper.

The doorkeeper had already been instructed. One glance at the card, and he replied that his master was out, although Qiu had only just risen. The visitor left, but his card remained: Gong Zhenlin, executive director of the Cannon Bureau, had called. Highly excited, Qiu hurried straight to Fukang Bank. “Heling reads the signs like a master diviner!” he told Hu. “Look—the elder Gong has come to seek my counsel, just as he predicted.” “Did you see him?” “Of course not. One meeting would have ruined everything. If he had asked me anything, I wouldn't have known what to say. Truly, ‘Let them question me, and my life is forfeit!’” “It isn't as terrible as all that. Don't be frightened. Come, let's go to Heling's.” There was little to do at the Sea Transport Bureau at the end of the year, so Ji was enjoying a quiet time at home. Seated by a sunny window on this winter day, he was teaching his little son to recognize characters. At the sight of Qiu's expression, he smiled. “There must be news.” “Indeed there is! All the way here I've been worrying. I've never tried a bluff like this before. I don't know whether I can carry it off.” His concern was that neither the proposed transaction nor the supposed merchant behind it actually existed. A question about the foreigner's whereabouts would be enough to put him in difficulty. Under Hu and Ji's guidance, however, this was easy enough to manage. They carefully coached him in what to say, and at last a real smile appeared on his face.

“I must return his call. I'll need to borrow your chair and your steward.” Ji had yet to answer when Hu objected. “No! That would give the game away.” “Quite right, quite right. Never mind. I'll manage.” Qiu had plenty of friends himself. He borrowed a chair elsewhere, took his own doorkeeper along as an attendant, and thus equipped went to return the call at the Cannon Bureau. As soon as his card was presented, Gong Zhenlin opened the main gate to receive him. Gong's home lay behind the bureau. To show his friendliness, he conducted Qiu into his private quarters and first summoned his son, Gong Zhitang, to pay his respects. The young man addressed Qiu repeatedly as “Uncle” and behaved with the greatest deference. “Brother Fengyan, I've long admired your fame as an immortal of the wine cup. I'm fond of a drink myself and have some excellent vintages. Now that two kindred drinkers have met, you mustn't leave sober.” “I really ought not to impose on you like this!” “You're treating me as a stranger.” Gong told his son, “Go and see where Uncle Qiu's steward is. Have his bundle of clothes brought in.” “No need, no need. I'd intended to stay only a moment, so I brought no informal clothes.” “In that case...” Gong glanced from his guest to his son. “Zhitang, you're much the same size as Uncle Qiu. Fetch one of your fur robes and help him change.” Drinking in official dress would be rather stiff, Qiu reflected, so he dispensed with polite refusals. When Zhitang had a maid bring the robe, he put it on. It was a new lambskin robe of the kind commonly called ‘shredded radish’, exceptionally light and warm, and it fitted perfectly.

Before the wine came tea: Wuyi tea from Fujian, prepared to perfection and served in exquisite, spotless utensils. Qiu was at ease wherever he found himself. Though he and Gong had previously been no more than nodding acquaintances and this was his first visit, he behaved like an old guest, tasting the tea and admiring the utensils in complete comfort. Father and son deliberately avoided business, concentrating instead on their attentions to him, as though they could become intimate friends in a few moments. Before they had finished their tea, two servants carried in a jar of wine. “You're a great connoisseur,” Gong said. “Come and have a look.” Judging from the ceremony, Qiu expected a rare vintage. He rose gladly and accompanied Gong into the corridor. It was a twenty-five-jin jar of huadiao wine. The painted designs had faded badly, and dust had turned the clay seal grey. A faint inscription appeared beneath the dust. When this was brushed away, it read: “Made in the twelfth month of the thirteenth year of Daoguang.” “Oh!” Qiu exclaimed. “A full twenty years!” “Yes. I've had it myself for five or six. There were two jars altogether. We opened one for my mother's seventieth birthday the year before last. This one has waited for a guest worthy of its opening.” Naturally touched, Qiu bowed deeply in thanks. Yet he felt uneasy. Hu and Ji had not anticipated such lavish kindness. Once he owed a return for all this generosity, it would be difficult to deal harshly with his host.

While he hesitated, the servants removed the clay seal and the bamboo covering beneath it. “Have a look, Mr Qiu.” He leaned forward. Light fell directly into the jar, revealing that only half the wine remained and that its surface was covered with white growth. This confirmed how old it was. Qiu knew his wine: he nodded. “That's how it should be.” With a copper ladle, a servant carefully skimmed away the white growth, then poured the wine with equal care into a large green porcelain jar, leaving the sediment behind. He opened a ten-jin jar of new wine and added it. Immediately, the fragrance of fermented grain filled the air, and Qiu swallowed involuntarily. They went back inside and took their places. The Gong household's Fujian dishes were even more elaborate than those served at Wang Youling's. Qiu was in his element. Encouraged by father and son together, he drained three cups in succession. A springlike warmth stirred within his chest, and comfort spread through his whole body. When young Gong urged a fourth cup upon him, he declined. “It tastes mild, but it has a powerful kick. One shouldn't drink it too quickly. It wouldn't do to get drunk.” “You're far too modest, Uncle. You must have one more. I'll drink first, as a mark of respect.” Zhitang gulped down his wine in one draught and tilted the empty cup towards his guest. Qiu had no choice but to follow suit. The Gongs understood what he meant, of course: he wanted to discuss business before he became drunk. And it was indeed time to begin.

“Yesterday, when I called at the governor's yamen, His Excellency mentioned a memorandum of yours,” Gong began casually. “He praised it most warmly. Men as zealous and capable as you, he said, are exceedingly rare in official life these days.” “His Excellency is too generous,” Qiu answered calmly. “He is a man willing to get things done. Otherwise, I shouldn't have ventured to submit it.” “Quite so. Our governor certainly has determination. But accomplishing anything is difficult. Take this gun purchase: it comes with powerful backing from the capital. Who knows what connections that Prussian has, to reach a Grand Councillor himself? Naturally, that makes a difference to the price. His demands were outrageous. The governor entrusted this thankless commission to me, and it took endless bargaining to bring the price down to its present level. I've made myself the villain, and people outside still criticize me. Neither side is pleased. Others may not understand what I've suffered, but you surely will.” Qiu reflected that Gong was trying to overawe him with a great name. Whether the story was true he could not tell, and there was no point in challenging it now. Fortunately, Hu had given him a simple guiding principle: neither agree nor disagree. He nodded and answered with a single “Oh!” He did not even ask which Grand Councillor was involved.

“Now, may I ask whether the British merchant named in your memorandum is Hudson?” This required an answer. “Yes.” “That's rather curious.” Gong looked at his son. “Hasn't Hudson gone home?” The remark was meant for Qiu, and it alarmed him. Even the wisest man could overlook something; for all Hu's ability, he would never have guessed that Hudson was no longer in China. If the whole invention were exposed at one stroke, what a predicament he would be in! Fortunately, three things helped him. First, wine had already reddened his face, concealing his embarrassment. Second, he had escorted a shipment of guns, visited Shanghai and dealt with foreigners; he was not wholly ignorant of the subject. Third, there remained one excuse he could use. “There must be some confusion,” he replied. “Many foreigners have the same first and last names. It was probably another merchant called Hudson. As for me, I haven't actually met Hudson over this transaction. The approach came through a comprador.” The word was a foreign borrowing. Chinese managers employed by foreigners to negotiate business on their behalf were called compradors. It was an impressively fashionable expression, and hearing that Qiu knew it made the Gongs regard him with new respect. “Perhaps so,” Zhitang said. Being younger, he was more candid. “It was the Prussian who told us. He must have said it deliberately, out of jealousy of a rival.”

“Exactly.” Gong turned back to Qiu. “When bargaining with this foreigner, I naturally cited Hudson's price to try to beat him down. If he would match Hudson, we could both oblige our superiors and justify the purchase on its merits. My only concern was Mr Hu. He had taken such trouble to introduce Hudson, and by the rules his offer ought to have had priority. Giving the opportunity to someone else wasn't right. But backing from the Grand Council cannot be ignored. We had no choice, so I made a particular point of mentioning this to the governor. His Excellency said at once that Mr Hu understood the larger interests involved and was always considerate of other people's difficulties. Though this occasion might do him a slight wrong, there would be others on which to make it up to him. In wartime there are many military procurement contracts; he must be accommodated next time. His Excellency also said, ‘Mr Hu has many business interests. Perhaps some other project could provide him with a transaction. In any case, there's no need to contest this particular opportunity.’” Gong expounded his account at leisurely length. Qiu drank, but his thoughts stayed on the matter at hand; he missed not a word. The supposed subject was bargaining with a foreign merchant, yet they had ended up talking about Hu Xueyan. Quite a departure from the point! There was no way to establish whether the governor had actually said these things, but the intention to placate Hu was unmistakable. Qiu could make no commitment himself. He could only keep to his rule of neither agreeing nor disagreeing, murmuring polite acknowledgements.

“So may I ask again: is this Hudson you know the same Hudson who sold Mr Hu the guns last time?” There was no evading that question. Qiu decided that admission was better than denial and nodded. “Yes.” “Then why has the price fallen, when last time he charged thirty taels apiece?” “Last time we approached him. This time he's coming to us for business. Naturally, he can't hold out for a scarcity price.” Pleased with his answer, Qiu decided to add fuel to the fire. “To tell you the truth, I could bargain him down another three or five taels.” “Oh! Oh!” Gong had maintained his composure throughout, but this remark seemed to leave him at a loss. Apparently realizing that it was unwise to let Qiu see his discomfiture, he rallied, recovered his calm and took a sip of wine. “There's something you may not like hearing, but I must tell you. Hudson's goods aren't necessarily very good. The bureau tested the guns you escorted back last time, and their aim was poor. I wonder whether the guns he's offering now are the same.” Qiu could not judge whether the allegation about poor aim was true or deliberately invented, but the latter part was easy to answer. “My memorandum states it quite clearly: goods identical to the Prussian's.” “That makes it harder to understand,” Gong replied. “No one else can obtain that particular stock.”

This was dangerous. Qiu thought that if they continued, every flaw in his story would show, and however good the performance, he could not keep it going. Instead of answering, he put a direct question to father and son. “May I ask whether the Prussian is here? Could I speak with him face to face?” This was a delaying tactic; Qiu merely wanted to stop discussing the matter with the Gongs. Gong, however, thought he really intended to question the foreigner, and grew anxious. There were so many concealed tricks in the business that one conversation would expose the whole deception. “The foreigner is in Shanghai at present,” he replied. “If you have anything to say, tell me and I'll certainly pass it on.” After a few more cups, Qiu declared loudly, “I want to ask what entitles him to demand such a price!” His words and tone were aggressive enough to make Gong's expression change. “As I told you, there is powerful backing in the capital. That makes things very difficult here.” His voice became conciliatory. “In everything, I can only ask for your understanding and Mr Hu's.” There was little more to say. Qiu could neither accept nor refuse. He simply nodded. “I understand what you mean.” They had reached something of an impasse. Gong could hardly compel him to abandon his plan and withdraw the memorandum. All he could do was play the attentive host, repeatedly urging wine upon him in the hope that he would depart in good spirits.

The drinking lasted four hours. Well advanced towards drunkenness, Qiu arrived at Ji's house, where Hu happened to be. His detailed account surprised Hu. “So a Grand Councillor is behind it! No wonder they dare act so openly. Elder Brother, what do you think we should do?” Ji knew official life far better than Hu. “There may be no powerful patron at all—only a powerful name to intimidate us. Don't let it crush you before we begin.” “Exactly,” Qiu agreed. “I find it hard to believe that a dignified Grand Councillor would introduce business for a foreign merchant.” “Even supposing there is such a patron, they can't behave as they please. We have ways of dealing with powerful backing, too, though then we'd be fighting in earnest.” “How, Elder Brother? What means have you in mind?” “The most direct is to have a censor submit an impeachment memorial. Then let's see whether they still dare talk about their powerful patron.” This was a ruthless move. Once such a memorial had been submitted, even if Huang Zonghan's connections in the capital protected him personally, the transaction would at least be certain to collapse. But it would also create an irreconcilable enmity. For as long as Huang remained in Zhejiang, there would be trouble. Wang Youling, too, would inevitably be implicated and could no longer get along in the province.

Of course, Ji was only saying this for the momentary satisfaction it gave him. It was Qiu who drew inspiration from it and produced an excellent idea. “We might ‘draw the bow without loosing the arrow’. Have someone make an inquiry: we've heard of such a matter but don't know the details—could you enlighten us? Then see what Gong says.” Ji was puzzled. “Whom would we ask to inquire?” “Why, a censor, naturally.” Now Ji and Hu understood. Drawing the bow without loosing the arrow meant appearing ready to investigate. Gong and Huang would be frightened into making a definite offer. “An excellent idea. But where shall we find a censor? A letter from the capital would come too late.” Qiu would not have proposed it without a man in mind. An investigating censor surnamed Xie had taken leave to return home for a parent's burial. His leave had expired, and he was waiting only for the New Year to set off again. He and Qiu were close friends through literature and wine. There was every reason to expect that he would oblige.

“What do you think?” Ji asked Hu. “I resent the Gongs' behaviour. They act without the least restraint, as though certain that no one would dare speak.” “I'm not nursing an idle grievance, and I'm not trying to make money out of this. But I'm dealing with foreigners now. My standing is involved.” Ji understood. He reflected that if Hu could overturn a transaction already settled with the governor's approval and bring in a different foreign merchant, the news would enormously enhance his influence in the foreign settlement. On the other hand, it would undoubtedly displease Huang and the Gongs. Once they acted, they were bound to make enemies. In those few moments, Hu had decided. “This is what I suggest. We go ahead, and the profit goes to Qiu. First, he's done most of the work. Second, it will put something aside for his old age. Or he might pay an additional contribution for an actual official appointment—a grander title with a real post—and satisfy his taste for office. Only we must settle things amicably when the time comes.” “You can't, however amicable you try to be,” Ji said. “Snatch food from someone's mouth, and how can he not resent it?” “I've considered that, of course. A man of the world doesn't cut off another's livelihood. If we succeed in doing this business, besides Qiu's share we must naturally look after the Gongs and Governor Huang.” “That's more like it.”

The matter was settled. In practice, it had become Qiu's affair, and he did the running about while Hu attended to his own business. Thanks to You Laowu's help and Gu Yingchun's skill, matters in Shanghai went fairly smoothly. Hangzhou's affairs were also brought into order. By the twentieth day of the twelfth month, almost everything was ready, and Hu could spare time for New Year preparations. On the day the Kitchen God was sent off to heaven, Qiu came eagerly to Fukang with good news. Gong had spoken frankly with him: the gun transaction would be handled jointly. His proposal was to divide the purchase between two contracts. Five thousand guns would be supplied by Hudson, with Qiu handling the transaction. The governor's yamen would take two taels per gun for expenses; the remaining benefit would be Qiu's. Hu calculated. There had originally been twelve taels of padding on each gun. Now they were retaining only the odd two taels. In other words, surrendering five thousand guns meant sacrificing fifty thousand taels. This was no small sum. How could Gong willingly hand it over? He was yielding under pressure and making a painful sacrifice. Surely he would bear a grudge and wait for a chance to retaliate. Having to shield Qiu from the consequences would hardly be worthwhile for Hu. With the memorandum already submitted, Gong had to offer something. He could hardly object to letting others drink the broth while he ate the meat. But this proposal cut into his very flesh; it went too far. Yet Hu had promised Qiu all the benefit. To protect Gong's interests now would be to cut into Qiu's flesh instead, and Qiu might resent it. Caught between the two, Hu felt that they had acted too lightly.

“What's the matter?” Qiu asked, puzzled by his expression. “Congratulations on your windfall,” Hu said tentatively. “I owe it all to your support. Naturally, everyone has a share. I'll leave the distribution to you.” This reassured Hu. So long as Qiu had no intention of keeping everything to himself, matters would be manageable. “Heling and I won't take anything. But money must be comfortable to hold. Money that burns the hand is no use. We need to consider Hudson's contract very carefully.” After a moment's thought, he asked, “Tell me honestly, Qiu: how much money would you like?” It was a difficult question. Qiu did not understand what Hu meant and had no idea how much he might have. “As I said, I'll leave it to you. Whatever you give me will be enough.” “Then I must explain from the beginning. They're sacrificing fifty thousand taels by giving up those five thousand guns, but we can't make that much from Hudson. Why not? Let me show you the figures.” The memorandum offered identical guns at twenty-five taels each. Their actual cost was twenty, leaving only five taels of padding per gun, or twenty-five thousand altogether. After deducting ten thousand for the governor's yamen, fifteen thousand remained.

“Fifteen thousand divided three ways,” Qiu volunteered when Hu had explained this much. “Five thousand each.” His expectations were so modest that Hu felt almost guilty. “Five thousand would be too little after all your trouble. Take ten thousand. Heling and I want nothing.” “And the other five thousand? Surely you don't mean to give it to Gong?” “Exactly. And besides giving him that five thousand, we must ask how much more he wishes to add on top. Only then will your money cease to burn your hand.” At first Qiu objected, but after Hu had explained his reasoning repeatedly, he saw the point and agreed to discuss it with Gong on those terms. Naturally, they needed a way to present the arrangement. Hudson, they would say, was willing to reduce his price by another tael per gun. Together with the two taels already allowed for the governor's yamen, that made a deduction of three from the quoted twenty-five: the guns would thus be reckoned at twenty-two taels apiece. This was the net amount their side would receive. If “the higher authorities have other expenses and need to add something on top, that is quite acceptable.”

Hearing these terms, Gong's view changed. He knew Hu stood behind Qiu. He had thought Hu excessively ruthless; now he discovered a man who handled matters most handsomely. Friendship mattered, but weighing interests mattered more. Gong understood the strength of Hu's circle quite well. Wang Youling had earned a reputation as an able official and enjoyed considerable favour with the governor. Ji Heling, too, was a name that carried weight in Zhejiang official circles. Both relied on Hu as their principal adviser. Hu was adaptable and resourceful, and his greatest advantage was that everyone gladly worked for him. To miss an opportunity to befriend such a man would be a pity. Having made up his mind, Gong told Qiu, “To be frank, this affair has put me in a very difficult position. I needn't explain all the complications. You and Mr Hu are perceptive enough to understand them. In a word, I am deeply obliged for your consideration and concessions, and shall certainly repay them.” Qiu found this very gratifying. “We're making friends,” he replied generously. “There's no need to speak of repayment.” “Indeed, indeed! The proverb is perfectly true: ‘At home, rely on your parents; away from home, on your friends.’ Whenever one can make a friend, one should. When this is settled, I shall thank you separately. And naturally I must also pay my respects to Mr Hu. What would you advise?” “If you offer him a gift, he'll certainly refuse.” An idea occurred to Qiu. “I can suggest a kindness that will cost you nothing.”

“Excellent. Please tell me.” “You know Fukang Bank, of course—a name of real standing among Hangzhou's major banks. You could do business with Fukang and give him your support.” “Nothing could be easier!” Gong repeated eagerly. “I'd also like to invite Mr Hu for a visit. Would you kindly make the introduction?” “Certainly. Hu loves making friends. He'll be glad to accept.” “Then that's settled.” Gong returned to the official business. “We'll handle Hudson's side as you propose. As for any expenses above us, I must consult the governor before I can tell you.” He lowered his voice, assuming the air of a man confiding in an intimate. “Think what the governor faces! At New Year he must attend to everyone, from the capital down to our own province, the garrison general and the education commissioner among them. He can't get through it on less than three hundred thousand taels. People truly ‘see the monk eating his porridge, but never see him enduring his vows’!” From this, Qiu knew that the amount added on top would not be small. He said no more and returned to Fukang to give Hu a detailed account. Before he had finished, Liu Qingsheng came in smiling, evidently with something pleasing to report.

“Mr Hu, an unexpected sum has come our way. There's no need to worry about New Year now. Mr Gong of the Cannon Bureau wants to open an account and deposit eighty thousand taels!” Qiu, too, was delighted. “Well?” he asked with a smile. “Don't celebrate yet.” Hu felt caution rather than pleasure. He told Liu, “This money isn't unexpected. If he wants it back at any moment, we must have it ready. We can't put it to use.” “No! He's specified three months, with the interest left to us.” “Then that's another matter.” Hu considered. “Naturally, we'll give him favourable interest. Issue a receipt to the person who brought it and say that I'll call on Mr Gong at once, bringing the passbook myself.” Liu agreed and went to see to it. Only now did Hu's pleasure show. With evident satisfaction, he told Qiu that the outcome was unexpectedly complete. His greatest fear had been that mending one thing would damage another: this affair might spoil Wang Youling's relationship with Governor Huang. Now, instead of damaging that relationship, they had added another bond. How could he not be pleased?

“Still, we mustn't get carried away,” Hu added. “We can't even call this speculative buying and selling. We've only been selling what we haven't got! We've undertaken everything, and still don't know what Hudson will say.” “Never mind. Didn't you say Hudson had agreed to twenty taels a gun? We now have two taels' leeway. At worst, I'll do the job for nothing. Surely we can settle at twenty-two.” It was a generous declaration. Hu smiled and patted his shoulder, then took the passbook to the Cannon Bureau to call on Gong. Naturally, they began with mutual expressions of admiration and found themselves in perfect accord. After they sat down and tea was served, Hu first handed over the passbook and expressed his thanks. He then spoke of Wang Youling's recent circumstances. Once this connection had been established, they felt closer still, truly like old friends at their first meeting. “Over Mr Qiu's memorandum, you've shown such understanding of our difficulties and done so much to help resolve them,” Gong said. “I'm deeply obliged. I've reported to the governor in person. He, too, was very gratified and specifically asked me to convey his regards.” Gong did not say precisely what those regards were, but he meant that Huang appreciated the favour as well. Hu smiled with reserve and said little.

“Though I hold this post at the Cannon Bureau, my knowledge of foreign affairs is limited. I shall need much guidance from you.” “You flatter me.” Hu abruptly turned to the point. “May I ask where delivery is specified in your contract with the Prussian?” “Hangzhou. He's undertaken to arrange the transport.” “Brother Zhenlin, have you considered conditions along the route from Shanghai?” “I know it isn't very peaceful, so I've already asked the governor to send troops to meet the shipment at the border.” “Once it reaches Zhejiang, there'll be nothing to worry about.” “Oh!” Gong's attention sharpened. “You mean the waterway through Jiangsu is unsafe?” “Yes. The Small Sword Society will certainly covet that shipment. I'm not trying to alarm you, but the foreigner's undertaking to transport it cannot be relied upon.” Gong drew in his breath, plainly troubled by doubts. He stared at Hu for some time without speaking. “Brother Zhenlin,” Hu said frankly, “if anything happens, the foreigner can disclaim responsibility, or ask the authorities to pursue the robbers. How would you fight that case?” “Ah!” Sweat covered Gong's forehead. Rising, he bowed deeply. “Thank you for pointing this out. I nearly made a grave mistake. The contract must be amended. We cannot leave transport to the foreigner. He cannot guarantee it.”

“Exactly. You understand now.” “I understand, but I'll still need your guidance on what to do. We may also have to consult Mr Qiu. He's escorted a shipment and knows the route better.” “There's no need to ask him. I can be of service.” “Excellent!” Gong bowed again. Hu hastily returned the courtesy. At this point, there was no need for further circumlocution. He explained his friendship with You Laowu directly and offered help if Gong could use it. “I certainly must rely on you!” Gong's joy and gratitude were unmistakable. “Without you, this could have become an endless disaster.” He next asked Hu to provide someone to work for him. In official circles, a request of this kind was the most concrete expression of a relationship. Unfortunately, Hu was short of men himself and had to decline with thanks. He did, however, offer another suggestion. The guns supplied by both merchants could travel together. Governor Huang could issue a commission appointing Qiu as escort commissioner again, with responsibility for liaising with You as well. Qiu would be doing familiar work, and they could rest easy. This arrangement would save both time and freight charges, so Gong naturally agreed. They found more and more common ground and talked until late into the night. The following day, Gong returned the visit at Hu's home and insisted that Old Mrs Hu be invited into the main hall so he could kowtow to her. That afternoon, Mrs Gong arrived with gifts. The two families quickly became close enough to visit one another's private households.

Hu did, however, see Gong in a different light, and not a favourable one. From his words and manner, Hu judged that self-interest mattered more to him than affection. As the saying went, he knew a man when he needed him and forgot him when he did not. Gong could not be placed alongside Wang Youling, You Laowu, Yu Si or Ji Heling. Hu therefore warned his wife to take particular care in dealing with the Gongs. No courtesy should be omitted, but anything with consequences for their affairs should be left unsaid, lest it cause trouble. And trouble did indeed come through the Gong household. On New Year's Eve, after the ancestral rites, the family sat down to their reunion dinner. Wearing a newly made coat of thick fur, Old Mrs Hu occupied the place of honour. As she looked at her daughter-in-law, she spoke with mingled happiness and emotion. “I never imagined we'd see a day like this! We owe it to our ancestors' virtue, but also to the truth that harmony in a family makes everything prosper. Xueyan, you must always remember the old saying: ‘Never forget the wife who shared your poverty.’ Keep your conscience in its proper place.” Hu found it unpleasant to hear this on New Year's Eve, but could only answer, “I know.”

His wife said nothing. She attended to everyone, old and young, until they had finished eating, then asked her husband, “Are you going out?” “No. Naturally, I'll stay at home to see the New Year in.” At this, Mrs Hu had a few delicate dishes prepared for his late supper. Husband and wife sat drinking quietly beside the brazier. When she saw that no one else was in the room, she said something that startled and alarmed him. “You heard what Mother said. Xueyan, you must keep your conscience in its proper place.” “This is extraordinary. What have I done to wrong you?” “Very well. Those are your own words. Once New Year is over, dismiss that woman in Huzhou.” Hu's heart gave a jump. He steadied himself and played the fool. “Which woman do you mean?” “Hmph! Still pretending innocence? So you intend to deceive me to the end. Must I say her name?” “Go on, then.” “Furong!”

“Oh...” Hu assumed the air of a man reminded of something long forgotten. “One has the occasional passing amusement. It's all in the past. Why bring her up? Tell me, who said this to you?” “Someone did, naturally!” His wife pressed him. “What do you mean, a passing amusement, all in the past? Are you saying she's no longer in Huzhou?” “How should I know whether she's in Huzhou?” Even as he spoke, Hu ran through his wife's usual relatives and friends one by one. Who among them could know of Furong? After considering them all, he could think of only one: Wang Youling's wife. Yet Mrs Wang was capable and discreet. Nothing would induce her to tell Mrs Hu out of mere gossip, unless... Suddenly he saw it. The Wangs and the Gongs came from the same home district, and their womenfolk often visited one another. Mrs Wang must have let the secret slip in casual conversation, and Mrs Hu had heard it from Mrs Gong. With her husband resolute in his denials, his wife could only let the subject drop for the time being. But an uneasiness now lay between them, and the New Year was less happy than they had imagined.

CHAPTER TWENTY-ONE

On the night of the fourth day of the New Year, the household welcomed the God of Wealth. Hu Xueyan’s extraordinary success during the past year had made him feel as though he had indeed encountered the god, and he burned the ritual paper offerings with unusual devotion. According to custom, women withdrew from ceremonies honouring the gods. As he stood alone offering incense and kowtowing, with neither brothers nor a son beside him, he was suddenly overcome by sadness. What lay beyond him seemed utterly empty. Even if the God of Wealth favoured him with a fortune of tens of millions of taels, what use would it be? When the god had been welcomed, the family gathered in the rear hall to share the blessed offerings. Old Mrs Hu was delighted, but her son looked melancholy. Forcing down two cups of wine and half a bowl of noodles in chicken broth, he put down his chopsticks and returned to his bedroom. “What is wrong?” his mother asked her daughter-in-law anxiously in a low voice. “On the very day we welcome the God of Wealth! He was still laughing and talking at dinner. Why the sudden change? Have you said something to him again?” “No. I haven’t said a word,” Mrs Hu replied. “At the beginning of a new year, we all want good fortune for the household. I wouldn’t pick a quarrel with him.” Her mother-in-law nodded repeatedly, much comforted. “I know how good you are. He owes his success to you too. But he has so much business outside, and entertaining is unavoidable. You must be more broad-minded.” All had been well until that last remark. It provoked a sharp resentment in Mrs Hu. She wanted to say that she was broad-minded enough already, but swallowed the words.

Back in the bedroom she found Hu sitting alone under the lamp, lost in thought. Remembering his mother’s words, she forgot the offending sentence and thought only of his many affairs outside. Her heart softened. He had built all this from nothing, with his own hands. At home she ought to give way to him. “You hardly ate,” she said. “There is rice porridge with red dates and lotus seeds. Would you like something sweet?” Hu shook his head, his eyes still fixed on the clear glass of the foreign lamp. “Then come to bed.” “Leave me alone,” he answered impatiently. “Go to bed yourself.” His cold response to her kindness hurt her. What was he thinking of? Naturally, that fox-spirit in Huzhou! Jealousy rushed straight to her head. Controlling herself with difficulty, she made the bed with tears in her eyes. Then Hu spoke. “Listen. I think you ought to consult a physician about childbearing.” She was astonished. “Why?” She dared not turn round, lest he see the traces of tears. “Why? There is nothing behind us but emptiness. Doesn’t that worry you?” He meant that she had borne him no son. Angry and distressed, she turned abruptly and stared at him.

“Bearing no son is one of the seven grounds for putting away a wife.” After staring a moment, she burst out with this. It was a heavy accusation, and Hu too was taken aback. “How can you say such a thing?” He was genuinely bewildered. He knew his wife had a mind of her own and was no ordinary woman, but had not expected words sharper than a knife. “Why shouldn’t I?” she asked with a faint, cold smile. “Having children concerns two people. Is there anyone in the world who can bear only daughters and never sons? Since that is what you say, naturally I must give way, and you can seek someone more capable.” It all came back to Furong. Recognising the cause, Hu could not help smiling. “You are capable enough yourself. First the blossom, then the fruit. I only meant that we might consult a physician who treats women and try a course of Fertility and Menstrual-Regulating Pills.” His wife was formidable indeed. She would not quarrel without reason, and now grew calm, but her words remained firm. Seizing the opportunity, she came to the crucial point. “And if they don’t work?” Hu was on his guard and dared not press his advantage. “Then they don’t work,” he said, sounding a little aggrieved. “If fate has decreed that I shall have no son, what is there to say?” Softness overcomes strength: those two apparently self-pitying remarks left her with no answer. That night they shared a bed but followed different thoughts. Mrs Hu considered the whole matter from beginning to end and made up her mind.

The next morning his mother asked, “When do you intend to leave for Shanghai?” “When the lanterns go up.” “Today is the fifth. There are eight days before then. There is still time.” “Mother!” Hu asked in surprise. “Time for what?” She explained that his wife wanted to visit her own family. They must count the days so that she could return before he left. Her family lived in Tangqi, a water town near Hangzhou. The journey there and back was tiring. If time was so short that she had to turn round almost as soon as she arrived, it would hardly be worth the trouble. “How strange! Why didn’t she discuss it with me first?” “I asked whether you knew. She said she must have my consent before telling you.” That explanation satisfied both courtesy and reason, but it was not how things usually happened. On every previous visit, husband and wife had agreed first and then informed their elders. Why was this time different? Besides, once the God of Wealth had been welcomed, merchants began giving their New Year dinners. Hu intended to entertain extensively over the next few days and needed someone to manage matters. How could she leave just now? When he explained this, his mother answered, “I mentioned that too. She said you would entertain at the shop and wouldn’t need her; she could be of no help there. As for the family dinner, the date has already been fixed. It is tomorrow.” “This is absurd!” Hu was annoyed. “Why wasn’t I told first?”

His mother already knew about Furong and felt her daughter-in-law had been wronged, so she was inclined to protect her. Taking the blame, she said the arrangement was her own idea and had nothing to do with Mrs Hu. Seeing how matters stood, Hu thought it best to say little. He gave a cold laugh. “Let her please herself. At home she is the one in command, anyway.” His mother naturally understood the implication. “This household depends on her,” she warned him. “Don’t imagine that because you are outside, nobody can control you and you can do whatever you please. If that is what you think, there is trouble in store for you.” Nobody knows a son like his mother. Her words went straight to his thoughts and made him wary. Yet on reflection he could not entirely suppress his grievance. “Mother, of the three failures in filial duty, leaving no heir is the greatest. Don’t you want a grandson?” “Of course I do,” she answered calmly. “Your wife and I have discussed it. She is a reasonable woman. As her mother-in-law, naturally I should follow her plan.” “What is her plan?” “Don’t ask yet.” His mother smiled. “It will be to your benefit.” Unable to guess what the two women were plotting, Hu could only leave the matter for the time being.

The next day they gave the family New Year dinner. Then Mrs Hu took her younger daughter, aged eight, and hired a boat for the journey to Tangqi. She was away only five days, returning to Hangzhou on the eleventh of the first month. The couple’s relationship had always been fairly good. After this short separation, their slight disagreement seemed forgotten, and they laughed and talked happily as before. Hu intended to leave on the fourteenth, so as soon as his wife returned she had to pack for him. He needed little personal luggage. The bulk consisted of local products to be given away in Songjiang and Shanghai. Besides Hangzhou’s “four specialities,” there were many kinds of food and useful articles. Sorting each gift separately was tiring work. These local goods had been obtained in bulk on account. Naturally, some were kept for the household. Hu opened a packet of crumbly sesame sweets made with lard and scented with osmanthus. After one piece he wanted no more. “Hezhu,” he called to his younger daughter, “come and finish these.” She picked one up, took a bite and shook her head. “I don’t want it.” “Why? Aren’t these your favourite sweets?” “They don’t taste nice. The ones from Huzhou are better.” “Where did you have sweets from Huzhou?” The question was really unnecessary: obviously, at her grandmother’s house. Yet it was like a drop of water falling into an oil bottle. Hezhu was old enough to understand a little of grown-up affairs. Suddenly she grew cautious, could not answer, and looked at her father with a flushed face, as though expecting punishment for some wrongdoing.

Hu’s suspicions rose at once. Seeing that his wife was not nearby, he took Hezhu to the window and asked quietly, “Tell Papa where those Huzhou sweets came from. When I return from Shanghai, I’ll bring you a foreign doll.” She did not know what to say. After thinking for a long while, she answered, “I don’t know.” This annoyed him, though he did not want to frighten her into tears. “Very well. If you won’t tell me, please yourself. When I return from Shanghai, your sister will have new clothes and a foreign doll. You will have nothing.” Between the threat and the reward, Hezhu finally told the truth. “Mother brought them back.” “Mother went to Huzhou?” “Mm.” She sounded aggrieved. “I wanted to go too, but she wouldn’t let me.” “Oh! How many days was she away?” “One day to go, one day to come back.” “Two days, then.” Hu thought a moment. “When she came back, what did she say to Grandmother?” “I don’t know. I went over to listen, and she sent me away. She also said I mustn’t tell anyone she had been to Huzhou.” Only now did Hezhu realise how serious this was. “Papa, Papa, you mustn’t tell Mother that I told you she went to Huzhou.” “I won’t, I won’t.” He gathered her into his arms. “I’ll buy you the foreign doll.”

Having reassured Hezhu, Hu was deeply troubled. Naturally his wife’s journey to Huzhou concerned Furong, but what she had done was hard to guess. Had she merely made inquiries, or taken some other action? He knew she had an excellent sense of measure and was nothing like a violent, unreasonable shrew. That made it all the more necessary for him to avoid rashness. He must plan before acting—or, as the saying went, meet soldiers with generals and floodwater with earth: discover her move and devise the proper answer. Once he knew her purpose and actions, he was confident he could deal with them. But this was a powerful opponent, and he must be careful. At home the odds were against him. His mother above and his two daughters below all stood on his wife’s side. One against four, he could hardly prevail. His immediate task was therefore to gain an advantage, and he could do it only in secret. If his wife learned of it, a little reassurance from her would make her position unshakable. First he sought Hezhu out again and warned her not to tell her mother what he had asked. Then he approached his elder daughter, fifteen-year-old Meiyu. She understood a good deal of the world. Though firmly her mother’s ally, she admired her father, so he adopted a different approach. “Meiyu, would you like to come to Shanghai with Papa?” The proposal surprised and delighted her. She longed to see something of the world, especially the foreign settlement with its countless novelties. Yet leaving her mother seemed unsettling. Her dark eyes moved to and fro, and for a while she could not answer.
