“What do you think? Don’t you want to go?” “Who says I don’t?” Meiyu replied. “I’m a little afraid.” “Afraid? Then that settles it! I was hoping to rely on you, and you are afraid already.” “Rely on me?” She was utterly bewildered. “Papa, what could you rely on me for?” “To write things down and do calculations for me.” Hu sounded thoroughly serious. “My business outside has grown very large. I need someone to help, and it must be one of our own family. There are accounts nobody else can know about—not even Uncle Liu Qingsheng or Uncle Chen Shilong. I have thought it over, and you are the only person I can rely on.” This fabrication changed her feelings completely. Until now she had regarded herself as a frail girl, useless outside the home and fit only to help with household affairs. Suddenly she discovered that she could perform an important service. She felt grown-up at once. She stopped thinking of her mother, became bold, and saw no harm in venturing out into the world. But the first burst of courage faded under further reflection. “Papa, I’m afraid I won’t know how to keep the accounts.” “How do you keep the household accounts for your mother, then?” “Those are household accounts. Your money comes and goes in thousands and tens of thousands.” “Large or small, the method is the same. Household accounts are full of little items. Mine concern only a few things. They are easier to keep.” Encouraged, Meiyu’s ambition rose again. “Then I’ll go with you,” she declared. “But I must take A’cai.” A’cai was the maid who looked after her. Naturally Hu agreed, and the matter was settled.

Soon everyone in the household knew, though Mrs Hu supposed her husband was joking. “Are you taking Meiyu to Shanghai?” she asked. “Yes. She is growing up. I want her to gain some experience.” “Experience!” His wife was astonished. “They say the foreign settlement has bad ways. What experience is there to gain? If she comes home with bad habits, you will have ruined her.” Hu only smiled. What was amusing? A girl’s conduct affected her whole future. It was no laughing matter. He must be laughing at her ignorance! Mrs Hu resented it. “Am I wrong?” she asked, calmly but stubbornly. “Besides, they say the roads are unsafe. Meiyu is not to go.” “If the roads are unsafe, what about me? Aren’t you worried?” “You and Meiyu are different. With Master You looking after you, naturally I feel easy.” “Exactly. If she is with me, what is there to worry about?” Their words met point against point, needles hidden in silk, with all their force concealed. Yet Hu had gained the upper hand. Unable to defeat him in argument, his wife made one last move: she brought his mother into it.

With his mother he could not answer every objection so sharply. He returned to the story he had told Meiyu: he needed someone he could trust to keep accounts. This time the fabrication was more detailed. Some expenses for entertaining and social dealings had no receipts. Unless they were recorded at once, they became impossible to disentangle later. Nobody outside the family could be allowed to know these accounts, so he needed Meiyu’s help. Then he sighed. “If I had a boy, why should I have to take Meiyu? Even a nephew of my own would do. The trouble is that I have neither.” This was an inspired appeal to his mother’s feelings. She immediately began to think that, had Meiyu been a boy, at fifteen he could have gone out with his father to learn business. In five or six years he would be a capable assistant, and the growing enterprise would have someone to inherit it. Even if a boy were born now, more than ten years must pass before he grew up. That could not meet their present need. The Hu family had lost an opportunity. She could not help blaming her daughter-in-law for wasting all these good years. Once again Mrs Hu was at a disadvantage, and her husband was pleased with himself. But when he tried to discover more about her visit to Huzhou, he was disappointed. From what Meiyu said, her mother had told her nothing of it.

That evening a messenger came from the bank. Liu Bucai had returned from Huzhou and wanted Hu to come and speak with him. Obviously it concerned Furong. Otherwise, Liu was familiar enough with the household to call there himself. Having worked this out, Hu first watched his wife’s reaction. “How strange,” he said, sounding her out. “Why doesn’t Liu come here? Why must I go to him?” “Never mind that,” she answered with complete unconcern. “Go and find out.” Her composure was formidable indeed. Only when Hu met Liu did he learn that she had already seen Furong. She had simply introduced herself as the wife who had shared Hu’s hardships, left a five-thousand-tael banknote and taken her leave. “Such a thing!” Hu exclaimed. “I never imagined it.” “Nobody did.” Liu was embarrassed. “Furong sent me to ask your wishes before she decides whether to stay or go.” Hu returned to his former mode of address. “Third Uncle, please go back to Huzhou and tell Furong not to worry. I shall find a way.” “What way?” “I cannot explain just now. Whatever happens, I shall deal honourably with her.” This was precisely what Liu did not want to hear. Privately, he hoped Hu would give another twenty or thirty thousand taels, release Furong to find another home, and spare him this not altogether creditable connection through his niece. Hu’s words suggested the opposite. Disappointed, Liu could say little.

“How has your luck been over the New Year?” Hu asked, feigning leisure. This cheered Liu at once. “Excellent!” he said, grinning. “Victorious everywhere, with rich spoils.” He must have won a good deal. Hu thought this a suitable moment for advice. “Third Uncle, the pitcher is bound to break at the well, and the general is bound to die on the battlefield. Have you ever known anyone make his way in the world through gambling? You have a little money now. You ought to turn to serious work.” “All my debts are paid,” Liu replied. “I even won a deed to some land. I have asked Yu Si to arrange the transfer and put me in possession.” Then he grew reflective. “A man really cannot afford to be poor. Once he has a little money, people change towards him at once. In these last few days several people have offered to arrange a marriage for me, urging me to take another wife.” “That would be a good thing.” “There is no hurry.” Liu shook his head. “Let me enjoy a few carefree years first.” “That is wrong. Think of comfort before you have made your fortune, and hardship will come later. Third Uncle, I advise you to restore Shide Hall.” “What?” Liu was surprised. “Weren’t you going to have me help open Hu Qingyu Hall?” Hu had almost forgotten the undertaking himself. “Between ourselves, I shall tell you frankly. That must wait. Even if I open it, I shall have to find someone else. Third Uncle, your strengths lie elsewhere.”

This hurt Liu. “Xueyan,” he said reproachfully, “do you think gambling is all I can do?” “Not at all!” Hu felt apologetic and did his best to reassure him. “I know your abilities. There will be important matters in which I must depend on you.” “What about now?” “For now, it depends on your wishes. Your ambition was to restore the family business. That is why I advised it, and I can help you.” “My mind has changed. Even restoring Shide Hall would mean little. I certainly couldn’t stay behind a shop counter. I think I would rather go out into the world with you.” “Very well. First return to Huzhou and put Furong’s mind at rest. Tell her to live quietly at home and concern herself with nothing else. When I return from Shanghai, I shall make arrangements. Once you have delivered that message, come to Shanghai with Shilong.”

They parted with this agreed. Hu had already left the bank when an idea struck him. He had a five-thousand-tael note drawn and took it home. Finding his wife in the study, he handed it to her. “What is this?” she asked, pretending not to understand. “You gave away five thousand taels for nothing. I am replacing your private savings. Wouldn’t it be better to put your money in the bank and earn interest? Kept at the bottom of a chest, big money won’t breed little money.” His manner left her unable to fathom him. Their silent contest had reached its utmost limit. Uneasy, she thought that, since the secret was out, they had better speak openly. She began with an apology. “Xueyan, don’t blame me for not discussing it with you first. I had no choice. I did it for the whole family. We suffered for so many years, and now that your fortune has only just turned, you must not become entangled in love affairs. It was for your own good. After more than ten years of marriage, you know my heart.” She paused. “Of course, I have another plan, which I have discussed with Mother. You will understand in time. I am not an unreasonable woman consumed by jealousy.”

Those last words revealed her purpose to Hu. In any reasonably prosperous family, once a son passed thirty without a male heir, his parents began thinking of finding him a concubine. If another five or six years passed and the future remained uncertain, neighbours and clansmen would speak out in the name of fairness. Even the fiercest principal wife had to submit to the argument that leaving no heir was the greatest failure of filial duty, swallow her anger and let her husband take a second woman. Cleverly jealous wives therefore prepared in advance. They showed no anger and seemed positively eager to obtain a concubine, calling matchmakers in every few days. In collusion with them, on the pretext of selecting a woman whose appearance promised sons, they found a girl with broad feet and large hands, as stupid as an ox, to serve as the A’jiao of their husband’s golden house. As soon as she entered, they laid down countless rules. Commands within the women’s quarters were as strict as military orders; the concubine was treated like an enemy state, under such close guard that the husband could scarcely move. Hu considered his wife just such a formidable strategist and immediately declined the favour. “Don’t waste your plans. I shan’t thank you for them.” Then he turned to Furong. “Your journey to Huzhou was a mistake—a very great mistake. I told you it was a passing amusement, nothing to take seriously. I had my own way of extricating myself later. Now you have put me in a difficulty. If I follow your idea, give her a few thousand taels and send her away, everyone will say Hu Xueyan is afraid of his wife. Besides losing face, I shall make people think I cannot decide anything for myself. Tell me, will they still trust me?”

This argument left Mrs Hu stunned. Clever as she was, she had seen little of the world. How could she fully understand the habits and anxieties of business? She could only protest, “I went alone and came back alone. We met once, for less time than it takes to drink a cup of tea. Nobody could have known. Who would find out?” “Whether the spirits knew, I cannot say. But if you don’t want people to know of something, don’t do it. Never mind anyone else—I know already.” Hu deliberately stamped and sighed. “They are laughing at me in Huzhou now! Do you know what Pang said? ‘Running a great business is like an emperor ruling the realm. Execute whom you must, spare whom you should—everything depends on deciding at once. Above all, you must not let women hamper your steps. Yet it turns out Hu Xueyan must obey his wife! Suppose an opportunity arises and one immediate word decides between a fortune and the loss of all the capital. Then Hu says he must go home and consult his wife. Tell me, how can anyone join such a man in serious business?’” This invented speech made her turn pale and red by turns. Anxious and remorseful, she could not speak for a long time. Now Hu comforted her. “Don’t distress yourself. What is done is done. Regret will not help. For the moment, let them laugh. We will see when I return from Shanghai.” The more he spoke like this, the less reassured she felt. Disputes between husband and wife over a concubine invariably produced a storm. Even a good-tempered husband could not show absolutely no resentment. There must be some design behind it. And what had become of Furong? Had she withdrawn in the face of difficulty, or was she unwilling to let go? Mrs Hu needed a definite answer before deciding what to do. Now that the matter was out in the open, it ought to be settled cleanly. Waiting until his return from Shanghai invited further complications. Worse still, the resentment he might nurse throughout those days could change their relationship.

His business was important, Mrs Hu decided, but this was more urgent. She must ask him to remain. “Could you leave a few days later?” The moment she opened her mouth, as the saying went, he could see straight down her throat. He understood completely, but asked as though he did not, “Why?” “It is Meiyu’s first long journey. We must make her some more clothes,” she said by way of a pretext. “Two or three days’ delay would not matter, would it?” “If you say it won’t matter, it won’t.” He added an indirect warning. “But don’t cause me any trouble in those few days and make it impossible for me to leave. That would take half my life.” “What trouble?” Resenting her constant defeats, she complained, “No trouble can defeat you. Let each of us act according to conscience, that is all.” Her eyes reddened. Such weakness in a strong-minded woman is particularly moving. Hu felt a pang and put a hand on her shoulder. “After more than ten years together, don’t you know me? You have a conscience, and so do I. Otherwise we would not have reached the life we have today.” Thinking of that life made her more watchful and more certain she was right to keep him at home. She intended to ask Ji Heling to mediate and would concede whatever she could. Hu knew she meant to act, but not that this was her plan. Calm reflection showed him that their positions had reversed. At first he had carried a guilty secret and dreaded further questions. Now she was anxious and he was not. He could wait at ease, see what move she made and devise an answer in good time.

In this leisurely mood, with two or three extra days at his disposal, Hu suddenly felt like an outing. He invited Ji Heling and Qiu Fengyan to tour the lake by day, dine at Huangfan’er and then climb City God Hill to see the lanterns. Qiu accepted without hesitation. Ji declined the lake excursion but came to dinner. When the wine had warmed them, the conversation turned to Furong. One man was his sworn brother, the other a close friend with whom he could discuss anything. A little tipsy, Hu recalled his handling of his wife, felt pleased with himself and could not resist talking at length. That very morning Ji had been asked by Mrs Hu to mediate, so he was content to hear Hu make his own confession. Qiu knew nothing of this. Agreeing with Hu, he said, “Sister-in-Law Hu is indeed clever. She must have read the Code of Jealousy.” Hu had not understood. “What did you say?” “The Code of Jealousy—jealousy, as in envy; code, as in statutes.” “Wine has set you inventing stories again,” Ji said with a smile. “I have never heard of such a code.” “Naturally it is a literary jest, but not without reason. It depicts a principal wife’s jealous heart in the finest detail. Every man thinking of taking a concubine ought to read it.” Hu was interested. “Then tell us about this code.” “It has eight chapters: Personnel, Revenue, Rites, War, Punishments and Works, with Additional Regulations and the Statutes for Apprehending Offenders. There are citations and judgments. Admirable writing!”

“Recite a few provisions for us.” Qiu nodded, drank some wine and took a crisp “ringing-bell” roll, crunching it as he silently rehearsed the words. Then he suddenly laughed. “I remember! Here are two for you, from the military statutes: ‘Any wife who sees her husband enter a concubine’s room to converse and, on the pretext of household business, bursts in and breaks up their meeting shall be charged under the statute against unauthorised entry into a military headquarters. If she merely disturbs them without showing anger, the provision for mitigation shall apply: fifty strokes of the light bamboo, with no confession required. The judgment states: Before the jade-green bed, the parrot’s tongue is just being coaxed to speech; beyond the crystal curtain, suddenly comes the roaring of a lion. This is more than hanging washing over flowers: it suggests a sword concealed in the belly. If deliberate, the intentions are improper; if unintentional, the understanding is deficient.’” Hu understood these balanced phrases. “A fine judgment! Hanging washing over flowers—what a way to spoil the scene. She really deserves a beating on the palms.”

“There is another offence whose penalty is far from light.” Drawing out his voice, Qiu continued: “‘Any wife who judges that her husband and concubine are at a tender moment together, and suddenly calls the concubine away on another errand, shall be charged with unauthorised deployment of government troops...’” Before he finished, Hu burst out laughing. “Excellent! Unauthorised deployment of troops! What is the punishment?” “A hundred strokes of the heavy bamboo and military service on a distant frontier.” “Rather severe,” Ji said, laughing too. “You call it severe, but the author says, ‘To spare her life is already excessive leniency.’” Qiu went on with the judgment: “‘The battle is at its height, the rake enjoying a moment of spring; suddenly a golden tally recalls the troops, and the lady repeats her command three times. Once the siege of Baideng has been lifted, what hope remains of reaching Huanglong?’” “There is something in that,” Hu said. “What statute would a woman like my wife offend against?” Qiu considered. “There is this one: ‘Any wife who agrees to a concubine only because she has no choice, yet boasts of her virtue in hope of praise, shall be charged under the statute against an incumbent official erecting a monument to himself: one hundred strokes of the heavy bamboo and three years’ penal servitude.’ The circumstances are comparable, while the reputation contradicts the reality. ‘Usurping a reputation is prohibited; the regulations must be obeyed.’”

“Stop talking nonsense!” Ji felt that Qiu’s jokes were obstructing his work as mediator and prevented him from continuing. “My sister-in-law is nothing of the kind. Her wish to find Xueyan a concubine neither contradicts her real intentions nor usurps a reputation. Your Code of Jealousy does not apply.” Qiu caught the implication and adapted at once. “It is all fanciful nonsense, of course. Sister-in-Law Hu need not boast of her goodness. All her friends and relations know it.” “Every household has a difficult scripture to recite...” “Xueyan!” Ji interrupted. “What has become of your new favourite?” Hu had no reason to deceive him. “She is living quietly in Huzhou.” “Still under your name?” “Naturally.” Suddenly realising that Ji’s attitude did not entirely agree with his own, Hu asked, “Elder Brother, what do you think I should do?” “A thousand words come to one point: do not let this sow discord in your family. That would be a great misfortune.” “Exactly!” Qiu chimed in. “When the family is harmonious, everything prospers. Brother Xueyan, your good fortune is still rising. Now above all you need your wife’s help.”

Hu looked from one to the other and smiled. “Two fists cannot fight four hands. It seems I shall lose the argument today.” “Qiu is one of us, so I shall speak plainly. I have been asked to mediate. That alone shows your wife’s good sense. This morning I also paid my respects to your mother and received her personal instructions to settle this romantic lawsuit as your elder brother.” “Your mother’s command, your good wife’s request and your elder brother’s authority!” Qiu clapped his hands and laughed. “Brother Xueyan, you must surely obey.” Ji hastily waved him down. “That is not what I mean. Everyone is acting for Xueyan’s sake. First I want to know his wishes. His wife has told me that, provided they accord with reason and propriety, she will certainly meet them.” At this point Hu felt there was no need for further manoeuvres and spoke frankly. “I am not a dissolute man, nor have I reached a point where I can afford to be one. Having no son is one consideration; needing somewhere to rest as I travel is another. I therefore do not think that establishing a household in Huzhou wrongs my wife. I kept it from her out of respect. But she insisted on exposing the illusion, and now the play has become difficult to continue.” “It must continue even if you have to act with a stone mortar balanced on your head,” Ji replied. “Harmony matters most in a family. To achieve harmony, there must be forbearance. Your wife has shown it. What about you?”

“Haven’t I shown it too? I give way in everything and don’t quarrel with her. Surely I have treated her fairly.” “Yes, I know. But what about Furong? There must be some settled arrangement.” “The present situation is the arrangement.” “Then we cannot get any further.” Evidently Mrs Hu had imposed a condition. Was she still insisting that Furong be sent away? If so, there really was nothing to discuss. As they reached this deadlock, Qiu made a fair remark. “Both sides must yield something. It hardly seems right for Brother Xueyan to insist that everything remain as it is.” “Exactly! That is what I mean.” “And if it doesn’t remain as it is? Am I really to let everyone laugh at Hu Xueyan for being afraid of his wife?” “Certainly not,” Ji said. “I have understood your wife’s meaning. You may take a concubine, but she insists that you all live together.” “That is reasonable,” Qiu agreed. “Sister-in-Law Hu is within the bounds of propriety.” “It may satisfy reason and propriety,” Hu replied, “but there is still the law—the Code of Jealousy!”

This was an excuse without substance, yet not easy to answer with reasoning alone, unless Ji could offer a guarantee. Almost anything in the world could be guaranteed except peace between two rulers sharing a realm or two women sharing a husband. The difficulty vexed Ji, and he turned some of his annoyance on Qiu. “It is all your doing! Talking wildly about this Code of Jealousy and putting a weapon into his hands.” Good-tempered as ever, Qiu took no offence and accepted the blame. Pouring himself a cup, he drained it. “A penalty for me!” “Let me drink to you,” Hu said with a smile. “You did well to remind me.” “No, no!” Only now did Qiu realise that Ji’s complaint about giving Hu a weapon was no joke. He wanted no more of the subject. Waving his hands, he said, “Brother Xueyan, no more of the Code of Jealousy, or I shall become the chief culprit.” Hu merely smiled, looking entirely at ease. Ji felt something was amiss. As Hu’s sworn brother he could not evade responsibility; the family’s troubles were as much his concern as his own. He drank two cups in succession.

“Elder Brother!” Hu was quick to notice his displeasure. “Don’t trouble yourself. It is nothing so very serious.” “You don’t understand my position,” Ji sighed. “If you and your wife fall out, how could I ever face your mother again?” “We shall not,” Hu said firmly. “There will certainly be no rupture between us. Give a matter time and it can be settled. There is no need to hurry. Shall we leave it until I return from Shanghai?” Ji answered with a rueful smile. “What can I say? I only hope you mean what you say, bear your wife no resentment and listen to her advice.” “Where I can, I certainly shall. Where I cannot, I shan’t make her swallow an unbearable grievance.” There was nothing more to say, and they dropped the subject. After dinner they went to see the lanterns and returned late. Hu behaved as though nothing had happened, laughing and talking with his wife about the day’s excursions. The next day Ruiyun visited Mrs Hu with a message from Ji: Hu’s attitude had been excellent, the matter was sure to end satisfactorily, and she need not worry. These were words of reassurance. Unaware of the true state of affairs, and seeing no trace of resentment in her husband, Mrs Hu naturally believed the mediator’s message.

When the day of departure came, Hu Xueyan set off with his daughter and a maid. That night they moored outside Beixin Customs. Father and daughter sat by the lamp, eating snacks and chatting. Hu deliberately set out to win his daughter over, indulging Meiyu so thoroughly that she could not bear to leave him and kept refusing to go to bed. “Meiyu,” he asked when he judged the moment ripe, “do you know what makes life difficult for your father?” She nodded. “You're away all year round, Father. Of course you have a hard time.” “The hard work is the least of it. The worst thing is having no one to look after me wherever I go. This journey will be different, though. With you beside me, I shan't suffer.” “Then... I'll go with you whenever you travel.” “That would be lovely, but I'm afraid it isn't possible. Meiyu, will you be angry if I say something?” “No, Father. Say whatever you like.” “To tell the truth, a daughter is best at home, but a son is best on the road. If you were a boy, I'd take you wherever I went. Unfortunately, you aren't. Even if neither of us can bear to part, I can't take you on every journey. First, Grandmother and your mother would worry. Second, people would gossip. Whoever heard of a girl roaming the world? Third, it wouldn't be convenient for you, and you couldn't bear the hardships. So it can only be an occasional treat.” Meiyu said nothing, merely looking at him with troubled eyes.

“Let me ask you this. Suppose there were someone in one of the places I visit who could look after me in your place. What would you think?” Meiyu did not grasp his meaning. She simply answered instinctively, “Of course that would be good!” “Good girl!” Delighted, Hu patted her shoulder. “You're truly a good daughter to me.” Accordingly, the next day he told the boatman to make a detour to Huzhou before proceeding directly to Songjiang. “But Father,” Meiyu asked in bewilderment, “why have you suddenly decided to go to Huzhou?” “It's for your sake that I must go there.” This only puzzled her more. “For my sake?” At fifteen, Meiyu was beginning to think of love. Suddenly she wondered whether they were going to Huzhou because her father meant to arrange a marriage for her. The thought made her painfully shy: her face flushed, her heart raced, and she could scarcely get her words out. Now it was her father's turn to be surprised. Only after recalling what he had said did he realize that she had misunderstood. It was an amusing mistake, but he dared not laugh. Nor was this the moment to explain at length. Meiyu was too unsettled to consider his words carefully, and he would not achieve the effect he wanted.

“It's about something of my own,” he said. “I want you to help me decide.” So that was it! She had been entirely mistaken. She felt a little ashamed and a little disappointed, without quite knowing what to make of her feelings. One thing alone was clear: she dreaded her father's discovering her mistake. Fortunately, she could detect nothing unusual in his expression. Reassured, she composed herself and asked, “What do you want me to decide, Father?” “It's a long story. After we've eaten, I'll tell you everything.” They took a nap after the meal, and by the time they woke it was almost dark again. Heavy clouds covered the sky, promising snow. Hu ordered an early halt and sent the boatman ashore for a fresh fish and a large piece of mutton. Someone happened to pass with game from a hunt, and Hu bought a pheasant and a wild duck as well. Their supper was therefore sumptuous. “Today hasn't been bad,” he said slowly, his wine cup in his hand. “Don't imagine that travelling is always so comfortable. I'm in better spirits today because you're here. Sometimes, when I'm in a hurry, we pass the last place where we could have stopped and find ourselves beside some deserted village or desolate bank, with nothing to be had. Then I have to mix a bowl of soup from soy sauce and eat cold rice.” Was this how her father suffered on his travels? Meiyu's heart filled with pity. She said nothing, but her chopsticks slowed, picking at the grains without carrying them to her mouth. “Go on, eat!” Hu placed a piece of braised mutton in her bowl. “A thousand days at home are pleasant; a single hour away can be hard. Your mother doesn't know what I suffer when I'm away. Now you understand, don't you?” Meiyu nodded. She had felt no hardship herself, but since her father spoke of suffering, she too began vaguely to sense how difficult travelling could be.

“Meiyu!” Hu abruptly came to the point. “You're my eldest daughter, but I treat you as a son. There's someone in Huzhou I want you to meet. If you approve of her, I'll keep her. If you don't, I'll tell her to leave.” For a moment Meiyu did not understand. Then she realized what sort of “someone” he meant. She had heard vague reports that her father had married a woman in Huzhou. When she asked her mother, she had only been scolded and told to mind her own business. Now her father's words seemed almost unbelievable. “Really?” She meant: could this woman's staying or going truly depend on a word from her? Hu understood. “Of course,” he replied solemnly. “I can't make your mother understand. I can only discuss it with you.” “I...” Meiyu did not know what to say. She wanted only to help him, but could find no way to express it. After staring blankly for a while, she asked, “What sort of person is she?” “Her name is Furong.” He then spoke at length of Furong's goodness and the hardships of her life, until Meiyu could think of nothing else.

When he had finished, Hu asked, “Well, Meiyu, what do you think of her?” “This woman... Father, how did you come to know her?” Her father was unwilling to explain all the circumstances. “Someone made the match. They said that whenever I went to Huzhou, I had nowhere to rest and no one to see to my daily needs, so I ought to establish a household there. Men with large businesses all do it. There's nothing unusual about it. I thought she seemed a good person, and what they said was true, so I brought her to live there. But I made one thing clear beforehand: nothing was settled until I'd spoken to my daughter and obtained your agreement.” Hearing this again left Meiyu overwhelmed, both grateful and frightened by the honour. “Why should you need my agreement?” She shook her head. “How would I dare interfere in your affairs?” “You may not dare, but I insist that you do. Why?” Hu sipped his wine and explained point by point. “First, of course, I must tell Grandmother. If she agrees, your mother must agree too. And even after your mother agrees, I still want to ask you. I don't want anyone in our family to be at odds with her. Do you understand?” “I do. If people seem friendly but don't feel it, everyone is unhappy.” “Exactly! And why must you take a hand? Because Grandmother listens to you more than anyone, and your mother can't ignore your opinion either. If you speak for us, things will go smoothly.”

No one had ever attached such importance to Meiyu before. She felt that the responsibility was hers alone and answered at once, “Since you say so, Father, I'll speak to Grandmother as soon as we get home.” “What will you tell her?” She considered. “I'll say she's a good person and very unfortunate.” “Good in what way? What will you say if Grandmother asks whether you've met her? That's why I must take you to see her before we discuss it further.” By now Hu was confident that his daughter was his unwavering ally. Yet affection for her father was one thing; what Meiyu would think of Furong was another. His thoughts therefore left Meiyu for the moment as he considered how to arrange matters so that the two would take to one another at their first meeting.

After another night, they would reach Huzhou before noon. Beforehand, Hu carefully explained his friends and connections there and how Meiyu should address each of them. Once the boat was moored, he took her to Yu Si's house to settle her there for the moment. She greeted Yu as “Fourth Uncle” and A’qi as “Auntie Seven.” A’qi was particularly astute in such matters. Seeing that Hu had brought his daughter to her house, she knew there must be something he wished to avoid, and never mentioned Furong. Instead, she entertained Meiyu most attentively. Warm-hearted and eloquent, and bound to Hu by a deep friendship, she treated his daughter as someone infinitely precious and went out of her way to please her. Meiyu naturally knew whose standing had earned her this welcome, and admired her father all the more. “Stay here a little while. Auntie Seven's house is just like your own. Make yourself at home. I must call at the prefectural yamen first, and then I'll come straight back for you.” But Hu did not go to see Wang Youling. He went directly to Furong's and knocked. She was delighted to see him, though she could not quite conceal the hurt in her expression. Ushering him into the sitting room, she first asked where his luggage was. “On the boat. I'm only staying a day. I've brought someone especially to see you—my eldest daughter.” “Oh!” Furong's eyes shone as she looked at him. “Where is the young lady?” “At the Yus'. I'll bring her presently. She's a child. Coax her a little.” Furong understood: he wanted her to humour the girl and win her over. There was nothing difficult about that. “I can manage,” she said. “That's a small matter.”

What was the great matter, then? Furong felt that Hu's attitude and intentions must first be made clear. The message her Third Uncle had conveyed was vague: he had merely told her not to worry, without saying what grounds she had for reassurance. This was the first thing she asked. It could not be settled in a few words. Hand in hand, they sat beside each other on the edge of the bed, and Hu first asked what had happened when his wife came to the house. “I was making New Year cakes when someone said a Mrs Hu had called,” Furong began in an aggrieved voice. “As soon as we met, she said, ‘My husband's name is Hu Xueyan.’ I panicked. Having no clear standing like this is really unbearable. Ah!” She sighed, and her eyes began to redden. Hu grew anxious at the sight. This was no time for protracted complaints and exchanges of sentiment. Time was short; they needed practical arrangements. Yet he had to comfort her, so he patiently said, “Don't be upset. Bear it all for my sake. Don't worry. I'll certainly arrange everything properly. First tell me what she said.” Furong blinked twice, took out a handkerchief and blew her nose. Controlling her feelings, she described her embarrassment. “Your wife said, ‘Forgive me for coming uninvited, but I truly have no alternative. I know you're a girl from a respectable family and he's deceived you. People who understand each other needn't spell everything out. I only ask you to take pity on me.’ Her words were sharp enough, but her manner was fairly civil, so I said, ‘Mrs Hu, please tell me plainly what you mean.’ She said nothing, but took a red envelope from her handbag and put it before me. ‘These are the little private savings I've put aside over the years. If you'll accept them, I'll be endlessly grateful.’ Of course I refused, but she thrust it into my hand. Then she said, ‘Xueyan won't be coming for some time. Has he left any account books or contracts here? I can take them back with me.’ I said no. She seemed doubtful. After a pause she said, ‘Xueyan and I have shared hardship. There's nothing we don't discuss. To put everything in a few words: we're both women. You must understand my position and take pity on me. You're still young and so good-looking. There's really no need to accept an inferior place.’” Furong paused and turned her face away. “When I think about it, there's truth in what she said.”

Watching her expression and listening to her tone, Hu knew that even if she meant what she said, half of it was resentment. He therefore did not take it too seriously. Turning her by the shoulder, he lightly tapped the tip of her nose and smiled. “You're far too simple and helpless! If you hadn't married a man like me, you'd have plenty of suffering ahead. You say she was right, but answer me this: she said I wouldn't come back, so why am I here? Not only have I come, I've brought my daughter. Doesn't that make her utterly wrong?” “Some of what she said was right,” Furong replied. “It's so difficult for me. You two have shared hardship as husband and wife. What am I?” If they went on like this, nothing would be settled. Hu thought for a moment and decided to cut through the tangle. “Then tell me plainly: what do you want?” “Haven't I told you? It's so difficult for me!” There was no need to ask further. “Since you're in difficulty, let me suggest a solution.” Deliberately, he asked, “Would you like that?” “Tell me.” “My suggestion”—this time he tapped her forehead—“is that you continue to bear my name, Hu.” “Only if I'm allowed to!” “Why shouldn't you? Hu is my surname. I decide who bears it. Who dares say otherwise?” After that, whatever else Furong might have said, she could no longer find a way to say it. Hu had another question in mind: how would she feel if she had to return to Hangzhou and share a home with his principal wife? But as it reached his lips, he saw that it would be unwise. This was no time to introduce another complication. The immediate task was to secure her cooperation and “conquer” Meiyu together. Everything else could wait.

He therefore explained Meiyu's temperament and tastes to Furong. She agreed to everything, with one condition: Meiyu must acknowledge her position in the family, or she would not entertain her. “Don't worry about that. Leave it to me.” With this assurance, he left. Back at Yu Si's, he found A’zhu's mother there too. She had happened to come visiting. Meiyu had met her before and felt no strangeness, so she was talking to her with particular animation. After exchanging greetings with Hu, A’zhu's mother invited father and daughter to stay at the silk firm. He declined. “There's no need for that. But I do have a favour to ask. Make a couple of your special dishes for my daughter.” “Easily done! Whatever the young lady likes, she has only to name it and I'll start at once.” Meiyu was delighted by everyone's attentions, but she was still a girl of fifteen and would not be persuaded to choose. At last her father named two favourites for her. Both were stir-fried dishes and involved little trouble. A’zhu's mother agreed gladly, then asked, “Where will you be eating?” “At Furong's.” “Stir-fried dishes must go straight from the pan to the table. I'll take the ingredients and cook them there.” “Thank you. We'd better be going too.” Hu drew Meiyu aside and asked quietly, “What will you call your auntie when you meet her?”

The question bewildered Meiyu. He had already said “auntie”; what else was she to call her? “What would I call her except Auntie?” she asked. Hu had intended to plant the suggestion. At her answer, he smiled. “I thought perhaps you might refuse to call her that.” “I will!” Meiyu nodded emphatically. “Your auntie has the sweetest temper. In Huzhou, I depend on her to look after me. That means she looks after me in your place, so you ought to thank her when you meet. That's the proper way to behave.” “Yes.” Meiyu thought for a moment, then repeated, “Yes.” Reassured, Hu took his daughter to Furong's without further misgivings. As their two sedan chairs reached the gate, they heard Furong calling, “Bring them inside! Bring them inside!” The chairs were carried through the gate and set down before the hall. Furong went to the second and lifted the curtain herself. Meiyu had already been peeping out. This new auntie was a little dark-skinned, but really quite good-looking. Suddenly she understood: no wonder her father was so unwilling to part with her!

“My dear young lady,” Furong said with a smile, “I never expected you to come.” Meiyu naturally felt shy. She answered with a bashful smile, stepped out of the chair and only then murmured, “Auntie.” At this greeting, Furong was too embarrassed to accept the title without demur. Taking Meiyu's hand, she said, “Come inside and sit down. Are you cold?” She felt the girl's shoulders and upper arms. “You're wearing too little. Let's see whether you can wear my new silk-padded jacket.” “Thank you, Auntie!” Meiyu seized the opportunity to repeat the words her father had taught her. “You've been so kind in looking after things all this time.” She had not expressed herself very clearly, but her meaning could be understood: the person looked after “all this time” must be Hu, not Meiyu on this first visit. Furong naturally felt comforted. Yet she also drew a conclusion about the mother from the daughter: a girl brought up so well suggested that Mrs Hu was an excellent mistress of her household. This made her still less inclined to treat Meiyu as merely a child. She led her into her own bedroom and entertained her most courteously, addressing her as “young lady” at every turn, until even Meiyu found it grating. “Auntie, just call me Meiyu.” Furong was about to demur again when Hu, entering behind them, happened to hear. It was a rare opening, offered by Meiyu herself, and he must not miss it. “Exactly! You're family. All this ‘young lady’ makes you sound like strangers.” Furong took the hint and nodded. “Then I shall. Meiyu, come and try this silk-padded jacket.”

She opened her wardrobe, which held a good many clothes, and took down a new jacket of pale green satin padded with silk floss. Laid over Meiyu's shoulders, it proved rather long, with sleeves too wide to fit her. A grey-squirrel-fur waistcoat faced with rose-purple Ning silk, however, fitted perfectly. Once Meiyu had it on, Furong would not let her take it off. “But it's one of Auntie's good things,” Meiyu said, delighted yet uneasy about accepting it. Looking at her father, she added, “I mustn't keep it.” “It makes no difference,” Hu answered promptly. “Your auntie loves you even more than your mother does.” That single remark bound them closely together. They became inseparable, like two affectionate sisters. Hu felt entirely relieved and decided he need worry no further. His time was as precious as gold, and he would not waste it. He immediately went to the prefectural yamen to see Wang Youling. “How long can you stay?” Wang asked. “I was thinking of leaving tomorrow.” “Why such a hurry? Couldn't you stay a few days longer?” Had he not come, it would not have mattered; now he was here, there was naturally much to discuss, probably more than a single evening would allow. “I'll stay one extra day,” Hu said. Then he explained in detail the purpose of his journey and his family affairs.

“You really are formidable!” Wang said, laughing. “My wife admires yours above all women. Yet in your hands she's like Sun Wukong meeting the Buddha.” “It's too soon to celebrate.” Hu shook his head. “Sun Wukong still has one trick that even the Buddha might find hard to counter.” “What trick?” “She wants to bring Furong home to live with us.” “And what do you think?” “I'd rather leave things as they are.” “See how matters go,” Wang advised. “If there really is no alternative to living together, you'll have to make the best of it.” “It isn't anything else that worries me. Furong is too simple-hearted and no match for my wife. I'm away all year round. I'm afraid she'll suffer.” Wang considered. “If that's your only concern, I have an idea. But we needn't discuss it yet. Tell me, what has been going on between you and the Gongs?”

“Oh, I was just going to tell you. You must have heard something.” “A great deal, though on the whole it's favourable. The Gongs come from my home district, but I don't take their side. To tell the truth, we don't get on particularly well. Father and son can be ruthless, so quite a few people are pleased that you've got the better of them this time.” This made Hu uneasy. His rule was to offend no one and, beyond that, to help anyone he could. Business inevitably involved dealing with officials, especially business on a large scale. The slightest obstruction could affect an entire undertaking, so he was particularly anxious not to antagonize officialdom. He had spent much effort observing and studying these matters quietly and knew how dangerous gossip could be. Two men might have no quarrel at all, but once someone spread stories that the second was hostile to the first, even the first might become confused and begin to think the other had failed him as a friend. This was what people meant by suspicion conjuring ghosts. Hu constantly reminded himself of the danger and would not readily credit malicious talk behind someone's back. But he could not expect everyone else to be equally sensible, and he therefore had to explain. “Then tell me, Mr Xuexuan: do you believe I've caused the Gongs a loss?” “I don't think you're that sort of man.” “You understand me!” Somewhat reassured, Hu continued, “They haven't lost anything through me. On the contrary, I've helped them.” He then told Wang the whole story of the gun purchase.

Wang listened, nodding repeatedly. He felt that Hu had considered every side of the matter and handled it very well. From the guns they turned to Huzhou's militia, and Wang warmly praised Zhao Jingxian's abilities. This subject gave him particular satisfaction. Elsewhere, officials and gentry often disagreed over the organization of militia; Huzhou alone was an exception. Here they worked together without friction, and business could be conducted very pleasantly. “I've thought this over carefully, and there are two reasons. First, Zhao's examination standing is limited. If he were a local gentleman who had once worn a red finial and could not forget the authority he had enjoyed in office, he might expect me to wait upon him and bow to his wishes as though he were still a serving official of the first or second rank. Then we'd never agree. Second, the credit belongs to you. Xueyan, this is no empty praise.” Wang spoke earnestly. “There are capable merchants, but they don't necessarily understand public affairs. You alone understand every difficulty an official faces and everything he thinks. That brings us back to the foreign guns. Zhao admires me for giving attention to them, but he doesn't know that the credit is yours.” “I've neither earned credit nor done any work. With you, Mr Xuexuan, I wouldn't pretend otherwise. All I've done is carry an official letter on a journey I was making anyway. If there's anything you need in Shanghai this time, I can attend to it too.” “That's precisely why I wanted you to stay another couple of days. Huzhou is prosperous, and everyone is eager to help. The militia is well funded. I'd like you to procure a consignment of military equipment. I'll give you the list tomorrow. Please inquire about prices first.” “Easily done. I can attend to it as soon as I reach Shanghai.”

“There's something else, rather more troublesome.” Wang lowered his voice. “There are reports that ‘Jiangxia’ may be transferred. I must think ahead.” “Jiangxia?” Hu did not understand. “Huang of Jiangxia!” Only then did Hu realize that he meant Huang Zonghan. Officials liked to speak in coded references, especially when mentioning great men. They might substitute a place name, an ancestral commandery or the name of an ancient figure. Once explained, these references were nothing remarkable, but without much book learning one really might have no idea whom they meant. This was a weakness of his own. He could hardly start learning again at his age, like a man of eighty taking up the profession of trumpeter and drummer, but he ought at least to consult men such as Ji Heling more often. This was an incidental reflection, and he put it aside. Wang's future was a matter intimately connected with his own interests. He dared not treat it lightly and gave it serious thought.

After a long silence, Wang asked, “What is it? Have you another idea?” “First, may I ask how ‘Jiangxia’ has treated you, Mr Xuexuan?” “Quite well, on the whole.” “Then you'd like him to stay?” “Not necessarily. He's a very difficult man to serve. If someone else could replace him without harming my position, I'd be only too glad to see him leave.” “I understand.” Hu nodded. “The best thing of all would be to have Education Commissioner He transferred to Zhejiang.” He meant He Guiqing. At these words Wang slapped his thigh. “Of course!” he exclaimed. “You've woken the dreamer with a single word! We might ask him.” “Urge him, rather than ask,” Hu replied. “Urge him to start making arrangements as soon as possible. Naturally, that will cost money. We'll find a way to provide it.” Now it was Wang's turn to fall silent in thought. As he considered, he smiled and nodded, plainly delighted by what he saw. Hu felt secretly pleased that he could move a man so deeply.

“That's an excellent idea! I believe He Genyun would gladly agree. First, although an education commissioner holds the second rank, he is still not the equal of a governor in charge of a whole province. Second, Jiangsu is a dangerous province. Zhejiang may be smaller, but war has not yet reached it, and its military arrangements already have a foundation. If he can simply ‘defend the province and keep the people at peace’, his prospects will be splendid. Why shouldn't he do it?” “And then,” Hu said with a smile, exposing the thought behind Wang's words, “it would be easy for you to move beyond the prefectural grade.” “Of course! A transfer to the prefecture containing the provincial capital would also be possible. I ought to go myself, but if I crossed the provincial boundary to promote another man's appointment, it would attract too much attention. ‘Jiangxia’ is narrow-minded and would certainly be displeased. Apart from myself, there is only you. Would you make the journey for me?” Hu hesitated. He truly could not spare the time. Business in Shanghai urgently needed attention, and they did not even know where He Guiqing was. The Jiangsu education commissioner had originally been based at Jiangyin, but since the emergence of the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom he had been unable to remain there and had moved from place to place. With the roads so difficult, finding him might involve a great deal of trouble. Seeing his reluctance, Wang understood and changed his proposal. “Then I'll write a personal letter. Take it to Shanghai and hire a special messenger to deliver it. How would that be?” “Certainly. But where is the commissioner staying at present?” “Presumably Suzhou. Inquire when you reach Shanghai.”

With that settled, they discussed other matters affecting their interests. It was late at night when Hu took his leave. Wang sent him home in his own sedan chair, accompanied by four personal guards carrying lanterns inscribed with his official title. At home, Hu found Furong and Meiyu still awake. “Well,” he asked cheerfully, “what have you two been doing?” “Auntie and I have been tracing patterns for a pair of shoes to give Grandmother.” “Who will make them—you or your auntie?” “I'd like to learn from Auntie, but where would I find the time?” This gave Hu an idea. Finding a chance to draw Furong aside, he urged her to persuade Meiyu to stay. He had thought all along that taking his daughter with him would be an encumbrance. But he had another use for her and had been obliged to invent an entirely respectable reason for bringing her. Now that she and Furong had taken to one another, he was happy to change his plan. “I'm only afraid she won't agree, and I'll be rebuffed for nothing.” “Let her refuse. It isn't such a serious matter. You must look further ahead. If you mean to spend your life in the Hu family, first win Meiyu over. She's the eldest. A word or two from her on your behalf will be very useful in future.”

That was true, Furong reflected. Married daughters and their husbands counted as impartial family arbiters. When property was divided or other family affairs settled, they were invited to attend and uphold fairness. A wife's own relatives were interested parties and could not take such a role. For the sake of the future, it was worth making an effort over Meiyu now. That night, therefore, Hu slept alone. Furong took Meiyu to share her bed and deliberately set out to win her affection. Meiyu was won over: if her father agreed, she would willingly stay there for a while. Though the plan had been his own, Hu affected hesitation when it was put to him. At last he granted permission, promising to stop in Huzhou on his return from Shanghai and take her back to Hangzhou. If he stayed too long in Shanghai and Meiyu grew homesick, Chen Shilong would escort her home. To Hu, Furong's situation was like a game of chess. With Meiyu now placed on the board, victory was assured, and he could leave the matter for the time being. Calculating how much time these domestic affairs had already cost him, he would linger no longer. That day he had a hurried meeting with Yu Si and looked in at the bank. He had no time even to inquire about the silk firm's affairs. Taking Wang's letter and the list of military equipment to purchase, he boarded his boat that same day, ordered extra boatmen hired and travelled through the night, straight for Songjiang.

“You've come at just the right moment!” You Laowu exclaimed when they met. “Silk and tea prices have risen sharply these last few days. It's an excellent opportunity!” “What is it?” Hu asked. “Is there news of a ban on shipments?” “Exactly. Look.” You took a sheet from a drawer. It was a copy of a memorial submitted by Yiliang, Governor-General of Liangjiang. Its substance was that there was evidence of the Small Swords Society's collusion with foreigners. The only course was temporarily to stop shipments of silk and tea from Fujian, Zhejiang and Jiangxi to Shanghai. Deprived of their natural profits, foreign merchants would become eager to see the city recaptured, and only then would they cease supplying the Small Swords Society. “Everyone has been talking about it these last two days. And besides that, harsher measures are coming. The government forces have decided they must recapture Shanghai.” You went on to describe the recent fighting. After Hu left Shanghai, the gentry of Jiangsu had subscribed funds to recruit a thousand Sichuan volunteers. They were commanded by Liu Cunhou, a secretary in the Board of Punishments from Rong County in Sichuan who had been assigned to serve at the Jiangnan Grand Camp, and placed under Ji’erhang’a, Jiangsu's provincial judge. At the same time, two provincial examination graduates, Qian Dingming of Taicang and Wu Lin of Jiading, had organized militia to cooperate with the government counteroffensive. Jiading and Qingpu had therefore been recovered first, followed by Baoshan, Nanhui and Chuansha. Ji’erhang’a and Liu Cunhou were now jointly besieging the walled county town of Shanghai. Whether Liu Lichuan would be defeated at once remained uncertain. Foreign supplies were proving effective: he had food, arms and ammunition, and might well hold out for a year or so.

“We'll have to plan this carefully. Where is Brother Yingchun?” “In Shanghai.” You sighed and seemed about to say more, then stopped. “Brother Five, what's wrong?” “Ah! A family disgrace. Naturally, I needn't hide it from you, but I hardly know where to begin.” You was a man thoroughly at home in the world, brisk and direct in speech. Even when tact was required, he could always explain himself smoothly. He had never been one to hesitate and struggle for words. This occasion alone was different. Hu listened intently, and only after a long time did he understand: the Seventh Lady had run away and was living with Gu Yingchun in Shanghai. The common expression for this was “shacking up”, a profoundly disgraceful thing. In respectable gentry households, even the expression itself was never spoken. No wonder You was so embarrassed to mention it. Hu was astonished, not at the Seventh Lady's boldness, but that Gu should disregard both his obligations to a friend and his own good name. Still more puzzling, Gu had not hinted at it in any of his letters. They were intimate friends; Hu had brought the pair together and was to act as their principal matchmaker. What reason could Gu have for concealing it? Turning this over, he could not help saying, “Old Gu has behaved very badly!”

Now that the matter was out, You found it easier to speak. “We must be fair to people. In truth, Old Gu isn't to blame. It all comes down to our family's misfortune in having a sister like this!” “Oh? Why do you say he isn't to blame?” Once again You faltered, giving an incomplete account of what had happened. Half listening and half guessing, Hu gathered that the Seventh Lady had pursued Gu relentlessly after reaching Shanghai. Then one day she had kept him to drink at her rented lodgings. Whether by design or accident was unclear; at any rate, Gu had become hopelessly drunk, and in his confusion they had become lovers. “Afterwards, Old Gu knelt before me to beg forgiveness. Little Uncle, we must act according to our consciences. Even a sage might have fallen in those circumstances. All I could do was ask what he meant to do. He said he'd go to Hangzhou especially to ask you to arrange the marriage. That would have been a good result reached by a crooked road, and I could have accepted it. Who could have guessed that a Cheng Yaojin would suddenly appear and leave Gu helpless under three blows of his axe?” “How strange!” Hu was full of suspicion. “Does Old Gu already have a wife? Wasn't he honest with me before? If that's so, I must question him properly.” “No, no! It's the head of the Gu clan, a white-bearded man in his seventies who happened to come to Shanghai to visit his grandson. The trouble was that Gu was too punctilious and went to report the matter to him. If only he'd kept quiet! As soon as he spoke, the old man objected fiercely. No woman remarrying had ever entered the Gu family, he said, and he would not allow it. Gu begged repeatedly and sent people to intercede. There was only one answer: he could marry her if he liked, but the old man would open the ancestral hall and expel him from the clan. Now the whole affair is deadlocked.”

“Did Old Gu tell you all this himself?” “Yes. But I've had someone make inquiries, and it's true.” “Then what about Seventh Sister?” You sighed. “A woman's heart turns outwards. She's home fewer than ten days in a month and spends all her time in Shanghai. She and Gu have already set up house together. Yet she herself says he's never stayed at her place. Even as things stand, it's more than enough for me to bear!” “Brother Five,” Hu said soothingly, “who doesn't know Seventh Sister is a woman with a man's courage? You can't judge what she does by the standards applied to ordinary women. I don't believe people will laugh at you. Why keep brooding over it?” “That's true enough, but the matter must be settled somehow.” “Let's discuss it when I get to Shanghai. There must be a way.”

CHAPTER TWENTY-TWO

The two men reached Shanghai that same day and took rooms at Yuji Silk Warehouse. Gu Yingchun hurried over when he heard they had arrived. He looked slightly embarrassed on seeing Hu Xueyan, who naturally would not mention the Seventh Lady in such circumstances. First he listened to Gu's account of the Shanghai market. Silk prices had risen. With Pang Er's support, everyone was holding together and waiting for a satisfactory price. But the foreigners, too, seemed formidable. By every means they could devise, they went inland to buy silk themselves, brought it by roundabout routes to Shanghai, and assembled it for shipment overseas. “This cannot last,” Gu said excitedly. “First, it's troublesome; second, it costs a good deal; third, once the Liangjiang governor-general's yamen has issued its proclamation, it must uphold its authority. Naturally, troops will be stationed at the checkpoints to inspect shipments and prevent anyone forcing a passage. In my view, the foreigners will soon have to come to terms. You've arrived at exactly the right time.”

The report pleased Hu. Yet he had so much to do on this journey that he must put his business in order of urgency and attend to it item by item. His first question concerned He Guiqing's whereabouts. “That I don't know,” Gu said. “The provincial education commissioner has to visit the prefectures and departments to conduct the regular examinations of licentiates. I don't know where he is just now, but we can certainly find out. Leave that to me.” “It isn't only finding him. There's an important letter to be delivered by a special messenger.” “That can be arranged too. Give me the letter.” With this settled, they turned to Zhejiang's gun purchase. Since receiving Hu's letter, Gu had made preliminary inquiries, but the foreign merchant had gone to Ningbo and would not return to Shanghai for several days. They could only wait.

The two most urgent matters discussed, it was time to speak of the Seventh Lady. Hu had agreed with You Laowu on the journey that You must withdraw at this point. At a glance from Hu, he rose, saying that he had a friend to see. “Brother Five,” Gu said, “I'm giving Hu a welcome dinner. Come and have foreign food with us.” “What's so good about foreign food? All those knives and forks—I can't be bothered. You go.” As his figure disappeared, Hu smiled. “You've kept me nicely in the dark, Old Gu!” At this, Gu became agitated. “You mean Seventh Sister? If I'd deliberately concealed it, I wouldn't deserve to be called your friend. If even you won't understand me, I'll have nowhere left to turn!” “Don't get excited. Tell me slowly, and we'll think of something together. I refuse to believe I can't make this match.” These words greatly reassured Gu. “I was afraid I couldn't explain it properly in a letter, and I knew you'd be coming soon, so I decided to say nothing. I was waiting for you to act as my strategist. You don't know how anxious I am, with the affair in this state. It's just like...” He swallowed and could not finish. “Like what? Give me an image, and I'll understand where your difficulty lies.” “Like being trapped behind a wall raised by ghosts. I can't understand how I suddenly found myself in this predicament.”

Hu laughed. “Wine overcomes restraint, and there you were with someone you'd always liked. The raw rice has gone into the pot, yet you can't cook it into a proper meal. No wonder you're anxious!” “Exactly!” Gu clapped his hands. “A perfect comparison. To tell you honestly, when I go to her, my eyes feast and my stomach hungers, but nothing reaches my mouth—all because the rice cannot be cooked!” “What? You really haven't been intimate with Seventh Sister since that night?” Hu remembered You's account: she had told her brother that Gu had never spent a night at her place. Now Gu himself said much the same, and Hu could not help doubting it. He knew men's habits. The Seventh Lady, moreover, was bold, unconventional and careless of restraint. After that night's happy encounter, why had the lovers not come together again? It hardly seemed reasonable. He and Gu were close enough to discuss anything. To speak of bedroom matters might be indiscreet, but given the Seventh Lady's unusual circumstances, it was hardly an affront to her. He smiled. “Dry wood and a blazing fire, yet they burned only once? That's rather curious.”

“Once I explain, you won't think it curious. There are two reasons. First, since I intend to marry her formally as my wife, I ought to show her respect. That night was a different matter—as you said, wine overcame restraint. Second, the marriage still faces obstacles, and no one can predict the outcome. If it fails, I'd have wronged both her and Brother Five, quite apart from what my conscience would say. People who didn't know the circumstances would accuse me of seducing and abandoning her. The foreign settlement is full of gossips. With a reputation like that, who knows what a villain they'd make of me!” Hu's respect rose at these words. His smile disappeared. “Old Gu, with intentions like yours, this marriage cannot fail. It's still early. I'll go and see Seventh Sister first.” Gu found this profoundly comforting.

After a moment's thought, Gu answered, “Then let's have dinner at her place. There's still some food at home today.” His tone made it clear that he and the Seventh Lady were already like husband and wife, lacking only the fulfilment of their shared dream. Their affection was plainly strong. Here were two people perfectly suited to one another, a match that ought to follow naturally, and that meddling Cheng Yaojin had to appear, brandishing clan rules. Infuriating! Hu felt a surge of defiance. Striking his chest, he declared, “Don't worry, Old Gu. Leave that old clan head to me.” “Wait, Hu!” Gu said nervously. “He's a great-uncle of mine, and he taught my late father. You mustn't act rashly. Tell me, how do you propose to ‘deal with’ him?” “‘Deal with’ may sound rather unpleasant. I'm not trying to make him lose face. I'm trying to win his consent.” “That's right.” Gu brightened. “Tell me quickly, so I can share the pleasure.” “It isn't time for pleasure yet, only reassurance. We must see how things work out. I do have a plan, but I must speak to Seventh Sister first.” “When? Should I keep out of the way?” “That would be best.” “Then I'll take you there and go to a foreign provision shop to buy some game. You can talk while I'm out.”

Having agreed, Gu hired a “Hengsimei” carriage and took Hu to the Seventh Lady's lodgings in Qipan Street. She was overjoyed to see him. “Little Uncle, after Gu left last night, I cast the dominoes and divined that an honoured helper would come today. Sure enough, here you are! A bodhisattva come to save my life!” Then she glanced at Gu. “It's that unfortunate surname of theirs. We had to come up against a stubborn old Gu—a hidebound old stick! He's made me so angry my stomach's nearly acting up.” “Don't be angry. So long as you'll listen to me, I guarantee you'll be called Gu yourself.” At this, Gu rose and, following their agreed plan, excused himself to buy game at the foreign provision shop. Once he had gone, her manner changed. Her pride made her pretend indifference in front of Gu. Alone with Hu, however, she behaved as though she had truly found an uncle of her own. Her face was full of hurt and distress. Compared with her usual bold, carefree manner, it scarcely seemed the same person. “Little Uncle,” she said, her voice close to tears, “what am I to do, left hanging like this? All my life I've tried to hold my head high, and now I've landed myself in something I can't hold my head high about. That's why I seldom go back to Songjiang. I really can't face people. You must find some way to help me.” “Don't worry. There must be a way.” Hu asked carefully, “But I must understand. Is it that you love each other too much to part, or that your pride is involved?” “Both. When it comes to reputation, it's always the woman who suffers. Ah, I have myself to blame. I tried a fancy trick with a spear and wounded myself.”

Hu was exceptionally good at reading a person's tone. At once he sensed more behind her words. “What trick did you play?” Her expression became extraordinary: amusement, pride, shame and regret mingled in it. Even Hu, so practised at reading faces, could not guess what she had in mind. “Well?” he deliberately provoked her. “If you can't bring yourself to say it, never mind.” “I can say it. I'm only afraid... afraid you won't believe me.” “Leave that to me. Not to boast, but whatever else I can't do, I can tell when people speak the truth or lie, how much of the truth they tell and how far their falsehood goes. None of that escapes me.” “I believe that.” Her expression changed again, becoming earnest. “You're the only person I could tell. I wouldn't even tell Fifth Sister-in-Law. She would be sure to blame me. But first, Little Uncle, what are people saying about me?” “People? What people? I've heard only what Brother Five told me.” “What did he say?” How could Hu repeat such words as ‘wine overcomes restraint’? After considering, he answered, “Brother Five said Gu wasn't to blame.” Though discreetly phrased, the meaning was plain to her. “Naturally, the blame is mine! As though I'd made myself cheap. Heaven is my witness—nothing of the sort happened!” “What didn't happen?” Hu asked in astonishment.

Even a woman as free-spoken as the Seventh Lady blushed at that question. Composing her face and lowering her eyes, she replied, “You're my elder, Little Uncle, so there's no harm in telling you. To this day, Gu has never touched my body.” “So that's it!” Hu was more puzzled than ever. “Then where did ‘that affair’ come from?” “I made him believe he'd done it.” “Why?” “Why?” Now she raised her face. “Surely even that worldly, ingenious heart of yours can understand!” A little thought made it plain. She must have been afraid Gu would change his mind, deliberately made him drunk, and claimed that they had been intimate. His sense of duty and conscience would then oblige him to marry her. It was a stratagem Hu would never have dreamed of. How unlike other women she was showed fully in this device. She had gone to extraordinary lengths, and he could not help admiring the courage with which she had burned her boats. Yet their friendship was close; he truly regarded her as his own younger sister. More than admiration, he felt disapproval. “What an idea to have! Never mind Fifth Sister-in-Law—I blame you too. Gu has a conscience. What he told me showed him to be a true gentleman. But suppose he'd refused to shoulder the responsibility? Wouldn't you have got the reputation before getting the shoes, as they say? A respectable woman, with a story like that going about! You may not care, but you've made Brother Five lose face whenever he goes out. Think about it. Was it worth it?”

His words filled her with regret and agitation. “Oh dear!” She wrung her hands and drew in her breath. “You've reminded me, Little Uncle. I never thought I might make Brother Five lose face. What... what am I to do?” Hu had never seen her so anxious. He felt deeply sorry for her and was about to comfort her when another thought occurred to him. She feared neither heaven nor earth and would listen to no one. Here was a rare chance to teach her a lesson. He made his face sterner. “Seventh Sister,” he said, his voice quiet but cold, “you think only of pleasing yourself, never of other people. By damaging your own honour like this, you damage the You family's name. Your parents must grieve for it in their graves. You really must change your ways.” Mention of her parents stung her conscience still more. Her face flushed; tears trembled in her eyes. She could only look at him, pleading for understanding and help. Hu's voice softened into earnestness. “A woman is still a woman. Her ability must show in the right sphere. If she can do what a man by his nature cannot, that is real ability. If you're capable in exactly the way a man is, only a useless husband will let your strengths shine. Otherwise, it can never end well. Why? A husband with spirit may put up with almost anything, but never with a wife humiliating him in public.”

The Seventh Lady said nothing. It was not that she had no answer, but everyone she met praised her ability. They either called her a woman with a man's courage or said she was more useful than a man. This was the first time she had heard anything like Hu's words, and she needed to consider them carefully. The more she did, the more they resembled an olive: sour and astringent at first, increasingly sweet in the aftertaste. For years she had had the upper hand in public life, but only she knew her private suffering as a woman. Alone beside a solitary lamp, with cold bedding and an empty place beside her pillow, all those ringing cries of “Seventh Sister! Seventh Sister!” were useless. What she longed for was a husband and children. She would willingly cook and wash; at least her toil would have a purpose. “There are men and women just as heaven and earth have yin and yang, and all things have firmness and softness. If women were the same as men, there'd be yang without yin, firmness without softness. What sort of world would that be? And if both husband and wife have forceful, unyielding temperaments, how can they live in harmony? Seventh Sister, am I right?” Directly asked, she could no longer remain silent. “Yes. I've never heard this before. If someone had said it earlier, I wouldn't have developed such a temper.” “It's still not too late to change,” Hu replied at once. “Mountains and rivers are easier to alter than a person's nature.” She paused. “I'll try.” “Good. If you're determined and want to show what you can do, you can change. If you can't...” He deliberately stopped. Naturally, she asked, “What if I can't?” “Then, honestly, you'd better not marry Gu. Even if you did, your temperaments wouldn't agree.”

She thought this went too far, but could hardly argue and gave no answer. “You don't believe me, do you?” “It isn't that,” she hastened to say. “Gu comes often and spends plenty of time here. He's never said anything.” “I know,” Hu replied calmly. “For one thing, you're both being polite to each other at present. For another, men and women think differently before and after marriage. What Gu values in you is your good heart and frank, generous spirit. Don't turn your strengths into weaknesses. Turn your weaknesses into strengths.” This won her admiration. “There's wisdom in those words, Little Uncle. I'll listen.” “That's right. If you'll listen, naturally I'll concern myself with your affairs. Otherwise, why make a match only to be cursed for it?” He continued, “First tell me, Seventh Sister: would you be willing to change your surname?” Her eyes widened. “Change it? To what? Why?” “It certainly wouldn't disgrace you. Oh!” Something occurred to him, and he asked urgently, “There's another important question. Has the old Gu clan head ever seen you?” “No. I've never met anyone from their family.” “Then we're certain to succeed. We'll use my plan to carry you safely past him without his knowing.”

Hu's plan was to have Wang Youling acknowledge the Seventh Lady as his sister. They would not say that the relationship was adoptive, so she must take the surname Wang. Gu would propose marriage to the Wang family; the bride's family would consent, and Wang himself would present the document giving her birth details. Out of respect for a prefect, the old clan head would find it difficult to refuse even if he learned the truth. Since he had never met her, however, deceiving him would be easy. The Seventh Lady could scarcely stop smiling. “Little Uncle, you're a real Zhuge Liang! Even if that old Gu fellow were Cao Cao, he'd still be beaten by you. But...” Her brows drew together slightly, and her smile faded. “What is Prefect Wang's position, and what is mine? How could I presume to claim such a connection?” “Don't concern yourself with that. Leave it to me.” “There's also Brother Five. I don't know what he'll think.” “If it's for your good, there's no reason for him to refuse. Leave that to me too.” She considered the plan from beginning to end and could find no obstacle. Only one concern remained: could she pass for the lady of a prefect's family? This brought a fresh resolve. “I really will change,” she said. “I must look like a daughter of an official household.” “Exactly. Now you're in earnest.”

Just then, the rumble of a carriage approached. She knew the sound. “Gu's back!” Lifting the curtain, she looked out. Hu rose to look too. Two figures appeared in the dusk, dimly recognizable as Gu and You. When they came upstairs, he saw that he was right. As Gu handed her a large parcel of smoked quail and other game, he could not help studying her face. Her expression was open and relaxed; the underlying gloom of so many days had vanished. “Well? What good idea has Hu found?” Even You brightened at the question, looking eagerly from Hu to his sister. She was moved. She had thought he deliberately neglected her troubles and rarely visited because he meant to show his displeasure. She had resented him deeply. Only now did she see how much he cared. She became more restrained and considerate. “Let Little Uncle tell you. We must ask Brother Five about this.” With that, she went lightly downstairs to the kitchen. Hu explained his plan. Gu was delighted; You remained more composed. His objection was the same as his sister's had been. “I know your friendship with Prefect Wang. One word from you is certain to settle it. But we must take a look in the mirror. Even if we claim such a grand connection and he doesn't disdain us, other people will gossip.” “Brother Five, I can't admire that remark,” Hu said frankly. “Are you the sort of man who fears what others say?” You looked ashamed. “Among ourselves, I'll tell the truth. These last two years, I really have become rather afraid of trouble. The proverb is right: ‘For your first three years abroad, you can go anywhere under heaven; after another three, you can scarcely take a step.’ I often think of that now.”

Hu and Gu remained silent. They did not know whether You had something particular in mind and thought it best to say nothing. “Enough of that. We'll follow Little Uncle's plan. Tell me what preparations courtesy requires of me.” “That's a small matter. First, we must plan for Gu. To carry this off, we must treat the previous marriage proposal as having failed and begin afresh with a daughter of the Wang family. Only then will it look convincing.” “Exactly.” You added solemnly, “One thing: please tell A’qi she must stop living here. She must go back to Songjiang first.” This reminded Hu of something. He smiled at Gu. “Forgive me. I must tell Brother Five a rather amusing story.” If it was amusing, why not let everyone hear it? Why tell it behind someone's back? Evidently it concerned Gu himself. He was bewildered, and You was puzzled too. But when Hu told You what his sister had confessed, he really did laugh, loudly. A small part was amusement; most was joy. Whatever her flightiness or recklessness, his sister had, after all, remained chaste. Gu could contain himself no longer. He came over. “What's so funny? Tell me, so I can laugh too.” Neither answered. Instead, they exchanged a glance, silently consulting each other. “He ought to be told,” You said firmly. Naturally, it fell to Hu to do the telling. He drew Gu aside and revealed the Seventh Lady's secret.

“No wonder!” Gu exclaimed, immensely relieved. A mystery he had carried for days, unable to discuss it with anyone, was solved. When he had awoken towards dawn that night, he had found her sitting alone by the lamp in a light lined jacket, faint traces of tears beneath her eyes. She had told him that she had given him everything and made him swear before the lamp never to change his heart. Feeling that he had wronged her, he had done whatever she asked. Yet sometimes, in quiet reflection, he could recall nothing of that enchanting scene—her soft, warm, fragrant body in his arms—still less the rapture itself. To have passed one of life's rarest nights so muddled and unaware seemed more regrettable than Pigsy swallowing the ginseng fruit without tasting it. Only now did he learn that ‘Pigsy’ had been deceived. But being deceived was better than not being deceived.
