Gu was driving the carriage himself and had also noticed him. He stopped. “Where are you going?” “Back to Yiqing House.” “No need. We've come specially to fetch Sister A’qiao. We're all gathering at our place tonight. You must come too.” Chen therefore turned back, and the three went into Daxing Inn together. The Seventh Lady and A’qiao had never met. One was punctiliously polite, the other warmly affectionate; both were talkative. Holding hands, they ranged far and wide over all they had heard of one another. The Seventh Lady said that Gu had told her how capable and pretty A’qiao was. A’qiao replied that Second Miss had described this frank, lively lady who dared to visit a place like Yiqing House. They took to one another at once and seemed to regret not having met sooner. Gu, however, grew impatient. “My dear lady, you've talked for ages. Say something about why we're here!” They had come specially to invite her. As Hu and You were about to leave for Suzhou and Hangzhou, the Seventh Lady had ordered a farewell banquet from an Anhui restaurant. Hu, meanwhile, wanted everyone at Daxing Inn to try A’qiao's cooking. The result was a deadlock. “It makes no difference whether we eat at your place or mine,” the Seventh Lady said. “But first, I can't cancel the banquet, and it would be a pity to waste several taels. Second, my place is more convenient. The weather isn't hot yet. Even if your dishes are already cooked, they'll keep overnight. I'll come and eat them tomorrow!”

A’qiao naturally agreed without hesitation. Saying that she must change, she asked them to sit in the outer room, then quietly drew Chen aside. Taking out four foreign silver dollars, she said, “Young Master Chen, may I ask a favour? It's my first visit to the Seventh Lady. I can't arrive empty-handed. Please buy four kinds of food for me and bring them to her house.” “I don't know where she lives.” Then Chen had an idea. “But never mind. Leave it to me.” Once she had changed, all four rode together to the Seventh Lady's door. Now that Chen knew the address, he said, “I'll be back in a moment,” and turned away. At the mouth of the lane were a confectioner's shop and a fruit stall. He bought a basket of American oranges, a basket of Tianjin duck pears, and a large box of pine-nut candy. Two dollars remained. He asked the shopkeeper to take down an aged ham, and when the total came to forty cents more than he had, he advanced the difference himself. “These are Sister A’qiao's gifts to the Seventh Lady,” he said with a smile. “I'm the junior here, so today I shall eat for nothing.”

“Why stand on ceremony?” the Seventh Lady said. “Sister A’qiao, we're like family. I'll open the skylight and speak plainly: I don't care for all this, and I'm no good at it myself.” Gu could not help reproaching her. “Listen to yourself. She means well, and that's all she gets from you. Sister A’qiao knows your nature, but wouldn't anyone who didn't think you unfeeling?” “Not at all!” A’qiao put in quickly. “I know the Seventh Lady dislikes empty formalities. But we're so used to them that we can't change. Fortunately, Young Master Chen chose well. These are all useful things. Even if I hadn't brought them, she'd have to spend money buying them.” “That's true enough,” the Seventh Lady said, smiling. Then she added apologetically, “I always say whatever comes into my head. Don't take offence if I say something wrong.” Nobody else found these two sentences remarkable, but Chen was astonished. She had never spoken like that before. It seemed that Gu's quiet influence was having its effect.

Chen was about to make a teasing remark when he heard footsteps on the stairs. You and Hu appeared together, still talking as they walked. They offered brief greetings and continued their conversation. Chen gathered that they had been visiting someone who could be very useful in settling the trouble within the Zhejiang brotherhood. They were now discussing whether to invite him to Hangzhou as well. “Can't your conversation ever end? Talk later. Dinner's ready.” Then the Seventh Lady had another thought. “There aren't enough of us to make it lively. Why not invite Second Miss?” “No need, no need!” You waved his hands. “She's gone out on a banquet engagement. She'll come later.” Dinner was served in the main room. Six people sat at a round table that seemed rather too large. Unable to resist the Seventh Lady's insistence, A’qiao shared the place of honour with Hu. Men and women sitting interspersed was a complete departure from custom, and A’qiao had never occupied the seat of honour before. She was therefore rather constrained and kept well away from Hu. After the first round of wine, he asked her, “What have you and the Seventh Lady been talking about?” “All sorts of things. She's so frank. It was delightful.” “Why don't you come and keep her company more often?” You coughed. Only then did Hu remember that You was urging his sister to return to her family home. Wouldn't frequent visits from A’qiao give her an excuse to stay in Shanghai?

The Seventh Lady paid no attention to these considerations. “Little Uncle is right. Why don't you come to Songjiang with me for a few days?” “Excellent!” You was slightly surprised and hastened to encourage the idea. “Sister A’qiao, do go and stay there. It's easy to travel back and forth. You can return to Shanghai whenever you please.” “I should feel awkward imposing on your household.” Though she said this, her bright eyes kept turning towards Hu. His attitude would determine what she did. He naturally expressed approval, but Gu had a different opinion. “I don't think she need go to Songjiang or stay in Shanghai. Why not simply accompany Little Uncle on a visit to Suzhou?” “That's another possibility.” You looked at them both. “What do you think?” Hu genuinely found it hard to decide. On one hand, A’qiao's company would make the journey warm and delightful. On the other, after sharing a bed and living together, travelling together as well would hammer in the nail and bend its point: the case would become unassailable. He would be able only to go forward, never retreat. It therefore depended on what A’qiao herself wanted. She had come from misunderstanding Hu to understanding him, and from understanding him to accepting Second Miss's advice. Her mind was already made up. But she had known many people and understood the world thoroughly. She would never force his hand at every turn and make him wary of her, keeping a respectful distance. For the moment, she said nothing.

“Well?” the Seventh Lady pressed. “Songjiang or Suzhou?” Put like that, A’qiao could naturally only answer Songjiang. Gu was more perceptive in such matters than the Seventh Lady and spoke before she could reply. “Suzhou, of course.” “Suzhou it is,” Hu decided, though he still had to ask the woman concerned. “Will you come?” Here A’qiao showed her skill. She said neither yes nor no, but merely, “The Seventh Lady has been so kind...” She meant to accept, while still acknowledging the Seventh Lady. Though only a verbal courtesy, it made a favourable impression. “Never mind, never mind!” the Seventh Lady replied. “Once you're back from Suzhou, I'll come and take you to Songjiang.” That settled the matter. Everyone had packing to do, so they broke up early, agreeing to lunch the following day in Second Miss's little house and then board their separate boats.

CHAPTER TWENTY-THREE

Back at Daxing Inn, A’qiao packed the things they would need and asked Hu Xueyan about the purpose of the journey. There was no reason to conceal it. He knew, moreover, that she was no ignorant woman without judgment or a sense of what mattered, so he told her the truth. “What sort of official is an education commissioner?” “He oversees the examinations for licentiates.” “Does he have any extra income?” “That I don't really understand. I hear that Sichuan and Guangdong are lucrative appointments. I don't know about Jiangsu. But with war and disorder everywhere, there are many places he can't even visit. With his territory reduced, any extra income must be limited.” “If that's so, asking Commissioner He to seek office in a good province may not work.” “Why?” “It takes money!” She smiled. “Not that I understand these things. But once, at Yiqing House, a Mr Wang awaiting a circuit appointment gave a party and talked at length about the business side of official life. You have to send money to the great gentlemen in the capital, he said. The more money, the easier promotion becomes.” “Mm, mm.” Reminded of this, Hu privately formed a plan, but did not explain it. Too much depended on it; even to a woman like A’qiao, it was better left unsaid. “You must at least take some gifts,” she added. “I have those—four kinds of foreign goods.” “Where is Commissioner He from?” “Yunnan.” “Then wouldn't things from Yunnan be better?” “Ah, exactly!” Hu praised her warmly. “A’qiao, you have a very good head.”

Early the next morning, Hu went to Gu Yingchun for help in finding Yunnan specialities. They eventually found a Yunnan official awaiting appointment as an assistant departmental magistrate, who had escorted copper to the Jiangsu provincial treasurer's yamen. From him they obtained four local products: Xuanwei ham, purple datoucai, jizong mushrooms and dried salted beef. Unfortunately, there was not much of any of them, but their scarcity made them all the more precious. After lunch at Second Miss's, the party agreed not to see one another off. When the man Gu had arranged to escort Hu arrived, Hu courteously asked his name, and they boarded together. Their vessel was a ‘Wuxi fast boat’ towed by a small steam launch. Hu and A’qiao occupied the aft cabin, while the forward cabin was left to their escort.

His name was Zhou Yiming, and he came from Hunan. He had once served as a detachment officer in the Jiangnan naval force, but was fond of drinking and making trouble. After injuring his superior's younger brother-in-law, he had received twenty strokes of the military cane and been dismissed. Though badly behaved in drink, Zhou was generous and loyal to his friends. His naval service had acquainted him with many boatmen, so at first he went round the wharves seeking handouts, which people willingly gave. Sometimes they asked him to carry a message. Having accepted their support, he faithfully discharged their business, making certain that every errand was properly done. Gradually he earned a reputation and began helping at the Shanghai boatmen's tea association. Such associations existed in every trade and functioned much like guildhalls. Whether to arrange business, deal with officials or settle disputes over tea, members discussed their affairs there. Zhou became an important figure in the boatmen's association. In particular, when officials imposed requisitions for boats or other compulsory service, he handled the negotiations. He had official business in Suzhou on this occasion. Gu, who knew him, therefore entrusted Hu to his care. He would hire the boat and provide the escort, for an agreed twenty taels. Hu was famous for his generosity. As soon as they boarded, he put a thirty-tael note into a red envelope and presented it with both hands. Zhou tried to decline, but Hu was so earnest that he accepted with repeated thanks. His attentions throughout the journey were naturally all the more thorough.

Hu never liked taking a personal attendant on his travels, so Zhou volunteered to manage everything on arrival in Suzhou: hiring chairs, carrying luggage and finding an inn. The inn stood outside Chang Gate and was called Jinchang. Once they were settled, Zhou prepared to leave. “Your Honour”—he addressed Hu this way because Hu had purchased eligibility for appointment as a county magistrate—“I have a place here in Suzhou and shall go and look in. Tomorrow morning I must deliver documents and attend to business at the naval yamen. I'll come to wait on you at midday. Would that suit you?” “I have a rather troublesome favour to ask. Four gifts and a letter—could you deliver them now?” “Certainly. Where to?” “To Education Commissioner He. First we must find out where he's staying.” “That's easy. Leave it to me.” Hu had Jinchang Inn's bookkeeper prepare a formal visiting card, with the address below: “Lodging outside Chang Gate, Jinchang Inn, west side of the third courtyard.” He gave this to Zhou, together with the four Yunnan gifts and Wang Youling's letter. Hu had sealed the letter himself, enclosing a five-thousand-tael note as a gift from Wang to He Guiqing. The letter was important, so he gave particular instructions. “Old Zhou, one more trouble: you must explain to the doorkeeper that I need an acknowledgement in Commissioner He's own hand.” “Yes. Shall I bring it back today?” Hu reflected that one should not employ a man one distrusted, or distrust a man one employed. Zhou valued loyalty and had an established background. He answered at once, “If the card merely acknowledges receipt, you needn't come again. Tomorrow will do.”

Once Zhou had gone, Hu was eager to go sightseeing with A’qiao. Suzhou was unlike Shanghai. Women there liked visiting temples to burn incense and joining the crowds at festivals and processions, but for a man and woman to appear together, whether at Xuanmiao Temple or along Shantang by Tiger Hill, was to parade themselves before the public and invite gossip. A’qiao was a native of the district and might meet acquaintances, which required still greater caution. She was consequently reluctant. While they were gently arguing the point, with no decision reached, Zhou returned, holding his red-tasselled cap as a fan. He had run himself into a sweat, yet his face was all smiles. Thinking He had sent some instructions, Hu hurried out. “Delivered! Here is the reply.” Hu took the card. It read, “One letter from Prefect Wang received. The four generous gifts are also accepted with thanks.” A further line at the foot stated, “Your messenger has been duly thanked in person.” Zhou made a formal greeting, hands lowered. “Your Honour, I must thank you for giving me this opportunity. Commissioner He is most generous. He gave me twenty taels.” This enhanced Hu's own standing, and he was pleased. “Excellent. Keep it.” “I came specially to tell you that the commissioner is staying at the Suzhou Prefectural Academy.” “Oh. Did you see him?” “No. But his steward came out and said he was delighted.” Whether He was delighted by the five thousand taels, the four Yunnan gifts, or both, Hu could not tell. In any event, he owed it to A’qiao.

For that reason, Hu accepted her wishes and did not press her to go out with him. He still intended to take a walk alone, but first sought her advice. They were discussing Suzhou's famous gardens and old temples when the innkeeper hurried straight in. “Your Honour! Education Commissioner He has come to call. He's already out of his chair.” Hu was alarmed. First, he had no attendant to receive the visiting card. Second, he ought to put on official dress to welcome his visitor, and there was no time. For a moment he did not know what to do. A’qiao was more composed. “What is the commissioner wearing?” “Informal clothes.” “That's a relief,” Hu said. “There's no time. I shall have to receive him informally too.” He went out. A’qiao hastily tidied the luggage they had unpacked but not yet put away, then watched at the window, ready to withdraw as soon as He arrived.

He Guiqing met Hu at the middle gateway of the second courtyard. Though informally dressed, he was followed by two attendants in dark gowns and small caps, which revealed his standing. Hu nevertheless dared not take anything for granted. He stopped for a look. The visitor was about his own age, with an exceptionally fair, clean-cut face, exactly as Wang had described. There could be no mistake. He stepped forward and made a formal bow of greeting. “Your Excellency! I don't deserve such an honour.” “Please rise, please rise.” He returned a clasped-hands salute. “You must be Brother Xueyan?” “I don't deserve that form of address. I am Hu Xueyan.” “A great pleasure to meet you.” He began walking again, and Hu led him towards his rooms. In those few steps, many thoughts passed through the host's mind. The situation was awkward. An official of the second rank was calling on a new acquaintance at an inn, with neither a proper reception hall for such a guest nor servants to attend them. The ceremonies of official life would be difficult to observe. He would simply treat He as an intimate. Having decided, he first changed his form of address. He's courtesy name was Genyun; following the familiar respectful form he used for Wang as Mr Xuexuan, Hu addressed He as Mr Genyun. “Mr Genyun,” he said on bringing him into the reception area, “we mustn't neglect propriety. Please take the place of honour and let this county magistrate awaiting appointment pay his respects.” This was merely an opening flourish. Informal dress and so familiar an address showed that he had no intention of observing full official ceremony. He, a man of exceptional intelligence, understood at once. Putting himself in Hu's place, he rather admired this unconventional solution. He smiled. “Brother Xueyan, don't spoil the occasion. I've heard Xuexuan speak of you and have long felt I knew you. Let's dispense with formalities.” “Certainly. Obedience is better than ceremony.” Hu made a deep bow, then straightened. “Please come inside.”

This was truly dispensing with formality: at their first meeting, Hu invited him straight into the inner room. He hesitated briefly, then entered. But he immediately stepped out again on seeing a woman's mirror case and two articles of female clothing. “Your lady is here. I mustn't intrude.” “Not at all, not at all.” Hu called, “A’qiao, come and meet Mr He.” While He was still hesitating, his eyes suddenly brightened, and he no longer wished to withdraw. Watching A’qiao approach, swaying gracefully like a willow in the breeze, he asked Hu, “How should I address her? Is she your concubine?” “No. Just call her by her own name, A’qiao.” As they spoke, she smiled and greeted him. “Mr He.” Then she gracefully sank to her knees. “I don't deserve this. Please rise!” Propriety forbade physical contact between men and women, so he could not help her up and had to accept the kneeling salutation. She rose, invited him to sit and went lightly out. They heard her calling to the inn's waiter for tea in lidded cups.

Treated genuinely as one of the household, He dropped his reserve. Taking the chair in the place of honour by the window, he first thanked Hu. “You've honoured me with a special journey, and I'm especially touched by the gifts. My home is so far away in the south, with war between us as well. To taste its flavours here is a rare pleasure.” “To tell the truth, it was A’qiao's idea.” “What a delightful woman!” His eyes returned to her as she arranged dishes of snacks. “There's nothing very fine for you, Mr He, only a little token,” she said, bringing over four dishes. These were the provisions she had brought to eat on the journey: foreign sweets, candied dates, Hangzhou torreya nuts and Huangdai melon seeds from near Kunshan. “Thank you.” His gaze followed her pair of snowy-white hands. Suddenly realizing that such an unguarded stare was discourteous, he drew his eyes back to Hu. “When did you arrive, Brother Xueyan?” “Only today.” “From Hangzhou?” “No. I've been in Shanghai for several days. I had meant to send someone with the letter, but I've long admired you and wanted to meet you, so I made the journey myself.” “I'm most grateful for your kindness.” He clasped his hands. “How many days will you linger here?” It was his time with Ji Heling that enabled Hu to understand such elegantly literary wording as ‘linger’ instead of the plain ‘stay’. He answered with equal refinement. “My visit is expressly to pay my respects to you. I shall also take the opportunity to visit Lingyan and Tiger Hill, so I expect to sojourn here for three to five days.” “You are a fortunate man!” He indicated A’qiao. “A charming companion at your side, wine aboard and hills to admire—rare pleasures in life, even in peaceful times, let alone these troubled days.”

A’qiao did not understand his words, but guessed that they concerned her and were complimentary. Looking at this Mr He, so like a fair-faced young scholar, she could scarcely believe he already wore the red button of high rank. Then she remembered the storytellers' tales: a young gentleman in distress came first in the examinations and was sent out as imperial inspector of seven provinces, carrying the sovereign's sword, rewarding kindness and avenging wrongs. Such a man must look just like the Mr He before her. As these thoughts tumbled through her mind, her enchanting eyes kept returning to him. The ‘fair-faced scholar’ she was watching had feelings of his own that he could not put into words. Who was she? What was her relationship with Hu? So absorbed was he in these questions that he scarcely knew what he was saying to his host. Only when A’qiao quietly rose and her lovely figure disappeared did he come to himself, embarrassed and amused. He had better leave. If he stayed, who knew what foolishness his distraction might produce? “I must take my leave,” he said. “Please honour me at a little dinner tonight. I have much to ask you.” “You do me too much honour.” “Brother Xueyan, this is no empty courtesy,” He said earnestly. “I know your friendship with Xuexuan. In his letter he calls you ‘resourceful and worthy of complete trust’. There are many things I want to discuss with you.” “In that case, I shall obey.” “Excellent. I shall invite no one else, only the two of us. I'll send a formal invitation presently.”

Hu saw him out to his chair and returned to his room. A’qiao was clearing away the dishes. Remembering the glances she and He had exchanged, Hu felt a sour touch of jealousy and discomfort. “That Mr He looks younger than you,” she said. “Yes. I'd say he's only two or three years older than you. Just the right match.” “What nonsense!” She gave him a reproachful look. She said no more, and Hu had no inclination to speak either. He lay on the bed turning one thought after another over in his mind, bored and restless. Dusk was approaching when the innkeeper's hurried voice sounded outside again. “Your Honour! Your Honour!” The cries were alarming. Hu sprang up and went out. Behind the innkeeper stood an attendant in a red-tasselled cap, carrying a document case. He stepped forward and made a formal greeting. “Your servant He Fu pays his respects. My master has sent me specially to fetch you. The chair is at the door. Please set out now.” He presented a card: “I respectfully invite you to an informal dinner this evening at the shen hour.” It was signed, “Your junior and humble pupil, He Guiqing.” “Ah, good. I'll come at once.” Hu returned inside and found A’qiao holding a riding jacket ready for him to put on.

“I must leave you alone at the inn.” As he said this, a desire to test her suddenly occurred to him. “When I get there, shall I ask Mr He to send someone to fetch you?” The idea was absurd in the extreme. Host and guest were newly acquainted and of different standing, far from the intimacy that allowed their families to visit freely. Even if they felt like old friends and dispensed with ceremony, A’qiao's position was still undefined. How could she enter an official household? Even supposing she had acquired a recognized position as Hu's concubine, an invitation must come from the women of the He family. Mr He could not possibly invite a female guest himself. Her answer ought therefore to have been astonishment, or a smile and the Suzhou expression, ‘What an idea to come up with!’ She might even ignore it as unworthy of an answer. Instead, she merely said, “I couldn't presume.” What kind of hesitation did that express? It invited speculation. Hu smiled and pursued the matter no further. Once in the chair, he continued to examine her response. Calmly, without emotion, he weighed advantage and disadvantage as though considering a business venture that might yield enormous profit or swallow its entire capital. By the time the chair was about to stop, he had broadly made up his mind. He put the matter aside for now and rallied himself to deal with his new acquaintance of high rank.

He Guiqing was lodging in the west reception hall of the Suzhou Prefectural Academy. Screens divided it into three rooms. The outermost served as an office for handling documents, and he received visitors in the second, furnished as a study with tasteful simplicity. When Hu arrived, He was practising large calligraphy. He laid aside an unfinished pair of couplets and welcomed his guest warmly. He wore a lined robe of jujube-red Ning silk beneath a black soft-satin waistcoat with a straight fastening, and a little six-sided cap that folded like a fan and could be slipped into a pocket. In this attire, he looked less like an education commissioner examining licentiates than a fashionable young man-about-town in the foreign settlement. “Brother Xueyan!” He waved a hand with easy grace. “As you see, there are only the two of us. Nothing need be left unsaid.” This was no ordinary declaration. Hu was touched, but all the more cautious. “Mr Genyun, when Mr Xuexuan gave me the letter, he particularly instructed me to carry out any request you might make. I didn't care to repeat that lightly, for fear my abilities might fall short. Now I can say it, because I feel certain you would understand even if I failed. Please tell me freely what you wish.” This was as far as such an assurance could go. He put aside his remaining doubts and spoke openly. “Huang Shouchen passed in the same examination year as I did. While he stays, I can't make any move. Now I hear he may be transferred. By seniority, there would be nothing surprising in my succeeding him, so Xuexuan's plan for me is worth considering. But after a great deal of effort, if all I get is a chicken rib, it won't be worthwhile. What exactly is the situation in Zhejiang?” Hu did not understand the allusion to a chicken rib, tasteless to chew yet regrettable to discard. But he understood the general question: how desirable was the governorship of Zhejiang? “Naturally, Zhejiang cannot compare with Jiangsu. But in one respect it's better: there has been no fighting there yet.” “True, but it must run a supply office for the Jiangnan Grand Camp and help with Anhui's defence. Preparing a bride's trousseau for someone else is hardly worthwhile.” “Not necessarily,” Hu answered. “If it were an idle, uneventful post, you might not care to accept it.”

“That's true.” He felt that Hu had understood him very well. “In peaceful times, my appointment as education commissioner of Jiangsu would rank just below the education commissionership of Shuntian. That is because Shuntian embraces the capital. In talent, how could it compare with your Jiangnan? Whether the right man holds Jiangsu's educational office therefore affects the fortunes of the state and the rise or decline of its talent. Who could have expected that, after two hundred years, I should happen to hold it at a time of war? Everyone speaks of military preparations and neglects civil learning. Much of the territory has fallen, so I could have taken things easily. But if we fail to cultivate scholars now, a year of war could interrupt the succession of talent. I should be guilty of failing the country. I've therefore borrowed premises elsewhere to hold the examinations, travelling from place to place. I feel I've done my duty to the emperor and the people of Jiangsu.” Hu had heard that He pursued his work with considerable energy. Besides his regular duties, he often submitted memorials on military matters. Hu had thought he was interfering in others' business and almost making unnecessary trouble. Now, hearing how he held examinations in borrowed premises and travelled about, he realized that He had not neglected his own office. Respect rose in him, though he knew too little of the subject to offer a word of appreciation. He could only listen closely and keep nodding. A maid approached. “Master, please invite your guest to the table.” “Come. It really is only a little dinner,” He said, “and I'm offering you flowers borrowed from yourself.”

Indeed, four of the six dishes were made from Hu's four Yunnan gifts. In the middle stood a covered casserole. When the lid was lifted, Hu saw an unusual construction: a spout rose like a pillar through its centre. Inside were pieces of chicken in a very clear broth, faintly fragrant with fermented grain. He swallowed involuntarily. “This must be steam-pot chicken. I've long heard of it, but never seen it before.” “The broth is really the point. It's not difficult to make; the rare thing is the vessel. I've had people try to reproduce this steam pot at Yixing, but it never came out right.” Suddenly He asked, “Have you ever visited my part of the country?” “No. But I've long admired Kunming as a blessed place, with spring throughout the year, beautiful hills and clear waters. As they say, fine land produces outstanding men. Only such a place could produce someone like you.” “You flatter me. Surely Xuexuan has told you I'm not a native of Yunnan?” His willingness to mention this showed that he did not conceal his origins. Hu realized that He truly regarded him as a confidential friend. Yet it would be awkward to reveal that he already knew the whole story, so he answered, “A little. Mr Xuexuan greatly admires you too.” “My friendship with him is unusual, and so is yours. You mustn't stand on ceremony with me from now on.” “Certainly. Since you're willing to accept me, I shall respect you just as I respect Mr Xuexuan.” “I don't ask for respect, only that you make no distinction between us. Come, a cup to the joy of meeting. Let us drain it.”

They drained their cups and showed them empty. Refilling their cups sparingly and drinking slowly, they continued to discuss Zhejiang. Hu thought there was no need to urge any particular course upon him now. He simply described all he knew of the province's administration, people's livelihoods, customs and local conditions. He Guiqing listened carefully and occasionally asked a question, always about the situation on the ground. Hu could tell that his interest lay in military affairs. If defence seemed uncertain, the Zhejiang governorship might not appeal to him. At last He revealed something of his career plans. “I certainly shan't remain education commissioner. What I'll do afterwards is still undecided.” Hu's understanding of official life extended only as far as prefectures and counties. He could guess at provincial affairs, but appointments in the capital and the many special offices were beyond him. He therefore had no answer. “You know, our examination class—the yiwei year, the fifteenth of Daoguang—is the most successful now. That is because Grand Secretary Mu advanced us all those years ago. You know who he is?” “I'm ashamed to say I don't really.” “You can hardly be blamed. You aren't one of our kind of people...”

He went on to explain: Grand Secretary Mu was Muzhang’a, the powerful minister of the Daoguang reign. As chief examiner at the metropolitan examination in the yiwei year, he had spent the next fifteen years promoting his pupils. They filled key posts everywhere: the Grand Council, ministries and courts at the centre, and governorships, treasurerships and judicial commissions in the provinces. Thus, although Muzhang’a had fallen in the second year after the present Xianfeng Emperor's accession, his yiwei pupils had fully grown wings and could each fly high. Their teacher's fall had not harmed them. On the contrary, their influence had saved him from anything worse than dismissal. He had not suffered Heshen's fate of confiscation and death. “So I can't lightly throw away an opportunity,” He continued, turning to his own affairs. “I must make a move. These aren't peaceful times, and there is little future in an education commissionership. If I said I wanted Zhejiang, it would amount to undermining Huang Shouchen. We're friends from the same examination class; I couldn't justify that. Returning to my substantive post as vice-minister of rites holds no interest either. I've been thinking that a post such as granary vice-minister might serve as an intermediate step.” Hu knew that title because it concerned the grain tribute and both Wang and Ji had mentioned it. The granary vice-minister was stationed at Tongzhou and supervised the receipt and storage of tribute grain, with eleven granary supervisors below him. It was a lucrative office. After two or three years, a man could be appointed a provincial governor with the means to behave honestly: his official purse would already be full, and he need no longer squeeze the people.

Hu's quick mind turned at once to Zhejiang's sea transport. From Wang to Ji, the Sea Transport Bureau had faced many difficulties. Numerous accounts still needed Tongzhou's help to obtain approval. If He could take charge there, everything would become easier. “Mr Genyun, that is an excellent plan! On this subject, I can be of some small service. The grain tribute depends chiefly on Jiangsu and Zhejiang. As far as Zhejiang's sea transport is concerned, once you are established at Tongzhou, your word will be law. Everything will be done as you wish.” “Oh?” He asked. “Xuexuan has handed over Zhejiang's sea transport. How can you be so certain?” “He has, but the present executive director, Ji Heling, still has very close ties with him. Ji is my sworn brother.” “So that's how it is!” He was delighted and surprised. Such a fortunate connection was quite unexpected. “As for Jiangsu's sea transport, you must know more than I do. And since you'll be transferring from Jiangsu, whoever handles it will be someone you know. Naturally, arrangements will be easy. In short, you and the post are perfectly suited.” “With the right man in the right place, administration runs smoothly and people live in harmony.” He paused. “It was only a passing thought at first. Talking with you has given it substance. I've already written to the capital and mean to go there. The imperial order summoning me to an audience should come soon. I'll definitely seek a transfer to the granaries.”

For He to speak so openly meant he now regarded Hu as a confidant with whom he could discuss anything. Hu understood that friendships and connections were established and strengthened by some concrete expression of commitment at just such a moment. Fail to take that step, and even close friends could become mere acquaintances. He would not let this opportunity slip. “Mr Genyun, I can say that your plan could not be better. There is no time to lose. You should go ahead. But there's something I don't know whether I may venture to say.” “How can I know until you've said it?” He picked at his nails, looking down at his hands as though preparing to receive the presumptuous remark. “I hear that a provincial treasurer's journey to the capital costs at least twenty thousand taels. Is that true?” “One can't generalize. For a middling province it would be enough; for a first-rank province such as Jiangsu, it wouldn't. It would cover merely attending an imperial audience and reporting on one's duties. But if there is official business to transact—requesting funds or getting accounts approved—there is no limit to the departmental fees. How could twenty thousand suffice?” “Then it would be still less adequate if one were seeking an appointment.” “That too depends on the office, imperial favour and whether one has people at court. My own journey this time won't cost very much.” Hu looked at him directly, his brows drawn, and asked with deliberate clarity, “How much, exactly?” He did not reply at once. Blinking repeatedly and murmuring, he counted on his fingers. After some time he said, “Fifteen thousand taels would be amply sufficient.”

Hu smiled, then became serious again. “Mr Genyun, you know I run a bank. What we dread most in our trade is idle money. You must use some of mine for this journey.” He's expression became complicated: delighted surprise mixed with uncertainty, as though he had not quite understood. In fact, he had not. Only after reflection did he grasp the meaning, and even then he doubted his interpretation. He spoke hesitantly. “Brother Xueyan, do you mean you wish to lend me money?” “Yes.” Hu answered directly and clearly. “I'd like to lend you fifteen thousand taels. The interest would be especially modest. I have plenty of funds, and that is better than leaving them idle.” “And the term?” “Whatever you say.” Again the commissioner had no answer. He needed to calculate, but had no basis for doing so. He knew the granary vice-minister's post was a good one, but not what it yielded in a year. Seeing his hesitation, Hu offered a suggestion. “I'll introduce you to a remittance bank in the capital. Keep your funds there, and repay according to circumstances: more when you have more, less when you have less, with no fixed term. How would that be?” “Good, good. Let us do that. But I don't need so much. Ten thousand will be enough.”

Hu knew the other five thousand was already provided for: he himself had sealed the note inside the letter after listening to A’qiao. But he could not say so openly. He deliberately asked, “Why? Aren't you still five thousand short?” The commissioner likewise would not reveal that Wang's letter had enclosed five thousand. He merely said, “I can ask someone else to make up the shortfall. That should be enough.” Understanding perfectly, Hu nodded. “Then please tell me where I should send the ten thousand.” It was an ordinary question, apparently easy to answer, yet the commissioner could not speak. The whole affair was so sudden as to seem scarcely believable. Ten thousand taels was no small sum. At a first meeting, after a few words, a man offered it as a loan, without an intermediary or guarantor, without even settling the interest or the term. Was that not extraordinary? While he wondered, a thought struck him. Hu's conduct might be explained by his friendship with Wang, but did he also have some purpose of his own? A businessman's calculations were certain to be shrewd. Better ask first. “Brother Xueyan,” he said with difficulty, “is this money really idle, as you say?” At this question, Hu felt there was no need to maintain the fiction. He answered ambiguously, “Even if it weren't, I could hardly fail to do my utmost to help with your important affairs.”

“I'm deeply grateful. Only, if I accept such a favour, how am I to repay it?” The words were an ordinary expression of gratitude, but his eyes were different. They fixed directly upon Hu, waiting for an answer. Hu's acute understanding caught the meaning at once: this was not merely thanks, but an inquiry about his conditions. Naturally, there were conditions, but to state them would mark him as a fool. Moreover, he felt slightly displeased that He should rate his friendship with Wang so lightly. “Mr Genyun, what are you saying? I've had no schooling, but I've heard people explain the ‘Biographies of the Money-Makers’ and ‘Biographies of the Knight-Errants’ in the Records of the Grand Historian. Must I have some ulterior purpose before I can part with a mere ten thousand taels?” “Yes, yes!” He was greatly embarrassed and repeatedly clasped his hands. “I've spoken wrongly. Brother Xueyan, I never expected it. You are a man who has truly profited from learning.” Hu was inwardly amused and, naturally, pleased with himself. A few Han-dynasty stories heard from Ji had actually overawed an education commissioner of Hanlin background. It would make a fine story to boast of later to Wang and Ji. “Not at all. To say that is almost to mock me.” It was half truth, half modesty. But He really did regard him with fresh respect. “No wonder Xuexuan admires you. Even in his unsuccessful days, he was proud and exacting. He praised few of the people he judged, yet he always spoke differently of you. Now I see that you really are different.”

Hu answered with a reserved, modest smile and returned the conversation to the loan. “I can have the ten thousand ready as soon as I reach Shanghai. Shall I send it here, or would you prefer another arrangement?” “There is no need to send it.” He considered. “When I go to the capital, I'll first come to Shanghai and travel north by sea. The route is more peaceful, and I can also inspect the sea transport arrangements. We can discuss it when we meet in Shanghai. I shall probably have other troubles for you then.” “Excellent.” Hu volunteered eagerly. “Let me know beforehand when you are going. I'll attend to everything in Shanghai—finding you a residence and booking your cabin.” “Please don't speak as though you were attending to official duties.” He hesitated. “There is one thing. At the earliest, I cannot leave until about the Dragon Boat Festival. By then you may have returned to Hangzhou.” “Then I'll come back to Shanghai from Hangzhou,” Hu answered readily. “Besides, I have people in Shanghai. You needn't concern yourself with any of it.” By now, they had talked and drunk enough. Hu asked his host to favour him with rice. After the meal he sat a little longer, then took his leave. He again sent him by chair to Jinchang Inn, where A’qiao was sitting alone by lamplight, waiting for his return.

“Have you eaten?” “Yes,” A’qiao replied. “I've been wanting some of Lugaojian's pork in soy sauce for ages. Today I finally had it.” As she helped him undress and wash his feet, she asked what had happened at He Guiqing's. Hu could hardly tell her about going to the capital to seek a transfer, and apart from that there was little to say. He had not seen a single member of He's family. Once they were in bed, she asked from her pillow, “What about tomorrow? Where would you like to go?” “The business is finished. Where shall we spend the day? I can't come all the way to Suzhou and say I haven't even seen Tiger Hill.” This surprised her. “I thought your business would take several days. In that case...” “What is it?” Her hesitation surprised him in turn. “I'd meant to go home to Mudu. Now it seems I can't.” “That needn't matter. What do you want to do there?” “What an odd question! My home's in Mudu. How could I come to Suzhou and not go back?” “Oh!” Hu blurted out. “You're going to see your husband?” “Must you put it so unpleasantly?” She was flustered and angry. “I'm going to my parents' home.”

From her expression, she appeared to be telling the truth. Hu felt he might as well ask further. “Who's left in your family?” “My mother and a brother. I'll see them, take them a little money and come straight back to the city.” “How long would that take?” “Two days for the journey there and back.” “Two days?” He considered. “Go tomorrow, then, and return the day after. We'll leave as soon as you're back.” “Then I shan't be able to go to Tiger Hill with you tomorrow,” she said apologetically. “That doesn't matter. A’qiao, what exactly is the arrangement between you and your husband's family?” “What arrangement? So long as I give them money, they don't care about anything.” Her tone was contemptuous. “Do you send money every month?” “Sometimes every month, sometimes every two months. More when I have more, less when I have less. There's no fixed rule. It also depends on finding someone going that way. Always having to ask people is a real nuisance.” “Wouldn't it be better to make a clean break? That would save you the trouble.” She said nothing and seemed troubled. Hu wondered what the difficulty was. “A clean break is possible. I'm afraid they'll demand an outrageous sum.” “How outrageous? Country people can hardly ask for very much.” “It would take at least two thousand taels.”

Two thousand was indeed an outrageous demand. Even marrying a celebrated courtesan from a changsan house in Shanghai would cost no more. Fine woman though A’qiao was, her value in such a transaction did not amount to that. If he simply said, “Then two thousand it shall be,” he would not win a reputation for generosity. He would look like what the foreign settlement's new slang called a gullible customer. Of course, he felt this way because his interest in her had diminished since she involuntarily betrayed her feelings for “Mr He.” Otherwise, the thought of being made a fool of would not have arisen. “We'll discuss it when we get back to Shanghai,” he answered coolly. “I haven't that much money with me.” In fact, he carried three thousand taels in banknotes. It was an excuse. A’qiao had expected no such offer, however, and was not disappointed. The night passed without further incident. In the morning, Hu kept his promise of the night before and urged her to go to Mudu. “I feel bad leaving you alone at the inn. Why don't you come with me?” What sort of arrangement would that be? Country customs were restrictive. Even if she did not mind bringing a lover home, Hu would feel embarrassed. He waved the suggestion aside. “Never mind. Go on your own. I shall enjoy looking round the city by myself.” “Then I'll set out early tomorrow morning. I should be back about noon.” She asked Jinchang Inn to hire a sedan chair for the return journey. Hu felt it would be rather shabby to let her go empty-handed without making any gesture himself. He took out a hundred-tael note, saying it was for her parents to buy nourishing medicines. Naturally delighted, she seemed still more reluctant to part when she got into the chair.

She had scarcely left when He Guiqing sent another invitation, this time to lunch at the Lion Grove Garden. Hu had been wondering where to go and gladly accepted. He sent back a reply, tipped the messenger and took a sedan chair through Chang Gate. After drinking a bowl of tea at Xuanmiao Temple and buying a few small jade objects at the temple market, he hired another small chair outside the temple shortly before noon and went to keep the appointment. The Lion Grove was famous for its rockery, said to have been designed by Ni Yunlin himself. Its paths twisted, rose and fell in strange, unpredictable ways. He personally conducted Hu through it, pointing out its features with the utmost attentiveness. A circuit took about an hour and left them tired enough to find the food especially good. Only after they had eaten a fair amount did conversation become lively. Official affairs were unsuitable for such an occasion, and He knew nothing of commerce, so they talked of scenery and romantic pleasures. With a little wine in him, He grew more expansive and less guarded. When they reached the subject of family, he suddenly said, “Brother Xueyan, there's something I must ask, though I'm embarrassed to do so. My wife is frail and often ill, and she has the most generous disposition. She frequently urges me to take a concubine who could share her burdens and attend to my meals and daily needs. I do see the necessity. But as an official serving in Jiangsu, I am strictly forbidden to take a woman under my jurisdiction as a concubine. On this journey to the capital, I shall need someone close to look after me. Could you find a suitable woman for me in Shanghai or Hangzhou?” “Nothing could be easier. Tell me what sort of woman you like.” “Someone like A’qiao would be ideal,” He answered without thinking.

Hu started. Studying He's expression, he concluded that this did not seem to be a disguised request for A’qiao herself, and felt somewhat better. “I understand,” he said, nodding. “Before you leave, I shall certainly have something to report.” “Thank you! I'll send five hundred taels over presently. Please arrange it within that sum.” “It won't cost so much. Nor need you send the money. Once it's settled, we'll reckon everything together. I'll even ask for a reward.” “You put it too strongly. I ought to thank my matchmaker.” Hu had agreed, but back at Jinchang Inn he realized that finding another woman like A’qiao would be no easy matter. “Ah! How foolish I've been!” Breaking through the obstruction in his mind, he solved the difficulty, only to be left with a sense of loss. Why seek someone like A’qiao when A’qiao herself was already there? Yet letting her go felt different from giving up A’zhu. When he had redirected the match, joining A’zhu's red thread of marriage to Chen Shilong's, his conscience had been clear and he had felt positively pleased. Now, at the thought of sending A’qiao into another man's arms, his heart was sour with unhappiness. He paced back and forth, turning the matter over repeatedly. Was there no better way?

His thoughts went round and round like an ant circling a millstone until it was almost dark. Then someone called from outside, “Mr Hu!” The voice was familiar, though for a moment he could not place it. Going out, he dimly made out Zhou Yiming. “When I called at noon, you were out?” “Oh, I'm sorry to have missed you. Education Commissioner He invited me to the Lion Grove.” “And the young mistress is away too?” “She's gone home to Mudu. She isn't my concubine, by the way. There's no need to call her that.” This was something of a rebuff. Zhou could find no answer and said, merely to fill the silence, “Why haven't you lit a lamp?” “Ah!” Only now did Hu notice. Amused at himself, he gave half the truth. “I've been so absorbed in something on my mind that I forgot. Old Zhou, let's go for a drink.” “Certainly.” Zhou smiled ingratiatingly. “I'd been hoping to act as host and offer you a cup, but I was afraid you wouldn't honour me and didn't dare suggest it.” “Nonsense! Why wouldn't I? You're far too polite.” Hu liked him and wanted to talk, so he added earnestly, “I'll be your guest. But I won't go to a restaurant. It isn't that I'm afraid of making you spend too much. First, I've had too much rich food at lunch. Second, I'd like to see what Suzhou's little taverns are like and how they differ from Hangzhou's.” “Then I'll do as you say. There are plenty of places devoted to drinking in front of Xuanmiao Temple. They're clean, and we could sit awhile.” “Good. Let's go.”

Hu slipped on an outer jacket, told an inn servant to lock his door and hired a carriage with Zhou to go into the city. The area before Xuanmiao Temple blazed with lights and bustled with people. Since Jiangning had fallen, Suzhou had become the province's foremost city. Several hundred civil and military officials had appeared almost overnight. Most had not brought their families and had nowhere to go when work was done. They congregated here, some strolling, others drinking themselves tipsy, and the market remained busy until the second watch. Every tavern was full. At last they found seats facing the street in one called Yuandachang. They sat down and ordered Shaoxing huadiao. Two or three older women, neatly and cleanly dressed in blue cotton, promptly approached with baskets of braised snacks to accompany the wine. The duck heads and wings looked good enough, though their flavour was unremarkable. But Hu had come to savour the atmosphere of a Suzhou tavern, not its food, and did not much mind. Once settled, after their first round of wine, he looked about him and began to observe. Suzhou natives were easily recognized by their composed manners, courteous deference and scholarly air. The two men at the next table were examples: both white-bearded, both speaking the local dialect in wonderfully soft voices. Merely listening to their animated conversation was a pleasure. War blazed on every side, yet Yuandachang was full of warm wine, gentle voices and leisurely enjoyment. The two old men were recalling the Jiaqing years, discussing inkstones, Yixing Gongchun teapots and bamboo carvings—the elegant playthings of scholars in a peaceful, prosperous age.

“What is a man alive for?” Hu asked, suddenly moved. “Simply to eat and drink his way through life?” Zhou stared blankly. He could not answer; he could scarcely even understand the question. “I mean people like those two old gentlemen,” Hu explained, lowering his voice. “They're probably country gentry living on rents. We have plenty of such families in Hangzhou. An ancestor held office and acquired some land. Unless a spendthrift appears, quiet living leaves enough to feed a generation or two. The men themselves generally have some examination standing. The better ones are licentiates admitted to the schools; otherwise they've paid twenty or thirty taels for the status of an Imperial Academy student. They count as people of standing too. All year round they're busy doing nothing: they sit in teahouses by day and have a bowl of wine at night. They drift pleasantly on until sixty or seventy, then stop breathing and go home to meet the King of Hell. ‘I've had my turn in the world of the living,’ they say. Ask what they did there, and the answer is nothing! Even being a ghost would be meaningless for someone like that.” Whether he was mocking himself or teasing others was unclear, but Zhou understood this much. He too had ambitions and felt considerable sympathy. “Quite so. A man should accomplish something in his lifetime, if only to do right by his parents.”

At that, Hu felt they could talk. “Old Zhou, I hear you were quite a figure in the navy.” “I wouldn't say I had a name, but I got on well with people.” Zhou took a drink and poured out his grievance. “Boatmen used to call me ‘Officer’ and treat me with great respect. Now it's ‘Old Zhou’, and I have to run every kind of errand. It leaves a bitter taste.” “You'd like to return to the navy, then?” “Wishing won't help.” He shook his head. “My old commanding officer has risen higher still. He listened to that damned brother-in-law of his and hates me like poison. The only way to get back on the rolls would be to change my name and start again as a common soldier. How long would it take to get anywhere? I can only give it up.” “If you really want to go back, I could help. A naval commander can hardly be so very high an official. What if I asked Education Commissioner He to write a letter for you?” “With a letter from him, I wouldn't have to return to my old place. He and Governor Xu of Jiangsu passed the metropolitan examination in the same year. I could enter the troops under the governor's direct command. That would be far better than my old post.” “Very well. I don't know much about these things. Tomorrow I'll take you to see the commissioner, and you can tell him yourself.” Remembering how courteously He had treated Hu, Zhou concluded that they must be close friends and that success was assured. He was intensely excited, thanked Hu repeatedly and became still more attentive as host.

When Hu had reached a comfortable degree of tipsiness, he wanted no more wine. They ordered two bowls of noodles with a double topping between them: one came with pork braised until meltingly tender, the other with smoked fish. By exchanging toppings, they each had fish and meat. They ate and drank to their hearts' content for less than half a tael. Hu was thoroughly pleased. “It isn't how much money you have, but how you use it. I've seldom enjoyed a meal as much as this.” “That's because you knew I was treating you and expected nothing fine. You'd prepared yourself, so it seems good.” “That's what they mean by ‘contentment brings lasting happiness’. If you can step back a little in your thinking, there's nothing to trouble you.” That night, he approached the question of letting A’qiao go in this same spirit. Suppose he had never met her. Suppose she had died. Suppose some powerful patron had taken her from him. Each such reflection loosened his attachment a little. At last he made up his mind. “A gentleman helps others attain their happiness,” he told himself. Then he sighed, pulled the quilt over his head and went to sleep.

When he rose early the next morning, Zhou was already waiting. Acting as a temporary servant, he ran about attending to Hu's needs, so that even without A’qiao Hu felt no inconvenience. He had always preferred travelling without a servant for the sake of freedom and efficiency. But a man like Zhou might be useful to have beside him. On his return, whether in Hangzhou or Shanghai, he ought to look carefully for someone suitable. After Hu had washed, Zhou invited him into the city for morning tea. Understanding what was on his mind, Hu readily agreed. “Yes, yes. Afterwards, I'll take you to the commissioner and ask him in person for a letter.” They went to the Wuyuan teahouse. Suzhou teahouses differed from Hangzhou's. In Hangzhou, most had open halls and treated everyone alike. Gentry, pedlars and labourers were all customers once seated. In Suzhou, the different classes were separated and did not mingle. Hu enjoyed a crowd, so he and Zhou sat in the outermost hall, drinking tea and sampling the various pastries until ten. Judging the time right, they paid and strolled to the prefectural school to see He Guiqing. Out of regard for Hu, He treated Zhou courteously too, repeatedly asking him to sit. Zhou observed official etiquette, standing respectfully with his hands at his sides. At last he could not refuse and perched on the edge of a chair as though squatting. Hu felt sorry for his discomfort and explained their purpose briefly. “Governor Xu has gone to Shanghai to direct the troops in person,” He replied. Then he turned to Hu. “There is a good opening at present, though. It's tax collection. I wonder whether Mr Zhou would consider it beneath him.” “You flatter him. At which tax station?” “You've heard of the new levy called lijin?” “I've heard of it, but I don't yet know exactly how it works.”

“It was devised by a remarkable man from your own Zhejiang. Indeed, he comes from Xuexuan's jurisdiction: Changxing County in Huzhou Prefecture. His name is Qian Jiang.” Qian Jiang, courtesy name Dongping, was an Imperial Academy student from Changxing. Fond of bold talk and ingenious schemes, he resembled the wandering strategists of the Warring States. When the Opium War began, Yijing, an imperial clansman who was assistant grand secretary and president of the Board of Civil Appointments, received orders to direct military affairs in Zhejiang as General Who Spreads Awe. Qian presented himself at his headquarters with a plan: recruit brave men, surprise the British and capture their leaders. Timid Yijing dared not attempt such an extraordinary scheme and politely declined. Later, Lin Zexu fell into disgrace and was sent into exile. Qian, having advocated resistance to the British in Guangzhou, was likewise sentenced to military exile in Ili. They met there, and Lin greatly admired him. When Lin was pardoned and allowed to return within the passes, he arranged to clear Qian's conviction and brought him back. In the capital, Lin praised him among the high officials, and his reputation rapidly grew. Unfortunately, Lin died not long afterwards, leaving Qian without support. He then travelled with his schemes through the country between the Yangtze and Huai rivers. In Yangzhou, he met Lei Yixian and proposed two measures. The first was to obtain blank certificates for purchased ranks in advance, to be filled in and issued on the spot. The second was to introduce lijin.

The poor long to be rich, and the rich to be honoured: that is human nature. Merchants who had made fortunes, particularly the salt merchants of the Two Huai districts, were therefore especially fond of purchasing official rank. Even after contributing enough to become third-rank circuit intendants, they felt a blue finial insufficiently imposing. They were always seeking opportunities—funding military supplies, for instance, or contributing to river works—to spend large sums on a special recommendation. Only a second-rank red finial would satisfy them. Yet buying rank involved complicated procedures. Clerks at the Board of Civil Appointments had endless tricks. A man might remit his payment and still wait a year or two for the board's certificate establishing his rank. Naturally, this diminished enthusiasm. Qian's scheme catered precisely to wealthy merchants eager to taste official distinction: money in one hand, goods in the other. As soon as payment was made, the certificate would be completed and issued. Nothing could be more straightforward. Lei thought the proposal excellent and had Qian submit a memorial setting it out in detail. Since the scheme would deprive the board's clerks of their profits, the board initially rejected it. But the treasury was empty. The more than ten million taels accumulated under Qianlong and Jiaqing had been exhausted since the Opium War in the Daoguang reign by imperial commissioners commanding armies—Yijing, Qiying, Qishan, Saishang’a and others. Now, in confronting the uprising of Hong and Yang, the court wanted a good horse without having to feed it. If it forbade the horse even to find its own fodder, how could that be justified? Qian's ingenious proposal was therefore approved at last. Large quantities of blank certificates arrived from the board. Transactions were immediate and required none of the endless incidental fees. Quicker and cheaper, the new arrangement naturally drew crowds of buyers. With this revenue, Lei recruited local volunteers and was able to hold the Yangzhou–Zhenjiang area. But each sale of rank brought payment only once. A continuing stream required another source. Hence lijin.

Previously, the Qing had imposed only customs duties on travelling merchants. Its principal tax revenue came from the land and poll levy, but so much territory had been lost that receipts had fallen sharply. War had also depressed sales in the Two Huai salt market and reduced its tax yield. Lijin was to make up the shortfall: one li collected on every qian. The rate appeared slight, but small sums accumulated into a considerable amount. Lei first tried it at canal wharves such as Xiannümiao and Shaobo near Yangzhou. The results were good. The court then formally ordered Yiliang, Governor-General of Liangjiang, Xu Naizhao, Governor of Jiangsu, and Yang Yizeng, Director-General of Grain Transport, to introduce contributions of lijin for military funds in various places north and south of the Yangtze. After hearing He's account, Hu greatly admired Qian and longed to meet him. That was impossible for the moment, however, so he set the thought aside and returned to Zhou's prospects. “He served in the navy and knows people at wharves all along the canal and the Yangtze. If you give him this opportunity, he certainly won't neglect his duties or let you down.” “I know. Mr Zhou looks very capable, and with your recommendation I'm sure your confidence is justified. I'll write at once. Please sit awhile.” He withdrew to his study and wrote the letter himself. Though not yet a provincial ruler, he already had all the manner of a governor or governor-general. His characters, as large as walnuts, filled two sheets of eight-line letter paper. In keeping with the order of their examination success, he addressed Lei as his senior. Hu received the letter and thanked He for Zhou, who himself expressed his gratitude by kowtowing.

“Go back first,” Hu told Zhou. “I'll stay and talk with His Excellency.” Once Zhou had left, He told Hu that Xu Naizhao might be transferred from the governorship of Jiangsu. “A confidential letter from the capital arrived early this morning. I think I shall wait and see.” Why should Xu's transfer make him wait? After a moment, Hu understood: He must have a chance of succeeding him and wanted to observe developments. This change of plan would be decidedly unfavourable to Hu's side. He wanted to urge He to keep to the original course: first arrange a transfer as granary vice-minister, then seek appointment as governor of Zhejiang. That would make everything convenient for Wang Youling, Ji Heling and Hu himself, with helpful connections on every side. But he could not openly argue against something he had only guessed. If the guess was wrong, he would be shooting at no target and make himself ridiculous in He's eyes. Besides, Hu knew that hints and indirect approaches worked better than plain statements. After a little thought, he found his line of argument. “The governorship of Jiangsu used to be the finest post in the empire,” he suddenly remarked. “Now I should call it the very worst.” He naturally paid attention. “It's true that the post is no longer what it was, but hardly that it has fallen to the bottom.” “I'm only talking at random and seeking your advice.” Speaking slowly, Hu thought of reasons one at a time and offered them as they came. “First, the worst disorder is in Jiangsu. Less territory means less tax revenue.”

“Not so bad. We still hold the fertile Suzhou–Songjiang country.” Hu could hardly say that even Suzhou and Songjiang might be lost. “Holding it is hard enough. Liu Lichuan is still in Shanghai. But leave that aside. Second, Jiangsu has too many officials. The advantage of Zhejiang is that the governor stands supreme.” “Ah!” He nodded deeply. “There's sense in that. A governor and governor-general in the same city are indeed troublesome. Either the east wind overcomes the west or the west overcomes the east.” “It can hardly be easy for a governor to overcome a governor-general. But leave that aside too. Third, I've heard that General Xiang at the Jiangnan Grand Camp is difficult to serve. Is that true?” Of course it was. He reflected that the camp was full of arrogant troops and unruly commanders; Xiang Rong's difficult temper was the least of it. His intention of waiting in Jiangsu for a chance to succeed Xu began to waver. Seeing him silent, Hu guessed what he was thinking and pressed him with a further warning. “A local official must live or die with his city. Speaking privately on behalf of Governor Xu, my fellow native of Hangzhou, if he could be transferred elsewhere, it might truly be a case of the frontier old man's lost horse proving a blessing in disguise.” This struck home. He was extremely timid. However boldly he discussed warfare on paper, he was terrified of actual fighting. Jiangsu did seem to have become the worst of posts. Why seek trouble? Better go to the capital after all. Having decided, he could not say so openly. He merely nodded repeatedly. “Your argument is entirely right. I admire your insight.”

“What do I know? But as the saying goes, a bystander sees clearly. Without holding the post or having a personal stake in its gains and losses, one can see more plainly.” “Quite true. I need more guidance from men like you.” “You flatter me so much that you make me blush.” Hu took the opportunity to rise. “I must leave now, and take my leave of you before my journey as well.” “What?” He looked disappointed at once. “Are you going already?” “Yes. I mean to return to Shanghai early tomorrow.” “Then...” He considered for a long while. “We'll meet in Shanghai. It won't be very long.” “Certainly. As soon as I'm back, I'll have the money ready and wait for your instructions.” “There is also that other matter. I must ask you, whatever happens, to give it your attention.” Hu was momentarily puzzled, then understood. In fact, half the work was already done, and he could answer confidently. “Don't worry. Once I reach Shanghai, I shall have good news.” He was naturally delighted, and his excessive pleasure turned reflective. “To think that this visit should unexpectedly have made such close friends of us! Life is all a matter of affinity. It's truly beyond understanding.” Hu's circumstances resembled his in some degree. With Wang Youling, they were three men from distant corners of the country, brought together by some unseen force. Like the pieces of a tangram, apparently unrelated, they had combined into a pattern. It was wonderfully ingenious, and Hu felt deep sympathy with He's words. “Speaking of affinity, there's something else that will surprise you. I won't reveal it yet; that would spoil the pleasure. I only hope you'll reach Shanghai before the festival if possible, and shortly after if not. Then we'll talk again.” Hearing this, He would not press. “Very well. We'll talk then. Our next meeting is not far off, so I won't see you off on your journey.” “You needn't trouble yourself. Nor shall I call again to take leave.” Hu rose and bowed.

“Wait a moment.” He hurried back into his study and did not reappear for some time. He was writing on visiting cards himself. There was no time for letters, so he used seven or eight cards, one for each of the civil and military officials controlling the districts along the route from Suzhou to Shanghai. Ostensibly, they conveyed his regards; in reality, they introduced Hu. “Keep these in reserve,” he said, handing over the little stack. “The wording will tell you how close I am to each man. Judge for yourself which to use, whether to use them and how.” “These cards are as good as sending a hundred soldiers to protect me. I can sleep all the way to Shanghai. Thank you!” “I'll answer Xuexuan separately. Couriers travel between here and Zhejiang every day, so it's easy enough. I needn't trouble you to carry the letter.” As he spoke, He accompanied his guest out. Official propriety allowed him to go no farther than the second gate. After Hu returned to the inn, He sent four dishes for the journey, a copy of his newly printed poems and a small, heavy wooden box. On opening it, Hu found a steam pot. “How thoughtful of your master!” “My master said,” replied the attendant He Fu, “that his friendship with you is unlike any other. He told me to ask whether you need anything. If so, I'm to stay and attend to you until you've boarded your boat.” “No need. I have someone. Please go back and thank him for me.” From A’qiao's dressing case, Hu took a red envelope. There were many there, prepared for tips of varying amounts. The largest contained a five-tael banknote. He gave He Fu one of these.

Now Hu had only one thing left to do: wait for A’qiao. She had said she would arrive at noon, but the sun sank without any sign of her. Instead, Zhou returned to keep him company. “Mr Hu, I owe you so much for helping me. I've consulted someone who says His Excellency's letter carries great weight. I'm certain to get a good post.” He was smiling broadly. “Excellent!” Hu was pleased for him. “You ought to get to Yangzhou quickly. Wait too long, and the good posts will be gone.” “Never fear. There'll be stations all along the canal and both banks of the Yangtze. There are too many posts for others to snap them all up. I'll see you back to Shanghai first, then go to Yangzhou. It'll delay me ten days at most. That's nothing.” He was clearly sincere, and Hu would still need his help on the journey, so he nodded and said no more. They talked for a while. Seeing Hu restless, Zhou hesitated. Staying might annoy him, but leaving him alone at the inn would be worse. After considering, he suggested going out for a drink to take his mind off things. “Thank you, but not today. I'm waiting for someone.” “Oh—A’qiao?” Now Zhou understood his uneasiness. “Yes. She went to her parents' home in Mudu and promised to return at noon. There's still no sign of her. I don't know what's happened.” “If she isn't here now, she won't be back today. The regular passenger boat from Mudu arrived long ago.” “She didn't take the regular boat. She hired one for the return journey.” “Then I'll inquire at the Chang Gate wharves.” Zhou stood up. “How can you inquire when we don't know which boat?” “Never mind. Once I'm there, a question will tell me.” “Of course! You know everyone at the wharves. Thank you.”

Not long after Zhou left, an inn servant brought in a boy of fifteen or sixteen. He said he was a young attendant who carried messages to the inner quarters of the Pan household. Their mistress had sent him. “Please come over, Mr Hu. A lady would like to see you.” All this talk of mistresses and ladies, with the inn servant listening, embarrassed Hu. It might cause misunderstandings and gossip—always a nuisance. Instead of answering the boy, he addressed the servant. “There's another Mr Hu staying here, isn't there? He has the wrong man.” “No mistake, sir. He gave your name, Xueyan. That's why I brought him in.” “How strange.” Hu turned to the boy. “I have no friend in Suzhou called Pan, and I certainly don't know your mistress.” “It's the lady from Mudu who wants to see you. She's a close friend of our mistress.” “So it's A’qiao!” Hu was utterly puzzled. “Why did she go to your house instead of coming back to the inn?” “I don't know. She only said to ask you to come and see her.” Hu was in a quandary. How could he accept an invitation from the womenfolk of a complete stranger? Why had A’qiao gone to the Pans', and why was she asking him to meet her there? Everything raised doubts. Better not go.

Even so, he must find out what had happened. To establish whether the story was true, the first thing was to ask about A’qiao. “Have you seen this lady from Mudu?” “Yes.” “What does she look like?” The boy described her figure, features and clothes correctly. It seemed true, then, that A’qiao was at the Pan house. With that established, the next step was easy. “Very well. Wait outside, or go for a walk and come back. I must see someone I'm expecting before I can go with you.” Hu took some small change from the tea table and gave it to him. “Go and buy yourself some sweets.” “Thank you, Mr Hu. When should I come back?” “In an hour.”

Before the hour was up, the man he was waiting for returned. It was Zhou. His inquiries showed that A’qiao's boat had arrived as early as three that afternoon. “This is interesting. It seems the story is true.” Hu then told him about the unexpected invitation. “There must be a reason. A’qiao must have some difficulty about returning here. I'll go with you.” “You're right, but I don't want to go. It's the one chance in ten thousand that a man must fear.” Lowering his voice, Hu continued, “People can be treacherous. One wrong step may ruin everything. I'm always careful and try to offend no one, but I can't avoid jealousy. Someone may be plotting against me. Other matters can be explained. Anything involving the women's quarters of another household is best kept far away from. I'd like you to go for me.” Zhou had long experience of the world and had seen every kind of strange affair. Hu was afraid of an extortion trap involving a woman, he thought, and the concern was reasonable. He too must be careful if he went in Hu's place. He nodded. “I'll go. I'll simply ask A’qiao to come out and hear what she has to say.” “Exactly. Find out and come straight back to tell me.” As they spoke, the boy returned. Hu gave some convenient reason why he could not leave. The messenger could hardly object and took Zhou away.

It was some two hours before Zhou returned. “A’qiao had a great deal to say. There are things I don't fully understand.” He paused to collect his thoughts, then explained briefly. “Her husband's family sent someone who followed her here from Mudu. They seem to be looking for trouble. She didn't come back because she didn't want them to discover where she's staying. She says there are many things she must discuss with you in person. She's afraid the people following her are watching near the Pans', so she dare not leave now. She wants me to fetch her at midnight.” “Oh!” Hu was deeply surprised. “As far as I know, her husband's family are very docile. How can this be?” Zhou could offer no opinion. “You'll know when you see her.” “Wait!” Hu's eyes flashed, and his expression became stern. “You mustn't fetch her. If someone follows and accuses me tomorrow of abducting a respectable married woman, I can't afford that disgrace. Old Zhou, tell me about this Pan family.” “There are two prominent Pan families in Suzhou: the ‘Noble Pans’ and the ‘Rich Pans’. This household belongs to the same clan as the Rich Pans. A’qiao's friend is the master's concubine. His principal wife has died, so the concubine runs the household. That's why she can decide to let A’qiao stay.” “What's the master's name? Do you know?” “No.” “That doesn't matter. I'll call on him and explain what has happened. Then we can ask A’qiao to come out and talk in his presence. But this will mean asking you to accept a humble role.” Zhou understood: he was to act for the moment as a servant presenting Hu's visiting card. He did not mind and readily agreed. “I'll attend you.” They hired a sedan chair. Carrying the card case, Zhou accompanied Hu to the Pan house. When the card was brought in, the master was bewildered. His concubine understood, however, and explained. Once he grasped the situation, he immediately ordered that the visitor be received.

“This is a most presumptuous visit,” Hu Xueyan said with a deep bow. “May I have the honour of your name?” “My courtesy name is Shuya,” Pan replied. “I already know why you have come. I'll ask her to join you so that you can speak face to face.” “Thank you, thank you. I'm most grateful, and very sorry to disturb you so late.” “Excuse me for a moment.” Pan Shuya turned and went inside. Hu took the opportunity to examine the reception room and was astonished by the difference between the house's exterior and interior. The narrow, worn entrance suggested a family in decline, yet the furnishings were extraordinarily valuable. The pictures and calligraphy alone dazzled him. A set of four landscape scrolls on one wall represented the “Four Wangs,” one apiece. On another wall hung four calligraphic scrolls by Wen Zhengming, covering all four scripts: regular, cursive, clerical, and seal. There was also an enormous central scroll stretching from ceiling to floor, covered in wild cursive characters as big as bowls. Apart from the character for “one,” Hu could not read a thing. But the sheer size of the sheet of xuan paper, over two zhang long and seven or eight chi wide, was enough to leave him staring.

“Mr Hu, please have some refreshments.” A servant in an exceptionally neat blue cotton gown brought a silver box wrought in the shape of a plum blossom, its stalk forming the handle. Beneath the lid were five fine porcelain dishes, each with a different delicacy. Red, green, yellow, black, and white were all represented in brilliant colour. Hu recognised only the red one, which he took for rose-flavoured New Year cake. Using ivory chopsticks mounted in silver, he lifted a piece to his mouth. Smooth, glutinous, fragrant, and sweet, it grew more delicious as he tasted it—but the flavour was not rose. “What is this made with?” “Peach juice mixed into the flour and steamed.” Hu had never heard of such a thing. “Your household certainly knows how to do things finely!” The servant smiled with restraint, stepped back two paces, and stood silently by. As Hu ate, he thought that when he made a great fortune, he must live even more exquisitely than the Pans. That would make life worth living.

In the midst of his admiration and wandering thoughts, he heard voices behind the screen. Looking up, he saw A’qiao approaching with a maid. “I've been waiting so long for you,” she said at once. “Please sit over here.” The tactful servant led them to a couch farther inside, brought covered bowls of tea, and gave the maid a glance. Both withdrew to the veranda. “What's happened?” Hu asked. “One visit to your family, and all this trouble! If I'd known, I'd have sent Zhou with you.” “That wouldn't have helped. It's very strange...” The strange thing was that on the day before A’qiao returned, someone had called at her husband's home and announced openly that she had sent him to discuss ending their marriage, which now existed only in name.
