If her husband was willing to divorce her and marry again, he could receive a substantial payment. Her husband was an honest, simple man and did not know what to say. But an elder cousin on his father's side, called Xiaogouzi, was a scoundrel who enjoyed stirring up trouble. Seeing a valuable opportunity, he immediately said that everything could be discussed, but A’qiao must come and settle it herself. The visitor repeatedly sounded him out, and Xiaogouzi said that he wanted only two or three hundred taels. “A lie! He meant to lure me home and use me to extort money from someone. As luck would have it, I came back the very next day. Fortunately, word reached me in time. When he came to fetch me, I refused to go. My mother told me to leave quickly too. Who would have thought he'd get a boat and follow me down with two local ruffians? When I saw that, I daren't return to the inn. I warned the boatman not to reveal that Jinchang Inn had hired his boat for me. I went ashore, hired a little sedan chair, and came straight here. I still don't know whether Xiaogouzi knows I'm here.”

Hu nodded gravely as he listened. By the time she finished, his mind was made up. “You did the right thing. Don't worry. I'll handle it.” “How?” “Are you very close to the concubine in this house?” “We've been friends since we were children. I wouldn't have come to her if we weren't close.” “Good!” Hu was relieved. “Then stay here for the present. Stay a few more days.” A’qiao was surprised. “A few more days?” She frowned. “Until when?” Hu would have preferred her to remain until He Guiqing left for the north, but this was neither the moment to say so nor something he could easily explain. Then he considered that, close though the women were, her hostess was not the household's principal mistress. A’qiao's position as a guest was awkward too. Both sides had their difficulties. A brief visit was harmless; a long stay might invite gossip. “Let's proceed as circumstances suggest,” he said. “If you're imposing on them here, naturally I must show my appreciation. I'll send a gift tomorrow. If the master of the house kindly invites you to remain, stay on. Otherwise we'll find another way.”

“There's no difficulty about staying. I only want to know until what day. You've so much to do in Shanghai that you'll have to go back in two or three days at most. Surely you don't mean to leave me here alone?” “Of course not. I have other arrangements...” “What arrangements?” she interrupted, intensely serious. Another man might have felt unable to withstand her persistent questioning, but not Hu. “Don't be anxious. Naturally, the arrangements will be perfectly satisfactory.” He continued, “To put it briefly, I'm keeping you here rather than bringing you back to the inn because I don't want to give Xiaogouzi anything to use against us. Next I'll find out who visited your husband's family.” “Yes, you must find out. All the way on the boat I kept wondering why they had used my name and said I'd asked them to negotiate. Could it have been someone I know?” Her words struck Hu like a flash of lightning. Almost certainly this was You and Gu's doing. He had told them to wait for his instructions and keep out of the matter for the present. They must have disregarded him, and their cleverness had backfired, producing unexpected trouble. But he knew A’qiao was unsettled and ought not to be told too much just then. “Don't go guessing. Leave everything to me. If this goes smoothly, it may be settled very quickly. Perhaps everything will be clear by tomorrow or the day after. Stay here a few days with an easy mind. I'll send your clothes trunk over.”

“There's no need. My friend and I are much the same size, and she has more clothes than she can wear. But...” A’qiao returned to her point. “You must give me a day. How long exactly am I to stay? Then I can be at ease and have an answer if they ask.” “Well...” Hu saw that keeping her here until He Guiqing left, around the Dragon Boat Festival, would be impossible. In that case, he should settle the matter sooner. After considering briefly, he answered decisively, “Three days. On the fourth day I'll certainly come to fetch you.” She was satisfied, but added, “Do remember!” “I won't forget.” He took out a thick sheaf of banknotes and selected several of smaller denominations. “Here are two hundred taels for your expenses. While you're a guest here, don't stint over small sums. Give the servants whatever gratuities are appropriate, and don't be mean about it. Understand?” Of course she understood. She nodded. “Don't worry. I won't let you lose face.”

Hu then asked to see the host, thanked him, and took his leave. Back at Jinchang Inn, he kept Zhou Yiming with him and explained the situation in detail. The story was complicated, with many twists of cause and consequence. Even though Hu omitted much that did not need telling, Zhou listened with relish and rubbed his hands, eager to take part. “Country ruffians can't manage much. Let me send them packing.” “We don't even know where they are. Don't rush,” Hu said. “Let's agree on a plan before acting. Getting rid of those two fellows would be easy enough. It's Xiaogouzi I want to deal with.” “Oh!” Zhou settled down to listen. Apparently, there was more to come. “I want to teach Xiaogouzi a lesson and make him grateful to me as well. See if you can think of a way.” This was a difficult problem, and Hu had partly intended it as a test. After careful thought, Zhou proposed a plan. Hu considered it workable, and they began preparations that day.

The first step was to locate the two men. Country people were country people, with a rustic air they could not shed, and early the next morning Zhou found them near the Pan house without much difficulty. At the mouth of the Pans' lane stood a little tea shop of the kind popularly called a “tiger stove.” Its customers were mostly ordinary people from the neighbourhood. On arriving, they took a wooden basin and scooped up water to wash their faces and rinse their mouths, greeted one another, then drank tea, ate snacks, and talked loudly. Only two furtive, rustic-looking customers, sitting at the table behind the flatbread stall by the entrance, greeted no one. Their eyes followed every passer-by, paying particular attention to women. The signs were plain enough. “Xiaogouzi!” Zhou called out on a guess. Xiaogouzi had no idea that, while the mantis stalked the cicada, an oriole waited behind it. He turned and found Zhou smiling at him. “Were you calling me?” “Yes. When did you come into town?” “Yester... yesterday.” Xiaogouzi faltered. “I don't know you.” “How can you not know me?” Zhou looked puzzled too. “Let me ask: don't you live in Mudu?” “Yes.” “Then that's right.” Zhou sounded utterly certain. “An important man forgets easily. You may not recognise me, but I can't be mistaken. We once attended a dispute-settling tea meeting together. You were a great help to my friend.” This was another fabrication. Zhou reckoned that a man like Xiaogouzi was bound to have taken part in such meetings and settlements, so he lied boldly. Suspecting no trick, Xiaogouzi considered. “Which friend?” “His surname is Wang.” “Oh! You must be Fat Wang's friend. Yes, he got slapped for making advances to Widow Liu, and I intervened for him. How is he now?” “Quite well, quite well,” Zhou answered readily. “He often mentions you and says what a loyal friend you are. Come, let me treat you to a little breakfast.” He called to the stall, “Bring some crab-shell pastries and oil buns!”

“You shouldn't trouble yourself,” Xiaogouzi said, but his eyes kept turning outside. A woman was passing whose graceful figure from behind looked very much like A’qiao's. It was as good as writing his own confession. Zhou laughed inwardly and ceased to regard him as any sort of opponent. When the figure disappeared, Xiaogouzi reluctantly looked back, his face showing both annoyance and doubt. Zhou went straight to the point. “Are you waiting for someone?” “No, no!” “That woman...” Zhou pointed into the distance. “Her back looks so familiar. Where have I seen her?” Xiaogouzi could not imagine that he was being deliberately baited. Surprised and delighted, he began, “You... Ah, how foolish of me! We've been talking all this time and I haven't asked your surname.” Holding him in such contempt, Zhou could not even be bothered to invent one. “Zhou.” “Brother Zhou, you too thought you recognised that woman who just passed?” “Yes. I seem to have seen her in Mudu, and perhaps in Shanghai too.” He shook his head. “I can't remember.” This performance deceived Xiaogouzi completely. Rather than reply, he called to his companion, “Old Wu!” and jerked his chin towards the street. Old Wu dashed off, leaving Zhou still more amused. Lowering his voice, Zhou asked, “Are you following someone?” With an air of concern, he warned him, “Suzhou isn't the countryside, especially this past year or so. The governor-general, governor, military commander—there are any number of great officials with red hat buttons here. You'd better be careful.” “Well...” Xiaogouzi faltered. “It's nothing. Someone we know.” “Who? Do you mean that woman?” “Yes.” Thinking Zhou worldly and experienced, and remembering his claim to know her too, Xiaogouzi stopped concealing the truth. “You're right about both Mudu and Shanghai. Perhaps you'll know her name. She's called A’qiao.”

Zhou put on another performance. Straightening his back, drawing his face a little away, and lowering his eyes, he paused for some time. “So that's who it is! A’qiao from the high-class courtesan house. No wonder her back looked familiar.” “Yes, yes! Brother Zhou, you know she's at one of those houses.” Feeling a further explanation necessary, Xiaogouzi hurried on. “It's all her own family's fault. She ran away secretly from her husband's home. Carrying on like that has disgraced his family. What rotten luck!” “Why are you following her now? To catch her and take her back?” “Not catch her. She's neglected her duties as a wife. We want to persuade her to return.” “Xiaogouzi, if I may say so, this is just like your Suzhou saying: ‘Hang a salted fish under your nose—smell it, but forget your hopes.’ How can you expect to talk sense into someone like that?” Xiaogouzi nodded, opened his mouth, then swallowed his words. Zhou knew they had reached the critical point. His original plan had been to find a young runner from the detention quarters and have him recruit a colleague. With a chain and a pair of handcuffs, they would wait until Zhou discovered Xiaogouzi's lodging, then pin some arbitrary charge on him and haul him into custody. Hu would then use the visiting card He Guiqing had given him for the magistrate of Changzhou County to secure Xiaogouzi's release. That was how they meant to frighten him and make him grateful as well. Now it seemed there was no need for such elaborate measures: direct negotiation would suffice. Zhou had no doubt he could mould Xiaogouzi like dough, round or long, into whatever shape he wanted. But he had to consider Hu. Neither his standing nor the closeness of their acquaintance entitled him to act independently. He was merely running errands: Hu gave instructions, and he followed them. Carrying them out exactly was the best possible result. If he disobeyed, even an outcome better than expected could make Hu think him unreliable, because a man who would not obey was a man difficult to control.

For this reason, Zhou changed course. “Everyone has his own affairs, Xiaogouzi. I won't ask any more.” He paused. “It's a coincidence, but I have a chance to make a little money today. I can't manage it alone. Passing by and seeing you, I thought I'd ask you to help. Have you any time?” The proposal came so abruptly that Xiaogouzi did not know how to answer. Of course he welcomed any chance to make money. But first he must decide whether Zhou could be trusted, and second whether he could do the job. He needed an explanation before making up his mind. “If you've chosen me, Brother Zhou, naturally I'm willing. But what's involved? Could you tell me first?” “It's a long story. You're distracted at the moment, and I have something else to do. Let's see...” Zhou pretended to consider, then asked urgently, “Where are you staying? I'll call at noon.” “With a friend outside Chang Gate. But I may not go back at noon.” “Then let's arrange somewhere to meet. I'll invite you for a drink. Bring your friend Old Wu.” “Good.” Xiaogouzi agreed without hesitation. “You choose the place. We're brothers; it makes no difference who treats whom.” “Exactly. Yuandachang on Guanqian Street, at noon sharp. Whoever arrives first waits. We must meet.” With this settled, Zhou left first. He was careful enough not to forget to pay the stall for their breakfast.

He hurried to Wuyuan Tea House, where Hu was waiting by arrangement from the previous night. “That Xiaogouzi is completely in the dark. He knows nothing! To think he'd try making money this way—he has no idea of his own limits.” Zhou proudly described how he had found him, then added, “Why use an ox-cleaver to kill a chicken? A fellow like that isn't worth your trouble. We need only tell him straight. I'd meant to speak plainly on the spot, but since it was your business, I didn't dare take the decision myself.” “You do me too much honour.” Well pleased, Hu responded with equal courtesy, clasping his hands. “You've done me a great favour.” “Not at all. No need for formalities, Mr Hu,” Zhou answered earnestly. “Just tell me what should be done, and I'll do the legwork.” “Your method is excellent already. To settle it within a day or two would be easier than I could have expected, to tell the truth. Keep your noon appointment, then bring him to my inn so we can talk together. It would be best to leave the man named Wu out of it.” “Easy enough. I'll find a way.” “There's one more thing, and it's important.” Hu thought briefly. “Never mind. I'll do it myself. Just bring Xiaogouzi. Once you've got him there, leave the rest to me.” Those words reminded Zhou that Xiaogouzi might grow suspicious and deliberately fail to appear. Then he would have no satisfactory account to give Hu.

Without further talk, Zhou hurried out of Jinchang Inn. To save time, he hired one of the horses used for excursions into the hills, set his foot in the stirrup, swung into the saddle, and turned it towards the city. “Hey, sir! Where are you going?” The groom hurried to catch the bridle and looked up at him. These horses normally went out with a groom leading the way, and knew the route thoroughly. They advanced one slow step at a time on the outward journey, but moved very differently when home and their feed troughs were in sight. All were old, so none could go particularly fast. They were used only for hill excursions and never entered the city. Hence the groom's astonishment. Zhou knew the rules. Seeing that no exception would be made, he said curtly, “I'm going into town. Will you hire it to me or not? If not, I'll get down.” “I'm in business. Why wouldn't I? Only...” With no time for discussion, Zhou jumped down, tossed away the reins, and turned to go. His manner was poor, and the groom had a temper too. Spitting on the ground, he muttered, “Rotten luck! I've met a ‘master’ today.” In this use of Suzhou speech, “master” meant a ghost or devil. Zhou was already furious at failing to hire the horse. Now he could contain himself no longer. Turning, he strode back two paces and pointed. “Who are you cursing?” Alarmed by this menacing approach, the groom was afraid. Yet the elaborate preparations of Suzhou men for a fight were famous. In a dialect that would never sound fierce, he repeatedly demanded, “What d'you want? What d'you want?” while backing away, baring his fists, rolling his sleeves, gathering his skirts, and winding up his queue as though preparing for a fight to the death. Suzhou people also loved a spectacle, and a ring of onlookers soon formed. Encouraged by the support of his fellow townsmen, the groom raised his voice and accused Zhou of behaving unreasonably in rapid Suzhou speech. Even in a quarrel he remembered to add a few witticisms, which drew laughter from the crowd. Zhou was now in an awkward position. He was not afraid, but feared becoming so entangled that he would miss Xiaogouzi and spoil Hu's important business. He regretted his conduct but could find no way to retreat with dignity.

Fortunately, help arrived in the shape of Hu. Pushing through the spectators, he asked, “Zhou, why are you quarrelling with him?” “I wanted a horse to get into town quickly. His horses are particular about where they'll go. Very well! Even if a bargain falls through, civility remains. There's no need to curse me.” “Who cursed you?” The groom hurried forward to argue, but Hu stopped him. “No one speaks pleasantly in a quarrel. There's no need to debate who's right. I ask only this: has he cost you any business?” “Even if he has, I'll have to put it down to bad luck.” “Then there's nothing more to say. Go and attend to your customers.” Taking Zhou by the arm, Hu walked away. There was no need for further soothing or questions. They hired two sedan chairs into the city, got out at Guanqian, fixed their meeting at Jinchang Inn for noon precisely, and separated to attend to their respective tasks.

Hu had intended to find a silver foundry, but inquiries showed it was too far away. He would have to use a bank instead. Entering Yongxingsheng, whose premises looked suitably imposing, he asked at once, “Have you any official ingots fresh from the mould?” These were large ingots of fifty taels each, cast under the supervision of the provincial treasury for remittances to the capital and other official purposes, hence their name. A bank might not have newly cast ones on hand, but could exchange for them at a foundry or even have them made. Anything was possible if the customer would pay the premium. A clerk at Yongxingsheng, full of his own importance, braced his hands wide apart on the counter, tilted his head, and asked, “How many?” “Twenty.” Twenty meant a thousand taels. The clerk pulled over an abacus, rattled through the calculation of the premium, and said, “Not until this afternoon.” “I need them urgently. I'll pay extra for transport. Please arrange it.” They agreed on that charge too, and Hu handed over two Fukang notes payable on demand, one large and one small. The clerk gave them a sidelong look. “We don't accept those notes.” “Why?” “Their credit is unreliable.” Had he said they had no dealings with Fukang and could not accept its notes because they knew nothing of its position, Hu would have had no objection. But to call its credit unreliable was close to slander. Anger rose in him. He reached inside his gown for his thick sheaf of notes, which included those of the capital's celebrated “Four Hengs” and Rishengchang, with its head office in Hankou and more than twenty branches. He meant to put them on the counter and let the man choose. His hand had already touched them when he reconsidered. There was no need. Suppressing his anger, he asked, “Does your bank issue notes?” “Of course.” “Good. Its own notes must be perfectly reliable, then?” “Need you ask? Bring as many as you like. We'll redeem them all.” “I have none. Since you won't accept Fukang's, I must go elsewhere.” Hu clasped his hands. “My apologies.”

Outside Yongxingsheng, Hu found the insult hard to swallow. He would have liked to retaliate immediately, but that could not be arranged in a moment. Putting it aside, he found another bank, obtained twenty official ingots, and had one of its outside clerks deliver them to Jinchang Inn. The silver had scarcely been stacked when Zhou arrived with Xiaogouzi. Once they were introduced, Hu came straight to the point. “I'm a patron of Sister A’qiao's. She has asked me to speak for her. If her husband's family will release her, she's willing to pay a thousand taels so that her husband can marry again and buy a few mu of land. He could live comfortably enough. Zhou tells me you're involved in the matter. An emperor doesn't send hungry soldiers on a mission. On Sister A’qiao's behalf, I'll give you a hundred taels. What do you say?” The proposal was plain, yet Xiaogouzi found it abrupt. What puzzled him most was how this “Brother Zhou,” who claimed to be Fat Wang's friend and to have attended a tea settlement with him, could know so much about his affairs. Looking first at Zhou and then at Hu, he rolled his triangular eyes, which showed more white than black, and could find no answer. As he hesitated, a flash of brightness struck him. Hu had pulled away a sheet, revealing twenty large ingots beneath, all brand-new and glittering with silver light: a truly lovely sight. Beside them lay another pile, several medium-sized ingots and some pieces of refined silver, perhaps a hundred taels in all. Plainly, that was the reward intended for him. “Money moves the heart,” as the saying went. Hu, who had turned countless somersaults through the eye of a coin, understood this better than anyone. That was why he had gone out of his way to obtain official ingots. Knowledge of the world, insight into human nature, and command over other men had given him this unfailing prescription. Xiaogouzi knew, too, that A’qiao had become a valuable commodity. Storytellers always said a beauty was beyond price. If he held firm, eighteen thousand taels would be easy enough to get. What was a mere thousand? Such were his thoughts, yet his eyes refused to obey. They would not leave the gleaming pile of ingots. Naturally, he said nothing. Zhou moved his lips to press him, but Hu stopped him with a gesture.

Hu was patient and let Xiaogouzi think. Silver was like beauty: “Let a man see nothing to desire, and his mind remains untroubled.” Even if he caught a glimpse and was abruptly cut off from it, that could be endured. But when it remained visible and just beyond his reach, each look intensified his longing. Xiaogouzi was gradually reaching precisely that state. “Nothing need be forced,” Hu said at last. If he did not speak, Xiaogouzi could not, and they would be deadlocked. “If there's a difficulty on your side, say so.” “A difficulty?” Xiaogouzi asked blankly. Seeing how the money had bewitched him, Hu lifted a corner of the sheet and flicked it upwards like a conjuror. It spread through the air and settled exactly over the ingots. Only then did Xiaogouzi recover his senses. “I know you're a man of the world who understands how things are done,” Hu continued. “That's why I've spoken plainly. I'm acting for someone else. Whether it succeeds or fails makes no difference to me. I only need an answer to take back.” The money had effectively been put away. One word from him, it seemed, and the whole matter would be dropped. Such an opportunity was too painful to surrender lightly. “I'll find a way,” he answered involuntarily. “That's the spirit. We're both intermediaries. We can speak frankly and discuss any difficulties together. What way do you have in mind?” “I can't decide it myself. I can only do my best to persuade them. I can't guarantee success.” Xiaogouzi added, “And if there's some difference over the amount, what should I say? Please give me something to go on, Mr Hu.”

They had reached the bargaining stage, which meant the main issue was effectively settled. Hu considered briefly. “I'm very busy in Suzhou and have no spare time for haggling. Make things easy for others, and they're easier for you too. If you don't waste my time, I'll pay for promptness. If the documents can be signed first thing tomorrow, I'll add four large ingots myself.” “Tomorrow morning may be too soon.” “Noon tomorrow at the latest. If it can't be done by noon, there's nothing more to discuss. Someone else has a use for a thousand taels.” As Xiaogouzi wondered what this meant, Zhou supplied the perfectly timed response: “I've invited Clerk Zhang of the criminal office to drink with me tomorrow at noon.” Together, the two remarks implied that the thousand taels might go to Zhang. Money for a clerk in the criminal office naturally meant a lawsuit. Xiaogouzi grew still more alert. “Yes, yes,” he said, nodding repeatedly. “I'll certainly bring the husband here by noon tomorrow. I'll act as intermediary for the documents.” “Zhou will act for our side.” Hu took the hundred taels and put them before Xiaogouzi. “Take this now.” Xiaogouzi was delighted beyond expectation, though he offered the required polite objection. “That isn't the custom.” “People make customs. This has always been mine. Take your hundred taels first. It'll give you more energy for running about.” Hu added a brand-new wrapping cloth, silk outside and cotton within, bundled up the silver himself, and handed it over. Xiaogouzi calculated that if the affair succeeded, the twelve hundred taels would yield him another three hundred through the open intermediary's fee and the concealed twenty-per-cent kickback. Such a windfall had dropped out of nowhere, and he owed it to Zhou. After thanking Hu, he beckoned. “Brother Zhou, please come outside with me.”

Zhou accompanied him out. When he returned, he carried two medium-sized ingots and was smiling broadly. “The fellow has a conscience after all. He said one should remember the source when drinking water, and since the opportunity had come through me, he wanted to give me twenty taels. I was happy to accept, so I could return them to their rightful owner.” He set the ingots before Hu. “Nonsense. He gave them to you. What have they to do with me? Keep them. Tomorrow, when the papers are signed, we'll follow the custom for property transactions: ‘three from the buyer, two from the seller.’ The intermediary's commission is five li, divided between the two sides. You'll have another thirty taels. That's your rightful benefit.” Zhou had thus gained fifty taels out of nowhere. Overjoyed, he revered Hu as though he were a god and volunteered to fetch A’qiao. “No hurry. Let her stay at the Pans' a couple of days,” Hu replied. “There are two other matters I'd like to discuss.” The first was the insult he had suffered at Yongxingsheng that morning. He wanted redress. Did Zhou have a clever suggestion? “No mind is better than yours, Mr Hu. You think of the plan, and I'll do the legwork.” “I do have a plan, but I'm afraid it may be too harsh. Let me tell you a story about a remittance house first.”

The four largest remittance houses in the capital all had the character Heng in their names and were commonly called the “Four Hengs.” Great businesses could bully their customers, and their competitors too. A rising house called Yiyuan specialised in copper-cash notes. Courteous and accommodating in its business, and sound in credit, it prospered rapidly. Its notes circulated chiefly among ordinary townspeople. Once its good name was established, word spread from one to ten and ten to a hundred, until even official circles knew its reputation. Jealous of a competitor, the Four Hengs set out to damage it. They secretly collected its notes and presented them for redemption while spreading rumours that it was about to fail. A run followed. Yet for three days Yiyuan redeemed every note on sight, without even making people wait. On the fourth day calm returned, and its reputation was stronger than before. The Four Hengs naturally investigated its resources, only to discover an unshakable opponent. Yiyuan had four million in cash reserves. Whenever it issued a note, it set aside the full corresponding amount in a separate reserve. It never issued an unbacked note, so it could not be embarrassed. Zhou understood the point. “Mr Hu, you mean to collect Yongxingsheng's notes and give it a lesson?” “Exactly. But I'm afraid of repeating what happened between the Four Hengs and Yiyuan. One man makes a move today, and the other answers tomorrow. If I fail to bring Yongxingsheng down and it turns on Fukang, wouldn't I be asking for trouble?” “Yes, we must guard against that. Let me find out how strong it is. If its resources are thin, we can put it in check. Otherwise we'll need another method.” “Just what I mean. Make inquiries first. Fortunately, there's no hurry. Now for the other matter.”

The other matter was a gift for Pan Shuya. Hu wanted both to thank him for lodging A’qiao and to cultivate his friendship, for a man like that was well worth knowing. If he merely wished to discharge a debt of courtesy, the gift would be easy: spend a few dozen taels on four kinds of presents, and the obligation would be met. Friendship required something Pan would value, even something that would touch him. The family was rich; no costly object was likely to impress it. Local products from Hangzhou might have left an impression through their rarity, but Hu was in Suzhou and could not obtain them. Explaining all this posed another difficult problem for Zhou. “A gift should be something the recipient wants but can't get,” Zhou said. “The Pans have money. What they lack is prestige. Could you give them that?” “Beautifully put!” Hu clapped in approval. “Let's think of some distinction we can give him.” Encouraged, Zhou concentrated, blinking as he worked his mind, and came up with an idea. “See what you think of this. Your friendship with Education Commissioner He is close enough. Ask him to honour the Pan household.” Hu nodded gravely. “The principle is excellent. But how exactly?” “You could write to him. Whether to explain the circumstances fully is for you to decide. If you'd rather not, you can be vague. Just say that Mr Pan has been a great help on this visit, and ask the commissioner to call and thank him on your behalf. A second-rank official paying a visit with his full ceremonial escort—wouldn't that confer considerable prestige?” “Excellent! A brilliant idea. So brilliant, Zhou, that you don't know yourself where its brilliance lies.” This was a strange remark. Zhou was thoroughly puzzled and could only stare. Hu offered no explanation; the time had not come to reveal his intentions. He had decided to follow a common practice in official circles: purchase a concubine as a gift, arranging for A’qiao to become He Guiqing's secondary wife. Since she was staying with the Pans, He too would owe them gratitude. Thanking them for Hu would really be thanking them for himself. Zhou's suggestion contained this further significance, which made it exceptionally clever, though he himself did not know it.

“That's certainly what we'll do.” Hu was pleased, yet regretful too. “Zhou, you're very capable. It's a pity you can't come and work for me.” Zhou was stirred. He too felt that working for Hu was brisk and satisfying: every move seemed to give them the upper hand. Yet the lijin post in Yangzhou was an official appointment, however modest, with a good income. It would be a pity to abandon it. He could only express regret. “Yes. If the opportunity arose, I'd very much like to serve you.” “We can discuss that later.” Hu rose cheerfully. “I've nothing more today. I'll go and look round the city. Find out how matters really stand at Yongxingsheng. We'll meet at Yuandachang again tonight.” Hu visited Xuanmiao Temple, drank tea, and listened to a long storytelling performance. When the session ended, he strolled to Yuandachang, chose a good seat, and began drinking alone while he waited. By the time he had finished a jin of Huadiao wine, Zhou arrived, wearing a secretive smile. Hu smiled back. “It looks as though Yongxingsheng may be in for a headache.” “An extraordinary coincidence!” Zhou said eagerly. “An acquaintance of mine works there as an outside clerk. I invited him for tea, and now I have the whole ‘Romance of the Western Chamber’ in my head.” “Excellent! Have some wine first.” Hu poured him a bowl of warm wine himself. “We can drink and talk.”

“Yongxingsheng deserves a lesson. Its very origins are crooked...” Zhou began with the bank's history. The original owner, surnamed Chen, had built his business through thrift, enduring hardship for half his life. Yet he had scarcely been a proprietor for a year when a fever carried him off. He was barely into his forties and left a wife and a son. A widow and orphan were easily preyed upon. One of the clerks, also surnamed Chen, was deeply calculating. He lavished concern on the widow and attended to her every need, eventually gaining both the woman and her money. Nominally Yongxingsheng's manager, he was in fact its owner. “One turn deserves another!” Zhou took a long drink. “This present Boss Chen has a daughter. A clerk in the bank became involved with her. By the time the raw rice was cooked, there was nothing to do but take him into the household as a son-in-law. His nickname is ‘Skyrocket’—the fellow who offended you.” “No wonder he's so full of himself. He has the standing of a man awarded an imperial yellow jacket.” Hu asked, “This Boss Chen schemed against a widow and orphan, and his son-in-law behaves like that. The other men in the bank must resent them. How can it prosper?” “Exactly!” Zhou put down his cup and struck the table. “No weakness escapes you. If that weren't the case, why would my friend act like Zhang Song presenting a map and reveal their secrets?” According to Zhou's information, Yongxingsheng was already in a dangerous position. Chen had been too greedy, lending several sums at high interest that he could not recover. Cash flow was therefore strained. Its capital had only ever amounted to a hundred thousand taels, yet it had issued notes for more than two hundred thousand. Resenting the wrong done to the dead Boss Chen, the clerks all longed to see the living one collapse. Hu knew the business. A brief calculation showed him that bringing Yongxingsheng down would not be difficult. Present fifty thousand taels in notes, and it would suffer; present a hundred thousand, and it would have to close. A man of Chen's character could expect little support from other banks. Even where fellow bankers felt a duty to help, it was easy to relieve a temporary emergency and hard to cure insolvency. Yongxingsheng's difficulties were more than a passing shortage. Any money advanced would be lost. Nobody would willingly be so foolish. But then Hu reconsidered. What benefit would he gain by destroying it? None—only harm. Word would spread that Hu Xueyan of Hangzhou's Fukang Bank was ruthless. The Suzhou bankers might be outraged and unite against him, shutting Fukang out of the city for good.

“Let it go,” Hu said with a smile. “I don't like beating a drowning dog. We'll spare him.” Zhou, however, was dissatisfied. “Mr Hu, he ought to be taught a lesson. Besides, Fukang could make a name for itself.” Hu considered. “That's possible. Let me think it through.” They dropped the subject. Hu drank with an easy mind; such moments of relaxation were rare. Without noticing, he drank too much and became so thoroughly drunk that he could not remember how he got back to Jinchang Inn. When he woke the following day, his whole body felt weak. Too languid to go out, he sat resting at the inn, drinking strong tea alone and reviewing the previous day's events. One remark of Zhou's had considerable point. A quarrel with Yongxingsheng was not worth the trouble, but making Fukang's name in Suzhou was an excellent idea. Suzhou had become the most important centre in Liangjiang, handling immense flows of military funds and assistance remitted by other provinces. If Fukang was to spread branches everywhere and operate on a grand scale like Rishengchang of Hankou, Suzhou was a market it must enter. There were only two ways to establish oneself. One was literally to fight one's way in, compelling submission by force—the method of a street ruffian making his name. Hu could do that too: crush Yongxingsheng and let everyone see his power. But he would not. His unchanging principle was the Hangzhou saying, “People lift one another as they carry a flowered bridal chair.” That principle had brought him to his present position, and he would continue to follow it. The other course was to win acceptance through goodwill. Remembering Skyrocket's face still filled him with disgust, but business must never become a contest of temper. Considering matters calmly, he saw that Yongxingsheng might serve as a stepping-stone into Suzhou. The question was how to place it.

Boss Chen did not seem an easy man to deal with. Hu had seen many of his kind: half-wits, as men of the world called them, or “candles,” as the people of Shanghai said—no light until someone set a flame to them. To bring such a man under control, one had to begin harshly and turn kind: let him taste hardship before sweetness, and he would become perfectly obedient. With this in mind, Hu quickly formed a plan. He could influence two streams of official payments between Zhejiang and Jiangsu: the shared expenses of the Sea Transport Bureau, and the military funds for Huzhou's joint defences, together with assistance remitted directly from Huzhou to Jiangsu. For both streams, Yongxingsheng notes could be collected and sent straight to the Jiangsu provincial treasury and military finance office. Public funds would naturally be redeemed in cash. This was borrowing another man's knife, and it would immediately put Yongxingsheng in difficulties. Once it could no longer meet its payments, Fukang would step forward to support it. Then Yongxingsheng would be meat on the chopping board, to be cut as he pleased: he could either keep it going or take it over. There were risks, of course. The bank was a mess. Supporting it might be like jumping down a well to save a drowning man; taking it over might bring endless entanglements. This was the point on which the whole plan would succeed or fail. Hu thought hard. The safest course seemed to be to judge the situation as it developed. If it could be managed, he would intervene. If not, the Jiangsu authorities would be the ones demanding payment, and his own side would have nothing to do with it. Yet safe though that might be, it could leave him with nothing for his effort, or damage others without benefiting himself, merely destroying Yongxingsheng. At this thought he realised that it was too early to decide. Before doing anything, he must investigate further: what were its real profits and losses, what other property did Chen own, and if the bank failed, what proportion of its debts could be recovered in a settlement? Only with that information could he reach a decision.

When Zhou arrived, Hu asked, “How much does your friend at Yongxingsheng actually know about its affairs?” “I can't say. But inquiries would be easy. Most of the clerks are at odds with Boss Chen and Skyrocket. If they know the details, they'll certainly tell.” “Good. Ask your friend to investigate. It must be done secretly.” “I understand. But it will take more than two or three days. I'm afraid you may not be able to wait.” “There's no hurry. Write when you've found out.” “Yes.” Zhou paused, then added, “Once I've finished your business, I'll go to Yangzhou and see how things are. If there's nothing worthwhile there, I'll come and join you in Shanghai.” “I hope you will. If Yangzhou really doesn't suit you, you're welcome. But there's no need to force it.” Hu returned to Yongxingsheng. “What's your friend's name?” “Zheng Pinsan.” “What sort of man is he?” “Very honest, and quite capable too.” “That's rare. Honest men are often useless, and most capable ones are slippery.” An idea occurred to Hu. “If he's that sort of man, could you bring him to see me?” “Of course! He knows of you too.” “How?” “I've told him about you. But he'd also heard that the owner of Fukang in Hangzhou was a Mr Hu. When would be convenient? I'll bring him over.” “You're leaving tomorrow. Bring him tonight.”

* * * Xiaogouzi proved most eager to oblige. The noon gun had scarcely sounded when he arrived with his party, five men in all. Three remained in the courtyard with sacks and carrying poles; the one he brought indoors was, plainly, A’qiao's husband. Said to be surnamed Chen, he was about forty, a timid, thoroughly honest-looking fellow. Over a bulky padded jacket he wore a brand-new blue cotton gown, with straw sandals on his bare feet. Once inside, he shrank against the doorway, looking either embarrassed or frightened. “Sit down, please.” Hu turned to Xiaogouzi. “Everything agreed?” “Everything.” He took out two written agreements on mulberry-bark paper. Even the letter of divorce was ready. Hu read them through. They were drawn up very securely, and he expressed his satisfaction. “This will do.” Pointing to Zhou Yiming, he said, “Here's the intermediary for our side. You represent the other side. We still need a scribe. Let the bookkeeper at Jinchang Inn earn a little.” “Mr Hu,” Xiaogouzi hastened to interrupt, “we've brought our own scribe.” He called outside, “Mr Liu!” Of the five men, this Mr Liu alone wore a long gown. His furtive, ratlike appearance suggested no good character.

Hu suddenly grew suspicious. Then he realized that he had forgotten an indispensable move. Keeping up appearances, he drew Zhou aside and whispered, “I've overlooked something. Does this Chen fellow look like A’qiao's husband to you?” “How could anyone tell by looking?” “Suppose he's an impostor? The money would be a small matter; we'd make fools of ourselves. Yesterday I forgot to tell them to bring their clan head.” “That can still be done. I'll speak to Xiaogouzi.” “Going back and forth would waste time and cause trouble. So long as we establish his identity and know he isn't an impostor, it doesn't matter whether the Chen clan head comes.” “Who can tell whether he's an impostor?” Zhou said. “Unless we ask A’qiao herself to identify him.” That went straight to the heart of it. There was no better way. Hu considered, then resolved on a delaying manoeuvre. Zhou was told to take Xiaogouzi to lunch, while Hu left Jinchang Inn on the pretext of going to a bank to obtain silver, and took a sedan chair straight to the Pans' house.

With a visiting card and a generous gratuity for the doorkeeper, Hu frankly explained his purpose. Whether the master received him did not matter; he had come to see A’qiao. Pan Shuya was a young master who dreaded worldly social obligations. On hearing the doorkeeper's report, he was glad of the excuse to spare himself the trouble and asked A’qiao to go out directly. Seeing Hu arrive empty-handed, she was disappointed and could not help complaining. “You ought to help me make a proper return. They're so kind to me here that I really feel uneasy.” “Don't worry. I've already made plans. You'll certainly have every reason to hold your head high. But there's no time for that now. Come back to the inn at once and identify someone.” “Identify someone? Who?” She blinked her exceptionally long lashes, thoroughly puzzled. “Think. Who else could there be that only you could identify?” The question made his meaning plain, yet she was more bewildered than ever. “What exactly has happened?” She was displeased that he should handle so important a matter without consulting her. “Unless you explain, I won't go,” she said firmly. Hu quickly took the hint and smiled apologetically. “Don't blame me for acting on my own. First, I had no chance to tell you; second, I wanted to spare you worry. I meant well.” “Thank you for your good intentions.” She accepted his explanation, though some resentment remained. She also found her position awkward. “Face to face, like a gong answering a drum—how am I supposed to identify him?” “No, no. You needn't face him. Just look through a crack in the partition. Once you've identified him, there's nothing more for you to do.” He briefly explained how he had brought Xiaogouzi round.

“You have so many tricks!” A’qiao said with a smile. Then her face suddenly grew serious. She looked down at the brick floor and remained silent for a long time. Hu became anxious and began to regret his lack of care. That she and her husband were on bad terms was something he had heard only from Second Miss at Yiqing House. Her own conduct did suggest that she had almost severed relations with her husband's family, but much of what people in such establishments said was unreliable. As the saying went, they could deceive a man to death without paying with their lives. He had taken it all for truth and set about the matter in earnest; at the critical moment, he might merely bring trouble upon himself. A’qiao might not have meant to deceive him. Still, every household had its own difficult scripture to recite. She evidently had some private concern that deserved understanding. In the end, he had been rash and could not blame her. Whether to blame her was secondary, however. If she refused her consent now, how was he to explain matters to Xiaogouzi? To come to Suzhou on such an absurd errand and become a laughingstock was more loss of face than he could bear. He urgently needed a truthful answer. “Sister A’qiao,” he said gravely, “you can't put me off any longer. Tell me honestly what you really want.” “Why!” She was astonished. “When have I ever lied to put you off?” “Then why do you seem ready to beat a retreat, now that things have come this far?” She found this amusing. “I've never sat in court like a county magistrate. How can I beat the drum that closes the hearing?”

Her words sounded more troublesome still. On closer examination, there was a barb in them. Before undertaking the matter, Hu had neither told her nor obtained her consent: she had never ‘opened court’, so how could she now beat the drum to close it? She was a formidable woman. This was no time to reason with her, since the right was not on his side and he could not win the argument. He could only appeal to her feelings, even deceive her a little if necessary. First, he admitted his fault. “I've handled this badly. But I'll certainly follow your wishes and won't force you. The man is there now. Come and identify him first, and we'll decide afterwards. If he's the wrong man, there's nothing more to discuss. If he's the right one, it's entirely up to you. Whichever way you wish to go, I won't object.” After all, a human heart was made of flesh. Hearing this, A’qiao could hesitate no longer. In fact, she was not reluctant because of lingering affection for her husband. She was thinking of her own family: Hu ought to provide some money to support her mother in old age. This condition seemed best discussed along with the other arrangements, but she did not know how to raise it. That was the cause of her hesitation; Hu had misunderstood. “Then sit down a moment. I must tell my hosts.” She added, “Did you hire a chair?” “Easily arranged. I'll leave mine for you and hire another. When you reach Jinchang Inn, come through the side entrance. I'll have someone waiting.”

With this settled, Hu left first. He had twice used these chair-bearers from near Chang Gate and knew them already. After giving his instructions, he hired another chair and hurried back to Jinchang Inn. There he rented an additional room and told an attendant to wait expressly at the side entrance. When A’qiao arrived, he was to bring her in quietly, then show himself to Hu without speaking. Only after everything was arranged did Hu return to his own room. Before long, Zhou brought Xiaogouzi and the others back from lunch. All their faces were red; they seemed to have drunk a good deal. After further courtesies, Hu launched into a wide-ranging account of Suzhou's scenery. Zhou understood that he meant to gain time and joined in. The conversation was lively, but never touched their business. Xiaogouzi could hardly bear it. At last, finding an opening, he interjected, “Mr Hu, we still want to get back to Mudu today. It'll be inconvenient if we're too late. Shall we begin?” “Oh, yes. Forgive me,” Hu replied apologetically. “Just a little longer. As soon as the bank's man comes and we have the full amount of silver, we'll begin. It's only a matter of putting down a mark. It won't take long.” Xiaogouzi had to wait patiently again, though his uneasiness became increasingly apparent. Watching coolly, Hu grew more suspicious and secretly devised a second plan. He was about to find an excuse to consult Zhou privately when the attendant appeared. Showing presence of mind, the man came with a pot to replenish the tea and gave Hu a covert glance. Even Zhou failed to notice.

Hu excused himself and went to see A’qiao in another part of the inn. “In a moment I'll bring someone out. Look carefully, but don't speak. I'll come back shortly.” Returning to the others, he beckoned to the supposed husband. The shrinking middle-aged man merely looked at Xiaogouzi, seeking guidance with his eyes. “Mr Hu, whatever you want to say, say it to me.” “Nothing important. But it isn't something for outsiders to hear.” Hu beckoned repeatedly. “Come here, please.” A countryman might be unused to polite society, but why be so reluctant to exchange a few private words? Xiaogouzi could hardly obstruct him further. Chen had no choice but to steel himself and follow his host outside. Hu was no ordinary man. Seeing Chen as wooden as a puppet, with Xiaogouzi pulling the strings, he had already guessed most of the truth without waiting for A’qiao's identification. He led him out to face the window behind which she was concealed. His first question was, “What is your actual surname?” “Chen.” The answer came readily enough to be true. Hu asked his second question. “What relation are you to A’qiao?” This exposed him. He stammered and muttered incoherently. Just as I thought! Hu silently reproached himself. Without that last-minute inspiration, Xiaogouzi would have cheated him of more than a thousand taels. He would have capsized in an open ditch—a humiliation he could not even complain of, since publicizing it would give people an irresistible story against him.

Inwardly both angry and amused, Hu kept his expression and voice unchanged. Instead, he offered reassurance. “Old Chen, I know all about Xiaogouzi's trick. Tell me the truth and I won't make trouble for you. I won't expose you to him afterwards either, so you needn't be put in a difficult position.” This last assurance touched the honest fellow where it mattered. “Mr Hu, if I tell you the truth,” he asked earnestly, “you really won't tell Xiaogouzi?” “Really. Do you want me to swear an oath?” Reassured, Chen revealed everything. He was an elder cousin of A’qiao's husband. He owed Xiaogouzi money and had been forced to submit to him and impersonate her husband. The agreement was that his old debt would be cancelled and he would receive a large silver ingot besides. What an absurd affair! “Aren't you afraid of being taken to court?” Hu asked. “I am,” Chen answered miserably. “But Xiaogouzi says there's nothing to fear. The intermediary and the scribe are all our own people. If a complaint reaches the county yamen, we'll just say the document is false and nothing of the sort happened.” The scoundrel! Hu thought. Xiaogouzi was a shrewd one and deserved a lesson. He whispered, “Don't be afraid. Whatever he tells you to do afterwards, do it. Just insist that you haven't told me the truth, and he won't blame you.” A simple-minded man needed instructions of this sort. Chen understood and nodded repeatedly. “I know. I know.”

They went back inside one after the other. Xiaogouzi's expression shifted uncertainly, but relaxed at once when Hu spoke. “Come, let's begin. Draw up the documents, then take your silver and get back to Mudu early. That will save everyone trouble.” Zhou knew nothing of what had happened. He assumed that Chen's identity as A’qiao's husband had been confirmed, a satisfactory conclusion. Cheerfully, he set out brush and inkstone and had Xiaogouzi spread the documents on the table. Zhou first signed his mark as intermediary. Xiaogouzi and the scribe followed, each taking the brush to draw a cross. Last came Chen, who could not even draw a cross and had to make an inked handprint. With the formalities complete, it was time to hand over the payment. Hu said, “Old Zhou, you're the intermediary. Hold the documents for now, and give them to me after the money has been paid in full.” He gave a slight signal with his eyes. Zhou understood at once: there was another move to come! He snatched up the papers, folded them in half and then in quarters, and gripped them firmly.

Hu continued, “Marriage is a serious matter. Whether people unite or separate, everything must be clear. The documents are drawn up, but only one of the two parties is present. Even the man is someone we've just met.” He turned to Zhou. “As intermediary, what would you say if a dispute arose later?” Knowing the question was deliberate, Zhou pretended surprise. “What dispute could there be?” “Exactly!” Xiaogouzi hastened to add. “There can't possibly be any dispute.” “Not so.” Hu pointed at Chen. “He doesn't much resemble A’qiao's husband to me. I asked him privately just now, and he insisted he was. Leave that aside. These documents still need one formality before they can be accepted. When we conduct affairs for others, we must make everything secure. If trouble arises when either party remarries, it will be a serious matter.” “Quite right,” Zhou put in. “It's no easy thing to act as intermediary. If this were merely a dispute about a debt, at worst I could repay the money. But if we've mistaken the person, how could I provide another A’qiao in compensation?” “Precisely,” Hu said. “Whether he's the genuine man or an impostor, we can't settle without A’qiao here to identify him, so let's leave that aside too. At least we must be able to prove that the documents are genuine.” Hearing that A’qiao was absent, Xiaogouzi felt greatly relieved. His mind grew more agile. “You're quite right, Mr Hu. That's exactly why we have intermediaries and a scribe—to prove the papers genuine. I don't understand what further witness you want.” Hu smiled faintly. “We have them, certainly. But let's speak plainly. If a dispute went to court, the magistrate couldn't rely on Old Zhou's testimony alone. Why don't we register the documents at the county yamen's revenue office and have them stamped with an official seal, like the red deeds used for buying land? I'll pay all the expenses.” Zhou was first to approve. “Excellent! That will lessen our responsibility as intermediaries,” he told Xiaogouzi.

Xiaogouzi mumbled without agreeing or refusing. This move was utterly unexpected. A countryman felt apprehensive at the mere mention of the county yamen. Its clerks brought to mind the fierce-faced judges in the City God's temple. If a clerk in the revenue office said, “We must go out to the village and investigate first,” the whole fraud would be exposed. Yet the procedure was perfectly proper, and Xiaogouzi could think of no excuse to refuse. His face reddened with anxiety. Then, seeing Zhou's knowing smile and the documents clenched in his hand, he suddenly understood. Before any silver had reached him, the others had secured evidence against him. He was in for a terrible fall. The thought struck like a blow on the head, sending stars before his eyes. In his panic he lost all sense of tactics and reached for the papers. He failed to seize them, but Zhou broke into a sweat, hastily thrust them inside his clothing, jumped back two paces and pressed both hands over his chest. “Hey! What are you doing?” Realizing that he had virtually exposed himself, Xiaogouzi turned ashen. He pointed at Zhou in agitation. “This is too much trouble! I won't concern myself with it any more. Take out the papers and tear them up. Let it be as though none of this happened.” Zhou was quick enough to see that he should now play the angry accuser, leaving Hu to intervene and negotiate. He raised a hand to rebuff Xiaogouzi, put on a fierce expression and said, “Wait. Let's make this clear. What exactly are you up to? I've treated you as a friend with all sincerity. Don't behave like a fool and leave me unable to account for myself to Mr Hu.” “No, no, that's not it!” Xiaogouzi protested vehemently. “I meant well too, but this really is a troublesome business to meddle in. Brother Zhou, do me a kindness and return the papers.” “Return them?” Zhou's expression changed, and he gave a cold laugh. “Do you think it's that easy?”

Xiaogouzi stared at him wide-eyed, without blinking, as though he had never truly seen his face before. Hu understood his feelings. Zhou still lacked finesse; he should not have turned hostile so abruptly. Hu hurried to intervene. “Let's talk calmly. Something written in black and white can't simply be torn up. Tell us what makes this so ‘troublesome’. Explain your difficulty, and we can discuss it.” Xiaogouzi's difficulty was precisely that he could not explain it. In desperation he seized upon someone else as a shield. Pointing at Chen, he said, “He's an honest fellow who's never been inside a yamen. He certainly won't agree to register the papers at the revenue office. Doesn't that put us intermediaries in a difficult position? Luckily, no money has changed hands. Let's cancel everything. Here's the husband; you can discuss it face to face and begin again. If you reach agreement, I'll be there to act as intermediary. If you don't, I've merely made a journey and run an errand for nothing.” His argument twisted reason, but he managed quite a speech. Hu smiled. “We've already agreed and drawn up the papers. What is there left to discuss? If he doesn't wish to go to the yamen, never mind. It'll only take a little more trouble. We'll all go by boat to Mudu and ask your Chen clan head to witness the matter. Surely that will do?” The fraud would still be exposed, but at least not until they reached Mudu. Xiaogouzi thought he could gain a little breathing space. He braced himself and answered, “Very well.” “Then when do we leave?” “Whenever you like. We can go at once.”

Xiaogouzi sounded resolute, but the other honest fellow lacked even his small skill in pretence. Chen could no longer keep calm. He tugged at Xiaogouzi's clothes and whispered, “We can't go.” “What do you mean, we can't?” Xiaogouzi snapped. “What are you afraid of?” “Yes, what?” Zhou added coldly. “The worst that can happen is a lawsuit.” This made Chen more anxious still. Having already told Hu the truth, how could he continue muddling along with Xiaogouzi? Yet he could hardly say openly that their host knew of the impersonation and no amount of bold talk would help. He merely wrung his hands. “Let's talk it over a little more.” Hu saw his distress and seized upon the opening. “Then let's talk. The matter must reach a satisfactory conclusion. Go and discuss it among yourselves.” This temporarily eased the strain. Xiaogouzi and his companions withdrew to confer in whispers. Hu and Zhou exchanged a smile and likewise sought a quiet place to assess the situation and decide their next move.

“He is an impostor, just as we thought.” Hu told Zhou what Chen had said, then frowned. “I'm afraid this will mean more trouble for you.” “Gladly!” After two days of unfailing success in Hu's service, Zhou's confidence had grown considerably. Eager for action, he declared, “I'll go myself and see it through, whatever it takes.” “Don't assume it'll be easy...” In Hu's analysis, Xiaogouzi must have found the proper course blocked, yet could not bear to give up that pile of gleaming ingots. He had therefore risked this inferior scheme in the hope of getting lucky. If that was right, there must be some obstacle on A’qiao's husband's side. They must first discover it before acting. “Easy enough,” Zhou said. “I'll put pressure on Xiaogouzi. We have evidence against him. He won't dare withhold the truth.” Once the truth was forced out, it proved that Hu had misjudged the matter this time. Xiaogouzi, who followed no honest occupation, had intended to obtain the money by fraud and disappear. A’qiao's husband knew nothing of the affair. Of course, Zhou elicited these facts through indirect questioning. Xiaogouzi proposed that they wipe the slate clean. He would accompany Hu to Mudu, bring the parties together and reopen negotiations. He promised not to manipulate matters or inflate the price for his own profit. His only hope was that, if an agreement was reached and put in writing, he might still earn an intermediary's fee. Hu accepted. Generously, he destroyed the document then and there, appointed Zhou as his representative, and sent him off to Mudu at once.

CHAPTER TWENTY-FIVE

Once the men had gone, A’qiao could come out of hiding. Hu Xueyan felt that the time had come to explain everything. After a moment's concentrated thought, he asked, “A’qiao, how would you like me to find you a husband?” He had deliberately chosen this abrupt opening to turn her thoughts in a new direction at once. That could not be achieved so easily. Her lively eyes blinked as she tried to understand his meaning before deciding how to answer. “What do you mean?” She shook her head, setting her jade earrings swinging. “I really don't understand.” “Do you think I'm joking?” “I don't know. I've had some experience of you now. You have so many tricks that even Zhuge Liang couldn't see through them.” Hu laughed. “Is that praise or abuse?” “Neither. It's the truth.” “I'm telling you the truth too.” His smile vanished and he spoke with complete seriousness. “I guarantee you'll be happy with the match I arrange. In future, remember that I've done you some good, and speak for me when you have the chance.” This was frank enough, and clear enough. A’qiao understood quickly. The promise that she would be happy struck a particularly pleasing chord. But who was the man? Hu answered before she could ask. “You've met him. Education Commissioner He.” Her face grew hot and her heart beat rapidly. She tried to conceal it and appear unmoved, but her eyes could not deceive Hu's penetrating gaze.

“Well?” he asked deliberately. “Commissioner He is a true fair-faced scholar, famous in official circles for his good looks. He'll soon go to the capital and then receive a provincial appointment. I hear his principal wife is unwell. If anything should happen to her, he might even make you his lawful wife. Then wouldn't you be a great official's lady, riding in a sedan chair with eight bearers?” What a delightful prospect! A’qiao's heart blossomed with joy, and a smile appeared at the corners of her mouth. It vanished almost at once. Suddenly on her guard, she thought the proposal too unexpected. Most likely Hu was testing her. If she believed him and the trick was exposed, she would have given him endless grounds for ridicule. Other matters could be joked about; this was no joke. Being too innocent and trusting could leave her in an impossible position. Her expression darkened. With a cold little laugh, she withdrew to the narrow space behind the bed curtains to change. Hu was naturally surprised by the sudden alteration, but soon understood. He could hardly blame her. “You don't believe me, do you?” he asked calmly. “Tell me what would convince you.” That was precisely what A’qiao was asking herself. She could think of no way to establish whether it was true. For now, her safest position was to show complete indifference. Deliberately sounding impatient, she replied, “I don't know. Stop bothering me.” Her defence admitted not even a drop of water. Hu paced slowly, considering how to reach her. Later, something he said could convince her that he was serious. Truth was truth and falsehood falsehood; the facts would emerge in time. He might as well say what needed saying now. She would remember, and once she believed him, his words would take effect.

He therefore went on “talking to himself,” describing He Guiqing's circumstances and the steps he intended to take. Inevitably, he ended by asking, “Now it depends on what you think.” A’qiao had long since finished changing, but deliberately remained seated behind the bed. His orderly, vivid account began to stir her hopes again. Still, she would not disclose her attitude. Whatever course she took, the essential thing was to keep up appearances. “What do I think?” She emerged gracefully and began folding her clothes. “I don't know.” Hu knew that further pressure would achieve nothing. Reversing his approach might be more effective. He assumed a disappointed expression. “If you're unwilling, nothing can be done. Other things may be forced, but this requires consent on both sides. Fortunately, I haven't spoken plainly over there yet. Otherwise I'd have offended everyone.” A’qiao feared that the cooked duck might fly away—that her cleverness would cost her the opportunity. Yet honestly admitting that she was willing would undo all her elaborate pretence. Caught between the two, she desperately found another tactic. She searched her memory for the sufferings that had begun when she became a child bride at seven: her mother-in-law's cruelty, washing coarse cotton clothes in icy water despite winter chilblains, and summer nights in the woodshed when mosquitoes kept her awake until dawn. Gradually her heart ached and her eyes grew hot. She began to sob.

A pretty woman's tears possessed immense power. Hu had a way of dealing with almost anything, but he feared tears like these. Alarmed, he asked, “Why, what's happened? Tell me if you've been wronged. What are you crying for?” “Where can I speak of my wrongs?” A’qiao seized the opening, filling her voice with resentment. “People like us are only playthings for rich men, like a cat or a caged bird. When they fancy us, they spend money to buy us; when they're tired of us, they give us away. Told to go east, we daren't go west. What is there to say?” “That's an ungrateful thing to say!” Hu was exasperated. “I'm doing this for your good.” “Who knows whether it's good or bad? Think about yourself. You decide everything without consulting anyone, and then say it's for my good!” She meant something specific: the business Zhou had gone to settle. Hu felt himself somewhat in the wrong and could only remain silent. Silence brought calm, and calm made it possible to understand. Thinking over her words, he perceived compliance beneath apparent opposition, pleasure beneath apparent resentment. Inwardly, she was perfectly willing; she merely had to retreat before advancing. That was human nature, and could even be taken as proof that she still had a conscience. To force her to say outright that she wanted to become He's concubine was impossible—and even if it were possible, what would be the point? Once he understood this, her tears no longer seemed formidable. What he must do now was win her affection and leave her feeling grateful, so that in future she would always consider his interests with He Guiqing. He remembered Ji Heling telling him the story of the First Emperor's parentage. He himself was rather like Lü Buwei. The thought brought an involuntary smile. “I cry, and you laugh!” A’qiao continued her performance, rolling her eyes and pouting. “Men have no conscience. One can see right through them.” “Quite right,” Hu answered in the same spirit. “I admit it. But men are clever too. They seldom drive things to the point of leaving no way out. When conscience is called for, they still have one.”

A’qiao did not answer. Wiping her tears, she poured herself a cup of hot tea. Just as she raised it to her lips, it struck her that this was not proper. She placed it before Hu and poured another for herself. Drinking at his ease, he asked, “A’qiao, who exactly is there in your family?” “Haven't I told you? An old mother and a younger brother.” “How old is he, and what does he do?” “Eighteen. He's an apprentice in a cloth shop.” “Is he married?” “He hasn't even finished his apprenticeship. How could he think of that? Besides, marrying isn't easy.” “Not so difficult, either. A’qiao, I'll give you another thousand taels. Deposit it in a sound bank, use the interest to help with household expenses, and leave the principal untouched. When your brother finishes his apprenticeship, it can pay for a wife or a little cloth shop of his own.” She looked at him, blinking without a word. Thinking she doubted him, Hu generously took out a thousand-tael note and pressed it into her hand.

“Do you really want to help me?” “How could there be any doubt?” Hu laughed. “Do you truly think I have no conscience?” “I was only saying that. Everyone has a human heart. If you're good to me, surely I know it.” She added, “But if you really want to help, don't help in this way.” “How, then?” “My brother is clever, and good-looking too. He's famous in our town as a handsome young fellow...” “You needn't tell me.” Hu smiled. “One look at the elder sister tells me the younger brother must have fine features.” “Not in an effeminate way. He's tall and well built, and cuts quite a figure. But never mind that. I was thinking that if you'd look after him, I could bring him out to work for you. Wouldn't that be better than learning business in our little place?” She returned the note. “So that's it! Certainly. I'll help your brother advance, provided he wants to get on. Keep the money too. Consider it my gift towards your mother's ‘coffin fund.’” Though she knew she need not stand on ceremony with Hu, A’qiao still felt uncomfortable accepting it. “I'll kowtow in thanks on my mother's behalf. I'll leave the money with you for the present.” “No. Keep it yourself.” She would not take it, and he would not yield. Taking the note, he slipped it into the inner pocket of her lined satin jacket. The soft warmth he felt as his hand reached inside stirred his desire. Regret returned. He was reluctant indeed to send such a woman far away.

For a while Hu said nothing, his mind in confused agitation. A’qiao could not guess what he was thinking and returned to her brother. “His childhood name is A’shun. When should I bring him out?” Collecting himself, Hu said, “An apprenticeship is governed by a written contract. He can't simply leave whenever he likes. As far as I'm concerned, any time will do.” A’qiao knew that leaving before the term was complete meant repaying the cost of board. But with a thousand-tael note on her, she felt secure. “That doesn't matter. I'll arrange it properly.” “Good. Write and tell him to come.” Besides this, she had much to discuss with her family. Better to go home again herself. “When are you leaving?” she asked. “I've already lost time. Once Zhou gets back, if your business is settled, I'll leave first thing tomorrow.” “Then it's too late,” she said disappointedly. “For what?” “If you were staying another day or two, I'd have gone home once more. Now there's no point discussing it.”

By this time Hu's wandering desires had settled. He had given his word and could not go back on it. That being so, he might alter his original plan for A’qiao to remain with the Pans. “This is what I think. In conducting affairs, one must give people no grounds for criticism. From this moment, you belong to Commissioner He's household. We ought not to stay together any longer; it wouldn't look right. I originally meant you to stay at the Pans', but now you can decide. You may go to your mother's instead.” This surprised her. After considering it, she felt that Hu really did act unlike other men: his thinking was careful and his methods elegant. Since he put it that way, she would have greater standing before He Guiqing later. There was no need to say more. Then it occurred to her that accepting without comment would suggest she felt no attachment, as though she truly had no conscience. She must say something, but what? She could hardly argue that they might continue living together since she had not yet entered He's household. Wouldn't that be the behaviour of a woman in a courtesan house? Even there, once a girl agreed to marry a patron, her nameplate came down immediately. She could not claim that she might still receive customers until the day she left. Yet what else could A’qiao say? At last she found something. “If one's conscience is clear and one's conduct upright, what is there to fear? We know the truth ourselves.” “That isn't the point. Any appearance of impropriety must be avoided,” Hu replied. “I'll ask Zhou to take you home tomorrow. If you grow bored after a couple of days in the country, you can return to the Pans', or even come to Shanghai for a visit. As far as I'm concerned, from this moment I regard you as a concubine of the He household.” His words built a fence between them. Both suddenly felt obliged to observe propriety; their speech and manner grew polite, and distant.

Such restraint made their company uncomfortable. “Go back to the Pans',” Hu said. “I'll take you.” “And what will you do?” “I...” At a loss, he answered vaguely, “I'll look round the city.” She wanted very much to offer to walk with him, but her new position as “a concubine of the He household” made the words difficult to utter. Unable to express her concern, she hesitated. “Well? Let's go before it gets late.” “No hurry. I'll sit a little longer.” Sitting silently was dull, so she found something to talk about: Suzhou's gentry families. From the wealthy Pans they passed to the distinguished Pans, and from them to first-place examination graduates and chief ministers. Suzhou produced great officials in abundance; the subject could go on forever. As dusk approached, Hu felt that calling on the Pans after nightfall would be inappropriate and urged her to enter the city. He escorted her there, arranged to meet the following day, and took his leave without disturbing the host.

Having dismissed his chair, Hu wandered on foot. He reached Guanqian and passed an inn just as a sedan chair stopped before it. A man got out whose back looked familiar. Hu stared for a moment, then called in delight, “Elder Brother! Elder Brother!” The man stopped and turned. Now Hu could see clearly: it was indeed Ji Heling. “What a surprise!” Ji was equally pleased. “To meet here! What brings you to Suzhou?” “I was going to ask you the same thing. Why are you here?” “Making arrangements for this year's sea transport. I've been here several days.” “Then haven't you heard about the disturbances in the Hangzhou brotherhood?” “I have. It isn't my responsibility, but it concerns sea transport all the same, and I've been very anxious. My official business isn't finished, so I can't get away.” Ji asked, “How did you hear of it?” “This is no place to talk. Where are your rooms?” “Oh, this way.” Ji led him to his quarters, which also had a small courtyard. Someone came out to open the door, and Hu was taken aback to find a young woman. “This is Mr Hu, my sworn brother.” “Mr Hu!” Smiling, she welcomed him. “Please come inside.” Unsure how to address her, he merely nodded vaguely, though his eyes remained on her. She seemed not yet twenty, wearing a pale moon-white satin lined jacket beneath a long black satin waistcoat, with loose trousers and unbound feet. A long, glossy black braid hung down her back. Her appearance suggested a maid in plain dress, but her speech and conduct were dignified and composed, quite unlike a servant's. He could not make her out.

Ji ought properly to have introduced her, but said nothing. Hu grew more puzzled. Unable to ask in her presence, he could only speak of the brotherhood's disturbances and Wang Youling's appeal for help. “Good! With You to mediate, everything should be all right.” Ji was deeply relieved. “Now I can stop worrying. But what brought you to Suzhou?” “A long story.” Hu rose. “Come, Elder Brother. Let's eat out and talk over dinner.” Ji readily agreed. “But first, there's one arrangement to make. Why don't you move here and stay with me?” “I'll stay here tonight, but there's no need to move my luggage. I meant to leave tomorrow. Since you're here, I'll stay another day. The day after that I'll board outside Chang Gate, so it's better to leave things where they are.” “Very well. I'll have someone find you a room.” Ji summoned his newly engaged attendant, Changqing, and told him to ask at the inn’s desk for a clean, superior room. Afraid Zhou might return and be unable to find him, Hu also asked Changqing to make a special trip to Jinchang Inn and explain his whereabouts. These arrangements made, they went out together. Yuandachang was only a few steps away. Choosing a secluded corner, they sat over their wine while Hu related the full story of his visit. “You're just like the Old Man under the Moon whom people worship by your West Lake!” Ji laughed. “Always arranging happy matches.” “This is one good deed I have to do. A’qiao's heart has already changed. Why should I insist on keeping her? As for Commissioner He, it's entirely a business calculation—placing a bet, you might say. If I win, everyone benefits.” Ji understood that “everyone” included himself and Wang, and felt more strongly than ever that Hu was a friend worth having. Yet he was a man of some learning, and did not consider obtaining influence through a woman's relationship particularly honourable. He therefore offered no comment.

“Now tell me about the woman in your rooms,” Hu said. “What's the story?” Ji smiled. “What do you think it is?” “How could I guess? Tell me yourself.” “She's Ruiyun's younger cousin. She married in Changshu and was widowed last year. Her parents-in-law wouldn't have her, so she wrote to Ruiyun asking to come and depend on her. Ruiyun asked what I thought. Surely I'm not so mean that I begrudge feeding one idle person? I took the opportunity of this official journey to Suzhou to arrange to bring her back to Hangzhou.” “What a pity!” Hu said with deep regret. “Widowed so young.” His evident sympathy for the young woman gave Ji an idea, but he immediately checked himself. Better not meddle. He merely nodded. “Naturally, she'll marry again eventually. If you know a suitable man—someone like Chen Shilong, for instance—do keep her in mind.” “Certainly.” Hu's answer was earnest. “I'll find someone for her.”

That subject passed, and Ji asked about public affairs. “How are things in Shanghai?” “The Small Swords Society amounts to little by itself, but the foreigners are behind it. I'm afraid the county town won't be recovered soon. The longer things remain as they are, the more the foreigners benefit.” “How?” Ji had lately become very interested in foreign affairs. Looking hard at Hu, he said, “Explain your reasoning.” “First, the settlement was originally waste ground. Land without people is useless. Now the disorder has driven everyone to seek refuge there. People create a market; as trade flourishes, the foreigners' revenues increase. Second, both sides want to win them over. While the snipe and clam struggle, the fisherman profits. The foreigners are happy to manipulate matters between them.” “In what way?” “They speak as men to men and as ghosts to ghosts. If you want their help, you must first do business with them. Governor-General Yiliang of Liangjiang has now decided to cut off their supplies. I don't think that policy can last.” Hu went on to relate many strange stories involving foreigners in the settlement. They made excellent entertainment over wine for Ji and taught him a good deal. Yet he felt that Hu too had certain prejudices. The foreigners were shrewd, but their shrewdness rested on reason. If one had reason on one's side, negotiations need not be difficult. The worst obstacles were one's own suspicions or insistence on preserving the empty prestige of the “great Celestial Empire.” The foreigners wanted a plain, sincere statement, while one's own side kept putting them off with evasions.
