Under those conditions agreement would never be possible. These ideas, however, remained untested. Moreover, prevailing opinion favoured round abuse of foreigners. Anyone who offered a fair-minded word was certain to be denounced by the guardians of orthodoxy for failing to distinguish Chinese civilisation from the foreign barbarians, perhaps even accused of taking a thief for his father or being a traitor. Ji therefore hesitated to express his view openly, even to so close a friend as Hu.

They turned to Zhejiang's political affairs. Ji too thought Huang Zonghan's transfer was merely a matter of time. The clearest sign was Huang's own preparation for departure. He was not only pressing hard for the customary unofficial payments and benefits that fell to him, but reaching out for gains that should not have been his at all. These were the signs of a man ready to pack his bags at any moment. “Then, Elder Brother, do you think Commissioner He has a chance of going to Zhejiang?” Hu asked with concern. “How could we know? There's no need to worry about it now.” Hu frankly explained his particular interest. After this Shanghai silk business, banking would remain the foundation of his enterprises. That principle was settled. Yet Shanghai's prospects were so brilliant that he was reluctant to abandon it. His idea was that influence among officials and foreigners would strengthen his influence in commerce. If He Guiqing became governor of Zhejiang, Wang's old connection with him, added to Hu's own immediate rapport with him in Suzhou, would give them unrivalled official support. Whatever business he attempted, whether moving capital or passing checkpoints, all would go smoothly. “That's why I must judge which way the wind is blowing and prepare early. If there's no hope of He's appointment to Zhejiang, I must reduce my operations and proceed steadily, securing each step. If the appointment is reliable, I have plenty more plans to bring out. Otherwise, wouldn't I be mad to leave so much business waiting in Shanghai and Hangzhou and come to Suzhou to deal with men like Xiaogouzi?” At this, Ji naturally felt bound to consider the matter seriously. He nodded without answering and thought carefully over his wine.

“I think there's a chance,” Ji began with a conclusion that pleased Hu. “Their yiwei examination class keeps in close touch and stands firmly together. Once they secure a provincial post, they don't easily let it go. Zhang Fu, the governor of Jiangxi, headed the second class in their yiwei palace examination and was one of Muzhang’a's ‘Ten Disciples.’ He was dismissed in the first month of this year. Last month they promptly put forward another classmate, Zheng Dunjin, to become governor of Henan. Both the present governors of Jiangsu and Zhejiang belong to that class. I hear Governor Xu in Jiangsu has lost imperial favour; there have long been reports that he'll be moved. If Governor Huang goes too, they'll lose two important territories at once and naturally seek to recover elsewhere what they've lost. Looked at that way, He's succession in Zhejiang is very possible. There's another consideration: this gentleman would also like one of his own people to follow him.” Dipping his chopstick in wine, Ji wrote the surname Huang on the table. He meant Huang Zonghan. “What makes you think so?” Hu was listening intently. “For the same reason that I succeeded Mr Xuexuan at the Sea Transport Bureau.” “Ah! One word wakes a dreamer!” Hu understood at once. After a moment's thought, he struck the table. “It's more than a chance. It's practically certain.”

He went on to develop the argument further. Huang Zonghan was calculating and devious. Though currently in favour, he had plenty of enemies. With so many things amiss in his administration of Zhejiang, he must worry about who would succeed him. Officials protecting one another was a practice common to all eighteen provinces. A successor generally did his best to cover his predecessor's mistakes. It was not unusual for a popular official's deficits to be cleared by his successor at a superior's instruction. There were only two exceptions: where the successor's own interests conflicted with such protection, or where an old enmity offered a chance for revenge. It was the latter that Huang had to fear. Though Zhejiang fell under the governor-general of Fujian and Zhejiang, that official resided in Fuzhou. Zhejiang's governor was in every real sense the province's highest authority. If his successor discovered a fault, he could impeach him in a direct memorial without consulting the governor-general. There would be no room for anyone to soften the blow. Huang therefore had to find a friend to succeed him, and his friendship with He was beyond question. “Yes. My view is much the same,” Ji agreed. “But if the court means to give He an important post,” Hu objected, “and Governor Xu is to leave Jiangsu, why not appoint He there? He knows the province. Wouldn't that be the natural arrangement?” “No, for two reasons. First, He has often submitted memorials about military affairs in Jiangsu, with remarks that reflect badly on Governor Xu. As members of the same examination class, they must avoid any appearance of disloyalty. Even if the court appointed him, He would fear being accused of writing those memorials in order to replace Xu, and would certainly refuse.” Ji drank, then continued. “Second, the governor of Jiangsu must command troops in battle. Military merit counts for most at present. Ji’erhang’a, the provincial treasurer, is working hard against the Small Swords in Shanghai. In my view, if Xu is transferred, Ji’erhang’a will probably succeed him.” This analysis reassured Hu still further. He now felt sure that He Guiqing would become governor of Zhejiang; only the timing remained uncertain. A delay would disadvantage Hu but help Ji, for it would mean He first serving a term as granary vice-minister. When Ji's sea-transported tribute grain was inspected at Tongzhou, he could then enjoy considerable assistance.

Having worked through all this, Hu felt that either course would benefit them. His appetite for both wine and conversation increased, and he drank until thoroughly drunk before returning with Ji to the inn. The next morning an attendant told him that Ji had gone out early to pay calls, leaving word that he would certainly be back at noon and wanted Hu to wait. Sitting alone was tedious. Hu also needed news from Zhou and had to see A’qiao, so he decided to return to Jinchang Inn, leaving a message that he would visit Ji again that afternoon. Before going out through Chang Gate, he called on A’qiao, briefly explained what had happened, and said he must stay another day. This was good news to her. She decided to go straight to Mudu and bring her brother to meet him. “Good. We might as well settle everything. But you can't manage it alone. When Zhou returns, I'll ask him to take the trouble of going to Mudu once more and accompany you. You should meet my sworn elder brother too.” A’qiao therefore went back with him to Jinchang Inn, carrying a large bundle of clothes. Some were gifts from her friend; others had been newly made during the past two days. The Pans kept a cutting table set up all year and employed two seamstresses by the day. Except during the three great festivals, they made new clothes every day. Being so close to the source was wonderfully convenient. Naturally, A’qiao knew Hu's temper and would not wear before him clothes that were in fact brand-new but counted as second-hand because her friend had given them to her. Her newly made garments were less fashionable than those of the foreign settlement, but they had the virtue of dignity. She changed her hair and ornaments to match, abandoning elaborate cosmetics, dressing her hair to a smooth shine, and wearing only a green jade hairpin in the bun and pearl earrings. No stranger seeing her could have detected a trace of the pleasure quarters.

Just as she had finished dressing at Jinchang Inn and was preparing to accompany Hu to see Ji after lunch, their intended host arrived instead. Hu introduced them. A’qiao's manner was so respectful that Ji took a strong liking to her and praised her warmly to her face. Once she had withdrawn to the inner room, he could not hold back. “Xueyan, I know a little of the Liuzhuang method of reading faces. This beauty past her first youth has considerable good fortune ahead.” “Then I'm doing the right thing.” Hu smiled. “Watch her walk: her skirt scarcely moves. She's so composed, she looks like a great official's lady.” “Otherwise...” Ji stopped abruptly. “Why don't you finish?” Hu could not resist asking. “There's a great deal behind that ‘otherwise.’” After a long pause, Ji waved his hand. “Never mind. Saying it would only unsettle you. In any case, what you lose at sunrise you regain at sunset. It makes little difference.” Hu understood the expression. Giving up A’qiao was a pity, but there would be compensation, naturally through He Guiqing. Because Ji put it that way, Hu began to take those future compensations especially seriously. The autumn harvest depended on spring cultivation. From this moment, he felt, he must make fresh efforts with He. After considering, he changed the subject, though it still concerned He and A’qiao.

“Elder Brother, there's something I meant to ask. I'd like you to write a letter for me.” “To whom?” “Commissioner He. It must be beautifully written, preferably in the four-and-six style...” “How did you think of that?” Ji interrupted with a laugh. “You're setting me an examination. Parallel prose requires reference books. To put it bluntly, one assembles a composition from quotations like an otter laying out its catch. Where am I to find something like the Peiwen Treasury of Rhymes while travelling?” Hu did not understand the explanation, but guessed that he had asked something difficult. He knew that not everyone could compose those elegantly balanced four- and six-character phrases, and regretted having embarrassed Ji by proposing it so casually. Seeing his thoughts, Ji hastened to change his tone. “Never mind. Since it's for you, I'll have to make an attempt. Tell me what you want to say.” Hu was delighted. “First, thank him, naturally with the customary expressions of admiration. Second, explain that A’qiao is staying with the Pans, that I owe them a debt, and ask him to thank them on my behalf.” “Third,” Ji added with a smile, “ask him to take care of the lady.” “That's what I have in mind, but I don't know how to put it.” “I do,” Ji said confidently. “I'll find a couple of allusions to hint discreetly at the meaning.” “Exactly.” Hu spoke with admiration and a touch of regret. “Your brush is a formidable thing. At school as a boy, I remember reading two lines: ‘Others carry treasured swords; my brush is like a blade.’ I used to wonder how a writing brush could be more powerful than a sword. Now I understand the words carved on some brushes: ‘Sweep away a thousand armies.’ They're perfectly true.”

“Not quite so formidable.” This reminded Ji of something Hu lacked. “I've wanted to tell you something for a long time. With your present responsibilities, you really must make proper use of several people. However fine the peony, it needs green leaves to support it. Relying on yourself alone, even with three heads and six arms, there will be times when you can't be everywhere.” The remark touched exactly the point troubling Hu. Slapping his thigh, he exclaimed, “Precisely! I've long meant to ask your advice. I've made plans too. I want two men: one to represent me in social dealings—I have him already, Liu Bucai—and another to handle my writing. There's a man surnamed Huang in Huzhou who was to come to Hangzhou with me, but other circumstances ended that plan. I don't think his abilities are very great, either. What I want to discuss with you...” He struggled to express himself. “I still don't really know how to use such people.” Ji pictured Hu's circumstances and saw his difficulty clearly. He began with the broader point. “To speak frankly, you've read too little to know how to expand your establishment. Money alone is no use. You need people. It doesn't matter if you lack knowledge yourself, provided you respect those who have it. It doesn't matter if the people you employ lack ability, either. Once you're known to welcome men, capable ones will naturally come to your door.” From the story of paying a thousand in gold for a horse's bones, Ji went on to Lord Mengchang's retainers, the imitator of a cock's crow and the petty thief. Hu listened with mounting excitement and found inspiration everywhere. When Ji finished, he exclaimed in admiration, feeling that an obstruction in his mind had suddenly cleared.

“I understand!” Hu nodded repeatedly. “Rushing about like this is no way to carry on. I must find a spacious, comfortable place and support a group of men with nothing particular to do. If they do nothing for three years, never mind. One useful act may be worth three years of their upkeep.” “Now you truly understand,” Ji said with deep satisfaction. “That's what household retainers are. The salt merchants of Yangzhou preserve much of Lord Mengchang's tradition. You might take notice of them.” Hu did not answer. He calculated carefully for a long time, then sprang to his feet. “That's settled. When I return, I'm changing my methods.” “How?” “Employ people!” Hu clapped his hands. “I'll stay at headquarters and go out myself only when there's no alternative.” “Exactly. Only then can your establishment grow. I'll help you.” “Naturally. You're my Zhuge Liang.” “I don't deserve that.” Ji laughed, then seemed a little uneasy. “You're expansive by nature. Keep some limits in mind when following my advice. If you suddenly spread yourself too widely and can't sustain it, that will be far from what I intended.” “Don't worry, Elder Brother.” Only now did Hu feel he had the advantage over Ji. “So long as we're talking about moving sums within a few hundred thousand taels, there will be no trouble.” “As long as you're sure.” Ji rose. “I'll go back and write that letter for you as soon as I can.” “Have you an engagement, or calls to make?” “Neither.” “Then why not begin here?”

Hearing them, A’qiao came out too and urged Ji to stay for a simple meal. There was nothing objectionable about that, and he agreed. “Don't prepare too many dishes,” he said. “There's only one thing I want. Is there a Lugaojian shop nearby?” “They're everywhere. I'll send someone for pork in soy sauce.” “Not the pork. I want the stuff they use to seal the pot while they cook it.” When a great cauldron of pork was ready to simmer over a low fire, strips of noodle dough were used to seal the lid, keeping the steam and flavour in. The dough was edible, but hardly fit for a distinguished table. A’qiao laughed. “They sell that to beggars!” “Never mind,” Hu put in, knowing Ji's ways. “Just send someone to buy it.” The conversation turned to Lugaojian. Hu and Ji shared the same puzzle: why did all Suzhou's shops selling pork in soy sauce and other cooked meats use that name? Were they branches belonging to one proprietor, or like the Xiaoquan scissors shop in Hangzhou, with only one genuine establishment and all the others imitations? “Most are imitations, of course,” A’qiao said. “But why Lugaojian? What a curious name. There must be a story behind it.”

“There is.” With perfect seriousness, A’qiao told the legend. An ancestor of the Lu family had begun with a little shop selling pork in soy sauce. A beggar came every day, and the owner, a kindly, generous man, always took up his knife and cut him a large piece of meat. Eventually the beggar began sleeping beneath the family's eaves. One day he suddenly disappeared, leaving only a ragged straw mat. It lay discarded in a corner, and nobody paid it any attention. Once, when a batch of meat was almost ready, the owner found that it needed one fierce burst of heat to finish it. The best fuel would be straw, which Suzhou people called “rice firewood”, but none could be found at the moment. The old mat came conveniently to hand. Who could have guessed that burning it would send the aroma of the pork drifting for several li? Business prospered from then on. To remember the origin of their good fortune, they named the shop Lugaojian: Lu's Straw Mat. “Gao means grain stalks,” Ji observed. “A learned man must have chosen the name. But I still don't understand why the mat made the aroma of the pork travel for several li.” “Naturally, it carried an immortal's influence. That wasn't a real beggar. It was Lü Dongbin come down to earth.” “So Immortal Lü was amusing himself among mortals.” “Nonsense!” Hu laughed. “Whenever someone prospers, there's always a fantastic story about him. It's the same when a business succeeds.”

“To inspire such a wildly improbable tale would itself be something to be proud of,” Ji replied. “May future generations tell many strange stories about Hu Xueyan.” “I don't want fame after death,” Hu answered casually. “I want it while I'm alive. If one day Fukang signs are as common everywhere as Lugaojian signs in Suzhou, I shan't have lived for nothing.” “That isn't impossible. It depends on whether you can set yourself the ambition.” Ji was encouraging his sworn brother. Hu replied without thinking, “The resolve is mine; success rests with others.” “Well said!” Ji was full of admiration. “Xueyan, your words are truly extraordinary.” “Don't flatter me, Elder Brother,” Hu said, pleased despite his modest reply. “It isn't flattery. Those two phrases show real understanding. The old saying is, ‘Man makes the plans, but Heaven determines success.’ What sort of man cannot command his own fate? Your way is right: first beware of lacking ambition, then of lacking the right men.” Hu's face grew hot. He felt that he did not deserve this praise. What he had meant was little different from leaving success to Heaven: whether things worked out depended on other people. Ji had interpreted “rests with others” as “finding the right people”. That had not been Hu's intention, though the interpretation was certainly wiser than his own meaning.

“To have ambition without knowing how to recognize and employ people is what we call ‘great ambition and little ability’. Such a man is born to suffer,” Ji continued. “When unsuccessful, he thinks his genius has been buried and is full of grievances. If chance brings him a great opportunity and he rises high, things become worse.” Listening intently, Hu could not help exclaiming, “Why should that be?” “Because the higher he climbs, the harder he falls. He has risen through chance, or because someone deliberately raised him up. Holding the place once he's been put there is no easy matter. When he tumbles, even if he doesn't lose his life, he'll be badly battered. A man whose ambitions exceed his abilities suffers whatever happens. Look through history: many heroes from humble beginnings became kings and emperors when circumstance favoured them, only to wake from their brief dream and lose their lives. Most came to grief through precisely that failing.” Hu understood and learned a great deal. Every long talk with Ji left him feeling enriched and deeply aware of the pleasures of friendship. Yet this pleasure differed greatly from what he felt with Yu Si, You Laowu, or even Wang Youling. “To tell the truth, my understanding falls far short of yours,” he said with complete sincerity. “A man really ought to read.” “‘Understanding the world is learning too.’ A man who rises through memorizing books and writing eight-legged essays may be worth less than an illiterate who understands people and their affairs.” “Now you're airing a grievance again!” Hu knew that officials who had passed the examinations looked down on men who had purchased rank, but able men among the latter equally despised bookish fools among the former. “Call it a grievance or call it the truth. Either will do.”

“Then let me say something truthful—and entirely serious.” A thought had occurred to Hu. “Elder Brother, do you still intend to sit the examinations?” Ji was a licentiate, commonly called a xiucai, so this meant the provincial examination. Naturally, he had considered it. “It isn't so easy. I waited for employment for years and have only just obtained a post. If I resign to take the provincial examination, even if luck favours me, there's still the metropolitan examination. Where would the money come from?” “Why worry about that? Leave it all to me.” “Given our friendship, if I truly had the ambition to try my fortunes in the autumn examination, I should have to trouble you. But when I consider it, there seems little point.” “Why? This year is jiayin; next year, yimao, is the year of the great examination. There's more than a year to prepare. You could study properly.” Ji had long abandoned the idea and shook his head. “In troubled times, a man can win distinction anywhere. Why must he seek his standing in an examination hall? The greater the disorder, the more opportunities there are. I imagine you understand why better than I do.” This was another revelation. Hu saw that it was true. All his business had been connected with the state of the country. In a peaceful, prosperous age, he might not have done so well. Thinking further, he realized that peace would have given his ability to adapt no occasion to show itself. He might simply have led an ordinary life and rotted away like grass and trees. “Only troubled times bring out men of talent!” he exclaimed. “Others have said that too.” Ji sounded approving. “In five thousand years of history, talent flourished most at the end of Qin and beginning of Han, and when Wei, Shu and Wu divided the empire. Those were troubled times.” “And now? This too is an age of disorder. I wonder how many men of talent later generations will find in it.” “Not a few. To speak only of the present, don't undervalue yourself, Xueyan. You're a rare talent yourself.”

Hu smiled without answering. Just then A’qiao came to call them to the meal. The dishes ordered from a restaurant were plentiful, with a large platter of Lugaojian pork besides. Naturally, the humble food unfit for grand tables was there too. “Come and eat with us,” Hu told her. “There isn't any rule permitting that.” She declined with a smile. “There are no outsiders here,” Ji put in. “It's the first visit to Suzhou for both of us. We want you to tell us about its people and customs.” Further ceremony would now seem unfriendly. A’qiao reflected that she would have to attend to the table in any case. Standing would be awkward; better sit. She therefore took a place at the side, pouring wine and serving dishes as hostess while talking with Ji about everyday matters. Suzhou women were skilled in conversation, and she had experience besides. Her tactful words and pleasant voice increased Ji's liking for her. The meal consequently lasted a long time, ending only after four. No sooner had Ji left than Zhou Yiming arrived. The negotiations over A’qiao's affairs had gone smoothly. Only payment remained before the transaction could be completed. “Congratulations!” Hu said to her with a smile. “You've thrown off your fetters.” “Thank you for all your trouble, Mr Zhou.” After thanking him, she added apologetically, “I'm afraid I shall need your help again tomorrow.” Hu explained that Zhou was to accompany her to Mudu once more and bring out her younger brother. Naturally, he agreed without hesitation.

By the time they had discussed everything, it was supper time. Hu asked Zhou to stay and eat. He himself drank tea to keep him company, chatting while privately considering a plan. When he had made up his mind, he asked casually, “Old Zhou, have you ever imagined what your life would be like if you prospered?” Zhou had no answer ready. “I've never thought about it,” he replied frankly. “I get through one day at a time.” “Surely you've thought about what sort of official you might become, or what sort of wife you'd marry?” “I have a wife at home. She came to our family as a child, and she's two years older than me. A very good woman. I've always wanted to bring her here, but never managed it.” “There must be a reason. Why haven't you managed?” “Isn't it easy enough to see? It all comes down to money.” Zhou spoke with deep feeling. “These last two years, I've barely managed on my own, running errands for people and unable to settle anywhere. I daren't do anything so rash.” “What would have to change before you could bring her?” Zhou's expression brightened. “Now there's hope, thanks to your help. If I get a post in Yangzhou with a dependable income of two hundred taels a year, I'll send for her and let her enjoy a few peaceful days.” “That isn't much. In my view, a man like you ought to have at least fifty taels a month to be properly valued.” “Where could I find such good fortune? If anyone gave me that, I'd serve him faithfully for the rest of my life.”

“Do you mean that?” Zhou had spoken without thinking, but now he saw that Hu looked quite serious and dared not answer carelessly. “We're only chatting,” Hu said in a gentler tone. “There's no obligation.” Even so, Zhou had to consider it carefully. He could not quite tell what Hu intended. “If you wanted me, sir, I'd naturally be willing.” “That's not what I mean.” Hu waved his hand. “I don't like anyone to work for me out of obligation.” “I mean it. Working for you is a real pleasure. Never mind fifty taels a month—I'd be delighted with half.” Seeing his sincerity, Hu explained his intention. After that day's long conversation with Ji, he had decided to employ Zhou. He proposed an annual salary of six hundred taels, with a further bonus at year's end according to the profits. Zhou should think it over carefully before answering. If he preferred to go to Yangzhou, Hu would understand: a post at a lijin station did, after all, make a man part of officialdom. “Who wants that kind of official standing? I needn't think it over. I can tell you now: I shall do whatever you ask.” “Excellent!” Hu said gladly. “From now on, you're one of our own.”

The new relationship made Zhou more constrained rather than less. He could no longer sit there drinking by himself and hurried through his meal. After clearing the table himself, he asked about A’qiao's journey the next day. “I'm entrusting her to you. Once the document has been drawn up tomorrow, accompany her to Mudu. When everything is settled, bring her brother to Shanghai. I'll write down my addresses there and in Hangzhou for you.” Hearing this, A’qiao came over. “And what about you?” “I'll see what Elder Brother Ji wants. I'll spend another day with him tomorrow, and I really ought to leave early the day after. With Old Zhou to look after you, you can take your time and stay a few extra days in Mudu. If anything comes up afterwards, I'll send him to make arrangements with you. In short, once you've escorted the Buddha, you must see him all the way to the Western Paradise. I won't consider this great business finished until you're properly settled.” First, Zhou was present, and A’qiao did not want an outsider to glimpse the private understanding between her and Hu. Second, her view of Hu had changed again during the past two or three days. She therefore made her attitude clear. “What's all this about escorting the Buddha to the Western Paradise? I don't understand!”

Whether she truly failed to understand or only pretended, she plainly did not welcome his well-meant promise to see everything through. Hu too realized that his words had been a little indiscreet and wisely dropped the subject. He turned to Zhou. “Go home early. If you have any unfinished business of your own, clear it up as soon as possible. There's something I ought to tell you now. In my work, we have to move quickly. There may be nothing to do for ten days or a fortnight, but once something comes up, we act at once. To say something that may sound unreasonable, there may not even be time for you to go home and tell your family. Naturally, I'll look after them. Whatever difficulty arises, however great, I'll settle it. Anyone I send out on business—to put it in a literary phrase—will have no worries about those left behind. Remember that when you work for me.” “Your Honour...” “Wait!” Hu cut him off. “We must change how you address me. I bought this ‘Your Honour’ with silver. I'm not a real magistrate presiding over cases in court. If a stranger chooses to address me that way, I may feel undeserving, but I do have a board certificate and count as an official of sorts. The court's established forms must be respected, so to insist on refusing the title would be discourteous. In business, we have no first or second official masters, only first or second proprietors. Yet I don't like dividing people into employers and employees either. I have two other ‘friends’, Liu Qingsheng and Chen Shilong, both able assistants. They call me Mr Hu. Do the same. There are other things you can teach me; but in business, if I may boast, you must learn from me. Think of the title xiansheng, ‘Mr’, in its other sense: your teacher in business.” “Oh, dear!” A’qiao frowned in mock distress, with the beguiling petulance of a Suzhou woman. “What a lot of words!” Zhou answered seriously. “Many words, but every one useful. Mr Hu, I am ready for your instructions.” “Then it's settled. Come early tomorrow.”

Just as Zhou was about to leave, an inn servant brought in someone A’qiao recognized: an attendant from the Pan household. “That's Pan Fu,” she told Hu after seeing him through the window. “I wonder why he's come. If it's anything to do with me, don't agree too readily.” She gave him a gentle push. Hu received the man in the outer room. After paying his respects, Pan Fu took a plum-red invitation from his card case and presented it. Pan Shuya, signing himself Hu's humble younger friend and pupil, invited him to lunch the next day. He had added an emphatic request: “Do please honour me by coming.” This was unexpected. Pan was a young master through and through, reluctant to bother with people who did not concern him. For that reason, on his several recent visits to the house, Hu had not asked to see its master. Such a sudden invitation must have a purpose, and Hu naturally asked what it was. “Nothing but admiration for you, sir,” Pan Fu replied. “No other guests have been invited. My master especially wishes to entertain you alone.” Hu could not imagine what Pan intended, but there was no need to puzzle over it now. He would learn at lunch. He took a reply card, confirmed that he would attend and asked Pan Fu to convey his thanks. “My master also asked whether you'll remain here tomorrow morning or go elsewhere. Please let us know where to send the chair.” “Probably here, but there's no need to send one.” “He insists. Without it, he says, he would not be showing proper respect.” In that case, further refusals were unnecessary. After Pan Fu left, Hu and A’qiao discussed the invitation. They agreed that the emphatic request and the offer of a chair must mean Pan had an important favour to ask. Even A’qiao, who had stayed in the house for several days, could not guess what it was.

“Never mind,” Hu said. “Let Old Zhou accompany you into the city. Sound out the Pan mistress while you're there, and find some way to let me know before I meet him tomorrow.” A’qiao still seemed reluctant to leave, but could say little in Zhou's presence. At last she hired a chair and went into the city. The night passed without incident. Early the next morning, Hu went in for a stroll. Ji was out, so he returned quietly to Jinchang Inn without disturbing Ruiyun's cousin. Just after eleven, the chair from the Pans arrived. It was a grand official chair. On inquiry, Hu learned that soon after Pan's birth, his father had followed the example of the Yangzhou salt merchants and spent twenty thousand taels to buy him the rank of circuit intendant. As a third-rank official, he was entitled to a large chair covered in green woollen cloth. He could even have mounted outriders, though he had not adopted that part of the official display. The chair itself was splendid: glass windows on three sides with coloured silk curtains, bright tassels along the eaves, and brass-covered poles polished to a shine. Inside were a covered tea bowl, fruit, snacks, a water pipe and two novels, Flower Shadows Behind the Curtain and An Old Rustic's Unvarnished Words. On a long journey, there would be no lack of diversion.

Hu had never ridden in such a large chair before. Watching the four bearers, he remembered one of Ji's jokes. Each man, Ji said, could be described in four characters. The first held his head high: “head up, spirits lifted”. The second “dared not let wind”, since he was directly in front of the gentleman, who would suffer the first blast. Of the two behind, the nearer man's view was blocked by the chair: he “couldn't tell east from west”. The last simply followed every step: “no ideas of his own”. The Grand Councillors were said to be much the same. Their leader naturally held his head high. Since he alone customarily spoke during an imperial audience, the second dared not let wind. The third was new to the council and still ignorant of its workings; not knowing east from west described him perfectly. The last, commonly called the “curtain-lifting Grand Councillor”, naturally had no ideas of his own. This brought Hu's thoughts to Peng Yunzhang, He's fellow graduate and a Grand Councillor. Where did he stand? If he was the one who dared not let wind, how could he speak on He's behalf? Hu must ask He about it when an opportunity arose.

While his thoughts wandered in this fashion, they reached the Pan house. The chair was carried right up to the eaves of the great hall. Only then did Hu discover that Pan Fu's words were unreliable: besides the host, two other guests were present, both dressed like wealthy young gentlemen. After host and guest exchanged bows, Pan made the introductions. Hu had guessed correctly. One was Wu Jizhong, the other Lu Zhixiang. Both came from distinguished families, with fathers and elder brothers holding posts in the capital; both were themselves licentiates. They exchanged the customary expressions of long-standing admiration, and Pan led them into the garden. It was large, but the buildings looked old. Only a boat-shaped pavilion of nanmu timber was new, and it was here that Pan entertained them. Male servants waited outside. Within, two maids attended them, exemplifying the prettiness of Suzhou girls: matching cotton tunics trimmed with patterned borders, loose-legged trousers, tightly drawn waists, glossy braids and nails dyed bright red. Their voices were as clear as orioles'. Pan, Wu and Lu were all “Young Master”; Hu alone was “Master Hu”. At noon, the meal was served in the pavilion. Pan offered Hu the seat of honour and forestalled his refusal. Hu was the only guest, he explained. Wu and Lu were not even fellow guests invited to keep him company. The three were jointly his hosts, and had something to consult him about. Pan Fu's words had been correct after all.

Hu had already expected a request. After three rounds of wine, he asked first, and Pan explained the circumstances. It had begun with A’qiao's conversation. While passing idle hours with the Pan mistress in the women's quarters, she had entertained her with stories heard from You Laowu, Second Miss and Hu himself. His adventures were unusual enough, and A’qiao's eloquence and vivid embellishments made them especially absorbing. The mistress was fascinated. The stories then travelled by way of the pillow to Pan's ears, changing his view of Hu entirely. Young men of privilege never chose ordinary, upright gentlemen as friends. They wanted “interesting” people: brilliant talkers, striking figures or men who handled affairs with style. Hu seemed to Pan precisely such a man. What impressed him most, however, was Hu's loyalty to his friends. For that reason, he had an important favour to ask. “Brother Hu, Suzhou has never been so unsettled. The government troops do more to disturb the people than to protect them. All three of us would like to see the foreign settlement in Shanghai, and we'd like you to look after us.” “Certainly,” Hu answered calmly. He supposed this meant such small matters as buying houses. “Gladly. Leave it all to me.” “This is what I have in mind. I have some ready money to entrust to you. What could you put it into? It isn't a great sum—about a hundred and twenty or a hundred and thirty thousand taels.”

A hundred and twenty or a hundred and thirty thousand, and he called it a small sum! What an expansive way of talking. Hu was about to answer when Wu spoke first. “My situation is much the same as Shuya's. I have a hundred thousand taels and would also like you to take the trouble to employ them for me.” “Mine is a little different,” Lu said. “I have a chest of things I'm uneasy about leaving in Suzhou. Could you advise me where to put it safely?” “What sort of things?” “A chest of paintings.” “The Lu family's collection is famous,” Pan explained. “Some of its finest pieces have been handed down since the Ming.” That alone showed how precious the chest must be. Hu dared not answer lightly. He merely nodded. “We can discuss it further.” “Discuss it” was an evasion. He had already decided against such a thankless burden. A thankless burden alone might be tolerable; the real danger was that something could go wrong. Antiques and ancient paintings could not be replaced with identical objects. It was a prudent decision.

Lu, however, wanted Hu to guarantee the paintings' safety during their removal from the endangered city to the settlement under foreign protection. He therefore mentioned You Laowu. “I hear you are a close friend of the leaders of the grain-transport brotherhood?” There was no denying this, nor any need to. “Yes. Both generations of leaders in Songjiang think well of me.” It occurred to Hu that Lu must want You's help. He might as well be generous without waiting to be asked. “If there's anything you need, so long as it's within my power, I can intercede.” “Yes, that's what I should like you to do.” They went on to talk at length about the Songjiang brotherhood's influence, leaving their immediate business aside. As Hu maintained the conversation, he observed the three men calmly. He soon understood that their wish to move to Shanghai arose half from fear of war and half from longing for the settlement's prosperity. The first thing to arrange for them there would therefore be a house for each. The plans quickly took shape in his mind: Western houses with all manner of imported furnishings—soft sofas, great dining tables, and fireplaces burning coal or wood. This also suggested a way to make Pan's and Wu's money productive. It would mean flying the kite far out on a long line; if they expected quick gains, there was nothing to discuss. If they took a long view, it could greatly assist his own business too. With two hundred thousand taels available for a long period, why not open another bank in Shanghai? Only then did he realize what an excellent opportunity he had found. He thought it through carefully, then waited for a pause in the conversation. “There's something I'd like to ask.”

“Of course. Please do.” “You both honour me with your confidence, and I must do my best. But you must have some intention for this money. Is it for trade or for lending at interest? If the latter, for a long term or a short one? I need to know your general purpose before I can act.” Pan glanced at Wu, seeking his view. Wu spoke only for himself. “Brother Hu, I don't know what I should do. I can only tell you my thoughts. If we have to flee, our income in Suzhou will stop. We shan't be able to collect the rent rice from our fields. Who knows whether our shop properties will even survive, let alone yield rent? In that case, all eighteen members of my household will depend on this money for their living. That's the truth. Please act accordingly.” “Mine is much the same,” Pan said. “There are only thirteen in my own household, but a great many in my clan. If they all flee to Shanghai and cannot maintain themselves, I'll have to help.” “I understand. If Suzhou falls, who can say when it will be recovered? Six months or a year, three years or five—nobody knows. Since this money must support you in exile, it must provide a steady stream. Security comes first.” “A steady stream—exactly!” Wu said with relief. “That's what I mean.” Hu nodded, laid down his chopsticks and placed both hands on the table, assuming a grave expression. “You're laying a heavy responsibility on me. I can only do my utmost. I think we should make provision on several fronts. First, you need homes of your own in the settlement. Second, we should calculate your monthly expenses and set aside enough to lend at interest. Spend the interest and leave the principal intact. With a house and daily expenses provided for, your home base will be secure. Then we can act more freely with the remaining money, buying land or trading. Even at the worst, if that portion is entirely lost, your living will remain secure and your foundations unharmed. Would that suit you?” “Of course! Excellent.” Wu turned to Pan. “Shuya, Brother Hu is truly a man of foresight. Admirable!”

Since Pan had brought Hu into their circle, this praise reflected honour on him, and he was delighted. In his excitement he called to a maid, “Tell the mistress there's a card case in the iron chest. Bring it here with the key.” “Wait!” Hu stopped her hastily. “Don't give me anything yet.” “It makes no difference. I have fifty or sixty thousand taels in notes at home. I'll hand them over to you first.” “No. In banking, trust comes first and proper procedure second. Once we've agreed the arrangements, you can deposit your funds at the bank and receive passbooks. The interest and the length of the deposits must both be considered carefully.” “Very well. Tell us what to do.” Hu began with buying land and building houses, and continued through to trade in foreign goods. A broad plan emerged. The budget for buying land and building was to be limited to ten thousand taels. The rest would be divided equally: half in a five-year deposit and half in a demand deposit to serve as trading capital. Hu would introduce them to a bank. In practice, the whole amount would be available for a long term, because even the trading half, though withdrawable on demand, would be employed according to his advice. If he was short of funds, he could simply advise against a particular transaction. Whichever way matters went, everything would depend on a word from him.

“Good. Let's do that.” Pan turned to Lu. “What about you? What are your plans?” “After listening to all this lively discussion, naturally I must make plans too. If we build our houses together in Shanghai, it will be easy to visit.” One after another, they spoke of the pleasures of living close together and seeing one another every day. Hu observed coolly. These three wealthy gentlemen differed from Pang Er, Gao Si, Zhou Wu and their circle. Zhou, Gao and the others had at least managed businesses themselves and were comparatively shrewd—which, paradoxically, made them easier to deal with. These three had never known the difficulties of earning a living. Their hopes might be too high and unrealistic; their lack of worldly experience might leave them unable to judge good from bad. While they were talking, everything sounded excellent. Once plans were carried out and fell short of their ideals, ugly complaints might follow. Such thankless effort would hardly be worthwhile. “Have any of you been to Shanghai?” he asked. “I went once, when I was four, and remember nothing. The farthest either of them has been is Changshu.” “Then you've never really seen the settlement.” “Exactly. I'm forty-two now. When I was four, it was still the Jiaqing reign. There was no foreign settlement then.” “People all say how lively it is, but I must tell you this: its real prosperity lies in the future. Only a small area is busy now, and all sorts of people mingle there. It isn't suitable for refined gentlemen like yourselves, with your music, chess, calligraphy and painting. I have thought of a place where you could buy a large piece of land for your homes. It's still like the countryside. Once the foreigners extend their roads that far, it will become a quiet place within a busy district, ideal for living. But that's only my opinion. You must see it yourselves before deciding.”

“If you say it's good, that's enough. Buy it first.” “Third Brother Pan is right,” Hu replied frankly. “But this is our first undertaking together, and we have many years ahead. I want everything to go well the first time. Here's my suggestion: if any of you would like to come, I'll accompany him to Shanghai for an inspection. How would that be?” “An excellent idea!” Lu said eagerly. “I've long wanted to visit, but I was afraid of making a fool of myself without acquaintances or any knowledge of the settlement's customs. With you there, what have I to fear?” This stirred Pan and Wu as well. But Wu was devoted to his mother and reluctant to leave her side, while Pan had some property to dispose of and could not go far. They therefore agreed that Lu alone would make the journey. “When shall we leave?” he asked. “I'd thought of setting off tomorrow.” “Good heavens!” Lu was astonished. “How could I possibly be ready?” For a businessman, a long journey was commonplace; he could leave at a word. For a man like Lu, it was a great event. First an auspicious day for travel must be chosen. Then luggage must be prepared and gifts assembled for friends and relatives. Farewell banquets would follow on successive days, with calls to take leave in between. If he could depart within ten days, that would be quick. Hu understood all this. There was no point in bargaining over the date. Even waiting another two or three days would achieve nothing, while his own time was too precious to waste. “Fortunately, there's no urgency about this particular matter. Take your time. Once you've fixed the day, I'll send someone especially to fetch you, or come again myself. I guarantee you a safe, comfortable journey to Shanghai.” “Nothing could be better.” Lu fetched an almanac and first chose a day near the end of the month. Then, remembering that the Dragon Boat Festival was approaching and that he wanted to spend it at home, he finally settled on the auspicious seventh day of the fifth lunar month.

By the time they finished discussing business, the sumptuous meal was nearly over. Four substantial dishes were brought out to conclude the feast, but they could do no more than look at them. The eight little plates of pickles, however, were swept clean. Hu Xueyan drank a bowl of fragrant rice porridge, patted his stomach, and rose. “I must take my leave. I shall probably set off tomorrow, so I will not come round to say goodbye again. After the Dragon Boat Festival, I shall certainly try to find time to come and escort Brother Zhixiang myself. We can talk further then.” Pan Shuya wanted him to stay a little longer, while Wu Jizhong and Lu Zhixiang both invited him to dinner. Hu felt there was no need to indulge these wealthy young gentlemen too much. He found excuses to decline all their invitations, tipped the Pan household’s maids and servants generously, and rode out through Chang Gate in the same splendid four-bearer sedan chair. It was only two in the afternoon. Resting with his eyes closed, he considered his plans. There was just one thing left to do that afternoon: have the document drawn up restoring A’qiao’s freedom. That would take no longer than a cup of tea. He could spend the rest of his time with Ji Heling. When he went into the city, he might also visit Sun Chunyang, the southern-goods shop he had long heard of, which was said to date from the Ming dynasty.

It was a sound enough plan, but the four-bearer chair proved his undoing. The district outside Chang Gate was a major junction of land and water routes, and Jinchang Inn had become a veritable residence for traveling officials. Since the fall of Jiangning, more major government offices had been established in Suzhou, bringing a corresponding increase in officials awaiting appointments, seeking commissions, or traveling on official business. For convenience, many preferred to stay at Jinchang Inn. The sight of the imposing sedan chair naturally set them asking what eminent official it carried. Hu’s easy manner and generous spending had won over every attendant at the inn. Eager to please him, they embellished his accomplishments without restraint. He was an influential figure in Zhejiang official circles, they said, and equally well connected in Liangjiang. Governor Xu came from the same locality as he did; Education Commissioner He was an intimate friend and had visited him twice in person. Governor-General Yi had sent a guardsman with a whole banquet of bird’s-nest dishes. The chair belonged to Young Master Pan, Suzhou’s richest young gentleman, who had held the rank of circuit intendant from the day he was born. They made Hu sound like the all-powerful Patriarch Tongtian, with three heads and six arms, able to command the winds and rain. As it happened, the Pan, Wu, and Lu families were all punctilious about social courtesies. They sent dishes for his journey and gifts of local produce, carried by handsome, smartly dressed servants. This seemed to confirm both the breadth of his connections and every word the attendants had said. Visitors streamed in to make his acquaintance, cultivate a connection, or even beg his assistance. Hu was overwhelmed and scarcely knew which way to turn. Only when the lamps were lit did he get a little peace.

“Mr Hu,” Zhou Yiming warned, “you cannot go on staying here.” “Indeed I cannot,” Hu replied with a rueful smile. “Isn’t this a calamity I have done nothing to deserve?” “I would not quite put it that way. Some people could not attract this sort of attention however hard they tried. It is simply that you do not care for such a display. I think you should move to an inn inside the city.” “I am leaving tomorrow. Better to stay put than make another change. I need only keep out of the way myself.” Fortunately, the most important piece of business had already been settled. Taking the document concerning A’qiao with him, Hu arranged to meet Zhou again the next day, then went into the city and straight to Ji Heling’s lodgings. His account of that day’s banquet at Pan Shuya’s astonished Ji, who was naturally delighted for him. “Wealth and distinction really are forcing themselves upon you! Xueyan, I never imagined you would meet with so many opportunities.”

Ji was a scholar, however, and never forgot the need for self-examination. Hu was enjoying such smooth sailing, with unforeseen opportunities presenting themselves one after another, that Ji could not help worrying about him. He went on at length about the need to preserve prosperity once it had been attained, urging Hu to proceed as warily as though approaching a deep abyss or treading on thin ice. He must be careful at every turn: one false step could not be afforded. The advice was somewhat pedantic, but Hu admired this elder brother above all others. He heard the affection and gravity behind the words, considered every one of them sound, and took them all to heart. At last they turned to their travel plans. “I keep putting back my departure, and there has been no letter from Shanghai. I am terribly anxious,” Hu said. “How many more days will you be in Suzhou, Elder Brother? If it is only a day or two, I might as well wait and travel with you.” “There is no need. My date is uncertain. You go first, and we shall meet in Hangzhou.” “Very well. Tomorrow morning I shall look round Sun Chunyang and buy a few things. I shall definitely sail in the afternoon, so I will not come to say goodbye tomorrow.” “And I shall not see you off. We can dispense with both formalities,” Ji replied. “Speaking of Sun Chunyang reminds me of a story I heard just before leaving Hangzhou. Let me tell you. It concerns Fang Yuhe.”

Like Sun Chunyang, Fang Yuhe was a very large dealer in goods from both northern and southern China. Its proprietor, Fang, came from Huizhou, a district famous for producing pawnshop appraisers, whose people were known as the “Huizhou camels” for their capacity for hard work and endurance. He attended to everything himself, and his business flourished until it ranked first in its trade in Hangzhou. Yet two years earlier goods had begun to disappear, and the missing stock consisted of the most expensive delicacies: shark’s fins, edible bird’s nests, dried scallops, and the like. Fang investigated both openly and in secret. First he examined his own staff to discover who might be light-fingered. Then he made inquiries among other dealers and restaurants, looking for anyone who had bought stolen goods of uncertain origin. He found no trace. Only recently had he discovered the method, quite by chance. The trouble lay in the torches: bundles of bamboo bound together, about a cun across and three chi long, normally sold by the bundle. The valuable delicacies were hidden inside these and carried out of the shop. Fang kept his head. He could not simply accuse a customer buying torches of conspiring with his staff to steal goods. The customer could deny it and counter by accusing him of falsely branding an honest man a thief, leaving Fang facing a lawsuit. After considering the matter, he betrayed nothing and left the bundle containing the stolen goods where it was.

Before long someone came to buy torches. The clerk who attended to this “customer” was one of Fang’s most trusted employees, a member of his own clan, both capable and honest. Fang was puzzled. Surely so loyal and reliable a man could not be the thief? Perhaps he had merely happened to serve the customer by chance. Fang decided to wait and see. A few days later he found stolen goods in the torches again. This time a different man came to buy them, but the same clerk named Fang attended to him. That could no longer be coincidence. Fang sent a young apprentice to follow the “customer” in secret, and the boy trailed him all the way to a grain-transport boat. The explanation was now plain. No wonder nothing had been found locally: the stolen goods were being carried to other towns aboard the grain boats. One day Fang called his kinsman aside and quietly asked, “Do you have any friends on the grain boats?” “No.” So he said, but a slight look of alarm crossed his face. Fang now had no doubt. The question was what to do about it. At this point Ji asked, “Xueyan, if you had been the proprietor, how would you have handled the matter?”

“I do not know much about the northern- and southern-goods trade. But from the sound of it, there must have been accomplices in the shop.” “Yes, there were.” Hu considered for a moment. “I may not know the rules of the trade, but the principles of dealing with people are the same. I have my own way of handling it. First tell me what Fang did.” Fang reasoned that a man who could carry on stealing for two years without being discovered must be exceptionally capable. Besides, since others were involved, exposing the affair would damage the firm’s reputation. He would also have to dismiss a number of experienced employees, which would hurt the business. He therefore decided to give the man greater responsibility, promote him, and raise his pay. Grateful for this kindness and eager to repay it, the clerk naturally put an end to the thefts. When Ji finished, Hu nodded. “The proprietor had the right idea, but his way of carrying it out could have been better.” Ji was astonished. He had thought Fang’s handling of the matter could scarcely be improved upon. To hear Hu still find fault made him feel rather indignant on Fang’s behalf. “Oh? Then I should like to hear what better method you have.”

“You must never unmask a thief. Once you do, it leaves a mark that cannot be rubbed away, and however you manage things, you cannot continue working together for long. I will make a prediction now, and time will test it: that kinsman of Fang’s will leave within a year at most.” “Hmm.” Ji began to see some sense in this. “Then would you simply turn a blind eye?” “How could I?” Hu replied. “My method would be to establish the facts in secret, then promote him and raise his pay without ever saying I knew. I would put him in sole charge of detecting theft. Would he still steal the very goods he was appointed to guard?” “Exactly!” Ji exclaimed. “You really are cleverer than any other merchant. ‘The antelope hangs by its horns and leaves no trace.’ That is mastery so complete that the art disappears.” “Still, there is another side to it. Unless the man really has ability, the consequences could be very bad: it would amount to rewarding theft. So what I have said is only an exercise in strategy on paper. Elder Brother, I often think of something you once told me: ‘The art of command lies in the commander’s mind.’ Business and warfare are much alike. You must act according to the person and speak according to the situation. Beyond adapting to changes, you must find opportunities within them. That is the highest skill of all.” “I think you have very nearly reached it,” Ji said, then added with deep regret, “If only you had read a few more books.” Hu could only shake his head. Ji wanted to urge him to devote himself seriously to study, but, considering how busy he was, where could he find the time? There was nothing more to say.

The next morning Hu had scarcely risen when a minor official from Zhejiang, visiting Jiangsu on government business, sent in his card. Zhou Yiming had been right: he could no longer stay here. He asked the inn to notify his boatman that he would leave that afternoon, then hurried out to escape. Before going, he left instructions that if Zhou came, he should be sent to meet him at Wuyuan Teahouse inside the city. Hu would wait until he arrived. Once in his sedan chair, he found the situation almost laughable. Life could produce the most unexpected troubles. He was the last man who wanted an official career, yet people insisted on treating him as though he possessed all an official’s importance. What was one to make of that? He was also irritated, of course. To be driven out of his own lodgings first thing in the morning was difficult to accept. He entered the city in this disgruntled mood and lost interest in doing anything. He sat drinking tea at Wuyuan, listening to a man nearby hold forth on current affairs. The speaker’s thick Hunan accent was hard to follow. He spoke very loudly, gesticulating and spraying saliva in a thoroughly ungraceful manner, and Hu found him exasperating. Yet everyone around the man was listening with rapt attention. Curiosity got the better of Hu, and he made himself listen carefully too.

Gradually he understood. The man was describing Zeng Guofan’s defeat at Jinggang, sixty li outside Changsha, the Hunan provincial capital. In his anguish Zeng had thrown himself into the water, but had been rescued. Hunan’s provincial treasurer, Xu Youwang, and judicial commissioner, Tao Enpei, had already resented him. Here was a vice-minister living at home in mourning for a parent: why must he meddle by organizing militia forces and encroaching on their authority? They jointly petitioned Governor Luo Bingzhang to impeach Zeng and disband his troops. Luo was a sensible man, and had recently engaged Zuo Zongtang, a distinguished scholar from Xiangyin, to assist with military affairs. Zeng had already submitted a memorial impeaching himself, Luo reasoned; it would be wrong to kick a man when he was down. Nor, with the fighting so urgent, was this the time to reduce the army. Luo firmly rejected Xu and Tao’s request. The very next day, however, Taqibu, deputy commander of the Changsha brigade serving under Zeng, defeated the Taiping forces at Xiangtan. Hunan’s provincial commander, Bao Qibao, submitted a memorial claiming the victory for himself. Comparing Zeng’s self-impeachment with Bao’s claim to military glory, the court saw that the man who had lost a battle deserved reward, while the man who had “won” had never even sent out troops. An imperial edict dismissed Bao. Taqibu was promoted from deputy brigade commander directly to Hunan provincial commander, skipping the rank of brigade commander and taking command of the province’s Green Standard forces.

If a subordinate received such advancement, his commander’s position must plainly be secure. Xu Youwang and Tao Enpei became deeply uneasy. They feared Zeng might bear a grudge, or Taqibu might seek to avenge him. Either could find some fault with them and submit an impeachment that the court would surely uphold. The two therefore arranged to visit Zeng at his headquarters in Gaofeng Temple outside Changsha’s south gate, where they kowtowed, offering congratulations and apologies together. It was a most satisfying story, and the listeners all applauded. “Vice-Minister Zeng’s defeat has actually secured his position,” the man said. “His troops’ morale is better than before, thanks to the court’s far-seeing judgment and its fairness in rewards and punishments.” “Exactly! Exactly!” several voices agreed. Then the conversation broke up into a confusion of remarks. Hu felt his spirits rise. People truly did have a sense of justice, he thought. From the look of things, the regime of Hong and Yang could not last. Once the war ended, the displaced would need to be resettled and every neglected enterprise revived. What business opportunities would there be then? He must think it through when he had a moment. To make a great deal of money, he would have to move before everyone else. His thoughts roamed far and wide until he caught himself and laughed: he was getting much too far ahead. Looking up, he found only a few customers left. The morning’s tea trade was over, and it was nearly noon. Why had Zhou still not come? He had wasted the entire morning. With a sigh, he rose and paid his bill, deciding to buy some local specialties at Sun Chunyang, then return to the inn, pack, and board his boat.

He had just stepped out of Wuyuan when he met Zhou Yiming face to face. They greeted each other, and Hu asked, “Where have you come from?” “Chang Gate. I went to the Pan household first thing this morning to see Sister A’qiao. We arranged to go to Mudu tomorrow morning. She asked me to escort her to Jinchang Inn, and only there did we learn that you had come into the city.” “Oh? Where is she now?” “At the inn, packing. She sent me to fetch you. When she heard from the attendants that you were leaving today, she had some of the luggage sent aboard already.” “I see. Do you know where Sun Chunyang is?” “Yes, in Wuqufang.” Zhou led the way, and they walked at an easy pace to the shop just north of Wuqufang. A huge tree stood outside, too broad for a man to encircle with his arms. Its bare branches bore a few new shoots, proving that it was not dead. Zhou told Hu that the tree dated from the Ming dynasty, and that Tang Bohu had once studied on this spot.

Hu had no interest in the historic site. What interested him was Sun Chunyang’s signboard. Its gilt ground had darkened, and the three characters of the name were barely legible, yet the shop itself was full of life. At a glance he saw everyone attending to his duties, briskly and solemnly. A white-bearded old man stood in the middle of the shop holding a water pipe. Looking from side to side, he pointed with the paper spill in his hand, directing clerks and apprentices as they served customers. The curious thing was that there were customers but no goods in sight. A customer would make a purchase, pay, and then walk toward the back with a small slip of paper. What was the arrangement? “That is Sun Chunyang’s system,” Zhou explained. “The business is divided into six departments. Not Personnel, Revenue, Rites, War, Punishments, and Works, as in government, but southern goods, northern goods, delicacies from the sea, cured meats, preserved fruits, and candles. You pay at the front and get a ticket, then collect your goods at the back.” “But if customers cannot see the goods, how do they choose? What if they are unsuitable?” “There is no need to choose. You get exactly what you ask for: genuine goods at fair prices. Sun Chunyang has earned its reputation. Its goods are the finest, its weights are full, and it cheats neither young nor old. If you are dissatisfied here, you will not find anything better elsewhere.” “It cannot have been easy to build such an unassailable reputation.”

Hu went to the counter himself and bought tea snacks and candles, along with several hams that he intended to take back to Hangzhou and compare with Jinhua hams. Having paid and received his ticket, he went to the appropriate department and asked for his purchases to be delivered to Jinchang Inn. Sun Chunyang proved unassailable in another sense too. They politely refused: delivering purchases to customers was not their practice. “That is a mistake,” Hu said quietly to Zhou. “A shop’s rules should not be rigid. Some things allow no compromise; others need improvement. The world changes every day. Once there were no foreigners here; now there are. That is change. What matters in business is the ability to adapt. Sun Chunyang has survived from the Ming dynasty because until now very little has changed since those days. Things are different today. The restrictions on maritime trade have been thrown open, and circumstances are changing profoundly. If they cling unchanged to the same old rules handed down for hundreds of years, I doubt this famous name will survive much longer.” Zhou also thought it unreasonable for a shop to refuse delivery of such a large purchase. He carefully considered Hu’s words, knowing that Hu was teaching him. When he followed him into business, he must remember this lesson: adapt to circumstances and always consider the customer’s needs.

Hu had intended to have lunch in the city before returning to Jinchang Inn. Now, encumbered with several large baskets of snacks and other purchases, he had to hire a porter and accompany the load out of the city. At the inn he found that A’qiao had packed his trunks and belongings neatly and stacked them to one side, ready for the boatmen to collect. He called an attendant, ordering lunch and asking for his account to be prepared. After the meal he paid the bill, and A’qiao escorted him to the boat. Once aboard, however, she said it was still early and she might as well sit for a while. Zhou tactfully found an excuse to go ashore. Hu was eager to be home and impatient to set off, but with A’qiao still there he could hardly order her away. Her silent, preoccupied air puzzled him. “Is there something else you want to tell me?” he asked. Absorbed in her own thoughts, she had not quite heard. She blinked and forced a smile. “What did you say?” “I asked whether you had something else to tell me.” “Something to tell you?” She hesitated. “Perhaps I have. Perhaps I haven’t.” What she meant was merely that she could not bear to leave and wanted to stay a little longer. Hu found her manner strange. Unless he understood it, he knew the puzzle would trouble him all the way home. He sat down first, leaned sideways, and pulled out an oblong stool, indicating that she should sit too.

He waited for her to speak while she searched for something to say. At last a question occurred to her. “Why exactly did Young Master Pan invite you to lunch yesterday? Was he asking you to buy land and build houses in Shanghai?” “So you know already.” “I know something about it, but not very clearly.” Hu gave her a brief account of their meeting. “Then you will be coming back to Suzhou after the festival?” “Not necessarily. It depends on whether I have time. I doubt I shall manage it; I shall probably have to ask Old Zhou to make the journey.” “By then…” A’qiao said. “I wonder where I shall be?” This was an indirect inquiry about her own future: where was she to go, and with whom would she settle? Hu replied, “By then, I think there is sure to be good news.” “Good news? What good news?” The meaning was plain enough. He was naturally referring to He Guiqing’s setting her up in a home of her own. Hu could not tell whether she was pretending not to understand or had really failed to think of it. He felt a flicker of irritation and could not be bothered to explain. He merely smiled.

“If you have time, you had better come yourself.” “Why?” “I may have something to tell you then.” “What? Why not tell me now?” “Because the time has not come yet.” A’qiao added, “Perhaps I shall, perhaps I shan’t. We shall see when the time comes.” Her evasiveness only deepened his suspicions. Hu calmly put her remarks together with her reluctance to leave, and at last understood what was in her mind. She was still wavering. One hand had already taken hold of He, while the other was unwilling to let go of Hu. Yet this was not a clever attempt to gain an advantage. They had spent these days together, affection had grown easily, and she could not cut it off all at once. Understanding this, Hu felt he should make his position clear, but not so harshly as to wound her needlessly. In a tone of earnest persuasion, he said, “You must stop letting your thoughts run away with you. Your future is settled. All you need do now is enjoy your good fortune.” “Ah,” A’qiao sighed softly. “Where am I to find any ‘Heavenly Official Bestows’?” Hu stared, then understood. Suzhou people liked to leave the last word of a familiar phrase unspoken. “The Heavenly Official Bestows” omitted the word “blessings.” He smiled. “You really do not know how fortunate you are. There, there.” His manner showed that he wished to discuss it no further. “Please go ashore. I shall have Old Zhou take you back.”

“It is still early!” A’qiao refused to go. Besides, she now really had remembered some things she wanted to say to him. Never mind, Hu told himself. So many days have passed already; why begrudge her one afternoon? He would see what she was up to. He took out the pine-nut sweets and other tea snacks he had bought at Sun Chunyang, opened the packets one by one, and covered the table with them. “Take your time. You can eat while you talk.” A’qiao smiled. “You are a little annoyed with me, aren’t you?” “I have changed my mind. I am not leaving today. I shall give you dinner before you go, as well as these snacks.” “And you say you are not speaking in anger?” “There, there!” Afraid she might really misunderstand, Hu added, “How could I be angry with you? There is nothing to be angry about. You must still have a great deal to say. Tell me everything while I am here.”

“That is true. I want you to take a message to Shanghai.” A’qiao picked up a preserved yangmei berry and put it in her mouth. “Please tell Second Miss…” Tell her what? Her hesitation was irritating. “Well?” Hu prompted. “What do you want to tell her?” “Let me ask you something. What exactly are things like in Young Master You’s household? I mean Mrs You. Does she keep him on a very tight rein?” Before she could go further, Hu understood. “You want to advise Second Miss to ask him to take her into his household, don’t you?” “Yes. Keeping her in a rented place outside is hardly a proper arrangement.” “You need not worry about that. The Seventh Lady is there; she will arrange things between them. Mrs You is a most accommodating wife and does not interfere with his affairs.” “Then why have they not celebrated the marriage already?” The reason, of course, was that You’s circumstances had not been going well, and he was in no mood for a wedding. There was no need to tell A’qiao this. Hu merely replied, “I have not asked him, so I do not know why. I shall pass your message on to Second Miss.”

Just then a head appeared at the cabin door. It was the boatman, urging them to depart. It was getting late, he said; once the water gate closed, they could not leave until morning. “Never mind,” Hu replied. “I have Education Commissioner He’s visiting card. I can request official assistance.” The implication was that as soon as A’qiao left, he intended to sail, even if the water gate had closed. Once she understood that, she really could not linger any longer. She rose. “I am going.” Hu did not ask her to stay. He sent someone ashore to fetch Zhou while he saw her off. When she had stepped gracefully onto the bank, the boatman withdrew the gangplank and was preparing to cast off when Zhou came running. “Wait! Wait!” he shouted. Hu, who was standing at the cabin door, asked at once, “What else is it?” “Sister A’qiao has dropped a ring on the boat.”

The gangplank was put back and A’qiao came aboard again. Hu asked what sort of ring she had lost. She gave evasive answers and kept her head down, searching the deck. It looked suspicious. Deliberately ignoring her, Hu stood still, neither speaking nor helping her search. He found it amusing and wanted to see how she would bring the performance to an end. A’qiao, however, thought he had seen through her lie, was displeased, and was deliberately creating an impasse. Her embarrassment began to turn to anger. She straightened up, planted her feet, and declared with a girl’s petulance, “I will not leave until I find that ring!” Then she sat down sulkily and looked away, furious at his indifference. This surprised him. Had she really lost a ring? Perhaps he had misjudged her. With an apologetic smile he said, “You have not told me what sort of ring it is. Even if I wanted to help, I would not know what to look for.” The reasoning was weak, and A’qiao challenged it. “A ring is a ring. Must I describe it exactly before you will trouble your precious hands to help me?”

“All right, all right!” Hu waved a hand. “I am about to leave. Why must we have a quarrel as well?” He steadied himself and considered. The only solution was to cut the tangle with one stroke. “Come, let us go ashore.” “Ashore?” A’qiao asked in surprise. “Where are we going?” “Into the city. Stop looking for your ring. I shall replace it. You can choose one yourself at a jeweler’s.” It was like a sudden cry of “Check!” in a game of chess: A’qiao was trapped and did not know how to respond. She faltered, “Never mind. I do not want you to replace it.” Hu answered instantly. “Then stop looking. Sit a little longer, and let Old Zhou take you back to the Pan household. I shall write to you when I reach Shanghai.” A little more time with him, and a promise like that, were enough to satisfy her. The tense look on her face faded without her noticing. She made certain of his promise. “You said it yourself: you will write. We shall see whether you keep your word.”

“I certainly shall. If I have no time to write myself, I shall ask Young Master Gu, or the Seventh Lady.” “The Seventh Lady can read and write?” “Very well indeed. She has a good deal of learning. More than I do.” A’qiao found this a fascinating discovery. “You would never guess!” She still sounded a little doubtful. “The way she looks, she does not seem a literary sort of person.” “You mean she lacks a scholarly air? You must not judge by appearances. The Seventh Lady has a way of doing things entirely her own. You could never dream of it.” He told her the Seventh Lady’s remarkable exploit: deliberately getting Gu Yingchun drunk, then falsely claiming that he had slept with her while drunk, until he was forced to swear by heaven that he would marry her and never prove faithless. A’qiao listened in astonishment. “That really is something new. Who ever heard of doing such a thing? A woman’s reputation is more important than anything. Even if something of that kind had happened, she would try to clear herself. Here nothing happened, and she smeared her own face with mud! The Seventh Lady certainly has an extraordinary mind.” “Indeed she does. But she is formidable too. How else could she have made Old Gu so obedient?” Hu produced a learned quotation. “‘Before you can take, you must first give.’ The Seventh Lady went about it the right way.”

A’qiao fell silent, her expression slowly growing somber. After a long while she said, “I could never learn to be as clever as the Seventh Lady.” Her look, together with those words, carried a good deal of unspoken meaning. Hu smiled and declined to take it up. Seeing this, A’qiao knew that he had, as the saying went, swallowed an iron scale weight: his heart was set like iron. To linger any longer would be humiliating. She sprang to her feet, turned her face aside, and said coldly, “I am going.” Hu did not answer her. He merely called out, “Put down the gangplank!” The plank had not been removed, and he could see that perfectly well. He had called out deliberately. A’qiao understood: he was driving in the nail and bending its point over, as the saying went. He was making her departure doubly certain. Even if she changed her mind, she could no longer stay. How ruthlessly he was behaving! The delicate affection she felt for him had turned to resentment, which now grew still stronger. “Hmph!” she sneered. “You are infuriating. Anyone would think I was the god of pestilence. You are so afraid I might not go!”

Under this reproach, Hu could only give a bitter smile. One hand was in his pocket. His fingers touched the little golden goat attached to his watch chain, and suddenly emotion surged through him. He almost cried out, “A’qiao, don’t go!” But she was already leaving. In her anger she walked quickly and heavily, making the gangplank dip and sway beneath her. Though she held the bamboo pole the boatman extended as a handrail, it was still dangerous. Terrified that she would miss her footing and fall into the water, Hu stared with his mouth open, frightening himself until he forgot every word he had meant to say. By the time he recovered and tried to speak, she was already in her sedan chair. He could only call out, “Old Zhou, please take good care of her!” “I will. Do not worry.” Zhou waved again. “I shall return to Shanghai in a few days. If anything urgent comes up, write to me care of Jinchang Inn, and they will forward it.”

CHAPTER TWENTY-SIX

On reaching Shanghai, Hu Xueyan again put up at the Daxing Inn. Before he had even settled his luggage, he wrote a note and had a man from the inn take it to the Seventh Lady’s lodgings, asking Gu Yingchun to call. In less than an hour Gu arrived, driving his Hengsimei carriage himself. After their first greetings, he said nothing but looked Hu’s luggage carefully over. “What is it, Gu?” “Where is A’qiao?” “She hasn’t come,” Hu replied. “Things have taken a turn you could never have imagined.” “What has happened?” “It’s a long story. We’ll talk when we have time. Tell me, has Brother Five come back?” “Not yet.” Gu returned to his question. “What about A’qiao? What has changed? Give me the gist of it.” Unable to understand this particular concern for her, Hu asked a question of his own. “Did you send someone to Mudu to discuss her affairs?” “Never mind that for the moment. Just tell me what has happened to her.” “That lovely flower has found her owner, and I arranged the whole thing. Before long she will be Education Commissioner He’s concubine.” He went on to explain how he had transplanted this celebrated flower. Eloquent as he was, the affair had too many twists to be disposed of in a few words.
