If you hadn't come, I'd already have taken him back to Shanghai. What are your instructions now?” Hu sighed and shook his head. “One thing after another—it's like holding a handful of tangled hair. I can't answer you yet. You and Fushan had better stay here for now.” Zhou went upstairs to arrange rooms. Left alone, Hu leaned against his pillow, resting without sleeping and considering his affairs one by one. He realized that he had made a grave mistake and thought of the saying, “A gentleman attends to the essentials.” His own essentials were banking first and silk second. For the bank, Pan Shuya's money was ready to hand. New silk would soon reach the Huzhou market. Was he going to trade in it this year, and if so, how? He must decide promptly and tell Chen Shilong what to do. If he kept attending to incidental matters and neglected his proper business, he would end in an impossible position. He therefore made a firm decision. Tomorrow he would hear what Yang Fengmao had to say. If the business proved troublesome, he would follow Qiu's suggestion and leave the guns in Shanghai for the time being, then hurry back to Zhejiang with the Seventh Lady and attend to real work. He would deal with other matters if he could; if not, they must wait. Having settled that, he made further arrangements, assigning manageable tasks to others. Liu could look after the Pan family's business; Zhou could handle He Guiqing and A’qiao. The mere change of outlook lifted much of the weight that had burdened him for days. Neither man would do his task as well as Hu himself, of course, and it was hard not to worry. But he was exhausted and could no longer attend to everything. Resolving to let go, he recalled two lines of verse seen somewhere and recited them aloud: “Shut the door and push the moon beyond the window; leave the plum blossoms to decide things for themselves.”

Of the three incidental matters, however, one could not be neglected. With his thoughts concentrated, he could consider it more thoroughly. Why travel all the way back to Hangzhou and then turn towards Huzhou? There was a canal from Suzhou to Huzhou. Suzhou lay east of Lake Tai and Huzhou south of it; that ought to be the shorter route. “Old Zhou, how does the water route from Suzhou to Huzhou run?” “Do you mean the canal? I've travelled it. From Suzhou to Wujiang it's called the Beitang River; from Wujiang to Pingwang, the Guantang River. At Pingwang it divides. The southern branch to Jiaxing is the Nantang River. The western branch, through Nanxun to Huzhou, is the Xitang River. A hundred and twenty li altogether.” Hu made up his mind. He trimmed the candle, ground ink and wrote a letter himself. Just as he finished sealing it, Fushan returned.

“Huang Yinbao lives at Shuitantou in Xiatang,” Fushan reported. “Mr Liu and Mr Qiu are both there. Mr Liu is banking at pai gow.” “Pai gow?” Hu was surprised. “With whom?” “The people of the house—older maids and young maids, a whole roomful. Only Mr Qiu is drinking.” Hu laughed. “One a drunkard, the other a gambler. They're the same wherever they go.” “Did you see them yourself?” Zhou asked. “How did you know who they were?” Fushan blushed. “I know an attendant there. He's from Mudu too. I asked him to take me in and show me.” This lent some support to Hu's suggestion that the youth had already ventured into the web of enchantment. Zhou smiled and said nothing, while Hu praised him. “Very capable. You can find your own way when you're out on an errand. Good! Have you ever been to Huzhou?” “No.” Encouraged by the praise, Fushan volunteered at once. “But that doesn't matter. If you need something done, I'll go.” “Take a letter for me. The address is on the envelope. Call the man Uncle Four. Get his reply and come straight back.” Hu handed him the letter and ten taels, adding, “One may live frugally at home, but must have money on the road. Take enough; account for whatever you spend.” This meant that actual travelling expenses would be reimbursed. Zhou thought of explaining, but then reflected that Hu might deliberately be testing Fushan. Better not reveal the point. He kept silent.

Fushan inquired that night about the passenger boats to Huzhou and left early the next morning. Hu rose late, refreshed himself and waited for news from Yang Fengmao. Meanwhile, he gave detailed instructions for arranging A’qiao's marriage to He. Liu and Qiu returned from spending the night at Huang Yinbao's, bringing the inevitable round of jokes. Soon it was time for the noon gun. Yang kept his word and hurried back while they were gathered round the lunch table. All four rose and invited him to join them. He had already eaten, so Hu did not press him, but took him into the inner suite for another private talk. “When did you get back?” “This morning. I had a few things to say at Third Granny Yu's.” Yang paused, blinking repeatedly, as though he had much to say and did not know where to begin. This put Hu on his guard. Yang had gone to the Yu house instead of coming straight to the inn. Clearly, “their own people” had held a private discussion unsuitable for outsiders. It seemed they had not yet reached the point of sharing fortunes and misfortunes. Hu must judge carefully how close they really were. “Uncle Hu, first there's something I must mention. Third Granny Yu hopes to claim a connection above her station by taking your concubine as her sworn daughter. Would you consent to honour us in that way?” This was wholly unexpected. But Hu's mind worked quickly; several thoughts flashed through it, and he grasped the probable intention. They had only just met, and the business they were discussing involved great differences between safety and danger, good fortune and disaster. Only a family tie making them “their own people” would reassure them. For the public business, he would gladly agree; the closer personal connection would be welcome too. But he had another concern. If Furong acquired such a powerful sworn mother, she might become impossible to control, creating future trouble between wife and concubine. He hesitated to consent.

Men of the brotherhood knew how to change course with the wind. Seeing his hesitation, Yang said hastily, “Of course, it was presumptuous to seek such a connection. If it can't be managed...” “No!” Hu interrupted, afraid of being misunderstood. Only the truth could remove suspicion. “Third Granny Yu honours us more than I could wish. The difficulty is that my wife is a tigress. I don't even dare take my concubine home. If my wife behaves violently and my concubine suffers, I shall have wronged Third Granny Yu. That's why I dare not agree.” The words were candid yet tactful. Yang understood their deeper meaning. “On that point, set your mind at rest. Third Granny Yu knows the ways of the world through and through. She'll only help settle your household troubles.” He waved his hand emphatically. “She'll never back her sworn daughter against you and make things difficult.” “Then what more can I say?” Hu assumed an expression of complete satisfaction. “Rather than choose a day, let us take the day we have. My concubine shall kowtow to Third Granny Yu this afternoon.” “Good. Leave the arrangements to me. To be frank, Uncle Hu, this will give my master something to say to the other side. Everything had been agreed; it was hard to go back on his word. Now he can say, ‘This concerns my sworn younger sister's family. There is truly no alternative. I can only apologize.’” Only now did Hu understand why Yang had first gone to the Yu house. The arrangement involved Third Granny Yu and had to be explained to her beforehand. It had taken considerable thought and showed the Yu family's sincerity. He was reassured.

“And the other matter?” Hu asked. This was the great question of accepting an amnesty. Yang answered steadily. “My master naturally favours it, but it won't be easy. It's like a boat already running east with the current. Turning back to travel upstream against the wind is hard work. He would like you to come and discuss it face to face.” “Certainly.” Hu agreed without hesitation. “Where is he now?” “In Tongli. You know the place?” Naturally, Hu had heard of it. Wujiang's county town was tiny; people joked that a shout of “Hello” at the east gate would be answered at the west. Tongli, northeast of the county town, was a famous large market town within the county. Bordering Qingpu, it was one of the richest parts of the southeastern land of fish and rice. “So he's in Tongli. No wonder you could go and return within a day. When shall we leave?” “Early tomorrow. Would that suit you?” “Yes. How do we go?” “By boat, of course. I'll arrange it. Riding is convenient too; one embankment road takes you straight there.” “Better go by boat.”

“Very well.” Yang paused. “But there's something I should tell you first. Several of the other side's leaders are in Tongli too. Would you like to meet them?” Hu considered, then answered firmly. “Without entering the tiger's den, how can one get its cub? I'll meet them.” “Then you'll have to go along with their ways. They're reckless womanizers and gamblers, a worthless lot. But if you'll mix with them, anything can be discussed.” An idea struck Hu. “Brother Yang, may I bring someone?” “Naturally.” Yang sounded a little reluctant. “Who would it be?” “Someone entirely trustworthy and one of our own: Third Master Liu, just outside. We're related. Food, clothes, women, gambling—he knows them all, and gambling is his particular expertise.” “If he's your relation, naturally there's no difficulty.” Yang rose. “I'll report to Third Granny Yu.” “Good. I'll follow shortly. Tell my concubine first that I'm very pleased she'll become Third Granny Yu's sworn daughter. I'll provide whatever the ceremony requires.” “No.” Yang interrupted. “Third Granny Yu was quite explicit. She's already ashamed to have accepted your generous gifts and won't let you spend more.” Hu thought there was no need to argue now. He could simply follow the proper forms himself. He gave a vague, accommodating answer. As soon as Yang had gone, he summoned Qiu, Liu and Zhou to discuss how to divide the work.

The business was complicated, and the amnesty involved matters that could not be spoken of freely. He could not explain everything at once and gave only the essential instructions. First, Zhou was to go into the city and buy lengths of cloth and other gifts for Furong to present to her sworn mother. Second, Liu must pack and prepare to leave for Tongli the following day. Finally, Qiu was to go to the Yu house and discuss the adoption ceremony with the Seventh Lady. “What about you?” Qiu asked. “Why not come to the Yus' with us?” “There's somewhere important I must go first. I'll join you there shortly.” The important place was Pan Shuya's house. Yang's words had inspired Hu to try an unconventional approach: he would use gambling as an opportunity to win over those rough adventurers. For that he needed ample capital. He had only a little over ten thousand taels in banknotes with him and meant to borrow twenty thousand in silver from Pan.

As soon as his visiting card went in, Pan came out to welcome him. “Xueyan, you deserve a penalty! Why didn't you come to see me when you reached Suzhou?” “How did you know I was here?” “I saw Education Commissioner He this morning. He told me.” “I see. Naturally, I deserve a penalty. But consider: why would I call on him unless something made it unavoidable? I hadn't even meant to disturb you. I know wealthy gentlemen like yourselves dislike pointless social calls. Since I couldn't spare time to amuse you, and haven't finished the business you entrusted to me, what was the use of coming?” Pan laughed. “I can never outtalk you. Does that mean you've come on business today?” “Yes. One doesn't visit the temple without a purpose. I have two favours to ask. First, I'd like you and your friends to support me in Tongli.” “What long arms you have!” Pan interrupted. “Reaching all the way to Tongli to make money.” “Exactly the opposite. I'm going to give some away, not make it. Otherwise I wouldn't have had to trouble you. I mean to gamble on a grand scale.” Now Pan understood what “support” meant. Hu was no gambler, though, and why should he travel so far for a great gambling session? “There must be a reason?” “Certainly. There are people I want to befriend. You'll understand when we reach Tongli.” Hu followed immediately with his second request. “For that purpose, I'd like to borrow twenty thousand taels. When my money arrives from Shanghai in three days, I'll repay you at once.”

“Why talk of ‘at once’ or anything of the sort?” Pan thought for a moment. “Would gold leaf do?” “Certainly. If I borrow gold leaf, I'll repay you in gold leaf.” Pan lent him five hundred taels of gold leaf. But he was less interested in supporting him in Tongli. “The place is mad for gambling. Even ordinary families will entertain for three days when a son turns one or a grandson reaches his first month, and gamble for all three days. All sorts mix together there. I don't want to go.” “Then I won't press you. If this business goes well, I'll have a proper game with you all when I come back. There's someone I want to introduce too: a very amusing fellow who'll get on well with all of you. I've put your business in his hands as well. We'll discuss everything when I return.” “Good. We shall await you.” Pan then asked, “Would you like to see our other guest?” He meant A’qiao. Hu had already decided what to do and answered at once, “No need. I know she's staying with you and has grown plumper. A contented mind makes a well-fed body. She's comfortable, and I'm quite at ease.” He took his leave, returned first to Jinchang Inn and locked the gold leaf in his chest. Zhou then arrived with an ample assortment of ceremonial gifts. Hu inspected them one by one and was satisfied. With Zhou accompanying the gifts behind his chair, they went into the city together.

At the Yu house, Yu Shaowu opened the main gate to receive him. Looking inside, Hu saw a pair of tall red candles burning in the hall, along with incense shaped like the character for longevity. The tables and chairs had fresh red satin covers embroidered in gold. Four new palace lanterns hung beneath the eaves. Everything was festive, arranged like a birthday celebration. Furong had not yet performed the ceremony, but Shaowu had already changed his form of address. “Uncle! Everything is ready. We've only been waiting for you to begin.” Within, distinguished guests filled both sides of the hall. Qiu had been given a place of honour, with several men keeping him company. When Hu appeared, their attention naturally shifted. Third Granny Yu clearly regarded the adoption as a great event. As he exchanged courtesies, he wondered whether she simply felt an affinity with Furong or had some other intention. There was no immediate answer, so he went along with the occasion. Finding an opening, he told Shaowu, “I'll go in and pay my respects to your grandmother first.” “She's waiting for you, Uncle. I'll take you in.” Excusing himself to the company, Hu followed through the inner gate. The rooms within were festive too. The Seventh Lady came forward smiling, wearing a green jacket and black skirt, with a large, deep-red camellia at her temple. Against her snow-white skin, the colours looked especially vivid. She curtsied. “Congratulations, Little Uncle!” “You honour me.” Hu returned the greeting with clasped hands. “Thank you for all your help these past two days.” “Little Uncle, come here a moment.” She was too impatient to wait for Third Granny Yu. Hu realized that she must have something he should know before meeting the old lady. He sent an apologetic glance across the room and followed her aside.

“We must treat it as though Auntie Furong became Third Granny Yu's sworn daughter as a child,” she said softly. A man of the world needed only a hint. This would make it easier for Yu Wucheng to explain his position. Otherwise, the adoption would plainly look like a deliberately staged performance. “I understand,” Hu said at once. “Third Granny Yu has brought out the private savings from the bottom of her chest to entertain everyone today. It will be a grand evening.” “Ah, that reminds me. I meant to ask: everything seems very elaborate. Is it because she likes Furong, or has she another purpose?” “Both. She wants to give Auntie a celebration, and she wants word to spread through the brotherhood that she's adopted a sworn daughter.” “Ah! Old ginger is the hottest indeed.” They entered the main inner room together. Third Granny Yu and Furong wore matching clothes: bright-red lined jackets of Ning silk and pale-blue skirts, all brand-new, seemingly made overnight. To honour Third Granny Yu and raise Furong's standing, Hu addressed her directly as “Mother”. The old lady was pleased, and Furong more pleased still. Having the famous Third Granny Yu of the Yu family as her sworn mother was a great comfort. What troubled her was that, as a concubine, she could not wear a red skirt even on such a day. Third Granny Yu wished to show her consideration without breaking customary rules. After consulting the Seventh Lady, she had engaged four seamstresses, set up worktables and had these two matching outfits made overnight, so that anyone could see they were mother and daughter. Furong was deeply grateful already. Now Hu's use of the same address effaced the distinction of her lesser status and delighted her further. “Master Hu,” Third Granny Yu said, her smiling eyes narrowing to slits, “I shall presume on this connection and call you ‘son-in-law’ from now on.” Holding Furong's hand tightly, she continued, “Now we're truly one family. You must keep Wucheng's affairs in mind.” “Naturally. I must attend not only to Elder Brother's affairs, but to Shaowu's too.” These were more than ordinary courtesies. Hu understood that this was a performance for their friends in the brotherhood. Taking Third Granny Yu's cues, he answered every word perfectly, leaving no opening. All the formalities were solemn and dignified. The ceremony passed smoothly, followed by a banquet of twelve tables. With Qiu as his “escort”, Hu went round offering toasts, attending to everyone with great care.

The banquet was followed by gambling: the dice-shaking game, pai gow and everything else. Hu did not join in this time. Accompanied by Yang, he passed through the inner gate to take leave of Third Granny Yu. “Mother, I'm going to Tongli to see Elder Brother tomorrow. Have you any message for him?” “Nothing for him. But I have a few words for you, son-in-law.” “Please tell me.” “I'm very happy today. To be honest, I'm more than halfway into the grave. To have such an unexpected joy now—Heaven has treated me well.” “Well said, Mother.” Hu smiled. “I'm only afraid Furong and I haven't done enough for you. Once Elder Brother and I have settled this business, I'll take you to Hangzhou to spend the summer by West Lake.” “Good! I went there to offer incense last year and mean to go again this year. But that is for later. Leave it for now.” She paused. “Son-in-law, I have something very important to entrust to you.” Hu felt slightly uneasy. “Why put it that way? I've already said I'll do everything I can. Elder Brother's affairs and Shaowu's are my own.” “I know. But although your elder brother is no longer young, some of the things he says and does are very immature. He's far less seasoned than Fengmao, and farther still from you.” Hu smiled. “Mother, you make him sound so bad that even I feel inclined to defend him.” “He's my own son, and my only one. Why would I deliberately belittle him? It's simply the truth. Before outsiders, I must cover his shortcomings. Before you, I needn't. You'll see in time. What I ask is really a warning: if Wucheng says or does anything improper, please bear with him for my sake.”

Hu found this puzzling, but there was no time to examine it closely. He readily agreed. “Set your mind at rest. When I meet him, I'll respect him as my own elder brother. He's always had a great tree to shelter under, and I've heard that he's had a young master's temper from childhood. Whatever he may say, I certainly won't take offence.” “Son-in-law!” Third Granny Yu was moved. “Those words are a blessing to the Yu family. I need say no more. When you return, I'll give you a proper welcome.” “A welcome and a celebration of success,” Hu added to please her. “May your golden words come true.” She turned and called, “My lady, come out.” She meant Furong. With Yang present, Furong had not felt free to appear earlier. At the summons, she came out with measured, dignified steps. “These past two days have counted as a visit to your mother's home. Your husband has come to fetch you today. Go back together.”

If Furong went back now, she would have to return tomorrow when Hu left for Tongli. Why make the needless journey? Staying where she was would also demonstrate her devotion to her new mother. Furong paid close attention to such social considerations. Having decided, she smiled. “I'm more comfortable here with you, Mother. I'm not going back.” Hu did not want her to go back either. That night he had matters to discuss with Liu and Qiu. They might talk late, or go to Huang Yinbao's to drink through the night. With Furong present, he would have to watch both his words and his movements. Her answer suited him perfectly, and he supported it at once. “Let her stay and keep you company. I'll fetch her when I return from Tongli.” “As you please. This is your home too. Or you could stay here yourself.” “There's no need. Brother Fengmao and I still have a little business to discuss.” Hu seized the chance to take his leave. “We set off early tomorrow, so I'll say goodbye now.” He bowed. After exchanging reminders and good wishes, he and Qiu found Liu at a gambling table. Yang accompanied them back to Jinchang Inn, where they agreed when to board the boat next day. He then left.

“I don't think Yu Wucheng will be easy to deal with.” Hu looked troubled. “I must have another force in reserve.” He asked Zhou, “Do you know Tongli?” “I know all the waterways and landing places in this district.” “Good.” Hu turned to Qiu. “Once we've left tomorrow, you and Old Zhou follow us. Find an inn, stay there and wait for my message. You'll have to put up with it for a day or two. Neither of you must leave.” “Very well.” Qiu smiled. “I've bought two collections of poetry and haven't opened them yet. I can drink and read at the inn.” “Exactly. That will do.” Hu asked Zhou, “Which inn? Decide now.” Zhou thought for a moment. “I can't recall any inn in Tongli. Whenever I've passed through, I've stayed on the boat or at a friend's house. I've never used an inn.” “Then we'll send messages through your friend's house,” Liu suggested. “Good. He's in your line of business, Third Master Liu. Go to East Street in Tongli and ask for the proprietor of Yanghetang Pharmacy. You'll find me.” Hu nodded. “Settled. Once you've found lodgings, Old Qiu must stay out of sight. Old Zhou can inquire along the waterfront about what Yu Wucheng is doing in Tongli. But keep it discreet.” “I understand.”

CHAPTER TWENTY-EIGHT

Only after arranging for this reserve force did Hu Xueyan feel at ease. Early the next morning, he had just finished washing and dressing when Yang Fengmao arrived. They breakfasted together and boarded the boat waiting at the Chang Gate landing. The two oars flew. They passed beneath Wujiang’s famous Chuihong Bridge and reached Tongli at noon. The boat drew up at the back door of a house; once they stepped onto the landing, they had arrived. On the journey Yang had explained that their hosts, the Zhu family, were rice merchants. The eldest Zhu brother was a disciple of Yu Wucheng, and therefore Yang’s junior fellow disciple. Whenever Yu came to Tongli, he stayed here. Eldest Brother Zhu treated his master with the greatest respect, so Hu and Liu Bucai could also make the house their quarters. Hu had left all the arrangements to Yang. Although he thought it might be inconvenient to stay with a family he had never met, he could hardly object. Fortunately, Zhu was attentive and easy-going. They took to one another at first sight, and much of Hu’s anticipated discomfort disappeared. After introductions and greetings, Zhu said to Yang, “Elder Brother, Master has gone to Qingpu. If he does not return tonight, he will certainly be back tomorrow morning. He asked you to apologise to our honoured guests for his absence, and said they must stay here.” He turned to Hu and Liu. “Our house is small. I fear we cannot entertain you properly and shall put you to some inconvenience.” Hu naturally replied with the customary thanks and modest assurances. As he did so, he considered how to make good use of the half-day ahead rather than let it go to waste.

Before he had decided, a servant came to announce lunch. In this land of fish and rice, food was plentiful and delicious. An ordinary meal resembled a banquet, yet Zhu still said, “Forgive this poor reception. Tonight we shall give you a proper welcome.” Besides the four hosts and guests, three others joined them: the third Zhu brother, the accountant and the family tutor. They talked pleasantly of Wujiang’s scenery and local life. After lunch Yang asked whether Hu would like to take a nap in the guest room before deciding what to do, or go for a walk. “I have long heard that Tongli is a blessed place. Let us go and admire it.” Accompanied by Yang and Zhu, they went out through the front door, having arrived by the back. Before them stretched a long street paved with exceptionally even blue-grey stone slabs, its rows of buildings presenting a remarkably orderly appearance. Nine out of ten passers-by wore silk robes. Even country people in straw sandals were dressed in spotless short jackets and trousers of fine blue cotton. Most carried a long pipe of mottled bamboo. Some wore white-jade thumb rings; others had jade ornaments at their waists. These villagers alone gave some idea of the grace and refinement of the people of the Wu region. Outside a house hung with lanterns and festive decorations, Zhu stopped. “Would you two like to go in and amuse yourselves?” Several gambling tables were visible through the gate. “May strangers go in?” Hu asked. “Certainly. That is our custom here.” They went in and looked about. There was pai gow and the dice-shaking game. Hu was interested in local customs and wanted only to observe, so he declined to play. Liu, following his three rules—keep cool, wait, strike hard—was not yet willing to play either. They entered several more houses, making a circuit of each before leaving, until they had almost reached the northern end of the long street.

Neither guest seemed particularly entertained, and Zhu felt uneasy. Quietly he asked Yang, “What about calling on Little Jinxiu?” Yang hesitated. Hu, sharp of hearing and quick of mind, understood that Little Jinxiu must be a celebrated local beauty. A pleasure house was enjoyable only when one went with friends familiar with it; otherwise it could be thoroughly dull. He promptly intervened. “Please don’t trouble yourselves. A walk like this is quite enough.” As they spoke, they came to another lively house, different from the others. Its stone-framed gate stood wide open. Vendors of cooked food stretched from outside the entrance into the house, apparently even into the courtyard beyond the second gate. The people coming and going were not uniformly well dressed as elsewhere, but a mixture of every sort and station. Hu could not make out what kind of establishment it was. Liu recognised it at once. The others offered private gambling in gentlemen’s studies; this was a true gambling house. “If we mean to play, this is the sort of place,” he said. “‘A man who opens a restaurant cannot be afraid of big appetites.’ Here one can gamble freely.” Zhu understood and admired his discernment. “Third Master Liu has a good eye! This is the only proper gambling house in Tongli. Would you like to look inside? It is the only place that plays White Star Treasure.” At the name, Liu’s fingers began to itch. “That is a contest of minds. It is popular in eastern Zhejiang. How did it reach your town?” “It came from eastern Zhejiang originally.” A Shaoxing man named Zhang had opened a distillery in Tongli. An inveterate gambler, he had first gathered his friends to play behind closed doors. Before long others heard of it and joined them, and the operation grew. Just then a new police inspector, Mr Wu, arrived in Tongli. As Zhang’s fellow townsman, he took advantage of the situation, protected him in opening a regular gambling house, and collected a share of the gaming fees without lifting a finger. Money poured in daily; in two years he had amassed a hundred thousand. After hearing this account, Liu judged that the play must be substantial and worth a look.

In the main hall they found pai gow and the dice-shaking game, but relatively few players. When they passed through a side passage into the second hall, the scene was quite different. Three sides of a large square table were packed three rows deep: the first row seated, the second standing, the third standing on benches. Shoulders touched shoulders and heads pressed against heads, leaving scarcely a gap. Fortunately Zhu had some local standing. He found acquaintances willing to make room, and the party squeezed in. Whether it was the dice-shaking game of Jiangnan or Cantonese fan-tan, in which counters were gathered and counted, the result was an unknown quantity. White Star Treasure alone was a game whose result could be deliberately set by the house. That was why Liu called it a contest of minds: the players were matching wits with someone who was not in the room. This man, the setter, stayed upstairs. To prevent cheating and keep the fortunes of the table from disturbing his cool judgement, the staircase was closed off. A small opening in the wooden partition allowed the treasure box to travel in a basket. A boy upstairs attended to the errands. When the bell rang, the basket was hauled up, and he took the copper box to the setter, who reclined on an opium couch amid clouds of smoke. Once the result had been set, another bell signalled that the basket should be lowered. Only when the box reached the table did the players place their bets. The betting was exactly as in the dice-shaking game, except that four pai gow tiles—Heaven, Earth, Man and Harmony—represented the Vermilion Bird in front, the Dark Warrior behind, the Green Dragon on the left and the White Tiger on the right. Though the result was deliberately set, it still had a “pattern.” Liu borrowed another player’s chart of the results and studied it. The setter, he decided, was an expert: his choices were so unpredictable that they seemed to fit every pattern and in fact fitted none. Liu resolved to watch a little longer.

The same result, or “Old Treasure,” had already appeared three times in succession, each time the Earth tile. When the fourth box was opened, it too was Old Treasure. For the fifth round, the bell upstairs failed to ring. The croupier remained composed, but the players grew impatient and urged him to hurry. He sent someone to ring the bell and ask for the box. They rang and rang without any response. Only on the third attempt did a bell answer. Yet when the players looked at the box, they hesitated over their bets. After four repetitions of Old Treasure and such a long delay before the fifth, they imagined the setter upstairs must have exhausted his ingenuity to devise an infallible choice. This round would be especially hard to guess. “If I follow the pattern, it ought to be this gate,” someone said, placing his stake on Heaven. “You can’t follow the pattern now. It must be Old Treasure,” another declared, betting accordingly. “Quite right,” a third agreed. “All that delay was to work up the nerve to set Old Treasure again.” These two reinforced one another’s conviction, unconsciously influencing the others, who followed them with their stakes. When the box was opened, cheers broke out. It was indeed another Earth tile, and the house had to pay heavily on the most popular gate.

The sixth round took even longer. When the box was at last brought down, fewer people bet on Old Treasure. Yet Old Treasure appeared again. Astonishment now outweighed every other response: six Earth tiles in succession, and the surprise only grew as the run continued. “There’s a gambling ghost about!” someone told the croupier. “Burn a string of paper ingots for it.” “Nonsense! There’s no such thing.” With fewer and fewer players backing Earth, the house was collecting large stakes and making small payouts. The croupier was well satisfied and rejected the suggestion. When the ninth round produced Old Treasure again, the gamblers looked at one another and held back. No one believed it could appear yet another time. The man who had spoken of a gambling ghost now told a story. During the Qianlong reign, a gambling house had once thrown four nineteen times running in a single night. At last the players discovered the secret and all placed single-number bets on four, forcing the establishment to close its box and shut its doors. “What was the secret?” “The Qianlong Emperor’s dragon boat was spending the night in Tongli on his southern tour. With the true dragon present, how could anything but four appear?” “Of course!” Four was the Green Dragon. The questioner understood, but the present case still puzzled him. “What is happening now, then? The Emperor is in the capital. There can be no true dragon in Tongli. And the Earth tile is Entrance!” “That is why I say there is a gambling ghost.” “Then you think Old Treasure will come up again?” “I don’t know.” The man shook his head. “Even if I knew it would, I couldn’t bring myself to bet on it. To my mind, this round certainly won’t be ‘two eyes in a straight line.’” That expression described the Earth tile. The other gamblers agreed with him. Liu, who had been listening and watching coolly throughout, had an idea of his own. If one was following patterns, a strange pattern demanded a strange response: one should keep backing Old Treasure. If it was a contest of minds, then setting Old Treasure until no one dared bet on it was the cleverest strategy of all. On that reasoning, there might well be several more repetitions to come.

He had observed the first two rules, coolness and patience. Now it was time to strike hard. Just as the croupier was about to lift the lid, Liu called softly, “One moment, please.” “Certainly.” The croupier withdrew his hand. “We wait for every wager.” “What is the limit on a gate?” “A thousand taels.” “A thousand it is.” Liu took a roll of banknotes from his clothes, selected one and laid it on Earth. Every eye turned towards him. He was a stranger, and his unhurried manner, treating a thousand taels as casually as a string of copper cash, made him seem all the more mysterious and intriguing. Under more than a hundred watching eyes, the box was opened. Once again it was “two eyes in a straight line.” The room boiled over. Astonishment, envy, anger and regret found expression in a confusion of voices and gestures. Liu’s face remained unchanged. He merely turned and said quietly to Zhu, “A lucky chance.” Now everyone knew that this unfamiliar high-stakes gambler was Zhu’s friend, and admiring looks followed. To men of this world, reputation mattered above all. Zhu was naturally proud of a friend who had won such acclaim with a single wager. His face seemed gilded with delight, his heart as pleasantly warmed as though smoothed by an iron. Eager to cultivate his customers, the croupier added his compliments and told the settling clerk at the Green Dragon corner to waive the house commission, known in the trade as “water money,” normally three or five li. Liu, for his part, knew how to make a handsome gesture. When the clerk paid him three thousand taels in counters, he took an ivory counter worth a hundred taels and tossed it towards the Green Dragon corner.

When the box was placed on the table again, everyone waited to see how Liu would bet before deciding for themselves. There was a term for this too: a “lantern.” A lantern illuminated the path, and it might be red or black. Gamblers avoided black luck and sought red. Suppose people had been backing Old Treasure throughout, while one man had missed several rounds and only joined in when, as the saying went, he consulted the almanac on New Year’s Eve and found all the auspicious days already gone. That man was plainly unlucky. A player skilled at reading such signs would withdraw his stake and move it elsewhere. Liu, however, was a red lantern. He had dared to back Old Treasure when no one else would, and had won. What magnificent luck! Everyone wanted to follow him. As soon as he placed another thousand taels on Earth, wagers rained down beside it. The box was opened. The croupier and settling clerk exchanged stricken looks, while the players rejoiced. On this round of Old Treasure the house paid out more than twenty thousand taels. The whole room erupted. Even gamblers from the front hall came rushing in. Liu was treated like a god; the men on either side pressed themselves away, afraid of crowding him. At that moment someone tapped his shoulder. He turned to see Hu signalling with his eyes, then pursing his lips towards the door to indicate that they should leave. Liu was intensely reluctant to rise, but he did not dare disregard Hu. At last he ostentatiously took out his gold watch, glanced at it and nodded, as though the hour of an appointment had arrived. He gathered up his banknotes and stood. The hangers-on who made their living around gambling houses saw that he had won six thousand taels and crowded round with attentions. Liu understood the customary courtesies. When he went to the cashier to exchange his winnings, he bought a hundred taels’ worth of small counters and gave one to everyone who approached, refusing no one.

Even as he distributed these shares of his good fortune, he complained to Hu. “You shouldn’t have hurried me away. I had worked out the setter’s pattern. There were at least three more Old Treasures to come.” “It was precisely because you had worked it out that I hurried you away. Everyone was following your bets. A couple more rounds and you could have ruined the place. Why should we arrive in Tongli and immediately bring someone else to grief?” “Uncle Hu,” Zhu said, adopting Yang’s form of address, “you really understand the ways of the world, and you have a proper sense of honour.” Liu did not agree. At the gambling table there were no fathers and sons; considering friendship and loyalty only meant losing oneself. But in front of their host, and seeing Zhu’s respect for Hu, he could only keep his thoughts to himself. On reflection, he had won six thousand taels in a matter of moments. Truly, if only one could gamble without losing, it would be the finest occupation in the world. A smile came to his face. “Third Master Liu plays well, but Uncle Hu does still better by not playing,” Yang told Zhu. “No wonder he is so well liked. We ought both to learn from him.” “You are far too kind!” Hu rubbed his face with a smile. “You two are making me blush.” “Enough compliments,” Yang said. “Where shall we go next?” “Uncle Hu and Third Master Liu must be tired,” Zhu replied. “Let us return to my house, rest a little and have a drink.”

They walked leisurely back to the Zhu house. Its finest accommodation was a pavilion overlooking the water. When the guests arrived, some women relatives of the family had been staying there, but it had now been vacated, and Zhu invited Hu and the others inside to rest. They had scarcely sat down when an old servant called softly from the doorway, “Eldest Young Master!” With a glance he drew Zhu outside and whispered, “Mr Zhang from the gambling house is here. He says he wants to see one of our guests, and he has brought four kinds of gifts. Will you come and see him?” This was an unexpected visitor indeed. Zhu could not imagine whom he wanted to see: none of them had any previous connection with him. Puzzled, he hurried to the reception hall. Since the two knew each other, there was no need for preliminaries, and Zhu asked his purpose at once. It emerged that Zhang wanted to see Hu. From the idlers who had solicited gifts from Liu, he had learnt that Hu, out of kindness, had deliberately removed the “lantern” and saved the gambling house from a grave disaster. He had come expressly to offer thanks and make a friend. “Uncle Hu is my master’s friend and related to him by an adopted family tie,” Zhu said. “He is generous to everyone. Thanks are unnecessary, but he will certainly be willing to make a friend. As for these four gifts, however, you really needn’t have brought them.” “I know. A few things to eat are hardly an adequate token, but I felt awkward coming empty-handed.” Zhang too realised that these modest gifts were inappropriate. Offered as payment for a kindness, they might seem to belittle Hu’s intentions. He hesitated, then said, “Do this: don’t mention them to Mr Hu. But since they are here, taking them back would be a nuisance. Just leave them in the kitchen.” “That is sensible. Come along, and I shall take you in.”

Zhu led him straight to the waterside pavilion, introduced him and explained why he had come. Hu modestly disclaimed the unexpected praise, but Zhang was utterly sincere. He bowed to the ground and nearly went down on his knees. “Mr Hu, you have done me an enormous service. To tell you the truth”—he pointed to Liu—“in twenty or thirty years of gambling I have never met anyone like Third Master Liu. If he had played a little longer, with everyone following him and backing Entrance on the same side, I would have been ruined today.” “How so?” Hu asked. “Did Old Treasure keep coming up?” “Sixteen times in all. It really is something extraordinary. Fortunately”—Zhang still seemed shaken at the thought—“Third Master Liu was the only one who saw through it. Once he left, no one dared back Old Treasure. Taking the whole session together, the house still came out ahead.” Liu naturally looked pleased. With a deliberate smile he said, “I merely answered a strange pattern with a strange wager and happened to strike lucky.” “Gambling is about seizing an opportunity. When a chance like that comes once in a thousand years, Third Master Liu alone can take it. It sounds incredible, but the setter prepared only four Old Treasures, while sixteen appeared. The trouble began with the fifth.” “Ah, I remember,” Liu interrupted. “The fifth box wouldn’t come down. They rang three times before they got it. What happened?” The setter had been struck by a sudden illness and lost consciousness on his opium couch. The boy who carried the box did not understand. He pushed and shook him but could not wake him. Panicked by the insistent bell below, he simply sent the same box down again. After the sixteenth round, faint crying was heard upstairs. Someone unlocked the staircase door and went up. Cut off from those below and unable to summon help, the boy had grown more and more terrified until his face was drained of colour. As for the setter, his body was already cold.

It was an unheard-of occurrence. Even Liu, who had spent half his life in gambling houses, found it scarcely believable. In peaceful, prosperous Tongli, untouched by the alarms of war, even the Zhang family’s dog nursing the Li family’s kitten could become an endlessly relished piece of news. A marvel like “a dead man setting the treasure” was bound to cause a sensation. At the very moment Zhang was visiting Hu, teahouses and taverns everywhere were discussing it. The two guests at the Zhu house instantly became the talk of Tongli. Qiu Fengyan and Zhou Yiming, who had arrived that afternoon and were rewarding themselves with a quiet drink in a tavern, heard the story too. They exchanged delighted smiles. Qiu remained restrained, but Zhou could not contain himself. During his time with Hu he had learnt something of the art of building a name. He revealed who Hu and Liu were, explaining that they were not simply Zhu’s friends but friends of Zhu’s master, Yu Wucheng. In everyone’s mind, Yu’s name at once acquired a new resonance as well.

News travelled remarkably fast. Early the next morning, as Yu Wucheng returned from Qingpu to Tongli, he stopped for tea in a village along the way and was already being asked about Hu Xueyan and Liu Bucai. Thus, when he first met Hu in Eldest Brother Zhu’s waterside pavilion, his opening words were, “You have only just arrived, brother, and already your name is on everyone’s lips. Those of us who have spent decades in the brotherhoods must acknowledge ourselves outdone!” There was an unpleasant edge to this, which Hu naturally detected. He could only reply, “We owe it all to your reputation, Brother Yu. Such pointless attention is better avoided. That is why I have not ventured outside today, but have waited here expressly for you, ready to follow your instructions in everything.” Their first encounter had scarcely begun before host and guest seemed at odds. Alarmed, Yang Fengmao tugged at Yu’s sleeve. “Master,” he said softly, “please come this way.” Drawing him aside, Yang explained in detail how highly Third Granny valued this new bond of adopted kinship. Finally, with particular gravity, he said, “Before I left, Third Granny called me aside especially to give you this message: Uncle Hu is an exceptionally capable and loyal man. She says that in all her decades of experience she has seen plenty of ruthless men and plenty of kindly, honest ones, but this is the first time she has met a man who is both ruthless and kindly.”

“What?” Yu asked. “I do not understand her. How can a man be both ruthless and kindly?” “Kindly in his nature, ruthless in his methods. I must say Third Granny’s judgment is extraordinary. No one else could have found those words.” “And do you think she is right?” “Of course she is!” Yang continued to relay the maternal instructions. “Third Granny says it is no way to go on, living here dependent on others and having to swallow their slights. Our chance to improve matters rests entirely with Uncle Hu. You must treat him with particular respect.” “And what happened at Boss Zhang’s gambling house yesterday?” “That,” Yang replied with an excited expression, “brought you credit too, Master!” He recounted the whole affair. “That is unusual. She was right to call him kindly,” Yu said. “That fellow Liu looks like an old hand at the pleasures of life, yet he obeys Hu meekly enough. You can see from that that Hu has some ability.” “More than a little. Once you talk to him, Master, you will see for yourself.”

When Yu resumed his conversation with Hu, his manner was quite different. He was exceedingly courteous and insisted that Hu and Liu take the places of honour on the raised couch. In reckoning their relationships, Liu, as Furong’s uncle, belonged to the senior generation, so their forms of address differed accordingly. Yu called Hu “Old Hu,” but addressed Liu formally as “Third Master Liu.” Liu in turn respectfully called him “Elder Yu,” which, compared with Hu’s “Brother Yu,” seemed to put Liu a generation below him again. In the brotherhoods everyone reckoned such relationships separately. The titles might be confused, but in practice they were all friends on an equal footing. Yu enforced strict rules among his disciples. Yang and Zhu remained standing to attend to their needs, while he sat in a grand armchair beside the pavilion window, talking at length with Hu about the Songjiang grain-transport brotherhood. He referred to the Old Master as the “Songjiang Chief” and told many stories of their adventures together in their youth, lamenting that life was harder now than it had been. Liu could only sit and listen. As he did so, he studied Yu. Although over sixty, the man dressed like a wealthy young idler, in satin shoes and a satin robe, with snow-white cuffs that he kept turning up and down. When lowered, the cuffs covered his hands, so he had to raise a thumb to hold the cuff back before he could move freely. This was a characteristic gesture among men of the brotherhoods, but Yu’s imposing build and splendid clothes gave it a particular flourish. Whenever his thumb rose, the ring of glass-clear green jade upon it flashed brilliantly, adding still further to his air of distinction.

What both fascinated and puzzled Liu, however, was the way Yu’s satin robe, glittering in the slanting sunlight, moved without any breeze. A bulge would appear here, something would wriggle there. What could cause it? He watched intently for a long time without solving the mystery, until his curiosity became almost unbearable. Just as he was about to ask, the answer appeared. Zhu brought in a large platter of cherries from Dongting East Mountain in Lake Tai. Yu took a cluster and held out his open palm. A furry little squirrel promptly emerged from his sleeve. Its large, bright eyes darted about; then it raised its forepaws, grasped a cherry in Yu’s palm, and began nibbling. Liu broke into a broad smile. “Elder Yu, you certainly know how to amuse yourself! Why keep a squirrel on your person? Is it not a nuisance?” “Once it is tame, there is no trouble.” “You keep it there all day?” “Yes.” Yu nodded. “We hardly ever part.” “Does it not bother you, crawling all over you from morning to night?” “It sleeps sometimes, naturally. Put it in my pocket and it settles down. If you like it, Third Master Liu, take it and amuse yourself.” “No, no!” Liu waved his hands. “A gentleman does not deprive another man of something he loves. Besides, to tell the truth, I should find it rather creepy having it crawl all over me.”

Yu smiled without answering, then turned to Zhu. “Will the meal be ready soon?” “Whenever you and Uncle Hu wish, Master. If you are not particularly hungry, it would be better to wait a little. The shark’s fin stewed with ham needs more time over the fire.” “Then let us wait. Bring Uncle Hu some refreshments to take the edge off his hunger. Once we have discussed our business, we can enjoy our wine properly.” The significant words were “discussed our business.” Hu feared that Yu might not wish Liu to hear their secrets, and gave him a casual-looking glance. Liu understood and rose. “You talk. I shall use the time to go into town and see a friend.” “Then I shall accompany you,” Zhu volunteered. Liu intended to see Zhou Yiming, their reserve force concealed from view. He could hardly let Yu’s people know about him. Clasping his hands, he said, “Please do not trouble yourself. You are our host and must stay here. Besides, I know Tongli well; there is no danger of my getting lost.” This was untrue: it was his first visit to Tongli too. Unless he said so, however, Zhu would send someone to guide him. Sure enough, his host pressed the matter no further and let him go alone.

Yu, Hu, and Yang then conferred in private. Yu said that he was willing to follow Hu’s arrangements and explained the position frankly. The men who had been preparing to seize the boatload of foreign guns were all under the direction of Lame Changgen, one of Zhou Lichun’s capable subordinate leaders. They needed Yu because this water route lay within the Songjiang brotherhood’s sphere of influence: he had to approach the Songjiang Chief and clear the way. Now Songjiang had adopted the position that, since both sides were friends, it could only stand aside and remain neutral. Changgen therefore hesitated to act. The proposed way out suited him very well, but he would have to discuss the terms with Hu. “Naturally,” Hu said. “How can I meet this friend?” “That still has to be arranged. Old Hu, I am a plain-spoken man.” Yu’s tone became solemn. “There is something I want to ask you first. You are family now, and my mother’s judgment is never wrong, so of course I trust you. But I have suffered at the hands of those officials, and cannot put much faith in them. When my son first wanted to take the provincial military examination, I told him, ‘There is nothing so wonderful about being an official. Do not bother with it.’ But my mother wanted her grandson to make a name for himself; she arranged everything and escorted him to the examination herself. As for this amnesty, it makes no difference to me personally. If it succeeds, the men can draw military pay and at least feed themselves. Bringing them over would also be a service to the court. What I fear is that those grand officials will say one thing and mean another. If something goes wrong, blaming you will be no use. And for me it will then be more than a question of whether I can still get along in the brotherhoods!”

This long speech, with its barbed insinuations, left Hu rather puzzled. What exactly did Yu mean? He seized on the phrase “something goes wrong” and thought hard until the meaning gradually became clear. “You mean that once the men have gone over, the officials might turn on them and disown their promises?” “Exactly! If they merely turned their backs on them, we could still manage. What I fear is—” Yu shook his head. “If they really did that, it would be terrible.” “Do you mean”—Hu found the question difficult to utter—“that they might kill the men who surrender?” “There is no telling.” “They will not!” Only now did Hu speak with absolute firmness. “I guarantee they will not. Brother, let me tell you plainly: my contact is Education Commissioner He. He is about to receive an excellent appointment. The leading grand councillor in the capital graduated in the same examination year as he did, and so did many provincial governors. His year is very much in favour, and their words carry weight.” “And how close are you to Commissioner He?” “He has asked me to find him a concubine. That is all there is to our friendship!” “Then there is nothing more to say.” Yu looked pleased. “Did he mention what advantages he could offer?” He hurriedly added, “I do not mean for me. I mean for Changgen and his men.”

“On that point, brother, you can imagine the answer without my telling you. If they abandon darkness for the light, the court will naturally reward them. Official appointments will certainly be available.” Hu went on, following He Guiqing’s instructions. “The men should at least receive a special gratuity equal to a month’s pay. After that, their pay will come from the military finance office wherever they are assigned. A single month’s gratuity may seem a little meagre, but there is really no help for it. So much territory has been lost that tax receipts have fallen greatly. You know the circumstances as well as anyone.” Yu certainly did: the fact that he and his followers had nothing to do was itself evidence of the decline in imperial revenue. He nodded. “The gratuity is not the main thing. Changgen wants to choose where his men are stationed after they become government troops. To be frank, he wants to remain in this district. That is something”—he seemed to find it difficult to say—“we really must arrange.” Hu was no expert in such matters, but common sense told him this would be difficult. After a moment’s thought he asked, “Then let me ask you, brother: if he were ordered to fight the Small Swords Society, would he agree?” “No. They have all stood on the same gangplank. How could he bring himself to do it?” “Then we have a difficulty. The troops stationed here are all intended to fight the Small Swords Society. If the military situation became urgent, a single order would require them to march. Refusing to go would be disobedience. Imagine you were their commanding officer. How would you deal with it?” “I had not thought of that.” Yu scratched his head, looking deeply troubled.

Hu could see that Yu had probably thumped his chest and promised without reservation that this could be arranged; hence his present anxiety. While Hu was still puzzling over a way to help him, Yang spoke. “Master, you must tell him it would be better to accept a posting farther away. If he remains in his home district, the Small Swords men may fail to understand his position. Or they may come to him for refuge in an emergency. If he turns them away, he will hurt their feelings; if he helps them, harbouring rebels is no trifling charge. Why not move away and escape that dilemma?” “That puts it very clearly,” Hu said, taking the opportunity to persuade him. “Give him that answer, brother. If Changgen understands reason and will listen to it, he is sure to stop making demands that others cannot fulfil.” Their arguments relieved Yu. “That will do for today.” He rose. “I think we should be able to reach agreement on the main points. Let us eat.”

They had to wait for Liu before beginning the banquet, but he was slow to return. They took some refreshments and sat talking until it was quite dark, when he finally hurried in. He apologized to his host, but found a moment to signal to Hu that something had developed with Zhou. Hu’s face and manner betrayed nothing. At dinner he talked and laughed freely with Yu about every imaginable subject. Afterwards they drank tea. Hu gave a yawn that might or might not have been deliberate, and Zhu suggested that the guests rest. He escorted them to their rooms, and they exchanged goodnights. Hu and Liu had separate rooms connected by a door. As a precaution, Hu first made sure that no member of Zhu’s household was staying nearby, then beckoned Liu in and asked for the details. “Old Zhou knows this district well and has friends everywhere along the waterways. From what he has heard, old Yu is in a very awkward position. Has he said anything to you about it?” “A little, but nothing about being in an ‘awkward position.’ What does Zhou say?” “He has heard that this is the Songjiang brotherhood’s territory. Many people know about your friendship with You Laowu. So when the Songjiang Chief announced that he was withdrawing, it might have been called neutrality, but everyone else took it to mean that he was no longer backing old Yu. Loyalty matters in the brotherhoods, but it depends on personal acquaintance. Yu has lost all his own territory and relies here on the Songjiang Chief’s name. Once the Chief stops backing him, nobody pays him any heed.”

Comparing this account with what he had seen of Yu’s circumstances, Hu found Zhou’s information quite credible. Yu was indeed in a predicament. He lacked the power either to bring anything about or to prevent it, and had become a man of little consequence. If he retained any usefulness, it lay in the thread that still connected him with Changgen. “I do not see why you need to humour old Yu so much,” Liu said. “He is like the dregs left after brewing medicine: his strength is spent and he is no use.” “That is not the way to put it. Once we have made a friend, we cannot be too calculating.” “Friendship is one thing; serious business is another. If he is no use any more, why keep yourself entangled with him?” “No.” Hu was not yet ready to tell him about Changgen. “I need him to lead me to someone important. That is why I must still work with him.” “Whether you work with him is your affair. But have you considered whether the other man will?” That brought Hu up short. Yes: Changgen must also know how sharply Yu’s standing had fallen. Whether he would trust Yu as openly as Hu did was therefore very doubtful. Perhaps the people Zhou meant when he said that nobody paid Yu any heed were precisely Changgen’s men. The thought convinced Hu that placing Zhou in reserve had been an indispensable move. He quietly told Liu about his private discussion with Yu and their agreement to arrange a meeting with Changgen. Then he instructed Liu to see Zhou again early the next morning and ask him to use his friends along the waterways to investigate Changgen thoroughly, particularly his relationship with Yu.

The next morning Liu again slipped out alone on the pretext of visiting a friend. Hu took morning tea with Yang and Zhu. They said that Yu had gone out early on business and would not return until the afternoon. Hu understood that he had gone to arrange the meeting with Changgen. After lunch, thoroughly bored, Hu was thinking of using the spare time to inquire into the silk market when Liu hurried back. The moment he saw Hu, he beckoned discreetly, drew him into a secluded spot, and asked in a low voice, “Has old Yu returned?” “How did you know he had gone out?” “Never mind that for the moment.” “He has not come back yet.” “Good, good! You were clearly destined to be saved.” “What?” Hu was badly startled. “What do you mean?” “Zhou Yiming is a capable fellow. What he has discovered will give you a shock. Changgen is preparing a Hongmen banquet—a feast that conceals a trap. It is meant to catch not only you, but old Yu as well.” “This—” Hu steadied himself and thought for a moment, then asked calmly, “Take your time. What has happened?”

According to Zhou’s information, Changgen had heard that the Songjiang Chief had changed his mind and that Yu was talking about an amnesty. Suspecting Yu of intending to betray his friends, he had decided to carry matters through without half measures and seize Yu as well. He planned to abduct them and demand the boatload of foreign guns as ransom. His scheme was to invite Yu and Hu to his house for a meeting, trap them there, and move them to a secret place. Once he had obtained what he wanted, he would take the guns and join the Taipings. Fearing that Hu might refuse to venture so far into the tiger’s den, he had also prepared an alternative venue: a private brothel in the busy part of Tongli. Two sisters who had fallen into prostitution lived there, the younger named Miaozhu and the elder Miaozhen. Miaozhen was Changgen’s exclusive mistress. Like Zhu’s house, theirs had a landing just outside the back door. The captives could be bundled into a boat in the middle of the night without anyone knowing. The report was astonishing, but also highly doubtful. Hu could scarcely believe it. Such conduct would be a grave violation of the brotherhoods’ code. If Changgen intended it, his preparations must be extremely secret. How could Zhou have discovered them so easily? “I thought the same,” Liu replied when Hu raised the question. “But Old Zhou is adamant that the information is completely reliable. He says he happened to meet someone who knew the inside story. He admits it was an extraordinary coincidence, but says your luck is running high: that is why you have this chance to escape disaster.” “Very well. We can test it easily enough. What did you say the sisters were called?” “Miaozhen and Miaozhu.”

Hu nodded and looked around. A writing desk stood by the window, with a brush and inkstone. The inkstone was covered in dust, only half an inkstick remained, and the brush he took from its rack had a worn-out point. They would have to make do. He poured a little tea into the inkstone himself, began grinding the ink, and beckoned Liu closer. “Find any scrap of paper,” he said softly, “and write this for me. Just one sentence: ‘If not at Changgen’s, then at Miaozhen’s.’” He went outside to keep watch. In his haste Liu could find no paper. Necessity supplied an idea: he spread a snow-white Hangzhou silk handkerchief on the table, wrote the ten characters, folded it, and handed it to Hu, who carefully hid it in the pocket of his underjacket next to his skin. Hu now changed his plans. Claiming that he wanted an afternoon nap, he shut himself in his room to consider how to meet this possible and unexpected turn of events. Liu meanwhile joined the gaming table arranged by their host. Shortly after four, when refreshments were being served, Yu returned and immediately asked for Hu. By then Hu had actually fallen asleep. Zhu woke him and invited him to the waterside pavilion to meet Yu.

“I have seen Changgen. He was delighted to hear you had come, and wants to give you a welcoming dinner tomorrow evening, when you can discuss everything in detail,” Yu said. “I told him all you said. He quite understands that the provincial treasury is not what it once was. A month’s gratuity will at least give the men something to show for it.” Yu spoke enthusiastically, but Hu was noticeably cool. He asked calmly, “Where does he intend to give me dinner?” “Wherever suits the guest. If you do not mind the journey, you can go to his house. He lives at Pingwang, which is not really so far away. Otherwise, here in Tongli. He has a long-standing mistress here, a well-known private courtesan. Her name is—” He tapped his forehead. “My memory has grown poor these last two years. Why has it suddenly escaped me?” “Is it Miaozhen?” “Miaozhen, yes, Miaozhen! Old Hu, how did you know?” “Brother,” Hu answered in an exceptionally cool voice, “I shall show you something.” It was, of course, Liu’s silk handkerchief. Hu spread it on the table, revealing the ten large, hastily written characters: “If not at Changgen’s, then at Miaozhen’s.” Yu’s face clouded with suspicion. “Old Hu, what does this mean?” Hu did not answer, but continued with his own point. “Brother, we are in the same boat now, with our lives bound together. Whatever you know, you must not conceal it from me.” His grave expression told Yu that there was much behind this, and that the situation might be urgent. Taking Hu’s arm, he said, “Come. Let us talk in my room.”

The quarters Zhu had prepared for his master were not only elegant but secure: a little courtyard thick with flowers and trees, with three single-storey rooms along its northern side. Yu occupied the innermost room. He led Hu inside and sat beside a small round rosewood table at the window, facing outwards so that nobody passing could escape his notice. The precaution was really unnecessary. Ever since the plot to seize the foreign guns had begun, these three fine rooms had been forbidden ground. Apart from Zhu and Yang, nobody dared enter without permission. “Old Hu, I imagine you must have another channel of information,” Yu said. “Since you say our lives are bound together, do not keep it from me if your side has other plans.” A worldly man’s eyes were sharper than shears: he had seen the clue at once. Hu naturally concealed it no longer. “We have no other plans. Another channel of information, yes. But that too came about unexpectedly. I shall tell you every detail presently.” He paused. “First let me ask you something. What sort of man is Changgen? Are his ties with you strong enough?” “He has always been a schemer. His nickname is ‘Outdoing Wu Yong.’ As for his ties with me, that is harder to say.” “Why?” “I am not particularly close to him personally, but his master belonged to my generation. He was called Bingkui, the Golden-haired Dog. I once saved his life; that is too long a story to tell now. Changgen was one of his favourite disciples. On his deathbed, the Golden-haired Dog told his disciples, ‘I cannot repay my debt to Yu in this life. Whenever you see him in future, you must treat him as you would me.’ Only after they nodded their assent did he breathe his last. That is why his disciples all call me Master Yu, and why Changgen came to me for help.”

“Then this man is betraying his master and dishonouring his forebears!” Yu was appalled. Within their brotherhood, that was an accusation of the gravest misconduct. An offender faced the punishment of “three knife thrusts, six holes,” without mercy. Yu grew so tense that for a moment he could not speak. “You probably find it hard to believe, brother?” “Yes.” Yu nodded slowly. “Every time Changgen lifts his lame leg, he has another scheme. I do not suppose he is a good man. But even if a man ignores loyalty, he must consider the consequences. If he acts on the first day, does he not fear what I may do on the second?” “You act on the first, and I shall act on the second” was much like “Three years is not too late for a gentleman to take revenge.” Both promised retaliation; the difference lay in the timing. One allowed three years, while the other demanded redress the very day after an injury. Yu’s question was reasonable, but Hu could answer it. As Yu himself had said, a man who ignored loyalty would still consider advantage and danger. Changgen believed that Yu had lost his power. A tiger brought down to the plains might be bullied by dogs; there was nothing surprising about it. Hu could not put that bluntly, however, for fear of hurting him. “You are right, brother,” he replied. “But Changgen is already preparing to flee to the other side. Naturally, he is not afraid of your acting on the second day.” “The monk may escape, but his temple cannot—” “Settling accounts with him comes later.” Growing impatient, Hu interrupted and brought him back to the point. “First we must deal with what is before us. It is safer to believe this warning than to dismiss it.”

Yu shook his head. “It is not a question of belief. We must establish whether the information is true.” He looked up and fixed Hu with a searching gaze. “Where did you hear it?” “From a Hunan man named Zhou. He used to work at a naval yamen and knows the waterways well. He obtained the information.” “Can you bring him here for us to meet?” “Of course. I shall ask Third Master Liu to fetch him.” Liu was summoned from the gaming table. In Yu’s presence Hu explained the errand, taking particular care to say that it was Yu who wanted to meet Zhou. This was a hint. Zhou would surely understand what had happened and could prepare his answers in advance. While they waited, Yu sent for Yang and Zhu, closed the door, and told them what Zhou had discovered. They disagreed: Yang believed the report, while Zhu thought it unreliable. Zhu argued that so many people visited the sisters Miaozhen and Miaozhu every day that their threshold was almost worn through. With all those eyes about, such an abduction would be impossible. Besides, the river behind their house was close to the wharf, with boats coming and going throughout the night. Quietly putting Yu and Hu aboard a boat and carrying them out through the water gate would be no easy matter.

“You were brought up as a rich man’s son. You have never experienced this sort of trick,” Yang countered calmly. “Once he sets his mind on it, there are any number of ways. To tell the truth, I see Changgen as another Wei Yan, with the traitor’s bone in his skull. The story is seven or eight parts true out of ten. Fortunately, our friend Zhou brought us the news early, so we still have time to take precautions. Even so, it will be difficult.” “Why?” Yu asked. “Say what you mean and ask Uncle Hu’s advice.” “Uncle Hu, do you think we should take a gentle approach or a forceful one?” “What do you mean by a gentle approach?” “Expose his trick when we meet and persuade him not to proceed.” “No, no!” Yu shook his head vigorously. “That sort of softness will only make him despise us. If he really dares do this, he has the heart of a wolf and the guts of a dog. Why would he listen to human reason?” “That is true. A gentle approach may be useless,” Hu said. “But if we use force, it must be done properly. The first and most important thing is to get the evidence into our hands.” “Exactly!” Yang slapped his thigh. “Uncle Hu has put the drop straight into the oil bottle. Nothing could be more precise. There are plenty of ways to act forcefully, but everything depends on the evidence.” “We can discuss how to obtain evidence later,” Yu said. “First tell us what forceful measures you propose.” Strangely, Yang hesitated and fell silent. Only after repeated urging from his master did he admit, “My plan will not do.” It all came back to evidence. His scheme required Yu and Hu to enter the trap first and then find a way out, thereby obtaining solid proof of Changgen’s crime. If their coordination failed, they might be unable to escape and might instead provoke Changgen into killing them. Then even an immortal could not save them.

Before they reached any conclusion, Liu arrived with Zhou. Zhou stood below Hu in status, but with Yu and his disciples he was a friend on equal terms. Moreover, by bringing the warning he had already done Yu a great service. They therefore treated him with marked courtesy, and some time passed in polite conversation before they came to the point. Naturally, Hu had to put the question. “Old Zhou, your information makes a good deal of sense. Still, there are questions about it. So much depends on this that we must establish the facts. Can you tell us how you obtained it?” Had Hu asked him alone, Zhou would readily have told the truth. With Yu and his disciples, whom he was meeting for the first time, present, he could not help feeling wary. Yu detected his hesitation and spoke with great sincerity. “Brother Zhou, speak freely. Not half a word will escape anyone here. If you do not believe me, I shall swear an oath upon my mother—” Zhou’s expression changed at once, and he waved his hands repeatedly. “You must not do that!” After a moment’s thought he asked, “May I ask, Master Yu, whether you know all the wicked things Changgen has done?” “Some, but I cannot claim to know everything.” “Have you heard how he mistreated a widow?” “Yes.” Yu nodded. “He began an affair with her and then demanded money whenever he lost at gambling. He forced her to give up all her private savings and jewellery. Then he wanted her to sell the land set aside to support ancestral rites. When she refused, he threatened to expose and disgrace her. She felt that whatever she did, she could no longer face the world, and hanged herself. Is that the affair?” “Yes. Her surname was Wei. She had a brother serving under Changgen, but Changgen was careless and paid him no attention—” “I understand.” Yu needed no more explanation. “Is this Wei a close friend of yours?” “No, I have only just met him. One of my sworn brothers is his close friend. When I mentioned Changgen to my sworn brother this time, he brought Young Wei to meet me. There is no doubt that the information is true. Unfortunately, Wei does not yet know the details.”

“That is enough already,” Yu said. “Would Young Wei be willing to come forward as a witness?” “He would not,” Hu answered. “And even if he did, a statement without proof could simply be denied by Changgen.” “Then I shall go and meet him alone!” Yu declared. “No. Going alone would achieve nothing, brother. He would certainly make no move. I think we must abandon the matter. I am grateful that you have agreed to leave that boatload of guns alone, and I shall repay your kindness in some other way—” “Oh, come!” Yu interrupted. “Old Hu, you cannot say that. For things to reach this miserable state! If I submit to such humiliation, how can I ever show my face again? Here is what we shall do: you go back first. I shall talk to the Songjiang Chief and make certain your guns reach Hangzhou. As for Changgen, of course I shall not let him off. I may be camped on borrowed ground, but I shall still fight this out with him.” Seeing that Yu was letting wounded pride govern him, Hu decided they should not continue the discussion. He must first cool down and lose some of his anger. Hu signalled to Liu and waved his hand. “You cannot swallow hot porridge in a hurry. Let us discuss it later. With you here, brother, there is nothing that cannot be managed.” “Exactly!” Liu understood the unspoken request and chimed in. “I shall play a round of pai gow with Elder Yu first, to give his mind a change.” He practically dragged Yu away. There were plenty of idle dependants in Zhu’s household; as soon as the game was set out, people gathered, and they soon had enough players for the small version of pai gow. Liu deliberately insisted that Yu take the bank, keeping him occupied so that Hu and Yang could devise a plan at leisure.

Liu had guessed exactly right: this was precisely what Hu Xueyan wanted. Hu now understood how much real influence Yu Wucheng possessed, what abilities he had, and how he thought and behaved. He felt that a discussion with Yang Fengmao would be more useful than one with Yu. There was, of course, another indispensable participant: Zhou Yiming. The three sat close together in the waterside pavilion to work out a plan. Hu began by explaining his position. His purpose had changed. Getting that boatload of foreign rifles to Hangzhou was now a secondary concern; his chief aim was to help Yu Wucheng regain his standing and thus prove worthy of Third Granny’s regard. In the brotherhood, such a gesture counted for everything. Yang’s feelings toward Hu had changed again and again, from indifference to considerable admiration; now they had become profound gratitude. “Uncle Hu,” he said frankly, “my master may not yet understand what is in your heart, but I understand it completely. Give us your instructions, and whatever we can do, we shall do with all our strength. Since this is what you have in mind, may I ask how you think my master can recover his position?” “On two fronts: with the authorities and within the brotherhood,” Hu answered at once. “As far as the authorities are concerned, successfully arranging this surrender would naturally be best. Failing that, there must be action to put the men down by force. That, too, would be a great service.” Yang understood. His heart began to pound, but he was not yet ready to commit himself. He watched Hu intently, waiting for him to continue. “Within the brotherhood, we must make your master’s name ring out again!” “Exactly.” On this point Yang agreed wholeheartedly. “That is what I have always wanted. But we need an opportunity. If only he could accomplish one or two things that would really impress people!”

“The opportunity is right before us. But let us put that aside for a moment. An idea has just occurred to me; see what you think of it. There is a saying: ‘Repair the plank road in plain sight, but secretly cross at Chencang.’ Lame Changgen’s whole attention is fixed on your master and me. With both eyes on Tongli, he is neglecting everything else. I want to take advantage of that opening to get the arms shipment out of Shanghai at once. Fortunately, we have people in Songjiang to look after it. Nothing should go wrong.” “Yes, yes!” Yang nodded repeatedly. “That is a risk worth taking.” “But there is another part to it. I should like Shaowu to escort the shipment. Of course,” Hu added quickly, “if anything does go wrong, he will certainly not be held responsible. My idea is that once the arms reach Hangzhou, this service will allow us to put his name near the top when recommendations for rewards are submitted to the throne. It should do him some good, and it will give us something to show Third Granny.” “Excellent. If you have chosen him, Uncle Hu, what more is there to say? I shall go back to Suzhou and tell him myself.” “You need not go. I shall arrange it.”

They next discussed how to deal with Changgen. Hu and Yang agreed that everything depended on evidence. Once they had proof, any course would be open to them. They could call in government troops to surround and suppress his men with full justification; or, on a smaller scale, they could convene an incense-hall tribunal under their own brotherhood’s rules. Confronted with the evidence, he could have no defense and would have to submit to their punishment, even the sentence of “three knife thrusts and six holes.” “At present all we have is this report. There are no letters or written documents, and no one will come forward to testify. What can we do to him?
