Naturally, I could find a way to have him brought before a magistrate and interrogated under torture. The resentment that would earn me is a minor matter. What matters is the damage to your leader’s reputation: people would say he had used official power to harm another man. I am sure he would never accept that name.” “Certainly not, certainly not,” Yang said repeatedly. “Once a man acquires that reputation, he can scarcely hold his ground in the brotherhood.” “So unless we abandon the matter and keep clear of his trap, there is only one course left: ‘How can you catch the tiger’s cub without entering the tiger’s den?’” “I have thought of that too, but it seemed too dangerous.” “Provided the rescue is properly coordinated, there is no danger. Here is what I propose...”

Hu’s plan was to accompany Yu Wucheng to this Banquet at Hongmen, prepared for the negotiations to break down and for both of them to be kidnapped. When their captors’ boat reached a checkpoint, men would board unexpectedly on the pretext of an inspection and rescue them. Changgen’s treachery would then be established. Whether to settle the affair through the authorities or within the brotherhood could be decided afterward. Yang listened closely, working through every stage, and found Hu’s plan more thorough than his own. Their ideas for the first part were the same; the difference lay in the escape. Yang had intended to station men in ambush and stage a rescue like the opera Seizing Adou by the River. Hu would use official authority as cover, “besieging Zhao to save Yan.” One meant a rescue by force, the other by strategy; the latter was plainly superior. “Uncle Hu, I have complete confidence in your ability to meet whatever happens. My only fear is that my master’s violent temper may provoke Changgen into a rage. Apart from that, with the rescue properly arranged, we cannot fail.” “Success depends on who knows what,” Hu replied. “Changgen thinks he is hidden while we stand in the open. In fact, it is he who is exposed and we who are hidden. If word gets out, we shall be the ones exposed again.” “Yes,” Yang said solemnly. “I suggest that only you, Mr Zhou, and I know of this. Once the arrangements are complete, we can tell my master.” “Exactly.” They gave nothing away. After the meal, Liu Bucai again kept Yu company at the gaming table while the three resumed their discussion. When every detail had been settled, they went about their separate tasks.

The first task, naturally, was to inform Yu Wucheng. He objected to parts of the plan. Having his own son escort the rifles, for instance, might allow people to say afterward that he had been the first to betray Changgen. That would sound very bad. But he had always relied on others to accomplish things. Yang was his most capable disciple, while Hu had shown himself superior at every turn to anyone on Yu’s side. Their newly established family connection made it still harder to object. He therefore agreed with an expansive air. “I leave it all to you. Whatever you say, I shall do!” “There is one point on which I need your decision, Brother Yu. Once everything has been exposed, shall we settle it officially or privately? If it is to go through the authorities, I shall make the arrangements. If it is to be settled privately, that is a matter for your brotherhood, and I cannot interfere.” Yu considered. “Privately, I think. Bringing in the authorities would not be a good thing.” “Then we shall do as you wish. I shall be with you throughout, in any case, ready to follow your instructions whenever anything arises.”

The words “with you throughout” sank deep into Yu’s mind. They gave him the sense that here was a man who would share his troubles and good fortune alike, and his feelings toward Hu changed accordingly. He was generous by nature, with something of a spoiled young gentleman’s reckless habit of acting on impulse. “Fengmao,” he said at once, “tell your fellow disciples and all the younger men that from now on Uncle Hu’s word carries exactly the same weight as yours or mine.” “Yes,” Yang answered with willing sincerity. “We would not dare treat Uncle Hu with anything less than respect.” “You are too kind, far too kind!” Hu felt both pleased and abashed. “With such affection from you and your disciple, how can I ever repay you?” “My dear Hu, you have it the wrong way round...” “Master!” Yang interrupted. “This is not the time for that. Uncle Hu still has urgent business to attend to. We can talk over supper tonight.”

Hu knew that in the world of the brotherhood, the more seasoned a man was, the more readily he took offense or grew suspicious. Every point of etiquette had to be made clear. Zhou Yiming had appeared without warning, which already suggested that Hu was setting up a separate camp and acting on his own. To keep Qiu Fengyan hidden as well, another man working in the shadows, would be altogether improper. He therefore took the opportunity to explain. “There is something I must make clear to you, Brother Yu. Zhou and I have another friend, Qiu Fengyan, the officer appointed to escort that shipment of rifles. Both of them were worried about me and have now hurried to Tongli to help. More hands make the work easier. Since we are deploying our people, we ought by rights to be together; but too many of us in one place might attract attention. I should like your opinion: should we all lodge together or remain apart?” Yu had no means of deciding which arrangement was better, but he could understand what he was being told. Since Hu was worried about attracting attention, his own preference was obvious. “Apart would be better, apart would be better!” Yu replied without hesitation. “Mr Qiu belongs to the class of officials eligible for subprefectural and county magistracies. Like Third Master Liu, he is excellent company. It was through him that Third Granny came to take Mrs Hu as a sworn daughter.” “Oh!” said Yu. “Then I must show him some courtesy. I shall send an invitation tomorrow and ask him to dinner.” “That is unnecessary. Once the business is successfully concluded, we can celebrate properly. If you would like to meet him, I can bring him here tonight.” “Excellent! I only hope he will forgive the informality.”

With that settled, Hu went with Zhou to see Qiu. At the inn they found him holding a volume of Huang Zhongze’s Complete Works of Liangdang Studio, reciting poetry with a tipsy, misty gaze. At the sight of Hu he laughed. “My dear Hu, I truly admire you! Come, come, let me offer you a cup first.” “Wait, wait. I shall drink with you over supper later. For the moment, ‘the military situation is urgent.’ Put down your cup.” To deprive Qiu of his wine was certainly to spoil his pleasure. But his admiration for Hu was genuine, and he accepted whatever Hu said. He joined him at another table to discuss the business in detail. Hu explained the plan for the secret shipment and had Qiu write three letters on the spot. One was to the Songjiang Chief, explaining the circumstances and requesting protection along the waterways. Another, written in Qiu’s own name to Wang Youling, set out Yu Shaowu’s appointment to escort the rifles, providing a record on which a future recommendation for reward could be based. The third introduced Zhou Yiming to He Guiqing, saying that Zhou had confidential matters of importance to report in person.

When the letters were finished, Hu invited Qiu to the Zhu house for supper and a meeting with Yu Wucheng. Qiu, the Wine Muddlehead, suddenly became exceedingly cautious. Secrecy should come first, he argued, and there was no need for him to meet Yu. Hu insisted, however, that since the meeting had already been promised, a last-minute change might arouse Yu’s suspicions. Qiu therefore had to go. The two exchanged expressions of admiration; wine made friendship easy, and Yu found him very congenial. When they spoke of Shaowu’s escort assignment, Yu, though he disapproved of it, now felt obliged to commend his son earnestly to Qiu’s care. Supper lasted far into the night. Qiu and Zhou then took their leave together, returned to the inn for a short nap, and boarded boats hired in advance. One went north to Suzhou, to see He Guiqing and notify Yu Shaowu that he should join the others in Shanghai. The other went east, first to Songjiang to see the Old Master, then back to Shanghai to ship the rifles.

Arranging the rescue at the checkpoints would take some days, so they first employed the delaying tactic they had agreed upon. Yu told Changgen that Hu insisted on entertaining him first as a mark of respect. A visitor should always call on the local man, but the local man should first extend hospitality. Yu therefore offered a compromise: he would give a small dinner at which the two sides could meet and talk. Once the terms had been settled, they could accept Changgen’s invitation. This was perfectly reasonable. Changgen suspected no hidden purpose and felt that postponing his own plan for a few days would do no harm. He readily agreed. At noon on the day after Qiu’s departure, Yu held a grand banquet at the Zhu house. Changgen arrived limping, with no fewer than twenty followers. Whether this was a display of importance or a precaution because he felt unsafe, no one could tell. The hosts had to scramble to provide extra tables, while Hu hurriedly told Liu to obtain more gifts. He had prepared eight sets, each consisting of cloth for an outfit and a red packet containing two taels; now twelve more were needed. This was no mere display of wealth. He meant to win the men over. At some future moment when his life hung by a thread, even this slight bond of goodwill might make an enormous difference. After the customary exchange of courtesies over seating, Hu, as the visitor from afar, took the place of honor next to Changgen. The conversation consisted, naturally, of polished pleasantries. Afterward Liu took the bank at pai gow to entertain the “honored guests,” while Yu led Hu and Changgen to the waterside pavilion for serious business. Yang was the only other person present.

“Changgen,” Yu began, “my mother has been fond of our friend Hu’s concubine since she was a child, and has taken her as a sworn daughter. It is a case of ‘the flood washing into the Dragon King’s own temple’—members of one family failing to recognize one another. A remarkable coincidence, when you think of it. Hu is not an initiate, but he is a truer friend than many within our ranks. His friendship with the Songjiang Chief and You Laowu needs no explanation. And you must have heard of Yu Si of Huzhou; they are in business together. So I must ask you to show consideration over that matter.” “Master Yu, there is no need to put it so strongly.” Changgen appeared entirely sincere. “We meet people here and there, only to discover that they are our own. Out of respect for Third Granny and yourself alone, I could have nothing more to say. Besides, I very much want to make our friend Hu’s acquaintance.” “I am grateful, very grateful!” Hu clasped his hands. “Since you are being so accommodating, I must make some gesture in return...” “Nonsense!” Changgen waved this aside. “There is no need to discuss that matter again!” The question of the rifles had at last been addressed. They turned to the proposed surrender.

Changgen was an accomplished actor. He had no intention of surrendering, yet he haggled over every condition and argued back and forth as though he were perfectly serious. Above all, he insisted that once his men were incorporated into the government army, they must remain stationed in the triangle formed by Jiading, Kunshan, and Qingpu. Hu patiently argued with him until they reached an impasse. Then Yu could contain himself no longer. “Changgen,” he said in a low voice, “when you do anything, you should ‘think of yourself for the first half of the night, and of others for the second.’ Let me ask you this: once you have accepted the amnesty, if your superiors order you to attack the county town of Shanghai, will you go?” “Well... Master Yu, you know my position.” “Exactly!” Yu seized on his reply. “And it is because other people understand your position and do not want to put you in a difficulty that they intend to move you elsewhere. Otherwise, you may still feel a bond with the Small Swords Society, but they may not feel any obligation to you. Suppose they suddenly try to swallow you up. What will you do then? To be frank, you would not even be free to give way. Why? First, once you become government troops, the Small Swords will no longer regard you as friends; they may even try to wipe you out. Second, if you retreat, you shake the army’s morale. Military orders are immovable as a mountain; they make no allowance even for fathers and sons. Surely you have seen the opera Executing the Son at the Camp Gate?”

Unable to answer this, Changgen brooded for some time, then assumed an earnest expression. “Master Yu, my dear Hu, I really do have difficulties. The men’s pay is barely enough to keep them alive; it will not support their families. At home they have other ways of making a little money. If they are transferred and cannot look after their dependents, none of them will have any peace of mind. What you say, Master Yu, could not be clearer, and I shall leave the decision to the authorities. But ‘even the emperor does not send hungry soldiers into the field.’ Whatever happens, I must ask them to grant six months’ bonus pay to provide for the men’s families. If their homes are unsettled, their minds will be unsettled, and they will not fight with all their strength. Am I not right, my dear Hu?” “Yes, yes. You understand the situation perfectly.” Hu spoke with great sincerity. “I shall certainly press your case. Six months may be difficult, but I promise to obtain three. More would naturally be better.” “Enough, enough! We have got this far, Changgen. It would be unreasonable to keep arguing!” “Very well.” Changgen appeared a little reluctant, as though Yu were invoking his seniority and he dared not disobey. “I shall do as you say.” “Excellent! At last we have reached an agreement.” Hu turned to Yu. “Brother Yu, I should like to return to Suzhou tomorrow. Official business moves slowly; settling this may take five or six days. But we need exact figures for the men and horses, so the authorities can make their plans.” He wanted Changgen’s muster roll. Yu understood, but found the request difficult to frame. If Changgen made an excuse and refused, a man of Yu’s standing would suffer an intolerable loss of face.

Unexpectedly, Changgen was most accommodating. Before Yu could speak, he said, “Quite right, quite right!” Then he called, “Guisheng!” One of his followers, a remarkably powerful-looking man, strode proudly in to receive his orders. A pistol hung at his waist, decorated with a scarlet silk tassel. “Bring me my document wallet.” When it arrived, Changgen took out a sheet of paper and handed it to Hu. It listed 2,700 men and 350 horses, followed by the quantities of their weapons: long spears, broadswords, white-waxwood staves, and more than forty foreign rifles. Hu had never personally handled a negotiated surrender, but conversations with Wang Youling, Ji Heling, and Qiu had given him some understanding of how to distinguish appearance from reality in such affairs. Very few bandit leaders reported their strength honestly. They either inflated it or concealed part of it, and the direction of the discrepancy revealed their intentions. A man sincerely wishing to surrender wanted to be taken seriously, so he exaggerated his men and horses to increase his bargaining value. A man driven by desperation to surrender temporarily merely to survive would conceal some of his forces, preserving strength for a later change of sides. What Hu now wanted to discover was Changgen’s actual strength.

“You have dealt so frankly with me that my work as intermediary could not be easier. I am deeply grateful. There is just one thing I should like to ask: when I return to Suzhou, may I submit this list of yours to the authorities?” Submission meant that the list would become an official record. “Once a word enters a government office, nine oxen cannot pull it back”: when Changgen surrendered, his men and horses would have to be inspected and counted against it. Hu was testing his attitude. Anyone seriously contemplating surrender would consider this carefully; anyone who was not would attach no importance to it. The test produced its answer. “Submit it by all means!” Changgen replied. “When the time comes, they can count according to that list. I will give you a written guarantee: not a man short, not a horse missing.” The more emphatic he was, the less credible his words became. Misfortune could arrive without warning. Among 2,700 men, someone might suddenly fall ill and die. How could he guarantee that not one would be missing? Hu’s thinking ran too deep for either Changgen or Yu to suspect his purpose. They merely felt that the discussion had reached a suitable stopping point, and agreed that on the day Hu returned from Suzhou they would drink to their success in Miaozhen’s chambers.

After business, some entertainment was in order. The gaming in the main hall had expanded from one table to two: pai gow at one and the dice-shaking game at the other. There were also two mahjong tables in the side rooms. Yu accompanied Changgen over to take the bank, but Hu objected. The banker had won money, he said, and ought to continue so that the other players had a chance to recover their losses. Living in Hu’s company day and night had deepened Liu’s understanding of him. He caught the meaning at once and changed his objective: he would no longer try to win. Winning at gambling is difficult; losing is easy. But even when losing, Liu employed some skill. By unobtrusive observation he knew exactly who had lost heavily and who had won a little. Using the possibilities for arranging hands in the full version of pai gow, he eased up or held firm as appropriate, redistributing the gains and losses. Before long, seven or eight players out of ten had recovered their stakes and were showing a profit. Liu reckoned his own loss at three thousand taels, then rose with a smile and “abdicated his throne.” His loss left Changgen’s followers delighted; all declared him a gambler of the first order. Changgen took the bank next. Custom required a leader playing against his followers to let them win something, and he soon lost a thousand taels. Hu wanted to lose some money to him, but could not see how to manage it.

“Well?” Changgen asked, unaware of Hu’s intention. “Aren’t you going to try your hand?” “I am a novice at this,” Hu replied with a smile. “Let me watch a little longer.” Whether from a sudden burst of enthusiasm or some other motive, Changgen abruptly raised his voice. “My dear Hu, how about a wager between the two of us?” “Certainly!” Hu answered just as readily. “I shall be happy to oblige. You mean head to head?” In such a game there was no distinction between banker and ordinary player. Changgen knew how to make a handsome gesture in public. “Naturally! Neither of us will have an advantage. What shall we stake? You decide.” He meant how much money, but Hu deliberately answered a different question. “A sincere heart!” Everyone looked from Hu to Changgen. Changgen paused, blinking as though deeply puzzled, then broke into a broad smile. “Yes, yes! A sincere heart! My dear friend, I shall not lose to you.” He meant that his own heart was sincere too, though the claim might be true or false. It was a figurative declaration prompted by the occasion and could not be taken literally. Hu brought the conversation back. “I was joking. You, I, Brother Yu—which of us is anything but sincere with our friends? Why wager on that? Come, let us play for money!” He turned to Liu. “Third Master, lend me ten thousand taels.”

Liu counted out ten thousand taels in banknotes and handed them over. Hu laid them at the Heaven Gate position on the table. Changgen called for Guisheng to bring his document wallet again, then placed it in the middle, indicating that he would settle after the result was known. At a gaming table this was an arrogant gesture, implying a right to impose on someone of lesser standing. Yu found it offensive. “I shall have a wager too!” he said. A seasoned man needed no more than a hint. Changgen immediately reached for the wallet, saying with an apologetic smile, “If Master Yu is playing, I should not dare accept the wager. Later, you must take the bank for a few rounds and let us play against you.” It was an acknowledgment of Yu’s rebuke, and Yu let it pass with a smile. Changgen ventured no further liberties. He properly laid a stack of banknotes beside him, then asked, “The full game or the small one?” “The small one is quicker!” Changgen shuffled the ebony pai gow tiles, picked out two hands, and took up the dice. “Odd comes in, even goes out.” He threw a five. Since that meant the outer hand came in, he drew it toward himself and turned it over. His eyes widened in dismay: a dead ten!

Hu did not want to win those ten thousand taels. He was no expert gambler, but he understood gamblers’ feelings. Sometimes the money was a small matter; it was the humiliation they could not bear. Changgen’s present circumstances were especially easy to guess. He was so hard pressed that he was ready to take desperate risks. Ten thousand taels was no small sum. A soldier’s pay was between one and a half and two taels; even three months’ bonus pay for his 2,700 men, if they joined the government army, would come to less than ten thousand taels. To lose it all in a single turn of the hand—Hu felt uncomfortable merely imagining it. If Changgen could afford the loss, that would be one thing. But he plainly could not. Losing would only drive him toward more desperate schemes, as though he were being forced to “take to Liangshan” as an outlaw. These thoughts flashed through Hu’s mind, and his hands moved just as quickly. While everyone else was still staring and sighing over Changgen’s bad luck, he seized his own two tiles. Everything favored Hu. Changgen had already conceded defeat and pushed his ten thousand taels in notes across, looking decidedly embarrassed. The others all watched Hu’s tiles, and the impatient ones called, “Turn one over first!” With thumb above and middle finger below, Hu slowly felt a tile. Even the least sensitive fingers could have identified it: an Earth tile. He must not expose it, for the moment he did, his victory over Changgen would be certain. Ignoring the spectators’ encouragement and concern, he continued his performance. At the second tile he started, frowned, then shook his head. He pushed both tiles back into the unarranged heap and casually retrieved his own banknotes.

“What have you got?” Changgen asked, picking up one of Hu’s tiles and feeling it. “Ding-seven, a dead ten,” Hu answered languidly. “An amicable draw!” How could it be ding-seven? Changgen did not believe him. His middle finger carefully traced what was unmistakably a “two-six” tile; with that tile, the hand could not be a dead ten. He felt the other and understood. The total was indeed ten, but the combination was an Earth Gang. “An amicable result is a rare pleasure!” he said. “Harmony is best. We have had our wager. Good friends should play against each other once, never twice. Thank you for your hospitality, Master Yu!” “But it is still early. Won’t you stay a little longer?” “No more gambling,” Changgen replied. “We shall have plenty of time together. When our friend Hu returns from Suzhou, we can meet again.”

After he left, Yu asked Hu quietly, “What hand did you really have? I cannot believe you failed to beat a dead ten.” “An Earth Gang. His circumstances did not seem good, and I could not bring myself to take his money.” “You certainly know how to part with money! Throw a copper coin into water and you at least hear a splash. Your ten thousand taels have simply dried up without a sound!” His words suggested regret, but he was deliberately teasing. Hu could not immediately tell what he meant and could only smile. “My dear Hu, no wonder even my mother admires you!” Yu now explained his thinking. “You have extended your friendship. We shall see whether the cripple is a man or a beast. If he is a man, he will not do anything foul. If he is a beast, we shall treat him as a venomous snake and strike straight at its vital spot. His death would be no loss.” “Exactly my intention,” Hu replied. “If we have to act harshly now, he will have only himself to blame. Not only shall we have easy consciences; even if someone comes forward on his behalf, there are reasons to be heard on every side of the table, and we can put ours before everyone.” “Quite right! You know every nicety of brotherhood conduct. I cannot imagine where you learned it all.” Hu smiled. “Enough of that. I shall leave early tomorrow and should be back in three to five days. Everything here is in your hands, Brother Yu.”

On the fifth day, within the time he had set himself, Hu returned to Tongli with Zhou Yiming. They began deploying their people at once. Zhou and Yang were to hold the checkpoints at the two ends of the canal, Eldest Brother Zhu would provide support, and Liu would play the part of a convivial guest, accompanying Hu and Yu to their Banquet at Hongmen. Once everything was arranged, Changgen’s invitation arrived. The dinner was set for two days later. The reason for the delay, rather than entertaining Hu immediately on his return, was that Miaozhen’s cook needed two days to prepare a lavish feast of delicacies from land and water. Business, of course, still had to be discussed separately. On the day the invitation was delivered, Changgen came in person to ask for news. He brought a blue cloth bundle. What it contained was a mystery; since the guest said nothing, the hosts could hardly ask. After a few pleasantries, he inquired about the results of Hu’s journey. “Four months’ bonus pay...” Hu set out the three principal terms: four months’ bonus pay; the possibility of recommending Changgen for a fourth-rank military appointment; and a posting still to be determined, but certainly outside his present area. He watched Changgen closely, curious to see what evasions he would offer.

“If we are going to come over, we cannot keep complaining about the terms. With you there, my dear friend, our men will never be allowed to suffer. I shall do as you say.” Changgen untied the blue cloth himself. Inside was a stack of old registers, their covers bearing the words “One Heart, One Purpose.” “These are the muster rolls. I have only this one set. There was no time to have a fair copy made, so I must ask you to look at the originals.” Hu and Yu exchanged astonished glances, unable to understand his intention. The books were greasy and grimy, unpleasant even to hold. Inside, the entries were covered in alterations and corrections. Some were marked “deserted,” some “dead,” and others “transferred to such-and-such a unit.” These were genuine working registers.

“Excellent, excellent!” Hu could only treat this as evidence of real sincerity. “Let me borrow these originals for two days. I shall divide them among several people and have them copied quickly.” “There is no need to trouble yourself. Other people would not understand some of the changes. I shall send my own men to copy them. But,” Changgen added, turning to Eldest Brother Zhu, “I intend to send three men. They will have to impose on your hospitality for two days.” This seemed a further demonstration of good faith, treating the Zhu house as a place where he could transact confidential business. Before the host could answer, Yu agreed for him. “A small matter, a small matter! Send them over by all means.” “Thank you! Then it is settled. I have something else to attend to today, so I shall not keep you. Please come early in the afternoon the day after tomorrow. There are still many things on which I want your advice.”

Once Changgen had gone, Hu felt both deeply anxious and greatly excited. Drawing Yu aside, he asked quietly, “What do you think, Brother Yu? The fellow does not seem to be playing tricks.” “Yes, I cannot quite understand it either. He has even brought the original registers. It almost looks as though he means it! I think we should ask Zhou to investigate again.” “Quite right!” Zhou was accordingly sent to discover Changgen’s real intentions. If he genuinely wished to surrender, his attitude had changed completely. What could account for such a sudden reversal? They needed a convincing explanation before they could believe it. Before Zhou’s report arrived, however, news came from Suzhou. He Guiqing sent Hu a letter by special messenger. The Jiangsu Military Affairs Office had reported that armed bands of “bandits” were continually moving between Qingpu and Jiading, behaving furtively and claiming that they were gathering from various places to await an official inspection. He feared that they were using this pretext to stir up trouble and urged Hu to find out at once whether there really was such a gathering for surrender. If there was not, Qing troops would be sent to surround and suppress them. At the end of the letter he added a special injunction: “This matter is of great consequence. I earnestly request an immediate reply.”

CHAPTER TWENTY-NINE

That flimsy letter seemed to lay a heavy burden on Hu's shoulders. The safety of the district, Lame Changgen's fate and He Guiqing's future all depended on a word from him. If he said that the men were assembling for inspection and had no hidden purpose, the Qing troops would withdraw their encirclement. But if Changgen seized the chance to rebel, He would face ruin, and Hu himself might lose his head. If, on the other hand, he said the situation was unclear and impossible to judge, the troops might attack. It would be like killing men who had surrendered. How he could explain himself was a secondary matter; he would carry a debt of blood. How could he live afterwards? After consulting Yu Wucheng, he replied that inquiries had begun as instructed, and asked He to tell the military affairs office to hold its position and exercise particular vigilance until the truth was clear. This put off the immediate difficulty, but the facts urgently needed establishing. Where had Zhou Yiming gone? Hu felt as though a jar of gunpowder were heating on a stove, ready to explode at any moment. Until it was removed, he could have no peace. He therefore decided to tackle the matter directly.

That evening he learned that Changgen was staying with Miaozhen. He asked Eldest Brother Zhu for a guide and went straight to her rooms. His unexpected arrival greatly surprised Changgen. Though tense within, Hu appeared perfectly at ease. He first took stock of Miaozhen. Her face was not especially beautiful, but she was tall and graceful, with an excellent figure, and at the flowering age considered the finest in a courtesan's life. Her conversation and social manner showed unusual distinction. Hu felt it a pity that she should be paired with a rough adventurer like Changgen. Only after small dishes had been set out for a drink did he glance at her and tell Changgen, “There's a letter I'd like you to see.” “Oh.” Understanding, Changgen said, “Come this way.” He led Hu into Miaozhen's bedroom and seated him by the dressing table. Changgen sat on the edge of the bed, leaning towards him, and waited. “I'll take your word. Whatever you tell me, that is what I'll report to the authorities.” Hu handed him the letter. After reading it, Changgen looked troubled. He considered silently for a moment. “Brother, what do you think my intentions are?” It was a weighty question. Hu answered carefully. “If I didn't trust you, I wouldn't show you this letter.” Changgen nodded, satisfied. “Good. I know your difficulty. Tell me what I should do.” “You honour me.” Hu thought for a moment. “We can hardly blame the troops. These times are so unsettled that they must take precautions. If a misunderstanding arises, frankly, we shall be the ones to suffer. Why not wait? Once an inspection date is fixed, everyone can assemble, and the troops will have no reason for suspicion.” “Very well. Let's have a drink.”

Back in the outer room, Changgen immediately summoned Guisheng and ordered him to send men out that night in every direction, telling his followers to return to their original quarters. Hu was deeply satisfied by this prompt decision. With his inner guard lowered, their conversation over wine grew increasingly congenial. Before Zhou returned to report, Hu learned why Changgen had changed his attitude and decided to accept the amnesty—at least, according to Changgen's own account. In a word, it was Hu's conduct. His generosity over that pai gow hand had been the chief cause, but not the only one. Changgen admired the way Hu understood and practised loyalty among friends. What truly won his trust, however, was Hu's ability. Even loyalty needed the right means of expression. Living and dying together might be its highest form, but dying together on the same day of the same month and year was less enjoyable than living together over wine and meat. Changgen frankly admitted that he trusted Hu to provide the wine and meat. Such confidence moved Hu unexpectedly. Yet his usual rule was that the more respect people showed him, the more consideration he owed them. He repeatedly disclaimed the credit, saying that Changgen was a true friend to grant him such favour. He also praised Yu Wucheng warmly, making Changgen understand that respect shown to Yu would please him even more than respect shown to himself. They drank far into the night. Yu grew anxious and sent Zhu to inquire, using the excuse that a letter had arrived from Suzhou and Hu must return to read it. Once home, they explained what had happened, and Yu's esteem for him rose still higher. Early next morning, Zhou brought information broadly matching Changgen's account. Zhou now had another task. Hu's arrangements in Suzhou had been seven parts precaution and three parts amnesty. The precautions were no longer needed; the concealed men at the checkpoints should be withdrawn. Three parts preparation for the amnesty was insufficient, however, and arrangements for Changgen must be made at once. Hu sent Zhou ahead to inform He, intending to return to Suzhou himself overnight after that evening's banquet.

The banquet meant as a trap became a celebration of success. Attended devotedly by Miaozhen and her sister, and urged on continually by Changgen, Hu became as thoroughly drunk as Yu. When he woke, he could not for a moment tell where he was. An unthinking movement of his hand brought it against skin exquisitely soft and smooth. Then came the scent of cosmetics and the pale gleam of a powdered face. A young woman lay sleeping beside him in the dim bed curtains, but her face was turned away, and he could not see who she was. Collecting himself, he remembered the drinking games, but nothing of the party's end. He shook the arm beside him, pale as a lotus root, and woke her. It was Miaozhen's younger sister, Miaozhu, far more beautiful than her elder sister. “Oh, Master Hu, you're awake!” Still fully dressed, she sat up quickly. “Would you like tea?” “Yes. Cold tea—a great cupful!” His throat was so dry that speech was difficult. “You drank far too much. Master Yu was insensible too.” She lifted the curtains, got out of bed, brightened the lamp and poured a large cup of lukewarm tea. Hooking up the curtains, she brought it to his lips. He drank it all, caught his breath and asked, “What time is it?” “Almost four.” “I'm afraid I've kept you from sleeping half the night. I'm very sorry.”

“Why say that? You're Seventh Master Li's friend.” By Seventh Master Li she meant Changgen. “Was he drunk?” Hu asked. “Seventh Master Li never gets drunk.” “Oh!” Hu was surprised. “Can he hold so much?” “He can't hold much, but he knows how to drink.” Hu laughed teasingly. “That's an amusing way to put it. You say he knows how to drink, and then that he can't drink much.” “Oh, Master Hu, don't pick holes in what I say!” Her voice and manner were cloyingly coy. “I mean he can play tricks when he drinks.” “I'm not picking holes. You really do say amusing things.” Hu cupped her face in his hands. “Think of it yourself: playing tricks with drinking!” “It's true. You mustn't talk nonsense. Do you know Seventh Master Li well?” “In one way, yes; in another, no.” “And what about you?” she retorted. “One foot in and one foot out whenever you speak!” “There's an explanation. We haven't known each other long, so I can't say I know him well. But our friendship is already deep, so in that sense I do.” “Once you know him, you'll understand. Watch him during drinking games and toasts. You may see him pouring wine into his mouth when it's really going onto the floor or into his sleeve. He knows his own capacity and always stops at seven-tenths of it. But he'll never say he can't drink any more. At that point...” She smiled and left the rest unsaid. That was when the tricks began.

Hu found this apparently irrelevant chatter extremely useful. Drinking and gambling were the best ways to reveal a man's character. Changgen's way of drinking showed exceptional self-control, but also that he was difficult to push. When he would not agree to do something and others insisted, he resorted to tricks. A little caution therefore returned to Hu's mind. Miaozhu was perceptive. Seeing the distraction in his eyes, she asked what he was thinking. “About Seventh Master Li's drinking tricks. Next time I must watch him and stop him playing them.” “That won't be easy. He has too many tricks for you to guard against.” “Oh!” Hu grew more wary. “What do you think of him?” She considered. “Extremely capable.” “And his temper?” “Everyone has a temper. His good point is that he doesn't lose it without reason. That's what my sister likes about him.” “And you? Do you feel the same as your sister?” “Of course.” Her manner grew languishing. “Oh, when we meet one of those foul-tempered customers, earning our living this way is a real torment. There's no hurtful thing they won't say.” “Then you'll like me as your sister likes Seventh Master Li. I never lose my temper.” “Really?” “Of course.”

“Then I like you.” Miaozhu threw her arms round him and drew a deep breath, suddenly seeming unable to contain her delight. Hu quietly enjoyed the warmth of the embrace. Comparing the sensation with the women he had known, he found something especially appealing in Miaozhu. Furong was reserved, A’qiao experienced, while Miaozhu had a tender, lively charm of her own. He gave himself over to their present intimacy. After loving embraces and countless endearments, he fell into a deep, contented sleep. When he woke again, sunlight flooded the window. His first thought was that he must go to Suzhou. Somehow, the thought made his heart sink, like a child enjoying the New Year holidays who suddenly hears that lessons are beginning again. He was utterly unwilling to go.

Never mind! He hardened his resolve and decided to steal a day of leisure. Turning over, he tried to sleep again. But the lingering fragrance in the pillows and quilts drifted round his nose and stirred his heart; sleep would not come. His tossing disturbed Miaozhu, who was dressing in the back room. She came quietly to see what was happening. Through the new gauze bed curtains, Hu watched her. Her light makeup seemed rich, for her lips were naturally red and her skin exceptionally fair. In the morning sun she looked like a dew-covered peony. Through the blue-green curtains she was a blossom in mist, exciting his desire to kiss her again. As soon as she raised the curtain, he reached out and pulled her towards him. The movement was so sudden and forceful that she was genuinely startled. “Oh!” She patted her chest. “You frightened me!” “I'm sorry.” He smiled apologetically and shifted farther into the bed to make room for her to sit. “What a fierce gentleman you are!” She was still patting her chest. “My heart is pounding even now.” “Surely you weren't that frightened? I don't believe it.” “Feel it, then.” Hu put his hand to her breast and smiled triumphantly as he touched her. Only then did she realize she had been tricked. Twisting away, she caught his hand, slapped it and gave him a reproachful look before thrusting it beneath the quilt.

“Miaozhu,” Hu pleaded with an unabashed smile, “lie with me a little longer.” “No. You mustn't.” She rose to go. “Don't go!” He yielded. “I won't bother you. Surely you can stay and talk?” She smiled and sat down again. “It's still early. Sleep a little more. What would you like to eat today? Shad?” “Good.” “Then I must tell the cook early.” She held down the quilt to keep his hands beneath it. “I'll be straight back.” She kept her word. As she tidied the room, she chatted with him intermittently. This made it still more impossible to sleep, but Hu knew the customs of such houses. Before lunch, everyone except the cook and male odd-job servants was still in bed. The maids and attendants did not begin their day until noon. If he got up, someone would have to attend him. Why disturb their pleasant dreams? Hu was always considerate towards servants. He therefore continued to linger in bed, talking while turning business over in his mind, enjoying a rare spell of leisure.

He remained there until nearly noon, then rose. After washing, he was about to seek Changgen when an unexpected visitor arrived: Zhu, with surprising news. You Laowu and Gu Yingchun had both come, and Yu wanted him to meet them at once. “Excellent!” Hu was delighted. “I'll tell our host and come immediately.” In Miaozhen's rooms at the rear, he learned that Changgen had left early. Hu had been sound asleep, so Changgen had not disturbed him. He had left word inviting Hu to stay another day and dine there again that evening. Hu wished to repay Miaozhu's attentions, return Changgen's hospitality and welcome You and Gu. Using Miaozhu's form of address for her sister, he told Miaozhen, “Sister Zhen, today I should provide the entertainment. Arrange two tables, please. Both the food and wine must be good.” He laid a fifty-tael note on the table. Miaozhen refused it firmly, saying so much money was unnecessary. After repeated offers and refusals, Hu could only take it back. Instead he gave twenty taels in gratuities. The maids, attendants and male servants came to thank him, every face beaming. The word that “Master Hu is the finest guest of all” soon spread.

At the Zhu house, Hu at once sensed something unusual. You and Gu were not the only uninvited arrivals. Five others were there, all middle-aged and well dressed, yet with an unmistakable air of boldness belonging to men of the brotherhood. He could not place them. As You introduced them, he learned that they were leading figures in the Suzhou, Songjiang and Taicang region. One addressed him as Little Uncle, plainly marking him as one of You's fellow disciples. With that foundation established, Hu found the greetings easy enough. Their purpose remained puzzling, however, and he took You aside to ask. “We've come for nothing—but it's better that way. If our strength had been needed, matters would have been serious.” You smiled at this cryptic opening, then explained. He had returned to Songjiang the day before yesterday. There was no time yet to discuss Wang's commission in detail. On arriving, he had heard that Changgen intended to harm Hu and Yu. The Old Master was deeply concerned. After consulting You, he had invited these men to come and mediate. If mediation failed, they might have to use force. The Old Master was personally making arrangements, with a large body of men awaiting orders. “I can never thank him enough for treating me like this.” Hu was genuinely moved. “The business is settled now.” “So I heard as soon as I arrived. Little Uncle, you're remarkable. Changgen is notoriously difficult, yet you've brought him round. Still, I think our presence can lend you useful support.” “Exactly. Frankly, from what I've learned of him, I still have two or three parts in ten of doubt. With your standing brought to bear, we can be completely secure.” “Good. I'll give a dinner.” “Tonight is mine. We'll dine with the courtesans. You can give yours tomorrow at noon. Would this house do?” “Zhu's is the only suitable place. But...” You hesitated, as though something were difficult to say. “Brother Five, speak freely. What could our friendship prevent you from saying?” Hu was truly curious. “First forgive me, Little Uncle. However close we are, you're still outside our threshold.” Hu understood at once. “Say no more. I know. Naturally, I should stay away.” Their friendship was close enough to need no further explanation. You changed the subject. “Old Gu reached my place yesterday. He has much to tell you too. Apparently the foreigners have yielded. I'll attend to the guests and send him out to speak with you.”

Gu brought excellent news. The foreigners had finally softened and agreed to pay a high price for the silk. By his calculation, the transaction would yield a profit of a hundred and eighty thousand taels. Would Hu sell? “Of course!” Hu replied gladly. “Never mind a hundred and eighty thousand—even eighty thousand would make me sell. Business must be built gradually, flying the kite far out on a long line. Besides, I have too many affairs on my hands. I must clear some of them.” “We can sell, but the foreigner has a condition: a three-year contract, with all our future silk sold exclusively to him.” “That would be acceptable too. But prices change every year. How would they be fixed?” “We would negotiate them at the time, of course. He guarantees us a profit. Broadly, the price would be the overseas quotation less his margin.” “That may not be sound. It would guarantee his profit. Suppose the overseas silk price fell and, after his margin was deducted, what remained didn't cover our costs?” “Yes, I've thought of that. But in the end, whatever else a man will do, he won't trade at a loss. That's true of Chinese and foreigners alike. If the overseas price falls and he won't buy, neither will anyone else. Besides, foreigners conduct business differently from us. They take care to develop their sources of supply and won't make excessive demands. We can discuss our concerns with him. So long as we hold to mutual benefit, we can agree a contract. When can you reach Shanghai?”

“Most of my business needs doing in Shanghai. But I must go to Hangzhou too. Seventh Sister's affairs are important.” “Oh! Didn't Brother Five tell you?” “Tell me what? No.” “He explained frankly to Mr Xuexuan that we wanted the sworn family connection for the weight of his name, to persuade our old clan head. Mr Xuexuan was very understanding. Since that was the purpose, he said, we might as well propose the marriage first. The weather is growing hot; there's no need to trouble Seventh Sister with a journey. When we marry in the cool of autumn, he'll find time to attend the feast and complete the sworn-sibling ceremony then. If he can't come, I can take her to him afterwards, combining her customary post-wedding family visit with the ceremony.” “Excellent! Since he says so, obedience is the best respect. I needn't return to Hangzhou for now. Once Changgen's business is finished, I'll go from Suzhou to Shanghai. What about Old Qiu?” “He was due to leave Shanghai today. I've met Yu's son too: mature beyond his years and thoroughly dependable. Brother Five has made arrangements throughout Songjiang. The passage is sure to go smoothly. Set your mind at rest.” This succession of good news lifted Hu's spirits and put him in an expansive mood. He decided to entertain on a grand scale. There was no time to choose another date; that evening's banquet must be enlarged. He put Liu Bucai in charge. After consulting Yang Fengmao and Zhu, Liu invited everyone locally connected with the Grain Transport Brotherhood. Another difficulty was Changgen's position: before visiting dignitaries like You, he could hardly occupy the chief seat, yet making him merely another guest would slight him. Liu explained this to Hu and proposed listing Changgen as a fellow host, with his name first on the invitations. That would honour him handsomely.

By evening the distinguished guests had gathered, at least forty in all, but Changgen, one of the hosts, had still not appeared. Hu was hard pressed to attend to everyone alone, and his private misgivings made it more unpleasant still. “Sister Zhen, where has Changgen gone?” he asked quietly. “Surely you have some idea?” “I can't guess. One of his men came for him early this morning. They spoke privately for a while, and he left without saying anything further. I think we should serve the meal. We can't keep the guests waiting.” Four tables were laid. After much polite yielding over places, everyone sat down. Liu had prepared a list of Tongli's celebrated courtesans and passed it round. Those wishing to summon an acquaintance marked her name. Notes went flying out, and the beauties arrived one after another. Those with familiar customers joined them; Liu matched the others as he thought suitable. Strings, flutes and singing followed in succession, with chairs and horses at the front and boats at the back. The excitement was extraordinary. Passers-by stopped to stare and ask which wealthy guest could put on such a display. When told that Changgen was the host, some wondered how he had suddenly come to such magnificence. Changgen himself was equally surprised. Finding Miaozhen's house so crowded, he hesitated to push his way in and stopped an attendant. “Who's giving this party?” “Why, Seventh Master Li, that's a funny question! Aren't you hosting it with Master Hu?” Changgen understood: Hu was giving him face. Rather than enter the hall at once, he went round a side passage to the back, found Miaozhen and learned the details. Then he entered the hall, clasped his hands and bowed all round. “Forgive me! For a host to arrive late is a grave discourtesy. There is nothing to say. I'll drink three penalty cups.” He took Hu's cup and drained it three times, then greeted the guests in order of seniority. His manners were both graceful and attentive.

When the banquet ended, the tables were cleared for serious gambling. Once the guests were settled, Changgen drew Hu aside and spoke reproachfully. “Old Hu, you handled something badly. There was nearly serious trouble.” “What?” “You ought to have told me before shipping the guns out of Shanghai.” “Oh!” Hu hastened to admit his fault. “An oversight. I'm sorry.” “I only learned this morning. It took me until the afternoon to settle things.” He then disclosed the state of his forces. Not all his more than twenty-seven hundred men obeyed him willingly. One group was unreliable, and he had held it down for the moment by the weight of his seniority. When he abruptly changed course and made peace, they turned against him and prepared to follow the original plan, seizing the boatload of guns under Qiu's escort. Fortunately, the plot leaked. One of Changgen's trusted men learned the details, hurried to Tongli through the night and roused him from Miaozhen's bed at dawn. He went to the border between Qingpu and Jiading and managed to intercept them. “I stopped them, but it took a great deal of effort. The guns have passed Jinshanwei now. With the Old Master's men there, they're safe. But...” He shook his head and would say no more.

Hu felt both grateful and uneasy. Changing his form of address, he said, “Seventh Brother Li, you've done me a great service. If you're in difficulty now, it's my turn to help. Tell me. Whatever lies within my power, I'll do.” Changgen thought for a long time, then spoke firmly. “You're different from other men. I'll tell you the truth. Their leader was a disciple of one of my fellow initiates. I had him done away with.” Hu would dare almost anything and cared little for most dangers, but these words changed his expression. “What? You killed him?” Changgen nodded gravely. “Then won't his family come to settle accounts?” Hu exclaimed. “By the rules of our world, I wasn't wrong. He disobeyed; the business was too important and too urgent. No one can say I acted improperly. But public duty and private feeling are separate. The rules obliged me to put him to death; personal feeling obliges me to attend to what follows his death.” “I understand. Like Zhuge Liang executing Ma Su, whose family had an eighty-year-old mother—you can't ignore her.” Hu paused, then asked directly, “Do you need money?” “Yes. Compensation for his family, for one thing. Then some men won't speak openly but don't want to stay with me. Better let them go.” “Quite right. That makes a clean settlement. How much? I have ten thousand taels ready. More can be found, but it would take two or three days.” “That's enough. Two thousand for the family, ten taels apiece to those leaving—there are a little over three hundred of them. Lend me five thousand.”

He limped to the window, took the brush and ink used for writing invitations to courtesans, and laboriously drew up a promissory note. The handwriting was crooked, but the wording entirely proper: “Received on loan from my friend Hu Xueyan the sum of five thousand taels of standard silver. As we are close friends, no guarantor or interest is required. Repayment is agreed within three months. This note is made as evidence.” He signed it “Li Changgen”. While he wrote, Hu found Liu and prepared the money. When he returned and Changgen handed him the note, he did not even look at it, but held it to the candle and burned it. “Seventh Brother Li, my business partner Gu Yingchun tells me I've made a good profit on silk. Our own people should share misfortunes and blessings alike.” He handed over a bundle of banknotes. “Here is your share of the profit: ten thousand taels.” “But...but...” Changgen, normally so shrewd, capable and eloquent, could not find words. “We have many years of friendship ahead.” Hu patted his back and walked away smiling.

The gathering ended in complete enjoyment. After the guests had gone, Hu offered to settle the account in cash, but Miaozhen refused. Changgen had told her to put everything on his account. Besides, she had collected more than two hundred taels in gaming commissions and felt embarrassed to charge her guests anything further. Hu had to let her have her way. A late supper was set out, and they gathered round one table. Taking up his chopsticks, Hu said at once, “Let's finish early.” “Finish?” Changgen asked. “Aren't you staying here tonight?” Miaozhen urged him to stay too, but he insisted that urgent work must be done that night. Miaozhu's face fell. Pleading a headache, she excused herself and left the table. “This rather spoils the occasion,” Gu said. “Old Hu, why do it?” Hu said nothing. He rose and went to see Miaozhu. In her room he found her sitting alone at the dressing table, wiping away tears. “What's wrong?” He rested his hands on her shoulders and spoke gently. “Are you angry with me?” She shook her head. “No.” “Then why these sudden tears?” “My own feelings. I was born to a bitter fate, earning my living in this miserable trade.” Her voice was full of sorrow and resentment.

Hu could think of no suitable reply. After a moment he took out a two-hundred-tael note and pressed it into her hand. “I return to Suzhou tomorrow afternoon. Buy yourself something to eat with this.” “I don't want it.” She pushed it away. “I sell smiles, not tears.” Beneath the angry words lay a deeper feeling. Hu stood stunned, unable to speak for a long while. “Please go. Didn't you say you had important work to do in the middle of the night?” “I'm not deceiving you.” He changed his approach. “Then I'll do it here. Have you any writing paper?” “There's a stationer's next door. We can knock them up even now.” “Good. Send someone for the best letter paper and envelopes, and make a pot of strong tea. Mr Gu and I must discuss some letters.” He warned her solemnly, “They are confidential. That's why I meant to go home to write them. Since I'm staying here, you must never repeat anything you hear.” “Set your mind at rest. I won't even listen.”

Hu therefore kept Gu Yingchun with him and used Miaozhu’s dressing table as a desk. She was as good as her word. After providing paper, brushes and tea, she sent the maids to bed and withdrew into the adjoining room herself. “Gu,” Hu said quietly, sitting on the edge of the bed, “this whole amnesty business was only settled tonight, when Changgen came back. I’ll tell you everything that happened. Please write a letter to Education Commissioner He for me, and tomorrow morning Old Zhou can take it there specially.” “Aren’t you about to return to Suzhou yourself? Wouldn’t it be better to speak to him in person?” “When the situation was uncertain and nothing was settled, it was better not to leave anything in writing. As matters stand now, a formal written account is needed to show that we take it seriously. Besides, Commissioner He still has to discuss it with the military affairs office. An oral message might be misunderstood. Put it clearly on paper, and there can be no mistake.” By the time the long letter was finished, the clock was striking three. It was near the summer solstice, when the days were longest and the nights shortest. A faint dawn was showing outside, though the deep night was still cool as water. Imagining Miaozhu fast asleep, Hu did not want to wake her and suggested that he and Gu share the large bed. “Why should we?” Gu laughed. “With such warm, fragrant beauty waiting to fill your arms, it would be a shame to waste Heaven’s gifts. Naturally, I shall take the small bed and you two the large one.” The remark stirred Hu, and he changed his mind. “You take the large bed yourself. I’ll squeeze in beside her.” “There are pleasures in being squeezed together too. As you please.” Gu undressed and got into bed.

Hu quietly pushed open the adjoining door. A flame still flickered, and the gauze curtains hung half drawn. Wrapped in a lined coverlet, Miaozhu lay facing the wall, snoring faintly. He tiptoed in, closed the door softly, undressed, put out the light and felt his way into bed beside her. He had no wish to disturb her, but could not settle his own thoughts. In her hair she wore a string of pearl orchids, flowers particularly suited to a pillow: mingling with a woman’s hair oil, their scent grew fuller, rich and alluring enough to set the heart astir. Crowded into the little bed, Hu also recalled his time with A’zhu aboard Old Zhang’s Wuxi fast boat. Those memories brought a sense of melancholy and left him still more restless. Without realising it, he turned from side to side and woke Miaozhu. Discovering a man beside her in her sleep naturally frightened her. As though possessed, she suddenly raised herself halfway, clasped her arms across her body and stared sideways with wide eyes. “It’s you!” She let out a breath. “You gave me such a fright.” “You might say you gave me one!” Hu laughed. “Sneaking about like a ghost! Why creep in like that?” “Creeping about makes it more amusing.” He took her arm and drew her down again. “I didn’t mean to wake you. I simply couldn’t sleep.”

“Where is Mr Gu?” “In the large bed. He has only just lain down too.” “Then he may still be awake. Keep your voice down.” She asked, “Is the letter finished?” “Of course. We wouldn’t go to bed before finishing it.” “Who was it to?” “Someone in Suzhou.” “Aren’t you going back to Suzhou? Why write, then? Does that mean you’ll stay another couple of days?” The succession of questions plainly revealed her wish to keep him. Hu thought that the truth would only upset her again, so he answered vaguely, “Well, well, nothing is fixed.”

Miaozhu began asking about his family. Since her tone suggested nothing more than idle conversation to pass the time, Hu was unguarded. He told her frankly that his elderly mother was still living, that he had a wife and a concubine, and that he had no son yet. “Third Master Liu is so shrewd and capable. I imagine your ‘Huzhou wife’ must be formidable too.” “Not in the least. She is goodness itself, a truly gentle soul.” “That is your good fortune.” “Thank you.” Hu smiled with some satisfaction. “My luck is not bad.” “It is your Huzhou wife’s good fortune too.” “Not necessarily.” “To marry someone as capable and considerate as you, Master Hu, and live comfortably without a care about food or clothing! You are so well liked, too. Wherever you go, there is lively company and every distinction. Isn’t that good fortune?” “When I’m easy to deal with, I’m very easy. When I’m difficult, I can be very difficult indeed.” “I can’t see that. You seem the most accommodating of men.” “Being accommodating has its drawbacks. It is easy to get involved with women elsewhere. Someone jealous could be driven wild.” “It is perfectly ordinary for a successful man to have several wives and concubines.” Miaozhu suddenly asked, “If you have a Huzhou wife, surely you have a Shanghai wife and a Suzhou wife too?” “Not yet. I haven’t happened to meet anyone who suits me.”

Miaozhu longed to bring her face close and ask, “What do you think of me?” But she could not bring herself to offer herself so openly, and feared that he might think less of her. She held back. Then she reflected: with all her qualities, in what way was she inferior to anyone else? For him to say in her presence that he had not met anyone who suited him was rather hard to bear. “Then what sort of person would suit you?” Hu now heard where this was leading and chose his answer carefully. “That is hard to say,” he replied, deliberately evading her. “Beauty lies in a lover’s eyes. There is no fixed rule.” That left her nothing to say. She could hardly demand, “Am I not your lover?” Even if she could bring herself to ask, what pleasure would there be in it? Her heart was wholly devoted to him, yet he treated her as a roadside willow or a flower on a wall, to be plucked and thrown away at will. It chilled her. With that thought came an inexpressible sense of injustice. Sorrow filled her heart, her eyes grew hot, and tears began to roll down.

Their cheeks were touching. Both looked up at the bed curtains, so Hu could not see her crying, but her warm tears ran onto his right cheek. He could hardly fail to notice. Turning towards her, he exclaimed in alarm, “Why, you’re crying again! What is it?” “I have something on my mind. You don’t understand.” “What has touched your feelings this time?” “I was thinking that Sister Zhen will soon have a settled home. Seventh Master Li told her that once he has accepted the amnesty and become an official, he means to live properly and accomplish something. He plans to take her into his household. We are only a year apart and have never been separated since childhood. Now she will go her way and I mine. How can I help being sad?” “So it is sisterly affection.” Hu smiled. “I have an idea. Why don’t you marry Seventh Master Li along with your sister?” It was a disastrous remark. Miaozhu’s tears poured out like a river bursting its banks. She jerked round to face the wall, pulled the coverlet over her head and began sobbing aloud. Hu regretted it bitterly, yet was too bewildered to understand why a single joke should distress her so much. There was no time to examine the question. He explained as gently as he could, then apologised, asking only that she stop crying. Instead, her sobbing grew louder. At last there was a sound at the door. Gu had been woken and had come to ask what was wrong. “Listen!” Hu nudged her. “You’ve woken him.” She paid no attention. In fact she welcomed a third person who might mediate, giving her hopes a chance of fulfilment. She cried harder still. “The more you’re supported, the drunker you get!” Helpless, Hu rose to open the door.

“What has happened?” Gu asked as he entered, studying Hu’s face. It wore an expression between laughter and tears. “How should I know? We were talking quite pleasantly, and suddenly she said she couldn’t bear her sister leaving the profession to marry, and became upset.” Before he had finished, Miaozhu threw back the coverlet. “You heartless wretch!” she said bitterly, then turned away again and covered her face to weep. She was deliberately creating a mystery for Gu to investigate, and he duly fell into the trap. “Little Uncle, how have you offended her? She seems to hate you so much. I can’t understand it.” “Neither can I.” Hu could only pretend ignorance. He did not want Gu to intervene, so he shifted aside and gestured towards the door. “It is almost daylight. Go back to bed. You haven’t much time left to sleep.” At this, Miaozhu raised her voice, as though losing the third person would leave her helpless and unable to obtain redress. Gu hesitated. “What is it really about?” “She wants to belong to me, but won’t discuss it properly. Instead, she goes through the whole performance—first tears, then a scene, then threats to hang herself. Isn’t it absurd?” Taken by surprise, Gu said without thinking, “But that is a good thing!” “Good things take time and trouble. We must talk it over slowly and work things out before we can agree.” Hu yawned and again urged him to leave. “Please go. I want to sleep too.”

Once Gu left, Miaozhu stopped crying. Hu had at least given some indication of his position, and she waited for him to talk. Instead, he blew out the lamp, got into bed and said nothing. They had reached a deadlock. Ashamed and angry, and encountering his methods for the first time, she found her love turning to resentment. Unable to turn her thoughts aside, she pursued them deeper into a blind alley. The more she thought, the angrier she grew and the less life seemed worth living. When she looked at Hu and heard him snoring loudly, her thoughts were driven to the brink. Quietly she rose, found a sash through her tears and brought a chair to the foot of the bed. She tied the sash to the rail above the bed and put her head into the loop. Hu’s snoring was feigned. He was deliberately ignoring her to escape her entreaties. He knew that she had climbed over him and got up, though not what she was doing. Suddenly the bed shook. He opened his eyes and was horrified by what he saw. Leaping out barefoot, he caught her lower body and lifted her until the loop came free. Her breath had only just begun to fail. Once she had put her head into the loop, she had realised too late that she regretted it; in that instant everything in the world had seemed precious and everyone dear. Now, rescued, she forgot his coldness. Her whole heart was filled with gratitude. She threw her arms about his head and burst into uncontrollable sobbing. This woke not only Gu but Miaozhen and the people in both courtyards. They hurried over, though, uncertain of their welcome, most remained at the doors and windows, peering in and whispering. Miaozhen alone pushed straight inside. She found her sister sobbing on the bed and Hu sitting barefoot in a white foreign-cotton undershirt and trousers, looking thoroughly embarrassed. Gu stood to one side as though faced with an impossible problem. Miaozhen could only ask him, “Mr Gu, what is all this about? Has Miaozhu offended Master Hu?” Gu did not answer. He pursed his lips and glanced upwards. Following his gaze, she saw the white silk sash tied to the vermilion bed rail. Had Miaozhu tried to take her life? She wondered, but could not bring herself to ask. It seemed too incredible.

Hu was deeply troubled and divided in his feelings, but his mind was exceptionally clear. To meet whatever difficulties might follow, he felt he must first establish a firm position on the rights and wrongs of the matter. He therefore put on a stern expression. “Sister Zhen, there is something I must ask you. We have only just met, but with Seventh Master Li connecting us, none of us is a stranger. I come to Tongli as a guest, and Miaozhu wants to involve me in a court case over a death. I really cannot understand why she should treat me like this.” Miaozhen was alarmed, and even Gu thought the accusation excessive. He hastened to intervene. “Little Uncle, you mustn’t put it like that.” “There is nothing wrong with what I said.” Hu deliberately appeared aggrieved. “Put yourself in my place. If she had stopped breathing, I would have been dragged into a case over her death for no reason at all. Is that a matter to joke about?” Miaozhen still understood only half of it. She could not fathom why her sister had tried to hang herself or how she had survived. Hearing Hu speak this way, she felt sincerely apologetic. “Master Hu, I suppose Miaozhu must have offended you. Please don’t be angry. Let me ask her. Afterwards I shall kowtow and apologise.” “Very well!” Hu took the opportunity to rise. “Ask her how I have wronged her. We have known one another for only three days. What terrible grievance could she have against me, to do this?” On the bed, Miaozhu felt both remorse and injustice, and cried still more bitterly. Gu pitied her, but did not yet understand Hu’s intentions and could say little. He merely accompanied him outside.

“Little Uncle, how did it come to this? What did you say that hurt her enough to make her try to hang herself?” “Quiet!” Hu reproached him. “You ought to be helping me keep up the performance. Why do you speak for the other side whenever you open your mouth?” Gu gave a wry smile, then said as if to himself, “Why hasn’t Changgen appeared? I’ll find him.” Hu’s silence signified consent. Gu went outside, ignoring the many idlers who drew away at the sight of him, and continued straight to Miaozhen’s courtyard. “Where is Seventh Master Li?” he asked a maid. “He didn’t stay here last night. He went back to Shengze during the night, but he’ll return by noon.” Gu had to go back. Miaozhen was now talking to Hu. Both looked at him expectantly when he entered, as though hoping for his help. “Mr Gu, you must say what is fair.” Miaozhen sounded aggrieved from the outset. “My sister has high standards. No customer has ever caught her eye. Today she was ready to give up her life for Master Hu. Surely that alone deserves some answer from him.” “Not so fast.” Hearing resentment in her tone, Gu first tried to soothe her. “We can discuss it calmly. Come over here and tell me what has happened.” She followed him aside and stated her request briefly. Miaozhu had sworn to marry no one but Hu, while Hu had refused outright and seemed unwilling to reconsider. She hoped Gu would see justice done. But how could he do that? Whatever the circumstances, he could only advise Hu, who was free to listen or not. He was puzzled too. Hu was usually so accommodating. Even if he could not accept this affection, he ought to decline gently. Why had he spoken so harshly that Miaozhen herself was angry? “Wait here. Let me ask our Little Uncle first.” Hu had another account. To him, Miaozhen’s words bordered on coercion. Besides, practical circumstances made it impossible to agree. Exhausted in body and mind by the past few days, he had no patience for further entanglement and had refused simply and directly. He too seemed to be acting partly out of resentment. Yet Miaozhen’s angry words were understandable: she loved her sister and felt her pain. Hu’s exhaustion and short temper were understandable as well. Both were in a bad mood, and afterwards they could come to understand one another, helped by someone else’s explanation. The real question was what he meant by saying that practical circumstances made agreement impossible. Gu had to ask.

“Little Uncle, tell me what the difficulty is. Is it that our Auntie at home would never agree?” “Exactly. There has been a great quarrel over Furong, and it still hasn’t been settled. Why should I invite more trouble?” Gu thought for a while. “There must be a way to arrange that. What matters most is whether you like Miaozhu.” Hu found this hard to answer. He did not want to deny his own feelings, but neither would he openly admit them. He changed the subject. “There is another thing. I brought Furong on this journey. To take up with someone else while she is here—think how she would feel. Besides, how could I explain it to Third Master Liu?” Gu, seeing more clearly from outside, understood at once. Hu did like Miaozhu. His wife in Hangzhou was no insuperable obstacle; it was Furong who prevented this happy arrangement for the moment. “You are speaking honestly. I understand.” Gu warned him, “Miaozhu is completely devoted to you. If her hopes come to nothing, she may try again. Why burden yourself with a death when you could be living happily? It would be a terrible price.” The word “death” startled Hu. Deeply uneasy, he rubbed his hands. “Are there really people so foolish that they will give up their lives?” “There may be.” Gu’s face grew serious. “If she had died the first time, that would have been one thing. If something happens a second time, you will have stood by and let her die. Your conscience will never be easy.” Hu had scarcely slept all night. After these shocks and troubles, his head felt as though it would split, and his thoughts were clouded. He told Gu frankly that he must find somewhere quiet and sleep properly. He asked him to deal with the two sisters on his behalf and leave everything until the afternoon.

For quiet, the best place was still Zhu’s house. Hu entered by the back door, went to his room, told the servant assigned to him to refuse all visitors, shut the door firmly, undressed and got into bed. He was utterly exhausted and fell asleep as soon as his head touched the pillow. He did not rise until noon. Liu was waiting over tea in the outer room. Hearing movement, he knocked. As soon as Hu opened the door, he asked, “How did things come so close to someone dying?” After a good sleep, Hu’s feelings were steadier and his mind clearer. Instead of answering, he asked about Gu. “Has Gu come back?” “Yes. He was the one who told me.” “Then Elder Yu, You Laowu and the others know too?” “Naturally. They all think you are somewhat to blame.” Anyone else can accuse me of being heartless, Hu thought, but you, of all people, cannot. Aloud he asked, “And you?” “It makes no difference to me. Your affairs have nothing to do with me.” That indicated that if Hu really did marry Miaozhu, Liu would not object. What the future might bring was uncertain, but at least a small obstacle had been removed, which was some comfort. Still, this was a side issue. Hu decided to put it off with an accommodating manner for the present. Much serious business remained. He therefore made an immediate decision. “Go and pack. We shall return to Suzhou today, settle Changgen’s important business and hurry back to Shanghai.”

“I don’t think we can go today,” Liu replied. “I heard from You Laowu that they mean to give a banquet for you together tonight.” “A banquet?” Hu was surprised. “Why?” “They must have something to say. They’re shut up together now, discussing who knows what.” This reminded Hu of something. “Has Changgen arrived?” he asked quickly. “Of course. He has been the busiest man of all these past two days. I hear he went to Shengze early this morning and hurried back specially.” Hu nodded. “Today they have brotherhood affairs to discuss. Outsiders shouldn’t intrude, and we needn’t disturb them. Find Gu. We can go somewhere to eat and talk about our own business.” When Gu arrived, he suggested returning to Miaozhen’s. She knew that she had lost her composure and was deeply anxious. She had begged him to bring Hu to lunch so that she could apologise. Avoiding her would avoid trouble, but trouble often multiplied when one tried to escape it. Hu was in quite a different mood now. After a moment’s thought he answered decisively, “Very well. Let us hear what she has to say.” The three walked leisurely to her house. Her earlier haughtiness had given way to deference. “Please don’t be angry, Master Hu,” she kept saying. “Miaozhu is young and foolish. If nothing else, for Seventh Master Li’s sake, let us treat it as though nothing happened.” This wording made Hu uneasy. “Where is Miaozhu? Why don’t I see her?” “She’ll come. She’ll come. It’s getting late. Shall I serve the meal now, or would you like some refreshments first?” “No refreshments, and no wine either. Let us eat.” Gu had come expressly to act as a conciliator and agreed. “Quite right. In this heat, leave out the wine.” “Then let us have a little yangmei liquor,” Miaozhen suggested. “I steeped it last year and have been saving it. Today I shall offer it to Master Hu.” Gu promptly changed his tone. “That would be pleasant. Yangmei liquor dispels the summer heat. A cup would do no harm.”

Miaozhen arranged their places herself at a small round table with a marble top. The silver-mounted ebony chopsticks and Jingdezhen porcelain were particularly fine. After the cold dishes had been set out, she brought a white porcelain jar, removed its cloth seal and lifted the lid. A mellow, pure fragrance rose from the liquor. It was sorghum spirit steeped with white yangmei berries from the Dongting hills. The strength of the spirit had passed into the fruit, while the deep-red liquor itself tasted sweet and mild, slipped down easily and was especially suited to an early-summer midday. As they sat down and poured, Miaozhu appeared. She wore no rouge or powder; her glossy black hair was simply dressed, with a row of jasmine blossoms. Their fragrance reached the company before she did. She greeted Liu first, then the others, and finally said softly, “Master Hu.” Her eyes moved towards him, bright with tears. Apparently remembering that this was no time or place for grief, she mastered herself, lowered her head and sat beside him. No one, Hu included, referred to the dawn incident when her life had hung by a breath. Miaozhen exerted all her powers as a hostess, handling each matter with the ease of a musician plucking the strings while watching wild geese fly. The table became lively, yet no one’s eyes could quite leave Miaozhu. Whether still resentful or merely embarrassed, she kept her head lowered, occasionally raising her brows to steal a quick look at Hu and turning away before he could notice. No one could tell what she meant. Hu’s own feelings were complicated. Remembering his words and manner that morning, he thought he had been too harsh and felt guilty. Under the table he quietly reached for her hand. Alert to his movement, she moved it aside and left him grasping nothing. This touch of resentment only deepened his feeling. Smiling, he asked, “Still angry with me?” “How would I dare?” “It is not a question of daring,” Gu put in. “Miaozhu isn’t angry at all, are you?” “Of course not,” Miaozhen added. “Why should she be? Miaozhu!” She indicated Hu’s empty cup with a movement of her lips. Miaozhu hesitated, took the silver ladle from the jar and filled the cups, beginning with Liu’s and leaving Hu’s until last.

“Everyone else has berries. Why haven’t I?” Hu demanded deliberately. Without speaking, Miaozhu ladled out two berries, put them on a little dish and pushed it towards him. “Things one has to beg for don’t taste good. I don’t want them.” “I know you don’t!” She gave a cold laugh. “You simply find me tiresome.” “Miaozhu!” Her sister’s sharp call carried a warning. Hu felt uneasy. If the elder sister tried to discipline the younger and the younger answered back, it would spoil the whole occasion. Miaozhu did not answer back.
