Now that Xiangyin is going to Liangjiang, he will not let the Northern administration interfere in Southern affairs as the earlier governors-general did. Then he and Governor-General Liu are fellow Hunan men. Liu has suffered at Hefei’s hands, and Xiangyin will naturally avenge him if he gets the chance. That is one side. Hefei, of course, must guard against it. In maneuvering, he is the more formidable. He may strike first. We must take care not to be caught between them.” “Caught between them?” Hu was astonished. How could a struggle between Zuo and Li bring disaster on him? “When two sides are scheming against each other, there are only two basic methods. If your opponent depends on a patron, capture the leader to defeat his followers. If he depends on helpers, clip his wings. Xiangyin is the latter kind. If Hefei means to move against him, Little Uncle, he must first remove his helpers. I fear you will be the first to bear the attack.” Hu’s expression changed in alarm, though he was still perplexed. “Do you mean I should submit my surrender to Hefei? How could I do that and face Xiangyin?” “Surrender is out of the question, of course. I think you should cultivate Shao Xiaocun.” Xiaocun was Shao Youlian, a man from Yuyao in Zhejiang, capable in foreign affairs and long close to Li Hongzhang. He had recently been appointed Shanghai Circuit Intendant. The post had previously belonged to Li’s trusted associate Liu Ruifen. By investigating Sheng impartially during Liu Kunyi’s impeachment case, Liu Ruifen had offended Li, who arranged his transfer as Provincial Treasurer of Jiangxi. Liu’s departure and Shao’s arrival showed how thoroughly the lucrative Shanghai post, which controlled Jianghaiguan Customs, lay within Li’s grasp.

“Cultivating Shao Xiaocun—isn’t that simply flirting with Hefei? Must I actually kowtow before you will call it surrender?” The vulgar expression “flirting” made the point perfectly clear. Gu was silent for some time, then made a startling proposal. “Little Uncle, once we begin, why stop halfway? Spend two or three hundred thousand taels and force Shao Xiaocun out!” Hu was more bewildered than ever. “You mean I should become Shanghai Circuit Intendant?” “Yes!” Unable to answer, Hu rose and paced thoughtfully in measured steps. After a long while he suddenly called, “Seventh Sister! Seventh Sister!” The Seventh Lady was picking crabmeat for the late-night refreshments. At his call she hurried out. “Did you want me, Little Uncle?” “Yingchun wants me to become Shanghai Circuit Intendant. Do you think the idea is practicable?” She paused in surprise. “I don’t yet understand what this is about.” Turning to her husband, she asked, “Hasn’t the Shanghai intendant only just changed?” This reminded Gu of something he had overlooked. Shao had only recently taken office; without a serious fault, there could be no reason to remove him. He nodded. “It does look difficult.” “Besides, I am not made for official life,” Hu said. “Do I look like a man who can get up early to stand in attendance?” Red button or no red button, Hu was still a merchant. With his fortune made, he lived more extravagantly than princes, and whatever official ceremony properly belonged to his rank was merely part of his display. A substantive appointment would require him to perform its actual duties and observe its formalities. He need not go as far as the expectant intendants, who fawned on superiors and hurried ahead to stand waiting whenever a governor or governor-general went out, hoping for a glance. But even receiving and seeing off senior officials passing through Shanghai, an unavoidable local duty, seemed an ordeal to him.

The Seventh Lady began to understand. Gu had told her that Shao Youlian belonged to Li’s camp, just as Hu belonged to Zuo’s, and so they were opponents. Her husband wanted Hu to replace Shao, not because the post would benefit Hu, but simply to remove Shao. “Whether the plan could work or not, and whether Little Uncle is too accustomed to comfort to endure official life, the idea itself should never have entered your head!” Her remarks were always frank and penetrating. Both men asked why she thought the idea so wrong. “Let me ask you first,” she said to her husband. “Is Shanghai Circuit Intendant the most lucrative post in the empire?” “Do you need to ask?” Ignoring his tone, she continued, “And is Little Uncle the richest man in the empire?” That needed asking still less. “Otherwise why call him the God of Wealth? Stop talking nonsense.” “I am not. But if Little Uncle became Shanghai Intendant, others would. He made his fortune in business, yet people insist he made it in office. And Shanghai is notoriously lucrative. Suppose the extortionate censors were not properly attended to and insisted that all his money came from official corruption. He could jump into the Yellow River and still never wash himself clean!” Gu broke into a cold sweat. Taking the Shanghai post might indeed expose Hu to the confiscation of his entire property. “Listen to her, Yingchun. Now you know why I ask Seventh Sister’s advice.” “Do not flatter me, Little Uncle! There is something, though, that I…” She stopped abruptly, waited a moment, then said, “We can speak of it later.” With that she turned and left.

Hu paid no attention to her hesitation and returned to the subject. “As for Shao Xiaocun, I will not court him, and there is no need to force him out. What do you suggest, Yingchun?” “Neither draw close nor keep too far away.” “In other words, carry on as usual?” “Yes.” “Very well. Let us return to what we can do once Xiangyin arrives. I think I can then strike a decisive blow at Jardine Matheson.” The British trading house had expanded rapidly in China. Its relations with Hu were those of both friend and enemy. He had relied heavily on its supplies when procuring military equipment for Zuo, particularly modern Western arms. In silk exports, however, it was his greatest competitor. In selling silk to foreign firms, Hu had chiefly dealt with Jardine Matheson. The firm thought buying through him too expensive and began sending agents into the countryside itself. It offered more than Hu did, so the silkworm-raising households were naturally pleased to sell; yet it still paid less than it would have paid him. In effect, producer and foreign buyer divided Hu’s middleman’s profit between them. This did not greatly trouble him. He believed in fair dealing and often said, “Let everyone share the rice.” A good price for the households’ new silk helped rather than harmed him: loans he had advanced during the lean season or the pressing needs of year’s end could then be repaid smoothly. Surely that was a good thing.

One development, however, demanded a prompt response. In the fifth year of Guangxu, Jardine Matheson had established a silk-reeling mill beside Suzhou Creek. This year, the seventh of Guangxu, Huang Zuoqing of Huzhou had opened another, Gongheyong. A third, the Gongping Silk-Reeling Mill, financed by the British firm Gongping Trading House, was also being prepared at a vigorous pace. Neither Jardine’s mill nor Gongheyong had begun production. The chief reason was widespread opposition. One machine did the work of thirty people: what it produced in a day would take a month by hand. The livelihoods of many silk-producing households in western Zhejiang were therefore threatened. The Silk Guild had organized resistance; in reality, Hu had organized it, for the Guild’s managers followed his lead in everything. But the three modern mills could no longer readily withdraw. Unless they adopted machine reeling, Jardine and Gongping in particular would lose their European customers to Japan’s higher-quality silk. The three mills consequently joined forces and hired an Italian, Maidengsi, as chief engineer, to guide their technicians in operating machinery purchased from Italy or France. They also sent agents into the countryside to pay in advance for next year’s new silk. Their confrontation with Hu’s resistance had become a close struggle.

His advisers were divided. Most favored opposition; a minority wanted to move with the times. Gu had earnestly urged the latter course. “Little Uncle, these are no longer the days when the Celestial Empire stood above all. There is always a greater world beyond our own, and someone more capable than ourselves. However fierce you are, you must look at the direction things are moving. Machine-reeled silk has no breaks or fuzz; it is brilliant white. Beside yellowish native silk, it looks like a young lady standing next to a kitchen maid. There is no comparison. We cannot change that. How many people opposed the steam engine when it was invented in Britain? What happened in the end?” “Your argument is sound. But what will all those country households eat if there is no work for their hands? I shall do what I can. For every day I can protect them, I shall make the effort. If the tide finally sweeps their footing away, at least my conscience will be clear.” This was not a matter of conscience, Gu thought. If the three mills could actually be forced to close and auction their machinery, he might find partners to take them over and acquire a ready-made bargain. Naturally, Hu could hold the largest share if he wished. For now, however, this thought must remain unspoken.

Gu accordingly became eager to plan the resistance. The essential move was to control the raw material. At equal prices, Hu’s established ties gave him an advantage over the mills in buying silk. Unfortunately, Jardine and Gongping had ample funds and raised their purchase prices. Seeing the unfavorable turn, Hu suddenly began selling heavily. Once the two firms had bought at high prices and the market settled, he replenished his stocks ahead of them, making a handsome profit on the outward and inward transactions. Jardine and Gongping lost this first round. Although their stocks would supply enough material to begin production, future supplies were bound to become difficult. At this moment another opportunity came to Hu: Zuo’s appointment to Liangjiang. “Yingchun, we are talking about fair dealing. Jardine and Gongping use machines; we use our hands. Is that fair?” “That is an inequality we cannot remedy.” “Why not? Of course it can be remedied. It depends on whether those in authority are willing. Hefei only wants to befriend the foreigners; he would refuse. Xiangyin will do it. I shall persuade him.” Gu laughed. “Little Uncle, after all this talk, what exactly is he to do?” “Raise the cocoon levy. Make their costs so high that no profit remains, and they will certainly have to close.” Naturally, the levy would have to be applied unequally; if everyone’s costs rose equally, they would still be unable to compete. Gu thought this a powerful way of dealing with the foreign firms. But they might enlist Hart, the British Inspector-General of Customs, and use Li’s connections to bring the dispute before the Zongli Yamen. “They will not,” Hu said, taking a different view. “After two rebuffs, Hefei will not interfere as freely as before. Besides, the silk industry in Jiangsu and Zhejiang has nothing to do with his Northern jurisdiction. Even if he does try to meddle, do you suppose Xiangyin will listen to him?”

At this point the Seventh Lady came to call them to supper. The Gu household was decidedly Western in style. A long mahogany dining table stood in the middle of the room, surrounded by six chairs in the French court style. The seating, however, followed Chinese custom: the places at the ends of the table were treated as seats of honour. Gu and his wife sat to either side of Hu, effectively making their guest the host. With the late-night congee came ham, preserved eggs, meat floss, fermented bean curd with shrimp roe, radishes pickled in lees-flavoured sauce, and other preserved delicacies. Their bright colours under the crystal chandelier made them particularly appetizing. “I should like a little wine,” Hu said. “My muscles and joints have been aching these last two days.” Such aches called for tiger-bone and papaya liquor, a medicinal spirit made by Hu Qingyu Hall and famous throughout the country. Hu had little capacity for alcohol, so the Seventh Lady filled his stemmed glass only halfway.

“Seventh Sister,” he asked, holding his glass, “when are you coming to Hangzhou? Mother keeps thinking of you.” “I think of her too. I am afraid I cannot get away before the year's end, but I shall certainly come in spring.” “There is something I want to discuss with you both. Mother will be sixty-nine next year and seventy the year after. While Xiangyin is here, I want to celebrate both birthdays—the nine and the ten.” Hu's retainers and employees had long been discussing a splendid celebration for his mother's seventieth birthday. Now he intended to use Zuo Zongtang's prestige as Governor-General of Liangjiang to give her a grand celebration a year earlier as well. The Seventh Lady did not object to celebrating next year. But custom favoured celebrating an age ending in nine rather than the following round number; doing both seemed excessive. Still, it sprang from filial affection, and she did not wish to spoil the occasion. “Nine or ten, either is good, so long as the old lady is happy.”

“It is hard to establish a grand style of life, and hard to scale it back,” Hu said. “Foreign dealings have expanded these past few years, and foreigners have brought us many things, good and bad. Fewer people learn the good than the bad. If a man is bad to begin with, and then learns foreign tricks that we Chinese do not understand, there is no telling what he will do. He could sell you as a coolie to Gold Mountain before you even understood how you had reached a foreign country. Is that not frightening, Seventh Sister?” Not understanding his point, she murmured a noncommittal assent. “Someone came to me for help recently,” Hu continued. “He might simply have asked, but he had another approach. ‘Mr Hu,’ he said, ‘if you fail to do what you ought to do, people will talk. It is not worth it.’ I answered, ‘Loyalty and filial duty are the foundations of life. Beyond them, what must I do? So long as I fulfil the five human relationships, nobody has grounds to criticize my conduct.’ ‘Not so,’ he replied. ‘Beyond those five relationships, there is one thing that you, Mr Hu, ought to do.’ I asked what it was. What do you think he said? ‘Spend money.’” His argument was that Hu was famous for extravagant generosity, so any occasion requiring expenditure was properly his responsibility. Otherwise, he would cease to be Hu Xueyan. The man then asked to borrow five hundred taels, but could not say what he wanted them for.

“I knew perfectly well that he wanted to pay gambling debts. Had he told me honestly, such a small amount would not have mattered. Instead, he said, ‘You need not ask what I want it for, Mr Hu. Nobody needs a reason to borrow from you. Everyone knows how generous you have always been and how much money you have thrown away. If word gets out that you are questioning me over five hundred taels, people will think you insist on getting value for every coin and are unwilling to waste anything.’ Tell me, should I have been angry?” “Of course,” Gu replied. “It was outright blackmail. He meant that unless you lent him the money, he would spread malicious stories. Detestable!” “Utterly detestable! I thought: if I refuse, naturally he will say nothing good of me. But if I lend it, a man with such a spiteful tongue will take the benefit and sneer at me too. He will say, ‘Look, I called him a fool to his face, and he still did not dare refuse. He is like a candle that gives no light until someone strikes a match.’ What do you think I should have done?” “If it were me,” the Seventh Lady said indignantly, “I would give the five hundred—but he would never spend it. I would donate it to a charity in his name.” Hu sighed. “If only I had possessed your wit at the time, Seventh Sister.” “Why?” Gu asked. “What did you do wrong, Little Uncle?”

“I gave a cold laugh and said, ‘True, I have thrown away I do not know how much money in my life. But you are the one exception.’ I happened to have a thousand-tael note from Beijing's Four Great Heng banks in my pocket. ‘It seems I am destined to lose money today,’ I said. ‘There is no helping it.’ Then I struck a match and burned the note before his eyes.” “What did he do? Was he furious?” “He was not. He said something that made me furious.” “What?” “‘Do not try tricks for fooling children on me, Mr Hu. Fukang and the Four Great Heng are in the same business. You can report the burned note as lost.’” Gu and his wife fell silent. At last the Seventh Lady said, “Little Uncle, you suffered an injury you could not answer.” So he had. It had never occurred to Hu to register the note as lost. Once the man suggested it, however, he could no longer do so without proving the accusation that he had merely staged a children's trick. “Later, when people asked, I admitted the incident. If they asked whether I had reported the loss, I could only smile and say, ‘What do you think?’” “It is better when people ask,” Gu observed. “At least they can see your manner for themselves. The danger is those who hear the story and immediately assume you must have reported it, without thinking a question necessary. A'qi is right. You suffered badly from this.”

“One must learn from a loss,” Hu replied. “Afterwards I thought the fellow did have a point. Spending money is what I ought to do. I should never have asked his purpose. If my spending is wasteful, what about the money I earn? From my side, I earn through judgment, skill, energy, and effort. But I ought to consider the man who loses. If he regards his loss as money thrown away, then what I gain is that same thrown-away money.” “Your reasoning grows more mysterious all the time,” Gu said with a laugh. “Can earning money be a waste too?” “If you do not know how to use it, earning it is a waste. Have you heard of the ‘death-bell loans’ around Huai'an and Yangzhou?” Gu had never heard the expression, but the Seventh Lady knew it. Some rich merchants counted every penny, accumulated enormous fortunes, and yet ate and dressed miserably, clinging to each coin as though it were life itself. Unfortunately, they sometimes produced wastrel sons. With their fathers keeping such a tight grip on the purse, the sons borrowed wherever they could. Interest was even more savage than on the instalment loans of the Shanxi moneylenders. But there was one advantage: if the prodigal could not pay, the creditors would never press him. “When, then, did repayment fall due?” the Seventh Lady explained to Gu. “On the day his father died. As soon as the old man stopped breathing, the first thing was to summon a monk to chant the prayers at the deathbed. The moment the monk struck his chime, the creditors came to the door. That is why they were called death-bell loans.” “Better spend it oneself than leave it for unfilial descendants,” Gu said. “What one has gained oneself, one may lose oneself; that need not matter. But the proposition that every expense is your duty, Little Uncle—perhaps that still deserves some consideration.”

“I have thought it over repeatedly. Since people call me the God of Wealth, I ought to distribute wealth. Otherwise I invite trouble.” Hu abruptly returned to his original subject. “Take Mother's sixty-ninth birthday next year. I must celebrate it. If I do not, those who envy me will have something to say. They will say I have always loved appearances, and that with His Excellency Zuo now Governor-General of Liangjiang, I ought to be eager to borrow his prestige for a grand display. If I refrain, it cannot be because I do not want one; it must be because Zuo no longer treats me as before. Of course he would send Mother a birthday present, but only an ordinary one. He would do nothing special to enhance the occasion. Better for me, then, to recognize my position and keep quiet. Seventh Sister, would people not say that if I held no celebration?” She could not deny it, but answered differently. “There is nothing wrong with celebrating the sixty-ninth.” “And after celebrating it next year, I must celebrate again the year after. Otherwise people will say Mother's seventieth had long been planned, but I brought it forward a year to exploit Zuo's prestige. Having held it once, I let it suffice, because my circumstances have declined and I must economize where I can. You must understand, Seventh Sister, that this would be worse than not celebrating next year.” “Why?” “Do you not see?” Gu intervened. “Once that rumour spreads, Fukang's deposits will shrink.” “Shrink is hardly the word!” Hu quoted a literary saying: “Pull one hair and the whole body moves. A major storm would break immediately.”

The Seventh Lady could not picture precisely what such a storm would mean. But seeing an unusually apprehensive expression on his face, she could not keep back something she had long wished to say. “Little Uncle, I too must advise you to draw things in. My meaning differs a little from your mother's. She says you should reduce the display where possible, instead of expanding it further. I mean that you should stop businesses you need not conduct, and manage properly those you ought to keep.” Gu was the first to find this painfully offensive. “What do you mean? Does Little Uncle need you to criticize his business?” “Yingchun!” Hu laid a hand over Gu's on the table to stop him. “Seventh Sister is the only person still willing to tell me the truth. I want to hear it.” He nodded emphatically. Gu had noticed that Hu's temperament was no longer quite what it had been. He feared his wife's bluntness would offend him; even if Hu said nothing, the evening would be spoiled. Since Hu welcomed unwelcome truths, Gu had no reason to obstruct her, although he still gave her a glance urging tact. “I have kept some things inside for a long time, without an opportunity to say them,” she began. “Since you wish to listen, I shall speak plainly. I am not afraid of offending people. If even one or two of my remarks reach you, their resentment will be worth it.”

From this introduction Hu knew she meant to criticize the people he employed. This was a matter in which he took great interest and pride. He believed that his achievement—an establishment surpassing even the Yangzhou salt merchants at their height in the Qianlong and Jiaqing reigns—rested on his ability both to judge people and to use them. Naturally, discovering a person's strengths and faults required open observation and discreet inquiry. Yet when listening to judgments of character, he followed principles of his own. First he examined the critic: was that person open to criticism? Only then did he weigh the remarks, distinguishing what he ought to hear from what the speaker merely wanted him to believe. The Seventh Lady was among the very few people he felt he should admire. He wanted not only to hear her judgments but to ensure that she left nothing unsaid. He therefore encouraged her. “Nobody will resent you, Seventh Sister, because nobody will know what you tell me. Say whatever you have observed. Even if I am at fault, do not spare me. I shall be grateful for the truth, never angry with you.” His sincerity made her feel that criticizing particular employees would not adequately express her loyalty. She must go deeper, to the source of the faults.

“To be honest, Little Uncle, I respect you less than I did ten or more years ago. But my concern for you has increased, not diminished. Sometimes I think about your affairs until I cannot sleep all night.” Hu was visibly shaken. “We are friends who have endured hardship together, Seventh Sister. What I most admire is your courage and integrity. I know I am not as considerate of others in everything as I was ten or more years ago. Still, I have not treated people badly. My establishment is large, but the people I employ are capable, and everything is held firmly together, inside and out. I do not understand what worries you so much that you cannot sleep.” “What worries me is that a great tree catches the wind. You are a towering lampstand, Little Uncle. So many people borrow your light to find their way and move ahead quickly and safely. Yet you cannot illuminate yourself.” Hu found this use of the familiar saying particularly apt, and listened still more attentively. “Fortunately, you can see clearly. There are no outsiders here today. Tell me honestly: what faults must I change?” She hesitated. Her first thought was that his very belief in the competence of all his people and the security of his affairs needed changing. But that sounded like a wholesale condemnation and might provoke resistance. There was a practical difficulty too. If he asked whether he must replace everyone, where so many replacements could be found at once, and whether they would all be trustworthy, she could not answer. Gu partly understood her hesitation. Fearing that excessive criticism would merely unsettle Hu without practical benefit, he suggested, “A'qi, describe one or two small incidents. Little Uncle will draw his own conclusions.” “Very well.” She thought briefly. “I shall tell you of two occasions when others offended people on your behalf, without your knowledge, and the blame was entered against your name.”

The first concerned Hu's garden. After it was completed, he disliked the rockery and decided to rebuild it. Several specialists inspected it and produced plans, but none impressed him. Eventually he heard of an eminent master in Beijing, Ying Chong, a native of Henan. Early in the Xianfeng reign, Ying had been a retainer of Prince Yi, Zaiyuan. The Xinyou coup destroyed Zaiyuan's household and cost him his life. Having watched the great mansion rise and then collapse, Ying was deeply affected. He withdrew to the Western Hills, shut his door, taught his children, and ignored outside affairs. Generous gifts received during Zaiyuan's ascendancy meant that a few years of simple living would not leave him destitute. He had no wish to return to worldly employment. But Hu's humble entreaties and generous payment, reinforced by the persuasive Liu Bucai, who had been sent to invite him, eventually brought him to Hangzhou. Having inspected the existing rockery and several unused designs, Ying thought them reasonably good. Alteration would suffice; complete rebuilding was unnecessary. Hu disagreed and insisted on starting afresh. Ying privately thought this the consequence of having too much money. Yet he could not say so: such frankness before their acquaintance had deepened might lead Hu to think he lacked the imaginative resources to dare demolish and rebuild it.

Stung by the desire to prove himself, Ying shut himself away and did not come downstairs for a month, until he had completed a preliminary design. Even then he would not show it. Each day he walked with his staff among the Six Bridges and Three Tianzhu Temples, or explored the Northern and Southern Peaks in search of secluded and remarkable scenery. At night he spread out the plans by lamplight and revised them carefully. After three months the work was finally complete: seventeen drawings, one general plan and sixteen detailed sheets. Strange rocks, unusual ravines, and countless winding turns made a small space suggest an immense landscape. The result inspired delighted admiration. Overjoyed, Hu entertained him at a lavish banquet and asked him to supervise construction. Ying agreed. A rockery required exceptional stones. Hangzhou, the Southern Song capital, contained many famous gardens, including abandoned ones. Ying inspected them all, without finding much to satisfy him. One day he came to a ruined garden by Gongyuan West Bridge, said to have been the ancestral shrine of Zhao Wenhua, Yan Song's adopted son. A stone lying on its side there caught his attention. Three qualities defined a fine ornamental rock: slenderness, wrinkled texture, and openings through its body. Although half buried, the exposed portion possessed all three, and Ying judged that the hidden half must be equally fine.

As he examined it from every angle, an old man whose beard and eyebrows were completely white strolled over. He wore a short jacket and straw sandals and carried a spotted-bamboo pipe. His clothes were not those of a gentleman, but his bearing suggested a great official retired into seclusion. Ying greeted him respectfully. “May I ask your surname, sir?” “You are too kind. Zhao. And yours?” “Ying. Is anyone responsible for this abandoned garden, Mr Zhao?” “Certainly. I am.” “Ah! Forgive my ignorance.” Ying repeatedly clasped his hands in greeting. Returning the salute with his pipe raised, Zhao asked why he wanted the keeper. “I hoped to ask about this stone.” Zhao nodded, looked him over, and said, “You seem to share Mi the Eccentric's passion. Since you ask, I must tell you. The stone has a distinguished history: it came from Genyue in Daliang.” So it had belonged to Emperor Huizong's Genyue garden, carried all the way from Kaifeng six or seven centuries earlier. Its rarity was obvious. “Perhaps you have not yet discovered its finest feature.” Zhao turned and called, “Little Fourth, bring a drying pole!” In Hangzhou, a bamboo pole for hanging clothes was called a langgan. Little Fourth knew what it was wanted for. Without a word he inserted it into one end of the stone. Only then did Ying notice a bowl-sized hole running right through it. The pole easily emerged at the other end. “A true thread of sky!” Ying immediately imagined the stone incorporated into the rockery, with the midday sun shining through it into a cavern as a round shaft of light. What an exquisite scene that would make.

“Mr Zhao,” he asked directly, “could you bear to part with it?” Zhao studied him again. “Are you building a garden for yourself, or finding materials for someone else?” “To be frank, the God of Wealth, Hu, invited me to remodel his garden. If I obtain this remarkable stone, I shall have to revise my design again.” “So it is for him!” Zhao shook his head. “I will not commit that sin.” Ying was astonished. “What do you mean?” “Mr Hu is admirable in many ways and has done a great deal of good. Unfortunately, these past few years he has become proud, extravagant, indulgent, and idle, quite changing his nature. Those despicable flatterers under him have made him forget all limits. Diligence and thrift build a household; pride and extravagance ruin it. Consider this very stone. Had Emperor Huizong not built Genyue and imposed his flower-and-rock transport levies, how could the Jin armies have reached Bianliang? Since garden building is your profession, you must have worked for many wealthy and powerful families. How many of their owners have worthy descendants? As for Mr Hu, his establishment has grown too large to control. A true friend would urge him to withdraw while there is time. Anyone who continues encouraging his reckless expenditure will sooner or later feel the reproach of conscience.”

The speech left Ying sweating and deeply regretting his decision to emerge from retirement. Yet matters had gone too far for him to return his fee and withdraw his plans. He could only plead urgent business at home and firmly decline the supervision. Unable to detain him despite repeated entreaties, Hu asked him to recommend a replacement. Ying found it hard to refuse. The design also embodied much effort, and he feared seeing it ruined by an incompetent hand. Among Hu's retainers was Zeng Xiaosu, who knew something of the art and occasionally offered original ideas in conversation. Ying therefore said that Zeng could undertake the task. Hu always wanted to establish a man's abilities before employing him. He summoned Zeng, had him examine the drawings in Ying's presence, and asked how long construction would take. “With a great master here,” Zeng said, smiling, “how could I venture an opinion?” “Not at all!” Ying interjected, giving him a meaningful glance. “Please make an estimate, Brother Xiaosu.” Zeng understood that this profitable assignment was probably within reach. He concentrated on calculations for a while, then asked, “When would you like it finished, sir?”

“How about fifty days?” “Fifty days would require one hundred and twenty workers.” Zeng counted on his fingers. “There are four grottoes in the design: twenty craftsmen for each, leaving forty men to transport stone. Five days to pound the mortar, twenty for construction, ten allowed for alterations, and ten to complete the tops. If everything goes smoothly, forty-five days will suffice. You may arrange your grand banquet for fifty days from the start.” Hu neither agreed nor disagreed, but turned to Ying. “What do you think?” “The calculation is intelligent, but rather tight. Any slackening during construction, and fifty days will be insufficient.” “I have allowed five days' margin,” Zeng replied. “You may not realize, sir, that elsewhere I might hesitate to promise a fixed date because materials or labour could be short. Here, whatever workers, money, or materials are needed can be supplied. I am confident of finishing in fifty days.” “That is true.” Ying's approval was like the certification of examination officials. In the provincial examination years corresponding to Zi, Wu, Mao, and You, the court first appointed senior officials who had passed both higher examinations to test the eligible capital officials; only those who passed could be sent out as chief and deputy examiners. Ying had similarly certified Zeng's competence to supervise, and Hu consequently trusted him without reservation.

An auspicious day was chosen, and work began. The old rockery had already been demolished. On the cleared ground, one hundred and twenty craftsmen formed twelve circles and began pounding mortar. The steward, Hu Yunfu, had instructed them beforehand: “No calling out while you pound. The old lady dislikes the noise.” There was a special reason for this. The mortar, known in Hangzhou as niaojiang, used a particular kind of leaf which, soaked in water, produced a thick liquid resembling the wood-shaving infusion women used to dress their hair. This was added to lime and yellow clay before pounding. Several men stood in a circle around the mixture, each holding a waist-high T-shaped rammer. Its shaft was a piece of chestnut wood as thick as a rice bowl, with a rounded iron head at the bottom and a firmly fitted crosspiece two chi long at the top. At the leader's signal, the men stepped back, straightened, and swung their rammers upward. As the tools descended, they stepped forward and bent, driving the heads heavily into the lime and clay. Another worker continuously ladled on the thick leaf infusion. At first, white lime and yellow clay remained distinct; gradually they blended, and the longer the pounding continued, the tougher the mixture became. In Hangzhou, tomb builders packed it around coffins. Once dry, it became extraordinarily hard, virtually impervious to blades and weapons. The rarity of grave robbery there was attributed to this mortar. When a burial had to be moved, there was a separate method for breaking it: the tomb was opened, strong liquor poured over the mortar and ignited, and, after the liquor and flames were exhausted, the material became brittle enough to work with a hoe.

When the Ming founder built Nanjing's walls, he had charged Shen Wansan, the immensely wealthy man of the late Yuan, with construction. Massive stones were joined with boiled glutinous-rice paste, enabling the walls to endure for centuries. Niaojiang could perform a similar function. What mattered most was prolonged, even pounding, making the leader's signals indispensable. These were the familiar heave-ho cries of labour. Their rhythm, while expressing the workers' exertion, naturally directed the force and speed of each stroke, counted the blows, and regulated the length of their steps. As they worked, the men slowly moved round to their right, both to ensure even mixing and to measure the labour performed. Usually twelve to sixteen circuits were needed to bring the mortar to its full strength. Besides tomb building, it was used in rockeries, where only this material could firmly join the stones. But the distinctive pounding chant was often heard around burial grounds in spring and autumn, inevitably suggesting that another grave was being built nearby. Hu's elderly mother disliked hearing it; hence Hu Yunfu's order for silence. Without the chant, the workers were like soldiers deprived of commands. Their movements became disordered and slow. Eager to succeed, Zeng scolded and shouted at them. They dared not voice their anger at work, but talked bitterly as they left. Their complaint was not that Zeng lacked consideration, but that the Hu household was cruel.

Cruelty was indeed occurring, though Hu knew nothing of it. Whenever a great household undertook construction, contractors or foremen were apt to skimp on labour or materials. In building a rockery there was little scope to economize on the stone, but labour could be cheated. Because Zeng was shrewd, the contractors dared not inflate the headcount; instead they passed apprentices and assistants off as skilled craftsmen. The first two days went well, but by the third something was wrong. Racking his brains, Zeng devised a rule: no wages could be drawn in advance, and payment would be made at the end of each day. A specially built long bench more than eight chi high stood by the garden gate. For each group of twelve men, twelve wage packets were placed on it. Everyone had to reach for his own; nobody could pass a packet to someone else. Anyone whose arm did not reach received nothing for his day's work. Young apprentices left empty-handed and tearful, but short adults were equally helpless. Zeng proudly claimed credit for the arrangement: tall men had ample strength, he said, while even a strong short man had limited power. What use was a rockery builder without strength? This was the surest means of retaining the able and eliminating the unfit. Public opinion, however, became appalling. As the story spread, it was said that Hu abused his power by making men work without paying them. Some protested that a man famous for charity could never be so harsh. But witnesses were available, and even those wishing to defend him were silenced.

Another incident was still more outrageous. One year, early in winter, Hu held Buddhist rites for his late father's posthumous birthday and distributed food and clothing. Anyone willing to endure the embarrassment of accepting charity could queue for a blue cotton padded jacket and four white-flour steamed buns, each as large as a rice bowl. Hu had personally inspected the jackets and tasted the buns, taking every care. The charitable event should have gone well. Instead, people cursed him through clenched teeth. Again, the fault lay in his choice of subordinates and their reckless conduct. Some recipients, wanting a little extra, joined the queue a second time for another portion. A generous view would recognize that they had spent further time and effort to obtain it, rather than gained something for nothing. Even a strict response need have gone no further than a reprimand. But the organizers devised a novel system. After receiving a jacket and buns, each person encountered a group of daizhao, as barbers were also called, waiting at the exit with a razor in each man’s hand. A patch of hair was shaved off as proof that charity had already been received. Anyone unwilling to submit had to forgo the gifts. “Little Uncle,” the Seventh Lady said, still angry at the recollection, “imagine someone queuing before dawn and waiting until noon, without knowing of this rule. To refuse would mean all that hardship for nothing. To accept would leave a bald patch advertising that he wore charity clothes. What a choice! How could people help feeling bitter?”

Hu's face alternately flushed and paled. Despite the late-autumn weather, sweat dampened his back. “I knew nothing of this, Seventh Sister. When I return, I shall investigate and give the culprit a thorough dressing-down.” “There is no need. The man no longer works for you. That is why I have spoken.” “Then there are still others like him there?” She was silent, which amounted to assent. Since matters had reached this point, Gu decided to add his own counsel. He had followed Hu for years and knew much of the difficulty of establishing the business; his advice was therefore both extensive and penetrating. “You regard your pawnshops as a service to the poor, Little Uncle, and say you do not want to make money from them. But what pawnshop in the world makes no money? Because you have expressed that intention, even profits that ought properly to be earned are not appearing. Have you considered that?” “I have. I told them that a bank is a rich man's pawnshop, and a pawnshop is a poor man's bank. I deal with the rich. They pledge their credit or their connections; I can generally judge whether to accept the pledge and how much it is worth. There are too many poor people for me to look after personally, so I entrust them to the staff, who must act according to conscience. I have treated those Huizhou friends well. Surely they cannot be entirely without conscience.” Pawnshop appraisers came from Huizhou, hence his name for them. Gu realized from this speech that Hu knew nothing of the accumulated abuses in his own pawnshops. He also saw that his own observations could be of real use.

“Do you know how many pawnshops you own, Little Uncle?” Hu was taken aback. Scratching his head, he said, “There must be twenty?” “Count them,” the Seventh Lady urged. “Start with Hangzhou.” First came Gongji, the earliest shop Hu had established; then Guangshun and Tai'an, at Gongzhen Bridge outside Wulin Gate, the starting point of the canal, set up especially for the convenience of the grain-transport brotherhood. Across Hangzhou, Huzhou, Jiaxing, Haining, Jinhua, and Quzhou in Zhejiang, Suzhou and Zhenjiang in Jiangsu, and Hubei and Hunan, there were twenty-three in all. A pawnshop's operating capital was called its shelf capital. By convention it was stated in copper cash rather than silver, at one thousand cash to a tael: ten thousand taels thus became ten thousand strings of a thousand cash. Shops varied in size, with shelf capital ranging from fifty thousand to two hundred thousand such strings. At an average of one hundred thousand each, the twenty-three shops represented 2,300,000 taels. If their pledged goods were valued instead, the figure would at least double. “Let us put the total at four and a half million taels,” Gu said. “A return of one per cent is a low estimate for a business like this. That would mean forty-five thousand taels a month—more than one could spend. You could have me give up all my other work and concentrate on managing these twenty-three pawnshops.” Hu calculated: forty-five thousand a month meant 540,000 a year. Yet he could not remember annual pawnshop profits ever exceeding two hundred thousand. On that reasoning, the Huizhou friends were swallowing more than three hundred thousand taels a year.

“My monthly expenditure, including all entertaining, is only forty or fifty thousand taels. If the pawnshops were properly managed, I could put myself beyond defeat. Where do you think I should begin reforming them, Yingchun?” “Naturally, with an audit and inspection.” “One shop after another, or all together at a single order?” “All together, of course.” “Are you talking without thinking?” the Seventh Lady interrupted. “Where will you find enough people to inspect twenty-three shops at once? It is not merely checking accounts. The pledged goods on the shelves must be examined too, and outsiders cannot do that.” “Seventh Sister,” Hu stopped her, “if Yingchun proposes it, he must have a method.” “Exactly!” Gu answered with satisfaction. “My method is quick, thorough, and unlikely to offend anyone. Consider: if we inspect one shop after another, we naturally start with those we distrust, taking them by surprise. If faults appear, well and good. But if a shop proves entirely sound, its people will resent the suspicion, and it will be harder to obtain their best service afterwards.”

“Enough preliminaries!” the Seventh Lady said impatiently. “If you have a method, tell us.” “It leaves no sign of suspicion. Little Uncle, make a general reshuffle. Transfer all the managers and custodians of pledged goods among the twenty-three shops. Transfers require formal handovers, and each person taking over becomes responsible. Naturally, he will not dare be careless. In this way, both the accounts and the actual goods on the shelves will be thoroughly checked.” “That is ingenious. But moving a man from a small shop to a large one will cause no complaint; moving him from a large one to a small one certainly may.” “There is a remedy. Divide the shops into three classes according to size, and have those within each class draw lots for exchanges. The differences will be limited, and everyone will depend on his luck, leaving little ground for complaint.” “Besides,” the Seventh Lady added, “you can privately reassure and reward the few who are truly capable and have done well.” “Quite right. I shall arrange it when I return to Hangzhou.”

CHAPTER FOUR: THE BEAUTY STRATAGEM

Hu Xueyan remained in Shanghai until definite news of Zuo Zongtang arrived. Zuo had left Beijing on the eighteenth day of the tenth lunar month, but instead of taking a seagoing steamer south from Tianjin and passing through Shanghai on his way to assume the Liangjiang governor-generalship at Jiangning, he was first returning to Hunan to visit his ancestral graves. He was not expected to take up his post until near the year's end, when official seals were put away for the New Year holiday. Hu had intended to welcome him in Shanghai and return to Hangzhou only after Zuo left for Jiangning. Now he decided to go home first and come back later. On his second day in Hangzhou, he summoned Tang Zishao, manager of Gongji Pawnshop, and explained his plan to transfer all twenty-three pawnshop managers. Their handovers would naturally provide an opportunity for a thorough inspection of every shop. “Zishao, you are the senior man among the managers of my twenty-three shops. I want you to handle this. Draw up a scheme, preferably to be completed before the year's end. Then every shop can begin next year with a fresh set of accounts, the dividing line clear and everything in order. What do you say?” Tang was taken aback. A multitude of anxious thoughts crowded his mind. Collecting himself, he replied, “At the end of the year, Mr Hu, those who are doing well come to redeem their pledges, while those who cannot make ends meet must pawn things. Wouldn't a general reshuffle at our busiest time throw everything into confusion?” “There is something in that. But you can prepare the scheme first and let everyone get ready. Once the New Year is over, make the transfers in a quiet month.” “Yes. That is the proper way.”

On returning from these instructions, Tang immediately sought out Pan Maocheng, the custodian of pledged goods, and shut the door for a confidential discussion. The two had been defrauding the business together for years. Their worst irregularities involved clothing left unredeemed after the loan period expired. Gongji had so much of this that it had opened a second-hand clothing shop of its own, under the sign of Gongji Clothing House. Forfeited garments from the various pawnshops were sent there for sale. Some arrived unchanged; others had been switched. A nearly new sheepskin coat of the fine “radish-thread” variety, for instance, would turn into a plain-skin coat by the time it reached the clothing shop. Pawn tickets habitually described valuable objects as worthless. A gold repeater watch might be entered as “one broken brass watch.” The wildly cursive handwriting could be read by nobody but the appraiser himself, so customers never protested. With tickets and accounts written in this fashion, substitutions among forfeited pledges were impossible to trace. At Gongji, the switching was particularly flagrant: dark sable became dark lambskin, and silk garments became bamboo ones. A comparison with the clothing shop's stock-entry accounts would expose the irregularities, and then matters would look very ugly. After much discussion, they could see only one way out: have the whole transfer scheme abandoned. The year-end rush provided a reason to postpone it, but beyond that they could find no argument against it. Pan was at his wits' end. Tang, however, thought of one desperate expedient. It must be carried out secretly, without a word getting about, and whether it could be attempted at all depended on his concubine's willingness.

Tang came from Huizhou. Appraisers from that region did not bring their families when they went elsewhere to earn a living. Seeing how lonely he was away from home, Hu had given him a maid named Yueru as a concubine three years earlier. Within six months of her marriage, she had seemed transformed into another woman. Her yellowish hair had grown thick and black; her coarse skin had become fair and smooth. Her figure had always been good, but now her slender waist and full hips stood out more strikingly, inviting thoughts of pleasure. Most remarkable were her eyes. Once dull and vacant, as though she never had enough sleep, they had become bright and liquid; a glance from them seemed to flash with a power that seized the heart. Hu was greatly attracted. His manner and conversation often betrayed an eagerness to try his chances. Tang had noticed long ago and merely pretended not to know. Now, in desperate circumstances, he thought of using her beauty as his stratagem. If he could persuade Yueru, half the task would be done.

After considering his approach, Tang decided to frighten her with the consequences. “Disaster is upon us, Yueru.” “Disaster?” Alarmed, she asked at once, “What trouble have you got yourself into?” “You could say I brought it on myself.” He pointed to the jade hairpin in her hair and the emerald ring on her hand. “Do you know where those came from?” “Weren't they forfeited pledges?” “They should have been. I entered them as having been redeemed by their original owners and took them away. That counts as tampering with the records and fraud. If it comes out, there will be terrible trouble.” “There won't. Mr Hu is a very generous man. Tell him honestly and admit your fault. He won't make things difficult for you.” “That is no use. I am not the only person involved. It is bound to come out. Then he won't have to dismiss me: I shall have no face to remain in Hangzhou. I shall have to go home and live on what we have put by.”

Looking utterly miserable, Tang continued, “I have brought this on myself. What grieves me is that I have ruined you too.” “Ruined me?” Yueru was shocked. “How have you ruined me?” “Think. First, once the fraud is discovered, restitution must be made. I fear not one piece of your jewellery will remain. Second, you will have to come back to Huizhou with me and suffer hardships. How could you bear that kind of life?” She had often heard him describe his home country. Huizhou lay among countless mountains, with little land, many people and scant produce. The men therefore went away to trade, leaving the women to do men's work: carrying water, chopping firewood, everything. Their lives were harder than those of women anywhere in Jiangsu or Zhejiang. Then she thought of her own position. Before Tang's principal wife she would have to be humble and submissive, serving her morning and evening. She would rather die than endure that. The thought made her frantic. “Really, what were you thinking?” she reproached him. “Besides your salary, every month you get shares of storage fees, sales commissions, pooled extra interest, loan fees and redemption fees. Those extras are substantial, and there is a dividend at the year's end. Why couldn't you enjoy a comfortable life instead of devising further tricks?”

Though she had been married to Tang for only three years, Yueru already knew the customs of the pawnshop well. Every grade of staff shared in extras beyond the regular monthly wage: the inside posts of manager, pledge custodian, cashier and bookkeeper; the outside posts of appraisers at the counter; the intermediate ranks who wrote and checked tickets, wrapped bundles and attached labels; and even the apprentices. Valuable clothes required special care, for which a fee of one per cent of the loan principal was customarily charged, called cunxiang, the storage fee. When forfeited goods were sold, six-tenths of one per cent was deducted for the employees, under the name shiyong, the sales commission. The customary grace period did not exceed five days: redemption within five extra days incurred no additional interest, but a delay of more than six days required payment of two months' interest. The extra month's interest then went to the staff as gongchou, the pooled levy. The dangli, or loan fee, was one-tenth of one per cent of the principal advanced; the shuli, or redemption fee, was three-tenths of one per cent of the principal repaid. Thus, if a shop advanced a hundred thousand taels in a month and recovered fifty thousand, the loan fees would amount to a hundred taels and the redemption fees to a hundred and fifty. These extras were pooled and divided each month in differing proportions. As manager, Tang naturally received a large share: fifty or sixty taels in a lean month, over a hundred in a good one. His circumstances were decidedly comfortable.

Tang did feel regret, but he said, “What is done is done. Reproaches are no use. We must find a remedy now. If you are willing, I can think of something.” “What use is my being willing?” “Of course it is useful. Just tell me: are you willing or not?” “How could I be unwilling? But explain why a single word from me could help.” “Because you possess something useful. The question is whether you will lend it for a little while. If you agree, you need only offer it.” Yueru considered his words, then suddenly understood. Her face hardened. “To whom do you want me to lend myself?” “Who else? Mr Hu, naturally.” She gave a cold laugh. “I knew you would come up with some shameless scheme like this!” “Every man needs his face, as every tree needs its bark. Do you think I want to lose mine? But there is no other way in an emergency. Better to lose face before Mr Hu than be called shameless by everyone in the trade. Is my calculation wrong?” “Your calculation is sound. But though you can do without your dignity, I cannot.” “Only he, you and I will know. There will be no fourth person. Your reputation will be safe.” Yueru said nothing. Her silence plainly signified agreement.

“Mr Hu,” Tang said, “I should like to discuss this matter with Rongzhai. He has a good head and is sure to devise a suitable arrangement.” Rongzhai's surname was Shi. He managed Gongshun Pawnshop in Deqing, in Huzhou Prefecture, and was exceptionally capable. Under his sole management, its annual profit consistently ranked first. Originally fifth or sixth in size among the twenty-three shops, it was now the largest, with accumulated shelf capital of three hundred thousand strings of a thousand cash. Hu thought that consulting Shi Rongzhai was precisely the right way to proceed and agreed without hesitation. “Have you any message for Rongzhai, sir?” “Yes. When are you leaving?” “Whenever you wish.” “Good. Let me think, and I shall tell you.”

“Here is a suggestion,” Tang said. “On what day are you free for lunch?” That had to be asked of Madam Song, fifth among Hu's twelve concubines, who managed all his social engagements. A maid was sent to inquire. The reply was that he had engagements throughout the next ten days, and a list was copied out, clearly showing when he was to be a guest and when a host. “Why do you ask when I am free for lunch?” “Yueru has long wanted to prepare a few dishes to show her respect. I thought you might come for a simple meal, and give me your instructions for Rongzhai at the same time.” This pleased Hu. Besides seeing Yueru, he was eager to taste her cooking. He took the list and studied it. “I can miss both lunch engagements the day after tomorrow. Let us make it then.” “Yes, sir. Would you name a few dishes you would like?”

Yueru had originally helped in the kitchen. She was not a scullery maid, but her duties had consisted merely of running about and carrying food boxes. Naturally quick-witted, she had learned through watching and listening and become a good cook. It was because Tang cared about fine food and she could prepare it that Hu had chosen this otherwise unremarkable-looking maid for him. During the past three years, Tang had explained recipes from the Sanhuang Shiyue Qianyu and the Suiyuan Food Manual to her. She reproduced them and made improvements, developing several specialities that even Hu's cooks admired. But she took pride in her skill and would not readily display it, so it remained little known. “All Yueru's dishes are good,” Hu said, “though some take a great deal of trouble.” “Never mind that. Please ask for whatever you wish.” Hu nodded. “Kidneys with walnuts.” This was indeed laborious. Lamb or pig kidneys were first boiled in salted water with fresh ginger, then stripped of their membrane and sliced. Selected walnut kernels were peeled, crushed and mixed with the slices. The mixture was stirred constantly over a very low fire until oil came out of the walnuts and penetrated the kidneys. Good soy sauce, aged wine and spices were then added, and everything cooked through. It made an excellent dish to accompany wine.

“What else?” “The steamed eggs Yueru once made for my mother were good too.” “Ah, the three-delicacy eggs. Those are easy. Anything else?” “Those are the only two that occur to me. Be sure not to make too many dishes. It would be wasteful. Besides, one person's time and effort are limited. With too many dishes to attend to, the flavour is bound to suffer.” “Certainly. Please come early the day after tomorrow.”

Tang lived behind Gongji Pawnshop, having rented one section of another household's residence: three rooms upstairs and three below, with wings at front and back. An east-facing room in the rear wing served as Yueru's kitchen. Upstairs, the two outer rooms had been joined to make a sitting room; the innermost was the bedroom. On Hu's arrival, he was taken upstairs. A white-copper brazier burned fiercely. The windows had been newly papered, and although tightly shut, they admitted a bright light. Hu removed his black-fox-fur robe. Even in only his silk-floss-padded jacket and trousers, he was sweating. Soon footsteps sounded on the stairs and Yueru appeared, wearing a purple Huzhou-crepe padded jacket and loose-legged, lined trousers of fine woollen cloth. Hu particularly disliked skirts on young women. Apart from his mother, every woman in his household wore a jacket and trousers; Yueru did the same. She made her formal greeting, still addressing him as she always had: “Master.” “You have put on weight, and your complexion is better than ever. Your whole face is glowing.” “That is because it is so hot,” Hu said, touching his face. “You are wearing silk floss. No wonder.” Yueru turned to Tang. “Go and see whether Master's clothes bundle contains an unpadded jacket and trousers.” Tang suddenly slapped his forehead. “Of course! I should have thought of that earlier.” He rose and went out.

Yueru sat down and asked after the old lady, Mrs Hu, and the senior concubine who managed the household. The last was surnamed Luo, fourth in her family; as her home had been outside Luosi Gate, she was known as Madam Luosi. Yueru went on to inquire about the young master and young lady. By the time she had asked after them all, Tang had brought the clothes bundle from Hu's attendant. “Let me help you change, Master,” she said, taking it. With Tang present, Hu could hardly allow her to perform such a service. “No, no. I can manage myself.” “Then come inside to change.” Yueru led him into her bedroom and drew the door shut. Hu sat on the edge of the bed and exchanged his padded clothes for lined ones. Once dressed, he naturally looked about. Of all the furniture, only the bed was particularly fine: a large rosewood frame, a very thick mattress, a brand-new silk-floss quilt and snow-white pillowcases. Beside it lay a wax-yellow Buddha's-hand citron. He picked it up and sniffed. It carried a trace of osmanthus, presumably from Yueru's hair oil. “Have you finished?” came a voice outside the door. “Yes.” “Then I'll put things away.” The door creaked open, and Yueru came in to fold and wrap the padded jacket and trousers he had taken off.

Hu had already returned to the outer room. Tang, who was smoking his water pipe, rose. “Shall we eat now, sir?” “If it is ready. When are you leaving for Huzhou?” “This afternoon.” “Then I must give you my instructions for Rongzhai. First, the silk market has been poor this year, and the silkworm-raising households may have difficulty getting through the New Year. Tell him to have the counter staff be a little more generous in assessing their pledges.” “Yes.” “Second, don't sell the forfeited silk…” “Most forfeited silk turns yellow,” Tang interrupted. “Unless we sell it, the longer it sits, the yellower and less valuable it becomes.” “If you sell,” Hu said, “first make careful inquiries about the buyers. If they are buying for the Shanghai silk-reeling factories, you must not sell to them.” “Yes,” Tang agreed, then added a qualification. “But if they are determined to obtain it, there is really no way to stop them.” “Why not?” “They can buy the pawn tickets and redeem the silk.” “That is precisely what I want. If the owners cannot afford to redeem their pledges, it is something, at least, if they can sell the tickets for a little money.” “You have the heart of a bodhisattva, sir,” Tang said admiringly.

“It is hardly a bodhisattva's heart. If I lose nothing and can help someone, why shouldn't I? To tell the truth, once a man has standing, there are countless ways for him to benefit others at no cost to himself. It depends only on whether he has the will.” “Your intentions are good, sir. It is a pity some people do not realize it.” “Why must they? To confer benefits at no cost and still insist on praise is an official's trick. In business one must be straightforward. Behave like that, and those who understand will criticize you behind your back for fishing for a reputation. Your gilded shop sign will no longer hang securely.” “Quite so, sir. You see deeply into things. But…” “Enough of your ‘buts’ and ginkgo nuts and red dates!” Yueru interrupted loudly. “You will talk until you forget the time. Dinner is ready.” Looking up, they saw a table covered with dishes. Besides the walnut kidneys and three-delicacy eggs Hu had requested, there were chicken steamed with pine nuts, fish stir-fried with winter bamboo shoots, ham braised with yellow-heart cabbage, a large bowl of fish-ball and water-shield soup, and the pickled greens every Hangzhou household made in winter. “What wine will you have, Master? The Huadiao is already warming.” “Good. Huadiao will do.” After pouring the wine, Yueru began serving the food. “I was afraid you might be tired of Fang Yuhe hams, so I have used Xuanwei ham today.”

“You exaggerate. One never tires of good ham.” Hu picked up a piece of Xuanwei ham and chewed it. “Speaking of Xuanwei ham, let me tell you a funny story. Sheng Xingsun is particularly fond of it. Someone hoping to flatter him had a pair brought all the way from Yunnan and sent to his Telegraph Bureau. The gift card said, ‘A pair of Xuan legs.’ That offended his taboo…” “Sheng Xingsun's name is Sheng Xuanhuai,” Tang explained to Yueru. “So he was displeased?” she asked. “Indeed. He flew into a temper. ‘What do you mean, Xuan legs? Take them away!’ A few days later he remembered them and summoned the bureau's cook. ‘Where are my legs?’ The cook understood and replied, ‘Your Excellency did not want your two legs, so the gentlemen in the bureau have eaten them.’”

Hu spoke rapidly, almost in a tongue-twister, and Yueru could not stop giggling. “The story is not finished,” he continued. “Sheng Xingsun is a spiteful fellow, always taking advantage and then putting on a virtuous air. Someone who resented him decided to make fun of him and sent another gift. Again the card said, ‘A pair of Xuan legs.’ But the two hams were black and smaller than Jinhua hams, let alone Xuanwei ones. Wondering what sort they could be, he called in the cook.” “Did the cook know?” Yueru asked. “Of course he knew his goods. ‘Your Excellency,’ he said, ‘these two legs of yours are dog's legs!’” Yueru laughed again. When she could speak, she said, “So they were dog hams! I have heard of them, but never seen one.” “They are seldom seen,” Tang said. “Only one dog ham is put in a vat of hams, to impart its fragrance.”

“Dog meat certainly is fragrant. Unfortunately, my mother will not allow it into the house.” Hu turned to Yueru. “She often mentions your steamed eggs. Make her another bowl tomorrow.” “How kind of the old lady! If she likes them, I will make them and send them every day.” “Steamed eggs should be eaten straight from the steamer,” Tang said, suggesting a better plan. “Why not teach Young Madam Liu the secret? Then the old lady can have them whenever she wants.” Like an imperial household, Hu's establishment had several small kitchens. The one devoted to his mother was managed by Young Madam Liu. Teaching her the method would make everything much easier. “An excellent suggestion, Zishao.” Hu thoroughly approved. “Tell me, Yueru, why is it that however many fine ingredients one puts into steamed eggs, they always come to table clear on top and thick below, with everything sunk to the bottom in a hard mass? Only in your three-delicacy eggs is everything evenly distributed, tender rather than overdone. What is the secret?” “They must be steamed twice…” First she beat three eggs thoroughly with a teacup of ham stock from which the fat had been removed and a little salt, then steamed them until set, as tender as the softest tofu. Only then did she add the chopped ham, chopped dried mushrooms, shrimp and other ingredients. She beat another raw egg into the steamed custard, mixed everything thoroughly, and added mushroom stock according to the consistency. Steamed again, it became the three-delicacy egg dish Hu was now eating.

“One should never reveal a secret,” Tang said with a laugh. “Once explained, it is worth nothing.” “Not so,” Hu replied. “Merely knowing the method is no use without care and effort. The result will be neither one thing nor another, let alone better than anyone else's. Am I right, Yueru?” His words naturally pleased her, and her smile was sweet. “If you say so, Master, have some more while it is hot.” She scooped up a spoonful and held it towards his lips. “I can manage myself.” Hu caught her hand and prevented her from putting the spoon into his mouth. At this, Tang turned to the maid waiting at table. “Bring me a bowl of rice. Once I have eaten, I must catch my boat. Time is getting very short.” “When does it leave?” Hu asked. “At two.” “Then you must hurry. It is past one already. These days a small steamer tows seven or eight passenger boats together. They won't wait once it is time to leave.”

Tang hurriedly finished his rice and took his leave. Yueru went to see him downstairs, but he stopped her at the stairhead. “Stay and keep Mr Hu company. There is plenty of time; I shall catch the boat. I expect to be away three days. Be careful with the fires and candles.” “I know. Go without worrying.” She told the maid, “See the master downstairs, then help Mother Chen in the kitchen. I will attend here.” Yet she remained where she was until the footsteps had died away. Then she turned, shut the door to the staircase and slipped the movable bolt into place, cutting them off from the outside. Hu felt a stir of excitement. This was rather like the opening of The Plum in the Golden Vase: Mr Hu had become Master Ximen. Tang might look like the procuring Granny Wang, but if he missed his boat and came home to find them, he would suddenly turn into the cuckolded Wu Dalang. That would be no joke. Could Tang have conceived a malicious plan and laid a honey trap for him? Hu asked himself the question while studying Yueru's face. Her calm expression reassured him. Even if Tang had such wicked intentions, he would lack the courage to carry them through. Yueru had still less reason to join him in a blackmail trap. Apparently they wanted something and had resorted to this desperate means of obtaining it. There was nothing very serious to fear.

Reassured, Hu let his thoughts roam. “Yueru, how I regret having given you to Old Tang.” “Why?” “Must you ask?” He took her hand. “Are you pretending not to understand?” “I am not pretending. I am only lamenting my hard fate. If I must be a concubine anyway, why am I unworthy to live in the Twelve Chambers?” Hu had built a gallery-lined residence divided into twelve sections for his twelve concubines, hence its name, the Twelve Chambers. Hearing her resentment, he replied, “Don't blame me. How could I know you would become what you are today?” “What have I become? Yueru is still Yueru.” “Su Qin was no longer the Su Qin of old. A woman goes through eighteen transformations as she grows, but nobody has changed as much as you. Except for…” He swallowed the rest. She pressed him. “Except for what? Except that I can cook a few dishes, there is nothing about me that pleases you.” “Everything pleases me. Except…” “There you go again, beginning and then stopping. I hate half-finished remarks.” “I will tell you if you promise not to be angry. The one flaw in your beauty is that pair of large feet.” “What is wrong with large feet? Grand Secretary Li's mother has them too.”

She meant Li Hongzhang. The story went that when his brother Li Hanzhang was Governor-General of Huguang and brought their mother to live with him, Li Hongzhang came ahead from Tianjin to Wuchang to welcome her. When her official boat reached the landing, the city's civil and military officers crowded the quay. From there to the governor-general's residence, the procession included dozens of horses ridden by outriders and attendants, placards displaying offices and ranks, and the full ceremonial escort. It stretched so far that the gong and cries clearing the way at the front could not be heard at the rear. Beside the shafts of the old lady's great green-wool-covered sedan walked her two sons, both governors-general, one on either side. The people of Wuchang poured out to watch, all envying her good fortune. The old lady herself was naturally delighted. In her exhilaration, she unconsciously extended the tips of her feet beyond the curtain. Her feet were unbound, and the spectators began whispering. Li Hongzhang noticed and felt embarrassed. “Mother, please draw your feet in. It does not look seemly to show them.” This angered her, for she particularly hated remarks about her large feet. Mortification turned to fury. “Your father never objected to my large feet. Now you object!” It was a famous joke, and Yueru knew it. Hu smiled. “Very well. I do not object to yours.”

“There is really nothing to object to. You don't know the advantages of large feet.” “Then tell me.” She blinked thoughtfully, suddenly blushed and gave him a sidelong look. “I shan't.” Hu felt a pleasurable stir of desire. Smiling, he said, “Put your feet out and let me look.” “No!” she answered sharply, drawing them back behind her chair. Again he thought of The Plum in the Golden Vase. He longed to follow Ximen Qing's example: deliberately knock down his chopsticks and, while bending to retrieve them, take the opportunity to squeeze her foot. Before the thought had fully formed, however, she spoke. “You will see my feet in time.” “When?” She did not answer. He reached over and held her hand. “Come and sit nearer. I have something to tell you.” “Can't you say it from where you are?” “No. This is something that tastes better when one ‘bites an ear.’” In Hangzhou speech, biting an ear meant whispering. “There is nobody here. Why must you bite my ear?” Despite her words, she brought over a round rosewood stool and sat beside him.

Hu put his left arm around her soft, slender waist, leaned close and first breathed in the scent of her hair. Then he whispered, “Go and wash your feet now, will you?” “No,” she answered promptly. “But wasn't it you who said…” “Yes, I said it. But not today.” “Then when?” Yueru did not reply. She let him hold her tighter and tighter without trying to pull away. After a long while she murmured, “It is so hot.” Sitting a little straighter, she raised her left hand and undid the fastenings from her collar to the button beneath her arm. Her jacket fell half open, releasing a faint fragrance. Seated on her right, Hu needed only to lift his hand to touch her bosom. But he preferred first to settle the question. “Why won't you speak?” “What can I say? If Madam Luosi found out, how could I ever show my face in Yuanbao Street again?” “How would she find out? Every man who comes out with me knows how to keep his mouth shut.” Yueru fell silent again. To Hu, she now seemed willing, and he waited patiently. “I have some duck congee simmering. Would you like a bowl?” “Later.” Hu rose and gave her a tug.

Yueru straightened the bedding and washed her hands, then opened the door to the stairs and called the maid to bring up the pot of duck congee. She sent the maid away again, filled a bowl for Hu, and took half a bowl herself to keep him company. “Master,” she asked casually, “is it true that you mean to move all twenty-three managers to different shops?” “Yes. That is what Old Tang has gone to Deqing to discuss.” “Where do you mean to send him?” “I do not know yet.” “How can you not know?” “Heaven will decide. How could I know?” “What do you mean, Heaven will decide?” “We shall draw lots. The twenty-three pawnshops will be divided into three classes—large, medium, and small—and the managers will draw within each class. Suppose there are eight in the largest class: their eight managers draw together, and each goes wherever his lot sends him.” “Then if Old Tang draws Suzhou he goes to Suzhou, and if he draws Zhenjiang he goes to Zhenjiang?” “Exactly.”

At this, Yueru put down her chopsticks, covered her face, and stumbled back into the bedroom. Startled, Hu followed. She lay face down on the bed, her shoulders shaking with sobs. “Yueru! Yueru!” Though he kept nudging her, she paid no attention. The sound of her crying did seem to stop. “What is the matter? Why are you suddenly so heartbroken?” Facing the inner side of the bed, she complained, “How could I not be? You heartless creature! You have tricked me into your arms, had your taste of something new, and immediately thought of this scheme. You will have Old Tang take me into exile in another county, so you need never set eyes on me again!” Hu could not help laughing in astonishment. “Where did that come from? I never dreamed you would connect two things that have nothing to do with each other.” “Nothing to do with each other? If Old Tang is sent away, I must go with him. You do not seem to care in the least. You have had your pleasure, and that is the end of it.” Her accusation was not wholly unreasonable. After considering it, Hu said, “You need not necessarily go with him. I could buy you another house.” “To be your secret household?” “It would not exactly be that…” He was at a loss, but Yueru pressed on. “What else would it be? Even if we said Old Tang had bought it, how should I explain living alone in Hangzhou? People would ask. And someone would be sure to discover your visits. If your attendants said nothing, somebody else would tell Madam Luosi. One day she would come with a crowd to attack me. Then I should have no choice but to throw myself into a river or a well.” Unable to refute her, Hu stood speechless for some time. “You know the transfer plan came first. Even yesterday I had no idea we would share a bed today. The two things were entirely separate; now they seem tied together. Tell me, then: what can we do?”

Yueru deliberately paused as though thinking it over. “There is a way. But first I must ask: did you only want to take advantage of me today, or do you still want me?” “I still want you.” “Then there is only one thing to do. Leave everything as it is.” “What do you mean?” “Move the other managers wherever you please, but leave Old Tang at Gongji. He is the head of all your pawnshop managers, different from the others. There is good reason to leave him where he is.” “How could that be justified? Once I make an exception, everyone will object.” “Then move none of them. I know nothing about business, but surely it depends on knowing people. Arrive suddenly in a strange place and you are completely in the dark. By the time you can see your way, other firms have taken the business.” Hu turned the matter over anxiously, unable to find a solution that served both purposes. At last he sighed. “We shall have to leave everyone where he is.”

The servants in Yuanbao Street soon knew of Tang Zishao’s beauty trap. Hu’s mother, however, ruled the household strictly. She treated the saying “Those who bring you gossip are troublemakers themselves” as an inviolable law, so no one dared carry this secret into the Twelve Chambers. It remained unspoken nearby but traveled far away. Gu related it gloomily to the Seventh Lady, who refused to believe him. “Little Uncle is not that sort of man. If a woman could make him overturn a settled business plan, how could he have built up what he has today? He would have ruined himself long ago.” “I cannot be bothered to argue. He will soon be here to meet His Excellency Zuo. Ask him yourself.” “Of course I shall.” She continued defending Hu. “He must have his reasons for leaving the twenty-three managers in place. His judgment will not be wrong.” Hu arrived the next day and stayed, as before, at Gu’s house. He and Gu returned from their engagements after eleven that night to find the Seventh Lady waiting with the customary late supper. Over wine and conversation, she asked casually, “Little Uncle, I hear you have abandoned your plan to transfer the twenty-three managers. Why?” “Ah, Seventh Sister, please do not ask.” Her expression changed at once. “Why should I not ask?” “Pleasant things are worth talking about. Unpleasant things will only upset you as well. Why bother?” “Then it is true. Tang really did lay a trap for you to walk into. Little Uncle, how could you do anything so foolish?”

As she said “foolish,” her mouth twisted, her eyes turned askew, and her face became fiery red. “Something is wrong!” Gu cried, rushing to support her. She could no longer sit upright and fell headlong from her stool. Fortunately, the thick Persian wool carpet kept her head from being cut open. “A stroke!” Hu jumped up and shouted for servants. While some lifted her, others were sent for doctors. Hu ordered them to fetch Doctor Cao, known as an imperial physician because he had been summoned to take pulses in the palace during the Xianfeng reign. Gu trusted Western medicine and sent separately for a doctor he knew, Ailituo. It was past midnight, and knocking up doctors from their beds naturally took time.
