First, we have many years ahead of us, and opportunities to return one another's kindness. Second, I truly like them.” She immediately had the chair covers arranged. Peonies embroidered on pink satin gave the room a rich splendour.

“Seventh Sister, hold these skirt lengths against yourself. I embroidered them.” One was red, covered with a hundred butterflies in dazzling colours. “It is beautiful, but on me it would be an ugly woman making a spectacle of herself,” the Seventh Lady said. “A bride of about twenty, returning to visit her parents, would look splendid in it. I shall keep it for my daughter.” Hu sprang from his chair. “Yingchun! Will you be inviting me to eat red eggs?” The couple had only one son, but the Seventh Lady had often spoken of wanting a daughter. Hu had noticed her thickened waist, and her words now made him suspect that she was expecting. Gu smiled without answering, tacitly confirming it. Luo took the Seventh Lady's hand. “Congratulations! How many months?” “Four,” she answered softly. “Four months! Quickly, sit down. It would be dreadful to disturb the baby.” “It is all right. The foreign doctor says I should walk about regularly to make the birth easier.” “How broad-minded you are, consulting a foreign doctor even about pregnancy!” With no outsiders present, and knowing her companion's frankness, Luo teasingly asked whether she had even allowed the doctor to feel her belly. “Of course. How else could the doctor tell whether the baby was lying properly?” Luo had meant it as a joke; discovering it was true left her speechless. The Seventh Lady was quite unconcerned. “There is nothing strange or shameful about it.” Luo shook her head repeatedly. “I could never do that, even if I died.” Gu laughed. “Do not let her deceive you, Sister Luo. She is teasing. The doctor is indeed foreign—but a woman.” “I thought as much!” Luo breathed with relief. “Would you not be afraid of a foreign man's hand, covered in black hair like a bear's paw, touching your belly?”

The Seventh Lady merely smiled and took up the other skirt length. It was pale blue satin, embroidered along the lower edge with waves and, above them, two birds she could not identify. The design was both novel and graceful. “I like this one. I shall have it made tomorrow. When the skirt moves, it will look just like a flowing tide. How did you think of it?” “One of my customers, the Zhang family's second young mistress, is very learned. We get along so well that whenever I visit, we talk for half a day. Once, somehow, she mentioned an old line: ‘Her six-panelled skirt trails the waters of the Xiang.’ It gave me an idea, and I designed this when I went home. Pale blue satin soils easily. I shall embroider another for you to alternate with it.” “There is no need. I do not wear skirts very often.” Meanwhile, Hu and Gu were examining the Gu embroidery. Viewed from different angles, the spread-tailed peacock's colours changed. Camellias, bamboo, and rocks completed a composition that rewarded endless attention. “Why not frame it and hang it?” Hu suggested. Gu immediately summoned a servant and ordered a rosewood frame, with a sheet of glass obtained from a foreign trading house, preferably that very day. They next examined the coverlets and pillows. Laughing at herself, the Seventh Lady said it was almost like inspecting a trousseau, which made the servants laugh too.

“I am hungry,” Hu said. “Can we dine soon?” “Everything is ready. We shall begin at once.” The arrangement was much as on the previous evening, but Gu had specially engaged a Cantonese cook. The dishes were excellent and unusual, delighting Luo's palate and broadening her experience. One consisted of two fish, one red-braised and one steamed, on a double-fish-shaped porcelain platter, one side white and the other yellow. Even Hu had never seen anything like it. “Gold and Silver Fish,” Gu explained. “A dish presented as tribute.” “By whom?” Hu asked in surprise. “By the time cooked fish reached the palace, even if it had not spoiled, it would no longer taste good.” “Naturally, it is cooked there and eaten fresh. As for who presents it, you might never guess: the Duke Yansheng of Qufu in Shandong.” “Ah!” Hu remembered. “I have heard that his household serves its most distinguished guests what is called ‘household cuisine.’ Is this an example?” “Exactly. There are a hundred and thirty-six dishes. Their quality is no surprise; what is remarkable is that each requires a specially made plate or bowl. The service includes gold, silver, pewter, and porcelain. If one piece is missing, the whole table setting is unusable. When the duke entertains distinguished guests, a dependable old family servant has sole charge of the tableware.” “And for imperial tribute, surely the service is gold?” “Certainly. At great palace celebrations, such as the Tongzhi emperor's wedding or Cixi's fortieth birthday, the duke goes to Beijing to offer congratulations, taking his cooks, tableware, and rare ingredients. Permission must first be sought for a day on which the court will enjoy his household cuisine. The food is prepared and delivered at the appointed time, though some dishes are cooked inside the palace itself. That requires advance arrangements with the chief eunuch—and naturally a gratuity for gaining access. Fortunately, the duke's estates are extensive, so he need not worry about the expense.”

Hu was much attracted by this account. “Did today's cook come from the duke's household?” “No, he is Cantonese. But his grandfather did. There is an interesting story behind it.” Gu slowly raised his glass and said no more. “If it is interesting, tell us!” his impatient wife urged. “Do not keep us waiting.” “I only heard it a couple of days ago and cannot quite remember. Let me think.” “Take your time.” Luo offered him a piece of fish. “A story is best when it has a proper beginning.” “Very well. To begin: late in Qianlong's reign…” Bi Qiufan was then governor of Shandong. Ruan Yuan had enjoyed early success and been in the Hanlin Academy only a few years when a major examination of Hanlin and Household of the Heir Apparent officials was held. Qianlong himself set the questions. The prescribed subject for the examination poem was spectacles. It was difficult: spectacles had entered China from the West only late in the Ming, so ancient poetry and prose offered no established allusion to them. Moreover, the required rhyme was ta, an awkward choice that made the task harder still. Every candidate looked distressed. Ruan was originally placed second in the first class, but Qianlong promoted him to first, saying that his rhapsody was excellent. In fact, it was the poem that pleased him, particularly a couplet to the effect that four eyes had no need of these things, and double pupils had no use for them. The emperor had been unusually favoured by Heaven: even after eighty, his hearing and eyesight remained keen, and he wore no spectacles, a fact of which he often boasted to his ministers. Ruan had used the allusions to Shun's four eyes and double pupils to flatter him, implying that he perceived people and affairs so clearly that spectacles were unnecessary.

First place in this examination traditionally brought promotion through three grades. Ruan rose at once from Hanlin Compiler to junior supervisor in the Household of the Heir Apparent, and soon became educational commissioner of Shandong. Still under thirty, he had lost his wife and had not remarried. His father had come to live with him there. Bi Qiufan told the elder Ruan, “My daughter could marry the Duke Yansheng; I should like you to arrange it. The duke's elder sister could marry your son; I shall arrange that match.” Thus Ruan became a son-in-law of the Kong family. The duke's household paid particular attention to food, following the tradition of Confucius, who did not consider food too finely prepared. Four cooks therefore accompanied Miss Kong as part of her marriage establishment. One was surnamed He; his grandson was the cook Gu had engaged that day. “How, then, did he become Cantonese?” Hu asked. “Ruan later became Governor-General of Liangguang, a famously lucrative post, and entertained frequently. Although the food did not equal the duke's household cuisine, it far surpassed anything available commercially. Since the household name could not be used, some called it the Manchu–Han Grand Banquet. The Governor-General's cooks were often borrowed to prepare meals elsewhere. That is how Cook He's grandfather settled in Guangdong, and the family became Cantonese.”

At this moment the shark's fin arrived, and Cook He came before the diners wearing a red-tasselled cap to pay his respects. Such was the custom when the principal dish was served; host and guests were expected to reward him. Hu, generous as ever, casually picked out a banknote for a hundred taels. “How can four people finish such a dish?” Luo asked. “I almost feel the expense on Seventh Sister's behalf.” The fin came on a silver platter two chi and five cun across, enough for twelve people. Four diners could hardly do justice to it. The Seventh Lady had a plan. “We are all friends. There is no need for ceremony. Let us put half aside.” Even half was rather too much. After two small bowls, Hu rubbed his stomach and declared himself full. He then asked why he had never heard of this cook before. “He has only recently arrived from Guangzhou,” Gu replied. “He wants to open a restaurant, but the arrangements have not yet been settled.” “What arrangements?” “Someone is offering the capital. They must agree on terms.” “Ask whether he would be willing to come to me. What I lack now is a good cook.” “Very well. I shall ask him.”

After dinner they sat talking. When the clock struck nine, the Seventh Lady urged Hu to take Luo home. Nine was early in Shanghai, where the city remained awake through the night. In places such as Zhoujin Lane, devoted to song, women, and extravagant pleasure, business was only beginning. But both Hu and Luo understood that the Seventh Lady was deliberately giving them an opportunity to become closer, and neither objected. As they were entering their chairs, she told the bearers to place a large two-tier food box in the chair compartment. “In our household, inviting someone to dinner means inviting them to supper afterwards as well. Tonight I am asking Little Uncle to act as host at your house. There is a porcelain jar of shark's fin in the box. It was set aside beforehand; it is not leftovers.” “Thank you. Let us say that you are inviting Mr Hu, and I shall act as hostess for you.” The Seventh Lady laughed. “As you please. You can settle between yourselves who is host and who is guest.” Luo distributed tips to the servants, and she and Hu returned in the same chairs that had brought them. At home she began bustling about as hostess, but Hu stopped her. “There is no need. You would spend all that effort, and I could not eat another thing. It would only waste your time and make me uncomfortable. Have someone brew good tea, and let us talk.” “Then come upstairs.”

Upstairs the lamps shone brightly, and an atmosphere as warm as spring surrounded them. As their eyes met, affection naturally stirred. Luo suddenly felt a constriction in her chest. She straightened, lifted her face slightly, and drew several deep breaths before feeling better. “How old are you this year?” “A little over forty.” “You look younger than forty.” She sighed softly. “Did you know how I felt about you then?” “How could I not? I thought we were not destined for each other. Yet here we are again. It seems the bond remains.” “Unfortunately, I am no longer the woman I was. An ageing woman is like a yellowed pearl, no longer worth anything.” “Not true at all. To my eyes, you are more beautiful than before. Like a persimmon: once green and hard, now red and soft.” Hu swallowed. “One can imagine how sweet it would taste.” She glanced at him and laughingly called him greedy. “Sister Luo,” he asked, “do you remember a summer when I brought you the savings-club payment, and you were alone at home…?”

Of course Luo remembered. She had recalled it on the evening of their reunion. It had been the thirtieth day of the seventh month, the birthday of the Bodhisattva Kshitigarbha. After setting out the incense, the family had gone to watch lotus lanterns being floated, leaving her alone to mind the house. Hu had suddenly appeared. “What brings you here?” “Your savings-club payment. Today is the last day of the month. A day's delay would carry it into next month, and credit matters. Where is everyone?” “Watching the lotus lanterns. Actually, it would have been better if you brought it tomorrow. I have to pass it straight on to someone else. In one hand and out of the other—that would be simple. Money kept overnight will not produce little coins, and a thief might come. Your kindness could turn into harm.” “I had not thought of that. If I had, I would have found some way to gather it all and bring it after lunch.” He considered. “Let me take it back, then, so you need not worry. Tell me who is to receive it, and I shall deliver it for you first thing tomorrow.” “That would be wonderful!” she said happily. “You are saving me the journey. I do not know how to thank you.” “First, give me a cup of cool tea.” “Certainly!” They had been talking in the courtyard by the light of candles set in the ground. For tea, she invited him into the main room.

She brought tea, and Hu drank it all. He then behaved inappropriately towards Luo, and she objected. Just then someone outside called loudly, “Sister Luo! Sister Luo!” She immediately moved away from him and answered, “Coming!” At the same time she signalled that Hu should step out of sight. The visitor was a neighbour with a small inquiry, whom she answered in a few words at the door and sent away. Back inside, she kept well away from Hu. When he tried to approach again, she moved to the other side of the square table. “You ought to go. That thoughtless fellow’s sudden shout frightened me nearly out of my senses. Quickly, quickly—please go.”

They returned to the memory of that incident. Luo’s expression showed sadness and loneliness. “It must have been ten years ago?” Hu asked. “Eleven,” Luo replied. “I was sixteen that year.” He tried to pursue the old subject, but she said she did not wish to discuss it, at least not yet. “When, then?” he asked.

“I don’t know,” Luo replied. Then she suddenly asked, “Do you think my abilities fit me for nothing more than an embroidery shop?” The question checked Hu's amorous thoughts. “Let us discuss this seriously. I knew how capable you were when you were still in your teens. Nobody was shrewder at arranging savings clubs or calculating interest. Frankly, if you were a man, I would ask you to manage a bank.” “Compliments cost nothing.” She smiled. “But I am not convinced by your claim that only a man can manage a bank.” “Do not misunderstand. I am not saying that you are less capable. It is inconvenient for a woman—especially one as beautiful as you. The clerks would quarrel over you, and my bank would be ruined.” “How outrageous!” Her feet were not tiny three-inch golden lilies, but the larger sort that had been bound and then released, described as having ginger for sale in front and duck eggs behind. Laughing, she became a little unsteady and reached for the table, only to have Hu catch her hand. “Never mind the clerks. I might be unable to concentrate on business myself, worrying all day that some customer would marry you and take you away.” In Hangzhou, the expression he used meant taking a wife. It touched Luo's old sorrow. “Enough!” She drew back her hand, sat aside, and said softly, “I can only blame my unhappy fate.” “I feel unhappy too,” Hu offered in sympathy. “If only I had married two years later.” She gave a faint, cold laugh. “Fine words come easily to you.” “Whether they are merely fine words, time will show. But to return to business: you say your abilities extend beyond an embroidery shop. What larger enterprise have you in mind? Tell me.”

She lowered her eyes to the tabletop, her lashes moving as though absorbed in calculation. At last she looked up. “Let us talk tomorrow. Will you come for a simple meal?” “Gladly. I shall come early in the afternoon so that we can talk at length.” “No. Come for lunch and leave early in the afternoon. Evenings are inconvenient.” Hu considered his engagements. He had two invitations for lunch the next day, one involving official business that he could not miss. The day after, he also had an engagement, but it could be declined. Luo settled on that day, and he reluctantly agreed. “I shall make a couple of Hangzhou dishes for you. Now let me act as hostess on the Seventh Lady's behalf and offer you supper.” Hu had little appetite, but the thought of not seeing her the next day made him reluctant to leave. Supper would provide an excuse to linger. He nodded, asking her not to go to any trouble. “Everything is ready. Shall we eat downstairs?” Drinking a little together upstairs would have been more agreeable, but would involve extra work and contradict his request. He rose and followed her down. “What would you like to drink?” “Anything. I am no drinker; I shall merely keep you company.” “Then join me in some medicinal wine I have infused myself.” “Ah! That reminds me…” “Wait until I have laid the table.”

Four dishes appeared: ham, crisp eel, vegetarian mock chicken, and dried croaker preserved in wine lees, all sent by the Seventh Lady. Luo also brought a white porcelain jar. The medicinal wine she poured from it had an unappealing colour but an enticing fragrance. “This looks promising. Do you have the recipe?” “Yes. It is called Duke Zhou's Hundred-Year Wine. I can copy it for you.” “The more recipes of this kind, the better. I intend to open a pharmacy and sell medicinal wines.” Surprised, she asked what had suddenly given him that idea. “Several things. One is a request for a very large quantity of prepared medicines. I thought that opening a pharmacy myself would be both convenient and a way to ensure proper quality.” Who had made the request, and why so much medicine? Zuo's soldiers on the western campaign had begun suffering from difficulty adjusting to unfamiliar climates and conditions. Letters to the Shanghai transshipment bureau requested large quantities of pills, powders, plasters, and other remedies. This had prompted Hu's plan for a substantial pharmacy. He had already obtained an official communication from the Governor-General of Shaanxi and Gansu requesting tax exemption, and had sent buyers to Anguo County in Zhili, the largest centre for crude medicinal ingredients, to purchase authentic supplies. Nothing interested him more than this plan, which he regarded as a practical means of relieving suffering and encouraging the troops. Once started, he spoke without pause. Luo listened closely and asked concise questions whenever something was unclear. Seeing that she both understood the project and cared about his work, he grew still more enthusiastic. They talked into the third watch. At last he noticed neighbours looking curiously at the brilliant lights in her house and the chair bearers talking and laughing loudly outside. Ashamed of the disturbance, he could no longer justify staying. “The day after tomorrow at noon, then. If we talk any longer, the neighbours will curse us.”

On the third morning, Hu went as usual to Fukang Bank. He was told that Weiji had withdrawn nine thousand taels in seventeen bank drafts of differing amounts. He remembered the information but asked no questions. Feeling that his previous visit to Luo had been too conspicuous, he took only one attendant this time and took a Hengsimei carriage instead of a sedan chair. Alighting at the entrance to her lane, he sent the carriage away and walked to the house. It was not yet noon, and seven or eight customers were still waiting in her reception room. Luo rose without embarrassment. “Please sit down, Mr Hu. I shall be finished very soon.” “There is no hurry. Attend to your business.” Holding a cup of tea, he watched quietly as she gave clear, brisk explanations and directions. Her customers seemed to accept her authority: what she said was done, without argument. In scarcely the time needed to drink the tea, everyone had departed. “Admirable!” Hu smiled. “You really are capable.” “We do not know that yet. Wait until the land I bought for you rises in value before praising me.” He was bewildered. “What are you talking about?” “I shall explain over lunch. Sit a little longer while I go to the kitchen.”

Most of the meal was ready. Fish head and bean curd simmered on the stove; pieces of pork were in the steamer. Brined shrimps, crucian carp braised with spring onions, and vegetarian mock chicken had been prepared earlier. She needed only to fry crisp bean-curd-skin rolls and stir-fry shepherd's purse with spring bamboo shoots. “Nothing fine to offer you. But you eat shark's fin and sea cucumber every day and must be tired of them. A few simple, refreshing home dishes might persuade you to eat another bowl of rice.” “Exactly.” Hu sat down happily. “I had little appetite before, but now I am hungry.” She smiled, poured medicinal wine, and served him. He ate with relish, much to her pleasure. “I did not understand what you said about land. Please explain.” “I withdrew nine thousand taels yesterday from the account you gave me. Did you know?” “They told me.” “When the British concession renamed its roads two years ago, I noticed how methodically the foreigners proceeded. Wherever they built a road, land prices rose. Unfortunately, I had no spare money to buy any. A couple of months ago someone approached me about a plot on Shandong Road…” “Wait. Where is Shandong Road?” “Temple Street.”

When the British concession's roads were first laid out, they received English names for the foreigners' convenience: Consulate Road where the consulates gathered, and Customs Road where the Jianghaiguan stood. During the Warring States period, Shanghai had belonged to the fief of Lord Chunshen, Huang Xie of Chu. To relieve flooding in the Songjiang region, he had opened a channel to carry water to the sea. It was called the Huangpu after his surname, or Huang Xie Pu. Other names for Shanghai—Chunshen Pu, Chunshen Jiang, and Shenjiang—came from the same association. Later generations had built a shrine to honour his achievement, also known as Lord Chunshen's temple, but its site could no longer be identified. Tradition held that Yanzhen Temple, established in the Ming near Sanmaoge Bridge to worship the Three Mao Immortals, had originally been that shrine. The British therefore named a nearby road Temple Street. Place names in the concession were confused, and the Municipal Council had long wanted a uniform system. East–west roads were to bear the names of major Chinese cities, while north–south roads would take provincial names. Consulate Road became Beijing Road. Nanjing supplied the next great city's name, given to the road extending west from the Bund park. Temple Street ran north–south and became Shandong Road. This had happened two years earlier, but Hu had paid no attention and did not recognize the new name. Temple Street he knew. “Ah! Someone offered you land there?”

“The road is now being extended southwards. Land there is certain to rise, so I withdrew nine thousand taels and bought more than twenty mu. The transaction is complete.” Hu was astonished. Buying property could remain unsettled for months or years, yet she had finished in a single day. Had someone deceived her? Reading his expression, she asked whether he disbelieved her. “Not that. It simply seems very quick. Have you any documents for the land?” “Of course. I have official lease deeds and authority certificates.” He was still more surprised. “You have even completed the minor transfer? You really are capable.” “If you do not believe me, I shall show you.”

She brought three official lease deeds. Following defeat in the Opium War and the Treaty of Nanjing in Daoguang's twenty-second year, five ports had opened to foreign trade and foreigners had begun arriving in numbers. Their settlement, however, posed a problem. All land beneath Heaven belonged to the sovereign; Chinese land could not be sold to foreigners. Some accommodation had to be devised. In Daoguang's twenty-fifth year, the British consul and the Shanghai circuit intendant therefore agreed on land regulations establishing perpetual leases. A foreigner negotiated with an owner, paid annual rent for a plot, and built upon it. In addition, the owner received a sum roughly equal to ten years' rent, called a deposit but effectively the purchase price. Once a lease was agreed, the neighbouring locality had to be notified. The local headman accompanied representatives of the circuit intendant and consulate to measure the property, establish its boundaries, and record them with a plan on the deed. The consul forwarded it to the circuit intendant for examination. If all was correct, the official sealed the lease deed and returned it to the lessee. Such a document was called a daoqi, an official lease deed. It established rights and responsibilities clearly, making disputes easier to decide than under old Chinese deeds, whose vagueness could turn a dispute into years of litigation and bitter regret. As the saying went, “However wealthy you are, never buy property that brings you grief.” People accordingly devised a nominal arrangement: a foreigner would obtain a daoqi on a Chinese owner's behalf. After agreeing terms and receiving his fee, the foreigner issued an authority certificate acknowledging that he held the property for its owner, who could dispose of it freely at any time. This was called nominee registration, and Shanghai had foreign brokers specializing in it. Before buyers and sellers concluded their transaction, they paid the broker to issue a replacement authority certificate. The original daoqi need not be changed; it passed to the buyer with equal validity. This was a minor transfer. Luo's three deeds naturally came with three authority certificates, written in English. Hu had learned a little English through years of dealing with foreigners. When he saw that the named owner was himself, he understood why she had said she had bought the land for him.

“No, no! The land is yours.” Taking the deeds and certificates, Hu said he would have another minor transfer made into her name. “There is no need. Transferring it back and forth merely gives the foreigner more fees. But you ought to show the three authority certificates to Brother-in-Law Gu. He knows English and understands the foreign settlement. If anything is wrong, we can raise it with the foreigner promptly.” “I shall. But I truly do not understand where you learned to buy land and complete every formality in a day. Even a professional might not manage it so quickly.” “Nonsense. Foreigners are straightforward about business. Once buyer and seller agree, they need only register it and sign to collect a fee. Why should they create delays? The middlemen deliberately drag matters out for a couple of days to make their errand fees seem hard-earned.” She explained her own experience. After agreeing to buy the Shandong Road land, she had engaged a specialist to handle the minor transfer for ten taels. He claimed it would take five days. Having heard of this trick, she said she would pay the same fee but employ him only as an interpreter while she dealt with the foreigner herself. The business was indeed completed in a single visit. “Here is something amusing: the foreigner even invited me to a Western meal. He said no Chinese woman had ever come to his office before. He admired my courage and wanted to entertain me.” “Did you accept?” Hu asked, smiling. “No. I said I was brave enough to ask him to do business, but not brave enough to eat his food. When the interpreter translated it, he laughed heartily.” Hu laughed too. “Never mind the foreigner: I admire you myself. Now I understand. You think an embroidery shop too small to display your abilities, do you not?”

“I would not presume to say that. But you have plenty of funds available at your bank. Why do you not buy land?” “I have never considered it.” Hu explained that his view of money differed from other people's. Money ought to flow like spring water. Buying land and waiting for its value to rise was like keeping water in a pond: only Heaven could supply the rain that raised the level. A prolonged drought would dry it up. He disdained business that depended on such chance. “That view is out of date,” Luo said, boldly criticizing him. “Elsewhere, land rises slowly and is difficult to sell. The money does become stagnant water. But in Shanghai the foreigners are building roads day and night. Once a road is complete, the fields along it can carry houses, and prices rise at once. Buyers can also resell easily. With brisk demand and quick sales, land ceases to be immovable property and becomes movable capital. How is that different from your stocking silk and cocoons?” Hu was taken aback. He had not expected such an acute insight and felt genuinely outmatched. “I must be going. Let us have rice.” She brought a shallow bowl. He poured soup over it and quickly finished, then sent his attendant to hail a street carriage at the entrance to the lane. He went to the transshipment bureau to conduct business and receive visitors. After his evening engagements, he called on Gu and his wife at midnight.

“Here is something extraordinary. Sister Luo knows how to deal in land and negotiate directly with foreigners. Look!” Examining the deeds and certificates, Gu asked in surprise whether Hu had commissioned the purchase. Hu said no and explained everything. “Sister Luo is a formidable woman,” the Seventh Lady remarked. “Little Uncle…” She stopped and did not finish. Hu partly understood but did not pursue it. He merely discussed transferring the three plots into Luo's name. “I know this foreign registration broker,” Gu said. “He sometimes plays tricks. We had better spend fifty taels and make a full transfer.” Without asking what a full transfer involved, Hu left the arrangements to him. “What is Sister Luo's name?” Gu asked. “There you have me.” “Sister Luo is Sister Luo,” his wife said. “Surname Luo, given name Sijie. What is wrong with that?” Hu laughed. “Seventh Sister settles a matter with a single stroke. She has judgment.” Gu laughed too, though rather ruefully, and rose with an air of casualness. “I shall write her name in English.”

When Gu had gone into his study, Hu moved closer to the Seventh Lady and lowered his voice. “There is something I want to discuss. Since the two younger women in my household died in an epidemic, and with my wife's health poor, Mother still has to trouble herself with domestic affairs at times. It is hardly right. I am very fond of Sister Luo. I wonder… can anything be arranged?” “I have already considered it. If she would marry you, Little Uncle, you would be a tiger given wings. You would prosper still further. But whether she will accept the position of a concubine is difficult to say.” “Could you sound her out?” “More than that: we must find a way. What about two wives of equal standing?” “That would mean two separate households, leaving Mother with the work as before. If she will accept the lesser formal status, I shall treat her as a principal wife in every other respect.” “Very well. I understand. I shall persuade her. Your wife is kind and sensible too; she certainly would not mistreat her.” “Then…” “Enough, Little Uncle! You need give me no more instructions. I am more impatient than you. I should like to drink the wedding wine tomorrow.”

True to her word, the Seventh Lady visited Luo the next morning, helped her finish with the customers, and ate upstairs with her. During their casual conversation, Luo could not hide her admiration and excitement whenever Hu was mentioned. Seeing a real prospect of success, the Seventh Lady formed a plan. “I know you were born in the year of the Snake. What month?” “The month?” Luo suddenly laughed. “My childhood name was A'he…” “Then you were born in the sixth month, the lotus month.” Noticing an odd smile and an unfinished thought, she asked about the name. “When I was small, the boys teased me by pretending to be man-eating tigers, roaring ‘A-ho! A-ho!’ They said I would grow into a tigress. I refused to answer to that name. If someone wanted my help—another participant for a savings club, for example—calling me A'he ensured they would not get it. That is how everyone came to call me Sister Luo.” The Seventh Lady laughed. “There is a story behind it, then. A tigress is not such a bad nickname. At least, if people know your husband fears you, they will not dare bully you.” “I am not like that. Why should a husband be afraid? Never mind the past. Now there is even less reason to speak of it.” “Not necessarily. Someone will certainly fear you yet.” Luo hesitated, then asked with a slight blush whom she meant. The Seventh Lady nodded thoughtfully. “There will be someone. An ordinary man is not worthy of you. Even if he married you, his fear would be useless.” “Useless?” “He would fear you because you are capable. Anyone can see that you have the fortune to help a husband succeed. But he must have good material in him too. A weak fellow without ambition or ability might receive an excellent idea from you and be too lazy to act, or incapable of carrying it out. Feeling indebted, he would merely fear you. What use is that?” Luo listened carefully and considered. “You are right. There is a reason some men are afraid of their wives.”

“Exactly.” The Seventh Lady returned to her purpose. “Fortune comes from destiny. To help a husband prosper, you must marry a man with a good destiny, and have a good one yourself. Fortune without destiny is like a rootless tree. Nothing will come of it.” “Destiny is unreliable too. When I was little, everyone who read mine said it was excellent. Look at me now. Where is the excellence?” “What did they say?” “I did not understand much of it. Only that a jiazi day and a jiazi hour made an unusually rich and honourable destiny.” “Perhaps the wealth and honour lie ahead.” “What future is there? With a son, there might be hope. Like the White Lady: after a lifetime of suffering, her son became the top examination graduate and she could hold her head high at last. What have I?” “Could you not marry again and have one? There is a Wu Tiekou on Second Road whose predictions everyone calls extraordinarily accurate. I shall take you to see him sometime.” Had the Seventh Lady consulted him herself? She said she had, and that his prediction had certainly proved true. He had foretold a bijie period in the first half of this year. Asked what that meant, she explained that it was a period of friendship and brotherhood. Had they not become as close as sisters at their first meeting? Luo was persuaded and asked when they could go. “His business is tremendously busy. You must book in advance, whether for a full reading or the year's fortunes. I shall send someone to register and let you know the appointment.”

Back at home, the Seventh Lady immediately asked Gu whether he knew Wu Tiekou well. “We are companions at courtesan banquets. Why do you ask?” “I have a set of birth characters…” “Enough! It is all a charlatan's formula, saying whatever suits the listener. Believe him and you invite trouble.” “That is precisely what I want him to do. Let him examine these birth characters first, and then say what I instruct.” “What you instruct? Whose birth characters?” “Sister Luo's. Snake year, the fifteenth of the sixth month, a jiazi day and a jiazi hour.” Gu began to understand. “Very well. What do you want him to say?” “Before that, I have two questions. Will he follow my instructions? And can he make it sound convincing?” “He will certainly follow them—if you pay a larger fee.” “That is a small matter. I am afraid he may fail to make it convincing, or even reveal the trick. That would ruin my plan.” “He is devilishly clever and will not give himself away. Whether his account withstands scrutiny depends on whether the other person knows the subject.” “Why?” “An expert can find faults and expose gaps. His profession has a saying: submit your reading to challenge, and you put your life in another's hands.” “Tell him not to worry. His life will certainly be safe.”

On the afternoon of the third day, the Seventh Lady accompanied Luo Sijie to consult Wu Tiekou. He lived on Second Road, whose English name had been Rope Walk Road, translated into Chinese as Towpath Road. In the early days, boats could still use Yangjing Creek, but the shallow water made towing necessary. When the towpath was turned into a road, it retained that name. The local people could not manage the English street names, so they called Garden Lane, the first road opened, First Road. The next to the south became Second Road, followed by Third, Fourth and Fifth Roads, all running east and west, down to Yangjing Creek. Two years earlier, First Road had been renamed Nanjing Road and Second Road Hangzhou Road. Someone pointed out to the foreigners that there were two waterways between Nanjing and Hangzhou, the Yangtze and the Grand Canal. Since Nanjing was on the lower Yangtze, the name of a major port farther upstream would make a more fitting companion to Nanjing Road. Second Road was therefore renamed Jiujiang Road, and Third Road, formerly Customs Road, naturally became Hankou Road. Shanghai people were accustomed to the old names, however, and continued to say First Road and Second Road.

Second Road had been opened early, and its shops and businesses had long flourished. Wu Tiekou's place for receiving clients was in Fuhou Lane: the first house on the right. Two stone-gated houses had been joined together, making a large reception hall. Its walls were covered with inscribed plaques presented by high officials, wealthy merchants and distinguished men. Hu Xueyan had given one himself, bearing the words “Supreme Mastery of Ziping Astrology.” It hung on the north partition, beside a door leading to Wu's consulting room. Wu had a square face, large ears and a moustache that spread down on either side. He was only a little over thirty, but his large dark-crystal spectacles made him look older. He wore a lined robe of date-red satin beneath a black jacket patterned with round floral medallions. An enormous stone called pinxia was set in the band of his blue-satin cap. His fingernails were very long. On his left thumb he wore an archer's ring of Han jade, on his right ring finger a platinum ring set with a square diamond; a bright gold watch chain crossed his chest. He was dressed like a fashionable rake. “Mrs Gu!” He rose to greet them, four purses of different sizes dangling beneath his jacket. Removing his spectacles, he smiled. “How well you look.” “With a bijie period like this, how could I not?” She indicated Luo. “This is a dear friend of mine, surnamed Luo. You may call her Sister Luo.” “Certainly. Sister Luo. Please sit down, both of you.” There were two stools beside the rosewood desk, one opposite Wu and one to his left. The Seventh Lady took the former, indicating that Luo should sit beside him for ease of conversation. Wu put on his spectacles, settled into his rosewood armchair, rolled back his sleeves and took up his brush. Having asked Luo's birth year, month, day and hour, he wrote her Four Pillars on a writing tablet: ji-si, xin-wei, jia-zi, jia-zi. He added marks and annotations, laid down the brush and studied them intently.

He studied them for a full quarter of an hour. From the side, Luo could see his eyes blinking rapidly behind the dark lenses, and she began to feel uneasy. “Mr Wu,” she said at last, unable to contain herself, “is my destiny bad?” He removed his spectacles and looked at her. “What a pity!” Then he turned to the Seventh Lady and repeated with emphasis, “A very great pity!” “What is it? Please tell us frankly. A sensible person asks about misfortune, not good fortune. Sister Luo is broad-minded. There is no need to spare her feelings.” Wu nodded heavily, set his spectacles aside and pointed with his brush. “Sister Luo, yours is a Wood destiny. Beneath your day stem lies a Direct Seal, and the hour is also jia-zi: Wood has a fellow to support it and a Seal to shelter it. Judging by the day and hour pillars alone, this is a superior configuration, one that turns misfortune into blessing and danger into good luck.” Luo did not understand “superior configuration,” but she could tell that her destiny was good. “Please go on.” “Wood born in summer, in a si-Fire year as well: this tree would normally find it hard to survive. Fortunately, zi-Water nourishes it. Not only can it live; it is a great tree. Metal, Wood, Water, Fire and Earth are all present, and so are Wealth, Officer, Seal and the Food God. Moreover, these are a Direct Officer and a Direct Seal. If this were a man's horoscope, he would be like Lord Pan Wenrong of Suzhou: first in the imperial examination, a chief minister, living to eighty with children and grandchildren all around him, enjoying endless honour and riches. A pity it is a woman's destiny!”

Before Luo could speak, the Seventh Lady protested loudly. “What is wrong with a woman's destiny? Are examination champions and chief ministers not born of women?” “Do not be angry, Mrs Gu,” Wu replied calmly. “When I say it is a pity, I do not mean that Sister Luo's destiny is bad. Heaven would not forgive me if I called a horoscope like this bad.” Her anger gave way to pleasure. “Then what is there to regret? Please, Mr Wu, tell us honestly.” “I had intended to judge the horoscope on its merits and speak plainly. Now I hardly dare.” “Why not?” “With your temper, Mrs Gu, if I said something unwelcome, you might slap me. I could not afford such a loss of dignity.” “I beg your pardon!” She laughed apologetically. “Rest assured. Explain yourself clearly, and of course I shan't lose my temper.” Wu called for his water pipe, then told his young attendant to bring a fruit platter for the ladies. Repeatedly protesting against all this trouble, the Seventh Lady nevertheless summoned her maid to bring her silver water pipe. She lit a paper spill and began smoking with leisurely, bubbling draws. She and Wu were playing their duet with a perfect understanding, and Luo was already taken in. Desperate to learn what was so regrettable, she grew impatient at this interruption, even resenting the Seventh Lady's failure to consider her anxiety. Unable to say so openly, she pretended to cough, as though the pipe smoke were choking her, to hint that her friend might stop.

“Open the window,” Wu ordered. He put down his pipe and took up his brush again, first looking at the Seventh Lady to secure her attention. “A woman's horoscope must be read differently from a man's. In a woman's destiny, the element that controls her represents the Husband Star. Thus what we call the Direct Officer and Indirect Officer in a man's horoscope both stand for husbands in a woman's. That is a fundamental rule. You must understand it to see why Sister Luo's horoscope is regrettable.” The Seventh Lady knew something of astrology and followed him. Luo understood less, but, eager for what came next, nodded faintly too. “Metal controls Wood. This xin-Metal in the month pillar is the Husband Star for jia-Wood. The trouble is that there is another jia in the hour pillar. We have a name for that: Two Women Contending for One Husband.” The women exchanged a simultaneous glance. Luo's look conveyed a request, and the Seventh Lady spoke for her. “You mean another woman will compete with Sister Luo?” “Exactly.” “Can she win?” “If she could, there would be nothing to regret. When two women contend for one husband, the stronger wins. On the surface, each is jia-zi, with zi-Water generating jia-Wood. It is like children fighting: a parent comes out to help the child on one side, and another parent speaks up on the other. They seem evenly matched.” “Yes, yes, I understand!” Luo said repeatedly. “By the usual rule, Sister Luo, the jia-zi in the hour pillar ought not to beat you. Your Husband Star is right beside you: the pavilion nearest the water catches the moon first. You should have the advantage. Unfortunately, there is the configuration called geng-zi wang-wei. Chen, xu, chou and wei are the Earth of the four seasons, and Earth generates Metal. On the other side, Wealth benefits the Officer. That is excellent for the Husband Star but disastrous for you, because Wealth Damages the Seal. Imagine children fighting when one has parents and the other has lost theirs and is an orphan. Could the orphan defeat the other child?”

The Seventh Lady, who could follow the explanation, thought it marvellous. “Let me look, Mr Wu.” He turned the tablet round, angling it slightly towards Luo so that both could see. After studying it, the Seventh Lady pointed things out to her friend. “Look. This wei beneath geng is Earth. It is right beside your zi, which is Water, and Water controls Earth. Water is Wealth and Earth is the Seal, hence Wealth Damages the Seal. There is nothing to be done. You are destined to lose to the other woman.” “And what happens if I lose?” That, of course, was for Wu to answer. “Become a concubine.” The words were uncompromising. Repelled by his cold, unfeeling tone, Luo raised her voice. “And if I refuse to become a concubine?” “You will bring death to your husband.” “I have already lost one.” “You must still become a concubine.” “I insist on being a principal wife!” “Then you will still bring death. Every man you marry will die.” Luo's face went white with anger. “I don't believe…” Wu's iron certainty met an equally unyielding resistance. Seeing a quarrel about to break out, the Seventh Lady quickly tugged Luo's clothes. “Better defy your father than defy your fate. Hear Mr Wu out. If he makes no sense, there will be time enough to contradict him.” “If I make no sense, Mrs Gu, Sister Luo may slap me and I shall not lift a hand.” Wu pointed to the tablet. “Her husband's death can also be seen here. The Seal represents shelter. At home a woman depends on her father; once married, on her husband. The Seal is her support. If her husband dies, has that support not collapsed?” He raised his eyes to observe her reaction.

Luo's expression had softened somewhat. The Seventh Lady asked, “But why must she still become a concubine?” “Because after wei-Earth has overcome the first zi-Water, it goes on to overcome the second. There is no escaping it. If she truly refuses to become a concubine, there is nothing to be done. Everyone has their own aspirations; we cannot force them. But then there is no need to examine the Wealth, Officer and Food God in the earlier part of the horoscope.” “Why not?” “What use are they if the person is no longer alive?” Luo was badly startled. “Mr Wu, do you mean I shall die if I refuse to become a concubine?” “Certainly. Wei-Earth overcomes one zi-Water after another. Suppose jia-Wood refuses to retreat and confronts it. Very well: Wood controls Earth, and jia-Wood has assistance, so its strength is considerable. But look at wei-Earth. The ji-Earth in the year pillar supports it. That is not even the most important thing: the greatest power is si-Fire, for Fire generates Earth, supplying it without end. Which side is stronger? In the interaction of the Five Elements, what fails to overcome its opponent is overcome in turn. This wei-Earth is hard as rock, on which nothing can grow. If jia-Wood challenges it, it is like trying to split a mountain with a piece of timber. The timber breaks; the mountain remains.” Luo looked like a defeated fighting cock. Her fierce insistence on being a principal wife had vanished completely, although inwardly she still resented becoming a concubine.

The Seventh Lady now turned to the favourable side. “Then she will be all right if she becomes a concubine?” “It is not merely a matter of being all right. Only by becoming a concubine—that is, by accepting xin-Metal as her Husband Star—can we begin to discuss the benefits of those four characters at the beginning.” “You mean the four characters of the year and month pillars?” “Yes. Earth generating Metal is like a mother and child. Once Wood has married Metal, they belong to the same family. There is no reason for further conflict…” “Mr Wu,” the Seventh Lady interrupted, “I was asking about the benefits of those four characters.” “They are endless. The finest feature of this horoscope is the Food God represented by si-Fire. In a horoscope, male or female, the Food God always means intelligence and good looks. It is what the self produces. Here the Food God generates Wealth in the two Earth signs, ji and wei; Wealth generates the xin-Officer. That is the fortune of a woman who advances her husband. In other words, the brilliance of the Husband Star depends entirely on this Food God that she produces.” “Most enlightening!” The Seventh Lady turned to Luo. “Sister Luo, is there anything else you would like to ask Mr Wu?”

Luo hesitated, then gave her a look. Understanding that she wanted a private word, the Seventh Lady rose and went aside with her. Luo whispered, “Seventh Sister, ask him what sort of destiny would suit mine.” “I understand.” Returning to her seat, the Seventh Lady asked, “If she marries, Mr Wu, what sort of destiny should the man have?” “Metal, naturally.” “What about Earth?” She gave him the faintest signal with her eyes. Wu was extremely quick-witted. “Earth generates Metal. Better still,” he replied at once. “Oh.” She sounded as though she attached no particular importance to it, then turned to Luo. “Anything else?” “Nothing comes to mind just now.” That answer showed that Luo already believed Wu's pronouncements to be infallible, and that she had much more on her mind to ask him. The Seventh Lady felt that her plan now had at least a seventy or eighty per cent chance of success. It was time to stop. She beckoned her maid to bring her purse, preparing to take out a banknote to pay his fee.

“Thank you very much for today, Mr Wu. But I must trouble you to write out a detailed reading of her whole life.” “Well…” Wu looked reluctant. “I am afraid I may not have time just now.” “Miss a couple of dinners with courtesans, and you will have time.” He laughed. “That too is ordained by my destiny. With peach blossoms all along my path, if I don't dine with courtesans, I shall have to dine with the King of Hell. It would be a poor bargain.” He was half joking. The Seventh Lady pursed her lips in disdain. “I know you are busy. A delay doesn't matter, but the reading must be very thorough.” “As long as there is no time limit, careful work is certain to produce a fine result.” “Good.” Sorting through her banknotes, she asked, “How much should we pay you?” “You know my rules, Mrs Gu. I depend entirely on the good fortune of my distinguished clients. If a destiny is bad, I won't read it however much I am offered. If it is good, I am too embarrassed to ask much. Give whatever you please. You would never let me give my work away.” “Giving away a destiny would be giving away a life!” She laid a fifty-tael note on the desk. “I hope you won't think it too little.” “It is a little on the low side. But I certainly shan't object.” “I know that for a horoscope like Sister Luo's, this is not enough. We are bound to consult you again. We shall make it up to you later.”

As they took their leave, the Seventh Lady invited Luo to have a Western meal and watch Japanese conjuring tricks. Luo pleaded a headache and insisted on going home. Her friend understood: Wu's categorical pronouncements had stirred up endless thoughts, and Luo wanted to consider them privately. She did not press the invitation. They rode together in the Gu carriage, and on reaching her own house she told the coachman to take Luo home. After ten that evening, Gu Yingchun and Hu Xueyan returned together from an engagement at a courtesan's house in Baoshan Street. Knowing that the Seventh Lady had taken Luo to have her fortune told that day, Hu had come expressly for the news. “This Wu Tiekou really has some ability. He made even me believe him.” It was the Seventh Lady herself who had instructed him to say that Luo must become a concubine. If she could accept her own invention as truth when she heard it from someone else, his argument must have been extraordinary. Gu was now as eager as Hu to hear it. “It makes me laugh to think of it. Wu was most blunt. Every other word was either ‘bring death to your husband’ or ‘become a concubine.’ Sister Luo was truly angry. But do you know what happened in the end?” “Don't ask us,” Gu said. “Just tell the story.” “In the end she privately asked me to find out what destiny would make a good match for her. Wu said Metal, naturally. I asked, ‘What about Earth?’ That is where I really admire him. It was nothing remarkable that he understood my meaning; what was clever was his instant answer: ‘Earth generates Metal. Better still.’” “Little Uncle,” Gu said with a smile, “it looks as though happy events will come in pairs.” “It all depends on Seventh Sister's help,” Hu replied, beaming. “Did you hear?” Gu said to his wife. “Everything is in your hands.”

“Leave it to me! But we must not rush. Sister Luo is shrewder than anyone. If she detects a clue and decides we are deceiving her, she will refuse to listen to another word. I must wait for her to speak to me about it. If I raise it myself, I may give the game away.” “Quite right.” Hu nodded earnestly. “I am in no hurry.” “In that case, Little Uncle, you might as well return to Hangzhou first. Leave her alone for a while, and things may move faster.” Hu thought briefly. “I shall go back and return after the festival.” “Good. You can make some preparations there. Tell your mother first.” “She knows Sister Luo too. She is sure to agree.” “And Aunt?” “She has said herself that she needs someone to help her.” “You must make quite sure of her agreement,” the Seventh Lady urged solemnly. “If Aunt disapproves, I shan't arrange this. I have known her for years. It would not be worth creating ill feeling between us.” The Seventh Lady got on extremely well with everyone in Hu's household and was deeply respected because she knew exactly how to conduct herself in such delicate matters. Hu did not resent her frankness. He promised to tell his wife the truth and never leave the Seventh Lady in an awkward position later. “Then I shall wait for your letter.” “Good. I expect to leave in three or four days. Do you think I ought to see her again first?” “Of course. You can visit her every day if you like. Only be sure not to mention the fortune-telling.” Gu, who had said little, reminded his wife, “A full bowl of rice is easily eaten; a sweeping promise is hard to fulfil. Don't imagine you are absolutely certain. If Sister Luo really has plans for her future, she must be anxious to discuss them with you. But she may be embarrassed to come seeking your advice. You ought to visit her. That is how to show consideration for a friend.”

The Seventh Lady willingly accepted her husband's suggestion and drove over the following morning. It was already after ten when she arrived. Quite a few embroidery workers were still sitting in the reception room, but Old Ma alone was attending to them. “Where is your mistress?” “She says she is unwell and hasn't come downstairs.” Old Ma smiled helplessly. “I am all at sea on my own.” “I shall help.” The Seventh Lady sat in Luo's usual place. Having visited several times and taken a hand before, she was not entirely unfamiliar with issuing materials and payments and inspecting finished work. Whenever a difficulty arose, she sent the maid upstairs to ask before deciding. Everything was settled within half an hour. “I shall go up and see her. What is wrong with her?” she asked the maid. “She is not ill,” the girl whispered. “She cried all last night, until her eyes were swollen.” Startled, the Seventh Lady asked quickly, “Why?” “I don't know. I didn't dare ask.” She said no more, lifted her skirt and went upstairs. Luo's bedroom was completely dark. Guessing that the light hurt her red, swollen eyes, she stopped in the doorway. A voice came from behind the bed curtains.

“Is that Seventh Sister?” “Yes.” “Don't move. Let me get up and help you.” “No, no. I can see a little now.” Holding the doorframe, the Seventh Lady advanced slowly. “Be careful!” Luo was already up. She drew back a corner of the window curtain to let in some light, then turned her own face away. “Thank goodness you came. Old Ma really couldn't manage by himself.” “The light hurts your eyes. Go back behind your bed curtains.” That was what Luo had intended. Besides finding the light painful, she did not want her friend to see how swollen her eyes were. She agreed and returned to bed, telling the maid, who had followed them up, to bring tea and prepare lunch. “Don't trouble yourself. I feel as much at home here as in my own house. If I want anything, I shall tell them.” Sitting on a bench beside the bed, the Seventh Lady asked quietly, “What is the matter?” “I feel miserable.” “What is it that you cannot put aside?” Luo said nothing, and there was no need to ask further. Reaching through the curtains to touch her face, the Seventh Lady found her eyes swollen to the size of apricots, with traces of tears still on her cheeks. “You must stop crying,” she scolded. “A woman's eyes are everything to her. You must look after yourself. What if you cry yourself blind?” “How could I cry myself blind?” Changing the subject, Luo asked, “Where have you come from?” “Home.” The Seventh Lady called to the maid. “Bring a basin of hot water and a fresh towel—new flannel would be best.” She wanted to apply a hot compress to reduce the swelling. While doing so, she told Luo that Hu would soon return to Hangzhou for the festival. They would give him a farewell dinner in the next two or three days, and she wanted Luo to come.

“On what day?” “We must wait until the swelling has gone down and you can go out.” “That will only take a day or two.” “Then let us make it three days from today. Come early. We can eat early, and afterwards I shall take you to the theatre.” “All right.” Just then the clock began to strike. Luo silently counted twelve. “My clock is slow. It is already past noon.” She called to the maid, “Go and hurry the restaurant. The food should have arrived.” “It has.” “Then why didn't you say so? Will it be any good once it is cold?” She began scolding the maid. The Seventh Lady intervened, saying that anger would make deficient fire rise and harm her eyes. Only then did Luo stop. “Bring lunch upstairs,” the Seventh Lady instructed. “I shall eat with your mistress.” When the meal was brought up, Luo got out of bed, but still sat with her back to the light, never allowing her friend to see her eyes. “What has upset you so much? I thought you were a very straightforward person. I never imagined you could brood like this.” “It is not brooding. I resent my miserable fate.” “With a horoscope like yours, you call your fate miserable?” “How can I not? Think, Seventh Sister: either I remain a widow or I become a concubine. The more I think about it, the less I can accept it. I am determined to defy my fate.” “You still seem angry. Let it go. I shall take you to the theatre the day after tomorrow to cheer you up.”

“I don't particularly want to see a play. But I shall certainly come early.” “As long as you do. We can decide about the theatre then. With Little Uncle going to Hangzhou, would you like him to take a letter or anything else?” “Would it be convenient?” “Of course. He has servants and a boat. It belongs to his bureau and is towed by a small steamer, so it is fast and steady.” Luo nodded. Instead of saying whether she had anything to send, she asked about Hu's bureau. The Seventh Lady explained the Shanghai Transport Bureau that served the western campaign. “You know Lord Zuo, who recovered your Hangzhou?” “Yes.” “He is now Governor-General of Shaanxi and Gansu, with tens of thousands of troops fighting there. Conditions are very harsh. They depend entirely on the rear commissariats for supplies. Little Uncle manages one of the most important, the Shanghai Transport Bureau.” “What does it send?” “Everything. The most important things are guns and cannon. Lord Zuo's victories depend entirely on the Western weapons Little Uncle buys for him in Shanghai.” “What else?” “A great deal.” The Seventh Lady counted on her fingers. “Uniforms, food, medicines…” “Medicines have to be sent too?” Luo interrupted. “Of course. Especially in summer. Huoxiang Zhengqi Pills and Biwen Dan are sent by the hundreds and thousands of cases.”

“No wonder!” Luo suddenly understood. “What?” “He told me the other day that he wanted to open a medicine shop. So the rich water is not to flow into someone else's fields.” “There are plenty of other businesses where he could keep the profits in his own hands. But he doesn't dare give them free rein.” “Why?” “He needs people to help him. How can he manage without them?” “Isn't Brother-in-Law Gu a first-rate assistant?” “In outside affairs. He needs a good assistant at home too.” The Seventh Lady gave an example. “Take the coming Dragon Boat Festival. Think of the trouble involved in sending the gifts alone. From princes and great officials in Beijing down to poor relations, the list is enough to frighten you. Leave one person out, and you offend them. Give too little, and you offend them too.” “Give too much, and you can also cause offence,” Luo said. “And perhaps offend more than one person.” “Exactly.” The Seventh Lady said no more.

On the day of Hu's farewell dinner, Luo arrived just after the Seventh Lady had finished lunch. “Have you any time to spare?” she asked at once. “What is it?” “If you have, I should like you to come with me to buy things to send to Hangzhou. And I want someone to write a letter home for me.” Old Ma was readily available, the Seventh Lady thought. Why did Luo want someone else to write her letter? Plainly there was a reason. She said nothing about shopping and asked only about the letter. “What sort of person are you looking for?” “Preferably…” Luo hesitated. “Someone like you.” “I have hardly more learning than you. If you cannot write a letter, neither can I.” She thought for a moment. “There is no need for you to go shopping yourself. Tell me what you want, and I shall send someone. Yingchun will be home soon. I shall press him into service to write the letter.” “That will do.” The Seventh Lady summoned her steward, A’fu, and Luo gave him her instructions. Foodstuffs and household articles, all the foreign and southern merchandise sold in Shanghai, were rare and precious in the interior. The list grew so long that A’fu had to fetch paper and brush. “Thank you, steward.” Luo took out a fifty-tael banknote, but as she was about to hand it over, the Seventh Lady stopped her. “There is no need. I have a shop account book,” Luo said. A’fu would not take the money without his mistress's permission. The Seventh Lady guessed that the account book for collecting goods must have been a gift from Hu. Since Luo did not wish to use it, or accept presents from anyone else, there was no reason to insist. “Very well. As you wish.” Only then did A’fu accept the note and go to make the purchases.

Gu happened to return just then. After a brief rest, his wife conscripted him to write Luo's letter. “This is not an easy assignment,” he said with a smile. “Shall I work like a character-diviner who writes letters for people, putting down each sentence as you dictate it? Or will you give me the general sense, and I shall write it out for you to read and correct?” “Which is easier?” “Taking it down sentence by sentence, naturally.” “Then let us do it the easy way.” “Good. Come with me.” In the study, Gu spread out a sheet of paper and moistened his brush. He first wrote, “Respectfully submitted at the feet of my honoured mother,” then looked up at Luo across the desk. “Brother-in-Law Gu, please tell my mother that I am well in Shanghai and she need not worry. Is her liver-qi trouble any better? She must not stop taking her medicine. I am sending her fifty taels. She must not economize on medicine.” Gu wrote it down. “Yes. What else?” “I am also sending a basket of foreign and southern goods with someone. Will she decide what to distribute among our relatives? She must be sure not to let A’qiao eat too many sweets…” “Who is A’qiao?” “My daughter.”

“Should I mention who is bringing the things?” “No.” “Very well. Anything else?” “Yes.” Luo thought for a moment. “I shall go back to Hangzhou to see her at the Mid-Autumn Festival.” “Anything else?” “She must reply as soon as she receives this letter. And she must ask Mr Wu to write the reply.” “Hu, written with ‘ancient’ and ‘moon,’ or Wu, with ‘mouth’ and ‘heaven’?” “Neither. Wu as in ‘crow.’” “I see. Anything else?” “No.” Gu finished and read the letter aloud. Luo was satisfied. When he came to address the envelope, he asked how she wanted it written. “What is the proper form, Brother-in-Law Gu?” “The usual form is, ‘Respectfully troubling So-and-so to deliver this to So-and-so at a convenient opportunity,’ with ‘Entrusted by So-and-so’ below.” “Could we simply write, ‘Respectfully requesting delivery at a convenient opportunity’?” Of course they could. Gu had asked again because she had already said there was no need to identify the bearer, and he wanted confirmation. He could now be certain that she was deliberately avoiding Hu's name. Her reason for doing so was intriguing.

Only when she was about to leave did Luo speak to Hu. “Mr Hu, I have a letter and a basket. Would you be so kind as to take them to Hangzhou and send someone to deliver them to my family?” She handed him the letter. “Certainly. Where are the things?” “I have them,” the Seventh Lady answered for her. “When are you leaving, Mr Hu?” “The day after tomorrow.” “Then I shan't come to see you off.” “Please don't trouble yourself. What would you like me to bring back?” “Nothing comes to mind just now.” “Write to me if you think of anything. Or tell Seventh Sister.”

Once they had seen Luo into her carriage, the Seventh Lady hurried back inside and asked her husband, “What did she say in her letter?” “So Yingchun wielded the brush!” Hu said, a little surprised. “No wonder the handwriting looked familiar.” “I played the character-diviner for once. But I found it curious too. Why should she ask me to write such an entirely ordinary letter? What has become of whoever normally writes her letters home?” “There is certainly a reason. Tell me what was in it.” Gu could recite the whole letter from memory. When he had done so, he added, “One point is worth considering. She did not want to say explicitly that Little Uncle was bringing the letter and basket.” “Did she explain why she specifically wanted Mr Wu to write the reply?” “No.” Hu's question was different. “She has a daughter? She never told me.” “She has told you today, through Yingchun.” “Ah!” Gu understood. “So that is why she deliberately asked me to write it.”

“There are other reasons,” the Seventh Lady said. “First, she wants to see whether Little Uncle remembers old ties. You must have met her mother in the old days. If you remember them, you will go and see her.” “Of course. I had already decided to deliver the letter and things myself. With the festival coming, I must take a present too.” “That is the right thing to do. And she wants to test how you react when you see her daughter.” “Mm.” Hu nodded without committing himself. “Anything else?” Gu had used the phrase so often that day that it slipped out unconsciously. “She specified Mr Wu because she was afraid a character-diviner might not explain things clearly or write them properly, and might carelessly leave something out. Only Mr Wu can be relied upon.” Hu thought her reasoning entirely correct. After considering it for a while, he said with feeling, “Sister Luo's mind works very deeply.” “Deeply and quickly. I said that giving too little could cause offence; she said that giving too much could offend more than one person. Little Uncle, if you want this helper, whether the match succeeds will depend on the letter Mr Wu writes.” Hu understood. Back in Hangzhou, he first sent someone to attend to Luo's commission, adding a generous festival gift. Then, on a free day, he dressed simply, took few attendants and went in an easy manner to visit her mother. He addressed her by the old name, Auntie Luo, but she could scarcely recognize him. His unfamiliarity, added to her astonishment at the honour, made her extremely uneasy. Understanding her feelings, he began with news of her daughter, then gradually recalled old times. Only then did Auntie Luo relax. Once at ease, she naturally became both pleased and moved, repeatedly saying that she would never have dared imagine a man in his present position lowering himself to visit her.

CHAPTER SIX: A WINDING ROAD TO MARRIAGE

Ten days later, Luo Sijie received a letter from home. As she had requested, her mother had asked Mr Wu to write it. Mr Wu was the keeper of the Temple of Lord Guan, a warm-hearted man with a thorough understanding of the world. Reading Luo’s letter first, he had wondered why she had specifically requested him as the writer of the reply. Then, listening to Auntie Luo’s delighted account of Hu’s visit, he understood. Her daughter probably had not been certain whether Hu would call in person, which explained why she had omitted the name of the man carrying her letter and gifts. Yet his actions mattered greatly to her. Mr Wu must therefore tell her everything in detail: that was precisely why she had asked him to write. He had guessed her intention perfectly, and the letter fully met her expectations. His language was plain and clear. She first had Old Ma read it aloud, then worked carefully through it herself. Once she could understand most of it, she put it inside her clothes and went to see the Seventh Lady. “Seventh Sister, I have a letter. Would you look at it for me?” “From whom?” “My mother. It is very long, and Mr Hu seems to be mentioned in the middle. I am afraid there may be something important that I ought not to ask Old Ma to read.” “I am not much better than you. If you cannot make it out, I may not be able to either. But never mind. One guest need not trouble two hosts. You asked Yingchun to write before; let him read this one too.” “Is Brother-in-Law Gu at home?” “Yes. A foreigner is coming to see him, and he is waiting.”

Gu was summoned and given the letter. He read and explained as he went. “Everything arrived. Mr Hu also sent a very substantial gift, eight things in all: ham, tea, Huadiao…” “You need not read those out,” the Seventh Lady interrupted. “Does the letter call Little Uncle Mr Hu?” “Yes. That is how Hangzhou people who respect him address him.” “Go on, then.” “On the seventh day of the fifth month, Mr Hu called on your mother. He was extremely courteous and stayed two full hours, talking about your recent life in Shanghai…” Gu smiled and stopped. “What is amusing?” his wife asked in surprise. “Your mother says she was pleased to learn that you had met the two of us. She calls it ‘the happy encounter with benefactors.’ That is far more than we deserve.” “My mother is right. You are certainly my benefactors.” Luo asked whether the letter also mentioned her daughter. “It does. Your mother says Mr Hu liked her very much, asked all sorts of questions, and talked with her at length. He also gave her a present at their first meeting: a pair of twisted-wire gold bracelets.” “Just think, Seventh Sister! Such costly things for a child. But I do not quite understand. Why did he have those bracelets with him? Did he know before going that I had a daughter?” “Not necessarily. Little Uncle has so many social obligations that he keeps gold watches and all sorts of other things. When a present is needed, he can simply produce one.” “So that is the explanation.” Her doubt resolved, Luo asked Gu to continue.

“Your mother says you mentioned coming home, and she misses you very much. If you cannot spare the time, perhaps she might come to Shanghai instead.” Before Luo could answer, the Seventh Lady exclaimed, “Let her come! Bring her here for the summer. She can stay two or three months before going back.” Luo nodded. “Shanghai is cooler than Hangzhou. Let me think about it.” “There is another passage, a postscript from Mr Wu. Quite interesting.” Gu smiled. “He says that since Mr Hu’s personal visit, the tea drinkers at the temple have talked of little else for days. Everyone calls him a generous and loyal man. Mr Wu thinks he might even be the benefactor destined to enter your life.” The words touched the deepest part of Luo’s heart. Composed as she was, she could not help blushing. With great tact, the Seventh Lady deliberately changed the subject. “What tea drinkers? What temple?” “The Temple of Lord Guan, near our house. Mr Wu, who wrote this letter for my mother, is its keeper. He sets out tables and sells tea, with storytellers performing. That is how the temple’s worship and incense are supported.” At this point Gu’s foreign visitor arrived. While he received him, the two women continued talking. Luo would very much like her mother to stay, but had no suitable person to escort her. The Seventh Lady thought that no difficulty at all: she need only write to Hu. “No, that would not do.” Luo kept shaking her head, and only when pressed explained, “I owe him too much already.” “Then what harm in owing him one kindness more?” “I am afraid I could never repay him.” “There is a way of doing that too…” On reflection, the Seventh Lady decided not to speak too plainly. Luo asked no further question, and the matter was left for the time being.

They chatted until the lamps were lit. The Seventh Lady proposed an early dinner followed by a visit to a Western circus. Luo agreed to dine but declined the circus: it would finish late, and she would feel guilty at making her hostess escort her so far home. “That is easily settled. Stay here. We can talk some more as well.” After considering it, Luo accepted. When they returned from the circus after dinner, Gu had just arrived home too. “A’qi, please pack my things. Today’s visitor is the new manager of a German trading house. He wants to make a special journey to Hangzhou to see Little Uncle and take the opportunity to visit West Lake. I have no choice but to accompany him.” “You are going to Hangzhou? Wonderful! Bring Sister Luo’s mother back with you.” Gu paused, then remembered the letter and understood. “Gladly. I shall certainly arrange it.” With husband and wife having decided between them, Luo could do nothing but thank them. They discussed the journey, which Gu reckoned would take about half a month there and back. His wife had another idea. “Why not move into the British settlement? It would be easier for us to visit each other. Half a month is quite enough to find a house and move.” “Let me think.” “You need not. Let me think for you.” She considered whose house might conveniently be rented or bought, and an idea came. “Wasn’t Old Mi building a row of houses in a lane? Are they finished?” “Long ago.” “There are twenty-four houses in that lane—a long one,” Gu continued. “I am sure some must be available.” “Then that is settled.” Turning to Luo, the Seventh Lady explained, “Old Mi is Fukang’s deputy manager. He has made a fortune too. If the houses are his, one word is all it will take for you to move in.”

“There, you see!” Luo hastily rejected the suggestion. “I think it would be better to find somewhere else.” “Why?” She would only shake her head. At last the Seventh Lady understood. At this delicate stage in Luo’s relations with Hu, she wished to avoid suspicion and leave no obvious sign. The Seventh Lady found her shrewd, capable, and loyal to her friends, yet also somewhat affected. A frank woman herself, she had a way of cutting through complications that Luo could not manage. “I don’t care what twists and turns that wonderfully clever mind of yours is taking. To sum it up, and sum it up again: you are moving. Whether we rent, acquire the house under a redeemable pledge, or buy it, I shall decide. You need not concern yourself.” Luo yielded. “Then I shall do as you say, Seventh Sister. I leave everything to you.” Taking full charge, the Seventh Lady bought her one of the new houses built by Old Mi, Fukang’s deputy manager. The lane was called Fuhou Lane. Its twenty-four houses faced one another across a passage open at both ends. She chose one facing south. Downstairs were side rooms to east and west, a large reception room, and, at the back, a kitchen, servants’ quarters, and storeroom. The stairs were in the middle. Upstairs were five rooms of different sizes. The largest was a suite running the full depth of the house from south to north, ample accommodation for a beauty in seclusion. The other four were a sitting room, a dining room, and two guest rooms. The Seventh Lady personally selected all the furniture and ornaments, arranging them with an attractive richness and splendor. Everything was ready in only ten days, and she was thoroughly pleased with herself. On the eleventh morning she sent the carriage for Luo. “I have arranged your house. Come and see.” Luo was astonished and delighted. “It is wonderful! I only fear I lack the good fortune to live in such a house.” Ignoring this, the Seventh Lady asked what she disliked; anything could be changed at once. Luo frankly mentioned that curtains were still needed.

“The windows have been measured, and the curtains are being made. They will be ready tomorrow. When will you move?” “Wait.” Luo drew her down to sit beside her and hesitated. “To tell the truth, I love the house. But I am afraid it is beyond my means. House and furniture together must cost four thousand taels?” “Less than four thousand. I have a detailed account. You need not worry about affording it now. For the moment, regard it as my property, lent to you to live in free of charge. When you can afford it, I shall let you have it at the original price.” “Can such good things happen in this world?” “You don’t believe it? I hardly believe it myself!” The Seventh Lady laughed. “It looks as though Wu Tiekou’s words are coming true.” Luo remembered them perfectly. He had insisted she must become a concubine. If she insisted on being a principal wife, she would bring death to one husband after another. If she would neither accept the lesser position nor occupy the higher one, disaster would overtake her own life. In that case, the Wealth, Officer, and Seal represented in the first four of her birth characters would count for nothing. Only by willingly becoming a concubine could she enjoy good fortune. The Seventh Lady’s meaning was therefore plain. Yet Luo would neither acknowledge nor reject it. Her only course was to pretend she had not quite heard, ignore the implication, and deliberately change the subject.

“Moving is a troublesome business, Seventh Sister. I am afraid…” “There is no need to worry about every possibility. The furniture and fittings are all here. Give away what you can of your old furniture, and have a secondhand dealer take the rest in one lot. Packing clothes, jewelry, and household utensils cannot take more than a day.
