The proprietor, however, was ashamed of making and selling them. A close friend's introduction was required, and they were prepared only to order, never sold over the counter. Liu's popularity enabled him to find a suitable intermediary. He paid heavily for a batch. After trying them, Hu gave free rein to himself in bed.

“There is no remedy,” the Seventh Lady said, “unless you can accept the situation generously.” She meant: could Madam Luosi allow Hu to take another concubine and share his favour? Madam Luosi considered her position, halfway between principal wife and concubine. The old lady trusted and favoured her, and she lived peacefully with the principal wife, but managing the household inevitably earned servants' resentment. Suppose a formidable new concubine arrived and, egged on by servants, allied herself with the principal wife, disregarding the rule that earlier entry conferred seniority and opposing her openly and covertly at every turn. She might not be afraid, but she would constantly be angry. That danger could not be ignored. As she reflected, the Seventh Lady spoke again. “Last autumn Yingchun had a fever. During his convalescence he couldn't go out and was dreadfully bored, so we hired a storyteller to perform at home for two hours every afternoon. The book was Tales of Heroic Sons and Daughters. Its account of women's jealousy made considerable sense.” “What did the storyteller say?” “He divided jealous women into those who manage jealousy well and those who don't, with three grades in each. Those who don't are laughable, pitiable or terrifying. For example…” “Never mind those who don't,” Madam Luosi interrupted. “Very well. Those who manage it well are also divided into three grades: ordinary, skilful and divine. We can leave out the ordinary. Take the skilful. A first-rate woman like you might see Little Uncle marry someone who surpassed even you. Yet if you remained generous, showed no disturbance and cared as attentively as ever for his food and daily comforts, he would feel indebted to you and you would retain his favour. That is skilful jealousy.”

By that account, Madam Luosi thought, the principal wife belonged to the skilful grade. What, then, was the divine? She asked aloud. “Nothing particularly extraordinary, once explained. With your ability, it would not be difficult. In a word, combine kindness with authority. If she behaves properly, treat her well; cherish her even more than Little Uncle does. If she breaks the rules, speak to her and keep her in order. When she has children, understand their needs better than their own mother and be better at bringing them up. Then who in the whole household will not respect you? Who will not call you virtuous? That is truly divine jealousy.” Every word went straight to Madam Luosi's heart, and she saw a further implication. In the household hierarchy, the old lady came first, the master second, the principal wife third, and she herself only fourth. Apart from the servants, there were people to govern her but nobody for her to govern. If she personally selected several more concubines for Hu and trained them through kindness and authority until they sincerely acknowledged her, she would at last display the full dignity and power of the household's manager. A smile appeared on her face without her noticing. The Seventh Lady smiled too. “Well, Sister Luo? Would you like to practise this jealousy that does not look like jealousy?” “I only fear I may not know how. Keep an eye out for someone for me, Seventh Sister.” The Seventh Lady realized that she had decided to act on the advice. It had begun as casual conversation; even if meant as a plan, it would require long consideration. She had never expected such immediate acceptance.

At that thought, the Seventh Lady suddenly felt a weight on her shoulders. As the saying went, “If you want discord at home, take a concubine.” Women like Madam Luosi were exceedingly rare. Besides, Hu had chosen Luo for himself. Even if things had gone badly after she entered the household, the Seventh Lady could not have been blamed. This was different: it now seemed entirely her proposal. If trouble followed, everyone, beginning with Old Madam Hu, would resent her. She must therefore think carefully on her friend's behalf. “Sister Luo, things sound fine in the planning but are not so easy to carry out. If Little Uncle wants to marry someone from a courtesan house, you must refuse. Such women have habits that make them difficult to manage.” “Yes. She must be a girl from a respectable family. I shall make it clear to him first: he may look for someone himself, but I must see her. In fact, there is no need for him to look. I shall ask people to choose someone for him.” She did as she said. Over three or four years, the women she found, together with those Hu chose himself, made eleven additional concubines. Including her, they numbered exactly twelve, like the Twelve Beauties of the novel.

With more family members and an expanding business continually bringing new personnel, the house proved inadequate despite repeated extensions. Eventually the limits of the site meant either complete rebuilding or finding another home. Hu discussed it with Madam Luosi. He proposed buying land and building a new residence elsewhere, moving his two younger brothers there along with the various people who worked for him, and demolishing the vacated buildings to make a garden. He also wanted a gallery-lined residence where his Twelve Beauties could live together. Madam Luosi approved of the latter but objected to the separate house. “Asking Second Master and Third Master to move out will hurt your mother. The relatives will gossip too. You ought to reconsider.” At the thought of hurting his mother, Hu abandoned the proposal at once. “But there isn't enough room. We must do something. Have you a better idea?” “I hear the Liu house next door is for sale. The owner of the rice shop behind us has died, and his two sons keep quarrelling over the division of the estate and who should run the shop. They also want to sell the building and divide the cash. Why not buy both properties and break through the walls to join them to ours?” This revived Hu's appetite for grand display. Silk prices happened to rise sharply that year. Through his control of the silk trade with foreign houses, he made four hundred thousand taels in three months. He decided on a grand garden. “Let us pretend I never earned that money. I shall follow your suggestion, but on a larger scale. Streets must bound it on all four sides, making one great, regular block, with the grandeur of a prince's mansion.” Madam Luosi was naturally pleased by such distinction. Hu sent men to persuade the surrounding households, offering substantial inducements. All but two agreed to move and sell.

One holdout was a wine warehouse. It said the stored wine was too difficult to move and refused to sell, firmly but politely. The other was different. It was a tiny barbershop at the corner of Yuanbao Street and Wangxianqiao Straight Street, a place everyone had to pass when entering or leaving. To have a gap in the estate at such an important junction—and a dilapidated barbershop at that—was as intolerable as a peerless beauty with one eye blind. “What does she want?” Hu demanded. “If she wants a good price, let her name it. Whatever she asks, she can have.” “She” was Old Mrs Cui, the proprietor's mother. Her son was stubborn too, but the Hu household's frequent visits and courteous persuasion, together with the prospect of money, had begun to move him.

His mother, however, refused absolutely. Widowed young and left without support, she had struggled to bring him up, only to see him become a barber. Rather than blame herself for choosing that trade for him, she accused Heaven of blindness. Over time she had grown contrary and bitter, hating the wealthy in proportion to their wealth. Hu's promise to pay whatever she asked touched precisely her sore point. “Tell your employer that he may be the God of Wealth, but we are paupers. We have no dealings with him. Let him make his fortune. He is neither the King of Hell nor a judge in the underworld. I have no reason to fear him.” The negotiator was Zhang Zihong, a literary hanger-on in Hu's household, famous for his mild temper. Even he lost patience. “He may not be the King of Hell or an underworld judge, but he is a circuit intendant.” “Does that put him above the law? My son and I have only our two lives. Let him do as he pleases.” When Hu heard this, he was so angry that he ate nothing all day. His household retainers, accountants, managers and servants proposed all kinds of measures: send the county bailiffs, burn down the house, or forge a deed and sue her. Hu could not bring himself to do it. Madam Luosi also feared that coercion might lead to a death and restrained the servants from any rash act. Even after the great mansion was completed and Yuanbao Street repaved, the barbershop remained.

The completion was celebrated with three days of banquets. On the first day, the guests were the three principal provincial authorities, the prefect of Hangzhou, the magistrates of Renhe and Qiantang, and expectant circuit intendants, with local gentry invited to keep them company. Before the meal, Hu personally led them through the garden. Following its winding paths around a rockery, they saw an extraordinarily splendid tower rising among the trees to the southeast. What puzzled them was the gold light flashing from the carved railings all around it. At that distance, nobody could account for it. “Mr Hu,” Governor Yang Changjun asked, “what is that building?” “The residence of my wife.” Hearing that it belonged to the women's quarters, Yang could not inquire further, but private questions brought the explanation. It was called the Hundred Lions Tower. One hundred lions carved and polished from zitan stood on the railing posts. Their protruding eyes were cast in gold and glittered in the sunlight so brightly that one could scarcely look at them. “Why call the ladies' residence Hundred Lions Tower? Does he not know the saying about the lioness of Hedong roaring?” “No, that isn't it. The lady is called Madam Luosi, and he built the tower for her.” Yang asked how she had acquired the name and what her origins were. Once informed, he felt that Hu had gone rather too far and quietly wrote to Zuo at Suzhou in Gansu, expressing some criticism.

Zuo disagreed considerably with Yang but could not conveniently say so outright. As it happened, his eldest son also wrote to criticize Hu, giving him a suitable occasion to express his view. A man's enjoyments, he said, should be proportionate to his deserts. The world did not fully understand Hu's services, but he did. The western campaign owed its present success entirely to Hu; a little excess in his pleasures need give him no shame. He cited Tao Shu, his closest lifelong friend and the father of his child's spouse. When Tao was Governor-General of Liangjiang, his son-in-law Hu Linyi, a Hanlin academician living idly at Jiangning, spent his days seeking singers and beautiful women, all at the expense of his father-in-law's integrity allowance. Once Tao's household accountant asked whether Hu Linyi's extravagance ought to be restrained. “Let him spend,” Tao replied. “He will serve the country one day. Then, even if he has money, he will have no time to spend it.” Hu Xueyan's circumstances differed, but compared with the great benefits he secured for the country, even extravagant personal pleasures counted for little. These remarks eventually reached Zhejiang. Deeply grateful, Hu served Zuo with still greater loyalty and effort. Madam Luosi, however, grew uneasy. In private talks with the Seventh Lady, both agreed that a tall tree catches the wind: it was time to become less conspicuous. Yet Hu needed only to ask, “How are we to cut back?” and she had no answer. For Hu depended on credit; credit rested on the confidence others placed in him; and that confidence was created by the grandeur of his establishment. The display could only grow, never shrink. Otherwise, a single casual remark—“Mr Hu is no longer what he used to be”—would instantly set off endless speculation. Those who bore him grudges, and those who had no grievance but were merely envious, would fan the rumours. His credit would be shaken, with consequences too terrible to contemplate.

Hu Xueyan: Vanishing into Thin Air

CHAPTER ONE: THE CRISIS OF THE JIASHEN YEAR

Business in Shanghai had deteriorated further under the impact of France's war in Vietnam. France had long coveted Vietnam. In the first year of Tongzhi, the French emperor Napoleon II launched a major naval invasion. The Qing court, fully occupied with the rebellion of Hong and Yang, had no strength to protect Vietnam, though it was a tributary state. Vietnam was forced to sign a humiliating treaty and cede the three provinces of Qinghe, Jiading, and Dingxiang. Jiading was Saigon, where the French worked energetically to establish a base for further aggression against Vietnam and eventual advances toward China's Yunnan Province.

In the eleventh year of Tongzhi, internal disorder broke out in Vietnam. Its leader, Huang Chongying, commanded tens of thousands of men under yellow banners, hence the name Yellow Flag Army. The French colluded with him to seize Tonkin, crossed the Han River, and captured Lang Son beyond Zhennan Pass on the Guangxi frontier. Liu Changyou, Governor of Guangxi and a veteran commander of the Hunan Army, sent troops to help Vietnam suppress the disorder and also invited Liu Yongfu to join the campaign. Liu Yongfu came from Shangsi in Guangxi and had originally been a smuggler. During the Xianfeng reign, when Hong and Yang rose in rebellion, he followed an ambition of his own, leading three hundred sturdy followers through Zhennan Pass into Baosheng in Vietnam. A Guangdong man named He Junchang had occupied the place, but Liu supplanted him. His men carried black banners and became known as the Black Flag Army. Having accepted Liu Changyou's invitation and the Vietnamese king's offer to bring him into the royal service, he joined the Guangxi troops in attacks on the French from two sides and won a formidable reputation. Opinion within Vietnam was divided, however, and peace negotiations were eventually chosen. The three envoys sent to negotiate were detained by the French and compelled to sign the twenty-two-article Treaty of Saigon. Besides ceding territory and opening trade, Vietnam accepted French protection. To placate Liu Yongfu, he was appointed deputy commander of Sanxuan. He settled in the remote mountain frontier, farming and training his troops. His followers grew to as many as two hundred thousand, including twenty thousand picked men between seventeen and twenty-four. Tall, dark-faced, and powerfully built, they crossed forests and ravines as nimbly as apes, their morale exceptionally high. The French regarded him as a thorn in their side and offered a large reward for his head.

After the Treaty of Saigon, regret and resentment spread through Vietnam from the highest ranks to the lowest. King Ruan Fushi resolved to make full use of the Black Flags, but France struck first, capturing Hanoi with a powerful force. From Hue, the king ordered the Black Flags to drive the French out. If Vietnam were lost, Guangxi and Yunnan would be threatened; France had also formally demanded trading relations with China. At court, opinion divided between war and peace. The war party was led by Li Hongzao. Besides supporting Cen Yuying, Governor-General of Yunnan and Guizhou, in his support for Liu Yongfu, it secured the special appointment of Zeng Guoquan as Governor-General of Liangguang to organize coastal defence. Zuo Zongtang also urged war, and opinion among the scholar-officials grew more impassioned. Yet the peace party was far from weak. Li Hongzhang, naturally, favoured peace, and Zeng Jize, the minister to France, also opposed a rupture. The clearest understanding of the advantages and dangers, however, belonged to Guo Songtao, who had previously represented China in France. In the first lunar month of that year, the ninth of Guangxu, Li and the French minister Bourée had reached an agreement: China would withdraw its troops, and France would not invade Vietnam. But political upheaval in France brought a cabinet reshuffle. The new foreign minister, Challemel-Lacour, was ambitious: he recalled Bourée, repudiated the agreement, and urged the dispatch of more French troops to Vietnam. An imperial order then instructed Li, who was observing mourning, to proceed urgently to Guangdong, direct Vietnamese affairs, and command the defence forces of Liangguang and Yunnan. Outwardly, he appeared to be taking charge of a war, but Guo saw otherwise. From his home at Xiangyin in Hunan, he sent a special messenger with a long letter. “In dealing with the West, war has never offered a solution,” he argued. The foreigners wanted trade; China should discuss trade with them. Agreeing to negotiations would ease the situation in Vietnam. Sending Li to command armies with a great show of force, as if determined to fight to the finish, would compel France to fight. France had not originally wished for war. To force it into one was to fail, in military terms, to understand the enemy.

If China actually went to war, Guo continued, it would also be failing to understand itself. His words were bitter: “For more than thirty years we have waged war. Gathered together, men become soldiers; dispersed, they become bandits, spreading across the empire and leaving profound dangers in their wake. Add repeated floods and droughts, a decaying administration, robbers everywhere, and a population unable to sustain life. To provoke trouble on the frontier now and recruit still more troops for defence would, as the days and months passed, produce exhaustion beyond endurance.” In terms of military expenditure alone, China could not fight. Even if it won, what then? Victory would require demobilizing the newly recruited troops, leaving them “wandering with nowhere to return,” gathering “the hungry and destitute to pursue their designs.” China would be creating the sources of its own disorder. Guo next reported the discussion in Beijing: “The Grand Council has repeatedly criticized the contrast between the Governor-General of Yunnan's preparations for battle and the Governor-General of Guangdong's apparent unconcern. That is why Your Excellency has been entrusted with supreme command.” It seemed that Cen Yuying wanted to fight while Zeng Guoquan stood aside, and that a man of Li's seniority and authority was needed to bring the commanders into agreement and direct the whole undertaking. In reality, however, “the capital's purpose in entrusting this to Your Excellency is still to negotiate peace, not to seek war.”

Although in mourning, Li was fully informed about the court. He maintained several resident informants in Beijing, who reported every development to Hefei by the fastest available means. He knew that Prince Gong wavered between war and peace, while the strongest advocates of war were Li Hongzao, leader of the northern faction, and the men of the Pure Stream group, particularly Zhang Peilun, the Left Deputy Censor-in-Chief. Even if Li intended to negotiate peace, he dared not say so openly. Scholarly opinion carried great force, and the Black Flags' successes had further strengthened the war party. To advocate peace now would defy the sentiment of the whole country. He therefore delayed his departure. On reaching Shanghai, he held several talks with Tricou, the new French minister who had replaced Bourée, adopting a manner neither yielding nor aggressive and relying above all on delay. What would delay achieve? Li himself did not know. Behind the scenes, however, he worked hard to remove obstacles to negotiation. The first was Zhang Peilun, a pillar of the Pure Stream group. If Zhang could be won over and the clamour for war quieted, peace would be easier to arrange. Another obstacle was Zeng Jize. His opposition to a breakdown in negotiations did not mean that he favoured concessions to France. After returning from Russia to Paris, he had observed that French policy was still unsettled and that only a minority wanted war. He sent secret telegrams to Li and the Zongli Yamen recommending military aid to Vietnam and a firm line with Tricou. Li neither accepted nor rejected his advice, but wrote to Guo, hinting that he should influence Zeng. Guo's ties with Zeng were close; they had also served in succession as minister to France. Zeng would certainly respect his views.

During these one or two months of delay, developments in both France and Vietnam changed the situation. French policy grew more unified. Prime Minister Jules Ferry told parliament that he was determined to intensify military operations in Vietnam. Nine thousand reinforcements and another twelve warships were sent east, and Admiral Courbet replaced General Bouët as commander of the French forces. In Vietnam, King Ruan Fushi died and was succeeded by his younger brother Ruan Fusheng, under the title King Hehe, or “Harmonious Peace.” The title itself suggested a willingness to submit to France. Only a month after his accession, he signed the twenty-seven-article Treaty of Hue, formally acknowledging Vietnam as a French protectorate while continuing to recognize China as its suzerain. The annual tribute, previously carried overland through Zhennan Pass to Beijing, would henceforth travel by sea. This Franco-Vietnamese treaty helped unite French policy and gave the French troops a recognized basis for expelling the Black Flags. The war party within the Vietnamese government was furious. It killed King Hehe and enthroned Ruan Fuwu as King Jianfu. Though Li, now back at his post in Tianjin, continued negotiating with the French minister over Vietnamese sovereignty, the two countries were in fact poised for battle, and war seemed almost unavoidable. News of Peng Yulin's special appointment to direct military affairs in Guangdong deepened the panic in Shanghai. It was now the middle of the ninth lunar month, just when Madam Luosi returned from Shanghai to Hangzhou.

The day after her return, a special envoy arrived from Jiangning. He wore red and was covered in the dust of travel, but on his hat, fringed all over with red silk, rose a red rank button, with a peacock feather trailing behind. Four attendants followed, each with an official button of his own. They had come by road on five tall horses, raising clouds of dust to the jingle of bridle bells, so imposing a procession that passers-by turned to stare. Just inside Wulin Gate, the envoy raised his hand and all five reined in. One officer, wearing a dark blue button, rode forward for orders. “Ask the way.” “Yes, sir!” He slipped from the saddle and, holding the reins in one hand, caught a middle-aged man with the other. “Here, my friend, a place I want to ask about: where's Wubao Street?” “What? What did you say?” The officer came from Zeng Guofan's own home district. Of all Hunan speech, the Xiangxiang dialect was the hardest to understand; delivered rapidly by an impatient soldier, it became even more incomprehensible. Fortunately, he recognized the problem. “Yuan-bao Street,” he repeated, syllable by syllable, cupping both hands to suggest a silver ingot. “Ah, Yuanbao Street! That's what you mean, sir.” The man, surnamed Bu, was a clerk in the rites section of the Qiantang county office. Instead of answering, he asked, “May I ask where you have come from? Jiangning?” “Yes.” “Then you are going to Yuanbao Street to see Mr Hu?” “Mr Hu?” The officer hesitated, then understood. “Yes, yes. Mr Hu is His Honour Hu Xueyan.”

Clerk Bu nodded, stepped closer, and pointed discreetly. “Who is the gentleman on horseback with the red button?” The officer was growing impatient. The roads were open to everyone, and asking directions was an ordinary matter. Someone who knew the way and felt helpful could explain it; someone who knew but could not be bothered could say he wasn't sure. A helpful person who did not know could apologize and suggest asking someone else, while an unhelpful one could simply turn and walk away. But to ask directions and be questioned in return, almost as though under investigation, was a new experience. Seeing his expression, Bu hastened to explain. “Please don't think me tiresome, sir. The gentleman on that horse is a first-rank military officer. I dare not neglect him. If I know who he is, I can report to our magistrate, and any service he requires can be attended to promptly.”

So that was his kindly intention! The officer felt embarrassed, but did not know how to answer. The envoy had originally been called Gao Laosan, Third Son Gao. When he joined the Hunan Army, the recruiting official had given him the more elegant name Leshan, playing on the sound of his old name and the saying that the benevolent delight in mountains. Because he was third-born, he also received the courtesy name Renshu. Gao had originally served under Liu Songshan. When Zuo began his western campaign, Zeng assigned Liu and his battalion to him, an arrangement people jokingly called a dowry. Liu's brilliant service proved invaluable. Zuo and Zeng did not get on; in the gifted Zuo's eyes, Zeng had otherwise done nothing worthy of admiration. For this gift of Liu, however, he was sincerely grateful, and he always treated Liu with special regard. Gao had been Liu's mounted orderly. Honest and sincere, he was once assigned to attend Zuo during an inspection visit. He patrolled through the night without sleeping, so impressing Zuo that he asked Liu to transfer him to his own staff. Whenever recommendations for promotion were submitted, Gao's name appeared among the confidential ones. He was now listed for appointment as a brigade commander, with the honorary rank of provincial military commander: the summit of advancement in the Green Standard Army. In practice, he remained a military attendant, carrying out errands, with a position among Zuo's staff rather like that of a bodyguard attending the emperor. To say that this first-rank officer was merely a superior sort of mounted orderly would diminish his red button. His blue-buttoned subordinate therefore answered vaguely, “Lord Zuo has sent him specially to see Mr Hu.”

“I guessed as much!” Bu clapped his hands and raised his thumb. “He must have been sent by Lord Zuo. Excellent! Yuanbao Street is a long way off, at the other end of the city. I'll lead you there. Just wait while I hire a horse.” Wulin Gate was Hangzhou's main northern entrance, and Gongchen Bridge, at the beginning of the canal, stood outside it. Carriages, sedan chairs, mules, and horses were all available for hire at the gate. Bu rented a dapple-grey and proudly led the way. It was an old horse discarded by the Banner garrison: docile enough, but painfully slow. Horses had understanding too. Hired out for so long, this one knew that setting out meant a burden and a distant destination; every step was lazier than the last, since the faster it walked, the worse its bargain. On the return journey, it might not quite rush like a thirsty steed toward a spring, but its pace was transformed, its head and mane high as it hurried back to its manger. It was an old hand among horses. Nine county clerks out of ten were old hands too. Here, one old hand had met another, and they suited each other perfectly. Bu proceeded at a leisurely pace, with five officers following step for step as though they were his mounted attendants. Hangzhou's highest-ranking official was the garrison general, followed by the governor. Though both wore red buttons, none of their attendants did. Bu glowed with pride, especially when he met acquaintances. He would raise clasped hands or bend forward in greeting, always adding loudly, “I'm taking them to see Mr Hu!” Several times he nearly fell off in his excitement, saving himself only by clutching the saddle pommel. His antics made the passers-by smile, while Gao's expression grew darker and darker.

Near Yuanbao Street, Bu raised a hand at a corner to signal a halt, then squeezed his horse forward and rode ahead to the Hu residence. “Old Bu, what brings you here?” asked a servant who recognized him. “I've brought news. Lord Zuo, Governor-General of Liangjiang, has sent a red-buttoned officer to see Mr Hu. I met him at the city gate and guided him here.” “Where is he?” “Just behind.” The servant looked up. Sure enough, five horses were approaching, the red and blue buttons clear in the bright autumn sunlight. All dozen or so men at the entrance grew nervous. Zuo often sent red-buttoned guards with orders, but when he had been Governor-General of Shaanxi and Gansu, his messengers on public or private business had gone only to the transshipment bureau in Shanghai. This was the first to come directly to the Hu house. The unfamiliar caused alarm, and the quick-witted servants hurried to report instead of lingering to watch.

Madam Luosi was startled. The Hu family had gone to great lengths for a red button. Hu himself held circuit-intendant rank with the honorary title of provincial judicial commissioner, entitling him to a third-rank blue button. Had he accepted an actual circuit post, Zuo could certainly have obtained the additional title of provincial treasurer for him. But Hu could only be an official merchant. To turn business success into an official career, he would have had to give up trade. Every office imposed its own rules of conduct; he could not bear such restrictions, nor would he have made an outstanding official. He knew this himself, and all who cared for him agreed that taking office would foolishly abandon his strengths for his weaknesses. If he wanted official splendour, therefore, he had to purchase it. Purchased rank for himself stopped at the third grade, but money could buy honorary distinctions for his parents. For more than ten years, whenever flood, drought, or famine struck, he had donated silver, rice, padded clothing, and medicines in his mother's name, finally obtaining for her the title of a first-rank lady. By sharing in his mother's distinction, he too could wear a red button. In Madam Luosi's memory, visits from red-buttoned civil or military dignitaries had been rare, always announced in advance and requiring days of careful planning for the reception, hospitality, and treatment of their attendants. Such an officer's sudden arrival naturally left her alarmed and at a loss.

Hu was accustomed to such visitors, however, and Gao was an old acquaintance. He could receive him calmly and courteously. After giving Madam Luosi a few instructions, he changed into official dress and met Gao in the garden drawing room. They greeted each other as equals, one addressing the other as Mr Xueyan, the other replying with General Gao. Hu then went into the corridor, asked Gao's attendants their names, exchanged a few courtesies, and assigned someone to look after them. “Please change into something informal,” he said. At once, a servant entered carrying a bundle of clothes to help Gao dress. In official society, meeting in ceremonial robes fulfilled the requirements of courtesy, while conversation in informal clothes expressed friendship. Normally, though, a guest judged the closeness of the relationship for himself and had his attendant bring a change of clothes. Gao had never experienced, or even heard of, a host supplying them. Still, Hu was famous for his lavishness, so perhaps it was not surprising. “Please go and change yourself too, Mr Xueyan.” “Yes, yes. Then we can talk at leisure.” When Hu returned, Gao was wearing a brand-new iron-grey lined silk robe, with a tribute-satin riding jacket fastened by coral buttons and a dark satin cap topped with a red knot. He had also washed his face and looked refreshed and vigorous. “Do the clothes fit reasonably well?” “Thank you, thank you! Better than anything I could have had a tailor make for me. I won't stand on ceremony. Many thanks!” Gao repeatedly clasped his hands in gratitude.

“Is Lord Zuo still in good spirits?” Gao's smile slowly faded. “He's much worse. His eyesight has deteriorated badly. It's no small trouble.” “Has a doctor seen him?” “Yes, but to no purpose. The doctor wants him to stop reading official papers and books, close his eyes, and rest. Can you imagine him doing that?” “What exactly is the disease?” “The doctor can't say. A film has formed over his left eye, and his right waters whenever the wind touches it.” “Could he go blind?” “It's hard to say.” “I'll recommend a doctor,” Hu said, “and have him go back with you.” “Yes.” Only now did Gao produce Zuo's letter. It was brief. The military situation in Vietnam was urgent; by imperial order, preparations for both the northern and southern maritime defences had to be hastened, and troops were to be sent to assist Vietnam. Zuo therefore asked Hu to find time for a meeting in Jiangning. Any further details could be obtained from Gao.

Hu supposed that, as usual, it would mean finding arms and military funds. A man should not concern himself with the duties of an office he did not hold. He had received no appointment from the Governor-General of Liangjiang's administration; any service he rendered would be purely a matter of personal friendship. He might as well make that clear to Gao first. “You know that whatever Lord Zuo says, I can only obey. But Jiangning is not Shaanxi and Gansu. I fear I may find myself working hard and getting no thanks.” “Yes. Lord Zuo said that Jiangning has its own people, and that anything Mr Hu does for him is done entirely out of friendship. As far as official business is concerned, your transshipment bureau serves the western expedition. He can only consult you; he cannot issue a written order. That is why he wants you to come and discuss matters in person.” “And what does he want to discuss? Money or weapons?” “Weapons.” “Ah.” Hu felt a little easier. “As long as it isn't money, things are more manageable.” “When do you intend to leave?” “I must discuss that with my wife,” Hu replied frankly, meaning, of course, Madam Luosi. “Who is Lord Zuo sending to Guangxi?” “Mr Wang.” “Mr Wang?” Hu could not immediately recall a senior commander of that surname on Zuo's staff. “Yes. Commander Wang Langqing.” “Oh, him.”

Gao meant Wang Debang, who, like Gao himself, possessed an elegant courtesy name: Langqing. He came from Jianghua County in Yongzhou Prefecture, Hunan, a remote little county that had never produced any particularly outstanding figure. Within the Hunan Army, however, Wang was a distinctive and respected veteran. Early in the Xianfeng reign, he had devoted his family fortune to organizing a local militia and rendered valuable service in defending his home district. Later, he distinguished himself in Jiangxi and, as early as the seventh year of Xianfeng, received the civil rank of assistant department magistrate. After joining Zuo, he repeatedly won remarkable victories and became a famous fighting commander, receiving the title “Bold and Brave Baturu” and permission to wear the yellow riding jacket. In the fourth year of Tongzhi, his accumulated service brought him the rank of provincial treasurer. He followed Zuo into Xinjiang and performed services no less distinguished than those of Liu Songshan and his nephew, yet advancement never satisfied him. He held the honorary treasurer's rank for six or eight years without obtaining an actual post. Wang was an uncouth soldier. When summoned to court after his promotion, he spoke so crudely and with so strong a local accent that the two empress dowagers could not understand him. Thus, while nominally a provincial treasurer, he performed the duties of a brigade commander. In the first year of Guangxu, he returned home for mourning; in the sixth, he went back to Xinjiang. Soon afterwards, Zuo entered the Grand Council in Beijing and, as a grand secretary, took charge of the Ministry of War. At Prince Chun's request, he reorganized the Banner troops and specially recommended Wang to train the Firearms and Stalwart camps. Wang's men also worked on waterways near the capital, carrying earth and dredging rivers without complaint, which earned Prince Chun's approval. Zuo understood Wang's strengths well, but his weaknesses were considerable: he could command soldiers, not administer a civil office. When Peng Yulin asked for assistance, Zuo thought of him as the right man for the task. He requested imperial approval to send Wang to Liangguang under Peng's command and promised to supply weapons. This was what he wished to discuss with Hu.

Now that Hu understood the circumstances, he knew where matters stood. “Stay here for a couple of days, General Gao. Once I've discussed it with my wife, perhaps we can leave together.” “If you are coming with me, I will certainly wait. Otherwise, I should return first to report. You know Lord Zuo's temperament.” “Then you may as well go back first. When would you leave?” “Tomorrow.” A sumptuous banquet was provided, though Hu did not need to attend personally. Afterwards, Gao and his men were shown to guest rooms and looked after with the greatest care. Before leaving the next day, Gao naturally asked to see Hu for any final instructions.

The answer was that Hu would invite him to lunch and give him a letter for Zuo in person. At noon, they were taken into the garden for another lavish meal, this time including Gao's attendants. Five sets of gifts had been laid out in the hall. Each contained a robe and riding jacket, two bolts of machine-woven cloth, a large box of household medicines made at Hu Qingyu Hall, and two official silver ingots of fifty taels each. Gao received, in addition, a gold repeater watch and an ivory-handled revolver. “I meant to send you home by boat, but I fear it would be too slow. I'm afraid I must ask you gentlemen to endure another journey on horseback.” Gao rubbed his hands repeatedly, feeling that refusal would be discourteous and acceptance undeserved. “Such generous rewards are really too much.” “A trifle, a trifle! Do have another cup.” Gao would not drink much. His four subordinates, unused to such hospitality, felt still more awkward. Each kept his head down and ate three bowls of rice, then rose, made the formal kneeling salutation to Hu, and thanked him as they took their leave. In honour of the red button, Hu naturally had the central gate opened to see them off. Five horses stood abreast by the screen wall outside, the same mounts as before but with new saddles, bridles, and even whips. Hu had his own ceremonial escort; two mounted attendants accompanied Gao's party out through Wulin Gate. People pointed along the way, knowing them to be Mr Hu's guests.

After Gao had left, Hu discussed his movements with Madam Luosi. “The second instalment of the foreign loan is also due. I thought I would go to Shanghai and settle that first, then proceed to Jiangning. Wang Langqing has only just left Beijing, so a slightly later arrival at Jiangning shouldn't delay anything.” “No. Since Lord Zuo has sent an officer specially to invite you, respect requires that you go to Jiangning first. Mi Benchang is in Shanghai. Let him press the circuit intendant for the foreign-loan payment in advance. By the time you arrive, the funds will be ready and you can make the payment in person. Isn't that the natural order?” “I'm uneasy about the Shanghai market too. I'd like to have a look first.” “There is even less need for that. Mi Benchang is extremely capable; he is certain to have everything properly arranged. Take my advice. Go to Jiangning first, then Shanghai, and come home for the wedding. The timing will be just right. If you go to Shanghai first and then Jiangning, Lord Zuo may give you some further task, and it would be a pity to miss the wedding date.”

In Tianjin, after careful consideration, Li Hongzhang decided that Zhang Peilun, with his talent, ambition, and excellent qualifications, should be brought into his service. Zhang's father had held office in Li's home province of Anhui, giving them something of an inherited family connection. Li sent a special invitation and held several long conversations with him at the northern maritime administration. Li had an ambition of his own. In secret consultation with Prince Chun, he had been planning a modern navy. Having founded the Anhui Army himself, he knew that the army could no longer be put into proper order. In foreign armies, even ordinary soldiers had schooling and could read written orders; in China's army, even battalion commanders were illiterate. How could they compete? Besides, however well the army was trained, it could defend the country only after an enemy had set foot on Chinese soil. A navy could keep the enemy beyond the frontier. Li had therefore quietly begun developing the port of Lushun and establishing a naval school for the northern fleet. This great undertaking would require at least ten years and a peaceful situation in which to advance steadily, step by step. That was why he insisted on compromise with France: endure a moment's anger to secure the country's future for a century. Zhang agreed that this was the proper way to plan for the nation and offered many suggestions. They found themselves in complete accord. “I am an old man,” Li said. “You have extraordinary talent and a great future. In time, this seat must surely be yours.” There was already a hint of handing on his mantle. Zhang recalled Zeng Guofan's dictum that the first task in great undertakings was to find a successor. Zeng had disbanded the Hunan Army and fostered the Anhui Army because he had found Li. Li, who regarded himself as Zeng's foremost disciple, must now be following that teaching by choosing Zhang. This honour concerned the nation's destiny; Zhang should accept the responsibility and not disappoint him.

With this unspoken understanding, Zhang privately joined the peace party. Meanwhile, someone proposed to Li a way of using another's blade to strike at the Pure Stream group: send its most prominent men out of Beijing and give them important military responsibilities. Scholars who had only discussed war on paper would often fail when confronted with real troops. Their failures could then be used to break the group's power, while other habitual critics would learn caution. It was an excellent means of silencing opinion. Li thought that whether such an appointment amounted to destroying a man or raising him to high command depended on the man. Zhang belonged to the second category. Li decided to secure his appointment to direct the Fujian Navy Yard, founded by Zuo and expanded by Shen Baozhen, as preparation for his future service with the northern navy. The others could be dealt with by the borrowed blade.

That plan would require gradual preparation and patient execution. For the moment, besides having Zhang quiet the clamour for war, the most urgent task was to make the advocates with real military power retreat before the difficulties. Foremost among them was Zuo. He must be obstructed from every direction until his plan to support Peng Yulin met barriers at every step and could not proceed. This was why Li specially summoned Shao Youlian north for consultation. “Zuo of Xiangyin relies entirely on Hu Xueyan's efforts,” Shao said. “When the provinces were last asked to contribute to disaster relief, Liangjiang was assigned two hundred thousand taels. The Jiangning treasury was empty. Zuo asked to borrow from the Jianghaiguan Customs, and I said I would have to consult Hart. He retreated before the difficulty and ended by borrowing the money from Hu. Without Hu, he would be helpless.” “Hu is a thoroughly troublesome man,” Li said. “The foreigners still trust him, and that affects many of my dealings with them.” “Then there is a way to make them stop trusting him,” Shao replied. “Or at least trust him less than before.” “Yes, that is the right idea. But it will not be easy. We must plan carefully.” “There is an opportunity at this very moment.” The second repayment of principal was now falling due on the final loan that Hu had arranged for Zuo.

By the time Shao Youlian had met Li Hongzhang and agreed that striking at Hu Xueyan would be their principal means of obstructing Zuo Zongtang, Hu had only just reached Jiangning. When he discussed his itinerary with Madam Luosi, she strongly urged him to visit Jiangning before Shanghai. He thought her reasoning sound. Her praise of Mi Benchang had made him realize how well Mi could handle unexpected situations, which simplified matters. In Nanjing he must attend upon Zuo and could not control his own movements. In Shanghai, Mi would attend upon him. Any unfinished business could be left to Mi, allowing him to come and go as he pleased without missing the important duty of presiding over his daughter's wedding. He wrote to Mi and Gu Yingchun while preparing his baggage, most of which consisted of local gifts. Jiangning had more expectant circuit intendants than anywhere else, giving rise to a joke that its “circuit men were as thick as hairs.” They might go a whole year without an assignment, yet still had to maintain the appearance of third-rank dignitaries. Struggling to do so, they awaited visits from friends holding lucrative posts, hoping for a little help. Hu had many acquaintances there and was the God of Wealth. Everyone must receive attention, in gifts or silver. The silver could be drawn from Fukang in Jiangning, but the Hangzhou gifts filled an entire boat. A small steamer specially sent by the Yangtze naval forces towed it and Hu's private passenger boat through Jiaxing and Suzhou to Jiangning. Meanwhile, Li secretly telegraphed Shao, the Shanghai circuit intendant, summoning him to Tianjin for an important personal discussion. As a local official, Shao could not leave his post without authorization, so Li explained that a separate telegram would come from the Zongli Yamen. Shao was to prepare and sail north as soon as its official instructions arrived. They reached Shanghai only after Hu had left Hangzhou. But the sea passage to Tianjin took just two days and a night; when Shao saw Li, Hu was still on his way.

The ministers responsible for the northern and southern maritime administrations were thus each summoning a trusted man, but for opposite purposes. Zuo favoured war. Besides actively preparing southern coastal defences, he fully supported Peng Yulin, the imperial commissioner supervising military affairs in Guangdong. Li, though unwilling openly to defy respectable public opinion, secretly used every means to remove the war party's support and weaken its power and prestige. His first target was Zhang Peilun, the Left Deputy Censor-in-Chief, chief strategist for Grand Secretary Li Hongzao, leader of the war party. Bringing Zhang under control would be like capturing the leader to subdue the band. In terms of suppressing the advocates of war, winning Zhang over dealt with the root; attacking Hu dealt with the branches.

Hu, who would bear the first blow, knew nothing of this. On reaching Jiangning, he went first to rest at his own residence. He kept houses in the great cities but rarely visited them even once a year. Because of Zuo, this was his second stay at Jiangning that year. The “mistress” of this house was surnamed Wang. She had formerly run a brothel in Diaoyu Lane in Qinhuai's Old Quarter, but misfortune had struck her two adopted daughters in succession: one died for love, and the other eloped. The elopement could be left alone, but the death involved Madam Wang in a homicide case. She was finally acquitted and released, yet so disheartened that she no longer wished to earn her living by that precarious trade. The only alternative was to leave it and marry. Like Li Xiangjun's adoptive mother in Miscellaneous Records of Banqiao, she was a madam without being old, only a little over thirty and still attractive. There were men willing to offer riches for her. But Qinhuai courtesans inherited the Old Quarter's traditions from the late Ming and early Qing. They cared about refinement in food and daily life and admired poets and cultivated men. Those who wanted her had fortunes but no trace of elegance; those she wanted were gentle and refined but poor. She wished to leave the profession, yet could find no one to entrust her future to.

That was three years earlier. Jiangning Fukang had just acquired a new manager, Jiang Deyuan, transferred from another Fukang establishment. Well versed in the world of pleasure, he heard of her and hired her to manage Hu's residence. Normally it entertained especially important clients; when the proprietor visited, she became its hostess, presiding over the household. Those duties naturally extended to the bedroom. Comfortable living and freedom from restraint made her readily accept. When Hu came that autumn, the first thing to attract him was the pair of tiny curved feet beneath her skirt, slender as crescent moons. After a night together, he found Yuan Zicai's saying true: “A mature woman's charms surpass those of youth.” Besides generous gifts, he gave her the name Mother Wang Jiu, after the brothel keeper in the famous Southern Song tale set on West Lake, The Oil Vendor Wins the Flower Queen. Now, warned by Jiang, she had prepared Hu's favourite food and gathered plenty of news to entertain him.

Naturally, Hu cared most about news of Zuo. He was said to be increasingly old and infirm, but more overbearing than ever. Visitors and subordinates must never mention the western campaign: it opened a floodgate of talk about his achievements, his combination of kindness and authority in handling generals, and the miraculous unpredictability of his strategy. Then came the abuse, first of Zeng Guofan, next of Li Hongzhang, and sometimes of Shen Baozhen too. All three had preceded him in office, and many of their former subordinates remained in Jiangning, especially Zeng's. Whatever might be said of Li, people resented attacks on Zeng's character. Zeng's old followers often complained openly: “The present commander has grievances against the old commander. The rights and wrongs between them are hard to judge. Even if the old commander was at fault, he is dead and cannot hear the abuse. Why must we endure it? Besides, the arguments are neither just nor convincing. It all comes down to the same thing: he monopolized military funds and protected Ninth Marshal. We have heard it until our ears have grown calluses.” Hu wondered how Zuo could have declined so much in the mere six months since they last met. He was doubtful until Jiang confirmed it. “Many things cannot be done in Jiangning now. His Excellency begins with a lecture, then starts abusing people, talking without pause. When the allotted time is nearly over, a guard puts a teacup into his hand and someone outside immediately calls, ‘See the guest out!’ There is no chance to discuss business.”

“Surely that happens only occasionally?” “Almost every day. He becomes more excited with a larger audience. You needn't stand on ceremony, sir. Instead of attending a formal audience, go now and see him in the garden reception room or his office. Then you might discuss something useful.” Governors-general and governors generally received the provincial treasurer and judicial commissioner, together with circuit intendants and lesser subordinates, about once every five days, often on dates ending in three or eight. These formal visits, called “going up to the court,” took place in the official reception hall. Hu had arrived on the seventeenth of the tenth lunar month and intended to attend on the eighteenth. Accepting Jiang's advice, he instead put on his official robes at once and went straight by sedan chair to the Liangjiang governor-general's gates.

Seeing the God of Wealth, the gatekeepers were exceptionally attentive. On their own authority they opened the main gate and let his sedan be carried to the eaves of the reception hall. Word was sent inside, and instructions came back: “Ask His Excellency Hu to change into informal clothes. We shall meet in the office.” His attendant opened the clothes bundle, and Hu changed in the hall before being shown into the office, where Zuo was already waiting. Hu naturally made his full ceremonial greeting. Zuo helped him up himself and led him to the guest seats, where they exchanged the usual courtesies. As they spoke, Hu studied his eyes. A white film covered the left, while the right watered badly in a draught, forcing him to wipe it repeatedly with a silk handkerchief. Finding an opening, Hu said, “I heard your eyes were troubling you and had a special medicine prepared. It is cooling and clears the sight, with very good results.” Undoing a small brocade bundle he had brought, he added, “I also had a medicinal paste made for you. If it agrees with you, have your correspondence secretary write, and I shall send more.” “Thank you! Nowadays I depend on a few friends for help, not just with private matters; even official business must trouble you. When Shandong suffered floods, Liangjiang was assigned four hundred thousand taels for relief, and the provincial treasury could provide only half. Your generous help saved us. But Liangjiang still cannot repay you.” “Please don't mention it.” Hu nearly added that, with public funds deposited with him, he ought to be of service, but checked the words before speaking.

“With the situation in Vietnam urgent, the court has ordered Peng Xueqin to supervise military affairs in Guangdong. We have been friends for thirty years, and I must help him. Moreover, I have been commanded to prepare southern maritime defences. The waters off Guangdong and Fujian fall within my jurisdiction; I cannot neglect them. What infuriates me is that, since Zeng of Xiangxiang's time, officialdom in Liangjiang has grown steadily worse. Evasion and delay, with no thought for the wider situation—so once again I must rely on old friends.” Hu assented gravely. “Wang Langqing has left Beijing for Hunan to recruit six thousand men. He will need at least four thousand rifles. Li Shaoquan's elder brother-in-law has made a complete mess of the Jiangning Arsenal. If we order the Shanghai Manufacturing Bureau to produce them, first the money is not yet available, and second they cannot arrive in time for the emergency. So I thought the Transport Bureau might find a way. What do you say, Xueyan?” “I don't yet know the exact number of Western rifles in stock. But if you require four thousand, I shall find some means of supplying the full number.” “Good! I knew that a word to you would settle it. Nothing could be more satisfying.” Referring to himself respectfully by his personal name, Hu replied, “Guangyong owes everything to your patronage. I dare not fail to serve you with all my heart and strength.”

“You are too modest. There is something else. The Ministry of Revenue will of course arrange pay and provisions for Wang's recruits, but the cost of mobilizing them is considerable. Liangjiang must contribute what it can. Could you help us once more?” In the past, Hu would simply have asked how much. Circumstances were different now. After a little thought, he replied, “Your Excellency, money is desperately tight in the market. Even if it were not, you must consider your old subordinate. If I raise whatever you ask now and later cannot supply Shaanxi and Gansu, I shall be like a man who jumps into a well to rescue someone.” The old subordinate was Liu Jintang. Hu held a commission with the western expedition's Transport Bureau, and his responsibilities had an order of priority. Raising funds for Liangjiang was additional work, which he could undertake if he had capacity to spare. Otherwise, the western army must come first. Zuo understood and could not disregard the concern. “Very well. Tomorrow I shall speak to the provincial treasurer again. If there really is difficulty, we shall have to rely on you to come to our rescue.” “You are too kind. When should I return for instructions?” By instructions, Hu meant the answer. “Soon. There will be news within two or three days.” Hu rose. “I shall act as you direct. For today, I take my leave.” “Are you free this evening?” Realizing that Zuo meant to invite him to dinner, Hu quickly said that he had an engagement he could not miss. “Then I won't keep you. I know you are busy. There is no need to call again. When there is news, I shall send for you.”

After his farewell salute, Hu went to a banquet in a riverside house on the Qinhuai. The guests were prominent men in Jiangning officialdom, unusually well informed, and he learned much inside news. Li Hongzhang was said to have formally told the Zongli Yamen that China's strength was insufficient and the Vietnamese affair must be settled promptly: there was no other satisfactory course. The Yamen, however, favoured notifying the countries of the world of France's coercion and unreasonable demands, making clear that the fault lay with France. If French troops attacked, China should fight. Li disagreed, but even if he wanted negotiations, he had no one to negotiate with: the French special envoy Tricou had left for Japan. “China's difficulty is that we want peace but dare not make it, and want war but cannot fight it,” said Zhang Fengchi, an expectant circuit intendant serving as foreign-affairs commissioner at the governor-general's headquarters. “Now each side is trying to outlast the other. The question is which can do it.” “Who do you think will last longer, Mr Feng?” “Hard to say. In France, only the foreign minister was initially so intransigent, but opinion has now become united. Their premier told parliament that they were determined to fight to the end in Vietnam. Meanwhile, our court's two great pillars may not be fire and water, but they are certainly pulling in opposite directions and cannot agree. That is deeply worrying.” The two pillars were plainly Li and Zuo. Most guests were Liangjiang officials, but many had close ties to Li. Their quarrel was a dangerous topic: an incautious word could bring trouble. Everyone remained silent.

Everyone, that is, except one man. Yugui, an expectant circuit intendant in Shandong, was a Mongol Bannerman. He had formerly awaited appointment in Liangjiang, acted in an established circuit post and held many assignments. Senior in service and the oldest man present, he was called Brother Yu by everyone. Clear-minded and ready to shoulder responsibility, he should have risen as an able official, but his blunt speech had harmed his prospects. The Shandong governor had sent him to consult Zuo about dredging the Grand Canal. He had spent half a month in Jiangning without getting anywhere, leaving him full of grievances. At mention of the quarrel, he could not remain silent. “Lords Zuo and Li have illustrious achievements and the admiration of the empire. The court has rewarded them with titles and high office. Their past military services are past; there is no need to keep discussing them. A true hero doesn't boast of former valour. Why do it?” He plainly meant Zuo. With the great official so near at hand, the subject became more perilous still, and nobody dared say a word. Slightly tipsy, Yugui took their silence as approval and grew more animated. “In war, speed is everything. If we talk emptily all day and neglect real work, what happens when the enemy reaches the city walls while we are still boasting that the spring wind has already passed the Jade Gate? Think what a state we shall be in!” The guests exchanged frightened looks. His closer friends were particularly worried. If this reached Zuo, Yugui would certainly be summoned. A severe scolding would be the least of it. What if Zuo asked, “What troops do you mean at the city walls? The French?” In anger, he could impeach Yugui by name for alarming the public and undermining civilian and military morale. Dismissal would be the minimum punishment. Someone hurriedly changed the subject. “Brother Yu, tonight let us discuss only pleasant things. Drink, drink!”

Yugui wanted to continue, but their host, Zhang Fengchi, seized his opportunity. “Brother Yu's black-faced roles ring like great bells and will sober us up. Come, give us a passage to delight our ears.” Others agreed enthusiastically. “His singing is wonderfully stirring. Quickly, where are the musicians?” String and wind players and percussionists were all available and soon took their places. When they asked what to play, Zhang said, “His specialities are Exploring Mount Yin and Ascending the Heavenly Terrace. Let us ascend the terrace first, then explore the mountain.” “No,” Yugui replied. “I shall change roles today and sing a bearded character. Give me Executing Ma Su.” The drummer struck up and the fiddle began. As the introductory music ended, Yugui changed his mind. “Better make it Ascending the Heavenly Terrace after all.” He had improvised some words to attack Zuo through the example of the Shu general who lost Jieting: “His words outrun his deeds; he will never be of great use.” But he reconsidered. He was a visitor here, and Zuo was, after all, an elderly man of high standing. Excessive insolence would be improper; he had better not go too far. Watching all this, Hu was deeply affected. He remembered Zuo in his vigorous prime, when even Zeng Guofan had to yield to him. Who could have imagined such decline in old age, and such contempt from others? Grieving for Zuo, he also began thinking of withdrawing while the current still ran strong.

He had been in Jiangning ten days, yet Zuo had not sent for him. Given the earlier instruction, he could hardly seek another audience. He asked acquaintances to inquire, but learned nothing definite. At last the summons came. This time Zuo wasted no words. “Xueyan, I have made other arrangements for Shaanxi and Gansu. Allocate two hundred and fifty thousand from the Transport Bureau's public funds.” The money was plainly for Wang Debang. It was an order, with no discussion, and Hu could only assent. “Can it be paid here?” “Wherever you wish.” “Good. Here, then. Open an account for Wang Langqing and issue him a passbook.” “Yes.” “When will you leave?” “I have been awaiting your instructions. Now that they are settled, I hope to leave tomorrow.” “Yes, you must return for the wedding. I have already told them to prepare a congratulatory letter for your daughter's marriage. We have shared hardships; I feel sorry that I cannot attend the feast.” “You are too kind.” “I should like to send something distinctive as well. What would you suggest? Don't stand on ceremony.” Hu thought for a moment. “A pair of wedding couplets in your own hand would truly bring glory to our humble house.” “A small matter. There is no time today, but I shall certainly send them before the wedding.” “You are so busy with public affairs that I am asking more than I should. Since you have granted the request, I shall reserve the place of honour in the wedding hall.”

This was an indirect way of making the promise binding. Zuo could not fail to keep his word, leaving two blank spaces in the place of honour. Understanding, he called for an attendant. An answer rang from the corridor, and an officer wearing a bright blue finial entered to await his orders. “I have promised His Excellency Hu a pair of couplets for his daughter's wedding. Whenever you see me with a little time to spare, remind me, so that I don't fail in courtesy. Keep reminding me.” “Yes.” “Good. That settles it.” He asked Hu, “You are going to Shanghai first?” “Yes.” “Is there anything you need me to arrange?” Hu was uneasy about the foreign loan principal soon falling due. But Mi had sent no letter, so he supposed everything had been settled. There was no need to trouble Zuo. “I shall ask when something arises.” “Very well. I have not even found time to give you a dinner on this visit. It is hardly proper.” “You are too courteous. Is there anything you would like me to attend to in Shanghai or Hangzhou?” Zuo thought briefly. “Only those four thousand rifles for Wang Langqing.” “I shall certainly settle that.” “Nothing else. As you said yourself, I shall ask when something comes to mind.” Hu took his leave, then earnestly reminded the attendant officers that they must prompt Zuo about the couplets. Naturally, he also presented a red envelope marked “Parting Gift.”

As soon as he reached Shanghai, Hu regretted the time wasted in Jiangning. The city seemed transformed. Business was depressed. Acquaintances, on meeting, asked either for war news or where it would be safest to take refuge. Nothing of the sort had been apparent in Jiangning. Such conditions were a banker's greatest fear: rumours everywhere and people in panic. The wealthy believed cash in hand was safest, so deposits were withdrawn but not replaced. Several banks had already failed through lack of funds to meet payments. Fukang's excellent name protected it to some extent, but another danger was developing in secret. Mi kept his lips sealed and let Hu know nothing. Even what Hu could see was enough to cause a severe headache. First came Wang Debang's four thousand rifles. The Transport Bureau had only twenty-five hundred in stock, leaving fifteen hundred to buy. At eighteen taels of standard silver each, with freight, they would cost about thirty thousand taels. That was relatively minor. The trouble was that Hu had given Zuo an unqualified promise. Failure to deliver the full number would affect his credit. “You needn't attach too much importance to it, Little Uncle,” Gu said. “You can show Zuo of Xiangyin the order later.” “Yingchun, I have never fallen short of my word to him. This may be one of the last one or two commissions I carry out for him. What matters most is how one finishes. If I break my word at the end, he may suspect that, no longer needing his protection, I am less loyal. Besides, I cannot bear to destroy a name built over so many years for such a small matter. Think of something. You must help me.” Gu had always handled arms purchases, and no such appeal had ever been necessary. The sudden plea made him uncomfortable. After considering for some time, he said, “Let us see whether Japan offers a way. If there is stock ready, we can still make the deadline. But we shall not be able to bargain over the price.” “Price is a small matter. Speed is everything. Start today.”

After two days' work, Gu at last had a lead. Eager to tell Hu, he looked everywhere but could not find him. Late that night, just as Gu was about to retire, Hu arrived unannounced, looking unwell. Ruixiang attended to him herself, bringing ginseng broth. “You must be exhausted, Master. Are you hungry?” “Hungry, yes, but I can't eat.” “Think of something appetizing for supper,” Gu told her. When she had gone, Hu asked, “Has Seventh Sister gone to bed?” “Yes. She retires early.” “Then don't disturb her. I hear you have been looking for me all day.” Gu brightened. “I have good news. We have found the rifles.” “Excellent! Where?” “Japan. Interestingly, they were originally intended for the French.” “Better still. How did it happen?” The French had hurriedly sent reinforcements and wanted to obtain additional rifles locally in the East. They had found a Japanese arms dealer with two thousand for sale. Through extensive inquiries, Gu learned of the stock and had a telegram sent offering a high price for fifteen hundred. The reply asked twenty-five taels each, plus freight. “Has the bargain been settled?” “Yes, at his price, with freight for our account. Ten thousand taels have already been telegraphed to him. Delivery in Shanghai in half a month.”

“Twenty-five it is. At least that is one worry settled.” Hu suddenly asked, “Have you heard that Old Mi is secretly trading in goods from north and south without telling me?” Gu hesitated. “I have heard something, but know no details.” “They say a ship struck a French mine and sank, with a considerable loss.” “The loss can't be large. There would certainly be insurance.” Hu nodded, reassured. “Do you think I should confront him?” The matter was important, and Gu dared not answer hastily. After a long pause, he asked instead, “What do you think?” “As long as the risk isn't great, I think it better to say nothing. As the saying goes, ‘Once you have gone astray, you may as well tear down the cowshed.’ If I expose it, he may simply throw off all restraint and do business on a large scale. Then I shall have to replace him. The difficulty is finding anyone suitable.”

Hu then spoke of another worry. The second repayment of principal on the foreign loan fell due at the end of the tenth lunar month. Since the beginning of that month, Mi had repeatedly asked at the Shanghai circuit intendant's office, only to be told that the provinces had not yet remitted the money. When Hu arrived and called on Shao Youlian, he received the same answer, with one addition: “Don't worry. I shall press them as hard as I can. The money should all be in around the due date.” “It must be before the deadline, not after. You know how particular foreigners are about keeping faith.” “I know. But the money is not in my hands. What can I do? Mr Hu, five hundred thousand taels is nothing to you. If it hasn't all arrived before the deadline, advance it yourself. You will only lose a few days' interest.” That silenced Hu. “He wasn't wrong. Normally an advance would be nothing. Who could have known that this time I couldn't make it? Misfortunes have happened to coincide, and I cannot explain my difficulty.”

Gu had to think for a moment to understand Hu's phrase: several unlucky circumstances coming together made a coincidence of misfortunes. There were many. First, business was poor and money desperately tight. Second, Hu knew that his stocks of silk and cocoons had trapped him and had tried hard to escape. Yet through one mishap after another, his scheme to acquire modern silk-reeling factories and create an outlet for the stock had never succeeded. Silk remained in both Tianjin and Shanghai, without buyers even at reduced prices. Third, Zuo had already borrowed two hundred thousand taels for relief contributions and now required another two hundred and fifty thousand for Wang Debang. Although these were the Transport Bureau's public funds, their removal still reduced the cash available for Hu to deploy. Fourth, the wedding on the fifth of the eleventh month was approaching. Such a grand occasion meant heavy spending; at least another two hundred thousand taels must be ready. Finally, Mi was privately using customers' names to withdraw deposits for his trade in northern and southern goods. Gu estimated the amount at roughly a hundred thousand taels. “Today is the twenty-fifth of the tenth month,” Hu said. “This month has only twenty-nine days. There are fewer than ten days until the fifth of next month. How can I attend to the wedding with an easy mind until I have put our cash position in order?” “Don't be too anxious. After all, it is only five hundred thousand. And it isn't your personal debt. There must be a solution.” “Then we must look for it early.”

After some thought, Gu said, “We can only proceed step by step. Press the Shanghai circuit intendant while making our own arrangements to mobilize funds. If neither succeeds, there is a final course: ask HSBC for an extension. At worst, we pay extra interest.” “I thought of that too. But what if they say, like Shao Xiaocun, ‘Why don't you advance it yourself?’ I shall have no answer.” “They won't. Foreigners distinguish public from private affairs. They won't expect a private person to advance money for a public debt. If they do say so, tell them, ‘Better for you to advance it than for me to do it. Before, HSBC wanted to lend to Fukang. Fukang didn't want the money but eventually took it. Let this again count as a loan from HSBC to Fukang.’ See what they say.” Hu nodded earnestly. “That is true.” “If you agree, I can settle it with HSBC in advance. Then you can put your mind at rest.” “Not so fast!” Hu repeatedly waved his hand. He had his own concerns. Requesting an extension would amount to admitting that he could not even advance five hundred thousand taels. If that became known, it would damage his golden reputation. Zuo would doubt his resources and ability, and on the fifth of the next month the crowds of wedding guests would be bound to discuss it. The glory of the celebration would be greatly diminished.

“Let us take the first and second steps for now,” Hu said. “I shall handle the first and entrust the second to you.” The first meant pressing the circuit intendant's office; the second, finding ways to arrange funds themselves. In practice, that meant urging Mi to act. Because of their earlier friction, Gu was unwilling to undertake an arduous, thankless task that might achieve nothing. His face showed his reluctance. “What is it?” “I should like us to exchange roles. Leave the first step to me, and take the second yourself. You have every right to press Old Mi. If I do it, he will resent it and pay no attention.” “Very well. But we must act quickly.” “I shall go first thing tomorrow. I have acquaintances at the office. Come for lunch and hear the news.” “Good. These next few days we must see each other morning and evening.”

At noon the next day, Gu Yingchun brought excellent news: almost all the provincial contributions to the western military funds had been collected. The earliest payment had arrived at the beginning of the tenth month. “Can that be true?” Hu Xueyan was thoroughly puzzled. “Why did Shao Xiaocun tell me he had not received a single cash? Where did you hear this?” “From a younger fellow townsman whom I helped years ago. He is now the head clerk in the telegraph room at the Shanghai circuit office.” “Then there can be no mistake!” Hu was delighted and angry at once. “What game is Shao Xiaocun playing? I shall have a word with him!” “There is no need for that, Little Uncle. I think the best course is to ask Lord Zuo to send him a telegram.” Gu had also obtained highly confidential information from his fellow townsman: Li Hongzhang was looking for ways to strike at Zuo Zongtang. This suggested that Shao Youlian had an ulterior motive for deliberately obstructing Hu. But the report had not been confirmed, and telling Hu might only cause trouble. The best course was to have Zuo intervene with a sternly worded warning, making Shao think twice and release the money he had collected before the deadline, thereby discharging Hu’s responsibility.

Hu, however, had no way of knowing what lay behind Gu’s advice. His concern was still to save face before Zuo. In Jiangning, Zuo had asked whether there was anything in which he should intervene, meaning the western military contributions collected through the Shanghai circuit office. Had Hu then asked him to write and hurry Shao along, it would have been a perfectly natural answer; Zuo would have thought nothing of it. But Hu had already said that there was nothing he needed to trouble him about. To ask for his intervention now would amount to admitting that he could not advance five hundred thousand taels. He therefore replied, “There is no need to trouble His Excellency. Since almost all the provincial payments have arrived, I shall go and press Shao myself.”

Hu had always been able to keep his temper, but this time the strain of too many affairs made him lose patience. He went angrily to see Shao, only to be told at the door, “His Excellency has gone to inspect the Manufacturing Bureau.” This fruitless visit made him still more displeased. Returning to the Manufacturing Bureau, he ordered his correspondence secretary to write to Shao. The letter was decidedly discourteous, with something of an official’s peremptory tone; it also hinted that, if Shao could not pay on time, Hu would have to ask Zuo himself to deal with the matter. Delivered to Jianghaiguan Customs, it was immediately forwarded to Shao’s residence. Naturally, it made him uneasy. As the saying went, “It is not an official you need fear, but the man who has authority over you.” Since the suppression of the Taiping armies, provincial governors and governors-general had acquired powers unequalled since the founding of the Qing dynasty. Zuo was the incumbent Governor-General of Liangjiang. If he submitted a severe impeachment naming Shao, no argument, however sound, could win Shao a hearing. Besides, contributions from several provinces had indeed arrived; withholding them was indefensible. Very reluctantly, he decided to draw up a statement and send the money already received to the Transport Bureau. It came to about four hundred thousand taels. Hu would then need to advance only one hundred thousand to preserve his credit with the foreigners. But just as Shao finished his reply and was about to send it, a visitor arrived who overturned his decision completely.

The visitor was Sheng Xuanhuai. Having successfully established the telegraph bureau, he had become one of Li Hongzhang’s leading favourites and had also formed a connection with Prince Chun. Li had sent him to Shanghai to discuss with Shao how to “put out the fire.” This was Sheng’s metaphor for rescuing the present situation, and Li used it too. Li believed he had a way to turn the danger of the Sino-French conflict over Vietnam into a peaceful settlement. The actions of the war party, however, were like setting fires, while the lofty rhetoric of the Pure Stream group poured oil on the flames. Once the fire was extinguished, even oil would have nothing to feed. In other words, if the moves towards war could be stopped, the Pure Stream group would cease to be a threat. Who, then, were the arsonists? In Li’s eyes, Zuo came first and Peng Yulin second. As for men in the southwest, such as Cen Yuying, Governor-General of Yunnan and Guizhou, there were ways to keep them under control. Even Peng, deprived of Zuo’s support, could be made to recognise the difficulties and withdraw. Capture the ringleader first: once Zuo had been restrained, Li could control the whole situation and negotiate peace with France.

“Brother Xiaocun, do not be misled by all the cries of ‘War and self-strengthening,’ ‘Let the empire display its might,’ and ‘Unite against the common enemy.’ Those impassioned declarations ring to the skies, but they are merely the voices you can hear. The voices you cannot hear are the ones with real power. Without those silent voices behind him, His Excellency would have no reason to oppose Zuo of Xiangyin. Zuo is declining in his old age; at most, he has another three or five years of wealth and honours ahead of him. Why should His Excellency be unable to tolerate him? Conversely, if he cannot tolerate him, there must be a reason why Zuo has to go. Brother Xiaocun, you must first understand what is in His Excellency’s mind.” By His Excellency, he meant Li Hongzhang. Sheng was a consummate speaker. He portrayed Li’s attitude towards Zuo as generous and temperate, all forbearance and charity. What Shao heard, however, was perfectly clear: Li and Zuo had become irreconcilable enemies, and their struggle could end only with one or the other destroyed.

“Yes,” Shao said, suddenly alert. “I understand. But may I ask whose voices these are that cannot be heard?” “First, Empress Dowager Cixi, who holds all power in her hands. She has laboured for more than half her life, and two years ago she suffered an illness that nearly killed her. Think of it: how many fifty-year-old ladies do not long for a few peaceful years?
