Why should she want a war?” “If all power is hers, she need only say ‘Peace.’ Who would dare disobey her command?” “That is precisely her difficulty. She can say anything but that one word. Why? She put down the great rebellion of Hong and Yang. No empress dowager who ruled from behind the curtain has ever had military achievements to equal hers. How can she show weakness before her ministers? Besides, the Pure Stream group is so clamorous that she has to echo its lofty sentiments in public. In reality, her wishes are quite different.” “I understand. It is a difficulty she cannot voice.” Shao asked, “And the second?”

“The second is Prince Gong, who is in charge of affairs. He has always believed that, in dealings with foreigners, peace comes first. Now that he is older, he has even less appetite for grand ambitions.” “When the Anglo-French forces invaded, Prince Gong advocated peace and the imperial princes and grandees called him a traitor. No wonder he is afraid to speak. But Prince Chun has always favoured war. Why is he silent too?” “That is the crucial point. The Prince Chun of today is not the man he was. In recent years, the foreigners’ strong armour and powerful weapons…” Sheng paused and smiled. “Indeed, it was Zuo who taught him that lesson. The western campaign went so smoothly entirely because of the superiority of its firearms. When Zuo was in the capital, he explained this to Prince Chun in detail. The prince now fully endorses His Excellency’s policy of learning the foreigners’ strengths in order to counter them. A plan is being prepared to make Lushun a naval port and develop a substantial navy. Prince Chun is intensely enthusiastic about it. Naturally, he does not want a moment’s impatience to ruin a great undertaking.” “Quite so! With those three behind him, His Excellency has every reason to hold firmly to the course he believes right.”

“Speaking of holding to the right course, there is another man we must not overlook. Xiaocun, you have been abroad. Tell me: among all the men dealing with foreign affairs today, who is the foremost?” “The Old Man of Yuchi, of course. Even Marquis Zeng has to seek his advice on foreign affairs.” The Old Man of Yuchi was a name Guo Songtao had chosen for himself; Marquis Zeng was Zeng Jize, the imperial envoy to France. In fact, not only Zeng but Li Hongzhang himself had to consult Guo. Li had seen a great deal, but his insight was less penetrating than Guo’s. Moreover, although Li too had belonged to the Hanlin Academy, his scholarship could not match Guo’s. Guo could advance an opinion or develop an argument that embraced ancient and modern times, China and foreign lands, without contradiction. Expounded with Li’s eloquence, Guo’s ideas sounded more persuasive still.

“Now Peng Xueqin is asking for money to recruit troops, and Wang Langqing has already enlisted his full four thousand men in Hunan. These are the men Zuo is sending out to set fires. Once trouble starts, it will spread like a blaze across the plains. His Excellency is deeply anxious. To take just one example, French warships are lying outside the mouth of the Wusong. The French have told him to his face that they can attack the Manufacturing Bureau at any time. That is one of the lifelines of the Beiyang establishment. How can he help being anxious?” Shao was appalled. He had always assumed that any clash with France would occur in Guangxi or Yunnan. An attack on the Manufacturing Bureau at Gaochangmiao would mean fighting in Shanghai. As circuit intendant, he was responsible for defending his territory. Would he have to go into battle himself against the French? The thought terrified him. “People have been saying that in Shanghai too,” he stammered. “I always took it for a rumour. But if they told His Excellency themselves, then it is true!” “There is no need to be alarmed,” Sheng reassured him. “They do not act indiscriminately. If you do not strike, they will not provoke a quarrel. But if you are going to strike, they will forestall you.”

The meaning could not have been clearer. Shao immediately replied, “Whatever happens, we cannot let Zuo start this fire. To set a fire, you need materials. Without Mobil kerosene or matches that light at a stroke, there can be no blaze. Am I right, Brother Xingsun?” “Exactly. That is what they call removing the firewood from under the pot.” “And there is only one way to do it,” Shao said. “Hu Xueyan has all the kerosene and matches. Without him, Zuo could not start a fire even if he wanted to. The officials in Jiangning pay little heed to Zuo; whatever he tells them to do, they comply only in part. There is just one man who does exactly what he says, and that is Hu. For instance…” He offered a number of examples. When relief was needed for the fire in Shandong and the Jiangning provincial treasurer could not provide the money, Zuo had asked Hu for a loan of two hundred thousand taels and received an immediate response. Now Wang Debang was recruiting men to assist Vietnam; Hu was arranging not only the supply of four thousand foreign rifles but also a contribution towards the troops’ travelling expenses. The conclusion was that, to prevent Zuo from setting his fire, Hu Xueyan had to be put out of action.

“Benchang,” Hu said, pointing to Shao’s reply, “read this and you will understand. He makes it perfectly clear: as soon as all the provincial payments have been collected, he will send them over. Everything will be settled before the deadline, and if it is missed, he will take full responsibility. He is the Shanghai circuit intendant, after all. His word means something. There is nothing to worry about.” After reading it, Mi asked, “What deadline have the foreigners set?” “They have allowed another ten days. So long as the money is paid before the tenth of the eleventh month, it will not count as late.” “Ah. When do you intend to return to Hangzhou, sir?” The question greatly displeased Hu. “The wedding is on the fifth,” he said. “Today is the twenty-ninth of the tenth month. When do you think I ought to leave?” Even with a small steamer towing his boat, the journey to Hangzhou would take at least three days. Before the wedding there were many elaborate formalities; even if he did not have to arrange or preside over them, he had to put in an appearance. Whatever happened, he must therefore set out the next day, the last day of the tenth month. Rebuked, Mi dared not say another word, though inwardly he was in turmoil. Hu knew nothing of his anxiety; his thoughts were fixed on the foreign loan’s deadline. “Of course I must make provision for this,” he said. “Since payment is due on the tenth, there is no need to press Shao now. Go to see him on the fifth or sixth and collect whatever is available. By my estimate, it will be at least eighty per cent, if not ninety. We shall have to advance at most a hundred thousand taels, and that will settle the matter.” “Yes, sir.”

“How much cash have we now?” Mi’s heart gave another jump. Hu had examined the accounts and ought to know the answer. Why ask a question whose answer he already knew? So absorbed was Mi in this thought that he forgot to reply. Hu prompted him again. “How much?” “Ah! You have seen the accounts, sir. Somewhere around four hundred thousand.” The silver held throughout Shanghai amounted to only a million taels. If Fukang alone held four hundred thousand, how could that be considered little? Hu knew, however, that Mi had diverted some of it. Even if four hundred thousand was no longer there, he supposed that at least three hundred thousand must remain. An advance of one hundred thousand was therefore nothing to worry about. Still, it would do no harm to ask, “If you cannot arrange the funds, what do you intend to do?” An odd question! Mi thought. If ready silver was short, naturally he would draw on the other branches. What else was there to “intend”? Was Hu implying something? There was no time to consider it. For the moment, he could only offer sweeping assurances. “There will be no difficulty arranging the funds. I know the receipts and payments at all thirty-three establishments in Shanghai, Hankou and Hangzhou. Advancing a hundred thousand is nothing.” He added, “The two Ningbo branches regularly have over a hundred thousand taels on hand.” He was trying to conceal the fact that he had used customers’ names to divert deposits. “A shrewd fellow needs only a hint”: Hu took this as an indirect admission that Mi had diverted a hundred thousand taels or more and would find a way to replace it when necessary. This reassured him further.

What Hu did not know was how widely the rumours had already spread. People said that he was on the verge of collapse. According to one account, he had lost his contest with the foreigners over silk and cocoons. Although nothing had happened in Shanghai, the silk in his Tianjin warehouses could find no buyer even at a low price. Another concerned the foreign loan: he could not repay it when due. This report had two versions. One was that, proud though Hu was, he could not raise the money in time and had asked the foreigners for an extension, which was still being negotiated. The other was that the Shanghai circuit office had already forwarded the provincial military contributions to Fukang in successive payments, only for its manager, Mi Benchang, secretly to use them to fill the hole in his own accounts. Rumours needed supporting evidence if people were to believe them, and here the evidence took the form of a question: Hu’s daughter was to be married on the fifth of the eleventh month, so why was he still lingering in Shanghai? Because he could not balance his funds. Otherwise, a man of his habits would long since have returned to Hangzhou to prepare for the wedding. It was a powerful argument. Everyone could see how extraordinary his delay was. Yet Hu was known far and wide as the God of Wealth. Deeply troubled though people were, they still felt that someone with that name must possess resources beyond their understanding. They would wait and see. Until when? Until the end of the tenth month, to see whether he could get through the crisis. These reports, half true and half false, neither wholly rumour nor wholly fact, had mostly been circulated by Sheng and Shao through HSBC. Thus, on the anxiously awaited thirtieth of the tenth month, many people went to HSBC for news, and still more went to Fukang to watch what happened.

“Is Mr Hu here?” a well-dressed middle-aged man asked a Fukang employee. “I have come to see him.” “Mr Hu has returned to Hangzhou.” “Returned to Hangzhou?” “Yes. There is a wedding in his family early next month. Naturally, he has to hurry home.” “Oh? In that case, he ought to have left long ago. Why…” Why? Nobody could answer that question. The well-dressed visitor was an agent sent by Sheng to spread rumours. He went about telling people that Hu, seeing the situation was hopeless, had fled to Hangzhou. That afternoon, people began bringing Fukang notes to be redeemed for silver. The first presented a bearer note for five hundred taels. He explained that the money was for betrothal gifts: he needed actual silver, preferably official ingots fresh from the mould. Fukang’s employees had always been eager to oblige their customers. They made a special trip to the vault for ten brand-new large ingots. Several still bore the double-happiness characters cut from red paper: they had themselves been deposited by families celebrating weddings. The second customer redeemed eight hundred taels without giving a reason. The employees had no right to ask for one. Such a transaction was perfectly ordinary and gave no cause for surprise. The third was another matter.

He arrived with a handcart and two porters, and laid seven notes on the counter, totalling twenty-one thousand four hundred taels. A cash withdrawal on that scale generally meant a military camp was paying its men, and advance notice was always given. Sensing trouble, the employee put on a courteous smile. “Please come inside, have some tea and rest a little.” “Certainly, certainly. You are very kind.” The visitor strolled over to the guests’ seats and accepted the invitation. Mi had already been informed. Feeling that something was amiss, he hurried out to receive the man himself and politely asked his name. “Zhu. And yours?” “Mi—the character for ‘must’ under a roof,” Mi replied. “I understand that you wish to redeem your notes for silver?” “Yes.” “Over twenty thousand taels of silver weighs more than twelve hundred jin. That is upwards of four hundred large ingots, very awkward to move.” He continued, “At Fukang, we always try to make the best arrangements for our customers. What do you need this silver for, Mr Zhu? Perhaps we could remit it to the destination, or exchange these notes for smaller ones in whatever amounts you require. Would that not be much easier?” “Thank you for your consideration. I have an unavoidable use for this money that I am not at liberty to explain. In any case, the recipient insists on actual silver, and I have no choice but to comply. I know it is cumbersome to move. That is why I brought the cart and the men.” That left nothing more to be said. One further objection from Mi would be a blow struck at Fukang’s own golden reputation. He murmured his assent and at once ordered the vault opened and the silver paid out.

Silver came in many forms, and twenty thousand taels or more was no small sum. They could not pay it all in large fifty-tael ingots. They had to combine ingots of different sizes and allow for differences in purity, a troublesome business. The silver was stored in wooden boxes. Each box had to be opened, examined, reckoned and carried away in turn. A crowd gathered to watch, talking excitedly, until one question naturally emerged: were Fukang’s notes no longer trustworthy? Was that why people were demanding silver? By the time Zhu left, it was closing time. They put up the shutters and sat down to supper. Mi looked dejected and could scarcely swallow. He forced down half a bowl of rice, rose and beckoned several senior employees to follow him upstairs to his bedroom at the back for a private conference. “I think we are in for trouble. How much silver is left?” “A little over eighteen thousand taels,” the vault keeper replied. “Only eighteen thousand? What is the total of our receivables and payments due?” They consulted the general ledger and the daybook. Receivables consisted of deposits at foreign banks and notes drawn on other Chinese banks, totalling over one hundred and fifty-six thousand taels. For payments due, they could count only the remittances ordered by the other branches, about sixty thousand taels in all. There was no way to calculate how much would be claimed on the banknotes they had issued.

“In that case, you must make contact with them tonight. They are all Mr Hu’s businesses; we should support one another in an emergency. Get me figures for whatever silver they have. Ask them to stand behind us when things are urgent.” By “them,” he meant Hu’s pawnshops, silk firms and cocoon firms in Shanghai. Four senior employees spent half the night making their rounds. When they had a reasonably clear picture, the silver that could be brought together amounted to only one hundred and twenty thousand taels. Mi carefully recalculated what was receivable and payable. Altogether, about two hundred and thirty thousand taels could be made available. “That ought to be enough,” he said. “So long as no devilry breaks out, we shall be all right.” Suddenly remembering something, he shouted, “A’zhang! A’zhang!” A’zhang was the leading apprentice, almost ready to complete his training, and had always managed Fukang’s miscellaneous chores. He was already in bed, but was called up again. “Have you made the offering to the Great Immortal?” “The offerings are made on the second and the sixteenth. Today is the last day of the month.” “Make it early! Early! Do it now.” The Great Immortal was the fox spirit. On the second and sixteenth of each month, it received a bowl of spirits and ten white eggs. There was liquor to hand, but the eggs had to be bought. It was already midnight. A’zhang went out and knocked on shop shutters until he could buy some, then boiled them and set out the offering. It was two in the morning before he went back to bed.

The next morning, his fellow apprentice Xiaomao woke him. “A’zhang! A’zhang!” he cried in a panic. “The devilry really has begun!” “What are you talking about?” “Listen!” A’zhang listened intently. Apart from the usual sounds of the street, he heard nothing unusual. “What am I supposed to hear?” he asked in bewilderment. “The voices!” Now that it had been pointed out, the voices did seem louder than usual. But what did voices have to do with devilry? “Go and look! The shutters are still up, and the customers are already queuing down the street!” That frightened every last trace of sleep out of A’zhang. He scrambled up, hurriedly washed his face and ran into the banking hall. Mi was gazing up at the clock mounted high on the wall. It showed ten minutes to nine. There were still ten minutes before the shutters were due to come down. At that moment, Mi stamped his foot. “Better to open early than late. Open up!”

A’zhang, barely out of bed, joined in the work at once. As soon as the first shutter was removed, the crowd surged in like a tide and knocked him to the ground. “Someone will be killed!” he cried. “Someone will be killed!” Fortunately, the police had arrived. Shanghai people were accustomed to the red-turbaned Indian policemen they called “A-san,” but raised batons still had a considerable restraining effect. The several hundred customers were finally put back into a long queue. A junior police officer, known in Shanghai as “Three Stripes,” entered Fukang and asked in Chinese with a Shandong accent, “Who is the manager?” “I am!” Mi stepped forward. “You own this bank?” “I do not own it. I manage it.” “As long as you manage it, that will do. Get the silver out and send these people on their way. We cannot have the whole street disrupted.” “There is plenty of silver. Officer, please keep order and let them come one at a time.” Three Stripes nodded, then shouted towards the customers beyond the counter, “There is plenty of silver! Enough for everyone! One at a time!” This quietened them further. All the employees had been instructed beforehand to work as slowly as possible. Some customers brought passbooks and required interest to be calculated on their withdrawals, which slowed matters still more. In an hour, the six men at the counter served only forty or fifty customers, who took away less than ten thousand taels. It looked as though the situation could be kept under control.

Towards noon, a thin, small elderly man arrived. Opening a bundle wrapped in a handkerchief, he passed a bankbook over the counter and said, “A withdrawal of one hundred thousand.” His voice was quiet, but to Mi it was a thunderclap overhead. He hurried forward to deal with the customer himself and first examined the account name in the passbook: Fuji. Trouble, he thought. “May I ask your name?” “Mao.” “How are you connected with Mr Zhaofu?” “We are friends.” “I see. Please come inside and sit down, Mr Mao.” “Very well.” Mao strolled into the seating area, where an apprentice brought tea and tobacco. Once he was settled, Mi asked, “You have come to withdraw one hundred thousand taels on Mr Zhaofu’s behalf?” “Yes.” “Where is the money to be used? If you will let me know, I can have notes drawn up.” “Locally.” “How many notes would you like?” Mao raised his eyes and asked slowly, “Which bank’s notes are you going to give me?” Mi was taken aback. Fukang notes, naturally. There had to be a reason for asking something so obvious. He therefore sounded the man out. “Which bank’s would you prefer?” “HSBC.”

Mi’s heart jumped again. Fukang had only a little over sixty thousand taels on deposit at HSBC. To write a cheque for one hundred thousand, he would have to make up the difference with notes from other banks, and under the rules these could not be drawn against on the day they were deposited. He might persuade HSBC to make an exception, but he could not get away. Besides, if word spread that he had gone begging HSBC for a favour at such a critical moment, Fukang’s credit would suffer. Rather than appeal to HSBC, why not appeal to the man sitting before him? “Mr Mao,” he said, “could we divide the payment?” “How?” “Half in an HSBC cheque, and half in our own notes?” Mao smiled faintly. “There is no need,” he said. “Please give me back the passbook.” So he had been right, Mi thought: Zhang Zhaofu was playing a trick. The Fuji account belonged to Zhang, a cotton and yarn merchant and a friend of Hu’s whom Mi also knew. Once, while drinking at a courtesan banquet, they had quarrelled over a courtesan’s transfer from one party to another. Both had had too much wine. Sober the next morning, Mi felt deeply uneasy and made a special visit to apologise. Zhang had merely said coolly, “I am a friend of your employer’s. There is no need for this.” His meaning was that he did not regard Mi as a friend. Now he had sent someone to withdraw his deposit, clearly with unfriendly intentions. Yet why demand the money and then decide not to take it? That was a puzzle.

When Mao had his passbook back, he said, “You have cost me a dinner!” “A dinner?” Mi asked. “Who have you made a wager with, Mr Mao? And what was the bet?” “Zhang Zhaofu, of course…” Mao explained that he and Zhang had been taking tea that morning in the West Garden of the City God Temple when they heard of the run on Fukang. Zhang said its position was dangerous. Mao maintained that a bank with Fukang’s golden reputation was safe beyond question. Zhang then said that Fukang probably had less than one hundred thousand taels at HSBC. If Mao doubted it, he could put it to the test. If Fukang could write an HSBC cheque for one hundred thousand taels, Zhang would pay for a banquet at a changsan courtesan house; otherwise, Mao would be the host. This was disastrous! After that evening’s banquet, Mi thought, who could say how many people throughout the foreign settlements would be repeating the next day that Fukang had only fifty thousand taels at HSBC? The consequences were unthinkable. He had to turn the tide. After considering and reconsidering every possibility, he finally saw a way: collect the military contributions due from the Shanghai circuit office and deposit them at HSBC as Fukang’s available funds. Then, the next day, anyone demanding redemption or withdrawing a deposit could be paid with an HSBC cheque.

Whenever Mi visited the Shanghai circuit office to press for payment or ask for news, he called on a fellow townsman named Zhu. This time, as soon as they met, Zhu asked, “How have you found time to come here?” Mi was astonished. “Why should I not have time?” he countered. “I hear there is a run on Fukang. Should you not be at the bank looking after things?” Mi was alarmed. News of the run had reached the circuit office, which would make it harder to ask for money. But he was quick-witted enough to see that he could use the situation as his excuse. “A run is an exaggeration. It is true that more people than usual are withdrawing their deposits, but that is because of the edict of the twenty-first of the tenth month, declaring martial law along the river. People are preparing to flee. Fukang has ample funds; they can withdraw as much as they please.” He hurried on. “But before he left, Mr Hu told me to set aside money to advance towards the foreign loan repayment. Now I cannot have the full amount ready. Please ask His Excellency to send over whatever he has already collected, so I can see how much is still lacking and arrange for it.” “Certainly!” Zhu replied without hesitation. “You have come at just the right moment. His Excellency has only just arrived. I shall speak to him for you.” Mi was delighted and could not help congratulating himself on his clever move. But Zhu returned very quickly, with suspicion on his face.

“You can go back with your mind at rest. The foreign payment is due on the tenth, and this office will pay it directly. Fukang will not have to advance a single cash.” Mi changed colour. It lasted only an instant, but Zhu noticed, and his suspicions deepened. “Mi, let me ask you something. His Excellency blamed me for failing to think it through. There is a run on Fukang. If official funds are sent over to fill the hole in your finances, how are the public accounts to be settled afterwards? Was that what you had in mind?” How could Mi admit it? He waved his hands in repeated denial. “Nothing of the kind! Nothing of the kind!” “Really?” “Of course. How could I deceive you?” “I did not think you would deceive me. Otherwise, you would be making me shoulder the consequences. That would hardly be the act of a friend.” The words cut Mi to the heart. He could only offer a strained smile, thank Zhu and take his leave. His legs felt weak beneath him, as though Fukang were a cauldron of boiling oil or a blazing volcano waiting for him to leap into it.

Back at Fukang, Mi entered by the rear of the kitchen. The clamour outside the front door filled him with dread. He had scarcely come in when an employee named Du stopped him. “Mr Mi, do not go out to the front!” “Why?” “Two big depositors were here just now. One wanted two hundred and fifty thousand, the other one hundred and eighty thousand. I told them funds had been tight in Shanghai for the past year or so, and our manager had gone out to arrange the money. They said they would come back tomorrow. If you show yourself, that explanation will no longer hold.” At the end of his resources, Mi suddenly felt that a way had opened before him. The truth could serve as an excuse too. Du was a capable man, the senior clerk at the counter. He could shoulder a heavy burden; why not let him try? After a moment’s thought, Mi said, “Quite right! That is how you should answer them. Tell them there is nothing to worry about. Our silk alone is worth several million taels. There is no need for everyone to rush in and demand their money.” “I understand,” Du replied. “But even if we get through today, we must have an answer tomorrow.” “When those two big depositors come back, tell them I have gone to Ningbo myself to collect cash. It will take five days.” Mi added, “I really am going to Ningbo. I am leaving now.” “It is nearly lunchtime. Eat before you go.” “How could I swallow anything?” Mi patted his shoulder. “I am placing a great trust in you here. Once this storm has passed, I shall put in a strong recommendation for you with Mr Hu.”

But that afternoon still more customers arrived, and the large depositors were less accommodating than the two who had come that morning. The crowd surged angrily, and trouble looked imminent. The officer called Three Stripes demanded to know where Mi was. Du had no choice but to tell the truth. “He has gone to Ningbo.” “What is to be done here?” Nobody knew. Only A’zhang said, “We can only put up the shutters.”

CHAPTER TWO: AN UNFORESEEN CRISIS

Madam Luosi had already gone to bed when the maid Hong'er came to report a message from the inner gate: Xie Yunqing, the manager of Fukang Bank, wished to see her. “At this hour?” Her heart suddenly sank. Could Hu Xueyan have fallen gravely ill? She dared not pursue the thought. “Madam,” Hong'er prompted, “shall I ask him to come back tomorrow morning?” “No. Ask him what it is.” “He only said there was a telegram from Shanghai.” “But what is it about? Go and ask.” Then she reconsidered. If it were not urgent, he would not be seeking an audience now; if it was, she must not waste time. “Open the inner gate and invite Mr Xie in,” she said instead, adding, “Don't disturb the old lady.” As Hong'er left, the other maids helped her rise and dress properly, then accompanied her downstairs. She too had learned to master appearances and steady others by her bearing. Though anxious within, she walked with measured steps, her skirt scarcely stirring. Those who read character and fortune from a person's gait had always said that hers promised distinction. Proud of her composure, she would not allow her steps to become disordered.

Xie Yunqing was always punctilious. At the first glimpse of her approaching figure, he stood respectfully with his hands at his sides, his gaze lowered in an attitude of complete restraint. Only when a breath of the foreign perfume she used reached him did he raise his head and bow with clasped hands. “I am very sorry to disturb you so late.” “Please sit.” She glanced around, then addressed the maids by the door. “Your manners are getting worse. A guest arrives, and you don't even bring tea.” “Please don't trouble. I've received important news and dared not keep it from you, Fourth Madam.” “Then sit down and tell me.” She waved him to a seat and took the place of honour herself. Xie perched deferentially on his chair, his voice beginning to tremble. “A telegram has just arrived. There has been a run on the Shanghai bank. They put up the shutters at three this afternoon.” Madam Luosi's heart jolted. “There can be no mistake?” “None. The telegram also says that Mi Benchang cannot be found. He is said to have gone to Ningbo.” “Who sent it?” “Mr Gu.” A telegram from Gu Yingchun could not be mistaken. She maintained an outward calm, but her thoughts were in such turmoil that she could scarcely gather them. After a long pause, she asked, “Where is Mr Hu?” “Presumably on his way home.” “How could such a thing happen?” she murmured, almost to herself. “With all Mi Benchang's ability, how could he fail to hold things together and let it come to this?” Xie had no answer. Rubbing his hands, he could only say, “It's a very serious matter. Quite unimaginable.”

She suddenly shivered. Struggling to remain calm, she asked, “What about Beijing?” “Tianjin must have heard already. Beijing will learn of it a day later,” Xie said. “Pull one hair and the whole body moves. Tomorrow will be very hard to get through.” She felt an immense pressure descend on her shoulders, far heavier than any physical burden. She longed to escape it but dared not. If she could not bear this invisible weight, the entire family would suffer. Yet even the thought of lifting it drained her courage, before any question of whether her strength was sufficient. Then came the warning thought of harm to the family, and above all to Hu. She could only grit her teeth and support it with all her might. “Mr Hu is on the road. We dare not alarm the old lady, and the other madam cannot devise a plan. What do you suggest, Mr Xie?” He had come to ask her for a decision. He could only smile bitterly. There was an idea in his mind, but he dared not voice it. After a silence, she spoke again.

“In your judgement, there is bound to be a run tomorrow?” “Yes.” “How much silver would we need to meet it?” “That is hard to say. Here alone, Fukang has notes outstanding for more than one million four hundred thousand taels. The deposits are greater still.” “How much cash is in the bank?” “About four hundred thousand.” She considered the matter repeatedly. “With four hundred thousand in ready silver, I should think we can hold out for a day or two. By then Mr Hu will be back.” Xie thought that, judging by what had happened, even Hu might have no solution. Otherwise, why would the Shanghai branch have had to close its doors? But he could not say that plainly. He asked only, “And if we cannot hold out?”

Had she possessed a satisfactory answer to that question, he would never have needed to seek out his employer's wife in the middle of the night. “Tell me yourself, Mr Xie. What happens if we cannot?” “There will be trouble, and people will get hurt. Suppose those who arrive early, or can reach farther, take away the cash first, while the latecomers get nothing. Put yourself in their place, Fourth Madam. Wouldn't you be furious?” The question needed no answer. “Go on.” “The worst thing is to provoke a crowd's anger. Once that happens, even the authorities cannot suppress it. Besides smashing the bank to pieces, they may come here to make trouble. Where that would end is impossible to say.” She was horrified. Forcing herself to settle her thoughts, she went over the problem again. “They become angry because some receive their money and some don't. It is unfair. If no one receives anything, that is a kind of fairness too. What do you think?” “Fourth Madam,” Xie said calmly, “you have understood.” “Very well!” For the moment, she felt she could shoulder the burden. “We won't open tomorrow. But we must give the customers an explanation.” “Naturally. We shall say the closure is temporary and ask them not to be alarmed.” “That is the meaning, but the words must be tactful.” “I understand.”

“I hear you are often in touch with Provincial Treasurer De's household?” Xie continued. Treasurer De was Dexin, courtesy name Xiaofeng, a Bannerman serving as provincial treasurer of Zhejiang. His friendship with Hu was close, and the women of the two households often visited one another. Madam Luosi and one of his favourite concubines were sworn sisters. “Yes. What about it?” “Go to his residence first thing tomorrow, if you would. It would be best to see him himself and ask for help in person. With the authorities intervening to maintain order, we shall have a better chance of getting through this.” “Very well. I'll go. Is there anything else we should consider and do immediately?”

One question kept troubling her: should she tell the First Madam of this wholly unforeseen upheaval? Within the Hu family's inner gate, there were, as the saying went, three rulers in one state. Nominally, the old lady presided over everything, like Empress Dowager Cixi ruling from behind the curtain. The First Madam resembled Prince Gong, while Madam Luosi was like Shen Guifen, who had died two years earlier. A Hanlin scholar named Wu had once written a poem called “The Younger Sister-in-Law's Lament,” comparing Shen, who had been summoned from the governorship of Shanxi into the Grand Council, to a daughter returning to her parents' home. So beloved by her mother was this daughter that the daughter-in-law in charge of the household lost her authority: all domestic business was conducted by the daughter under her mother's instructions. If the empire was the Manchus' family property, then the Manchu Shen did resemble a daughter coming home for a visit, or returning as a widow, and taking over the management of her natal household.

The closest parallel in the Hu family was the old lady's affection for Madam Luosi, which resembled Cixi's trust in Shen. At the daily morning “audience,” when the day's important business was discussed, Madam Luosi usually raised a matter and the old lady approved it. Alternatively, the old lady would ask and Madam Luosi would propose a solution. Her suggestions were almost always followed. Only after a decision had been reached would the old lady turn to the First Madam and ask, “What do you think?” Sometimes even that was omitted. Truly difficult matters, however, were not put to the old lady at all, and bad news was particularly to be concealed. Madam Luosi decided what she could herself and asked Hu about what she could not. If he was absent and a decision carrying some responsibility or risk of blame had to be made, she would consult the First Madam, hoping not for a useful idea but for someone to share the responsibility. Tonight's news was too serious. It would terrify the old lady; even the First Madam might fall ill with anxiety. Yet to decide alone would be more responsibility than she could bear. Telling her, on the other hand, meant considering the consequences. Xie was right: to steady the situation, they must first keep their own composure. Rumours outside were one thing. A single admission from within the family that they could not hold on would bring complete and irretrievable ruin.

“Madam!” She started slightly and looked up. A'yun, her senior maid, stood in the doorway. She had replaced Ruixiang as Madam Luosi's most trusted confidante. Wearing a soft rose-purple satin lined jacket, she rubbed her sleepy eyes and suddenly looked astonished. “Haven't you slept?” “No. Pour me some tea.” A'yun brought it and said as she handed it over, “Hong'er told me Mr Xie came in the middle of the night—” “Don't ask questions.” Madam Luosi waved her away with some impatience. Just then, the watch gong sounded again and the morning bell began to ring. A'yun glanced back in alarm. “It's five o'clock. If you don't sleep now, it will soon be daylight. Madam Matchmaker is coming for her thirteenth chicken today. The old lady particularly asked you to be there. How will you manage unless you get a little sleep?” In Hangzhou's official households, a male matchmaker was respectfully called Master Matchmaker and a woman Madam Matchmaker. Arranging a marriage was known as “eating thirteen and a half chickens.” Under the procedures of the Six Rites, a matchmaker made as many as thirteen journeys between the prospective bride's and groom's homes. Each visit required a fine meal, with at least a chicken killed in the visitor's honour. The joke was that a greedy matchmaker would come for another meal just before the bridal chair departed, but in the rush could eat only half a chicken. Hence thirteen and a half. Today, the matchmaker for Hu's Third Miss was coming to discuss the final details. Her next visit would be for the half-chicken meal before the bridal chair arrived on the fifth day of the eleventh lunar month.

Madam Luosi did not answer her point. She only sighed. “Third Miss has a hard fate too.” Then she added, “Go to Mengxiang Tower and see whether the madam there is awake. If she is, say I want to see her.” “Now?” “Of course now!” She was growing angry. “What's the matter with you this morning? Can't you understand anything?” A'yun dared say no more and slipped away. Mengxiang Tower, where the First Madam lived, was some distance off. Madam Luosi had finished a cup of hot tea before A'yun returned, followed by A'lan, the First Madam's trusted maid. “Madam had just woken up. She called me to her bedside and asked what it was. I said I didn't know. She asked whether it was urgent. I said that, if you wanted to talk at this hour, I supposed it must be. So she sent A'lan with me to ask you.” Madam Luosi knew that the First Madam was habitually slow to act, but how could she still fail to distinguish what mattered? With a sigh, she called A'lan in. “Go back and tell her I must speak to her in person. I'll come at once.” When they reached Mengxiang Tower, the First Madam was up and smoking the first of her five daily water pipes. “You're very early,” she remarked. “And dressed already.”

“I haven't slept all night.” The First Madam blew out the burning paper taper and looked up. “Why?” Madam Luosi did not answer immediately. She glanced back. “A'lan, all of you go downstairs. Don't come up unless called.” A'lan hesitated, then led out the three maids who were tidying the bed and clothes, closing the door behind them. Madam Luosi waited until no sound remained on the stairs. “Xie Yunqing came to see me in the middle of the night. He had received a telegram from Shanghai. Fukang has put up its shutters.” For a moment, the First Madam did not understand. Surely closing the shutters at the end of the day was no reason to send a telegram? Then she suddenly grasped it. “You mean Fukang has failed?” “It happened yesterday afternoon. Mi Benchang cannot be found.” “Where is our husband?” “On the road.” “Then he must have left before it failed. It wouldn't have failed with him there.” Having said this, she relit her taper and went on smoking, the pipe bubbling steadily.

Madam Luosi was surprised. She had not expected such composure. Perhaps she really ought to ask her advice. “Madam, Xie Yunqing wants to know whether they should take down the shutters tomorrow.” She paused for a response. With “putting up the shutters” already understood, taking them down plainly meant opening for business. “Are you afraid that, once they're down, you won't be able to put them up again?” the First Madam asked. “Naturally.” “Then what do you think?” “I think that, rather than let other people force us to fail, we had better fail ourselves. No, no!” she corrected herself hastily. “Suspend business until our husband returns.” “There seems nothing else to do. When will he arrive?” “By my reckoning, tomorrow afternoon at the latest.” “Do you mean tomorrow, or today?” “Oh, I misspoke. Today.” “Today! Just this one day too late,” the First Madam said regretfully. She meant that, had Hu arrived a day earlier, he could surely have seen them safely through. Madam Luosi lacked that confidence. Only a wife married to him from the beginning could trust him so completely. But what use was that? In a crisis, she thought, you still have much to learn. Her competitive spirit revived, along with her usual decisiveness. “Madam, this burden now falls on both of us. We must discuss what to do together. Whatever the outcome, the responsibility will be shared.” “I understand. Put forward whatever ideas you have, just as usual.” “Just as usual” meant she could decide and act for herself. At such a moment, however, respect for the First Madam's position was necessary, so she continued in a tone of consultation.

“First, I think we must keep this completely from the old lady. We'll call the male and female stewards together shortly and give them instructions. Will you speak, or shall I?” “You speak.” “I'll do the speaking, but you must be present.” “I will.” “Madam Matchmaker is coming at noon, and the old lady wants me to attend too. I'm afraid you must entertain her on your own. I have to go to the provincial treasurer's residence.” “To see his second concubine?” “Not just her. I want to speak to Treasurer De himself. I shall have to wait there, and probably won't be back by noon. The old lady may ask.” “What shall I say?” “Isn't Treasurer De's eldest daughter going to Beijing for the selection of palace women? Say Mrs De has invited me to discuss it.” “Oh, I understand.” Madam Luosi rose. “Please get dressed. I'll call them together.”

Those summoned were the Hu family's seven stewards: four men and three women. The women mattered most, since the men seldom passed the inner gate except under special circumstances and were less likely to let the news slip. They assembled in a hall near that gate which the servants called the Common Hall. The male and female stewards used it for joint discussions, and Madam Luosi often addressed them there at festivals or when important instructions were needed. But this was the first meeting that required candles to be lit. Everyone felt an indefinable dread. The first cold spell of the eleventh lunar month had arrived, and even their fox-fur coats could not keep the dawn chill from their bones. Their teeth chattered. Guided by two rows of palace lanterns, the two mistresses, principal and subordinate, approached slowly and took their seats behind a large round table. They removed their black-fox muffs. A'lan and A'yun put gold hand warmers into their hands, then took gold water pipes from the younger maids and began to fill them. “No.” Madam Luosi waved A'yun away and glanced at the First Madam. “Go ahead,” the latter said.

Madam Luosi cleared her throat and spoke in a voice rather lower than usual. “Today is the second. Third Miss's wedding is on the fifth, three days from now. You must all work a little harder. Everything will proceed as usual.” Working harder was to be expected, but why the reassurance that everything would be as usual? The thought made Old Mother He's throat itch, and her chronic cough broke out violently. Everyone looked at her in annoyance, making her more nervous and the coughing worse. Madam Luosi, however, showed no irritation. “A'yun, pour Old Mother He some hot tea.” Another maid had already brought it and asked quietly, “Would you like me to help you somewhere else to rest?” “It will pass in a moment,” Madam Luosi intervened. Then, as the cough subsided, she asked, “Have you taken your tonic paste?” “Not yet.” Old Mother He smiled apologetically. “With Third Miss's wedding, everyone has been busy. I haven't had this year's prepared.” “You aren't busy; you're lazy. A'gao!” “Here.” “Send someone to have four batches of tonic paste made up for Old Mother He. Charge them to me.” A'gao, the steward responsible for outside errands and purchasing, answered, “Yes.” After Old Mother He had thanked her, Madam Luosi continued, “You are all old members of this household, and none of you is young. You should take something to build up your strength. When you have time, see Mr Cai at Qingyu Hall and ask for a prescription. Whatever quantity you need can be charged to the household.” Such kindness was common. Fusheng, the oldest and longest-serving, led the thanks as usual. Yet they remained puzzled. Had they been summoned at this cold hour simply to hear these few remarks? Of course not. Still, her unhurried composure had done much to ease their sense of impending disaster.

When she resumed, she first answered the question in their minds. “Why do I say everything will proceed as usual? Is there some reason it might not? In a way, yes. A telegram came from Shanghai yesterday. Conditions are poor, and Fukang must close for a couple of days.” She paused deliberately to study their reactions. They varied. Some were unmoved, whether because they had not understood or because they had no idea how grave it was. Others turned deathly pale, plainly believing that the family's decline had begun. The calmer ones waited solemnly for more. Only A'gao, the purchasing steward who dealt with the outside world, looked evasive, his eyes darting restlessly. She made a mental note of it. “Mr Xie came last night and asked what to do. I discussed it with Madam. The trouble has arisen at an awkward moment between outgoing and incoming funds, while our master happens to be travelling. Once he returns, all will be well. You have served him for years. You know he has his own ways of managing things, don't you?” “Yes,” Fusheng answered for them. “He has weathered countless storms in his life. This one won't defeat him either.” “It's simply bad timing. Think of us as a great ship whose captain happens to be on the opposite bank. We have to bring the ship across and take him aboard. Once he is at the helm, it will steady itself and sail on as before. For now, Madam and I are steering. We are confident of reaching the other side, but you must help her.” “Please give us your instructions,” Fusheng replied. “An old saying tells us to cross the river together in the same boat. However many people are aboard, they share one life. If they perish, all perish; if they survive, all survive. You must understand that.” Several voices assented. “In a storm, the worst danger is confusion among our own people. One wants to go east, another west; one wants to turn back, another to go on. Too many conflicting opinions bring disorder, and disorder overturns the boat. So everyone must stay steady.” She paused. “If anyone thinks we cannot reach the other bank and would rather swim back and escape ashore, say so.” Naturally, no one did. After a silence, Fusheng said, “Please go on, Madam Luosi.”

“Since everyone is willing to share the boat's fate, remember that harming others means harming yourselves. Listen carefully. First, this matter must not be discussed in any of the towers or halls, above all in the old lady's rooms.” “Yes!” “Second, as the saying goes, whoever brings tales is a troublemaker. Do not go about talking. If anyone asks, consider who it is. If it is someone with no business knowing, say you don't know. If it is a close friend with a real concern for the Hu family, you may reassure them sincerely: it's a temporary disturbance in the market, nothing serious.” Seeing nods and expressions of understanding, she felt easier and announced her third point, again beginning with a proverb. “A tall tree catches the wind. You may all have offended people at one time or another. Some will be delighted that Fukang is keeping its shutters up; others may take the chance to play tricks. Ignore strange behaviour and it defeats itself. If people are gossiping, pay no attention. If you discover someone plotting something, tell me quietly. Once the report is verified, I shall privately give the informant a substantial reward. A'yun!” The maid stepped forward from behind her. “Here.” “Whoever comes to the inner gate asking to see me, you are to meet them. Bring their words directly to me. If anything leaks out, you will answer for it. Do you understand?” Not only A'yun but everyone present understood. Information would be well rewarded, provided it was passed through Madam Luosi's trusted maid. The secret would be safe, and the message would reach her faithfully.

“Madam, do you have any instructions?” Madam Luosi asked, turning to the First Madam. She nodded, finished her pipe, and wiped her lips with a handkerchief. “Fusheng has seen more than anyone here. He was with our master before the Long-Haired Rebels rose. He has watched all his rises and falls. Tell us, Fusheng, how did our master make his way?” Fusheng coughed to clear his throat. “His greatest strength is that he never admits defeat. Twice, everyone thought he was certain to lose, but it was like a game of chess: he already had pieces lying in wait. Out of a hopeless position came a miraculous move. This time he must have a move prepared too, though we don't know what it is. Once he comes home, all will be well.” “You have heard him,” the First Madam said. “Third Miss's wedding is almost upon us. Go on preparing for it happily. If the sky falls, the tall ones will hold it up. Behave as though none of this had happened.”

Before noon, it seemed that all Hangzhou knew Fukang Bank was in trouble. Many people were “hawking the Court Gazette,” as Hangzhou people called running about spreading news. Some did so because nothing so extraordinary had happened since the fall of the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom. More were personally affected. Hu had so many enterprises that countless people depended on him directly or indirectly. Among the most anxious was Yueru, concubine of Tang Zishao, manager of Gongji Pawnshop. For some time, people around the Hu household had been making businesses out of supplying it. Madam Luosi disapproved, but Hu thought that benefits should stay among one's own people and that everyone was free to do business. There was nothing to condemn. Gradually it became a fashion, and Yueru was tempted to try. At Old Madam Hu's birthday, the banquets had drawn in almost every celebrated cook in Hangzhou. Yueru partnered with a cook named Sun, catered for one day, and made more than four hundred taels, to her great satisfaction. For Third Miss's wedding, the banquets were to be held at five locations. The Hu household's own cooks would serve the guests of highest standing; the other four were contracted out. A'gao was close to Tang, so Yueru knew him well. Through him she obtained one of the contracts, covering a hundred and twenty tables across the midday and evening sittings. Again she partnered with Sun, who supplied the labour while she advanced the capital. Now that Fukang was in trouble, the wedding could hardly be so grand. Yueru lived behind Gongji Pawnshop, only a few shopfronts from Fukang. She could clearly hear the clamour of people arriving to demand their money and shouting abuse outside its closed doors. While she was anxiously preparing to send for Sun, he heard the news himself and hurried over.

“Have you soaked the dried seafood yet?” she asked. “It went into the water yesterday. Otherwise, how could it be ready in time?” “Wonderful! Now we may have to eat all the shark's fin and sea cucumber ourselves.” “Has Third Miss's wedding been postponed?” “Even if it hasn't, it won't be much of an occasion now. And even if everything goes ahead as planned, who knows whether we'll get paid?” Sun stared. “Then what am I to tell the twenty cooks I've hired?” he asked miserably. Yueru felt angry but had to restrain herself. They had agreed that she would provide the capital, including those twenty men's wages. She could hardly blame him for worrying. “Mistress Tang, you hear more than we do. Have you heard what has gone wrong with Mr Hu?” “How should I know? I was having my hair done when I heard voices outside, first buzzing like flies, then roaring like a tide. I sent a maid to find out and learned that, for the first time since it opened, Fukang hadn't taken down its shutters for business. Later, people even began making trouble at Gongji Pawnshop. What have you heard?” “People say Mr Hu may never get up again after this fall. The higher you climb, the harder you fall. When the God of Wealth takes a tumble, his ingots roll everywhere and the little demons pick them clean. By the time he gets up, his hands are empty and he's the Barefoot God of Wealth.”

A god of wealth without even a pair of shoes: the misery of it was plain. Yueru sighed. “I can't understand how it came to this.” “He used to rely on Lord Zuo. Now Zuo is out of favour and Grand Secretary Li, Governor-General of Zhili, is in power. They say Mr Hu and Lord Li are at odds. If Hu falls, Li will kick him instead of helping him up.” “I don't really understand such things. Let's talk about our own business. I'm afraid this misfortune may make the Hu family reduce the wedding to a simple affair and cancel our banquets.” “Cancellation would be better. What I fear is that the wedding and banquets go ahead and we aren't paid.” “You underestimate Mr Hu,” she objected. “Even if the God of Wealth has fallen, surely he wouldn't fail to pay for our banquets!”

“True. He wouldn't refuse. But you may feel too embarrassed to ask. Think what a muddle everything will be in, Mistress Tang. Even if you can bring yourself to ask, you may not know whom to approach.” Yueru was silent for a long time. At last she asked, “Then what do you think we should do?” Sun swallowed and answered with difficulty. “First, we must find out whether the wedding will proceed as usual.” “I'm sure it will. I know Mr Hu's temperament.” “And if the wedding goes ahead, will the banquets?” “That goes without saying.” “No. It must be said. Whoever gives the order is the person we can look to for payment. You ought to find Second Master Gao at once and make it clear.” Second Master Gao was A'gao. This reminded Yueru that, even if she could not find him, she could at least go to the residence to ask for news.

Yueru had seldom entered the Hu residence in recent years. There were several reasons, but chiefly she dreaded meeting her old companions. Once a kitchen drudge tending the fires, she had unexpectedly “flown up to a branch and become a phoenix,” and envy was inevitable. Some called her Mistress Tang, others Madam Tang; neither sounded as pleasant as her own name. Since her affair had become common knowledge, the question she dreaded most was, “Has the master been to your place for a meal these last two days?” Today circumstances forced her to brave a visit. She entered through the back door of the main kitchen. Beside it stood an open hall where the maids and serving women from the different households collected boiling water and gathered to talk. Today two large baskets stood on a long table, and more than a dozen maids were wrapping osmanthus sweets in pieces of red paper. In Hangzhou, people expected these sweets at weddings in households great and small. White sugar was mixed with osmanthus blossoms, tinted with rose or mint juice, and pressed into small molds of various shapes. Each piece was about the size of a thumb: delicate, delicious, and fun to play with, a delight to children. For the Third Miss’s wedding, four hundred jin of specially enriched sweets had been ordered from Fang Yuhe. They had arrived that morning, and maids from the different households had been called in to help. A’ju, who tended the lamps, candles, and incense for Old Madam Hu, happened to be sitting by the door. A good friend of Yueru’s, she shifted along and patted the table. “Just in time to help.” Yueru sat beside her and glanced around. Those she knew greeted her silently with their eyes. Even the two most talkative girls said nothing today. Naturally, there were no smiles.

Yueru dared not speak loudly in such an atmosphere. “Will the Third Miss’s wedding have to be postponed?” she asked, putting her chief concern first. “Can’t you see we’re still wrapping the sweets?” A’ju answered quietly. “At first light, the First Madam and Madam Luosi told everyone in the Common Hall that everything was to go on as usual.” “How could this happen? How is the Third Miss? Has she been crying?” “Crying? What for? What has it to do with her?” “Such a thing happening just before her wedding—she must be upset.” “Being upset is one thing, but whoever heard of a bride crying? Still,” A’ju added, “she certainly can’t manage a smile.” Yueru lowered her voice almost to a whisper. “A’ju, do you think it’s serious?” “What do you mean, serious?” “I mean, could it…” “Could the whole thing collapse? Is that what you mean?” A’ju shook her head. “I’m afraid it’s hard to say.” “Collapse?” Yueru asked in alarm. “Really?” “Don’t carry on like that!” A’ju gave her a reproachful look. “Madam Luosi hates people making a fuss.” Realizing she had lost her composure, Yueru resumed a calmer tone. “What makes you think it might collapse?” “People are too wicked!” There was much behind those words, well worth probing, but before Yueru could ask, a serving woman from her own house hurried in. Tang Zishao wanted her home at once.

“Where are those pawn tickets?” Tang Zishao asked. Yueru opened her jewelry box and took out a stack of them, which he examined one by one. She could recognize a few characters, but the wild cursive scrawls on pawn tickets were utterly beyond her. When he selected three and laid them aside, she asked, “What are those for?” Tang had resorted to every conceivable form of fraud at Gongji Pawnshop. Besides tampering with goods whose redemption periods had expired, he would make lists of particularly valuable unredeemed articles and send them to the Hu residence. If one of the concubines in the Twelve Chambers took a fancy to something and wanted to keep it, a new ticket would be issued on the pretext that the original had been lost. There were also tickets sold by their owners, or acquired from dubious sources—picked from pockets or stolen by thieves—which Tang bought for next to nothing and entrusted to Yueru, to be redeemed when convenient. The three he had selected were to be redeemed now. One covered a hat ornament: an exceptionally large, flawless Persian emerald worth two thousand taels at current prices, on which only five hundred had been lent. Another covered a set of silver tableware weighing six hundred taels. That did not mean a loan of six hundred taels, for a deduction had to be made for the loss in remelting; its purity was also pronounced deficient, and interest was deducted. After one reduction and another, the six hundred taels of silver had yielded a loan of only three hundred. Yet making another set to match it would cost at least a thousand taels.

The third article was even more valuable: a pair of diamond bracelets set with twelve large diamonds and sixty-four small ones. Without counting the workmanship, the diamonds alone were worth eight thousand taels, but the loan had been only two thousand. Tang had bought the ticket from a petty thief for eight taels. The next day the owner’s servant had come rushing in, distraught, to report its loss. Tang had attended to him personally. “I’m terribly sorry. Someone has already redeemed the goods.” He had produced the ticket, which the owner’s side acknowledged was indeed the right one. But who had redeemed them? Again: “I’m terribly sorry. I have no idea.” Throughout the empire’s eighteen provinces, pawnshops followed the same rule: they recognized the ticket, not the person presenting it. The servant could only return dejectedly to report to his master. “Get these three tickets taken care of at once,” Tang now said. “Fukang holds a great deal of public money. Every authority from the Qiantang and Renhe county offices up to the governor’s yamen has grounds to seal the pawnshops. Unless we redeem the goods, we’ll simply lose them.” “If Fukang fails, what has that to do with Gongji Pawnshop?” “How can you ask such a question? Anything belonging to Mr Hu can be seized.” With that, Tang hurried away.

Yueru saw him to the door and took the opportunity to look at the commotion outside. Her house stood in a back street with little traffic, but the clamor from the main street was clearly audible. Among the voices she thought she could hear gongs and calls to clear the way. Listening carefully, she found she was right. Tang’s warning came back to her, and she started in alarm. Could officials really be coming to seal Fukang Bank and Gongji Pawnshop? The truth was precisely the reverse of her guess. Provincial Treasurer Dexin, accompanied by Wu Yun, the prefect of Hangzhou, was coming to urge Fukang to reopen, rather than to seal its doors. Earlier that morning, following Xie Yunqing’s suggestion, Madam Luosi had gone by sedan chair to the provincial treasurer’s yamen to visit his favorite concubine. The building was said to have been the residence of Qin Hui, the powerful Southern Song chief minister. According to another story, the two great pools enclosed by stone balustrades outside concealed water gates leading to the provincial treasury, guarded by the enormous soft-shelled turtles that Hangzhou people called “scabby-headed turtles.” Such legends were difficult to verify, but watching the turtles outside the treasurer’s yamen had been a familiar city pastime for decades. Normally Madam Luosi paid no attention to the people sitting or leaning against the balustrades as her sedan passed. Today she imagined them pointing and saying, “Look, that’s Mr Hu’s Madam Luosi in the chair. The God of Wealth has fallen and lost even his shoes. Now she has to show herself in public and beg for help.” These imaginings made her heart ache. Suddenly her eyes grew hot; she hastily wiped away the tears and steadied herself. It would be all right, she told herself. Whatever happened, she must not be the first to show alarm. Recalling how she usually behaved on these visits, she resolved to do everything as usual. Her sedan was unusually splendid, and she had always tipped generously. Before her card bearer could announce her at the side entrance, one of the treasurer’s attendants came out and opened both doors. The sedan passed along the covered passage west of the main hall, and she alighted at the garden entrance.

The treasurer’s favorite concubine was named Lianzhu. Second-born in her family and a year older than Madam Luosi, she had exchanged sworn-sisterhood pledges with her. Madam Luosi called her Second Sister; Lianzhu called Madam Luosi Fourth Sister. They greeted one another with their usual affectionate names and exchanged a few pleasantries. But once they were inside, even before they had settled into their seats, Lianzhu’s expression changed. “Fourth Sister,” she said, taking Madam Luosi’s hand, “what is happening? Early this morning I heard Fukang hadn’t opened, and I said it couldn’t be true. Only when the master came in just now and I asked him did I learn that the Shanghai Fukang has failed, and that there are crowds outside the bank here and trouble may break out. He kept sighing, and I’ve been worried too. How serious is it?” Her words threw Madam Luosi into fresh confusion. Her face felt hot. She struggled to remain calm, but it was quite impossible to laugh and talk as she normally did. “How could it not be serious? A gilded signboard is hard to polish bright and very easy to soil,” she said slowly. “The trouble is that our master is still on the road, with neither Shanghai nor Hangzhou able to reach him. Even if a woman like me comes out in public, who will listen? I can only ask the treasurer for help.” “Between our two families, there’s no question of asking a favor.” Lianzhu called a maid. “Go to the inner gate and send word to A’fu: as soon as the master has finished receiving visitors, ask him to come in.”

A’fu was Dexin’s personal valet. On receiving the message from the inner gate, he took the opportunity of filling his master’s water pipe to whisper, “Madam wishes to see you.” Dexin had several concubines, but “Madam,” without qualification, meant Lianzhu. What could be so urgent that she could not wait until he returned to the inner apartments for lunch? It must be something to do with the Hus. He turned to the expectant circuit intendant he was receiving. “My dear fellow, I’m not yet entirely familiar with this case. Let me look into it, and we can discuss it later.” Without allowing an answer, he lifted his teacup. An attendant in the reception-hall corridor immediately called, “See the gentleman out!” The expectant intendant was thus summarily dismissed. Four visiting cards remained: three expectant county magistrates and the serving magistrate of Haining Department. Dexin hesitated, then singled out two. “No time for these gentlemen today,” he said, almost to himself. A’fu took the cards and saw that one belonged to a man named Liu, who had given him a substantial gatekeeper’s tip. “Madam has given instructions about this Mr Liu.” “What instructions?” “He wants the assignment of escorting next year’s grain shipment. Madam said you must appoint him.” “If I’m bound to appoint him, there’s no need to see him.” “What shall I tell him, then?” “To wait at home for word.” “Yes, sir.” “As for this one…” Dexin picked up another card, paused, then cut through the difficulty at a stroke: he pushed that card away together with the Haining magistrate’s. “Say I’m feeling unwell. Ask them to come back tomorrow.”

He rose, returned to the inner apartments through a side door of the reception hall, and went straight to Lianzhu’s rooms. Madam Luosi hastily stood and made a formal curtsy. Dexin was a close friend of Hu Xueyan, whom he privately called Brother Hu; to Madam Luosi he used the familiar Sister Luo. His first question was, “Sister Luo, when will Xueyan be back?” “This afternoon.” “Ah!” He stamped his foot. “Just one day too late.” He meant that if Hu had arrived yesterday, today’s crisis would never have arisen. Madam Luosi had no idea how he might resolve it, but his willingness to do everything he could was evident. In adversity, people feel kindness all the more keenly. With tears glistening in her eyes, she curtsied again. “Everyone in our household is grateful for your concern, Treasurer.” “Please don’t say that, Sister Luo. Now that this has happened, I don’t even know whether I can be of any use.” “What do you mean, whether you can be of use?” Lianzhu put in. “If you put your authority behind it, it’s bound to help.” “Of course I shall. Whatever I can do for Brother Hu, I’ll do. You go home first, Sister Luo. Once I’ve had my smoke, I’ll send for Prefect Wu and discuss it with him.” He added, “After lunch I’ll go and see for myself. Keeping the doors shut can’t be the answer. Still, it’s difficult to say. In any case, we must find a sound way to handle it.” That last sentence reassured Madam Luosi. “You have so much to do today, Fourth Sister,” Lianzhu said. “I won’t keep you.” Walking her out, she whispered in the corridor, “I’ll keep after the old man. If only he’ll go to Fukang—he is the provincial treasurer, after all—he should be able to keep things under control.”

“Yes, Second Sister. I’m like a crab without legs just now. I’m depending entirely on you to act for me.” Madam Luosi lowered her voice still further. “Last time, you admired the design of the pearl ornaments I was wearing. I’ve had another set strung. I’ll send them over tomorrow or the day after.” “No, no. Why worry about such things at a time like this? Oh!” Lianzhu suddenly remembered. “What about the wedding?” “It will have to go ahead as usual, or there’ll be even more rumors outside. People are so worldly—I’m afraid some of the guests may not come.” “I certainly shall.” “Of course, of course!” Fearful of being misunderstood, Madam Luosi hurried on. “We’re our own people. Never mind that we haven’t collapsed yet—even if we were too poor to eat, you’d still come, Second Sister.” “Exactly. Send us word as soon as Mr Hu gets back.” “The treasurer will certainly be the first person he visits.” “Yes. Even if it’s late at night, that doesn’t matter.” “I understand. I’ll see whether the pearl ornaments are ready. If they are, I’ll have him bring them for you to wear.” The first thing Madam Luosi attended to on reaching home was this gift. Her claim that she had commissioned another set was deliberate. She owned several sets of pearl ornaments already. Choosing the one with the whitest, most lustrous pearls, she added a gold-mounted jadeite bracelet and had both sent to Lianzhu at once.

The gift arrived at precisely the critical moment. Although Dexin had a reputation as an able official among the bannermen, he had been born to privilege and was passionately fond of women and entertainment. He had heard that two traveling waterway troupes had come for the Hu wedding. In the great cities, opera companies consisted entirely of male performers; women formed separate companies, known as mao’er troupes. Only the waterway troupes mixed men and women. One of these companies, Fuhe, had a leading actress named Lingzhicao, who specialized in young female roles and was celebrated for both her beauty and her art. Dexin had heard his advisers talk of her and had long wanted to see her. Now that she was in Hangzhou, how could he miss the chance? He had sent a trusted retainer to ask the manager when she could come and sing for him privately. Shortly after Madam Luosi left, while he was satisfying his craving for opium, the retainer returned. On hearing that the treasurer had summoned her for official duty, the Fuhe manager had not dared delay: Lingzhicao would be brought that very afternoon. Delighted, Dexin changed his plans and made other arrangements for dealing with the run on Fukang. Just then Lianzhu came into his private office. Madam Luosi’s substantial gift had made her particularly concerned about the bank, and she had come specifically to find out what was happening. “I’ve already sent for Prefect Wu,” Dexin told her. “When he comes, I’ll give him very thorough instructions.”

“What instructions?” “To go in person and keep order.” “And you? Aren’t you going?” “Prefect Wu will be enough on his own.” “Are you certain he can handle it?” “Who can be certain about something like this? Even I can’t.” “Is that why you aren’t going?” “No.” “Why, then?” “I can’t be bothered to move.” “Old man, you make my heart turn cold! Hu Xueyan is your friend. He’s in desperate trouble and may lose everything he owns, yet you can’t be bothered even to go and see him. What sort of friendship is that? Have you forgotten your audience with the empress dowager before you were appointed provincial treasurer? If Hu hadn’t lent you ten thousand taels, would anyone in the capital have paid you any attention or shown you consideration when you arrived empty-handed?” Lianzhu paused, then spoke bluntly. “If you think Fukang’s difficulties are minor and Prefect Wu can settle them alone, you may spare yourself the effort. Otherwise, you must go yourself. Then, even if Fukang fails, you’ll have done your duty as a friend, and Hu Xueyan won’t blame you. What do you say?”

Dexin was about to answer when the door curtain rustled. Turning, he saw A’fu hurry in, beaming with excitement. The moment the valet saw Lianzhu, he stopped short and his smile vanished. “What is it?” she snapped. “Barging in, looking so shifty—you haven’t the least idea how to behave!” A’fu said nothing, merely stealing glances at Dexin, who kept signaling with his eyes. Their furtiveness aroused Lianzhu’s suspicions. “A’fu!” she shouted. “What is it? Speak!” “Yes, madam.” He forced a smile. “Nothing at all.” “Still refusing to tell the truth?” She turned to the maid preparing the opium. “Fetch Steward Zhang! I’ll have both his wretched legs broken.” Behind her back, the yamen servants called Lianzhu “the firebrand.” A’fu knew what she could do. His knees buckled and he dropped to the floor. “Please spare me, madam. I won’t do it again.” “Again? We haven’t finished with this time! Speak! Tell the truth and I’ll let you off.” A’fu hesitated. Even the master was afraid of her; surely telling the truth could hardly count as betraying him. “I came to report something to the master.” “What?” Dexin was now giving a succession of warning coughs. Lianzhu sat down with a cold smile. “Tell the truth and nothing will happen to you. But one false word—if I don’t have you beaten, you need never call me Madam again.” At this solemn threat, A’fu turned pale. Looking close to tears, he answered, “I came to tell the master that the Fuhe troupe’s manager has sent word. They’re bringing Lingzhicao over at once.”

“Oh? Lingzhicao? A man or a woman?” “A woman.” “Very well. I understand. You may go.” A’fu kowtowed and rose, but Dexin stopped him. “Wait! Tell the Fuhe troupe I’m busy with official business and have no time to hear Lingzhicao sing. We’ll discuss it in a few days.” “Yes, sir!” A’fu stuck out his tongue and slipped away. “Old man…” “Stop nagging!” Dexin interrupted. “I’ll go as soon as I’ve had enough to smoke. Will that do?” “There’s something else I want to say.” Lianzhu dismissed the maid. “I’ll prepare the master’s pipe myself.” This was a treat for Dexin. Lianzhu’s opium fulfilled all three desirable qualities—golden, tall, and loose—and each pipe seemed to give him fresh energy. Since teaching the maids her special skill, she had ceased performing this service herself, but nobody else did it so well. Her offer now went some way toward compensating him for missing Lingzhicao’s singing. Without speaking, she concentrated on preparing a pipeful, fitted it to the pipe, drew the handkerchief from beneath her arm, and wiped the ivory mouthpiece. She placed it between Dexin’s lips, held it to the flame, and tended the heat with her opium needle. Dexin drew in and exhaled clouds of smoke, finishing the pipe in one continuous effort. Then he picked up a small teapot and drank. The tea was too hot for an ordinary person to touch, but he was accustomed to it; after rolling his tongue about, he took several mouthfuls, popped a pine-nut sweet into his mouth, and said at leisure, “Now, what have you to say?”

“I was thinking,” Lianzhu said as she prepared another pipe, “if Hu Xueyan collapses, you’ll be in terrible trouble too. Just think how much public money is deposited there.” “That doesn’t worry me. I can seal his pawnshops.” “And private money? Will you seal his pawnshops for that too? Even if you can, what will you say when people ask?” “Yes…” Dexin drew in his breath. “That would be difficult to explain.” “Even if it weren’t, you must consider whether the people who entrusted the money to you want you to reveal it. Take the fifty thousand taels belonging to Vice-Minister Chong’s eldest son. When he asked you to deposit it with Fukang for him, he insisted again and again that nobody must know. Wouldn’t Vice-Minister Chong hate you if you told?” “Well…well…” Dexin frowned. “I didn’t want to have anything to do with it at first. Chong is a hypocritical moralist, unreasonable in everything he does. Working for him is thankless labor. But we belong to the same Banner, our families are old friends, and his eldest son has always treated me very respectfully, so I agreed. If I expose the business and ruin Chong’s reputation for incorruptibility, he’ll hate me for the rest of his life.” “And it isn’t only Chong. There’s Censor Sun’s wife. Her twenty thousand taels are her own private savings. Sun might as well have ‘incorruptible’ engraved on his forehead. If people find out his wife has that deposit, they won’t know it came from her own family, the reserve she brought with her in marriage. They’ll say it’s dirty money he made by selling his power of impeachment. If he then repudiates her and sends her back to her family, how could such a wrong ever be put right? Old man, you’re always saying you’d rather demolish eight temples than break up one marriage. What a terrible sin you’d have committed!”

This torrent of words left Dexin drenched in sweat. Forgetting even his opium, he sat up and began to take off his silk-wadded jacket. “Don’t—you’ll catch cold,” Lianzhu said. “And don’t panic. Let me explain things properly.” “Yes, yes! I really must seek the advice of my female Zhuge Liang.” “Smoke this pipe first.” By the time he had finished it, Lianzhu had worked out her plan. Yet she began with something apparently unrelated. “Old man, you’ve listened to opera all your life. Tell me, do you understand the rules of a troupe?” “Why ask me that?” “Never mind why. Just tell me whether you do.” “Of course I do.” “Then let me ask you this. When a troupe is invited somewhere, whether to perform at a private celebration or in a theater, its actors mustn’t display their art elsewhere before performing for the original host. Is that the rule?” “Yes. But it doesn’t apply here. I no longer want to hear Lingzhicao; if I did, summoning her would be calling her to official duty. Can theatrical rules bind the authorities?” “No, they can’t. But remember the saying: before beating a dog, consider its master. The Hus brought Fuhe here for their Third Miss’s wedding. Their guests haven’t had the first taste, yet you want the actors to perform for you beforehand. Isn’t that using official power to make the Hu family lose face?”

Although Lianzhu had come from a brothel in Houjiajun, Tianjin, her analysis was remarkably shrewd, and Dexin could not help conceding her point. “Fortunately, the matter is over. There’s no need to bring it up again.” “Why would I bring it up if there were no need? I’m not talking nonsense. The fact that you still don’t understand proves my point.” “This is strange! What haven’t I understood?” “The principle behind it. I mean that you must not only honor your friendship with Hu Xueyan: at this moment, you must also avoid upsetting him. If he really is going under, he’ll have to weigh what he owes to people. If anyone is to suffer, it will be those who disregarded their friendship and offended him. For his close friends, on the other hand—since he can’t settle the whole affair anyway, why leave the river water unused when he could wash a boat with it? If you understood that, you wouldn’t think all I’ve said was idle talk.” There was a great deal beneath her words. Dexin pondered for some time. “I truly hadn’t thought of that. You’re right. I’ve nothing to gain by offending him. If a dying man drags someone down into the grave with him, I’d be in more trouble than I could bear. It wouldn’t be worth it. Come, lie down. Let me prepare a pipe for you.” “Enough! I only smoke for amusement. I have no craving, so don’t ruin me.” Lianzhu lay down across the smoking tray from him. “Do everything you can to keep Fukang going. When Hu returns, have a proper talk with him.
